posts.title: The Smoke Machine Is Not the Problem
posts.body:
There is a meeting happening somewhere in America right now, in a church office with a whiteboard, and on the whiteboard is a number that has been shrinking for ten years. The number is the young people. Someone at the table says the word *relevant*. Someone else says *engage*. Within the hour the church decides what American churches have decided at that table for forty years: turn up the production. Better lights. A shorter sermon. A band that sounds like the radio, coffee in the lobby, a smoke machine if the budget clears. The theory never changes, the kids are leaving because church feels old, so make it feel new.

I have sat in that meeting. I have run that meeting. And I have five sons, which means the shrinking number on the whiteboard eats dinner at my table every night. What follows is not survey data. It is what a pastor sees from the front of a room and a father sees across a table, a smaller sample, a closer look. The closer look starts with a face. When the smoke machine comes on, nothing happens in it. Not hostility, hostility would at least be attention. Nothing. The show has been getting better for forty years and the room has been getting emptier the whole time, and the reason is not that the show still needs work. The reason is that they can smell it.

## Raised inside the ad

To be seventeen in 2026 is to have spent your whole life being sold to, every surface, since before you could read. The most sophisticated persuasion machinery in human history has been aimed at your attention since you could hold a screen, built by the largest companies on earth, tuned hour by hour against everything you have ever clicked, all of it working to manufacture wanting. Children raised in that weather develop what any organism develops under constant exposure: immunity. They know an ad when they see one, because ads are their native climate, and they know precisely what an ad is, a thing that wants something from you while performing the desire to give you something.

So when a church adopts the grammar of the ad, the branding, the hook, the sermon series with the streaming-poster artwork, the relentless cheerfulness of the pitch, they do not hear the gospel translated into their language. They hear an ad. And they extend to it exactly the trust they extend to every other ad, which is none. You cannot out-market a generation that was formed inside marketing. They were raised in the factory. They know how desire gets manufactured.

## Be fair to the men who built it

The attractional church was not built by cynics, and the current fashion of sneering at it is too easy. It was built by people who loved the lost, say that plainly, because it is true. In 1975 a young pastor named Bill Hybels went door to door in the Chicago suburbs asking people who did not attend church why they stayed away, and built Willow Creek Community Church in a rented movie theater around their answers. The logic was missionary logic: find every barrier standing between a secular person and the gospel, and tear down every one that is not the gospel itself. The organ, the pews, the offering plate, the coat and tie, the insider vocabulary, none of that is the cross. Clear it away. The warrant was Paul's own: "I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some" (1 Corinthians 9:22).

And it worked, for the people it was aimed at. The unchurched suburban adult of 1980 had a real objection, church as he had known it was formal, dull, and answering questions nobody was asking, and the seeker-sensitive church answered his actual objection. Millions who would never have crossed the threshold of a sanctuary crossed the threshold of a theater and heard about Jesus there, while the traditional church rearranged its committees. Whatever gets said next gets said about missionaries who read their field correctly, and the criticism that follows means nothing without that sentence.

But the model carried an assumption underneath the love: that the seeker is a consumer, and that the obstacle is the packaging. That was close to true of suburban adults in 1980. It is precisely false of their grandchildren, the most heavily marketed-to human beings who have ever lived, for whom slick packaging is not the welcome mat but the warning label. For them, the strangeness of the church was never the barrier. It was the evidence, the last visible sign that the thing might have come from somewhere other than the machine that produces everything else on their screens. We sanded off the strangeness to lower the threshold, and in lowering it we filed the church into the one category it can never win: content. The church will never be better content than the content industry. It was never supposed to enter that contest.

And I write *we* with a straight face. I shortened sermons that needed their length. I moved the hook to the front. I cut the strange parts, the hard texts, the long prayers, the silence, because I was afraid of losing the room. I lost the room anyway. Slower, politely, to a better screen.

The question worth a whiteboard is not how to make church feel new. It is what the attractional decades stripped out, what this generation is starving for. From where I sit, the answer has four parts.

## They will forgive uncertainty. They will never forgive spin.

Ask a hard question at my dinner table, one of my sons will, most weeks: suffering, hell, the Canaanites, the friend whose family came apart while a church watched, and the next half-second decides everything. If the father reaches for the packaged answer, the face across the table closes like a door. Not because the answer was wrong. Because it was handled, because the boy asked a real question and received a product.

A young person will forgive *I don't know* almost indefinitely. *I don't know why God allowed that. Here is what I do know, and here is why I stake my life on it anyway*, that sentence keeps a teenager at the table, because it is the sentence of a man standing under the same sky he stands under. What he will never forgive, even once, is spin: the confident non-answer, the pivot, the verse deployed like a customer-service script. These kids grew up fact-checking everyone; they assume every speaker has an angle until the speaker bleeds; and the moment they catch a church managing their doubt instead of meeting it, they file the church with the other institutions that handle people. A church that treats doubt as disloyalty teaches its young exactly one lesson, that the faith cannot survive contact with their real questions, and they will carry the questions somewhere the questions are welcome. The somewhere will not love them.

This does not mean a pulpit full of shrugs. Honesty about doubt is not the abandonment of conviction; it is the refusal to counterfeit it. I came to faith from atheism, which means every objection my sons raise lived in my own mouth first, and I tell them so. Speak that way and a doubter moves toward you. Perform a certainty you do not have and he will find the seam. He always finds the seam.

## They are drowning in content and starving for meaning.

The feed never ends. My sons have never once in their lives run out of things to watch, sit with that, because no generation before them could say it. And the feed, for all its infinity, has never handed them a single thing with weight: nothing that took centuries to compose, nothing that demands they change, nothing that will still be standing in ten years, nothing that knows their names. Infinite content turns out to be a starvation diet. The volume is the deficiency.

A church that offers more content joins a contest against opponents who spend billions to be unbeatable at it, and loses in the lobby. But depth is a category the feed cannot enter. The algorithm cannot sit with one text for an hour. It cannot make anyone memorize anything, grieve anything, wait for anything. So the old strange things the attractional model cleared out as barriers, the creed said aloud by a whole room, the psalm of lament, the doctrine taught without training wheels, the church's two-thousand-year argument with itself, were never the obstacle to reaching the young. They are the offer. I have taught the Trinity to teenagers straight, no cushions, and watched them sit up like something had finally respected them. They are not afraid of hard. They are bored of easy.

## They have algorithms. They need elders.

We segmented the church by age because the market segments by age, youth in the youth room with the pizza and the game, young adults in their own service, seniors at the early one, and we called it strategy. The result, one generation on, is a seventeen-year-old with ten thousand voices in his pocket and not one elder in his life. An algorithm knows what he clicked. An elder knows what he is becoming. Those are not the same knowledge, and only one can save him.

I was raised without a father, so I am not guessing at what the absence of older men costs a boy. I paid it. And when I came stumbling toward the faith out of atheism, what pulled me was not programming aimed at my demographic. It was older men who let me stand close enough to watch them live, men whose faith had scar tissue I could see, who did not perform for me because they had nothing to sell me. That cannot be streamed. It barely survives being scheduled. The church is nearly the last room in American life where an eighty-year-old and a fifteen-year-old sit under the same roof for the same reason, and we spent forty years engineering them into separate wings. My sons do not need the church to hand them one more screen of voices their own age. They need old people who know their names.

## They will not give everything to a thing that asks nothing.

There was a man who ran up to Jesus with the best question a person can ask, and Mark records what happened next with a detail no marketer would have kept: "And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, 'You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:21–22).

Watch the order. Jesus loved him, the text insists on it, and then raised the price to everything. The attractional instinct reads this story as a lost sale and starts drafting the recovery: chase him down the road, restructure the ask, keep him in the funnel. Jesus let him walk away sad. The love and the cost were not in tension. The cost was what the love looked like once it took the man seriously.

He did the same thing to crowds, which should bury the idea that Jesus measured success at the whiteboard. "Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?'" (Luke 14:25–28). Great crowds, the metric every church growth conference exists to produce, and he turns around and thins them on purpose, tells them to sit down first and do the math. He was not trying to lose them, he was refusing to win them falsely.

Bonhoeffer, watching a national church fold itself into the Reich, gave the disease its permanent name in *The Cost of Discipleship* (1937): cheap grace, "grace without discipleship, grace without the cross." He saw where a costless Christianity ends, and it is not in a bigger room.

The strange fact is that the young honor cost everywhere else in their lives. They wake at five for a sport that promises them nothing but the sport. They give their bodies to disciplines, their years to causes, their savings to a craft, the demand is not what repels them; the demand is what convinces them the thing is real. Then they walk into a church that asks for forty minutes, a decent mood, and nothing that will ever register in their calendar, their bank account, or their body, and they draw the only conclusion available. Nothing important is this easy. A faith that asks nothing is worth what it asks. They are not leaving because Christianity demanded too much of them. They are leaving because they suspect it was never going to demand anything.

## The whiteboard question

What this asks of pastors and parents is worse than a production budget, because none of it can be purchased or programmed. You cannot schedule honesty about doubt for the second Sunday of the month. You cannot hire depth. The only way to put elders in the room is to be becoming one, and the only way to offer the young a costly faith is to be visibly paying for yours. My sons will not remember my arguments; I have watched enough of them sail past five sets of eyes to make my peace with that. They will remember whether the thing cost their father something they could see, whether it made him tell the truth when a lie was cheaper, stay in the room when leaving was easier, keep loving people who wasted his love, rise early to sit alone with a book he had read ten thousand times as if it still outranked him. Children do not inherit our marketing. They inherit our actual gods.

So the meeting is asking the wrong question. The young are not asking the church to be interesting; they have interesting solved, and it is making them miserable. They are carrying the same two questions the rich young man carried out onto the road, whether it is true, and what it costs, and for forty years we have answered a different question, louder each time. The man went away sorrowful, and the text does not say Jesus chased him, and it does not say Jesus stopped loving him. It says the love came first and the price stood. A church willing to say both of those sentences to a seventeen-year-old will be smaller before it is deeper. It will lose a crowd before it finds a son. And the generation we are so anxious to win is standing in the lobby, watching us with the eyes of people raised inside the ad, waiting to see whether we believe our own gospel enough to charge them what it costs.
posts.excerpt: The show has been getting better for forty years and the room has been getting emptier the whole time. A pastor with five sons on what the young actually want from church: honesty about doubt, depth, elders, and something worth the cost.

posts.title: The Same Table
posts.body:
Two pastors are driving to the same lunch. The first is Reformed, confessional, careful, his library leaning toward the seventeenth century, and he is braced for chaos. He has seen the footage: the stadium, the white suit, healings announced into a camera and never into a hospital chart. Somewhere on the drive he has rehearsed the patient face he will wear if the man across the table says *the Lord told me*. The second pastor is charismatic, and he is braced for a lecture. He has met the Reformed brother before, the crossed arms, the citation deployed like a checkpoint, the settled suspicion that whatever the Spirit is doing in his church is manufactured, or worse. Each man has held the hands of the dying. Each walks in carrying a cartoon of the other.

I have been the first man in that car. The Pastors Connection Network puts pastors in rooms together, Reformed and Pentecostal, Baptist and Methodist, men who could not sign one another's doctrinal statements sharing one another's bread, and I did not come to those tables neutral. I came as a Reformed Baptist with a confession written in 1689 and expectations formed less by charismatic pastors than by charismatic television. The tables have not settled the doctrine of the gifts for me. They did something harder to shake: they put a face where the caricature used to sit.

The bracing came first, and the bracing has a history.

## A divide with an American address

The quarrel over the gifts feels timeless. Its modern form has a street address. In April 1906, at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles, revival broke out under William Seymour, a Black preacher, son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye, and from that mission Pentecostalism went out to the world. Twelve years later B. B. Warfield of Princeton published *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918), the scholarly spine of modern cessationism: the miraculous gifts attested the apostles and their message, and passed with the apostolic age. In 1960 the renewal jumped the denominational fences when Dennis Bennett, an Episcopal rector in Van Nuys, told his congregation he had spoken in tongues; by 1967 it was inside the Roman Catholic Church. In 2013 John MacArthur convened a conference and published a book, both named *Strange Fire*, arguing that the movement as a whole was offering God unholy fire.

A century of that history did not produce two arguments. It produced two caricatures, each assembled from the other side's worst exports. The Reformed man's picture of the charismatic is built from prosperity television, the jet, the seed-faith pledge, the blessings of God priced like inventory. The charismatic's picture of the Reformed man is built from the coldest church he ever walked out of, the congregation that would sooner split than clap, where the Spirit is confessed in the third person and expected in none. Both pictures are made of real material. Neither has a face. And pastors have been discipled by the pictures, refuting a caricature is easier than lunch with a brother.

## The case that the gifts have ceased

Take the cessationist at full strength, which means retiring the weak version he has abandoned. The weak version hangs everything on a clause, "but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:10), with "the perfect" read as the completed canon, prophecy expiring the day the ink dried on Revelation. Serious cessationists do not argue this; the passage will not carry it. Read it whole: "Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away. When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways. For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" (1 Corinthians 13:8–12). Face to face. Fully known. That is not the arrival of a book. The honest cessationist concedes it: this text promises the gifts will end and sets the horizon at glory. His case stands elsewhere.

It stands on architecture. The church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. The sign gifts, on this reading, were not the church's permanent equipment but the foundation's attestation: "It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will" (Hebrews 2:3–4). Attested, past tense, God notarizing a revelation now complete. Warfield pressed the pattern: Scripture's miracles cluster at the hinges of redemptive history, Moses, Elijah and Elisha, Christ and his apostles, trumpet blasts announcing new revelation. The revelation is complete. The trumpets have sounded.

Beneath the architecture sits the deepest concern, and it is not tidiness in worship. It is the sufficiency of the Book. My own confession states it plainly: the Second London Confession of 1689 calls the Scriptures most necessary, "those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased." If God still delivers fresh words through prophets, a second pulpit has quietly opened in every congregation that believes it, and the Reformation's whole wager, a conscience captive to the Word of God alone, is renegotiated every time a confident man prefaces his opinion with *thus says the Lord*. Wayne Grudem's patch (1988), that congregational prophecy is a lesser, fallible kind, Spirit-prompted impressions rather than oracles, meets a hard text: Deuteronomy knows no fallible category of prophet. On its terms, the man whose word does not come to pass has spoken presumptuously and is not to be feared (Deuteronomy 18:22). A prophecy graded on a curve is something Scripture never describes, and the cessationist declines to invent it.

None of this is a small doctrine of the Spirit. He confesses a Spirit who raises the dead, illumines the Word, and does more in one quiet conversion than in a stadium of announced healings. The scaffolding came down, he says, because the house stands.

## The case that the gifts continue

Now the other chair, at the same strength. The continuationist begins with the burden of proof: Scripture announces the end of the gifts nowhere except at the horizon the cessationist just conceded, face to face. What it says in the meantime, it says in imperatives: "Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). Commands presuppose a church with something to test. And Paul grounds the gifts not in apostolic credentialing but in congregational life: "Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (1 Corinthians 12:4–7). For the common good. An attestation of apostles might expire with the apostles; the common good of the congregation carries no expiration date, and two chapters later it becomes a command: "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1).

The continuationist has answers, not only proof-texts. To the sufficiency objection: prophecy tested by Scripture stands under Scripture, never beside it, the Bereans examined even Paul's preaching against the written Word daily, and Luke calls them noble for it (Acts 17:11). Testing is submission; a word that must pass the Book's inspection cannot rival the Book. To the embarrassment objection, the jets, the stagecraft, the healings that dissolve on contact with a medical record, a doctrine is not refuted by its abusers, or the Reformed man must answer for every frozen congregation and every hyper-Calvinist who never shared the gospel. Judging continuationism by prosperity television is judging the doctrines of grace by the meanest man who ever held them. His shelf is sober: D. A. Carson's *Showing the Spirit* (1987) is a patient exegesis of 1 Corinthians 12–14, not a stadium act. And the global church sits mostly in his pew: by the Pew Research Center's 2011 report on global Christianity, roughly a quarter of the world's Christians are Pentecostal or charismatic. Seen from Lagos or São Paulo, the gifts did not cease. They moved.

Then the counterpunch, and the Reformed man should let it land: there is more than one way to quench the Spirit. Credulity quenches him, prophecy untested, everything held fast, discernment renamed doubt. So does a liturgy of low expectation, a congregation that would be alarmed if God did anything on a Sunday, and has learned to call the alarm reverence. Paul wrote "test everything" to a church tempted to despise prophecy, which means despising is the failure he saw coming.

## What kind of question this is

Sort the question, because a quarrel that never names its own order grows without limit. The creeds bind the floor: one God in three persons; the full deity and full humanity of Christ, defined at Chalcedon in 451; the bodily resurrection; the Spirit confessed at Constantinople in 381 as the Lord and giver of life, who spoke by the prophets. Both men recite every word without crossing their fingers. No creed rules on whether the Spirit who spoke by the prophets still distributes prophecy; the fathers did not bind what Scripture left disputable. The gifts are a second-order question. This divides faithful churches; it does not divide the faith. Second-order is not nothing, the answer shapes how you order a service, how you weigh a member's *God told me*, what you pray beside a hospital bed. But it is the kind of question a Christian can get wrong and still be inside.

Paul establishes the floor in his opening line to the most gift-saturated, gift-troubled congregation in the canon: "To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours" (1 Corinthians 1:2). Together with all those. He is about to spend fourteen chapters correcting nearly everything this church does with tongues, prophecy, and the Supper, and he begins by binding it to every congregation on earth. Corinth got the gifts wrong in every direction, and Paul never once tells them they have stopped being the church of God. That is the apostolic temperature for this dispute. Ours runs hotter, and the heat is not zeal.

## Where I land, and the arrow still in it

I am open but cautious, the position of a 1689 man who has read his confession's first paragraph and his Bible's sentences and cannot make them close the same door. Open, because no text closes it: the terminus Scripture names for the gifts is face to face, and I will not announce on God's behalf a cessation he did not announce. Cautious, because the canon is closed and every claimed word must stand under the Book; because Deuteronomy's severity about presumptuous speech has no statute of limitations; because I have watched *the Lord told me* justify a divorce and empty a savings account, and the wreckage was not hypothetical. My tradition leans harder toward cessation than I do, "now ceased" is my own confession's sentence, and I hold the tension in the open rather than pretending it away.

The objection I cannot fully answer arrives from both sides at once, the sign it has found the joint in the armor. "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" is an imperative, and open-but-cautious obeys it in neither direction. I do not forbid what the cessationist forbids. I do not desire earnestly what the continuationist desires. I hold a door ajar and invite no one through it. At my church we test everything and are rarely given much to test, which may indict the age, or the pastor. If the cessationist is right, my openness leaks against the sufficiency of the Word I confess. If the continuationist is right, my caution is disobedience wearing prudence's coat, a way of holding a doctrine without ever paying for it. A door held ajar that no one is ever welcomed through functions like a wall with better manners, and I am not certain mine is more than that.

## What the table taught

The network was never built to settle this. It was built because pastors, whatever their pneumatology, are dying of the same things, isolation, criticism, the Sunday that never stops coming, and the tables it sets have no position paper at the door. What happens there is slower than debate and harder on caricature. The Reformed man hears the charismatic work through a text with care and no theater. The charismatic hears the Reformed man pray with actual heat. Each discovers the other keeps the same terrible hours: the same funeral homes, the same marriage dissolving quietly in the third pew, the same 2 a.m. phone call and the same dark drive toward it. I have been prayed for at tables like that by men whose theology of prayer I would edit, and I have walked to the parking lot knowing, past argument, that I had been prayed for. The other man loves the same Lord. He reads the same Bible, some weeks more of it aloud than I do. He buries the same dead.

This is the work Paul assigned a divided church: "eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all" (Ephesians 4:3–6). Maintain, not manufacture. The unity is the Spirit's making; the table only keeps us from tearing what he made.

The dispute itself will not survive the appointment both disputants are keeping. The chapter each side quotes at the other ends by telling every party that they are children squinting at a clouded mirror, knowing in part until they are known in full. Prophecies will pass away; so will *Counterfeit Miracles* and *Strange Fire*, and so will this essay. On the day the partial passes, one of the two men at that lunch will learn he was wrong about the gifts. I do not know which one, and in that light it will matter less than either of us has been living as if it does. What will remain is the first line of the letter, whether we called on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ together with all those who in every place call on it, or made our exceptions. The other man is already at the table. What the gifts debate keeps drowning out is the question of whether you will sit down.
posts.excerpt: The Reformed man arrives braced for chaos. The charismatic arrives braced for a lecture. Years of tables with pastors on both sides of the gifts divide taught me what neither caricature could: the other man loves the same Lord, reads the same Bible, and buries the same dead.

posts.title: The Trip Is Not the Work
posts.body:
The report-back Sunday has become its own liturgy. The team stands at the front in matching shirts, tanned and glad and a little hoarse, and the screen fills with photographs, the concrete-block church, the children reaching for the camera, the van, the market, the team with arms around people whose names are already slipping. Then the testimonies, and a pastor learns to hear what a testimony is made of. *It changed my life. I will never take hot water for granted again. God wrecked me down there.* Every sentence true, and every sentence about us. The country appears in its own story as a backdrop. And the question that never reaches the platform, the one I have learned to dread because for years I did not ask it either: what did our two weeks do for the place we went, and if the believers there were released from every obligation of hospitality, would they ask us back?

I do not write this from the lobby. I direct a missions initiative built around long-term partnership with national pastors in India and Thailand, and short-term trips are part of how that work breathes. I have planned the trips, raised the money, led the teams, preached the report-back, and taken the photographs. Whatever knife this essay holds, I have had to turn the edge toward myself first, and more than once.

## The case for going

The critique of short-term missions has become a genre, and like most genres it is cheapest for the people furthest from the work. So the strongest case gets stated first, in the form the trip's defenders would sign, because most of it is simply true.

A congregation's love for missions is sustained by people who have stood in the room. Budgets are abstractions until a man has eaten at a pastor's table on the other side of the world; after that, the line item has a face, and he will fight for it in the lean year when every other line is bleeding. Ask any missions committee where its most faithful givers were made and you will hear about trips, checks that have kept coming for twenty and thirty years, begun in two weeks. The trip is how a comfortable church puts its body where its money is, and bodies change what money cannot.

Calls are discerned there too. A real portion of the church's lifetime workers first heard the call on a short trip; the two weeks functioned as a doorway, and they walked through it and gave their lives on the other side. Shut the door because some people treat it as a photo booth, and the field loses workers it will not get another way.

And when a team comes under the direction of the national church, invited, aimed, put to use on that church's own terms, the visit itself preaches. It says to a congregation meeting in a rented room or under a tin roof: you are not forgotten; the body is larger than this village; the people who pray for you have faces. Hospitality in much of the world is not an imposition endured but an honor received, and the believers who host teams say so without being asked. The alternative to the bad trip was never a holier isolation. A church that never goes anywhere learns to love missions in the abstract and no missionary in particular, and abstract love does not survive a budget meeting.

All of that is real. A critique that cannot say it first is posturing, and there is plenty of posturing in circulation. But the case for going is a case for a certain kind of going, and it dissolves on contact with the other kind.

## The trip that exists for the traveler

There is a story that circulates wherever missions people gather, told each time as if it happened one town over: the orphanage wall painted by the June team, repainted by the July team, painted a third time in August, because the wall was never the point; the point was that teams need something to do, and painting photographs well. No one can source the story, which is its own kind of warning. It survives because everyone near the work recognizes it. It is a parable, and parables tell the truth.

Look at the marks of the trip that exists for the traveler, and count how many an honest church can check. The dates are set by our school calendar, not the field's seasons. The work is chosen for how it will look on the screen at report-back rather than for what the church there asked to have done. Unskilled hands are flown across an ocean, at a cost nobody wants said aloud from the platform, to do work that local hands could do better, faster, and for a wage a local family is praying for. The team photographs everything, including other people's children, held on strangers' hips for pictures we would never permit of our own children, taken without one glance at the parent standing off-frame. I have taken those pictures. It took me years to see what they were: vacation photography wearing ministry's clothes.

Underneath the aesthetics sits the structural harm. A congregation that learns its roof comes from abroad learns to wait for abroad, and the capacity God gave that congregation to build and give and sacrifice is quietly retired. A pastor who learns that donors respond to need learns to perform need, and something in a man dies when his poverty becomes his product. Hosting becomes a job. The shepherd God called to a village spends his year as a tour operator for his own funding, translating, arranging vans, absorbing enthusiasm, protecting his people from ours. That is dignity spent, his and the gospel's, in the eyes of every neighbor watching the whole exchange. The test is simple and severe: cancel the team and see what is actually missed. If the answer is the work, the trip was serving something. If the answer is the money and the audience, the trip was the product, and the field was the packaging.

## Where we learned to travel this way

The short-term trip feels ancient because it is dressed in the Great Commission, but it is younger than the fluorescent lights in most church basements. William Carey sailed for India in 1793 and never saw England again; he worked at Serampore until his death in 1834. That was the shape of going for most of the church's history, going meant staying, and the send-off was a kind of funeral. The question a short-term trip answers, *how can I serve over there within my vacation days,* could not have been asked for eighteen centuries. It is a creature of the jet engine and the postwar American paycheck.

New possibilities are not sins. But this one arrived in a church already thoroughly discipled by the market, and the trip took the shape of the culture it was born into: an experience, packaged, priced, scheduled around the buyer, documented for sharing, reviewed afterward in testimonies that are indistinguishable, grammatically, from reviews. We did not set out to make the poor of another country the scenery of our own spiritual formation. We simply never asked the question, and the market answered it for us.

While we were building the industry, the map changed under it. Philip Jenkins put the fact before Western readers in *The Next Christendom* (2002): the center of gravity in world Christianity has moved south and east, out of the old sending countries and into the places we still call the field. The average team now flies from a thinning church to a growing one and arrives carrying an assumption a hundred years out of date, that it brings the faith rather than visits it. We are not founders there. We are guests of a younger, poorer, faster-growing church, and a guest who behaves like a founder is not helping anyone.

Steve Corbett and Brian Fikkert, in *When Helping Hurts* (2009), handed the church a distinction it keeps declining to use: relief for the crisis, rehabilitation for the recovery, development for the long condition, and the warning that aiming relief at a chronic condition deepens it. Two weeks is the shape of relief. Almost nothing a team visits is a crisis; it is a long obedience, a church being planted, pastors being trained, children being raised in the faith across decades, and relief aimed at a long obedience interrupts it. The same book names the disease beneath the method: the helper's quiet god-complex, the assumption that material poverty is the whole poverty and that we are the un-poor. Sit long enough under the teaching of a pastor who has counted the cost of his own baptism and the arithmetic reverses. He lacks money. We lack what he has. The trip done rightly is where an American church discovers its own poverty; the trip done wrongly is engineered so that it never has to.

## Paul traveled, watch how

The command behind every trip deserves to be read at its full length. "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:19–20). The going is commanded. But look at what the going is for, make disciples, baptizing, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded. That is the work of years, of lifetimes, of languages learned and funerals attended. No one is discipled in a fortnight by visitors who cannot pronounce his name. The commission is carried, day by day, by the church that lives there, and a two-week traveler serves the commission only by serving the people who are spending their lives inside it.

Paul is the pattern, and Paul took short trips constantly, read Romans 15 and watch how he frames one. "I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while" (Romans 15:24). In passing. The greatest missionary the church has ever produced describes his visit as a joint in a larger body. It serves the mission ahead of him. It feeds a real relationship, *enjoyed your company* is not committee language. And it ends with the church sending him onward, toward work that was never about them. Even the money in his hands traveled that way. He was carrying a contribution from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26), relief moving person to person, church to church, inside relationships that had names.

When Paul wanted to describe his bond with a congregation that had backed him for years, he reached for one word. "I thank my God in all my remembrance of you... because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now" (Philippians 1:3–5), written from a prison the partnership had followed him into. From the first day until now. The unit of missions in the New Testament is not the trip. It is the partnership, and every visit is one heartbeat inside it.

And to the senders, the people who never board a plane but write the checks, the New Testament gives its own standard. "Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are... You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God... Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth" (3 John 5–8). In a manner worthy of God, the standard for support is set by heaven, not by the sending church's convenience. And the promise attached is staggering: the supporter becomes a fellow worker. The widow whose gift keeps a pastor teaching in a village she will never see is not adjacent to the work, she is in it.

## The discipline that separates help from harm

Sincerity does not divide the trip that serves from the trip that spends, every team is sincere. The divide is a discipline, and it can be stated plainly.

The national pastor sets the agenda, or the trip is tourism. He knows what the work needs; we know what our people would enjoy; whoever's question writes the itinerary owns the trip. In practice the test is a single freedom: is the man on the field free to say no, not this year, not that project, send two teachers instead of fifteen painters, send nothing but the support and your prayers, without fearing for his funding? A partner can say no. If he cannot, then whatever we are calling him, we have made him a vendor, and the trip is a purchase.

Go to serve an existing work, not to feel like the work. The team is scaffolding on someone else's building, useful for a season, dismantled without grief, never confused with the architecture. If the ministry only functions while teams are present, it is not a ministry; it is a set. So the question that precedes every booking: what will be true in this place in ten years, and does this trip serve that or interrupt it? Sometimes the honest answer reroutes the money. If local hands could do the job and need the wage, flying our hands over is not generosity, and the same dollars sent as a wage would build the wall and feed the family that painted it. A church that cannot bear that answer has confessed what its trip was for.

The trip is the beginning of a relationship, or it is theater. Judge no trip at report-back; judge it at year ten. The support that never lapsed. The pastor still known by name in the sending church, prayed for by name, asked after by name. The later visits that no longer need photographs, because the relationship stopped being content years ago. From the first day until now, that is the metric Scripture keeps, and it cannot be faked in two weeks, which is precisely its value.

None of this is a case for staying home. It is a case for going the way Paul went, in passing, in service, inside a partnership that existed before the plane landed and will be there after the photos are forgotten. The report-back Sunday will come again, and the photographs will go up, and some of them should. But the questions that make the liturgy honest have to come up with them. Who set the agenda. Whose work did we serve. Who would grieve if we never returned, the church we visited, or only we, missing the feeling.

The wall does not need a fourth coat of paint. The man who owns the wall needs a brother who will still know his name in ten years. Every trip is either the first step toward that brotherhood or a substitute for it, and the two weeks were never the work. The work is the long faithfulness the two weeks either serve, or perform.
posts.excerpt: Short-term trips begin lifetimes of giving and wreck works that took decades to build, sometimes on the same itinerary. A pastor who builds trips around national partners on the honest case for going, the harm nobody photographs, and the discipline that separates a partnership from a performance.

posts.title: The Church That Cannot Promise Safety
posts.body:
The prayer list tells you what a church actually believes. Sit in an American small group long enough and beneath the stated theology you will hear the working one: traveling mercies, a successful surgery, the interview on Thursday, the house that needs to sell. None of those prayers are wrong. But listen to the room when the answer is no, when the scan comes back worse, when the job goes to someone else, when the child does not come home, and a second theology surfaces, the real one, in a single bewildered question. *Why would God let this happen to me?* The question assumes a contract. I believed. I behaved. The hedge was supposed to hold. Suffering arrives as evidence that somebody breached the terms, I failed God or God failed me, and either way the faith itself begins to wobble, because the faith was resting on a premise nobody ever said out loud: that God's presence and my comfort rise and fall together.

I have heard the question in hospital corridors for fifteen years, and I have asked it there myself. It is not a stupid question. It is the honest cry of people who were handed a version of Christianity in which hardship reads as malfunction, a deviation from the deal, a signal that God has stepped out of the room.

And while we were asking it, the center of the Christian faith quietly moved to the parts of the world where no one has ever been able to afford the premise.

## The map has been redrawn

Philip Jenkins put the fact before Western readers in *The Next Christendom* (2002): the demographic center of gravity in world Christianity has shifted south and east, out of Europe and North America and into Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and the shift is not slowing. The representative Christian of this century is not a middle-aged American in a suburban sanctuary. She is more likely to live in Lagos or Manila or a village in the Indian countryside, worshiping in a congregation her grandparents' generation planted, under conditions the American church would classify as crisis.

Set the two facts side by side. The churches of the West, which can promise their members safety, are thinning. The churches that can promise their members nothing of the kind, where baptism can cost a family, a job, a place in the village, sometimes a life, are the ones growing.

A faith that spreads fastest where it costs most is telling us something about what the faith is. It is also telling us something about what we have made of it.

## Where the premise came from

The comfort assumption was not invented last Tuesday. It has a seventeen-hundred-year history, and the honest telling starts at Constantine, not at the prosperity preachers. From the fourth century forward, Western Christianity was mostly practiced from inside cultural power, the faith of the empire, then of the kingdoms, then of the respectable classes, and persecution became something that happened long ago or far away. Add the American chapter: a nation where church membership carried social advantage for most of its history, then a postwar boom in which the pews filled and the suburbs rose together, until blessing and belonging became almost impossible to tell apart.

The prosperity gospel is the version we allow ourselves to mock, health and wealth claimed in Jesus' name, faith as a vending machine. The mockery is cheap, because the respectable churches run a quieter model of the same engine. Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton, in *Soul Searching* (2005), named the actual folk religion of American Christianity moralistic therapeutic deism: God wants me to be good and to be happy, and he is available when I need something, and otherwise he does not intrude. Notice what that creed cannot process. A God whose job is my well-being has no explanation for my suffering except failure, his or mine. When the fire comes, moralistic therapeutic deism does not comfort. It indicts.

Luther diagnosed the root five hundred years before the sociologists measured the fruit. At the Heidelberg Disputation in 1518, he drew the line between the theologian of glory and the theologian of the cross. The theologian of glory expects to find God in strength, success, and visible blessing, and therefore reads suffering as God's absence. The theologian of the cross knows that God chose to reveal himself in the last place a reasonable person would look: a condemned man dying outside the city wall. Thesis 21 carries the whole weight: "A theology of glory calls evil good and good evil. A theology of the cross calls the thing what it actually is." By that standard, much of what the American church says about hardship, every silver lining rushed to, every insistence that the loss is secretly a win, is glory theology wearing a pastoral face. We are not the first church to prefer glory. We are the first that could afford it for this long.

I am not writing from outside this. I pastor a church with a heating system, an insurance policy, and a lockdown protocol. I check the doors. I have preached the hard texts softly because the room was grieving and I flinched. The premise is in my bloodstream too.

## The case for comfort, taken seriously

The comfortable church is not simply wrong, and its instinct deserves its strongest form before any verdict lands.

Peace is a biblical good. Paul told Timothy to pray "for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way" (1 Timothy 2:2), an inspired apostle instructing the church to ask God for roughly the conditions the American church enjoys. Religious liberty is not decadence; it is an answered prayer, bought over centuries at terrible cost, and despising it insults the people who bled for it. The persecuted church itself does not romanticize its chains, the pastors I have sat with pray for relief, for their children's protection, for the knock at the door never to come. Relieving suffering is Christ's own pattern; he healed bodies, he did not lecture them. And a Christian who prays for persecution to toughen up the Western church is volunteering other people's children for a fire he has never felt. All of this is true, and any account of suffering that cannot say it is posturing.

The error was never the comfort. The error is the theology we quietly built on top of it, the promotion of comfort from mercy to covenant. A mercy is something God gives that he did not owe, held with open hands. A covenant is the deal itself, and once safety becomes the deal, its loss becomes betrayal, and every hard providence turns into a crisis of God's character. The global church is not asking us to feel guilty for our peace. It is asking us to read our own Bible the way they are forced to read theirs.

## What the New Testament assumes

Read Peter's first letter as the churches of Asia Minor first heard it, small, exposed communities inside an empire that was beginning to notice them, and one sentence lands like a hand on the shoulder: "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed" (1 Peter 4:12–13).

Do not be surprised. As though something strange were happening. Peter assumes his readers will be tempted to treat suffering as an anomaly, and he forbids it. The fire is not strange weather in the Christian life; it is the climate, and more than that, it is fellowship, a sharing in the sufferings of Christ himself. Now name the American condition honestly. We are precisely surprised. Suffering strikes us as strange, which means the New Testament strikes us as strange, and one of the two of us is misreading the faith.

Paul goes further, into a sentence almost no American pulpit will linger on: "For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake" (Philippians 1:29). The verb translated "granted" is built on the Greek word for grace. Suffering for Christ is not the fine print beneath the gift. It is listed inside the gift, next to faith itself, graced to you. And to Timothy, flatly, without a loophole: "Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted" (2 Timothy 3:12). That is a promise verse. No one prints it on a mug.

Then there is the scene in Acts that measures the whole distance between the first church and mine. The apostles are flogged by the council and released: "Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name" (Acts 5:41). Counted worthy. They received the beating as a credential. I have led a church for fifteen years in which that sentence is functionally unintelligible, we would file the flogging under trauma, schedule the counseling, and ask where God had been. The churches of the global South read the verse and recognize their own week.

**They read these texts as descriptions. We read them as edge cases. That one difference in reading is the whole curriculum.**

## The reverse mentorship

I direct a missions initiative that trains national pastors in India and Thailand, and I will tell you plainly how I first walked into that work: carrying what we had. Money, books, method, curriculum, the accumulated resources of the world's wealthiest church, flowing in the direction resources have always flowed. Somewhere beneath the humility I performed sat an assumption I had never examined: that the teaching would flow the same direction as the funding.

It does not. The pastors I have sat with, and I will not decorate them with invented stories; the general truth is heavy enough, shepherd congregations for whom conversion has a price, in currencies I have never paid. They are not exotic saints, and treating them as scenery is its own kind of theft. They grieve the way anyone grieves. They fear for their children the way I fear for my five sons. They would rather the knock at the door never come. What they have that I do not is not courage as a personality trait. It is a settled, unsurprised theology of suffering, Peter's letter received as a letter to them, in which hardship is not evidence against God but one of the appointed places to meet him. They hold joy and grief in the same hands without either canceling the other. They know what their faith weighs, because it has been on the scale.

So the mentorship runs in reverse, and the sooner the American church says so out loud, the sooner the actual exchange can begin. We have the seminaries, the publishing houses, the budgets, the bandwidth. They have the working theology of the cross. We can fund the printing; they can teach us to read what we print. The posture this requires of us is the one the Western church has almost no muscle memory for, the student's chair, occupied without irony, in front of teachers who own less than our sound boards cost.

And the lesson is not reserved for some future persecution that may never reach an American zip code. Most suffering in my congregation does not come with a persecutor attached. It comes as the scan, the layoff, the miscarriage, the depression that will not lift, the parent buried, the child who walked away. Peter's fiery trial is larger than the arena. A church formed to expect suffering, to receive it as shared with Christ rather than as proof of his absence, is formed for the oncology waiting room, not only for the underground. The theology the global church carries is not a specialty tool for extreme circumstances. It is the ordinary theology of the Christian life, which we misplaced during the long peace.

## What has never been tested

The question the church of the global South puts to the church of the American suburbs is not the dramatic one, whether we would hold up under interrogation, whether our faith would survive the arena. Almost none of us will face that, and imagining we might is its own comfortable fantasy. The question is quieter and closer. What is our faith resting on that has never once been tested? How much of what we call trust in God is, on inspection, trust in the hedge, the income, the insurance, the institutions, the long American peace, with God's name attached to it?

One thing about the hedge is certain. It fails. It fails for everyone eventually; no privilege has yet amended the mortality rate. Some ordinary Tuesday the phone will ring in my house or in yours, and on that day the premise we have lived by will be weighed in about four seconds. The believers on the far side of the world already know what their faith is made of. They found out early, and they have been trying, patiently, without waiting for our permission, to tell us what they learned: that the fire is not strange, that the fellowship is real, that God was not absent in the one place we were most certain he could never be.

They found out early. We will find out late. But we will find out.
posts.excerpt: The churches growing fastest in the world cannot promise their members safety, and they grow anyway. What the global church knows about suffering, the American church misplaced during the long peace, and the mentorship we assumed ran one direction runs in reverse.
