posts.title: None of the Above
posts.body:
There is a slide that comes up at pastors' conferences now, a gray band rising across two decades, and I have watched rooms full of men photograph it with their phones. The religiously unaffiliated. The *nones*, we call them, because a survey offered a checkbox, religious affiliation: none, and enough people checked it that the checkbox became a species, the species a market, and the market a breakout session with a title like *Reaching the Nones*, and the session fills with pastors taking notes, because the numbers at home are going the wrong direction. I have taken the notes too. But I sit in those rooms with double vision, because everyone around me is studying a category, and I am remembering being one. Before I was a pastor I was the man on the slide. And almost nothing taught in that session would have gotten within a mile of me.

## The three people behind the checkbox

The church imagines the none as an atheist with an argument, Dawkins on the nightstand, a folder of objections, an ambush waiting for a Christian. Pastors train for that man. He is real; I came close to being him; and I have met him far less often than the brochures suggest. The stranger fact is that of all the nones he is the nearest to reach, because anger is a form of attention. A man still arguing with God has not left the building. He is standing in the doorway, shouting back into it. It is the other two who are gone.

The first is the indifferent. He bears the church no anger; anger would require the church to matter. To him, faith is roughly what ham radio is, a hobby some people keep, harmless, faintly antique, broadcast on a frequency he has never once tuned past. He is not lying awake suppressing hard questions about God; the questions have nowhere in his life to land. Nothing in his week touches a church. No one he loves attends one. When a Christian corners him about his soul, he experiences it the way you would experience a stranger urgently discussing your stamp collection, not offended, just puzzled that anyone thinks this is about him.

The second is the quietly burned. She grew up inside, the camps, the retreats, the youth group, the whole apparatus. She left without a speech. Sometimes there was a sharp thing: a divorce the church handled with casseroles for one side and silence for the other; a pastor who fell and a board that managed it like a public-relations problem; a real question at sixteen met with alarm instead of an answer. Sometimes there was nothing so sharp, only the slow discovery that the place seemed to need her more than it loved her. She did not deconvert. Ask her about Jesus and something still moves in her face. She backed out of the room quietly, and the room was so busy with its program that nobody noticed for a year, and when somebody finally called, the call felt like attendance follow-up. Which it partly was. It is why she never called back.

And then there was my kind. For years I would have appeared in nobody's pew and on everybody's slide. My atheism was not a wound I nursed or a rebellion I staged. It was furniture, a conclusion so settled I had stopped noticing it was a conclusion. I did not lie awake resenting God. I did not think about God at all, the way you do not think about Portuguese. This is the first thing pastors have to sit with, longer than we want to: most of the people we are strategizing to reach are not against us, because against would take effort. We round the nones up into a single armed enemy because an enemy is easier to plan for than a shrug.

## The postcard arrives pre-read

Be fair to the playbook before burying it. The church-growth toolkit, the Easter mailer, the sermon series with the streaming-poster artwork, the parking team in matching shirts, was not built by cynics but by people who looked at empty pews and lost neighbors and refused to shrug, and its logic was missionary logic: clear away every barrier that is not the cross itself. There are men and women in the kingdom today because somebody mailed a postcard. I will not sneer at a tool God has stooped to use.

But every tool carries a picture of the person on the other end of it, and this picture is wrong. Marketing assumes the problem is awareness, that the none is a customer who has not yet heard a good pitch. Set that assumption next to the actual people. The indifferent man has been pitched since before he could read. He has spent his entire life inside the most sophisticated selling machinery ever built, and the one survival skill that life refined in him is knowing, inside a second, when something wants something from him. The burned woman is harder still, because the pitch is part of what she left. She sat under the branding. She watched her church learn the grammar of the advertisement and call it outreach, and somewhere in those years she realized she could no longer tell whether the smile at the door wanted her or wanted her attendance, and she declined to keep guessing. When our postcard lands in her mailbox, better design this year, warmer copy, it does not reopen her question. It certifies the verdict she already reached.

You cannot market to people whose defining trait is that they stopped believing the marketing. The louder the campaign, the more it proves them right.

I write this with unclean hands. I have approved the mailers and argued about the font. I have stood in a lobby in the branded shirt counting cars, telling myself the count was about the lost, and it was, and it was also about the slide, and the budget, and me, and I could not always have told you the proportions. The nones can smell that mixture. Every strategy meeting about reaching the unaffiliated is a conversation about them, held without them, and people always know when they have become somebody's growth plan. Nobody has ever wanted to be a prospect. The indifferent man and the burned woman agree on almost nothing, except this: neither will consent to being your strategy.

## Come and see

So what reaches them? I can only testify, to what reached me, and to what I have watched reach others across fifteen years of ministry, and the first honest thing to say is that none of it scales. Everything that works is slow, personal, and useless to a funnel. That is its credential. The none has learned to trust only what nobody would bother to fake, and nobody fakes slow.

When Philip told Nathanael that the Messiah had turned up out of Nazareth, Nathanael answered in the voice of every none I have ever met: "Nathanael said to him, 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?' Philip said to him, 'Come and see'" (John 1:46). Sight-unseen contempt, a door already swinging shut, and Philip mounts no defense of Nazareth, takes no offense, builds no five-point case. Three words, and the three words assume the thing will survive being looked at. Marketing exists to control what people see. *Come and see* hands over the control. It is the least defensive sentence in the Gospels, and only a man who has actually seen something can afford to say it.

Which is the catch, and the reason we keep choosing the mailer instead. The invitation is cheap to say and ruinous to honor, because it commits the room to being what it claims. If the burned woman takes you up on it and finds the show, the fog, the funnel, the follow-up card timed by software, you have not lost a customer. You have confirmed a witness.

## Paul walked the city first

When Paul stood up before the philosophers of Athens, he had already done the thing most of our outreach never does. "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you'" (Acts 17:22–23). Passed along. Observed. Before he preached to the city, he walked it. He opens with honor, *very religious*, where a lesser missionary would have opened with the idolatry, then quotes their own literature back to them: "as even some of your own poets have said, 'For we are indeed his offspring'" (Acts 17:28). You cannot quote a poet you have not read. Paul paid the cost of attention. He knew their altars, their writers, and their ache before he asked them to know his Lord.

Hold that next to us. We want the unaffiliated inside our world and have never entered theirs. Most churches strategizing about the nones could not introduce you to one, not the category, a person; could not tell you what the man two doors down from the building fears at three in the morning, or which of his loves is breaking his heart. The none can always tell the difference between being known and being briefed on. Paul's five minutes on Mars Hill cost him days in the streets of Athens. Our version costs a subscription to a culture-trends newsletter, and it lands like what it is.

## Food and time

What actually got me was slower than an argument and more ordinary. People fed me. They fed me not as an event but as a habit, real tables, a long stretch of time, no ask at the end, no card under the napkin. Christians who were in no hurry, whose faith surfaced in conversation because it was load-bearing in their actual lives and not because I was the evening's project. Their unhurriedness was itself an argument, because you cannot rush a person and respect him at the same time, and I had been rushed by everything else that wanted me.

It took me years to notice that the pace was the risen Christ's own. On the road to Emmaus he walks for miles beside two disciples who do not recognize him, and he lets them talk first, asks what they are discussing, hears the grief out, and the unveiling never comes during the theology lecture. "When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him" (Luke 24:30–31). The recognition came at the table, at the end of a walk he refused to rush, on the very day he had conquered death. He, of all persons, had somewhere better to be. He matched his pace to theirs anyway.

Conversion moves at the speed of trust, and trust moves at the speed of meals. Almost no one's guard survives a year of dinners. But a year of dinners cannot be budgeted, delegated, or reported at the annual meeting, which is exactly why we keep choosing the postcard. The postcard produces a number by Friday. The table produces nothing visible for eleven months, and then, sometimes, a person.

## The verse we cut down to a weapon

The Christian who finally cracked my settled unbelief did not out-argue me. He did something rarer. He did not flinch. I brought out the objections, suffering, hypocrites, the wars fought under the cross, the science I thought had closed the case, and he did not change the subject, did not look wounded, did not reach for a pamphlet. He said, more than once, *that is a real question*, and then he answered what he could and told me plainly where his answers ran out and why he believed on the far side of the gap anyway. I lost no debate that day. What I lost was a theory, that Christians could not bear to hear it. A faith that could sit still while I swung at it was a faith I suddenly had to take seriously.

Peter wrote the manual for that man, and we have been quoting a third of it. Here is the whole sentence: "but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15). Apologetics culture kept the middle clause and amputated both ends. The sentence begins in the heart, honor Christ as holy, because the defense is downstream of a settled hope, never a substitute for one. And it ends exactly where we least wanted it to end: gentleness and respect, aimed at the very skeptic we were bracing to defeat. Notice, too, what sets the whole verse in motion: *anyone who asks*. Peter assumes a life strange enough, and a hope visible enough, to provoke the question. The defense answers an inquiry; it was never designed to open the conversation. Hope first, then the question, then the answer, and gentleness the whole way down. We have run the sequence backward for a generation, answers first, at full volume, to questions nobody was asking, from lives too ordinary to provoke any.

## What the slide cannot show

And if you are not a pastor, if you are the one the slide is about, reading over our shoulders, I am not writing to recruit you. You have been recruited at enough for one lifetime. I am writing to tell the men with the notebooks to put them down, because you were never a category, and because somebody once did for me what no campaign could have done: he learned my name before he mentioned my soul.

So, pastors, and I say this to my own house first: the man on the slide is a neighbor, not a decline curve. He stopped believing the marketing, and about the marketing he is right, and there remains one question he is still, silently, without knowing its name, willing to have answered: when the marketing is stripped away, is there anything left in the building? Anyone unhurried enough to eat with him for a year without a pitch. Anyone settled enough to hear his real objections without flinching. Anyone who can say *come and see* and then bear the seeing.

I know the question can be answered, because somebody answered it for me. Nobody mailed me anything. Somebody fed me, and took the years, and did not flinch, and did not hurry, and the man from the slide now writes to you from the other side of a pulpit, with five sons who watch him to see whether the thing still costs him anything. The gray band on that chart is made of people like him, one at a time, each of them measuring, most without a word for it, whether anyone will put down the funnel and pick up a fork. That is what the checkbox has been recording all along. Not the death of their belief. The exhaustion of ours.
posts.excerpt: You cannot market to people whose defining trait is that they stopped believing the marketing. What reaches them costs more: food, time, answered questions, and a Christian who does not flinch.

posts.title: The Pastor and the Machine
posts.body:
A machine will now draft your sermon. Not a rough one, either, orthodox where it should be orthodox, structured, supplied with an illustration and a closing turn, finished in less time than it takes most of us to find a first sentence. So the question pastors are asking one another, on network calls, and in messages that begin *just between us*, is not whether the machine can do it. The question is what it means that it can. If a sermon can be produced on demand, what was a sermon? If answers are free now, every verse explained, every Greek word parsed, every application generated while the coffee cools, what is a pastor for? And inside that question hides the one almost nobody asks out loud. Somewhere this Sunday a drafted sermon gets preached. Whose voice is that congregation trusting?

I do not write this from above the temptation. I pastor a church, I run a network of pastors, and I know the arithmetic of a week that eats the study first, the hospital takes Tuesday, the funeral takes Thursday, the marriage that is ending takes whatever was left, and Saturday night arrives with the page still blank. At that hour the machine's offer does not feel like corruption. It feels like help, and partly it is, and the part that is not does not announce itself. I have twenty-one books and a platform with my name on it, more reason than most to want the producing made easier, more to lose if the name stops meaning that the man behind it did the work. Read what follows as a man drawing a line he needs, not issuing a verdict on other men from safety.

## The panic has a long record

Start with the fear, because the fear deserves better than mockery. Every arrival of a new power over words has been greeted with a funeral for the old ones. Plato preserved the earliest version we have: in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates tells of an Egyptian king who, offered the invention of writing itself, refused to celebrate it, letters would breed forgetfulness, he warned, because men would come to trust the marks outside themselves and lose the memory within. The warning reaches us in writing. Around 1230, Dominican friars in Paris working under Hugh of Saint-Cher assembled the first great concordance of Scripture; for the first time a man could find any word of the Bible without carrying the whole of it in his memory. Cruden built one for English readers in 1737; Strong indexed every occurrence in 1890. Gutenberg's press was running by the mid-1450s, and within seventy years it had carried Luther's quarrel with Rome across Europe faster than any bishop could answer it. Radio began carrying church services in 1921. Then the recorded sermon, then the podcast, and at each arrival some version of the same grief: this will hollow out the man, empty the pews, replace the labor with its counterfeit.

Each time, the grief was wrong in the same way. The concordance did not kill exegesis; it put deeper exegesis within reach of pastors who would never own a library. The press did not kill preaching; it carried preaching farther than any living voice had gone. The technologies of study became servants of the very labor they were accused of ending. That is the record, and the alarm has been issued before, in better prose, and it aged badly.

But the fear deserves its strongest form, not its silliest, so here it is. Every previous tool extended the pastor's work and left the working to him. The concordance found the verses; a man still had to think about them. The press carried the sermon; a man still had to have written one. This machine is different in kind, the fear says, because it does not offer to assist the labor. It offers to perform it, the reading, the connecting, the composing, the finding of words, and what it hands back is a finished substitute for the very acts that made a preacher a preacher. The concordance was a better shovel. This is a machine that digs, and a man who no longer digs will discover soon enough what the digging was for.

That is the honest version, and it is mostly right about the machine and wrong about where the line falls. It draws the line at the technology, and the line has never run there; it runs through the man. Proof-texting by index, verses conscripted into arguments their contexts never made, was a corruption of study available from the thirteenth century on, and pastors found it. Preaching other men's sermons is as old as the circulation of other men's sermons; the borrowed manuscript did not wait for the internet. The counterfeit pastor is not a new invention. What the machine changed is the price. It took a fraud that once required effort and made it effortless, and the only thing still standing between any of us and the counterfeit is what stood there all along, not the state of the technology but the state of the man.

## The scroll must be eaten

There is a scene in Ezekiel that settles what a preacher is, and it is stranger than any account of preaching we would write. "And he said to me, 'Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel.' So I opened my mouth, and he gave me this scroll to eat. And he said to me, 'Son of man, feed your belly with this scroll that I give you and fill your stomach with it.' Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey" (Ezekiel 3:1–3, ESV). God does not tell the prophet to read the scroll or summarize it for the exiles. He tells him to eat it. The word has to pass through the man, belly and body, before it can pass through his mouth, so that what Israel finally receives is not a courier with a message but a man with the message inside him, altered by the carrying. Delivery was never the office. Ingestion was. And ingestion is the one act in the whole chain that cannot be delegated, because no one can eat for you.

This is why the panic, for all its half-truths, keeps missing the target: it assumes the sermon is information transfer, and mourns that information now transfers for free. If the sermon were information transfer, the case for resignation predates the machine by generations. Better explanations of every text I will ever preach have sat in commentaries for a century, and better sermons than mine have been free since preaching was first printed and then recorded. Any member of my congregation could stay home this Sunday and hear finer preaching than they will get from me, and they come anyway, because they were never chiefly there for information. A sermon is a shepherd who has been with God and with these particular people, standing up in front of them to say what he has seen. The preparation the machine offers to take off my hands, the slow reading, the dead ends, the hours in which the passage examines the man before the man expounds the passage, is not packaging around that act. It is the act. Hand it off, and something can still fill twenty-five minutes on Sunday. But the thing Ezekiel was sent to be did not occur that week, whatever occurred in the pulpit.

Jesus supplied the image's pastoral half. "When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know his voice" (John 10:4–5, ESV). The sheep do not follow credentials, or eloquence, or the quality of the material. They follow a known voice, known because it has called them by name before, in rooms the pulpit never sees. The voice a congregation trusts on Sunday is the one that prayed beside the hospital bed on Tuesday and stood at the graveside on Thursday. That knowing is built one visit at a time, over years, and it is the entire collateral behind every sentence the pastor speaks. Which answers the question of what a pastor is for when answers are free: he was never for the answers. He is for the presence the answers ride on, a man who has been with the flock and with God, and presence cannot be delegated. It can only be given or withheld.

So the line can be drawn plainly. A tool that sends the pastor deeper into the text and further into his people serves the office, the concordance served it that way, the commentary serves it, and a machine that gathers sources, checks a date, or argues with a draft the pastor has already labored over can serve it the same way. A tool that stands in for the pastor's own encounter, that reads so he does not have to read, wrestles so he does not have to wrestle, finds the words so that nothing ever passed through him at all, has stopped being a tool. It is a substitute, and what it substitutes for is not his labor but him. The same machinery can be either. Which it becomes is decided in the study, alone, with the door shut, which is why the deciding question was never about machinery.

## Secrecy is the tell

Paul defended his ministry to Corinth in a sentence that reads as if it were written for this year: "But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God's word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone's conscience in the sight of God" (2 Corinthians 4:2, ESV). The defense consists of renunciation, not eloquence, not results, but what the ministry refuses: cunning, tampering, the underhanded. And the alternative to cunning is named with precision: the open statement of the truth. Openness is not a courtesy Paul extends when convenient. It is the load-bearing wall of the whole apostolic claim, because a gospel about the God of truth cannot be commended by sleight of hand without becoming, in the commending, something else. He had already told the same church, "For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God's word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:17, ESV). The peddler asks what will move. The commissioned man asks what is true, and asks it in the sight of God, as a man who assumes he is watched even when the study door is shut.

The test that follows fits in a pocket: whatever you did to make the sermon, could you describe it from the pulpit in plain words and stand there while the congregation took it in? The congregation holds no veto over a pastor's study habits; the reason is that secrecy is the tell. A tool you can name from the pulpit is a tool. A tool you must hide has become a lie you are telling weekly, and the sermon built on it becomes the lie's delivery system, whatever the doctrine inside it says. A pastor who can say openly, "I use these machines to gather and to check, and every word I preach passed through me first," has nothing in the study he must pray stays hidden. A pastor who cannot say what he does has already ruled, in the court of his own conscience, that what he does breaks trust, and is doing it anyway, which is what cunning means.

And the stakes are not symmetrical. A congregation that learns its shepherd's sermons have grown slower and plainer because he declined the shortcut will forgive that in an afternoon; slower was never the complaint. A congregation that discovers its shepherd outsourced his soul, that the voice they trusted at the graveside was a stranger's in the pulpit, loses something no apology quickly retrieves, because the discovery does not discredit one sermon. It reaches backward. Every previous Sunday becomes an open question. The sheep flee from a stranger's voice, Jesus says, and the fleeing is not rebellion; it is the design, working. Borrowed sermons always carried this cost. The machine only made the borrowing easy.

One more thing has to be said, because some readers are auditing whether the church can handle a new power honestly, and they are right to. Nothing in this argument depends on the machine writing badly. Assume it writes well; assume it writes better than the man. The argument does not move, because it was never a claim about the quality of machine prose, and a pastor who rests his case on the machine's inferiority has built on shifting sand. The claim is about truthfulness, that the saying must belong to the one who signs it, that what he signs he must have ingested, and that whatever stands between him and saying so out loud is the exact measure of what has gone wrong. The claim holds in a world of brilliant machines and in a world with none; it held for the borrowed manuscript two centuries before the transistor. Integrity does not have a technology problem. It has only ever had a truth-telling problem, and every generation is issued new equipment for the same old test.

The watching world is not scandalized that Christians use machines; it uses them too. It is watching whether the community that claims to serve the God of truth will be one place the new power gets handled in the light, named, bounded, confessed when misused, or one more place it gets handled like everywhere else, meaning wherever advantage points, with a statement when caught. I spent years on the outside of this faith, auditing the church for honesty, and I remember exactly what I was looking for: not a position paper, but one community that would tell the truth about itself when lying had gotten cheap. The machine has just made lying cheaper across the board, which means it has also made the truth-tellers easier to see.

## What cannot be touched

So the pastors asking one another what this machine means for the office can be given a plain answer. It means what the concordance meant, and the press, and the microphone: new equipment in the study, which will serve whatever master is set over it. It also means one thing none of those meant, the price of the counterfeit has fallen to almost nothing, so the only cost still attached to a borrowed soul is the truth. What it cannot mean, what no technology has ever meant, is a change in the office itself. The scroll is still on the table. It still has to be eaten, by you, because nothing and no one can eat it for you, and the people in the pews are not waiting for the finest available words. They are waiting to hear whether the voice is one they know, whether the man in front of them has been with them, and been with God, and is saying what he has seen. The machine can produce everything about a sermon except a man who was there. That part of the office has not moved since Ezekiel opened his mouth. Eat the scroll, or hand the flock a stranger's voice. There is no third thing on the table.
posts.excerpt: A machine will now draft a competent sermon, which forces the older question: if answers are free, what is a pastor for? On the scroll that must be eaten, the voice the sheep know, and why a tool you have to hide has already become a lie.
