posts.title: The House Is Not Full
posts.body:
Every church I have ever served has said the same sentence from the front, and meant it: everyone is welcome here. Then the service starts, and the building begins to disagree. Please stand. The lyrics are on a screen a low-vision member cannot read, moving at a pace a slower mind cannot hold, in a room where a child who cannot sit still is felt as an interruption rather than a member of the body. There are steps where ramps should be. Somewhere in the third row is a family that will make it through today and quietly stop coming by spring, not because anyone was cruel, but because everything here was designed by people whose bodies cooperate, for people whose bodies cooperate. I have designed those services. I have trimmed the dead air, tightened the transitions, and never once asked whose exclusion the smoothness was made of.

Here is the tell, and it indicts me before it indicts anyone. The church will pray for a disabled member's healing far more readily than it will change its building, its pace, or its platform for them. The prayer costs a sentence. The ramp costs money, and something more expensive than money, the admission that the room was built wrong, by us, for us. We ask God to change the body in the pew because that is easier than changing anything that belongs to the church. And we call it faith.

**The claim, plainly: the church's theology of disability is often worse than the world's practice. The world, holding no doctrine that every human being bears the image of God, wrote accessibility into its building codes. The church, holding exactly that doctrine, asked to be excused, and underneath the architecture sits the deeper failure: we have treated disabled people as objects of our ministry rather than as members of Christ's body, which Scripture does not call welcome. It calls them indispensable.**

The legal fact first, because the church prefers not to know it. When Congress passed the Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990, religious organizations were exempted from its public accommodation requirements. There were constitutional reasons offered, real ones. But sit with the plain result. The law that redrew the entrances of grocery stores and movie theaters stops at the sanctuary door. A person using a wheelchair can count on getting into the bar. She cannot count on getting into the church. The world did this with no theology at all. We had Genesis: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). They had a building code. Their building code has done more for disabled bodies than our doctrine has, and that sentence should not be able to be true.

## What the objection gets right

There is a serious Christian objection to everything I am arguing, and it deserves its strongest form. Disability is not the design; it is the groan. "For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now" (Romans 8:22), and failing bodies are part of that groaning, which is why Jesus, everywhere he went, healed them. He did not hand the blind man a better theology of blindness. He gave him his sight. A church that stops praying for healing, that reframes every affliction as an identity to be accommodated, has quietly given up on the God of the Gospels and baptized the Fall. And many disabled people themselves ache for healing, for the pain to stop, for the seizures to end, for one conversation with a child the condition has locked away, and a theology that celebrates their condition can feel, from inside it, like being told to decorate a prison.

Nearly all of that is true, and none of it gets walked back here. Creation groans. The resurrection promises a body beyond pain, and hoping for it is not a failure of self-acceptance. Praying for healing is not an insult; I will keep doing it. And any writing that speaks over the disabled people who long for healing, that tells a woman in chronic pain her ache for relief is a false consciousness, has traded one cruelty for another.

But watch what the church has done with that true objection, because the move is the whole problem. We took a real hope and made it a schedule. Healing became the thing that happens before full membership, be fixed, then belong, and the healing prayer became the able-bodied church's exit from its own obligations. We pray for the body in the pew to change so that nothing about the church has to. And when the body does not change, the old arithmetic surfaces: somebody must not have enough faith. The person we would not build a ramp for now carries the blame for the prayer we prayed instead. That is not the hope of Romans 8. That is a theology that has found a pious way to keep the building.

## The question Jesus refused to answer

The arithmetic is old. When Jesus's disciples passed a man born blind, they asked the question every religious culture asks about a body that does not work the way bodies are supposed to: whose fault. "And his disciples asked him, 'Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?' Jesus answered, 'It was not this man who sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him'" (John 9:2–3).

The disciples are not being monsters; they are being theologians. A ledger somewhere must balance. It is the oldest pastoral malpractice in the world, and it survives, every time a congregation treats a wheelchair as a verdict, every time the mother of an autistic child is asked, gently, whether there is unconfessed sin in the home. Jesus refuses the entire frame. Not this man. Not his parents.

And then the sentence that has been abused almost as badly as the question: that the works of God might be displayed in him. The church has taken those words and made them a new cruelty, telling disabled people their bodies exist as other people's object lessons, inspiration for the able, sermon illustrations with a pulse. Read the chapter instead. The man himself, not his condition, the man, becomes the only person in John 9 who sees clearly. He stands up to the Pharisees with more nerve than his own parents can find, and ends the chapter as a worshiper while the sighted experts end it blind. Jesus moved him from the specimen everyone discussed to the confessor everyone should have heard. The chapter is a demolition of every church that explains its disabled members instead of listening to them.

Exodus goes further, and it goes where we flinch. When Moses tried to disqualify himself from the call, "I am not eloquent... I am slow of speech and of tongue" (Exodus 4:10), God answered with a question the church has been dodging ever since: "Then the LORD said to him, 'Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?'" (Exodus 4:11). It is a hard verse; I will not sand it smooth. But it says one thing beyond dispute: God refuses to be distanced from the bodies we distance ourselves from. The mute mouth and the deaf ear are not outside his making, and this is God's answer while he commissions a man with a speech impairment to be his spokesman. God's reply to my body disqualifies me was not healing. It was sending. The most consequential voice in the Old Testament stammered.

## The God who chose weakness

If Exodus looks like an anomaly, the New Testament makes it a policy. "But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong" (1 Corinthians 1:27), and the choosing runs all the way to the center, because the center of Christianity is a body that was pierced, executed in public, unable to come down. The world's gods are personifications of ability. Ours was crucified.

Paul learned the policy in his own flesh. Whatever the thorn was, the record of the prayer is plain: "Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me. But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness'" (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The most prominent unanswered healing prayer in the New Testament belongs to its greatest apostle. Be careful here, because people bleed on this verse. It does not mean God will explain your thorn, and it is not a script anyone else is permitted to read over your suffering. It means this much: Paul's body was not fixed, and Paul was not thereby disqualified, diminished, or benched. The power of Christ did not wait for the thorn to leave. It rested on the man who still had it.

And the risen Christ kept his wounds. "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:39). The resurrection body, the prototype of every body the church hopes for, came back scarred. Nancy Eiesland, a sociologist of religion who lived her whole life with a congenital bone condition, built her book The Disabled God (1994) on that scene: the Lord who returns in glory still bearing the marks, and known by them, is not a God who is ashamed of marked bodies. Heaven's first citizen has scars, and he showed them to the room.

Now set 1 Corinthians 12 on top of it all, the verse the church files under nice and Scripture files under load-bearing. "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you,' nor again the head to the feet, 'I have no need of you.' On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable" (1 Corinthians 12:21–22). Read the word. Not tolerated, not accommodated, not even welcomed, indispensable, the word you use for an organ, the word for what the body dies without. Welcome is what I extend to a guest in my house; indispensable is what I confess about a member of my body. A congregation without its disabled members is not a whole church being generous when it considers them. It is an amputated body that has learned to call its missing parts optional. No church says I have no need of you out loud. We said it with four steps and no ramp. We said it with a pace only certain minds can ride, with a platform where nobody shakes or stutters or signs, with a Lord's Table a walker cannot reach and a communion roster no one with Down syndrome has ever been asked to join, receiving, always receiving, and never once distributing the body of Christ to the body of Christ.

This includes the minds. A church knows, more or less, what to do with a wheelchair; it panics quietly before dementia, before the member who no longer remembers the creed or the pastor's name or, on the hard days, her own. John Swinton, a practical theologian at Aberdeen who was a psychiatric nurse first, argued in Dementia: Living in the Memories of God (2012) what the church should have known from its own doctrine: a person's identity is not stored in her brain, to be lost when the tissue fails. It is held in the memory of God, who does not forget her, and in the body of Christ, which remembers her faith with her and for her when she can no longer recite it. The congregation that keeps singing the old hymns with a woman who has forgotten everything but their tunes is not doing sentimental aftercare. It is ecclesiology, being the part of her that remembers.

## The banquet and the house

So what does a congregation owe its members whose bodies or minds do not cooperate? Jesus answered with a guest list, twice in one chapter. First as instruction: "But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you" (Luke 14:13–14). Then as parable, when the invited guests excused themselves and the host turned to his servant in anger: "Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame" (Luke 14:21). And when there was still room: "Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled" (Luke 14:23).

The church has read Luke 14 as a charity text for two thousand years, and the reading flatters us. Look again at the host's motive. That my house may be filled. The banquet is not complete without them. The master is filling his house with the guests he wants, and the list he dictates, the poor and crippled and blind and lame, is not the outreach program of the banquet. It is the banquet. A church that treats its disabled members as recipients of ministry has the parable exactly backwards. They are not the objects of the feast. They are the invited.

That reversal is the debt, and it is larger than a ramp, though it includes the ramp. It means the building, the pace, and the platform get remade around the confession that the body is incomplete without these members, not as a project for when the budget allows, but the way you act on what you believe is true. It means gifts, not just needs: a church asking what it cannot see, cannot preach, cannot know about patience and dependence and the actual meaning of grace until the members who live those words daily are teaching, serving, deciding, distributing the bread.

And to the reader whose own body or mind is the subject here, the one who has been prayed over without being asked, explained without being heard, welcomed to a room that was never built with you in mind, one sentence with no program attached. The failures named in this essay are the church's, and mine, and nothing in the Scriptures we mishandled ever called you a burden, an object lesson, or a problem of ministry; the word the apostle chose for you was indispensable, and the host of the banquet wrote your invitation before the church revised his list.

I do not know how to end this comfortably, so I will not try. The master's instruction is still standing; the house is still not full; and the emptiness of the seats is not a mystery about who declined. We built the room. We set the pace. We decided, without ever having to defend the sentence, which bodies a worship service assumes. And all the while, the parts of the body we treated as optional were the ones our Lord had called indispensable, so that when a church finally tears out its steps and slows its liturgy and places the bread in trembling hands to distribute, it is not being generous. It is being completed, late, at its own expense, in the image of a God whose power is made perfect in weakness and whose risen body still shows the scars.
posts.excerpt: The world, with no doctrine of the image of God, wrote accessibility into law. The church, holding that doctrine, asked to be excused. Paul's word for the members we treated as optional was indispensable, and the master's house is still not full.

posts.title: The Earth Is the Lord's
posts.body: Creation care is not an optional concern for environmentalists. It is central to Christian theology and practice. The earth belongs to God, and we are accountable for how we treat it. Climate change is a justice issue because it disproportionately affects the poor.

posts.body: The gleaning laws of Israel were not charity. They were justice, a way of ensuring that the poor had access to the resources they needed to survive. The book of Ruth shows what this looks like in practice.

posts.title: Why the Church's Comfort With Inequality Requires Explanation
posts.body: The church's acceptance of vast economic inequality is not neutral. It is a theological choice with theological consequences. It requires theological justification, and that justification is hard to find in Scripture.
posts.excerpt: The church's acceptance of vast economic inequality is not neutral. It is a theological choice with theological consequences. It requires theological justification, and that justification is hard to find in Scripture.

posts.title: The Prophetic Pastor
posts.body: The pastor is called to be a prophetic voice, to name injustice, to challenge the powerful, to advocate for the vulnerable. This is not optional. It is central to the pastoral calling. The pastor who remains silent is not being neutral. He is complicit.
posts.excerpt: The pastor is called to be a prophetic voice, to name injustice, to challenge the powerful, to advocate for the vulnerable. This is not optional.

posts.title: Justice Without Love Is Ideology
posts.body: Justice pursued without love becomes ideology. Love pursued without justice becomes sentimentality. The church needs both. The prophets combined fierce indictments of injustice with deep compassion for the vulnerable.
posts.excerpt: Justice pursued without love becomes ideology. Love pursued without justice becomes sentimentality. The church needs both.

posts.title: What the Beatitudes Are Actually Promising
posts.body: The Beatitudes are not spiritual abstractions. They are political statements about God's preference for the poor and God's vision of a transformed world. "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
posts.excerpt: The Beatitudes are not spiritual abstractions. They are political statements about God's preference for the poor and God's vision of a transformed world.

posts.title: What the Black Church Never Had to Rediscover
posts.body:
Every few years, my branch of the church discovers justice. A book climbs the lists. A conference adds a panel. A denomination drafts a statement, carefully worded, and we congratulate ourselves on the courage it took. Then the arguing starts, the word itself becomes suspect, and we set the whole subject down until the next discovery, each one announced with the surprise of a man who has just found the ocean.

I was one of the discoverers. Somewhere in my thirties I read Martin Luther King Jr.'s letter from the Birmingham jail, written in April of 1963, and came away feeling I had met something new, a fresh synthesis, Christianity finally catching up to its conscience. Then I looked at what King was actually doing on the page. Answering the charge of extremism, he called witnesses, and the first was twenty-seven centuries old: "Was not Amos an extremist for justice: 'Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.'" He was not improvising. He was quoting the eighth century before Christ, through a tradition that had been preaching Amos in secret while my tradition was quoting Scripture over the auction block. I had mistaken the oldest reading in the room for the newest, because the people who kept it alive were not the people I had been taught to read.

So let me say what this essay is before it goes any further. It is a white Baptist pastor paying a debt in public. I have no standing to appraise the Black church, and this is not an appraisal; a man does not grade the bank that carries his mortgage. What the Black church in America knows about the prophets, it learned in a school my spiritual ancestors built and could not have survived a week in. I write as a student who arrived several centuries late to the seminar, asking what was on the syllabus.

## The gospel they were handed and the Bible they found

Begin with what was offered, because the offer was an insult with a liturgy. The Christianity presented to enslaved Africans in the American South was edited by its beneficiaries. Slave states passed laws against teaching an enslaved person to read. Plantation missionaries preached under the eye of the men who owned the pews and the people in them, and the texts were chosen accordingly, "Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling" (Ephesians 6:5) wore thin from use, while Exodus was handled like contraband, which the masters correctly understood it to be. The catechisms composed for slaves taught obedience, contentment, and the wickedness of stealing, by which they meant a chicken and never a man. Whatever else that religion was, it was designed, and the design had one purpose: a Christ who saves the soul and leaves the plantation exactly as he found it.

They did not accept the edit. This is the fact that should permanently end the theory that Christianity was simply imposed on the enslaved and swallowed whole. They took the censored book and heard it, heard, mostly, since reading it was a crime, more honestly than the men who censored it, and they built a church to hold what they heard. It met at night. In the woods, in ravines, in brush arbors; the narratives of the formerly enslaved describe quilts hung wet to trap the sound and iron pots turned over at the threshold because the tradition said the pot caught the voices. Historians came to call what grew in those clearings the invisible institution, Albert Raboteau's Slave Religion (1978) carries the phrase in its subtitle, an entire Christian communion with no building, no charter, no legal existence, and no permission, where discovery meant the lash. They gathered anyway. American Christianity has produced no other body of believers who risked more to hear a sermon, and what they were risking it for was precisely the pages we had torn out.

What did they find on those pages? A God who takes sides in history and announces the side. "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings" (Exodus 3:7). In the church of my upbringing that verse was background, ancient Near Eastern context, a setup for doctrines that arrive later in the book. To a woman standing in a Georgia field it was a mirror with her own face in it. Egypt was no metaphor for her bad habits, it had acreage, an economy, an overseer with a name, and the exodus was not a typology to be diagrammed but a precedent to be pleaded, the case, already decided, that the Judge of all the earth hears people exactly like her and comes down.

Their theology survives because they sang it. The spirituals are the invisible institution's systematic theology, composed by people forbidden to write, and as readings of Scripture they are more serious than most of what sits on my shelf. "Go down, Moses, way down in Egypt's land; tell old Pharaoh to let my people go." That is not folk music with religious coloring; it is an interpretation of Exodus so plain it was dangerous to be caught singing it. When Jeremiah cried the question of a shattered people, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22), it was the enslaved church that answered the prophet across twenty-four centuries, and answered him in the affirmative: there is a balm in Gilead. They sang heaven, and they sang the river crossing, and often in the same song, a chariot that meant glory and also meant north, because they never granted the choice the white church keeps insisting on between the world to come and the world as it stands. We would spend the next century and a half debating whether the gospel is spiritual or social. The people in the brush arbor declined the premise. They had heard Luke.

"The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed" (Luke 4:18). That is the text Jesus chose for his first recorded sermon, Isaiah in his mouth, and he told the room it was fulfilled that day in their hearing. A congregation of captives did not need the passage explained. A congregation of the comfortable has spent two hundred years explaining it away.

## The one house they owned

When freedom finally came on paper, nearly every institution in Black American life still belonged to someone else, the mill, the bank, the courthouse, the school, and above all the ledger. One did not. The church had been theirs in the woods before it was theirs on a deed, and once it had walls it became the single institution Black Americans owned outright: pulpit, purse, and vote. Richard Allen had seen the necessity early, after Black worshipers were pulled from their knees during prayer in a Philadelphia sanctuary that had welcomed their money and resented their presence, he walked out and built, and by 1816 the African Methodist Episcopal Church existed as a denomination with Allen as its first bishop. What followed, north and south, was a church that had to be everything because its people were allowed nothing: school and mutual-aid society, credit union and printing press, political hall and burying ground, the one room where a man who was called boy all week was called deacon on Sunday. And the pastor, paid by his own people, answered to no employer white power could lean on. It is no accident that the prophetic voice endured in that pulpit. It was the only pulpit in America whose bills the empire did not pay.

That is the line King stood in, and he knew it. Frederick Douglass stood in it in 1845, writing in the appendix to his Narrative that "between the Christianity of this land, and the Christianity of Christ, I recognize the widest possible difference", the formerly enslaved man holding the slaveholder's religion to the Scriptures it claimed. Howard Thurman stood in it in 1949, asking in Jesus and the Disinherited what the religion of Jesus, himself a poor man under an occupying empire, says to those whose backs are against the wall. The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956 was organized through church basements and mass meetings in sanctuaries, sustained for more than a year on sermons and collection plates, led by the young pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church. By the time King sat in the Birmingham jail with Amos in his memory, he was not founding a tradition of biblical protest. He was the latest preacher in a pulpit older than the country's conscience. My church kept treating him as a beginning because we had never read the line he came from. The line was two centuries long. We were surprised by its newest sentence.

## Why we keep learning it late

The question that indicts me is not why the Black church saw all this. It is why mine keeps having to be told.

The easy answer is villainy, and villainy is in the record, my own denomination organized in 1845 so that slaveholders could be missionaries, and I have written elsewhere about that grave. But villainy explains the 1850s better than it explains last Tuesday, and the fuller answer is worse because it survives every reform: comfort. The same Bible reads differently on either side of the whip. Where the prophets cost nothing, they read as poetry, stirring, distant, safely about Israel. Where they name your Tuesday, they read as news. My tradition did not lack the texts; we lacked the wound that makes the texts legible, and rather than sit near the wounded and learn, we filed justice under electives. Amos became a unit in a survey course. Exodus became a typology chart. Luke 4 became a passage about preaching. The enslaved church could not afford the abstraction, and we could, that is nearly the whole difference, and it is not a difference in the book.

I owe the strongest form of the worry some readers are carrying by now, because it is not a foolish worry. It says: this talk of prophetic justice is how the social gospel returns, politics wearing a stole. There is a real lineage in which justice-language slowly swallowed the resurrection, until the church became a charity with hymns and had nothing left to say over a grave, and whoever fears that is remembering something that happened. But look where the fear points, and notice that the Black church at its center is the standing refutation of the dichotomy, not an instance of it. The same gathered people sang the blood of Jesus and let-my-people-go in one service. Thurman wrote about the religion of Jesus, not a program with his name attached. King's Amos arrives in a letter soaked in Scripture and church history, addressed to clergy as clergy. The tradition held together what white Protestants keep tearing in half and handing to opposing parties, the cross and the courtroom, the age to come and the age as it stands, and it held them together because it did its reading under a pressure that made amputating either half unaffordable. A comfortable church splits the gospel and calls each half a party. A suffering church could not afford halves.

## What a debtor owes

Here is where a white pastor writing on this subject usually reaches for the wrong ending, and I feel the pull of both versions. One is romance: the Black church rendered as a museum of moral heroism, a mascot for other people's renewal. It is not a museum but a living church, churches, rather, plural and arguing, with tired pastors and empty pews and prosperity hustlers and every sin mine has, plus a history mine inflicted. Sanding off its ordinary humanity is tourism wearing reverence. The other temptation is citation as payment, as if quoting King every January retires the debt, as if admiration were restitution. A man who owes you money and keeps praising your handwriting has misunderstood his situation.

What a debtor actually owes is changed practice, and for a pastor the practice is reading. I have begun to ask, of every text I preach, a question I learned too late: how was this verse heard by the people my church's fathers held in bondage, and why does my reading keep landing so much nearer the master's? This is not because suffering confers infallibility; it does not, and the Black church's theologians argue with one another like everyone else's. But the parts of the canon that comfort archives, affliction keeps in circulation, and a tradition that read Exodus in a clearing at midnight, under penalty of the lash, knows things about that book which I do not. The debt is a posture. Sit under before you quote. Learn the line before you borrow its newest sentence.

Amos is still on the syllabus. "But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24), the verse was not fresh when King quoted it, and it was not fresh when a field hand first heard Egypt named and recognized the address. The next rediscovery is already scheduled; my tradition will announce it with clean surprise, and there will be a panel. I keep thinking instead about the iron pot turned over at the threshold of the hush harbor, believers muffling the sound of the gospel so that the gospel could survive its official custodians. That detail will not leave me alone. The question it asks is not whether the singing was real. The question is which side of that door my church was standing on, and how long we intend, politely, to stay there.
posts.excerpt: Every few years my branch of the church discovers justice, announces it like news, and sets it down again. The Black church in America has held it for two and a half centuries, read in hush harbors, sung in the spirituals, preached from the one pulpit the empire did not pay for. I write as a student and a debtor, several centuries late to the seminar.

posts.title: Why Color-Blindness Is Not a Theological Virtue
posts.body: Color-blindness sounds virtuous but it is actually a way of denying the reality of racism and its ongoing effects. Justice requires seeing and naming racial injustice. The church that claims to be color-blind is blind to the suffering of people of color.
posts.excerpt: Color-blindness sounds virtuous but it is actually a way of denying the reality of racism and its ongoing effects. Justice requires seeing and naming racial injustice.

posts.title: The Most Vulnerable People in Your City Are Not in Your Pews
posts.body: The most vulnerable people in your city, the homeless, the incarcerated, the undocumented, are not in your church. This is not an accident. It is a failure of the church to reach across the boundaries that divide us. Justice requires going to them.
posts.excerpt: The most vulnerable people in your city, the homeless, the incarcerated, the undocumented, are not in your church. This is not an accident. It is a failure of the church to reach across the boundaries that divide us.

posts.title: Why the Prophets Were Expelled From the Sanctuary
posts.body: The prophets were not welcomed in the temple. They were expelled because their message threatened the comfortable religious establishment. The prophet who is comfortable in the sanctuary is not a prophet. He is a chaplain to the status quo.
posts.excerpt: The prophets were not welcomed in the temple. They were expelled because their message threatened the comfortable religious establishment.

posts.title: What the Exodus Demands of the Church Today
posts.body: The Exodus is not just ancient history. It is a paradigm for liberation that the church is called to embody today. God is on the side of the oppressed. The church that forgets this has forgotten its own story.
posts.excerpt: The Exodus is not just ancient history. It is a paradigm for liberation that the church is called to embody today. God is on the side of the oppressed.

posts.title: Sabbath Is Resistance
posts.body: Sabbath is not just rest. It is a political act, a refusal to participate in the logic of endless production and consumption that fuels injustice. To keep Sabbath is to declare that there is more to life than work and that people matter more than productivity.
posts.excerpt: Sabbath is not just rest. It is a political act, a refusal to participate in the logic of endless production and consumption that fuels injustice.

posts.title: The Pastoral Care of the Wealthy Congregant
posts.body: The wealthy need pastoral care too. But that care must include prophetic challenge, a call to use their resources justly and to align their lives with the kingdom of God. Pastoral care that affirms the wealthy in their wealth is not care. It is complicity.
posts.excerpt: The wealthy need pastoral care too. But that care must include prophetic challenge, a call to use their resources justly and to align their lives with the kingdom of God.

posts.title: Why the Church's Response to Poverty Has Been Mostly Charity
posts.body: The church has historically responded to poverty with charity rather than justice. This is not because charity is bad, but because it is insufficient. Charity addresses symptoms. Justice addresses causes. The church needs both, but it has prioritized charity.
posts.excerpt: The church has historically responded to poverty with charity rather than justice. This is not because charity is bad, but because it is insufficient.

posts.title: The Stranger and the Sword
posts.body:
Read the verse aloud in a room of American Christians and watch the sorting begin before the sentence ends. "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong" (Leviticus 19:33). One man hears a border bill coming and braces. The woman two chairs down hears ammunition and starts composing the post. For one full second, nobody in the room is hearing Leviticus. The verse was drafted before it finished being read, and a sentence that ends with the name of God now functions mostly as a way of finding out who is in the room with you.

I have preached this text and felt myself calculating, mid-sentence, which half of my congregation was about to write me an email, and I have softened the next sentence to lower the count. I have also quoted it at people, in arguments, online, as a move. A pastor who deploys Scripture to win rooms should not be the one you trust to describe the room. I am trying anyway. The verse deserves better than what we have done with it, all of us, me first.

## What the text says

Leviticus 19 is the summit of the Holiness Code, the chapter where "you shall love your neighbor as yourself" lives (Leviticus 19:18), the command Jesus ranked second in all the Law. Sixteen verses later it turns to the outsider and refuses to let the neighbor-command die at the covenant’s edge: "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God" (Leviticus 19:33–34).

Mark the verb. As yourself. The love commanded toward the neighbor is commanded toward the one who is not your kin, not your tribe, not your faith, whose presence in your town you never voted on.

And it is no stray verse. "You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21). "He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:18–19). The rabbis of the Talmud counted thirty-six places, some said forty-six, where the Torah warns Israel about its treatment of the stranger (Bava Metzia 59b).

The grounding is stranger than the command. The reason is never the sojourner's merit, his usefulness, his paperwork, his gratitude. The reason is memory, you were strangers, and the reason under the memory is God himself. Deuteronomy does not say the sojourner deserves love. It says God loves him, feeds him, clothes him, and then orders Israel to fall in step with what God is already doing. And Deuteronomy names the three people God takes as his personal clients: the fatherless, the widow, the sojourner, the ones who arrive at the gate with no household behind them and no one to speak their name.

I flinch at that list, and the flinch is older than my politics. I was raised without a father. Long before I believed a word of this book, it had already named me, the boy at the gate with no man behind him, and named a God who takes that boy's case without being paid. I did not come to this text neutral. Neither did you.

## What the word means, said honestly

The Hebrew word is *ger*, and this essay stands or falls on being honest about it. The ger of the Torah is neither a tourist nor an invading army. He is the resident outsider, the foreigner living inside Israel's towns, under Israel's law, within reach of Israel's hands. He gleans at the field's edge with the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). He rests on the Sabbath with the household (Exodus 20:10). He receives the same justice in court as the native (Deuteronomy 1:16–17), and a curse falls on anyone who bends it (Deuteronomy 27:19). Ruth the Moabite gleaned under these laws, and the Bible walks her from that field into the genealogy of Jesus Christ (Ruth 2; Matthew 1:5). The Torah's stranger is a person the text guards, not a problem it manages, once, the great-grandmother of the king.

Now the honesty. Scholars genuinely dispute the ger's precise legal standing. James K. Hoffmeier, in *The Immigration Crisis* (2009), argues that the ger was a foreigner residing with the community's sanction, something like a legally admitted alien, distinct from the *nokri* and the *zar*, the foreigner merely passing through, and that the sojourner texts therefore do not directly adjudicate the modern question of unlawful entry. M. Daniel Carroll R., in *Christians at the Border* (2008), argues that the texts disclose God's enduring posture toward the vulnerable outsider, and that Christian thinking begins with the image of God in the immigrant, not his legal category. Both men read the Hebrew, and their disagreement proves the one thing neither tribe wants proven. The verse carries no modern border policy inside it, in either direction. It does not tell a nation whom to admit or how to enforce its laws. It tells a people how the stranger who is among you, present, resident, within reach, must be treated. Anyone who tells you the Hebrew settles the border has already left the Hebrew.

Hold that distinction; it will indict both rooms before this essay ends.

## The strongest case from the right

Take it in the form its best defenders would sign.

God ordains government, and not as a concession. "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (Romans 13:1). Paul wrote that under Nero, not under a ruler he admired. And the authority is armed on purpose: the ruler "is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:4). A government that cannot say who enters its territory, and under what law, has surrendered part of the ordering work God assigned it, and disorder is never neutral. When law breaks down, the strong do not suffer first. The poor do. The trafficked do. The migrant himself does, delivered to smugglers and black markets wherever lawful process fails. On this reading a secure border is not love's enemy; it can be one of love's instruments.

Nor is a nation a church. Israel itself, the very nation commanded to love the ger, maintained legal distinctions between sojourner and native, and between the resident sojourner and the foreigner passing through. Boundaries and citizenship belong to the ordered world in which love has to be practiced. A government carries particular obligations to its own citizens, the widow and the fatherless already inside its gates, and weighing those obligations against others is moral work, not hardness of heart. And the conservative is right about one more thing: converting "love the sojourner" into an admissions policy is proof-texting, the same crime he stands accused of when he quotes Romans 13, a command to love no more specifies a visa quota than "You shall not steal" (Exodus 20:15) specifies a tax code. Christians who serve in government and enforce just laws are not violating Leviticus. Some of them are obeying Romans.

That is the case. It is serious and biblical, and the half of the church that waves it away with a chant has not answered it.

## The strongest case from the left

Now the other room, at full strength.

The command to love the stranger is among the most repeated instructions God ever gave his people, and it rests not on circumstance but on his character. He loves the sojourner. Present tense, no expiration. And when God took flesh, he pressed the identification further. In his own account of the last judgment, the Son of Man says to those on his right: "For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35). Christ does not say the stranger is your assignment. He says the stranger is, in some way he declines to soften, himself. The early church took him at his word: hospitality to the alien was ordinary discipline for centuries, practiced by people with no vote on any policy.

And the left is right about the reflex. When a Christian hears the word *stranger* and his first movement is threat assessment, cost, crime, culture, what it means for people like him, something has already gone wrong that no policy argument can repair. The heart is disobeying before the mind has finished reasoning. "It's complicated" is true, and it is also the most comfortable sentence in the language; whole congregations have lived inside it for decades, feeling nothing, risking nothing, while the Bible on their laps repeats its warning thirty-six times. The Egypt-logic cuts deeper still: you were strangers. You did not earn your birthplace. The accident of being born inside the gates is not a merit, and a Christian who treats it as one has forgotten the entire grammar of grace. The prophets judged nations, not only individuals, by what happened to the widow, the orphan, and the sojourner at their gates; to notice that is not conscription of the text, it is reading it.

That case is also serious, also biblical. And the half of the church that dismisses it as politics in a robe has not answered it either.

## The double indictment

The verdict falls on both rooms with the same weight, because both committed the same crime against the same verse.

The right has read the stranger out of the Bible it claims to defend. A tribe that will go to war for the inerrancy of Scripture falls strangely silent at one of the Torah's most repeated commands, and the silence is not exegesis. Watch the tell: Romans 13 is quoted at the sojourner with precision and volume, and Leviticus 19 is quoted at no one. A hermeneutic that always lands on the side of your own comfort is not a hermeneutic. It is a mirror.

The left has conscripted the verse into a program it does not contain. "You shall love him as yourself" gets stapled to a platform, fired across a feed, and retired until the next news cycle, a missile with a Scripture reference painted on the side. Watch this tell too: the verse is quoted for policy by people who have never obeyed it in person, no stranger at the table, no name learned, no cost paid, as though love of the sojourner could be delegated to a federal agency and called discipleship. A verse used to win arguments and never to wash feet has also been silenced. It has just been silenced loudly.

Same crime, opposite jerseys. Both tribes took a command addressed to *you* and turned it into a claim about someone else, the government, the other party, the voters who need correcting. I have stood in both rooms. I carried the verse into both as a weapon, and both times I carried it back out unobeyed.

## What is bound, and what is left free

So sort it, what the text binds, and what it leaves to prudence.

Bound, on every Christian conscience, in every political weather: the stranger among you must not be wronged or oppressed. He must receive the same justice as the native. He bears the image of God, which no legal status confers and none revokes. He must be loved, not tolerated, not processed, loved, with the same verb you spend on yourself. And Christ has staked his own honor on how he is received. These are not positions. They are commands, and they survive every election.

Left to prudence: how many a nation admits, by what process, with what enforcement, at what cost against which obligations. That is the sphere Romans 13 assigns to government, and Scripture declines to dictate its details, which is why faithful Christians reading the same Bible land in different places. Disagreement here is legitimate. The brother on the other side of an admissions number is a brother. Excommunicate the other room over a question Scripture left open and you have confused prudence with confession, broken fellowship over a quota.

But see the asymmetry, because neither tribe will say it. The bound part is the treatment of the person. The free part is the policy. A Christian may hold nearly any view of border law and remain faithful, and no view of border law, none, licenses contempt for the man standing in front of you. The policy is debatable. The image of God is not.

## The doors and the borders

The state carries a sword, and Romans 13 says God handed it the hilt. The church carries a towel and sets a table. Nearly every disaster in this debate comes from confusing the two, Christians who want the state to do the church's loving, and Christians who want the church to do the state's gatekeeping. The country's borders are the government's to administer, answerable to God. The church's doors are not the country's borders. Nothing decided in any capital tells a congregation whom to welcome at the door, whose children to feed at the pantry, whose name to learn, whose funeral to stand at. The person in front of you was never a policy question. He is the neighbor of Leviticus 19, and by the word of Christ he may be more.

I keep thinking about how I got in. I walked into a church years ago as a stranger to everything in it, an atheist, fatherless, fluent in contempt, and by every spiritual measure I carried no papers at all. Nobody at that door asked what I could contribute. Peter names the permanent Christian address: "sojourners and exiles" (1 Peter 2:11). And Paul describes the only naturalization that ever mattered to me: "So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God" (Ephesians 2:19). Every Christian in that arguing Bible study was once the stranger in this story. Both halves of the room. All of us let in on someone else's merit, loved before we were vetted.

Five sons eat at my table, and they are listening to how their father talks about strangers. Long after every bill of this decade is amended and forgotten, they will still talk the way I taught them. That is the piece of the border debate I actually control, and it is the piece I will answer for.

Israel was commanded to remember Egypt, you were strangers, and the memory was meant to make oppression impossible. The command closes with a signature, "I am the LORD your God," as if to say: this one is personal to me. The country will decide its policy, as countries do, and Christians will argue it, as Christians may. What no vote can decide is the older question, the one that sat on the table before any border was drawn and will outlast them all, whether the people who were carried in as strangers, loved as natives, and seated at a table they never earned can look at the sojourner and remember the door.
posts.excerpt: Leviticus 19 commands Israel to love the stranger as itself; Romans 13 puts a sword in the hand of the state. Both tribes have claimed one text and silenced the other. What Scripture actually binds in the immigration debate is harder than either side wants, and it is not a policy.

posts.title: The Door We Did Not Walk Through
posts.body:
Read the list slowly, because we have trained ourselves to read it fast. Hungry. Thirsty. A stranger. Naked. Sick. And then the sixth thing, the one the eye skips on its way to the point. "I was in prison and you came to me" (Matthew 25:36). Jesus put six needs in the mouth of the King, hung the final judgment on whether we met them, and the American church built a ministry for five. We run the food pantry. We stock the clothing closet. We keep the hospital rota and the casserole chain and the refugee welcome team, and we run them faithfully, and God sees it. Then the list reaches its last word and something in the collective body goes still. The prison is the one door on the King's own list the church, in the main, declined to walk through.

I am inside the church I am describing. I have kept a visitation list in my desk for fifteen years and no cell block has ever been on it.

Let me be fair to the reasons before I turn on them, because the strongest version is not cruelty. It is justice, and justice is not a small word to concede. Somewhere tonight a mother is lying awake because a man took her daughter and will not give her back, and no amount of pastoral warmth changes the arithmetic of that grief. The person behind the wall is often there because he left a wound in someone still bleeding, and to hurry past the victim on the way to the prisoner is its own quiet cruelty, dressed as compassion. Scripture does not pretend otherwise. It hands the civil authority a sword and says the one who wields it "is God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:4), an avenger who carries out wrath on the wrongdoer. A society that will not restrain the predator has not achieved mercy. It has abandoned the weak to the strong and called its cowardice love. Public safety is a real good. Desert is a real category. The blood of the innocent has a real voice, and it cries from the ground, and God is the one who taught it to cry. Any honest word about the prison has to begin by granting all of that without a flinch, or it forfeits the right to be heard by anyone who has buried someone.

So here is the claim, stated before it is earned, and it does not require softening a single thing I just conceded. **The church did not skip the prison because it weighed the demands of justice and found visitation wanting. It skipped the prison because it quietly decided that some image-bearers are disposable, adopted the state's verdict as its own, and built a gospel in which grace is what I receive and desert is what they get, which is the precise inversion of the thing we claim to preach.** You can hold the sword and still remember the man it fell on. We stopped remembering.

## The one need we agreed to outsource

Notice what makes the prison different from the other five, because the difference is the whole confession.

Hunger is nobody's fault in a way that stains the hungry. Sickness carries no charge sheet. The stranger at the border may frighten us, but we do not think he earned his exile by his own hand. The prisoner is the only person on Jesus's list whose need we can tell ourselves he deserves, and that single word, deserves, is the trapdoor the whole church fell through. Once a person's suffering can be filed under justice served, the obligation to go to him feels not merely optional but faintly wrong, as though a visit were a criticism of the verdict. We do not withhold the casserole from the cancer patient because he brought it on himself. We withhold ourselves from the prisoner because we have decided he did, and that the deciding settles the matter of whether Christ meant him too.

But read the King's sentence again and find the exemption. It is not there. He does not say I was wrongfully in prison and you came to me. He does not sort the cell block into the framed and the guilty and assign the visit only to the innocent. He says prison, flatly, the institution and everyone in it, and then he says the thing that should have ended the argument forever: "as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40). There is an honest scholarly question about who the brothers are, whether Jesus meant the poor and imprisoned as such, or his own messengers who landed in chains for carrying his name. Grant the narrower reading its full weight. It still does not rescue us, because a second command sits outside the debate entirely, addressed to the whole church with no interpretive escape hatch. "Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body" (Hebrews 13:3). As though in prison with them. Not as a patron mailing a tract through the bars. As a fellow member of one body, whose own freedom is the accident and whose neighbor's chains could have been his.

## A young institution and an old forgetting

Push the history back, because the reflex feels ancient and is not.

The prison as we know it, the vast machinery of cells and sentences and men warehoused by the thousand, is a young thing, barely two centuries old. It was invented in part by Christians who believed that a man left alone with a Bible and his own conscience would be driven to repentance, which is why they gave it a name built from the word penitence and called it a penitentiary. The theory was tender and the result was catastrophic, as tender theories often are, but notice what the founders assumed and we forgot. They built the whole cruel apparatus on the premise that the man inside was not finished, not disposable, still a candidate for the mercy of God. We kept their walls and lost their premise. We inherited the institution and mislaid the anthropology that was supposed to haunt it.

And the institution grew. The United States now imprisons more of its own people than almost any nation on earth, a fact so large it has become invisible, the way a wall goes invisible to the people behind it and the people in front of it alike. A whole population, disproportionately poor and disproportionately Black, lives inside a structure the church drives past without a turn of the head. This is not a partisan observation. The scale is simply a fact, and a fact of that size, met by a church of this size with near silence, is not an oversight. It is a theology, unspoken and therefore never examined. We have decided, without ever saying it aloud in a sentence we would have to defend, that these are not our people.

Here is where the diagnosis has to cut inward or it is worthless. When I ask why I never built the prison ministry, the honest answer is not that I ran out of Tuesdays. It is that the prisoner frightened me and did not flatter me. The food pantry photographs well. The hospital visit makes me feel like a pastor. The cell block offers nothing to my sense of myself except the disquiet of standing in front of a man I have been taught to fear and failing to find, in his face, the monster the fear requires. As long as I did not go, I could keep believing there were two kinds of people, and that I knew which kind I was.

## The gospel was written in a jail

Set the church's forgetting next to its own book, and the distance is almost unbearable.

The faith we are protecting from the prisoner was founded by one. Strip away the stained glass and look at what happened: an itinerant preacher was arrested on a religious charge, handed to the occupying state, condemned in a night court, and executed between two convicts by the approved method for insurrectionists and slaves. The central image of Christianity is a state execution. The Lord the church worships spent his last night in custody. And when he stood up in his hometown synagogue to say in one sentence what he had come to do, he reached for the prophet and read this: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed" (Luke 4:18). He was quoting Isaiah, who had said it centuries before with the door itself in view, anointed "to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound" (Isaiah 61:1). The opening of the prison. That phrase is in the job description Jesus read over his own ministry, out loud, and then rolled up the scroll and said today it is fulfilled.

Run the concordance and the pattern will not let go. Joseph interprets dreams in a cell. John the Baptist loses his head in Herod's dungeon. Peter is sprung from chains by an angel. Paul writes half the letters we read on Sunday from custody, and calls himself, without embarrassment, a prisoner of Christ Jesus. The book the church holds up as its charter was in no small part composed behind bars, addressed to a movement whose leaders kept ending up there, worshiping a Savior the authorities had filed under executed. A church that cannot find its way to the jailhouse has lost the ability to recognize its own family album.

## Not softer than justice, deeper

Now the ditch on the other side, because it is real and people leap into it with relief.

There is a way of talking about the prison that dissolves the victim, that treats every sentence as an injustice and every offender as a misunderstood innocent, that hears blood crying from the ground and answers with a sociology lecture. That is not the gospel either. That is sentiment with the cross removed, and it insults the very people it pretends to champion, because it cannot tell the murdered daughter's mother anything true. The recovery I am after does not require pretending that guilt is a fiction or that safety does not matter or that the man who did the terrible thing did not do it. It requires something harder than leniency and older than either party's slogan: the conviction that a person can be genuinely guilty and still be genuinely Christ's concern, that the same man can owe a debt to the society he wronged and bear the image of the God who made him, and that the second fact does not cancel the first but forbids us from ever using the first to erase the second.

This is the both/and the tribes cannot hold. One half keeps the justice and loses the man, locks the door, throws away the key, calls the throwing righteousness, and never once asks what Christ asks of the free toward the bound. The other half keeps the man and loses the justice, waves away the wound in the victim, romanticizes the offender, and offers a mercy so cheap it costs no one anything and therefore heals no one. Both halves are the same lie wearing opposite jerseys: the refusal to hold two true things at the cost of holding them. Christ held them. He told the woman caught in adultery both go and sin no more, the pardon and the verdict in a single breath, and neither word softened the other. He did not choose between mercy and truth. He was the place they met.

So what does the deeper thing actually ask, at the scale where an ordinary Christian lives? Not the overhaul of a penal system by people with no power over it, though the Christian may work for that too. It asks the smaller and more terrifying thing the King already named. Go. Remember the man as though you were the one in the cell, because on any honest accounting of your own heart the difference between you and him is not the size you have made it. Learn a name. Sit across a table from someone the whole world has agreed to file under his worst day, and let the agreement break on the fact of his face. Hebrews does not command the church to reform the prison. It commands the church to remember the prisoner, and remembering, in the Bible, is never a mood. It is a movement of the body toward the one remembered. God remembered Noah and the waters went down. God remembered his covenant and the people came out. To remember, in this book, is to show up.

## The list still has six things on it

The judgment scene ends and the King does not revise the list.

He does not, on reflection, drop the sixth item as too much to ask of a busy church in a frightened country. He leaves it standing where he put it, next to the bread and the water and the coat, as though visiting a prisoner were as plain a Christian duty as feeding a hungry man, which, in his accounting, is exactly what it is. The uncomfortable arithmetic of Matthew 25 is that he measures the nations by the least glamorous mercies, and he puts the prison among them on purpose. He knew we would prefer a gospel of five needs. He gave us six.

I have preached this passage for fifteen years and left the sixth clause to hang in the air unillustrated, and I know now what that omission was. It was not a scheduling problem. It was a refusal, mine and my congregation's together, to believe that the man behind the wall was included in the word whosoever we sing about so freely. We drew a line the King did not draw, exactly where it cost us nothing and comforted us most, around the people we were already afraid of. Then we called the line prudence and went back to the food pantry, which is good work, and easier work, and does not make us stand in front of anything that could indict us.

The mother whose daughter is not coming back is owed justice, and the man who took her is owed the truth about what he did, and neither of those debts is canceled by a single word I have written. But there is a third fact standing in the room with those two, and the church agreed a long time ago to pretend it was not there. Christ is in the prison. He said so, in the plainest sentence he ever spoke about the last day, and he did not add a clause excusing us from the one visit that frightened us most. The door is still on the list. It has been on the list the whole time. We are the ones who walked past it, year after year, telling ourselves the King could not possibly have meant that one, and he stood on the other side of it, waiting, filed under the worst thing anyone ever did.
posts.excerpt: Jesus put six needs in the mouth of the King and the church built a ministry for five. We run the food pantry and the clothing closet and the hospital list, and then we reach the sixth item and go quiet. A reckoning with punishment, mercy, and the image of God behind the wall.

posts.title: Why the Church Must Speak About Housing
posts.body: Housing is not just an economic issue. It is a justice issue. The church must speak prophetically about the housing crisis and work for solutions. Everyone deserves safe, affordable housing. This is not negotiable.

posts.title: What We Owe the Ones Who Come After
posts.body: We are accountable not just for our own generation but for those who come after us. Climate change, economic injustice, and systemic racism will be inherited by our children. Justice requires that we work to leave them a better world.

posts.title: The Long Arc
posts.body: The arc of history is long, but it bends toward justice. The church is called to bend it. This is not naive optimism. It is faithful hope rooted in the God who is working toward redemption. The prophets knew this. So must we.
