As a pastor I have sat across from people who built a faith answerable to nothing but their own conscience, and who were, for a season, the freest people I knew, and then the floor opened. A death. A diagnosis. A marriage that came apart in the hand. And what I have watched, again and again, is the discovery that there is nothing to say to oneself that one has not already generated oneself, no word from outside the grief to contradict it. The self had been enthroned, and then the self was the thing in ruins, and a king cannot rescue himself from inside his own collapsed house. What comes back to such people, when it comes, is rarely certainty. It is the relief of being under something again, a word they did not write, cannot revise, and are therefore, for the first time, able to trust on the night their own heart turns liar.

We thought authority was the cage and authenticity was the open door. We had it backwards. The sovereign self is the smallest room in the world, and its only window faces inward. When the dark comes, it comes for everyone; it is coming for me, and for you, there is no one in that room but you and a voice you can no longer trust.

Authority was never the cage.

It was the hand reaching in.

The trade is still on offer, in language so kind it does not sound like a serpent: *be true to yourself, trust your heart, your experience is the final word.* The answer the church owes the age is not contempt, because the longing underneath the trade is real, people want to be free, and they have been crushed by counterfeit authorities that deserved to fall. But the answer is still no. Not the no of a slammed door. The no of a physician to a patient who has begun to trust the disease.

I traded it once myself, at nineteen, for a self that would answer to nothing and no one. It took me years to learn what I had actually bought. A god who only ever agrees with me is not a god. He is a mirror with my own face in it. And I had been on my knees the whole time, in the dark, to me.
posts.excerpt: Somewhere in the last few decades a sentence changed shape in the Christian mouth. The old sentence was 'the Bible says.' The new one is 'I feel like God is.' We thought we were gaining freedom. We were changing kings.

posts.title: When Forgiveness Only Flows One Way
posts.body:
Ask most people who quote it what cheap grace means, and they will tell you it is what happens when a church makes salvation too easy. Forgiveness without repentance. The altar call with no aftermath. They are right, and they have aimed it at exactly one target.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote the phrase in 1937, in a Germany where most of the church had already made its peace with a monster. *Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of our church.* He put it in *The Cost of Discipleship* and defined it with a surgeon's precision: grace without discipleship, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ living and incarnate. The preaching of forgiveness that requires no repentance. Grace, he said, that we bestow on ourselves. It cost the recipient nothing, and, in our telling, cost the giver nothing either, though in fact it cost God his Son.

We have done a strange thing with that warning. We decided it belongs to the right.

The claim, before any of the evidence. **Cheap grace is not a conservative problem the left gets to diagnose from a safe distance. The left has a cheap grace of its own, boundless mercy for allies, frozen wrath for enemies, forgiveness handed out as tribal currency, and it is harder to see precisely because it does not look like grace at all. It looks like justice.** Once you see it, you cannot quote Bonhoeffer the same way again. And I am not pointing across the room. I am the one writing checks with it.

## What cheap grace actually meant in the room Bonhoeffer wrote it

Grant the obvious first, because the strong version of an argument is the only one worth making.

There is a recognizable American cheap grace, and it does live most comfortably on the conservative side of the room. The eternal-security teaching that curdles into a license. The businessman forgiven on Sunday for what he will repeat on Monday, assured it does not matter because grace. The man who treats the blood of Christ as a transaction that cleared his account and changed nothing, got the fire insurance and went home. Bonhoeffer's words land on that like a hammer, and the progressive Christian who aims them there is not wrong.

But the slogan-version of Bonhoeffer has eaten the man, so go back to the room he was actually standing in.

By 1937 the German Protestant church had largely folded itself into the Reich. The German Christians, the *Deutsche Christen*, had decided that Hitler's Germany was a fresh revelation of God's will in history, that the nation was bending toward something glorious, and that the church's job was to align with the movement of the moment. Against them stood the Confessing Church, which in the Barmen Declaration of 1934, drafted largely by Karl Barth, said the one thing the age would not permit: that Jesus Christ, not the spirit of the times, is the one Word the church is bound to hear. Bonhoeffer was Confessing Church, though, to keep the record clean, he was not himself a signatory at Barmen.

His charge of cheap grace was never first about lazy individuals getting saved without changing. **It was an indictment of a whole church that had granted itself absolution for its alignment, that had decided, because it stood with the right cause at the right moment, that it was no longer the thing in need of repentance.** The Confessing Church was a minority. It lost most of its public fights. Bonhoeffer ended in a Gestapo cell. The lesson he paid for is the one we turned into a bumper sticker: a church can sell grace cheap not only by forgiving too easily, but by aligning so confidently with a cause that it forgets it is still in the dock.

## The left's cheap grace: mercy for the distant, wrath for the man in front of you

Hold that, and the left's version comes into focus.

Cheap grace on the left is forgiveness extended in the abstract to everyone except the people actually standing in front of you. It flows freely toward the distant and the categorical, the marginalized in general, the oppressed as a class, the sympathetic figure who confirms your politics, and freezes solid toward the particular sinner whose sin is the wrong kind. It is the warmest possible language about mercy attached to the most merciless possible practice toward the unforgiven.

We keep a grace for victims and a wrath for villains, we are very confident about which is which, and we call the wrath justice so we never have to notice that we have only moved the cheapness to the other hand. The right gives cheap grace to itself. The left gives cheap grace to its allies and no grace at all to its enemies. Both have made grace cheap. They have simply chosen different people to be cheap toward.

Watch the second move, because it is subtler, and it is mine. Cheap grace on the left is also grace bestowed on the self through identification with the right cause. Bonhoeffer's exact charge was that cheap grace is the grace we bestow on ourselves, and the progressive does this not by saying *I am forgiven, so I can do as I please*, but by saying, underneath, *I am on the right side, so I am not the problem*. The cause launders the conscience. To stand with the oppressed becomes a way of standing outside the dock, of being, by virtue of my politics, one of the good ones, the awake ones, the ones the future will thank. And once I am one of the good ones, the call to repent quietly excuses me, because repentance is for the captured and the complicit, the people who have not yet seen what I have seen.

I have absolved myself by my alignment. That is grace without the cross. That is the exact thing Bonhoeffer named, wearing the one costume he did not live to see it wear.

## The tell is the same in both hands: forgiveness that costs the forgiver nothing

The signature of cheap grace, left or right, never changes. It is a forgiveness that costs the forgiver nothing.

Real grace is expensive to the one who extends it. It cost God the cross. It costs me, when I extend it, the surrender of my right to be the one who was wronged, the death of my satisfaction in someone else's guilt. *Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors.* The *as* is a hinge and a horror, because it ties the mercy I receive to the mercy I am willing to spend.

Then there is the parable nobody wants attached to their politics. A servant is forgiven ten thousand talents, a debt no laborer could clear in a hundred lifetimes, and walks straight out of his own pardon to seize a man who owes him a hundred denarii by the throat, demanding payment, deaf to the very plea he had just made and been granted (Matthew 18:23–35). The king's verdict is the most frightening sentence in the chapter: should you not have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you.

The horror of the parable is not that the servant was a hypocrite. **It is that he could not feel the contradiction.** He held an erased fortune in one hand and throttled a man over pennies with the other, and the two never met in his conscience, because he had filed the man he was choking under a different category than the one he himself had been forgiven under. That is the precise mechanism of cheap grace on the left. I have throttled men over pennies while carrying a forgiven fortune. I have done it in the name of justice, which is the most respectable way to do it.

## Forgiveness and accountability are not opponents, the cross holds them together

Here the theology has to slow down, because the cheap answer is to say *the left should just forgive more*, and that answer is shallow, and Bonhoeffer would have hated it.

The harder truth is that forgiveness and accountability are not two values to be balanced against each other. They are a single act the cross holds together, and we keep tearing it in half and grabbing the half that flatters us.

Miroslav Volf, a Croatian theologian, wrote *Exclusion and Embrace* in 1996 out of the wreckage of the Balkan wars, out of being asked by Jürgen Moltmann whether he could embrace a *četnik*, one of the Serbian fighters who had burned his people's villages. Volf's argument is not that we forgive instead of pursuing justice. It is that the will to embrace the other must precede the judgment about the other, or the judgment becomes a weapon and the self becomes God. We sin, Volf says, not first by hating the wicked but by drawing the boundary of the human community to leave the enemy outside it, so that the violence we then do feels like cleansing. Exclusion comes dressed as righteousness. It always has.

And the embrace Volf calls for is not cheap. It does not pretend the *četnik* did nothing. It does not bury the burned village. It makes room, while the wound is still open, for the one who caused it. That is the costliest thing a wounded person can do, and Volf insists it is the only thing the crucified God actually models, because on the cross God embraced the very humanity that was killing him.

Reinhold Niebuhr saw the political form of the same danger a generation earlier, and he saw it inside his own side. Niebuhr was a man of the left, a socialist, a labor preacher in industrial Detroit before he was anything else, and the burden of his work, from *Moral Man and Immoral Society* in 1932 onward, was to warn his own people about the self-righteousness that hides inside a just cause. The groups most certain of their own virtue, he argued, are the most dangerous, because they baptize their will to power as the will of God and lose the one thing that might restrain them: the knowledge that they too stand under judgment. **A movement that cannot imagine its own sin has already become the thing it opposes.** Niebuhr was not telling the left to abandon justice; he spent his life pursuing it. He was telling the left the truth it least wanted to hear. He could have been writing to a congregation. He was, in fact, writing to me.

Walter Brueggemann pushes it one layer further down, into the language we pray. Brueggemann spent a career arguing that prophetic imagination is not the same as moral certainty, that the prophets did not stand over Israel as the righteous over the wicked but stood *inside* the people, grieving a sin they shared. A prophetic posture can curdle into a permanent indictment of everyone but the prophet. And his reading of the Psalms keeps open a door we usually want shut: the imprecatory psalms, the ones that howl *break their teeth, O God*, are not models for our wrath but the place we are commanded to *bring* it, handed up to God, surrendered to the only One who can judge without sin, instead of executed by our own hand. The rage is real. The rage is even prayed. But it is prayed *to* God, which means it is taken *out of* my hands. That is the whole point of *Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord* (Romans 12:19). Paul does not say the debt is forgiven into thin air. He says I do not get to be the collector, and then he says the unbearable next thing. If your enemy is hungry, feed him (Romans 12:20–21). I had to give up the wrath and then hand the enemy bread.

## The hinge: I do not get to keep an enemy I am allowed to despise

So set the demand down without decoration.

Costly grace, turned left, looks like extending real forgiveness to the people my politics has taught me to hate. Not the abstract enemy. The actual one. The relative who voted the way that frightens me. The pastor whose theology I find cruel. The figure from the past whose statue came down, and whether or not the statue should have come down, the question of whether I can pray *Father, forgive him* without my teeth grinding is a different question, a more revealing one, and the harder of the two.

The cross took away my permission to keep an enemy I am allowed to despise without limit. Jesus did not say love your neighbor and feel however you like about your enemy. He said *love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you* (Luke 6:27–28), and he said it is no great thing to love those who love you, even sinners manage that, even the tax collectors, even the people on the right side of history manage to love the others on the right side of history. **The test of grace was never the ally. It was always the enemy.**

And there is one more demand, the one we never preach, because it cuts the wrong direction. We assume the burden of reconciliation falls on the offender, that he must come contrite and earn his way back before we owe him anything. Jesus puts the burden somewhere that should stop us cold. *If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there and go. First be reconciled to your brother* (Matthew 5:23–24). Not: if you have something against him. If *he* has something against *you*. The worshiper is sent away from the altar not to collect a debt but to settle one he may not even think he owes.

Be fair to the fear underneath the left's version, because it is a real and holy fear: that forgiveness has been weaponized by the powerful to silence the wounded, that *just forgive and move on* has been said to abused women and exploited workers and a whole race of people as a way of protecting the abuser and burying the wound. That fear is earned. The church has used a counterfeit grace to muzzle real pain, and the rage against that counterfeit is closer to God than the counterfeit was. Bonhoeffer himself stood with the persecuted Jews of Germany while most of the church looked for a way to call its silence prudence. But the answer to a grace that protects the powerful is not a grace that merely changes which people get protected. The answer is costly grace, which protects no one from the truth, abuser or avenger, names the sin in full, refuses to bury the wound, and still, with the wound open, opens a door the offender did not earn.

## The elder brother is the one left outside

There is an older brother in one of the parables who never gets the grace, and it is because he refuses it, not because it was withheld.

The prodigal comes home and the father runs (Luke 15). The robe, the ring, the calf, the music, all of it lands on the son who burned the inheritance in a far country, and the elder brother stands out in the field and will not come in. His complaint is not wrong on the facts. He really did stay. He really did work. The younger son really did squander everything. Every line of his grievance is true, and the truth of it is exactly what hardens him, because he built his whole standing on being the one who did it right, and a father who throws a feast for the one who did it wrong has demolished the economy he lived by. He cannot enter the joy without surrendering his ledger.

Here is the part that should stop every progressive Christian, and me first. The elder brother is the one the story leaves outside. Not the sinner. The righteous one. The one who was, by every metric, on the correct side, and who stayed there in the dark because the grace shown to his enemy was an offense he would not forgive. I have stood in that field. I have called it justice. The father came out and pleaded with him too, which is the mercy in it, but the parable does not tell us whether he went in.

So I will keep quoting Bonhoeffer. I am only trying to stop quoting him as a weapon and start hearing him as a mirror, the way he wrote it, the way he died for it, hanged at Flossenbürg on the ninth of April, 1945, two weeks before the Americans reached the camp, on the personal order of a regime that wanted him gone before the end it could already see. He had a chance to stay safe in New York in 1939 and came back to Germany to share the fate of his people. He paid for the costly grace he preached, in full, in his own body, to a country that had earned none of it. That is why his words still cut. Most of us are quoting a martyr to indict the other side while keeping, in our own left hand, the very thing he died saying was the enemy of the church.

I do not get to keep the enemy. That is the part I keep trying to negotiate around. I will extend grace to the distant and the categorical all day, because it costs me nothing and confirms my standing among the people whose approval I want. The grace that costs is the grace I owe the man across the table whose politics frightens me, the one I have filed under *villain* so I never have to file him under *neighbor*, the one whose hunger I am commanded to feed before I have finished deciding whether he deserves to eat.

Cheap grace has a left hand. I know, because I have been writing checks with it for years, and the signature at the bottom is my own.
posts.excerpt: Bonhoeffer's cheap grace is usually aimed at the easy-believism of the right. But the left has a cheap grace of its own, endless mercy for allies, cold wrath for enemies, and it is harder to see because it does not look like grace. It looks like justice.

posts.title: Should a Christian Follow a Political Party?
posts.body:
Ask yourself one question about your strongest political conviction, and notice how hard it is to answer honestly. Not *is it true.* That is the easy question, and it lets you off the hook. The hard question is *how did I come to hold it.* Trace it back far enough and you reach a fork. At that fork you either reasoned your way to the position from something prior, or you received it, pre-formed, ready to wear, from a tribe whose approval you needed and whose disapproval you feared. Be honest about which. Most of what I believe, when I trace it, I caught the way you catch an accent: by living among people who already had it.

That is the subject. Not whether your politics are right. Whether they are yours.

We talk constantly about the church captured by the political right. The pulpit that became a precinct. The cross fused to the flag, the sanctuary that learned to applaud a man before it would weep over a sin. That capture is real, I have named it before, and I will name it again, because it is killing the witness of the American church in front of a world that already suspected we never meant any of it. The other capture gets almost none of the attention. Put it on the table first.

**Capture is not a partisan event. It is a human one. And the left's version is more dangerous precisely because the left believes it is the side that thinks for itself.** The herd that is certain it is not a herd is the most thoroughly herded of all, because it has disabled the one alarm that might have warned it.

So this is not a piece about them. It is a piece about us. *Us* is the harder word.

## Your brain was built to outsource this

The precision matters here, because precision is where the mercy hides.

Jonathan Haidt, in *The Righteous Mind* (2012), gathered the research showing that moral reasoning runs mostly backward. We arrive at a judgment by fast intuition, then hire reasons after the fact, like a press secretary defending a decision the boss already made. And the intuitions are tuned by the group. We are, Haidt argued, *groupish*: built to bind ourselves into moral teams and to feel the team's enemies as not merely wrong but unclean.

This is not a defect in a few weak minds. It is the standard wiring of every mind, mine included. And the spiritual danger is exactly this: the binding feels, from the inside, identical to conviction. The man who has handed his conscience to his tribe does not experience it as handing anything over. He experiences it as having finally seen clearly.

**The takeover is invisible to the one taken over. That is what makes it a capture and not a choice.**

Consider what the party offers, and I mean the whole apparatus, the consensus of the people you cannot bear to disappoint. It offers to think for you about questions you have never studied. You will hold a fervent opinion about a policy you could not explain for ninety seconds, a foreign war you could not find on a map, a person you have never met. And the opinion arrives with the weight of something you earned at cost, when in fact you only absorbed the ambient certainty of your people. That is a tremendous relief. Thinking is slow and lonely. Belonging is warm and instant. The party does your moral homework and hands it back with your name on it, and the gratitude you feel for being spared the labor, you mistake for conviction.

## When the faith stops judging the politics

There is an older name for what the party has become.

In 1967 the sociologist Robert Bellah published "Civil Religion in America," not as a critic but as a diagnostician. He noticed the nation had its own gods and scriptures, its martyrs and high holy days, an entire apparatus of the sacred running underneath the religion of the churches and often louder than it. Bellah thought a civil religion could even be a restraining good. But he saw the hazard, and the hazard is the whole point: when the civil faith and the church faith fuse, the church has nothing left to say to the nation that the nation did not already believe about itself. The sacred canopy becomes a mirror. And a mirror cannot rebuke you. It can only show you, in flattering light, the face you brought to it.

Watch how the fusion happens, because it never announces itself. You begin with a real conviction, that the poor are neglected, the stranger despised, the church complicit in cruelties it still will not name, and on much of this you are right, biblically and gloriously right, and the prophets were saying it before your party was born. But somewhere in the defending of it, the root gets swapped while the flower keeps its color. You held the conviction because the God who set his image in every person commands it. Now you hold it because it is what decent, forward-looking people believe, and you have grown afraid of being mistaken for the other kind.

The conviction stays. Its root is cut. And a conviction cut from its root keeps its color for a while, the way a cut flower does, and then it dies, without your noticing, in the very vase you were so proud to set it in. **The faith was supposed to judge the politics. Now the politics tells the faith what it is allowed to feel.**

## The church that had nothing left to say no with

And then comes the part that should frighten anyone who follows a crucified Lord. A conscience you have outsourced cannot be recalled when the party goes wrong.

This is the lesson of the German church in the 1930s, and it is the lesson precisely because the men who failed it were not monsters. When the National Socialists took power in 1933, a movement rose inside the Protestant church calling itself the *Deutsche Christen*, the German Christians. They were not a fringe. They won church elections. They wanted a Christianity scrubbed of its Jewish roots and aligned with the blood and soil of the *Volk*, a faith that would bless the new order and crown the *Führer* as God's gift to the nation. They thought they were being relevant. They thought they were reading the moment.

Against them a remnant formed the Confessing Church, and in May 1934, at Barmen, they issued a declaration drafted largely by the theologian Karl Barth. It said one thing with terrible clarity: Jesus Christ is the one Word of God the church must hear and obey in life and in death, and the church will not recognize any other event, power, or figure as a second source of its proclamation alongside that one Word. That was not abstract theology. It was a refusal, a church drawing the line the German Christians could not draw. The state's ideology will not become our creed. The *Volk* is not our gospel. The *Führer* is not our Word. (Dietrich Bonhoeffer stood with the Confessing Church and helped shape its resistance, though he was not himself among the Barmen signatories; the line he kept cost him his life on a scaffold at Flossenbürg in April 1945, weeks before the war's end.)

The German Christians could not draw that line because they had nothing left to draw it with. They had handed their conscience to the nation years earlier, in a thousand small surrenders, and when the nation finally demanded the unthinkable there was no conscience standing outside the nation to judge it. The faculty had atrophied from disuse. They were not, most of them, evil men. They were captured men, and a captured man cannot resist his captor, because resistance requires a self that is not owned, and they had signed theirs away.

I am not comparing any American party to the Nazis. Hear that plainly, because it is the lazy reading and I refuse it. I am saying the mechanism is identical at every scale, that the same atrophy happens in a Michigan suburb as in a Berlin parish, only quieter, lower stakes, the same lost faculty. **The conscience you outsource for small things will not be there for the large ones. The muscle you never use does not come back when you need it.**

## The right made the identical mistake, with a mailing list

Now I have to turn the knife on my own tribe's mirror image, because if I do not, this whole essay is a cheap shot wearing a clerical collar.

The right made the same error, and it made it in public. In 1979 Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority, and in its own telling the move was not a surrender of the faith to a party. It was a rescue of the nation by the faith. But what actually happened across the decades that followed is that a platform learned to set the boundaries of the Christian conscience. A voter guide began to function as a catechism. A man's standing in the kingdom got measured by his standing in a coalition. The cross was asked to ratify a politics it was never consulted on.

The German Christians fused the faith to the *Volk*. A great deal of American religion fused it to a party and a flag. The direction differs. The idolatry is identical. Both took a human arrangement, a movement, a nation, a coalition, and seated it on the throne where Christ alone may sit. Barth would have recognized the right's version on sight, because it is the *Deutsche Christen* error in English.

The left simply tells the same lie in a different accent, and prides itself on being too enlightened to lie at all. That self-congratulation is not a defense against the capture. It is the capture's most effective cover, because a man who is certain he is immune never checks.

## Scripture is not sentimental about the crowd

We have sentimentalized the word *community* until it means only warmth. The Bible is warier of the crowd than we are, and we have edited the wariness out of our reading.

Exodus 23:2 says it without decoration: do not follow the crowd into wrongdoing. The Hebrew is blunter than our translations, do not go after a multitude to do evil. It is a commandment, set down in the middle of the law about courts and justice, and it assumes the most ordinary fact about us: that we will do in a crowd what we would never do alone, and feel righteous doing it because everyone around us is doing it too. The crowd is not a neutral container for conviction. It is a current, a pressure, a thing that pulls, and the law has to *command* us to stand against it, because standing against it is not natural. The herd is the default. The conscience is the exception, and it has to be commanded into being.

Paul says it again in the key of the new covenant. Do not be conformed to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind (Romans 12:2). We have read that a thousand times as a warning against the obvious vices. But conformity is rarely a vice you choose. The Greek is *syschematizo*, do not let yourself be pressed into the world's mold, and a mold does not ask permission. The renewing of the mind is the slow, lonely work of recovering a conscience that answers to God before it answers to your people, and it cannot be done in a crowd, because the crowd is the thing it has to be done against. The world that presses us into its shape now is not the world of the old sermons, of liquor and dice. It is the world of the people we love and admire and cannot bear to lose, which is the only world that has ever had the power to shape anyone.

Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon, in *Resident Aliens* (1989), named what the church forgot when it became chaplain to whichever order it preferred. The church is not a department of the nation's moral life, a values-supplier for one party or the other. It is a colony, an outpost of a different country, with a different citizenship and a different Lord, living in the empire as resident aliens, loyal in every lawful thing and bought by no one. The moment the church becomes the religious wing of a political movement, left or right, it stops being a colony and becomes a constituency. And a constituency exists to be counted, not to be a conscience. Lesslie Newbigin, who gave forty years to India as a missionary and came home to a Britain that had quietly stopped believing, said the same in another register: the gospel is not the chaplain of any culture's project but a rival announcement, a different account of what is finally real. A church that loses its nerve to be different has nothing left to offer the culture but agreement. Agreement is not witness. Agreement is the sound a mirror makes.

This is why the early church could say the sentence that founded its whole posture toward power. Ordered to stop preaching, Peter answered: we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Not God in addition to men. Not God once we have checked with the coalition. God *rather than* men, when the two collide, because there is an authority that stands outside every human authority and judges it, and a church that has lost access to it has nothing left to obey but the room. The book of Revelation pressed the same blade against the same wound. The beast of Revelation 13 is no cartoon. It is the political order divinized, the state demanding not merely your taxes and obedience but your worship, the mark that says you may not buy or sell, may not belong, may not eat, unless you bow. John wrote it to a church being asked to drop a pinch of incense on the emperor's altar and call it a formality. It was never a formality. It was a question about who owns your conscience.

## One man at a window

Set against all of it is one man at a window.

Daniel kept a window open toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day toward a city that no longer existed, in defiance of a law signed by a king he served loyally in every lawful thing (Daniel 6:10). He was not a rebel. He was the best administrator the empire had, the man the king trusted with the realm, and there is no record of him refusing a single lawful thing the empire ever asked. But there was a window in him that opened toward an authority higher than the empire, and when the empire and that authority collided, the window decided. He had not outsourced the window.

And before Daniel there were three men in chapter three who would not bow to the golden image when the whole assembly fell on its face at the sound of the music, who stood while everyone they knew knelt, who told the most powerful man on earth that their God was able to deliver them, but that even if he did not, even then, they would not serve the king's gods or worship the image (Daniel 3:17–18). *Even if he does not.* That is the sentence the captured conscience can never say, because the captured conscience has already decided belonging is survival. These men had decided belonging to God was survival, and the furnace was only the weather.

We have closed the window. We have bricked it over with the consensus of our people, hung a curtain of righteousness across the brick, and we pray now toward the party, three times a day, and call it faith. We have heard the music and knelt with the assembly and told ourselves that kneeling is humility, when it was only fear wearing humility's coat.

So how do you tell whether you have a conscience or a subscription? I have found one test that does not lie, and it is the one I least want to take. Name the issue on which you disagree with your own side. Not a safe one, not a matter of tone or tactics where the disagreement still flatters you as the reasonable one in the room. A real one. A place where the people whose respect you need would be genuinely disappointed in you, where you would pay a price, lose a little standing, get the look. If you cannot name one, if your conscience and your tribe's platform are a perfect, seamless overlay with no daylight anywhere between them, then you do not have a conscience on these matters. You have a membership. And a membership is not the same as a soul, though it is far more comfortable, and it never once keeps you up at night.

I do not exempt myself from a word of this. I have caught myself reaching for an opinion I had not earned, defending a position because my people held it and the alternative would have cost me a table I wanted to keep my seat at. I have closed my own window and prayed toward the consensus and felt the warmth of the crowd at my back and named the warmth courage. The frightening thing is how good it felt, how much it felt like conviction, like bravery even, while it was the precise opposite. While it was the surrender itself, dressed as resistance to surrender.

The test is never the easy disagreement. The test is the moment your own side asks you to call evil good, to cheer something, excuse someone, despise a category of person, bury a truth that is inconvenient to the cause, and you have to find out whether you have any conscience left that can say no to your own people. Most of us have never tried. We have never once disappointed our tribe on a thing that mattered to it, and we have mistaken that perfect record of agreement for integrity, when it is the surest evidence the capture is complete.

Keep the window open. It is the loneliest discipline in the Christian life, and it will cost you a seat at some table you wanted, and the lions are not always a metaphor. The men at Barmen lost their pulpits and some of them lost their lives. Daniel lost a night with the lions and counted it cheap.

And the crowd is going to be wrong. Yours and mine. It always has been. That is the whole reason the window faces a different city.
posts.excerpt: We talk about the church captured by the political right. The left's version is harder to see, because the left believes it is the side that thinks for itself. A pastor on the conscience we handed our tribe without ever signing the papers.

posts.title: What Happens After You Deconstruct Your Faith?
posts.body:
The people deconstructing their faith are usually right about why. That is not the line most pastors lead with, so I am leading with it. If you were handed a Christianity that was equal parts Jesus and a voting bloc, that policed your hemline and ignored your hunger, that protected the man behind the pulpit and disbelieved the woman in the pew, that taught you to fear questions because the questions had answers nobody could survive being asked, then the impulse to tear it down is not rebellion. It is closer to repentance. The online deconstruction wave did not invent the wound. It found a microphone for a pain the church had spent decades keeping quiet.

So I am not going to defend the building that hurt you. I have torn one down myself. At nineteen I built an atheism brick by brick to keep God at arm's length, and I defended it the way you defend a house you are afraid to leave. Tearing it down was the most honest thing I had done up to then. I have held the hammer. I still do. This is not a warning from a man who never doubted. It is a report from one who doubted enough to learn that doubt, by itself, builds nothing.

The claim underneath the whole essay. **Faith deconstruction can be the most faithful thing a person does, Jesus deconstructed the Pharisees on purpose and relentlessly, but deconstruction that never rebuilds is not freedom. It is demolition. And the swept, empty house does not stay empty. Something always moves in, and what moves in is rarely kinder than what you evicted.**

## The word meant something, and we lost half of it

Start with the word, because we have forgotten what it was for.

*Deconstruct* is borrowed, and the lender meant something we have misplaced. It comes from Jacques Derrida, the French philosopher, who introduced it in the late 1960s, *Of Grammatology* appeared in 1967, and in his hands it was never destruction. It was a method of reading. A way of taking a text apart to see what it was secretly built on, what it had buried in its own foundations, what it leaned on while pretending it stood on its own. The point of taking the thing apart was to read it more truly, not to leave it in pieces on the floor. Derrida spent his life inside the texts he deconstructed, not in some cleared field beyond them. He was not swinging a wrecking ball. He was a man on his knees in the basement, running his hand along the load-bearing walls.

Somewhere on the road from the seminar room into our group chats, the word lost its second half.

The wave that crested around 2015, the hashtag, the deconstruction podcasts, the exvangelical testimony threads, the entire architecture of people narrating their exit in real time on TikTok, kept the taking-apart and quietly dropped the reading-truly. I want to be careful, because the wound driving all of it was real, and much of it the church spent years hiding. But somewhere the method became a mood. We turned a way of reading into a permanent condition of suspicion, and we called the suspicion freedom.

There is a difference between renovating a house and standing in a field where a house used to be. Both start with demolition. That is the trap.

In the early days the two are indistinguishable, the same walls coming down, the same dust in the same air, the same neighbors asking what on earth you are doing in there. You can be three years into deconstructing your faith and genuinely not know whether you are building something truer or simply tearing down something false and intending to live, from now on, in the open. The dust is identical. Only the intention is different, and intention is invisible, even to yourself. **Especially to yourself.**

## A field is not a home

Here is what I have watched, pastorally, across fifteen years, in people I love.

The demolition feels like clarity for about two years. There is a real exhilaration in it, the relief of putting down a god who was never God, the rush of finally saying the forbidden thing, the company of others swinging their hammers beside you on the same timeline. It is a genuine joy and I will not mock it. But a field is not a home, and a person cannot live in suspicion forever, because suspicion is a posture and not a place.

Suspicion can tell you what to tear down. It cannot tell you what to do on a Tuesday in February when the marriage is hard and the father is dying and you need something to stand on that you did not invent that morning. Suspicion has no Tuesday. So the ones who only deconstructed, who never rebuilt, rarely end up as triumphant free thinkers. They end up tired. They end up with a sophisticated account of everything they no longer believe and no account at all of what they would die for. No one runs on that for long.

The philosophers who thought hardest about doubt knew this, and they were not pastors trying to keep anyone in the pews.

Michael Polanyi, a chemist before he was a philosopher, watched the twentieth century try to ground all knowledge in universal doubt and concluded the project was incoherent. You cannot doubt everything at once. To doubt one thing, he argued in *Personal Knowledge* in 1958, you have to stand on a hundred things you are not doubting at the moment. The man who claims to have suspended all his commitments has only hidden them from himself. There is no view from nowhere. There is no clean field. The mind that believes it has cleared the ground of every belief is standing, without knowing it, on ground it never examined, which is the most dangerous ground there is, because it is load-bearing and unseen.

Alasdair MacIntyre drove the same stake deeper. In *After Virtue*, published in 1981, he argued that human reasoning is not a free-floating faculty that works best stripped of every inherited loyalty. It is tradition-constituted. We think *from somewhere*, inside a story and a community and a set of practices that taught us what the questions even are. A person who imagines he has reasoned his way out of every tradition into pure, unencumbered freedom has merely become fluent in a newer tradition without noticing it is one, usually the thin, dissolving tradition of the late-modern West, which trains its children to believe they have no tradition at all. The unreconstructed deconstruction does not rescue you from this. It delivers you straight into it.

## Doubt always feels braver than belief, and that feeling is rigged

Charles Taylor named the water we are all swimming in.

In *A Secular Age*, in 2007, he described the immanent frame, a way of living in which meaning is generated entirely within history, with nothing breaking in from outside it. We did not choose it. We were born into it the way a fish is born into water. And inside that frame, doubt always feels braver than belief, subtraction always feels more honest than construction, and the person tearing down feels like a truth-teller while the person building feels like a rube who has not yet been disillusioned.

Taylor's point cuts against the feeling. The choice to stop in the empty field is not the neutral, default, grown-up position. **It is itself a faith, a faith in nothing in particular, and it is no less a leap than the one it replaced.** The field is not the absence of a story. The field is a story that tells you to call it an absence.

This is the part the field cannot admit, because the field has a stake in your not knowing it. A faith taken apart and left open does not become a neutral clearing. It gets occupied by whatever is strongest in the neighborhood. The spirit of the age moves in. The anxieties of the feed move in. A new and unexamined orthodoxy moves in, and you will defend it more fiercely than the one you left, precisely because you are sure you have left all orthodoxies behind, which makes the new one invisible and therefore unopposed.

I keep returning to the man in the parable who swept his house clean. Jesus tells it almost as a warning. An unclean spirit goes out of a man, and the man cleans the house, sweeps it, puts it in order, and leaves it empty (Matthew 12:43–45). Empty. And because it is empty, the spirit comes back with seven others more wicked than itself, and the last state of that man is worse than the first. I do not think Jesus is preaching about deconstruction. But the shape of the warning is the shape of our moment. An emptied house does not stay empty. The seven worse tenants do not arrive looking worse. They arrive looking like liberation, like the obvious opinions of decent people, like the only sane way to think, which is exactly how the first set arrived, before you learned what they cost.

We do not get to choose whether we will worship. We only ever choose what.

## The exiles were told to rebuild before they could see the end

The Israelites in exile had every reason to deconstruct.

The temple was rubble, literal rubble, not metaphor, and the theology that had promised *God will never let Jerusalem fall* lay in the ash with it. The certainties of their fathers were gone. If anyone ever earned the right to demolish a faith and live in the open, it was the generation Jeremiah wrote to in 587 before Christ, dragged a thousand miles into Babylon to grieve a God who had apparently lost.

And what does the prophet send them? Not *your old faith was a lie, walk free*. He tells them to build houses and live in them, to plant gardens and eat what they grow, to marry and raise children, to seek the welfare of the very city that holds them captive (Jeremiah 29:5–7). He tells the deconstructed to reconstruct, in exile, with no temple, on foreign soil, before they could possibly see how it ends.

They did not get their old certainties back. They got something better and harder. They got a faith that had passed through the fire and learned to stand without the props, and that faith produced, eventually, the synagogue and the canon and some of the deepest theology Israel ever wrote. None of it would have come if they had refused to build. Read the record: the ones who would not reconstruct assimilated into Babylon and dissolved, and history does not even keep their names.

A century later Nehemiah went back to the actual rubble of the actual walls, and the work of reconstruction had a detail the romance of demolition always forgets. The builders worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 4:17), because there were people invested in keeping the ruins ruined. Rebuilding is contested. Someone always profits from the field staying empty. That is worth knowing before you mistake the resistance you feel for proof you should quit.

There is a counterfeit reconstruction as dangerous as the empty field, and it usually arrives faster. It is the person who tears down the faith that hurt them and immediately rebuilds, on the same foundation, the same kind of certainty pointed the opposite way, the same contempt, the same tribe, the same refusal to be questioned, simply repainted. That is not reconstruction. That is the swept house redecorated for new tenants who are no gentler than the old ones.

## Faithful deconstruction has a model, and it is not Derrida

Jesus deconstructed the Pharisees' system constantly and on purpose.

He took apart their reading of the Sabbath, their fences around the law, their accounting of clean and unclean, their confidence that they could see. He pulled down a religious structure that policed the hemline and ignored the hunger, the original of every counterfeit you were handed, and he did it relentlessly, and the people who loved the old building hated him for it. But he never tore down to leave a field. He tore down to build a temple they could not see yet, raised in three days, made of his own body. **His demolition always had a destination. That is the line between the prophet and the cynic, and it is a thin, sharp line, and most of us have stood on the wrong side of it while feeling most righteous.**

There is a verse that has become the patron saint of everyone caught between the house and the field, and it earns its place. A father brings his suffering son to Jesus and is asked whether he believes. He answers with the truest sentence in the Gospels: "I believe; help my unbelief" (Mark 9:24). Notice what he does not say. He does not say *I have torn down my belief and will live in my unbelief and call it courage*. He does not say *I have resolved my doubt and have no more questions*. He holds both in the same breath, in the same body, and he holds them toward Christ, not in a field at a safe distance, but kneeling in front of the only One who could do anything about either. That is reconstruction in a single line. It is not the end of doubt. It is doubt brought home and given somewhere to stand.

Thomas is the other patron, and the church has slandered him for centuries by calling him a doubter as if doubt were the sin. Thomas said he would not believe the resurrection unless he put his hand in the wounds (John 20:24–29). He wanted evidence. He wanted the demolition of an easy, secondhand faith of people who had not been in the room. Jesus did not rebuke the demand. He walked through a locked door and offered him the wounds. *Put your finger here.* The risen Christ met the deconstruction by handing over the load-bearing wall and saying, test it, lean on it, put your weight where the nails went. Thomas did, and what came out of him was not a field. It was the highest confession in the Gospel: "My Lord and my God." Doubt was not the enemy. Doubt was the way in. But it had to walk all the way to the wounds.

Augustine, who tore down more than most before he built anything, gives the *Confessions*, finished around 397 after Christ, its strange double motion. Every page is an accounting of what he had believed and abandoned: the Manichees, the astrologers, the rhetoric, the ambition. And every page is also a building, a slow construction of praise on the ruin of all of it. He did not deconstruct his way to nothing. He deconstructed his way to God, and the wreckage was the road. "You have made us for yourself," he wrote, "and our heart is restless until it rests in you." That restlessness is the engine. It is the thing the unreconstructed deconstruction tries to medicate by calling the field home, and the field never quiets it, because the field is precisely the absence of the rest the heart was made to find.

Lesslie Newbigin spent forty years as a missionary in India and came home to a Britain that had quietly stopped believing while he was gone. He thought longer than almost anyone about faith in a world that treats doubt as the only honest posture, and his answer, sharpened in *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* in 1989, was that there is no commitment-free standpoint from which to evaluate the faith. Every knower stands somewhere. Every act of knowing rests on things held without proof, trusted in order to see anything at all. The imagined field, where you have cleared away all belief and now reason in pure suspended air, is not humility. It is the proudest illusion the modern world sells, and it sells it cheap. The choice is never between commitment and the absence of commitment. It is only ever between commitments. You are going to build on something. The unreconstructed deconstruction is dishonest exactly there, because it claims to have built on nothing while standing, the whole time, on the floor of an unexamined age.

## What I would say to the one in the dust

Keep tearing down what is false. Do not stop short out of fear.

The half-deconstructed faith, where you have seen the rot but lack the nerve to name it, is its own misery, and I am not sending anyone back into the house that did the harm. Tear out the rot. But decide, while the hammer is still swinging, whether this is renovation or razing. Decide whether there is anything you are tearing *toward* and not only away from. The goal of taking a faith apart was never the taking apart. Derrida knew that, in the basement, on his knees, with his hand on the wall. The goal was to find what was load-bearing, what could actually carry the weight of a life, and to build again on that, and on nothing less.

There is one wall I have found that does not come down no matter how hard I have swung. It is a man on a cross who refused to defend himself, and an empty tomb three days later that I cannot explain away and have spent thirty years trying. Everything else in my faith I have taken apart and rebuilt, some of it more than once, and I expect to do it again before I die. But that wall has held my full weight every time I threw myself against it. It held the weight of my father's absence. It held the night I was certain there was no God. It is still holding.

Church hurt is real. The wounds are real, and the One who carries his own scars into a locked room to be touched is not asking you to pretend otherwise. He is asking you not to die of exposure in a field while you wait for proof you have already been offered.

You can tear everything else down. I have. The field has no roof, and the rain is coming, and it always comes, and a hammer was never a shelter and was never meant to be one.
posts.excerpt: The exvangelical wave got the diagnosis right. The wounds are real and the church earned most of them. But deconstructing your faith and never rebuilding is not freedom, it is an empty house, and empty houses do not stay empty.

posts.title: When History Becomes Your God
posts.body:
Say the phrase out loud and feel what it does. *The right side of history.* It doesn't argue. It announces. It is the rare sentence that ends a debate instead of starting one, and that is precisely why it has become the most quoted line in American moral life, said from podiums and pulpits, printed on corporate statements the week the wind shifts, posted by the millions every time a consensus turns. It feels less like an opinion than like a weather report on the future. And it feels, when you are the one saying it, *wonderful.*

That is the first thing to admit, because I have felt it too. I have stood in a room certain that time itself was on my side, that to stand on the leading edge of the present was to stand near the heart of God. It is a very good feeling. Good feelings have always been the cheapest disguise sin puts on.

The claim is blunt, and the rest of this essay is me earning it. **"The right side of history" is not a neutral phrase. It is a piece of theology, a complete, working faith with its own god, its own salvation, and its own final judgment, and the American church, left and right, adopted it without ever deciding to.** Once you see the religion inside the phrase, you cannot unsee it. And you have to choose which faith you actually hold.

## The phrase has a noble birth, and that is the trap

Start by being fair to it, because the version worth refuting is the strong one.

The most famous mouth to say it was fighting actual slavery. Theodore Parker, the abolitionist preacher, told a Boston congregation in 1853 that he could not see far down the moral universe, that his sight reached only a little way, but that from what he could see he was sure it bends toward justice. A hundred years later Martin Luther King Jr. carried that sentence into Birmingham and made it the heartbeat of a movement. In their mouths it was not a slogan. It was a confession of providence. There was a *hand* in that arc. The arc bent because Someone was bending it.

That is the version everyone half-remembers. That is the trap. We kept Parker's confidence and quietly fired Parker's God.

Because the phrase did not stay in the pulpit. It passed through the nineteenth century and came out the other side stripped of the one thing that made it true. Hegel had already taught the educated West to read time itself as Spirit climbing toward freedom, history as a rational escalator, going up on its own. His *Phenomenology of Spirit* landed in 1807, and for two centuries his confidence has been the groundwater under thinkers who never read him. By the time the phrase reached us it meant something Parker never said: not that God bends the arc, but that the arc bends itself, automatically, and our only job is to guess its direction and lean.

We kept the arc. We threw away the hand that bends it.

## What the phrase actually worships

Strip a sentence down to what it promises and you find its religion.

"The right side of history" promises that your sacrifices will be vindicated. That your enemies will face a reckoning. That the dead who fought for the cause will not have died for nothing. That there is a verdict coming, and it will fall on the just side. Read that list again. That is not politics. **That is the freight the resurrection used to carry**, judgment, vindication, the moral arc of the cosmos resolving in favor of the good, repackaged for people who can no longer say the word *God* in public without flinching.

Charles Taylor gave the condition a name. In *A Secular Age* (2007) he calls it the immanent frame: a way of living in which all meaning is generated inside history, with nothing breaking in from outside it. We were born into that frame the way a fish is born into water, and inside it, "the right side of history" is the only transcendence still allowed at the table. It lets you feel the pull of something cosmic and vindicating, without a God who might also judge *you.* It is eschatology with the accountability surgically removed.

It is heaven for people who have stopped believing in heaven.

And here is the modern accelerant Parker never had to reckon with: the platforms. The phrase thrives now because the internet runs on it. The algorithm rewards the certainty, not the doubt. A consensus can form, harden, and reverse in a single news cycle, and the timeline rewards whoever called it first and loudest. We have built a machine that pays out in status every time you correctly predict which way the crowd will move, and then we baptized the machine and called the payout righteousness. The "right side of history" stopped being a long arc you trusted God to bend. It became a leaderboard you check hourly.

## The problem the phrase cannot survive

Here is the question that breaks it, and there is no good answer.

If history has a "right side," who told you which side it is, *before* history finished? You are claiming to read a verdict that has not been handed down. And the record of people who were certain they had read it correctly is the most damning record there is.

A century ago the people most sure they stood on the right side of history were not the villains of the story. They were the progressives. They were the educated, the scientific, the forward-looking, and a great many of them were eugenicists. This is the sentence my own tribe least wants to hear, so I will say it slowly. In 1927 the Supreme Court of the United States ruled, eight to one, that the state could sterilize a young woman named Carrie Buck against her will, and Oliver Wendell Holmes, as fine a progressive mind as the century produced, wrote the line that should haunt everyone who reaches for our phrase: *"Three generations of imbeciles are enough."* They believed they were curating the future. They believed the arc ran straight through them. Tens of thousands of Americans were sterilized on the strength of a certainty that felt, from the inside, exactly like ours feels now. Righteous. Modern. Ahead.

The future did not redeem them. The future buried them and called the next thing progress.

So did the architects of a hundred other "inevitable" futures. The Belgian administrators in the Congo in the 1890s knew they stood on the advancing edge of civilization. They had the science, the maps, and the serious opinion of their day. History was not their judge. History was their alibi, right up until it wasn't.

**"The right side of history" just means the winning side, and the winning side has included monsters in every century, each one convinced it was modern.**

## What Scripture means by "the future"

Now the harder turn, the one that costs me as much as anyone.

The biblical word for the future is not *progress.* It is *judgment*, and then *mercy*, and the two are never pried apart. The prophets did not read trend lines. Amos did not poll the room. He stood in a prosperous, confident, upwardly mobile nation, a nation sure the day of the Lord would be its vindication, and told them that day would be darkness, not light, that God hated their festivals and would not glance at their offerings, that what God wanted was justice rolling down like water (Amos 5:18–24). By every available metric Amos was on the wrong side of history. He was on the right side of God. The entire prophetic tradition is an argument that the gap between those two is the only gap that finally matters.

The church learned this once, at the cost of an empire, and then forgot it. When Rome fell in 410 the pagans blamed the Christians for abandoning the old gods. Augustine answered with twenty-two books. *The City of God*, finished around 426, is the longest refusal in Christian literature of the idea that any earthly order, even the best one, even the one you were born into and love, can carry the weight of ultimate hope. Two cities, Augustine said, built by two loves, tangled together in every nation and every heart, and not to be sorted out by an election or a century or a trend. Rome was never the kingdom. The Christian who wept for Rome as though the kingdom had fallen with it had simply confused his two cities.

We make the identical confusion. We have only swapped the city for a date on the calendar.

And the resurrection, the hinge of the whole Christian claim, is the precise opposite of "the right side of history." It is not the arc bending upward. It is a corpse standing up in a borrowed garden on a Sunday no trend predicted. The first witnesses were not riding the momentum of their moment; their moment had just executed their Lord. The right side of history, that weekend, was a sealed tomb, a squad of imperial soldiers, and the settled verdict of every serious person in Jerusalem that the matter was closed. Then the matter was not closed. **The future did not produce the resurrection. The resurrection produced the future**, broke it open from the far side, against the grain of everything the present could see. This is what Lesslie Newbigin spent forty years insisting to a Britain that had quietly stopped believing, and what N. T. Wright has spent a career arguing since: the kingdom does not arrive as our achievement riding the escalator up. It arrives as God's gift, and it keeps arriving through the people the trend lines had already written off.

## This is not a critique of the left. It is a critique of the church.

Brace for the move my readers always want me to make here, the pivot where I reveal this was secretly about the other side all along. I am not making it, and I am also not letting my own side off.

The identical idol lives on the right, dressed in different clothes. The Christian who insists a vanished America was God's ordained order has made exactly the same mistake in reverse: he has fused the kingdom to a moment in time, except his moment sits behind him instead of ahead. **Nostalgia and progressivism are the same idolatry facing opposite directions.** The progressive worships a future that has not arrived; the reactionary worships a past that never was; and both will defend their chosen moment with a devotion they no longer spend on the cross. The God of Scripture stands outside both, unimpressed by the calendar, asking the same question he asked in the garden. *Where are you.*

So this is the harder essay. It is written to the people I agree with, by a man who agrees with them, about the way our agreement started carrying a weight that belongs only to Christ.

Watch how the capture actually happens, because it never announces itself. It does not feel like apostasy. It feels like relevance. You begin with a real conviction, that the poor are neglected, the stranger despised, the church complicit in cruelties it still will not confess, and on all of it you are right, biblically and gloriously right. Micah 6:8 is not a suggestion. But somewhere in defending those convictions a substitution occurs, so quietly you never sign the papers. The *reason* shifts. You held the conviction because the God who set his image in every person commands it. Now you hold it because it is what decent, forward-looking people believe, and you have grown afraid of being mistaken for the other kind. The conviction stays. Its root is cut. And a conviction cut from its root keeps its color for a while, the way a cut flower does, and then it begins, without your noticing, to die in the very vase you were so proud to display it in.

The tribunal I had installed. I have caught myself weighing a sermon not by whether it was true but by whether it would age well, whether, ten years out, I would be embarrassed to have preached it. A real question. But look at the judge I had seated on the bench. The future. The applause of a generation not yet born. I had swapped the God before whom I will actually stand for a jury of imagined grandchildren whose approval I craved, and I had done it while feeling more righteous, not less. That is this sin's signature. It does not arrive as compromise. It arrives as conscience.

## The test, and the verdict

Here is the test. It is simple, and it is brutal, and I have failed it.

Take the conviction you are proudest of, the one that makes you feel, when you hold it, like one of the good ones. Now imagine history turns against it. Imagine your grandchildren are taught you were a fool, that the future you bet your name on lost, that the room you were so glad to stand in emptied and the door locked behind you. Would you still hold it?

If the only thing keeping the conviction alive is your confidence that tomorrow will agree with you, then it was never faith. **It was forecasting. And forecasting is not a fruit of the Spirit.**

Hebrews keeps a different ledger than the one we are all so anxious to be written into. Its eleventh chapter runs the roll of the faithful and then says the part we skip: that many of them did not receive what was promised, that they were stoned and sawn in two and wandered in deserts in animal skins, that the world was not worthy of them (Hebrews 11:36–38). By every metric available in their lifetimes, they lost. They were on the wrong side of history. The God who keeps the real record called them faithful, and that verdict is the only one that will finally hold.

I do not know which way history is going. Neither do you. We have both pretended to, and we have both used the pretending to dodge the only question that was ever ours to answer, not where the world is heading, but where we are standing, and before whom.

There is one side worth being on. It was never the side of history.

History is going to die. The One who walked out of his own grave will be standing in the wreckage when it does, asking the question no trend can answer for you.
posts.excerpt: \"The right side of history\" is the most successful piece of secular theology of our age, and the American church swallowed it whole. Here is what we traded away.

posts.title: Why the Church Stopped Talking About Sin
posts.body:
Ask a certain kind of church a hard question about the doctrine of sin and watch what happens. You will not get silence. You will get fluency. We can name sin at a scale our grandparents never managed, systems, structures, the long arithmetic of history, the way an economy grinds the poor without any single villain pulling the lever. That is a real skill, and most of it is true. But notice the word that has gone quiet underneath all the noise. Sin in the singular. Sin in the second person. Sin as something a person did. Sin as something I did.

I am inside the church I am describing. I helped the word go quiet.

So let me be fair to my own side before I turn on it, because the version worth telling is the strong one. For a long stretch of American Christianity, *sin* meant a short list of private vices, what you drank, what you watched, who you slept with, while the public sins went unnamed from the pulpit. The segregated congregation. The exploited worker. The war blessed without a tremor of conscience. The word had been shrunk until it fit inside other people's bedrooms and never reached our own balance sheets. A generation reacted, and the reaction was right. We enlarged the word. We said sin is bigger than your private habits, it scales, it hides in systems, it poisons the air a whole society breathes. Amos knew this. He stood in a prosperous nation and condemned an entire economy rather than a few greedy men, and told them God hated their festivals and would not glance at their offerings until justice rolled down like water. Recovering that was not a fad. It was obedience.

The claim, stated before it is earned. **Progressive Christianity recovered structural sin, which was a genuine gain, and then lost personal sin, which was a catastrophe, and the recovered half, cut loose from the lost half, has quietly become the most respectable form of self-righteousness the modern church has produced.** Once you see the trade, you cannot unsee it. Sin becomes always what *they* do, what the system does, what the dead did. Never what I am doing at this desk.

## The optimism that outran the evidence

This has happened before, almost beat for beat, and the last time it happened it did not end the way the optimists expected.

The American mainline did not abandon the doctrine of sin in one dramatic act of unbelief. It mislaid it slowly, across the long Protestant afternoon between the Civil War and the First World War, and it mislaid it for reasons that felt like growing up. The confidence of the nineteenth century had trained the educated West to read the human story as a climb, Darwin misread as moral progress, industry misread as providence, a missionary empire misread as the kingdom arriving on schedule. Liberal Protestantism breathed that air. The harsher furniture of the old faith, wrath, judgment, the bondage of the will, the rot native to every heart, came to seem like the cramped theology of a frightened age the species had outgrown. Sin, where it survived in the preaching, softened into ignorance, or maladjustment, a residue of bad environment that better schools and better laws would slowly wash out.

H. Richard Niebuhr fixed the whole drift in one sentence that still draws blood. Looking back in 1937, in *The Kingdom of God in America*, he described the gospel liberalism had built: "A God without wrath brought men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross." Read it slowly. Every clause is a thing quietly removed. No wrath, so no judgment. No sin, so no need of a cross. A religion of uplift with the offense at its center surgically taken out. Niebuhr was not sniping from outside the church. He was a churchman grieving from inside it, naming what his own tradition had done to itself while it believed the whole time it was maturing.

His older brother had drawn the same blade five years earlier and aimed it at the optimism underneath. In 1932 Reinhold Niebuhr published *Moral Man and Immoral Society*, and the title carried the argument. Individuals, he allowed, can sometimes be brought to consider an interest beyond their own. But groups, nations, classes, movements, almost never can. The larger the collective, the more naked its egotism and the more total its self-deception. He had watched a Christian civilization march singing into the trenches of 1914, and pastored autoworkers in Henry Ford's Detroit, and seen what a churchgoing industrialist did to the men on the line. Human evil does not evaporate under sunlight. It organizes. It scales. It learns to wear the face of the common good.

But Niebuhr's deepest charge was not that the liberals were naive about systems. **It was that they had grown naive about the self.** By moving evil out into circumstances and structures, into everything outside the will, the modern reformer had quietly exempted his own heart from the diagnosis. And a reformer who believes his own heart is clean is the most dangerous man in any movement. He has no brake. He has audited the sin in everyone but the auditor. Niebuhr would later call original sin the one Christian doctrine empirically verifiable by a glance at the morning paper, and the one the modern church was most determined to be rid of. We got rid of it. Then the century showed us, in the camps and the purges and the ovens of supposedly Christian Europe, exactly what we had set down.

That is the warning we inherited. We learned half of it.

## The half we kept

We were the children of that correction, and we took the part of it that flattered us.

We seized Reinhold Niebuhr's insistence that sin is structural, that it scales, that it hides in systems, that a society can be guilty in ways no single citizen intends, and we built a whole theology of justice on it, and the theology was largely true. But we let go of the half his brother named, the half that costs. We kept *immoral society*. We lost *moral man*, which in Niebuhr's hands never meant the individual was clean. It meant the individual was the only place where the disease can actually be confessed. We took the doctrine that indicts the system and dropped the doctrine that indicts the one analyzing it. We ran the exact play Niebuhr had warned the liberals against, and we ran it in his name.

Here is the mechanism, and I am describing my own heart, not a stranger's. When sin is only structural, it is never mine. A structure has no soul to examine at midnight. A system cannot kneel. If the locus of sin is the institution, the economy, the inherited arrangement of power, then I am no longer a sinner, I am, at worst, a beneficiary, and at best an ally, and either way the verb has slid off of me and onto something I can study from a clean distance. I get to keep the moral weight of the word while shedding its personal cost. **I get to be against sin without ever being a sinner. It is the most comfortable position in the history of moral thought. We found it. We called it justice.**

Forty years after Reinhold's book, a Kansas psychiatrist noticed the silence and said the obvious thing out loud. In 1973 Karl Menninger published *Whatever Became of Sin?*, a bracing book from a secular clinician who had watched the culture, and the churches inside it, retire the word entirely. Sin had become sickness, or crime, or syndrome, or social pathology; it had become anything that could be assigned to a cause outside the patient and treated without a verdict. Menninger's worry was not theological prudery. It was that a society which can no longer say *I have sinned* has lost the one category that takes responsibility seriously, it has traded the chance of repentance for the comfort of explanation. He was writing to a whole culture. He could have been writing to my congregation, and to me.

## The bend in the will

To see why the personal can never be quietly swapped for the structural, go back to the oldest map of the diseased heart in the Christian tradition.

The Augustinian stream of theology, and the phrase gets pinned on both Augustine and Luther, so hold the attribution loosely, gave the condition its enduring name: *incurvatus in se*, the soul curved in on itself, the will bent inward so that even its loves and its labors and its justice finally bend back toward the self and serve it. This is the engine under everything else. It is not first a matter of bad rules or bad systems, though it builds those by the thousand. It is the original torque in the will, the gravity that turns a person into his own horizon. And the point we have lost is that this curve is not out there in the institution. It is in here, in the one doing the looking, including the one looking with the sharpest eye for injustice. You do not escape the curve by becoming an excellent critic of other people's curve. The critic is curved too. The reformer is curved.

Sixteen centuries later, Cornelius Plantinga built the same truth into a phrase made for our exact evasion. In *Not the Way It's Supposed to Be* (1995), he defined sin as "culpable shalom-breaking", the willful vandalizing of the way God meant things to flourish. Hold both words, because together they block our trick. *Shalom-breaking* is as wide as the world; it reaches every fractured system, every wrecked economy, every structure that grinds the poor, and it licenses all the structural analysis the prophets ever demanded. But *culpable* keeps a name attached. It keeps a will in the sentence. It will not let the breaking float free of the breaker. Plantinga's whole burden was that the modern church had grown fluent in the breaking and gone silent on the culpability, could describe the wreckage at length and never locate a hand, least of all its own, on the hammer. That is our condition exactly. We have an eloquent account of broken shalom and no one in it who is culpable but the absent and the dead.

## The Pharisee changed parties

Scripture will not let me off this lightly, and the place it pins me is a parable I have preached without flinching.

Two men went up to the temple to pray (Luke 18:9–14). The Pharisee was not wrong about anything visible. He really did tithe. He really did fast. He really was, by every public standard of his day, on the right side. His sin was not in his analysis. It was in his pronoun. *God, I thank you that I am not like other people*, and that is the sentence the modern progressive heart composes in the dark, word for word, only with the list updated. Thank you that I am not like the racists, the colonizers, the fundamentalists, the ones who do not see, the ones still asleep in the pews I walked out of. We keep a running litany of the people we are grateful not to be, we recite it daily, and we have taught ourselves to call it conviction. The other man kept no list. He could not see past himself far enough to compile one. He beat his chest and said *God, be merciful to me, a sinner*, not *be merciful to the unjust structures*, true as that prayer would have been, and Jesus said it was that man, not the structurally literate one, who went home justified.

Notice what indicts us. It is not that the Pharisee faked his virtues. He had them. It is that real virtue became the very ground he stood on to look down. The most religiously serious man in the story goes home unforgiven, and he goes home unforgiven for the one sin that hides perfectly inside being right.

David did not write Psalm 51 about a system either. He wrote it after a night with Bathsheba and a murdered husband, and the line that breaks it open, *against you, you only, have I sinned*, is not a denial that Uriah was wronged.
