The exile changes Babylon not by conquering it but by being a good neighbor in it: by raising children who know who they are, by building things that bless the people around them, by seeking the genuine welfare of a city that is not his home. The witness is in the gardens. It is in the houses. It is in the quality of a life lived faithfully where no one is watching for it. A church that learns to seek the welfare of its city, its actual city, its schools and streets and struggling families, without demanding the city's allegiance in return is a church that has understood the letter. Most of our energy goes the other direction, toward demanding the allegiance and neglecting the welfare. The exiles were told to do the opposite, and they were told it would be enough.

## What is on the far side of seventy years

Jeremiah's letter does not end with the instruction to settle in. It ends with a promise, and the promise matters precisely because it comes only after the long obedience.

For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (Jeremiah 29:11). That verse has been printed on a million coffee mugs and stripped of everything that gave it weight, because it has been torn out of its setting. It is not a promise of a comfortable life. It is a promise made to people who have just been told they will die in Babylon, that beyond the seventy years they cannot see, beyond their own lifetimes, God has not abandoned the story. The exiles had to build a life they would never see vindicated. They had to plant gardens whose harvest would feed grandchildren they could only imagine. The hope was real. It was also long.

I find this clarifying rather than discouraging. The church in the West may be in for a long exile. The recovery, if it comes, may not come on my watch or in the lifetime of anyone reading this. We may be the generation that plants gardens for a harvest we will not eat. **But exile is not the end of the people of God. It is the place where the people of God remember that their hope was never in the empire to begin with.** The temple fell, and the faith did not. Babylon rose and Babylon fell, and the faith outlived it. The exiles who built houses and sought the welfare of the city were not the ones who lost. They were the ones who kept the story alive long enough to hand it back.

So build the house. Plant the garden. Seek the welfare of the city that no longer agrees with you, and pray for it, and refuse the furnace, and do not pack your bags for a return to a Christendom that is not coming back.

There is a strange freedom in accepting the exile rather than fighting it. The energy the church spends trying to claw its way back to the center is energy it cannot spend on the work in front of it, the neighbor, the city, the slow formation of a people who know who they are in a place that has forgotten. Acceptance is not surrender. The exiles who built houses in Babylon were not surrendering; they were refusing to waste their lives in a bitterness that accomplished nothing. They were free to live, because they had stopped pretending they were somewhere else. The church that accepts its exile is freed in the same way, freed from the nostalgia that drains it and the panic that distorts it, freed to do the only thing it was ever finally asked to do, which is to be faithful in the place it has actually been sent. That place is no longer the center. The center was never the point.

The exile is long. It is not the end. It was never the end.
posts.excerpt: The church in the West keeps treating its loss of cultural power as a catastrophe. Scripture treats exile as something else entirely, the place where faith learns what it is made of.

posts.title: Is the Church Really Dying? What the Numbers Say
posts.body:
Hand a pastor a graph of religious decline and watch what happens to his face. Some go pale, already drafting the eulogy for the faith. Others wave it off, certain the numbers are liberal propaganda and the pews will fill back up any Sunday now. Both reactions are a way of not looking. The first treats the data as a death sentence; the second treats it as a lie. **The truth about the numbers behind the decline is more disciplined and less dramatic than either camp wants: the trends are real, the meaning is contested, and almost every precise figure you have heard quoted with confidence is shakier than the person quoting it admitted.** Reading the data honestly is its own spiritual discipline, because the temptation is always to make the numbers say what your fear or your hope already decided.

I want to read them carefully here, which means I will hedge, and the hedging is the point. When someone tells you that exactly such-and-such percent of a generation has left the faith, your first question should be where the number came from, how it was measured, and what the margin of error was, because survey questions about religion are notoriously sensitive to how they are worded, and small changes in phrasing move the results more than most people realize.

## The rise of the "nones" is real, and its meaning is not obvious

The single largest, most replicated finding in the sociology of American religion over the past several decades is the rise of the religiously unaffiliated, the so-called "nones," people who, asked their religion, answer "none" or "nothing in particular." On the broad shape of this, the major data sources tend to agree: the share of Americans claiming no religious affiliation has grown substantially since roughly the early 1990s, rising from a small minority to something in the broad neighborhood of a quarter to a third of adults in recent years, depending on the survey and the year. I give you a range on purpose. Different instruments produce different figures, and anyone who hands you a single decimal point as gospel is selling certainty the data does not contain.

Ryan Burge, whose book *The Nones* (2021) is the most careful popular treatment of this group, makes a point that cuts against the apocalyptic reading: "none" is not the same as "atheist." The unaffiliated are a sprawling, internally contradictory category. Some are committed secularists. But a large share, often the largest share, are the "nothing in particular" respondents, many of whom still believe in God, still pray, still hold a vaguely spiritual outlook, and have simply dropped the institutional label. Burge has shown that the growth has been concentrated heavily in that "nothing in particular" middle, not in hardened atheism. What is collapsing, in other words, is affiliation, the willingness to claim a religious brand, more than belief itself. That is exactly what you would expect if what is dying is Christendom, the cultural default, rather than faith as such.

This is the first place the numbers lie when handled carelessly. A rising "none" figure gets reported as a rising tide of unbelief. Much of it is actually a falling tide of nominal, culturally-pressured affiliation, the very thing Christendom inflated and its collapse is now deflating. The honest reading is that the data shows a real and significant disaffiliation, the meaning of which is genuinely mixed.

Burge adds a further complication that should keep everyone humble. The trend lines are not perfectly smooth, and there are recent signs in some datasets that the rapid rise of the unaffiliated may be slowing or leveling off, though I state even that cautiously, because a few years of data do not make a trend, and the people who declared the decline unstoppable were too quick, just as the people who would now declare it reversed are too quick. The discipline is to hold the long, well-attested shape of the change, a real, decades-long rise in disaffiliation, while resisting the urge to read next year's headline as destiny. Sociology describes what has happened. It does not prophesy. The church that treats a survey as a prophecy has confused two very different kinds of book.

## The number that gets weaponized

There is a particular kind of statistic that does the most damage, and it is the dramatic figure about the young leaving the church.

You have heard versions of it, that some large fraction of young people raised in the church abandon it as adults. There is real signal underneath these claims. Multiple long-term datasets do show that younger cohorts are markedly less affiliated and less religiously active than older ones, and that each generation in recent decades has entered adulthood somewhat less attached to institutional religion than the one before. That much is well-supported and worth taking with full seriousness. But the precise retention and dropout figures that circulate in church-growth seminars are often built on small samples, particular definitions of "raised in the church," and methodologies that do not bear the weight placed on them. The honest statement is directional, not decimal: yes, the young are less affiliated, and the long trend is real; no, the terrifyingly exact percentage on the conference slide should not be trusted without knowing its source.

It helps to understand why religion surveys are so slippery in the first place, because the slipperiness is not a flaw to be corrected but a feature of what is being measured. Religious identity is one of the most context-dependent things a person reports. Whether someone calls themselves Christian can shift with the wording of the question, the order of the questions before it, the mode of the survey, even the cultural moment in which it is asked. When the social cost of claiming no religion falls, as it has fallen dramatically over the past few decades, people who were always functionally unaffiliated begin saying so out loud, and the numbers move sharply without any underlying change in belief. Some of the steepest part of the "none" curve is almost certainly this: not new disaffiliation but newly honest reporting, a closet emptying rather than a faith collapsing. This is why I refuse to hand anyone a clean percentage. The instrument is measuring honesty and affiliation and belief all at once, and it cannot tell you how much of the movement belongs to each. Anyone who pretends it can is reading confidence into a number that does not contain it.

Christian Smith's research adds the texture the raw numbers miss. Studying the actual religious lives of American teenagers and young adults, Smith found that the dominant faith of the young was not atheism but something he named *moralistic therapeutic deism*, a vague belief in a distant God who wants people to be nice and happy and who shows up mainly to solve problems. The striking finding was not that the young had reasoned their way out of Christianity. It was that many had never been given a robust Christianity to leave. They were handed the thin, comfortable, culturally-adjacent version, cultural Christianity in its final, watered form, and they let go of it because there was almost nothing there to hold. **The data does not show a generation that examined the faith and rejected it. It shows, in large part, a generation that was handed the wrap and never the gift, and quietly set down the wrap.**

Robert Putnam, who documented the broader collapse of American community life in *Bowling Alone* (2000), points to a wider current the religious numbers are riding. Church attendance did not fall in isolation; it fell alongside union membership, civic clubs, bowling leagues, and nearly every form of in-person associational life. Some meaningful portion of religious decline is not about belief at all but about the general dissolution of the habits of gathering. That does not make it less serious for the church. It does mean that reading the church's numbers without the surrounding collapse of community is reading them out of context, and context is precisely what the weaponized statistic strips away.

This matters more than it first appears, because it changes the diagnosis. If people are leaving churches mainly because their faith collapsed, the response is apologetics, better arguments, sharper answers. But if a large share are leaving because the entire infrastructure of gathering on a schedule with other human beings has eroded across the whole society, then the church is facing a different problem, one it shares with the bowling leagues and the Rotary clubs and the dying downtown congregations of every kind. The crisis of belief and the crisis of belonging are tangled together, and the data cannot fully separate them. A church that diagnoses a belonging problem as a belief problem will spend its energy on arguments when what people actually walked away from was a table. The honest reading holds both: there is a real erosion of conviction, and there is a real erosion of community, and they reinforce each other, and untangling which is which in any given person is beyond what a survey can do.

## What Charles Taylor adds that the surveys cannot

Statistics measure behavior and self-report. They cannot measure the thing Charles Taylor spent *A Secular Age* (2007) describing: the shift in the conditions of belief itself.

Taylor's argument is that the deepest change is not how many people believe but what believing has become. We have moved, he says, from a world in which faith was the unquestioned default to a world in which it is one contested option among many, held under constant cross-pressure. This is invisible to a survey, because a survey can only count the boxes people check, not the weight those boxes carry. Two people can both check "Christian" while living in entirely different spiritual universes, one for whom it is an inherited assumption, another for whom it is a daily decision against the grain of everything around them. The numbers cannot tell these apart. The collapse of the first kind looks, on a graph, identical to the collapse of faith itself. It is not.

This is why I distrust the graph as a guide to the spiritual reality. The graph is real. It is also blind to the most important variable, which is whether the faith that remains is deeper or shallower than the faith that left. A church can shrink in numbers and grow in conviction. Christendom, on the way down, may be trading breadth for depth, and no survey instrument in existence can see that trade.

## Scripture has never trusted the headcount

The God of the Bible has a long, almost provocative habit of doing his work through the smaller number, and it is worth holding against our anxiety about the graphs.

When Gideon raised an army of thirty-two thousand against Midian, God reduced it, first to ten thousand, then to a mere three hundred, for an explicit reason: lest Israel boast that its own hand had saved it (Judges 7:2–7). The fear was not too few. The fear was too many, because a victory won by a crowd would have been credited to the crowd. The decisive deliverance in the story comes through the deliberately diminished number. When Elijah collapsed in self-pity, certain he was the last faithful man alive, God corrected him not with a revival but with a remnant: I have kept for myself seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Not a majority. A remnant Elijah could not even see, faithful in obscurity while the prophet assumed the faith had died with him.

And Jesus himself was almost careless about the size of the crowd, to the alarm of anyone running the numbers. The gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, he said, and those who find it are few, while the easy road, the wide gate, the crowded path, leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13–14). That is not a verse for a growth strategy. It is a warning that bigness and faithfulness are not the same measurement, and have sometimes been opposites. **Scripture never once treats the headcount as the score. The faithful have been a remnant more often than a majority, and the times they were a majority were rarely their best.**

There is a pastoral danger in the statistics that I have watched do real harm, and it deserves naming. A church that absorbs the apocalyptic reading of the data begins to lead from fear, and fear is a terrible foundation for ministry. The fearful church grasps, manipulates, and chases the culture in a panic to stop the bleeding, and in doing so it hands the watching world a portrait of a faith that does not believe its own promises. Why would anyone join a people who are visibly terrified that their God is losing? The early church grew in part because it was conspicuously unafraid, unafraid of plague, unafraid of the empire, unafraid even of death, and that fearlessness was itself a kind of evidence. A church that reads the decline numbers and responds with terror has already lost something more important than the numbers measure. The data should sober us. It should not frighten us, because fear preaches a smaller God than the one we claim, and the people reading our fear can tell.

So when the graphs come, and they will keep coming, read them with the discipline they deserve. The decline is real; do not be the pastor who calls the data a lie. The decline is also not the death of God; do not be the pastor who reads it as the final verdict. Much of what the numbers record is the long-overdue deflation of a faith that was inflated by culture and never by conviction. The remnant the numbers cannot see is the part that was always doing the work.

Gideon went to war with three hundred and won. Elijah was wrong about the seven thousand. The narrow gate was never crowded. **Count carefully, and then remember that the One who keeps the only ledger that matters has never been impressed by the size of the line at the wide gate.**
posts.excerpt: The statistics about the dying church get quoted in two directions, apocalypse and denial, and both are usually wrong. A careful look at what the data on the 'nones' actually says, and what it can't.

posts.title: What Actually Dies When Christianity Loses Power
posts.body:
When something large dies, the first grief is indiscriminate. You mourn everything at once, the good and the rotten, the essential and the accidental, all of it heaped together in the loss. Only later, when the shock thins, can you begin the harder work of sorting: this part I will carry forever, that part I am quietly relieved to be free of. The church in the West is in the first stage. Christendom is dying, and we are mourning all of it at once, the way you do at a funeral before you have had time to think. **But not everything that is dying deserves to be mourned, and the most important spiritual work of this generation is learning to tell cultural Christianity apart from the faith it was wrapped around, because they are dying together, and only one of them is supposed to.**

This is a distinction the comfortable years let us blur. When the culture and the faith point the same direction, you never have to ask which one you actually serve. The default did the sorting for you. Now the default is gone, and the question can no longer be avoided. What, exactly, are we afraid of losing? And is all of it worth keeping?

## The difference cultural Christianity was built to hide

Cultural Christianity is the version of the faith you can hold without it costing you anything, because everyone around you holds it too.

It is Christianity as respectability, as social glue, as the assumed background of a decent life. It fills pews at Christmas and Easter and weddings and funerals. It says grace at the table out of habit and votes its tribe out of loyalty and would be offended to be called anything but Christian, while carrying almost none of the actual weight of following a crucified Lord. It is not hypocrisy exactly, most of the people holding it are sincere. It is something subtler: a faith that has been so thoroughly merged with a culture that no one can tell anymore where the gospel ends and the customs begin. Under Christendom this version flourished, because the culture rewarded it and demanded nothing in return.

The death of Christendom is, first and most visibly, the death of *this.* The nominal believer is leaving. The person who attended because attendance was expected, who identified as Christian because identifying otherwise was unthinkable, that person is melting away with the social pressure that produced them. And here is the part the church struggles to say out loud: the loss of the nominal believer is not, in itself, the loss of anything the gospel ever promised to keep. Jesus never recruited the nominal. He kept thinning his own crowds. When the teaching got hard in John 6, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him, and he did not chase them; he turned to the twelve and asked if they would leave too. Christendom reversed that dynamic for seventeen centuries, swelling the crowds by lowering the cost. The collapse of Christendom is simply the cost returning.

I want to be careful here, because this is the point where the argument can curdle into something ugly, a smug satisfaction at the departure of the lukewarm, a relief that the crowd is thinning so the remnant can feel pure. That is not the spirit of any of this, and Jesus weeping over Jerusalem forbids it. The nominal believer leaving is still a person, often a person the church failed, handed a faith too thin to hold, never shown the real thing, never given a reason to count the cost because no one ever told them there was a cost. We do not get to be glad they are gone. We get to ask why the only Christianity many of them ever encountered was the cultural counterfeit, and whether the church that handed them the counterfeit was not itself the problem. The death of cultural Christianity indicts the church before it indicts the people who are leaving it. They are setting down what we gave them. The question is why we gave them so little.

## What Bonhoeffer saw from a prison cell

Dietrich Bonhoeffer saw all of this coming from inside a Nazi prison, and his letters from those months contain one of the strangest and most prophetic phrases in modern theology.

Writing to his friend Eberhard Bethge in 1944, in the letters later gathered as *Letters and Papers from Prison*, Bonhoeffer began sketching what he called a "religionless Christianity." He saw that the world was becoming what he named *mündig*, come of age, no longer needing God as the explanation for the gaps in its knowledge or the prop for its morality. The old religious scaffolding, he argued, was collapsing, and good riddance to much of it. He had watched the respectable, churchgoing Christianity of his own nation bless the regime that was murdering its way across Europe. He had seen what cultural Christianity was worth when the test came: nearly nothing. The pastors who had the most religion had the least faith. Bonhoeffer was not mourning the death of religious Christendom. He was asking what kind of faith could possibly survive its death, a faith stripped of its cultural supports, a Christianity that followed Christ rather than merely invoking him.

He paid for that faith with his life, hanged at Flossenbürg weeks before the war ended. And the witness of his dying is the answer to his own question. **What Bonhoeffer proved is that when cultural Christianity dies, the faith that remains is smaller, costlier, and immeasurably more real**, the faith that will follow Christ to a gallows because it was never propped up by anything but Christ in the first place.

Charles Taylor names the modern condition Bonhoeffer was living into. In *A Secular Age* (2007) he describes the "cross-pressures" of our moment, the way belief and unbelief now press on everyone, so that the believer feels the pull of doubt and the unbeliever feels the haunting of transcendence, and no one gets to rest in an unexamined default. Cultural Christianity cannot survive cross-pressure, because cultural Christianity was always an unexamined default. Real faith can survive it. Real faith was always examined; it was always chosen against alternatives. The cross-pressured world is brutal to nominal belief and oddly clarifying for the genuine kind.

## Two things are buried in the same grave

So let me say plainly what I think dies, and what does not, because the grief needs sorting and no one else seems eager to do it.

What dies: the assumption that a respectable person is a Christian. The political reflex that fused the faith to a flag and a party and a nostalgic vision of a nation. The crowds that came for belonging and stayed for nothing. The cultural prestige of the pastor, the automatic deference, the reserved seat at the civic table. The mistaking of church membership for discipleship. The whole apparatus by which the culture did the work the Spirit was supposed to do. These are dying, and when I am honest, I cannot fully grieve them, because much of this was the very thing that hollowed the church from the inside while it looked strong from the outside. A church that has to be defended by social pressure is already dead; it just has not been told.

What does not die: the gospel. The cross and the empty tomb. The presence of God with his people. The Scriptures, which were written largely by and for a persecuted minority and lose nothing when their readers become a minority again. The communion of saints across twenty centuries. The Spirit, who was not granted by Constantine and cannot be revoked by a census. None of this is tied to Christendom. None of this depends on a culture's agreement. The faith that raised the dead in a hostile empire does not need a friendly one to survive.

There is a second list worth making, harder than the first, because it concerns the genuine goods that Christendom carried and that we will miss when they are gone. The instinct to care for the weak, which Tom Holland traced to Christian roots, was real, and a culture that forgets its source may forget the instinct. The shared moral vocabulary that let strangers argue about right and wrong because they assumed a common frame, that is going, and its loss is not nothing. The hospitals and universities and charities that grew from Christian conviction, the assumption that mercy is a duty and not a weakness, the strange Western reflex that the powerful owe something to the powerless, these were genuine fruits, and they may not survive the death of the tree that bore them. I do not want to pretend the only thing dying is the rot. Real goods are dying too. The honest position grieves them while refusing to confuse them with the gospel itself. The goods were downstream of the faith. They were never a substitute for it, and they cannot be preserved by a culture that has discarded their source. That is the sober part of this essay, and I will not soften it: some good things are going to be lost, and the way to keep them is not to defend the culture but to be the church that produced them in the first place.

Lesslie Newbigin understood that the danger was never the death of Christendom but the church's failure to distinguish it from the death of faith. He came home to a post-Christian Britain and found a church paralyzed by grief over the wrong corpse, mourning its lost status as though its lost status were its life. He spent his last decades trying to wake it to the difference: the West was now a mission field, and that was not the end of the church but the recovery of its true work, which Christendom had let it forget.

## The seed has to go into the ground

Jesus gave us the only frame that makes sense of a death like this, and he gave it just days before his own.

Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). He was speaking of himself, of the cross that was days away. But he stated it as a law of the kingdom, not a one-time exception. Life comes through death. The seed that refuses to die stays a single seed, preserved, intact, and utterly barren. The seed that goes into the ground and is buried and broken open is the only one that multiplies. Christendom was a seed that refused to fall, a Christianity preserved so carefully by the culture that it slowly stopped bearing fruit. Its death is terrible to watch. It may also be the only way back to a harvest.

Jesus said the same thing in the form of a paradox we have domesticated past recognition: whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). This is true of churches and not only of souls. The church that spends its energy trying to save its life, its position, its prestige, its cultural power, will lose the thing it was protecting. The church willing to lose all of that for Christ's sake will find what it was actually for.

This is the test that separates the two things dying in the same grave, and it is a test we can actually run. Take any feature of the church's life that feels threatened right now and ask of it: is this the gospel, or is this Christendom? Is this the seed, or is this the husk that grew around the seed? The reserved seat at the civic table, husk. The conviction that Jesus is Lord whether the civic table agrees or not, seed. The expectation of cultural deference, husk. The call to love the neighbor who does not defer, seed. The political reflex to win, husk. The willingness to lose everything and follow anyway, seed. Run that test honestly across the whole inventory of what we are afraid to lose, and a strange thing happens. Most of what frightens us turns out to be husk, and most of what we will actually keep turns out to be the part no census can touch. The grief is real. It is also, on inspection, mostly grief for the husk, and the husk was never what kept us alive.

Hebrews promises that this sorting is, in the end, God's own work. He has promised to shake the heavens and the earth once more, the writer says, and that phrase, *once more,* signals the removal of what can be shaken, so that what cannot be shaken may remain (Hebrews 12:27). Christendom can be shaken; it is being shaken; it is, by the evidence, coming down. **The shaking is not the enemy of the kingdom. The shaking is how you find out what the kingdom actually was, underneath everything the culture had built on top of it.**

The fear underneath all our grieving is that the shaking will not stop until there is nothing left, that the seed in the ground is simply dead, not buried, and no spring is coming. I cannot prove otherwise from a chart, and I will not pretend to. But the witness of the church's own history is that it has died and risen more times than anyone counting has expected. The faith was supposed to be finished when Rome fell, and it outlived Rome. It was supposed to be finished when the Enlightenment dismissed it, and it outlived the philosophers who wrote its obituary. It has been buried in more soils than I can name, and the burying has a way of preceding a harvest no one predicted, because the God of this faith specializes in the kind of life that only comes after a death. That is not optimism. Optimism is a reading of the trend lines. This is hope, which is a reading of the character of God, and the two are not the same, and only one of them survives a funeral.

When the dust settles, the church will be smaller. It will also be unmistakable, in a way it has not been able to be for a very long time. The people who remain will be there because they chose it against the grain, not because the culture handed it to them at birth. That is not a defeat. That is a seed in the ground.

Grieve what is worth grieving. Bury the rest, and do not dig it back up. Something is supposed to grow here.
posts.excerpt: Not everything that is dying in the church deserves to be mourned. The hard work of this moment is telling the difference between cultural Christianity and the faith it was hiding.

posts.title: The Church Grew Fastest When It Had No Power
posts.body:
By the year 300, before any emperor had lifted a finger to help it, the Christian movement may have numbered in the millions across the Roman world. It had no army. It held no offices of consequence. It controlled no schools, no courts, no press, no levers of the imperial machine. Its members were disproportionately the people Rome counted as nothing, slaves, women, the urban poor, the kind of people whose deaths did not trouble the historians. And yet within a few generations this powerless movement had so saturated the empire that an emperor would find it expedient to join it rather than crush it. **The early church grew not despite having no power but, in a sense we have nearly lost the ability to understand, because of it.** That is the fact a declining Western church most needs to sit with, because it is being handed back the exact conditions under which the faith first spread like fire.

We have spent so long assuming that influence requires position, a voice in the room, a seat at the table, a hand on the wheel, that we read the loss of those things as the loss of the faith's future. The first three centuries say otherwise. They say the future of the faith was never tied to its position. It was tied to its life.

## The math does not work, and that is the point

Rodney Stark, a sociologist rather than a theologian, took up the question with cold-eyed numbers in *The Rise of Christianity* (1996), and his answer is more unsettling than any sermon. The church did not grow through mass conversions or dramatic public victories. It grew at a steady, almost modest rate, somewhere in the range of forty percent per decade, Stark estimated, the same rate by which modern movements like the early Mormons grew. Compounded over three centuries, that ordinary rate produces an extraordinary result. A few thousand at the death of the apostles becomes a few million by Constantine. The growth was exponential precisely because it was relational and unhurried, person to person, household to household, friend to friend.

But Stark's most provocative finding is *why* people stayed. When plague swept the cities of the empire, and it did, catastrophically, more than once, the pagans fled, abandoning even their own sick to die alone in the streets. The Christians stayed. They nursed the dying, their own and their neighbors', often catching the disease and dying themselves. The simple fact that basic care raises survival rates meant that Christian communities came through the plagues stronger, with more survivors bound by gratitude and awe. The watching world drew the obvious conclusion: these people have something we do not. They are not afraid of death the way we are afraid of it.

That is witness without power. Not an argument won in the forum. A body, fevered and dying, refusing to leave the bedside of a stranger. The math of the empire said the Christians should have died out. They multiplied, because the thing they had could not be killed by the thing the empire used to kill everything else.

Stark pressed the point further, into territory that should make a modern church uncomfortable. The early Christians, he showed, were disproportionately attractive to the people the empire treated worst. They welcomed women in a culture that discarded infant girls on rubbish heaps to die, and so their communities had more women, more marriages, more children, more growth. They cared for widows and orphans the wider society ignored. They crossed the ethnic and class lines that everyone else policed. The result was that the church became a refuge for exactly the people who had nothing to gain from the existing order, and a great deal to gain from a community that treated them as though they mattered to God. This was no marketing strategy but the simple outworking of believing that every person bore the image of God, applied without exception in a world that made endless exceptions. The empire ran on a hierarchy of worth. The church ignored the hierarchy, and the people at the bottom noticed first.

## Patience was a strategy nobody chose

Alan Kreider, returning to him from a different angle, argues in *The Patient Ferment of the Early Church* (2016) that the early church's defining trait was patience, and that this was not a tactic but a character, formed in people who genuinely believed God was at work and they did not have to force the outcome.

This matters because it cuts against everything a results-driven, growth-obsessed church instinctively reaches for. The early Christians did not evangelize the way we do. They did not, for the most part, stand in public and preach to crowds; that was rare and often dangerous. They did not run programs. What they did, Kreider shows, was live in a way that was patiently, persistently strange, and that strangeness raised questions in their neighbors that the Christians were then ready to answer. The candidates for baptism were often made to wait years, formed slowly into a new way of being before they were admitted. The church was not trying to maximize conversions per quarter. It was trying to produce people whose lives were the argument.

A church that has lost its power is freed, whether it wants to be or not, from the illusion that it can force the harvest. It can only be patient. It can only ferment. **When you have no power to coerce belief, the only thing left is to live in a way that makes belief plausible, and that, it turns out, is the only thing that ever truly worked.** Christendom let us forget this, because Christendom gave us levers, and levers are faster than lives. The levers are being taken away. We may discover that we were always meant to ferment, not to push.

There is a cost to this recovery that I do not want to soften. Patience is agonizing for a church trained to measure itself by quarterly results. Fermentation cannot be reported on a chart. The early church's slow formation of disciples over years, its refusal to inflate its numbers by lowering the bar, its willingness to let a person mature before declaring them a member, all of this runs against every instinct of a movement anxious about its survival. When you are afraid you are dying, the temptation is to grasp for the fastest growth available, and the fastest growth is always the shallowest. Kreider's point is that the early church grew deep precisely because it refused to grow fast, and that the depth was the durability. The candidate who waited three years for baptism was a candidate the next persecution could not easily frighten away. We have largely inverted this, building wide and shallow, and the shallowness is now draining out the same door it came in. The early church's patience was not passivity. It was a confidence that the work was God's and the timing was God's, and that confidence is the precise thing a panicked church most needs and least has.

## God chose the foolish thing on purpose

None of this is an accident of history that the New Testament merely records. It is the announced strategy of God, and Paul states it with a bluntness that still scandalizes.

The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, he writes, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:18). Then he drives it further than comfort allows. God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong. God chose the low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). Read that as a description of the church's social makeup in the first century and it is simply accurate. The movement really was composed of the foolish, the weak, the low. But Paul does not apologize for this; he claims it is the design.

The center of the faith is an instrument of imperial execution. The cross was Rome's way of displaying its power, the most public, most humiliating death the empire could inflict, reserved for slaves and rebels, a billboard of who was in charge. And the church took that symbol of total powerlessness and made it the throne. The God of the Christians did not overcome the empire by becoming a greater empire. He overcame it by being crucified by it and rising anyway. The method is in the message. You cannot preach a crucified Lord and then insist that the kingdom advances by strength.

This is why Paul could write, of his own weakness, the sentence that should govern every church now learning to live without clout: God's grace was sufficient for him, for God's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Not tolerated in weakness. Not despite weakness. Made perfect in it. The thinning of the church's cultural power is not, on this logic, the frustration of God's work. It may be the precondition of it.

Notice that Paul had asked God three times to remove the weakness, the thorn in his flesh, and three times the answer was no. He wanted strength and was given grace instead, and he came to understand that the two were not the same and that the grace was better. This is the prayer the Western church is praying right now, mostly without realizing it. Lord, restore our power. Lord, give us back the culture, the influence, the deference, the thorn-free strength we used to have. And if the pattern of the thorn holds, the answer is the same answer Paul received. No. My grace is enough. My power works through what you are calling your weakness. The church that keeps demanding its strength back may be asking God to undo the very condition in which his power is most clearly his own and not ours. The thorn was not Paul's failure but the thing that kept the power from being mistaken for his.

## Hauerwas and the temptation we keep failing

Stanley Hauerwas has spent a career insisting that the church's first political task is not to seize the levers of the state but to be the church, a community whose common life is itself the witness, a people who do not need to run the world in order to show the world another way to live. The book of Acts is his evidence, whether he cites it or not. Look at what the church actually does in those first chapters: it devotes itself to teaching and fellowship and the breaking of bread; it holds its possessions loosely and meets the needs of its own; it bears witness boldly and is hauled before the authorities for it; and when the authorities threaten, it does not organize a faction to take power but prays for boldness to keep speaking (Acts 2:42–47; 4:23–31). The early church's response to opposition was never to grasp for control. It was to ask God for courage and go back to the work.

There is a deep consistency in this that Hauerwas presses harder than most are comfortable with. The church does not first have a message and then, separately, a way of life that may or may not match it. The way of life is the message. A community that forgives because it has been forgiven, that shares because it has received, that welcomes the stranger because it was once a stranger to God, that community is making an argument no sermon can make, an argument the watching world can examine and not refute, because the evidence is a set of actual people living an actual life. When the church has political power, it is tempted to let the power accomplish what the life was supposed to accomplish, to enforce by law what it could only ever commend by witness. And every time it makes that trade, it weakens the very thing that made it credible. The kingdom advances by being a contrast, not a coercion. A church that rules looks like every other ruler. A church that serves, forgives, and suffers looks like its Lord, and that resemblance is the only argument that has ever finally persuaded anyone.

The case for seizing power is not stupid, and it deserves its strongest form before it is answered. Law teaches; a people is shaped by what its institutions honor and punish, and to walk away from those institutions is to hand the vulnerable over to whoever does seize them. The defender's exhibit is abolition and the civil rights movement, the church spending real public power on behalf of the weak, and history vindicating it. But look again at how that fight was actually won. It was won as witness, marchers who took the fire hoses and the dogs and answered them with hymns, suffering endured in public until the watching country could no longer look away. That was the plague-bedside method at national scale, not the capture of offices. The power that told was the power to suffer, not the power to rule.

We keep failing this test, and I include myself and my own tribe in the failure. Every time the church senses its power slipping, the loudest voices call for more power, capture the institutions, win the elections, reclaim the culture by force of numbers and law. It is the most natural instinct in the world, and it is the precise instinct the early church did not have, because it had no power to be tempted by. Now that ours is genuinely going, we will find out whether we believe what we say about the cross, or whether Christendom taught us to trust the sword after all.

The early church conquered Rome by refusing to fight it on Rome's terms. It out-loved, out-suffered, and out-died an empire that had every advantage. **The question for the church after Christendom is not how to get our power back. It is whether we ever needed it, or whether the power was the thing that nearly cost us the gospel in the first place.**

I want to name what this asks of pastors in particular, because we are the ones most tempted to measure our faithfulness by our reach. For a long time the pastor in the West was a person of standing, consulted, deferred to, given a microphone in the public square by default. That standing is going, and its going feels, from the inside, like a loss of effectiveness, even a loss of calling. It is neither. The early church had no pastors with public standing; it had elders who were as likely to be arrested as honored. What it had instead was a community whose ordinary members lived in a way that made the gospel visible, so that the witness was carried not by a few professionals with platforms but by the whole body, scattered through the city, loving in ways the city could not explain. A pastor after Christendom is not a public figure managing the church's influence. He is a person forming a people whose shared life is the argument. That is a smaller role and a truer one, and I am still, most days, learning to want it.

A dying man held the hand of a stranger in a plague-emptied city, and an empire was changed. That is the method. It was always the method. We just got rich enough, for a while, to forget it.
posts.excerpt: The early church conquered the Roman Empire without a single seat in its government. It is worth asking how, because the method was not power, and we have spent centuries forgetting it.

posts.title: How Fear Took Over the Church
posts.body:
The man across the desk is not angry, though it sounds like anger. Sit with him long enough and you find what is actually under there. He is afraid. He is afraid for his grandchildren, afraid of what the country is becoming, afraid that the people running things despise him and everything he loves, afraid in the specific, sleepless way of a person who has been told every night for years that the barbarians are at the gate and only vigilance can hold them off. The politics is the surface. The fear is the engine. And I have learned, slowly and against my own instinct to fix things with sentences, that you cannot argue a frightened man into peace. You can win the argument and lose the man, and send him home more afraid than when he came, now afraid of you too.

This is the thing about political capture that we keep misdiagnosing. We treat it as an information problem, if I can just show him the better facts, the truer frame, the correct theology of government, he will come around. But capture is not finally an information problem. **It is a formation problem, and the formation runs on fear, and fear does not yield to better information any more than a drowning man yields to a lecture on swimming.** The question for the pastor is not how to correct the frightened person's conclusions. It is how to disciple the fear itself, how to form a person whose loves and reflexes have been so reshaped by a steady diet of dread that the dread now feels like discernment.

I do not exempt myself. I have felt the pull of the dread, the way it offers a counterfeit of vigilance, the way being afraid can masquerade as being awake. The pastor who imagines he is above the fear is usually just better at hiding it, including from himself.

## Scripture names fear as the enemy, not a neutral fact

We tend to treat fear as morally neutral, an understandable response to a frightening world, regrettable but innocent. Scripture does not treat it that way. It treats fear as a power to be cast out. *There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love* (1 John 4:18). John sets fear and love in direct opposition. They cannot occupy the same space. To the degree a person is ruled by fear, he is not yet ruled by love, and the casting out of the one is the perfecting of the other. This is not a counseling insight John stumbled onto. It is the architecture of the Christian life.

Paul tells the same young pastor we keep returning to: *God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control* (2 Timothy 1:7). The spirit of fear is not from God. That sentence ought to reorganize how we hear the anxiety in our congregations. When a member's politics has become a vehicle for dread, for the conviction that everything depends on the next election, that the enemy is closing in, that vigilance and outrage are the highest virtues, that member is not being more discerning than his neighbor. He is operating under a spirit that Paul says God did not give. The kindest and truest thing a pastor can do is recognize that the fear is the captivity, and that freedom from it is not naivety but the very thing the gospel promises.

The Psalms model the alternative without ever pretending the threats are imaginary. *God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea* (Psalm 46:1–2). The psalmist is not denying that the earth gives way. He is locating his security somewhere the earthquake cannot reach. *Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth* (Psalm 46:10). The frightened church needs to hear that God's exaltation among the nations does not depend on its anxiety, and that the command in the storm is not *fight harder* but *be still.* Isaiah says it to a people facing real exile: *fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand* (Isaiah 41:10). Real danger. A larger God. That is the whole pastoral move, and you cannot make it with an argument.

## Why argument fails and formation works

James K. A. Smith spent three books, beginning with *Desiring the Kingdom* in 2009, arguing a thesis the church had largely forgotten: that human beings are not primarily thinking things but loving things, and that our loves are shaped less by what we believe than by what we repeatedly do. We are, he argued, liturgical animals. Our hearts are calibrated by the rhythms and rituals we practice, and those rituals are running whether or not we choose them. The mall has a liturgy. The stadium has a liturgy. And the daily three hours of cable news, with its repetitions, its rhythms, its dependable cycle of threat and outrage and the warm relief of being on the right side, is among the most powerful liturgies our people undergo. It is forming their fears by repetition the way the Psalms once formed their peace by repetition.

This is why argument fails. You are trying to change with a single sentence what a thousand evenings of repetition have built. The frightened man's fear is not a conclusion he reasoned his way to and can reason his way out of. It is a disposition that has been trained into him, a reflex laid down by liturgy, and reflexes are not undone by debate. They are undone the way they were made, by a counter-liturgy, a competing set of repeated practices that train the heart toward peace as relentlessly as the screen trained it toward dread.

**You cannot lecture a person out of a fear that a liturgy formed. You can only out-form it, with a deeper and slower liturgy of your own.** This is enormously freeing for the pastor, because it relieves us of the impossible job of winning every argument and gives us the actual job, the one the church has always had, of forming people through Word, sacrament, prayer, confession, and the long rhythm of gathered worship. We were never supposed to be debaters. We were supposed to be the keepers of a counter-liturgy strong enough to reshape what people love and therefore what they fear.

## What the counter-liturgy actually trains

Consider what the gathered worship of the church does to a frightened person over years, if we let it do its work and stop interrupting it with our own anxieties. It puts the words of Psalm 46 in his mouth until *I will not fear* becomes a reflex rather than a struggle. It bends his knee in confession every week until he is reminded that he, too, is among the sinners and not only among the threatened, which is the single most decapacitating fact for the fear-based politics, because that politics requires a clean self and a guilty enemy. It places the Lord's Table in front of him and makes him receive grace he did not earn, in the company of people he disagrees with, until the reflex of receiving grace begins to compete with the reflex of dispensing blame.

It prays, week after week, for the very leaders the screen has taught him to fear and hate, *for kings and all who are in high positions*, and the act of intercession does something no argument can. You cannot hate a man fully while you are honestly praying for him. The liturgy of intercession is corrosive to the liturgy of contempt, and it works by repetition, not persuasion. It sits the man under preaching that names a God sovereign over the future he is frightened of, not occasionally but every Sunday, until the sovereignty of God over the nations stops being a doctrine he affirms and becomes a settledness he inhabits.

Eugene Peterson called the pastoral vocation a work that proceeds at the pace of grace, slow, unglamorous, resistant to the metrics that measure everything else. Discipling people out of fear is the purest form of that slow work. There is no Sunday on which you can announce it accomplished. There is only the patient setting of one liturgy against another, year over year, trusting that the counter-formation is real even when the screen seems to be winning, because the One whose Table it is has promised that perfect love, given time and repetition and the means of grace, casts out fear.

## Naming the fear is itself pastoral

There is a step before the long formation, and it is the one we most often skip because it feels too simple to matter. Before you can disciple a person out of a fear, you have to help him see that he is afraid. The captured man almost never describes his condition as fear. He describes it as realism, as vigilance, as finally being awake to what is actually happening while everyone else sleeps. The fear has disguised itself as clear sight, and the disguise is most of its power. A man who knows he is afraid can be comforted. A man who believes his fear is simply accurate perception cannot, because to comfort him looks, from inside the fear, like asking him to stop caring.

So part of the work is the patient, unhurried naming of the thing, and it cannot be done with a confrontation. You do not tell a frightened man he is frightened; you sit with him long enough, ask enough about what keeps him up at night, that he hears himself say it. The pastors I have sat with who do this best are not clever. They are present. They let the man talk past the politics until the fear surfaces on its own, and then they do not pounce on it or correct it. They name it gently and let it sit in the open, where the gospel can finally get at it. Because a fear that has been spoken out loud, in the presence of someone who did not flinch and did not argue, has already lost some of its grip. It has been moved from the place where it ruled him in the dark to the place where it can be brought, honestly, before the God who keeps saying *fear not* to people in far worse danger than ours.

## The pastor's own fear comes first

There is a hard turn here that I have to make on myself before I make it on anyone else. The reason so much of our preaching feeds the congregation's fear instead of healing it is that we are afraid too. We are afraid of losing members, afraid of the building's finances, afraid of the cultural ground shifting under the church, afraid in the particular pastoral way of a man who has staked his life on an institution that appears to be receding. And a frightened shepherd cannot disciple a flock out of fear. He will, without meaning to, transmit his own dread in the very act of trying to address theirs. The anxiety in the pulpit becomes the anxiety in the pew, multiplied.

So the first person who has to be discipled out of fear is the one holding the microphone. The pastor has to sit under Psalm 46 himself, has to be still and know, has to let the sovereignty of God over the nations become a thing he rests in rather than a thing he merely teaches. He has to stop measuring the kingdom by the metrics the fear uses, attendance, cultural position, electoral outcomes, and recover the older measure, the one Isaiah's God offers a people headed into exile: *I am with you.* Not *you will win.* Not *the danger is not real.* *I am with you.* That is the only ground from which a man can stand before frightened people and not merely amplify their fright.

## Fear is also good news about your people

There is a turn here that changes how a pastor feels walking into the hard conversation, and it is worth dwelling on. If the politics is a symptom and the fear is the engine, then the angry, rigid, exhausting member who corners you after the service is not primarily an opponent to be managed. He is a frightened person to be loved, and frightened people are not finally hard to love once you have seen the fear under the armor. The armor is loud and off-putting on purpose; that is what armor is for. But a man does not armor himself against a world he feels safe in. The very intensity that wears you out is the measure of how afraid he is, and the fear is the door the gospel walks through.

This reframe does not make the member easier to be around, but it makes him possible to pastor, because you are no longer trying to win. You are trying to reach the scared person inside the position, and that is a thing you actually know how to do. It is the oldest pastoral work there is, sitting with the frightened, the bereaved, the cornered, and speaking the *fear not* of Scripture into the specific dark they are in. The political shape of the fear is new; the fear is not. Pastors have been discipling frightened people out of fear since the church began, because the world has always given people plenty to be afraid of, and the answer has always been the same. *Fear not, for I am with you.* You have said it at a hundred bedsides. You can say it to the man whose dread has dressed itself as a politics, once you have learned to hear, under the noise, that it was dread all along.

The frightened in your congregation will not be argued into peace, and they will not be shamed out of their politics, and they will not be saved by the better cable network you wish they watched. They will be re-formed, slowly, by a community whose worship trains a deeper love than the one the screen is training, or they will not be re-formed at all. The work is unhurried because love is unhurried, and love is the thing that casts out fear. There is no faster way, and the search for one is usually just the fear, looking for a shortcut. Be still. The future the man is so afraid of is held in hands that were nailed open, and they have not let go yet.
posts.excerpt: Political capture runs on fear, and you cannot argue a frightened person back to peace. A working pastor on why fear is the engine under the polarization, and why formation is the only cure.

posts.title: How Do You Pastor a Church Addicted to Cable News?
posts.body:
You can hear it in the prayer requests. Not the ones spoken aloud, those are still about surgeries and prodigals and jobs. The other ones. The aside in the hallway, the comment dropped after the benediction, the thing a good man says with real fear in his voice about what is coming for the country if the wrong people win. I have learned to listen for the fear underneath the politics, because the fear is the tell. It tells me where my people actually live, and more often than I want to admit, it is not in the world the sermon described that morning. It is in the world a screen described to them the night before, and the night before that, and for three hours every evening for the last fifteen years.

That is the situation, and pretending otherwise is the first failure. **Your most committed members are being discipled forty hours a week by a medium that knows their fears better than you do, and you get them for forty minutes on a Sunday, if the kickoff is late.** This is not a metaphor. It is an arithmetic problem, and the arithmetic is not on our side.

I am not writing this as a man above the problem. I have caught my own attention pulled the same direction, felt the same pull toward the screen that promises to tell me what is really going on. The capture I am describing is not a sin other people commit. It is a current we are all standing in, and the pastor who imagines himself dry is usually the one already soaked.

## The formation we are competing with is better than ours

Eugene Peterson spent a career insisting that the pastor's work is slow, local, and unglamorous, the cure of souls, he called it, borrowing the old phrase, a craft more like gardening than like broadcasting. In *Working the Angles* he warned that pastors who abandon that slow work for something more visible become, in his blunt word, shopkeepers, managers of religious consumer demand. He wrote that before the smartphone. He was describing a competition for attention that has since become a rout.

Consider what the cable network actually does, because we should respect a rival before we name its lie. It is present every day. It speaks the same message at the same time across millions of homes, so your people are formed in unison with strangers they will never meet but feel they know. It tells a story with heroes and villains and a coming reckoning, a complete narrative of sin, judgment, and salvation, with everything except a savior who dies for his enemies. It asks nothing of the viewer but attention and rewards that attention with the warm certainty of being on the right side. It is, in the precise sense, a liturgy. It forms loves by repetition the way a liturgy forms loves by repetition, and it does so with a consistency most of our churches have never achieved.

We tend to think we are competing on the level of ideas. We are not. We are competing on the level of formation, and the screen has more hours, more repetition, and a tighter feedback loop than we will ever have. A man does not leave the faith over an argument he lost. He drifts, one evening at a time, into a different story about what he should fear and whom he should hate, until one Sunday the sermon sounds naive and the news sounds true. Paul saw the shape of it without the technology: *the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths* (2 Timothy 4:3–4). The genius of the modern version is that it lets a person accumulate those teachers while still calling himself orthodox. He keeps the doctrine and outsources the fear.

## Name the capture without naming the network

Here is where many of us go wrong, myself included on more than one Sunday. We sense the capture and we attack the symptom. We name the network from the pulpit, or worse, we name it sideways, a knowing aside, a little dig that the people who agree with us catch and enjoy. And in that moment we have stopped pastoring and started competing. We have entered the same arena, played by the same rules, and conceded that the question worth fighting over is which channel is right.

The deeper work is to name the capture itself, the condition, not the channel. You can stand before a room that is divided three ways politically and say, with no partisan fingerprint on it, that there is a kind of fear that is teaching us to see our brother as our enemy, and that this fear does not come from God. You can say that a steady diet of outrage will hollow out a soul as surely as a steady diet of pornography, and for the same reason: both train us to consume a human being as a means to a feeling. Nobody in the room can dismiss that as the other side talking, because it indicts the room. It indicts you. *For God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control*, Paul again, to the same young pastor (2 Timothy 1:7). The diagnosis is not that my people vote wrong. The diagnosis is that they are afraid, and their fear is being farmed.

**The enemy is not the channel your people watch. The enemy is what the watching is doing to their capacity to love the brother sitting three pews over.** That is a pastoral problem, and it is the one Scripture actually equips us to address.

## Romans 14 is the most underused chapter in a divided church

We reach for Romans 14 about food and holy days and then quietly file it under "first-century problems." That is a mistake. Paul is doing something there that we desperately need: he is teaching a congregation how to remain one body while holding genuinely different convictions about contested matters. *Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls* (Romans 14:4). *Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God* (Romans 14:10).

Read that as a man whose congregation is divided over a contested election and it reorganizes everything. Paul does not flatten the convictions. He does not say the matters are unimportant or that everyone is equally right. He says something harder. He says the brother who disagrees with you is the servant of another master, and that master is able to make him stand, and your contempt for him is a usurpation, you have climbed onto a judgment seat that belongs to God. The political opponent in your congregation is not your project to fix. He is your brother to honor, and the day is coming when you both answer to the same Lord for how you treated each other while you waited.

The distinction we have to recover is the one Romans 14 assumes and our age has lost: the difference between the things worth dividing over and the things that are not. The first-century church divided over whether you could eat meat sacrificed to idols. Ours divides over tax policy and border policy and which strongman to fear most. I am not saying these questions do not matter. I am saying they are not the gospel, and a church that treats a policy disagreement as a test of fellowship has confused a disputable matter with a damnable one. That confusion is precisely what the capture produces. It takes a contested question and inflates it into a creed, so that to disagree is no longer to differ but to betray.

## Build the alternative liturgy or lose by default

Hauerwas and Willimon saw this coming in 1989. *Resident Aliens* argued that the church's first political act is not to take a position on the issues of the day but to be the church, a community whose common life is itself a witness, a colony of heaven in a world that has forgotten heaven exists. They were writing against the assumption that Christianity's job is to make America work better. Their claim was sharper: the church is a *polis* of its own, an alternative society, and its members are dual citizens whose deeper loyalty relativizes the shallower one. "The church doesn't have a social strategy," they wrote. "The church is a social strategy."

I resisted that book for years because it sounded like retreat. I have come to think it is the opposite. The reason cable news captures our people is that it offers them a community of meaning, a tribe with a story and an enemy and a sense of belonging, and too many of our churches offer them a service to attend and a building to maintain. We cannot out-shout the screen. But we can do the one thing the screen cannot do. We can put a person who voted one way at a table beside a person who voted the other way and have them pass the bread to each other and call each other brother, and mean it. That table is an argument no broadcast can answer. It is the demonstration that something binds these people deeper than the thing dividing everyone else.

This is why Ephesians 4 is not decoration. *I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace* (Ephesians 4:1–3). Note that Paul commands them to *maintain* a unity that already exists, *one body and one Spirit . . . one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all* (Ephesians 4:4–6). The unity is not something we manufacture by agreeing. It is something Christ already accomplished and we are charged to guard. The captured congregation has not lost a unity. It has stopped maintaining one it still possesses, because it has been taught by a more diligent teacher that the people across the aisle are the threat.

## The slow recovery, and why it has to be slow

So what do you actually do on Monday. Not much that will feel like enough, and that is the hardest part for those of us who want a strategy that works by Christmas.

You preach the whole text, including the parts that wound your own side, so that no one can predict your politics from your exposition. You catechize, relentlessly and unfashionably, because a people who know what they believe are harder to capture than a people who only know what they feel. You build the practices that form loves, the table, confession, the Psalms in the mouth, the long prayer for the very leaders your people fear, because James K. A. Smith is right that we are shaped more by what we repeatedly do than by what we occasionally think. You sit with the frightened man and you do not argue him out of his channel; you ask him what he is afraid of, and you stay long enough to hear that underneath the politics is usually a father's terror for his children's world, which is a fear the gospel actually has something to say to.

And you accept that you will not win the forty-hour war with forty minutes. You will win, if you win, the way Peterson said you win everything in this vocation: slowly, locally, by being present over years in a way no broadcast can be, until the relationship you have built outweighs the relationship the screen has built, and the man trusts your voice enough to question the other one. There is no shortcut. The shortcut is what the network sells, and selling shortcuts is how it captured him in the first place.

## Resist the capture in your own ministry first

There is a version of this essay I could have written that would have let me off the hook, and it is the version most of us prefer to read. It treats the captured congregation as a problem out there, a flock that has wandered while the shepherd stood faithful at the gate. That version is a lie, and the lie is comfortable, which is how I know to distrust it. The pastor is in the same current as the people, watching some of the same screens, feeling the same pull toward the certainty and the outrage and the warm sense of being among the right ones. The capture does not knock on the study door and ask permission. It seeps in through the same channels it uses on everyone, and it deforms the ministry in ways we are slow to name.

It shows in which sins we preach against and which we leave alone, and the pattern usually maps with embarrassing precision onto the sins of the other tribe. It shows in whose funerals we are warm at and whose we are merely correct at. It shows in the private relief we feel when a member who annoyed us politically leaves the church, a relief that should frighten any man who has read the parable of the ninety-nine. Hauerwas and Willimon insisted that the church is meant to be a community of character that produces a particular kind of person, and the pastor is the first product on the line. If outrage has formed me before it formed them, then every counter-liturgy I try to build will carry the contamination, because a shepherd cannot lead a flock somewhere he has not gone. The work of un-capturing the congregation begins, humiliatingly, with the un-capturing of the man who is supposed to be doing it, which is a work only the Spirit does, and only in a man honest enough to admit he needs it.

The congregation will not be saved by a better argument than the one on television. It will be saved, if it is saved, by a deeper belonging than the one on television, and that belonging is built one shared table, one honest conversation, one un-takeback prayer at a time, by a pastor patient enough to lose every news cycle while quietly winning the soul. The screen has the hours. We have the years. And we have a table the screen will never set, where enemies eat as brothers because a third party has made peace between them at his own expense. We have not yet begun to use it.
posts.excerpt: Your people are being discipled forty hours a week by a screen that knows them better than you do. A working pastor on shepherding a congregation whose first language has quietly become cable news.

posts.title: How to Preach to a Politically Divided Church
posts.body:
Somewhere around the third sentence of the sermon, the room sorts itself. You can feel it happen. A phrase lands and one section of the congregation leans in, recognizing an ally, while another section pulls back a half inch, bracing for betrayal. You have not said anything political yet. You said the word *justice*, or the word *order*, or you named the poor, or you named the unborn, and the room did the math before you finished the clause. They are not listening to your argument. They are listening for your jersey.

This is the condition of preaching now, and the temptations it produces are two, and they are opposite, and most of us oscillate between them. The first is to choose a side, to give the half of the room that already agrees the satisfaction of hearing you say it, because the warmth coming back at you feels, in the moment, like effectiveness. The second is to go silent, to preach only the safe, internal, spiritualized text, to wall off whole books of the Bible because they will be heard as a vote, until your preaching has nothing to say about anything anyone is actually afraid of. **One temptation makes you a chaplain to a tribe. The other makes you a chaplain to no one. Both are a dereliction, and both feel like wisdom from the inside.**

I have done both. I have preached the sermon that flattered my own instincts and called it courage, and I have ducked a text I should have preached and called it prudence. The work I am describing is not work I have mastered. It is work I am still learning to do without flinching toward either ditch.

## The whole counsel is not optional, and it was never safe

Paul, saying goodbye to the Ephesian elders, makes a claim about his own preaching that should unsettle every one of us who has trimmed a sermon to keep the peace: *I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God* (Acts 20:27). The whole counsel. Not the comfortable counsel. Not the half that plays well with the donors. The whole of it, which means the parts that comfort the afflicted and the parts that afflict the comfortable, the texts that wound the left and the texts that wound the right, the God who defends the widow and the orphan and the immigrant and the God who will by no means clear the guilty.

The shrinking Paul refused to do is the shrinking we have perfected. We have learned to preach a Bible with the political nerve removed, a private gospel about my heart and my anxiety and my personal walk, carefully sealed off from anything that might be overheard as a position. We tell ourselves this is keeping the main thing the main thing. It is not. It is editing God down to the size of a room that will not be offended, and a God who cannot offend the room is not the God of Amos or Jeremiah or the carpenter who turned over the tables.

The instruction to the young pastor is famous and we have domesticated it: *preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching* (2 Timothy 4:2). Read it slowly. *Reprove. Rebuke.* Those are not gentle words. They are the words of a man who expects his preaching to cut, who knows that *out of season* means the times when the cutting is unwelcome, which is exactly when the temptation to shrink is strongest. The verse that follows is the one about itching ears, about people accumulating teachers who tell them what they already want. Paul sets the whole counsel directly against the itching ear. To preach the whole counsel is, by definition, to tell the room something it did not come to hear.

## Brueggemann and the difference between a memo and a poem

Walter Brueggemann gave us the language for why so much of our political preaching fails even when it is brave. In *Finally Comes the Poet* (1989), he argued that the preacher's task is not to deliver prose to a settled world but to speak a poem into a world that has gone numb, to crack open the reduced, flattened imagination of people who have stopped expecting God to do anything. The prophets, he said, did not win by stating the obvious more loudly. They won by reframing reality so completely that the listener saw his own life inside a story he had been refusing to see.

This is the key the divided room hands us, if we will take it. The reason a congregation hears politics is that the politicians and the broadcasters got there first and supplied the only frame the people have. They handed your members a reduced map, a flat world of two teams, where every question has a red answer and a blue answer and nothing else. When you preach in prose against that map, naming positions and taking sides, you are playing on their board, and you will be scored by their rules. But when you preach as the poet Brueggemann describes, when you open the strange, larger world of the text until the familiar fight looks small inside it, you are not taking a side in their argument. You are dissolving the frame that made the argument seem like the whole of reality.
