The silence you are in is not the absence of God. It is the absence of the feeling of God, and the two are not the same thing, and learning the difference may be the most important work your faith ever does.

Keep walking. The dark is not the end of the road. It is the part of the road where you finally learn whose hand you are holding.
posts.excerpt: The silence is not punishment and it is not your failure. The tradition has a name for it, and the name is the beginning of surviving it.

posts.title: What If Christianity Is Wrong?
posts.body:
The question does not knock. It is already in the room.

You are driving, or you are awake at two in the morning, or you are halfway through a hymn you have sung a thousand times, and it surfaces with no warning and no mercy. *What if we are wrong.* What if the whole thing is a beautiful, two-thousand-year-old story that frightened people told themselves so they could bear the dark. What if the building you have given your life to was built on nothing, and everyone inside it is too invested to say so out loud. The question feels less like temptation than like clarity, like a curtain pulled back, like the one honest thought in a life of performed certainty. That is what makes it terrifying. And it is the exact phrase a believer types into the search bar when the house is asleep, what if Christianity is wrong, half hoping for an argument strong enough to make it stop.

I want to say something most pastors will not say from a stage. I have asked it. I came to faith from atheism, so the question is not a foreign army to me; it is my own first language, and it never fully leaves. There are mornings I wake and for a few seconds the whole edifice looks like wishful thinking, an elaborate consolation built over a void, and I have learned not to panic at those seconds. A faith that has never met the question has only been sheltered, never tested, and sheltered faith breaks the first time the weather turns, usually at a funeral, usually too late to find out it was never load-bearing. So let us actually ask it, all the way down, without flinching. What if we are wrong.

## The doubt is not the neutral position

Start by noticing what the question quietly assumes.

It assumes that doubt is the neutral ground and belief is the leap, that the skeptic stands on bedrock and the believer floats out over the void. But this is not neutral at all. It is a particular faith with its own unexamined creed. To say that the universe is finally meaningless, that consciousness is an accident of chemistry, that love is a neurological event evolution dressed up to keep us breeding, that justice is a preference with no foundation outside the skull, these are claims as large as any in the Apostles' Creed, and the person making them cannot prove a single one. He holds them by faith, the same way I hold mine, except that he has been told his faith is the absence of faith, and he believes it, and the believing is the most unexamined thing about him. **Everyone is believing something they cannot prove.** The honest question is not whether you have faith. The honest question is which faith carries the weight of an actual life, a deathbed, a betrayal, a child in a hospital bed, without collapsing into a consolation it has no right to.

Charles Taylor gave this its name, and the name is part of the answer. In *A Secular Age* (2007) he describes the modern condition as one in which every belief is haunted by its alternatives. The believer feels the pull of unbelief in the empty hour; the unbeliever feels the pull of belief in the cathedral, at the graveside, under a sky of stars that will not stop suggesting something. None of us holds a position the others cannot reach. Five hundred years ago, Taylor argues, atheism was nearly unthinkable, not because people were stupid but because the whole world pressed belief upon them. Now belief is the contested thing, and we feel the contesting in our own chests, every one of us. Taylor's point is not that the cross-pressure proves anyone right. His point is that it is the air we all breathe, and the man who thinks his doubt is pure reason is exactly as naive as the man who thinks his belief has never wavered. We are all standing in the same wind, and the wind does not settle the question. It only humbles everyone in the room.

## If we are wrong, we are wrong about a tomb

The question deserves a real answer, not just a reframe, so here is where I plant my feet.

If we are wrong, we are wrong about a tomb. The whole structure stands or falls on one morning outside Jerusalem, and the New Testament is not coy about this, Paul says flatly that if Christ has not been raised, the faith is futile and the preachers are liars and the dead are simply dead. There is no inspirational fallback, no Jesus-as-good-teacher consolation prize. It is the resurrection or it is nothing, and the writers stake everything on it precisely where a fraud would hedge.

Tom Holland is worth listening to here, because he is no apologist. In *Dominion* (2019) he describes spending a long secular career assuming Christianity was a footnote to the real story of the West, and arriving, against his own expectations, at the opposite conclusion. Something happened in the first century that turned a scattering of terrified Galileans, men who had run, denied, hidden behind locked doors, into people who would die rather than recant a thing they claimed to have seen with their eyes. People do not die for a story they know they invented. They die for a body they are sure was missing and a face they are sure they saw, and they kept dying for it, in arenas, for three hundred years, with every incentive to stop. You can call them deluded. You cannot easily call them liars, and you cannot explain them away as cleanly as the secular story needs you to. **The resurrection is either the worst-attested fraud in history or the hinge of it. There is no comfortable middle**, and the discomfort of that is itself a kind of evidence, the story refuses to shrink into something safe.

And notice what Scripture does with doubt, because it is not what your fear expects. It does not banish the doubters. It builds on one. Thomas says he will not believe unless he puts his hand in the wounds, and Jesus does not rebuke him from a safe distance or shame him out of the room. He shows up. *Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side.* The risen Christ accommodates the doubter, invites the hand into the wound, makes room for the man who needed evidence and would not pretend otherwise. The faith was never afraid of Thomas. The church that is afraid of its Thomases has lost its nerve and forgotten its own founding scene, in which the resurrected Lord met honest doubt not with a threat but with a wound to touch. And the father in Mark 9 prays the truest sentence a doubter ever prayed, *I believe; help my unbelief*, holding both at once, faith and its absence in a single breath, and Jesus heals the boy anyway. He did not wait for the man to resolve the contradiction. He worked through the crack. He always works through the crack.

## The morality you cannot stop believing

There is a second answer, quieter than the tomb but it has kept me up on its own nights.

If we are wrong, we are wrong about the things we cannot stop believing anyway. That the weak deserve protection. That a person is worth more than his usefulness. That cruelty is not merely inefficient but evil, actually evil, evil in the dark, evil whether or not anyone is watching or remembers or is harmed in a way the ledger could measure. The strongest secular answer does not concede this: moral realists argue that the wrongness of cruelty is a fact as real and mind-independent as a mathematical truth, seen and not invented, binding whether or not anyone decreed it and needing no God to be so. The harder question is not whether the conviction is real but where it came from, and whether it survives being cut from its root. Holland's whole argument in *Dominion* is that the modern West is running on borrowed Christian capital, spending moral convictions it did not earn and cannot account for, certain that human dignity is real while having quietly bulldozed the only soil in which that idea ever grew. Where does the worth of the weak come from, if we are wrong? Not from nature, which is indifferent. Not from evolution, which favors the strong. It came from a crucified God who chose the powerless and called them blessed, and the modern moral conscience is his fingerprint on a culture that has stopped believing in his hand.

The atheist who weeps at injustice is a believer with cold feet. He has kept the morality and burned the mortgage that paid for it, and the house stays warm for a while after the fire goes out, a generation, maybe two. I lived in that house. I know how warm it stays, and I know the cold that comes when you finally notice no one is keeping the furnace lit. You can believe the universe is meaningless and still flinch at a child's suffering, but the flinch is a memory, not a foundation. It is borrowed. It will not survive the people who think it through.

This is the part the question never accounts for when it visits at two in the morning. It comes dressed as the brave option, the cost-free clarity, the thought that finally tells the truth no one else will. But it is not cost-free, and it is not the truth no one will tell. It is a wager with a price tag the night conveniently hides. To say *we are wrong* is to say that the dignity of your own children is a fiction, that the love you would die for is a trick of chemistry, that the injustice that makes your hands shake is a preference and nothing more. The question presents the bill for belief and pockets the bill for unbelief. It asks what it costs to be wrong about God and never once asks what it costs to be wrong about the void. Both bets are total. Both stake the whole of a life. The only dishonesty available in the room is to pretend that one side of it is free.

## You cannot escape the wager

So what do you do with the question that is already in the room.

You let it sit. You do not medicate it with louder worship or kill it with a quick apologetic you do not actually believe, because a doubt that is suppressed only goes underground and rots into the thing that walks you out the door at fifty. You hold it the way the psalmists held theirs, out loud, addressed to a God you are not yet sure is listening. *Why do you hide your face? How long must I wrestle with my thoughts?* You read the people who asked it harder than you and stayed. And you make a wager, because there is no position that escapes the wager, only positions that pretend to. The skeptic wagers his one life on emptiness, on the bet that the tomb stayed shut, that the dignity he can't stop defending is a fiction, that the love he would die for is a chemical. You wager yours on the tomb. Both of you are betting your whole existence on something you cannot prove. The honest ones on both sides know it.

Here is what fifteen years of pastoring has shown me, buried under all the certainty people perform on Sunday. The people whose faith finally held were never the ones who never doubted. They were the ones who took the question all the way down, hit what they thought was the bottom, and discovered it was not the bottom, that underneath the worst night there was a floor they had not put there. Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote some of his deepest faith from a Nazi cell, expecting to be hanged, and was hanged, in April 1945, weeks before the camp was liberated. Doubt did not destroy him. It burned away everything that could be taken until what was left could not be, and what was left went to the gallows quietly, having already settled the question the rest of us run from.

You are afraid the question will end your faith. It might end a version of it, the inherited one, the unexamined one, the sheltered one that was always going to break. Let it.

What if we are wrong. And what if, having asked it honestly, all the way to the floor, you find you cannot get the stone to stay in front of the tomb.
posts.excerpt: The question arrives uninvited, usually at night: what if the whole thing is a story we told ourselves? A faith that cannot survive the question was never faith. It was shelter.

posts.title: When Fear Starts Rewriting What You Believe
posts.body:
The first thing fear does is dress itself as discernment.

It tells you the worry is wisdom. It tells you the dread is just spiritual seriousness, that the knot in your stomach at three in the morning is a kind of vigilance God requires of the faithful. So you pray harder, and the praying becomes a way of managing the panic, and somewhere in there the God you are praying to starts to look like the thing you are afraid of. You did not decide this. No one decides this. **Fear rewrites your theology while you sleep, and you wake up believing in a God you would never have chosen on a clear morning.**

I know this because I have lived inside it. I came to faith out of atheism, which means I know what it is to build a god out of nothing and call it nature, to assemble a universe with no one home in it and learn to live in the cold of that. What I learned later is harder to admit. A Christian can do the same thing in reverse. You can keep the name of the God of Jesus Christ and quietly swap the face. The new face is the one fear gives you, and it is the question that drives people to the search bar at two in the morning, why am I afraid of God, why does the faith that was supposed to free me feel like a hand at my throat. The honest answer is that fear got into the foundations, and it did not knock.

## What fear actually does to a mind

Consider the machinery before you blame the soul.

Fear narrows. That is its whole job. The amygdala does not write essays; it sounds an alarm and shuts down the slow rooms of the brain where reflection lives, the rooms where you weigh, qualify, hold two things at once. Jonathan Haidt, in *The Righteous Mind* (2012), describes the rider and the elephant, the small rational rider perched on the back of an enormous emotional animal that goes where it wants. Under threat the rider does not steer. The rider explains. The rider produces reasons, fast and fluent, for wherever the elephant already lunged, and the reasons feel exactly like thinking because, structurally, they are. And so a frightened Christian produces frightened theology and calls it conviction, because the rider is very good at making the panic sound like principle. The theology is real. It just isn't reasoned. It is the alarm, given vocabulary.

This is how the gentlest people end up with the cruelest doctrines. Not through study. Through dread. The man who would never strike a child preaches a God who will not stop striking. The woman who forgives everyone forgives herself nothing, because the God in her chest keeps a ledger she can never close. Neither of them argued their way there. They were carried there by a feeling that learned to talk.

And you can watch the same thing happen at the scale of a whole culture, which is why the search query keeps changing form but never disappears. Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* (2007), describes the modern condition as the loss of a world we could take for granted, the buffered self standing alone in a disenchanted room where there used to be a cosmos full of meaning pressing in from every side. We are afraid in a way our grandparents were not, because the floor that held them has been pulled up and we know it is gone, and no amount of certainty puts it back. **A church that is afraid does not preach the kingdom. It preaches the bunker.** It draws the line tighter, names the enemy faster, mistakes its own anxiety for the holiness of God. The fortress feels like faithfulness. It is fear with a steeple.

## I have preached the bunker

I want to be precise about this, because it is easy to write these sentences as though the failure belongs to other pastors, the loud ones, the ones on television. It does not. There were seasons when I read the headlines before I read the Psalms, and the headlines won, and what came out of me on Sunday had the cadence of the gospel and the marrow of dread. The people felt it. Fear is contagious from a pulpit the way a yawn is contagious across a room; it does not need to be argued, only modeled. I taught a frightened God to a frightened room, and we comforted one another in the wrong thing, and we called the comfort faith because it came with chapter and verse.

The terrible mercy of it is that fearful religion works, for a while. It organizes the world. It tells you who is safe and who is not, what to defend and whom to suspect, and the organizing feels like clarity, and clarity feels like God. This is the trap inside the trap. The frightened God is useful. He gives you something to do with the dread. He turns the formless three-in-the-morning terror into a project, a doctrine to guard, a boundary to police, an enemy to name, and the project is so absorbing that you never notice you have stopped worshiping and started bracing.

## The fear that heals and the fear that hides

Scripture is not naive about any of this. The most repeated command in the book is aimed straight at it.

Three hundred times, give or take, the line returns. *Do not be afraid.* It is the first word of the angel at the empty tomb and the first word of the angel over the shepherds. It is what God says to Abram in the dark, to Israel pinned against the sea, to the disciples white-knuckled in the boat. If you wanted the one sentence God says more than any other to human beings, that is the sentence, and the frequency is the revelation. The command is not given to the brave. It is given to the terrified, over and over, because the terrified are who we are, and God knows it, and keeps saying it anyway to people who keep not believing it.

But fear has a counterfeit even here, and this is where the search for honest answers gets hard. There is a fear of God that Scripture commends, the beginning of wisdom, the trembling reverence of a creature before the Creator, and frightened religion is very good at impersonating it. The two are not the same, and learning to tell them apart may be the most important diagnostic work a believer ever does. The fear of the Lord in the Psalms produces nearness. The worshiper draws closer, sings, lingers in the courts, cannot stay away. Anxiety produces distance. It backs out of the room. It builds rules to keep God at arm's length so the relationship never has to risk anything real, because intimacy with a God you suspect of cruelty is unbearable, and so the anxious soul chooses management over communion every time and calls the management holiness.

You can test your theology against this, and the test is brutally simple. Does your picture of God make you want to come near, or to hide in the trees like Adam? Adam's first theology after the fall was fear, and the first thing fear told him was that God was hunting him. *I heard you in the garden, and I was afraid, so I hid.* God was not hunting him. God was walking in the cool of the day, calling his name, asking the only question fear cannot answer, *where are you*. The fear had already rewritten the relationship before God said a word. The hiding was the theology. Adam met grace and read it as a manhunt, because fear had gotten there first and recolored the whole face of God.

## The verse we quote and do not believe

*Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment.* John writes it plainly in his first letter, and we read it as a greeting card, and we miss the surgery in it.

Look at the clause we skip. Fear *has to do with punishment.* John is not being sentimental; he is naming a mechanism. Fear is what runs the soul that expects to be punished, and a soul that expects punishment will build a punishing God to match, because the architecture of the inner life always projects itself onto the ceiling. We do not see God as he is. **We see God as we are braced for him to be.** And the bracing is the theology. The bracing is what we defend on Sunday, pass to our children at the dinner table, and mistake for orthodoxy for the rest of our lives. The frightened man does not have wrong information about God. He has a wrong posture toward God, and the posture generates the information.

Walter Brueggemann spent a career insisting that the Psalms refuse to lie about fear, and that the refusal is the recovery. In *The Message of the Psalms* (1984) he traced the movement from orientation through disorientation to a new orientation, and he warned against the thing the frightened church does instinctively, skipping the middle. We want to jump from the settled psalm to the praising psalm without passing through the terrified one, and the skipping is exactly what keeps the fear in charge underground, unspoken, running the show from a basement no one will enter. You cannot cast out what you will not name. The Psalter names it constantly. *My heart is in anguish within me, the terrors of death have fallen upon me.* That is Psalm 55, and it is not weak faith. It is faith dragging the fear into the light where it can finally be seen for what it is, a feeling and not a fact, a weather system and not the face of God. A church that cannot pray the frightened Psalms out loud will preach a frightened God by accident, every single time, because the fear it would not speak does not leave. It just changes pulpits.

## How the rewriting gets undone

So how does it get undone. Not by trying harder to be brave. Bravery is another thing fear can fake; a clenched jaw is not a quiet heart, and white-knuckled certainty is just panic that learned to stand up straight.

The undoing is slower and more humiliating than that. It begins with naming the fear as fear and refusing to let it keep its disguise as discernment, refusing to dignify the three-in-the-morning dread with the word *wisdom* when it is only adrenaline with a theology degree. It continues in the company of people who love you enough to tell you when your God has started to look like your dread, because you will be the last to see it; the rewriting is invisible from inside the rewritten mind. And it ends, if it ends, the way it began for the disciples in the boat, with a man asleep in the storm who wakes and is not afraid, and whose not-being-afraid is the only sermon that finally lands. They had a frightened theology too. *Do you not care that we are perishing.* He cared. He simply was not afraid, and his lack of fear was the revelation. The God they actually had was sleeping through the thing that was killing them, and the storm was no threat to him at all.

There is a difference, then, between a faith that has conquered fear and a faith that has buried it, and the difference shows up under pressure. The buried fear runs the buried God. It waits. It surfaces in the diagnosis, the late-night phone call, the child who walks away, and when it surfaces it brings its theology with it, fully formed, the punishing face you built without consent in a thousand frightened hours. The conquered fear is different. It still comes, Jesus sweat blood in a garden, so do not tell me the goal is never to feel it, but it no longer writes the doctrine. It is felt and named and brought into the light, and the God on the other side of it is not the elephant's god but the real one, the one who keeps saying the sentence to terrified people because terrified people are the only kind he has ever had.

The honest prayer in all of this is old and short. *I believe; help my unbelief.* The father in Mark 9 does not pretend his faith is whole. He brings the cracked thing and asks for it to be mended in the asking, holds out his fear and his faith in the same hand and lets Jesus take both. That is the prayer for the frightened believer. Not a performance of certainty, which is only fear in costume. A confession that the dread has gotten into the foundations, and a request that the God who is not what we are braced for would show his actual face.

Most of us are not defending the faith. We are defending the fear, and calling it the faith.

Look hard at the God you are most certain of when you are most afraid. That is not God. That is the elephant, explained.
posts.excerpt: Fear does not announce itself as fear. It arrives wearing the clothes of conviction, and you wake up believing in a God you would never have chosen on a clear morning.

posts.title: When God Stops Making Sense
posts.body:
You did everything you were told and the math still did not work.

You prayed and the marriage ended anyway. You tithed and the diagnosis came anyway. You raised the kids in the faith and one of them walked away anyway, and somewhere in the wreckage you ran the equation again, the one you were handed in your first year of believing. Faithfulness in, blessing out. It was supposed to balance. It did not balance. And the not-balancing produced a quieter terror than open atheism ever did, because the God you doubted was not a God you had rejected. He was a God who had stopped adding up, and that is the question that drives a believer to type the words into the dark, why doesn't God make sense, why did I do everything right and lose anyway.

I came to faith from atheism, so let me be honest about what I expected on the way in. I expected the universe to make more sense once God was in it. I expected the equation to finally resolve, the loose ends to gather, the cruelty of things to acquire a reason. What I found instead was a God who would not be solved, and it took me years to understand that the unsolvability was not the problem with the faith. **It was the faith.** I had come looking for an answer and been handed a person, and at first I could not tell the difference between those two things, and the whole crisis lived in that gap.

## We were sold a calculation

Somewhere in American Christianity the gospel got reduced to a transaction, and the transaction promised coherence above all.

Tim Keller spent a career taking that apart. In *Walking with God through Pain and Suffering* (2013) he showed that the older, sturdier faith never promised the books would balance in this life, that the assumption of a clean moral ledger, good rewarded and evil punished on a schedule we can audit, is not Christianity but a folk religion wearing its clothes. The prosperity preachers promised the balance outright. The self-help-with-a-cross crowd promised it in softer language, the abundant life as a return on spiritual investment. But the actual Scriptures hand you something stranger and far less marketable. They hand you Job, and Job is the book the equation cannot survive.

Here is a man the text itself calls blameless, and the calamity falls anyway, all of it, in an afternoon. The livestock, the servants, the ten children, the health, the standing. His friends arrive, and they are the theology most of us were raised in, whether we noticed or not. They run the math out loud. Suffering means sin, they reason, so confess the sin and the suffering will lift, because that is how the equation works and the equation must work or the universe is unsafe. They are not cruel men. That is the part we miss. They are orthodox men, careful men, men defending the coherence of God against the obscene evidence of their friend's body, and they spend thirty-some chapters defending it, building the case, quoting the tradition. And at the end God turns to them and says they have not spoken rightly of him.

Read that slowly. The men who defended God's logic are the men God rebukes. The man who shouted at heaven and demanded an accounting is the man God commends. The book is an assault on the equation, written into the canon, left there on purpose by people who knew exactly how dangerous it was to the comfortable version of the faith.

## The answer that refuses to be an answer

And when God finally answers Job, out of the whirlwind, he does not answer the question.

He does not explain the suffering. He never mentions the wager in the prologue, never tells Job why, never produces the chart that would make the afternoon add up. He asks instead about the foundations of the earth, the storehouses of the snow, the wild donkey who scorns the city, the war horse who laughs at fear, the eagle who makes her nest on the crag. It looks like evasion. A frightened reader hears it as a divine non-answer, God changing the subject because he has no defense. It is not evasion. **It is God refusing to be reduced to a function that Job can compute.** And Job's response, when it comes, is not new information. It is relationship. *I had heard of you with the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.* He did not get the answer. He got the Answerer. Those are not the same thing, and the entire book turns on the difference.

This is harder for us than it was for Job, and Charles Taylor told us why. In *A Secular Age* (2007) he describes the buffered self, the modern person sealed inside his own mind, for whom meaning is something we manufacture rather than something we receive. We are the first people in history trained from birth to expect the cosmos to be transparent to reason. We assume that if a thing is real it can be explained, and that if it cannot be explained it is probably not real, or not worth our trust. So when God does not make sense, we hear it as evidence against him, a failure of the system to deliver the transparency the system owed us. Job did not have that reflex. He had the older reflex, the one we lost, the capacity to stay in the room with a God he could not parse, to remain in relationship with an unexplained Person rather than walking out in search of an explanation that fit. We have lost the reflex, and the losing of it is why our doubt cuts deeper and heals slower than his ever did.

## The chart is always cold

I have stood at enough hospital beds to know the equation does not comfort anyone. It only condemns.

When you tell a grieving mother that God has a reason, you have made yourself one of Job's friends, and you have not noticed that the book you are quoting from is the very book that silences you. I have done it. Early on I did it from a kind of fear, the fear that if I could not explain God I would lose him, that an unexplained God was a God halfway to vanishing. So I explained him. I explained him to people who needed his presence and got my chart instead, and the chart was cold, the chart is always cold, because it is the thing we reach for precisely when we cannot bear the silence. We hand the grieving a reason because a reason gives us something to say, and our terror of having nothing to say is so great that we will wound the suffering to relieve it. The friends of Job talked for thirty chapters. The kindest thing in the book is the seven days at the start when they sat with him on the ground and said nothing, because his suffering was very great. Then they opened their mouths, and the comfort ended.

There is a difference, though, between a God who does not make sense and a God who is senseless, and everything hangs on it. A senseless God is chaos with a name, caprice, a coin flip, a force with no coherence behind the silence. The God of Job is not chaos. He is coherent in himself and only opaque to us, the way the foundations of the earth are coherent and only opaque to a man who was not there when they were laid. The opacity is not in God. It is in the gap between his vantage and ours, and that gap is not an insult. It is simply the truth about a creature standing before its Creator. To demand that God be transparent to you is to demand that he be your size. He declines. The declining is mercy, though it does not feel like mercy at the time.

Keller pressed exactly this point, and it is worth following all the way down. A God small enough to be fully explained by you would be a God too small to save you. The very incomprehensibility that feels, in the hospital corridor, like abandonment is the flip side of the thing you actually need, a God whose purposes run deeper than your sight, which means deeper than your catastrophe. If you could audit his reasons, he would be a manager, not a maker. And a managed universe holds no rescue you did not already foresee. The unexplained God is the only kind worth crying out to, because he is the only kind who might be doing something in the dark that you, from inside the dark, cannot yet see. **The same opacity that wounds you is the only ground there is for hope.** Take away the mystery and you take away the rescue in the same motion.

This is the thing the equation can never hold, and why the equation finally breaks every honest person who clings to it. The equation assumes you can see the whole board. It assumes the relevant variables are the ones in your line of sight, your faithfulness, your prayer, your tithe, your obedience, and that the output should follow from those inputs on a timetable you can read. Job's friends believed they could see the whole board. That was their error, dressed up as orthodoxy. They thought God's justice had to be legible to them or it was not justice, and so when the evidence stopped fitting their math, they did not doubt the math. They blamed the man. The equation always ends there. When reality refuses to balance, the equation does not confess its own poverty. It finds someone to condemn, your friend, or God, or finally yourself.

## Lament is the language of people who still believe

The Psalms live in this exact gap, and they are louder about it than we are comfortable with.

*How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?* That is Psalm 13, and it is not a crisis of faith. It is faith doing the one thing only faith can do, which is to address the silence rather than walk away from it. The atheist does not write Psalm 13. The atheist has no one to shout at; the silence is just silence, the universe being what it always was. Lament is the native tongue of people who still believe and cannot make it add up, and Scripture is full of it, a third of the Psalter, by some counts, because God is not embarrassed by it. He canonized it. He put the angry prayers in the book and called them prayer. The church that has no room for *how long* has a smaller God than the one who inspired the question, a God who can only be praised and never wept at, and that God will not survive a hospital corridor at midnight.

So what do you do when God does not make sense. You stop demanding that he do, not because the demand is wrong, since Job demanded and was praised, but because the demand was never the point and resolution was never the promise. You learn the difference between an explanation and a presence, and you learn it the hard way, usually at a graveside, usually after the charts have all failed you. You pray the angry Psalms instead of swallowing them, because the swallowed prayer rots into the unspoken doubt that finally walks you out the door. And you wait in the silence the way Job waited, not because the silence is comfortable but because the alternative is to walk out of the room where God actually is, into a room where everything makes sense and no one is home. That second room is on offer. It always is. It is clean and bright and explicable and empty, and a great many people have moved into it and called the emptiness honesty.

The cross is the place this all converges. The most God-forsaken cry in Scripture comes from the mouth of God himself, *my God, my God, why have you forsaken me*, and it is a question, and it is not answered from the sky, and three days later the answer turns out to be a Person and not a sentence. That is the pattern. It has always been the pattern. **The God of the Bible does not hand you the equation. He climbs into the part of it that does not balance** and dies there, and rises, and the rising is not an explanation either. It is a presence that outlasts the question.

You wanted a God who would make sense. You were given a God who makes scars, and shows them to the doubter, and says, put your hand here.

Stop solving him. Start following him into the dark, where the seeing finally happens.
posts.excerpt: We were sold a God who would add up. The God of the Bible refuses the equation, and the refusal is not a flaw in the system. It is the system.

posts.title: Why Does God Allow Suffering?
posts.body:
The reasons start arriving before the casket is in the ground.

Someone tells you it was God's plan. Someone tells you that God needed another angel, which is not even good theology, but they mean well and you nod. Someone tells you everything happens for a reason, and you can see in their face that they need this to be true more than you do, that they are not comforting you so much as steadying themselves against a world where a thing like this could happen to a person like you for no reason at all. Someone, eventually, tells you that God will use it. Maybe he will. But you notice that all of them, every one, has arrived with a reason. As if the unbearable thing about your loss were the absence of an explanation, and a good enough sentence might close the wound.

It will not. And the oldest book in the Bible on the subject agrees with you. If you have ever asked, into the dark, why God allows suffering, and gotten back only the sound of people filling the silence, you are in older company than you know.

## Thirty-seven chapters of being wrong

The book of Job is long, and it is long on purpose, and the length is the argument.

A righteous man loses everything in an afternoon, his wealth, his servants, and then, in a single sentence the narrator refuses to slow down for, all ten of his children, killed when the house fell on them at a feast. Job sits in the ashes. He tears his robe. And then his friends arrive, and they do the one thing in the whole book that anyone does right: they sit with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and they say nothing, because they see that his suffering is very great.

Then they open their mouths, and for the next thirty-some chapters they explain. They are not villains. They are orthodox. Everything they say is the conventional theology of their day, and much of it sounds like the theology of ours. God is just. God does not punish the innocent. Therefore Job must have sinned, and if Job will only confess, the suffering will lift and the equation will balance. Suffering is the effect; sin is the cause; find the cause and the universe makes sense again and the friends can go home to their own children with the world still safe.

They are wrong. The book tells us at the very start that they are wrong, we, the readers, were shown in the first chapter that Job is blameless, before the friends ever spoke a word. So we watch thirty-seven chapters of confident, articulate, theologically respectable people explaining a man's suffering, and we know the whole time that every explanation is false. The book is, among other things, a sustained portrait of religious people doing harm with their certainty. They came with reasons. The reasons were a second affliction laid on top of the first, and the second one they delivered with their own mouths.

## When God finally speaks

Then God answers. After all the human explaining, the voice comes out of the whirlwind, and here is the thing that should stop us cold. God does not explain.

He does not tell Job about the scene in heaven from chapter one, the wager, the accuser, the reason behind it all. Job never learns why. He dies, at the end of a long restored life, still not knowing why his first ten children were taken. Instead God asks questions, dozens of them, vast and strange and beautiful. *Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Have you entered the storehouses of the snow? Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades? Do you give the horse his might? Who provides for the raven its prey?* It is not an argument. It is a tour of a creation too large and too wild for Job to have authored or even to comprehend. God does not say *here is the reason.* God says, in effect, *you are speaking about things larger than you knew, and I am here, and I am not absent, and I am not asleep.*

And Job is satisfied. Not because he got the explanation, he did not, but because he got God. *I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.* The encounter did what the explanation could not. He had wanted a reason, and he received a presence, and the presence turned out to be the thing he had actually been after the whole time, underneath the demand for an answer.

Then comes the verdict the church loves to skip. God turns to the friends, the orthodox explainers, and tells them he is angry with them, *for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.* The men who defended God are rebuked. The man who accused him, who demanded an audience, who refused the easy reasons and hurled his complaint at the sky, he is the one who spoke rightly. **Let that land on every comforter who ever arrived with a verse and a theory: God preferred the honest complaint to the tidy defense.** He was angrier at the men who explained his ways than at the man who shouted at him for them.

## Why the explanation would not help anyway

Here is what I have come to believe after years of sitting in these rooms. Even if you could have the reason, it would not do what you imagine it would do.

Suppose God pulled back the curtain and showed you the entire chain of causes, the whole architecture of how this loss serves some good you cannot now see. Suppose you understood it completely, the way Job's friends were so sure they did. Your child would still be gone. The understanding would not return what was taken. It would only convert your grief into a transaction, you lost this in order to gain that, and a person you love is not a price paid for a benefit received. To accept the explanation would be to agree that the trade was worth it. And there is no parent alive who would make that trade, and God, mercifully, does not ask you to. The reason, if you had it, would ask you to sign off on the death of the one you love as a fair exchange. You would refuse. You would be right to refuse.

The free-will defense, the soul-making theodicy, the greater-good argument, the philosophers have built these, and they are not nothing, and I have read them carefully and even taught them to students with a clear conscience. But every one of them works at the altitude of the argument, and grief does not live at that altitude. Grief lives in the kitchen at six in the morning, with one fewer place to set at the table, with the coffee mug that is still in the cabinet because you cannot make yourself give it away. No syllogism reaches that kitchen. No proof has ever set a fourth place. Only a presence reaches the kitchen.

## The ones who stopped explaining

The people who have written most truly about loss are the ones who had built explanations first, and then watched a death take the explanations apart.

C.S. Lewis wrote *The Problem of Pain* in 1940, a clear, ordered, persuasive account of how suffering fits inside a good God's world. It is a fine book. It is a book written from the outside, by a man who had thought hard about grief without yet being inside one. Then his wife Joy died in 1960, and he wrote *A Grief Observed* (1961), and it is the same man and not the same man at all. The later book does not explain. It records. It refuses the consolations the earlier book had offered so calmly, and the refusal is not a loss of faith. It is faith arriving in the kitchen, where the proofs do not reach. Lewis did not retract *The Problem of Pain.* He simply discovered that a true thing said from a safe distance does nothing for the person under the rubble, and he had become the person under the rubble.

Nicholas Wolterstorff was a philosopher by trade, a man whose whole working life was argument, when his son Eric died on a mountain in 1983 at twenty-five. He wrote *Lament for a Son* (1987), and a philosopher's book it is not. It is fragments, refusals, a flat insistence on the size of the thing. *Don't say it's not really so bad,* he wrote. *Because it is. Death is awful, demonic.* He would not let the theodicies he himself could have constructed shrink the loss to a manageable size. And what he found, where the explanation should have been, was not a reason but a revised picture of God: *God is not only the God of the sufferers but the God who suffers.* He did not get an answer. He got a companion in the ash heap, which Job got too, and which turns out to be the only thing the book of Job ever promised.

## The harm the reasons do

I want to be honest about something the church does not like to admit. The reasons we hand the grieving are not neutral. They are not merely unhelpful. They wound, and they wound in a particular way, and we should name it.

When you tell a grieving mother that God took her child for a reason, you have told her that God is the agent of her child's death and that he had a purpose worth her child's life. You may not have meant that. You almost certainly did not. But that is the sentence she now has to live with, and she will turn it over at three in the morning, and it will curdle. Either God is cruel, having traded her son for some greater good she is not permitted to see, or the comforter was talking nonsense to fill a silence they could not bear. Those are the only two places the sentence leads, and both are worse than the honest *I don't know* the comforter was too frightened to say.

Job's friends did this. They were not malicious. They were anxious. A man was suffering in front of them with no apparent cause, and the absence of a cause threatened their whole picture of an orderly, just universe, so they manufactured a cause and laid it on him. *You must have sinned.* They did it to keep their own world intact. The explanation served the comforter, not the sufferer. It always does. When we explain a grief that is not ours, we are most often steadying ourselves, building a small wall of reasons between us and the terrifying possibility that this could happen to anyone, including us, for nothing. The reasons are not for the bereaved. They are for the frightened.

The most faithful thing the friends ever did was the seven days of silence at the beginning, before they opened their mouths. If they had simply stayed in the ashes and said nothing, the book of Job would be a story about good friends. It became a story about bad theology the moment they decided that the silence needed filling. Most of us cannot leave the silence alone either. We should learn to. The silence, held with someone, is closer to the presence of God than any reason we could invent to break it.

## The God who entered it instead

So the Christian claim is not finally a reason. It is a person.

When God moved to address the suffering of the world, he did not send down a fuller explanation. He did not transmit a better theodicy from a safe distance. He came. He took a body, and the body could be hurt, and it was. He stood at the grave of his friend Lazarus, knowing he would raise him within the hour, knowing the happy ending was minutes away, and the shortest verse in the Bible records what he did first. *Jesus wept.* He did not skip to the resurrection. He did not tell Mary and Martha to cheer up because the explanation was coming and the good ending was already loaded. He stood in the stink of death, among people who were furious he had come too late, and he cried. The God who weeps at a grave he is about to empty is the only God worth having when you are standing at one that will not be emptied this side of the world's end.

That is the answer the Bible gives. Not the reason you asked for. The presence you actually needed. A God who came down into the suffering rather than narrating it from a safe height. A God who, in Job, refused to explain, and in Christ, refused to stay away. The two refusals are the same mercy from two directions.

I cannot give you the reason. I have stopped trying, and I have come to think the stopping was obedience and not defeat. What I can tell you is that the absence of a reason is not the absence of God. He has been in the ashes with Job. He wept at the grave with the sisters. He never told Job why, and he was not, for one moment of that whole long book, absent from him.

He showed up instead. He is still doing it. He has not explained a thing.
posts.excerpt: Everyone arrives with a reason. The book of Job spends thirty-seven chapters refusing every reason offered, and when God finally speaks, he never gives one either.

posts.title: Where Is God on Holy Saturday?
posts.body:
We are very good at Friday and Sunday. We have almost nothing for Saturday.

Walk into almost any church and you will find a theology of the cross. We can preach it. We have the atonement worked out in five competing models, and we can argue them at conferences over coffee. Walk into the same church on Easter and you will find a theology of the resurrection, with trumpets, with lilies, with a sanctuary so full the ushers bring out folding chairs. The two great days of the Christian story are covered. We have books on them. We have hymns for them. We have built our whole emotional architecture on the pivot from one to the other, the Friday we mourn briefly and the Sunday we celebrate loudly.

There is a third day, and we have almost nothing.

Holy Saturday. The day the body lay in the tomb. The day after God died and before God rose. The disciples lived a whole day inside it, a real day with real hours, and the Gospels say next to nothing about it because there was nothing to report. No miracle. No appearance. No word from heaven. Just a sealed stone and a dead teacher and a group of people whose entire understanding of the world had collapsed on Friday afternoon and would not be rebuilt until a morning they had no reason to expect.

That is the day most of the grieving are actually living in. And almost no one is preaching to them there.

## The day with no content

Notice what Saturday is not. It is not Friday.

Friday is catastrophe, and catastrophe at least has shape. Friday you can name what is happening, he is dying, it is finished, the worst is occurring before your eyes. There is a terrible clarity to Friday. The phone rings at the hour phones should not ring. The doctor uses the word. The grief has an event to attach itself to, an hour you can point to, a thing that happened.

Saturday has no event. The catastrophe already happened. It happened yesterday, and now there is only the long flat stretch of after, when the casket is in the ground and the relatives have gone home and the dishes have been returned to their owners, and you are left with a Tuesday, and another Tuesday, and the slow horror of discovering that life intends to keep being ordinary around a hole it refuses to acknowledge. The mail comes. The bills come addressed to a name that no longer answers. Saturday is not the wound. Saturday is the endless afternoon in which you find out the wound is not going to close on the schedule everyone implied.

Saturday is not Sunday either. This is the part we will not sit still for. We rush the grieving toward Sunday, *they're in a better place, you'll see them again, God works all things together.* All of it may be true. None of it is Saturday. On Saturday the resurrection has not happened yet, and to a person living inside their Saturday, our Sunday talk sounds like someone narrating the ending of a film to a man who is still watching, in the dark, the part where the hero dies. We are not comforting him. We are refusing to be in the theater with him.

The disciples did not have Sunday on Saturday. They had only the dead body and the dark. And the faith they were given, the faith we inherit from them, includes that day. It is on the calendar. The church, in its wisdom, did not skip from Good Friday to Easter. It left Saturday standing, empty, unprogrammed, a whole liturgical day with almost nothing in it but waiting. We forgot what to do with the gift. We treat the empty day as a scheduling problem on the way to the lilies. It was meant to be a place to stand.

## Lamentations does not look away

The Old Testament has a Saturday book. We do not read it.

Lamentations. Five poems written after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, after the temple burned, after the covenant people watched the visible center of their faith reduced to ash and rubble and corpses in the street. The poems do not soften it. *How lonely sits the city that was full of people.* They describe mothers boiling their own children in the famine. They name God himself as the one who did this, *the Lord has become like an enemy.* This is in the Bible. The people of God kept it, the way they kept Psalm 88, because they knew that a faith with no language for the ruin is a faith that goes mute exactly when its people need words most.

And here is what the famous middle of the book is actually doing. In chapter three, in the dead center of the rubble, comes the line everyone quotes, *his mercies are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.* We have made it a chorus. We have sung it at sunrise with our hands raised, in sanctuaries with good coffee in the lobby, a thousand miles from any burning city. But read where it sits. It sits buried in the middle of the most relentless grief in the canon, and the poems do not stop after it. The lament resumes. Chapter four is more ruin. Chapter five ends not in triumph but in a question left open, *unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.* That is the last verse. The book ends on a Saturday.

The hope in chapter three did not end the grief. It was spoken from inside the grief, and the grief went on around it, before it and after it, unhealed. **That is the only kind of hope that is any use on Saturday, not the hope that ends the waiting, but the hope you can say in the middle of the waiting without the waiting being over.** The hope that has to wait for the grief to finish before it can be spoken is no hope at all to a person on the long middle day. The hope of Lamentations is spoken with the city still smoking. It is the only kind that reaches you here.

## The Christ who descended

There is a line in the old creed we say without noticing it. *He descended to the dead.*

On Saturday, the church confessed, Christ did not skip ahead. He went down. He entered the realm of the dead and was, for a day, among them, God himself on the wrong side of the grave, keeping company with everyone who had ever waited in the dark for a rescue that had not come. The creed does not explain the mechanics, and I will not pretend to. But it refuses to let Saturday be a blank. It insists that something was true of God on the silent day, and the something is this: he was in the place of the dead. He did not hover above it. He was in it.

Hans Urs von Balthasar, the Swiss theologian, wrote that Holy Saturday is the day God knows what it is to be dead, not merely to die, which is Friday's work, but to be dead, to lie in the silence with no power moving, no light, no word. He called it the day of God's solidarity with the lost. I do not need you to follow the whole theology, and parts of it are contested among people who care about such things. I need you to hear the center of it, which is not contested at all. Whatever Saturday is, God has been in it. Not narrating it from Sunday. In it. On the inside of the stone, in the dark, on the day with no miracle, keeping the exact silence you are keeping now.

## The disciples did not know it was Saturday

Here is the part that should change how we read the whole story. The disciples did not know they were living in Saturday.

We know. We have the book. We have read to the end, and so we cannot fully feel what that day was, because we cannot unknow the morning that is coming. But they could. To them it was not the middle day of a three-act drama. It was simply the day after the end of everything. The story, as far as they could tell, was over, and it had ended in defeat, and there was no act three because there was no reason on earth to expect one. They were not waiting for Sunday. You do not wait for a thing you have no concept of. They were simply grieving, in a locked room, a man they had watched die.

That is the condition of grief exactly. You do not get to read ahead. When you are inside the loss, you do not experience it as a chapter with more chapters coming. You experience it as the end of the book. The mind cannot manufacture a Sunday it has no evidence for, and the well-meaning friend who insists the Sunday is coming is asking you to feel something the disciples themselves could not feel on the original Saturday. They had walked with him for three years. They had watched him raise the dead with their own eyes. And on Saturday they still sat in a locked room and grieved as people with no hope, because the hope had been crucified the day before.

So if you cannot feel the resurrection right now, you are not less faithful than the apostles. You are in precisely their position. They could not feel it either. **Faith on Saturday is not the ability to feel Sunday. Faith on Saturday is staying in the room, keeping the body company, refusing to leave even though the story appears to be over.** That is all they did. It turned out to be enough.

## Against the rush to Sunday

I want to say something plainly to the church, because we are the worst offenders. We cannot stand Saturday.

It has no program. There is nothing to do on it, no victory to claim and no catastrophe to mourn dramatically, only the flat unbearable middle. And so we hurry people through it. We schedule the grief. We expect the bereaved to be functioning by a certain Sunday, smiling by a certain holiday, back among us by some unspoken deadline we would never say aloud but enforce with our discomfort whenever they are not. We mean to be kind. We are mostly being afraid.

We do it because Saturday frightens us. A grieving person who is not recovering on our timeline is a standing reminder that our theology has a gap in it, that we built a faith of Fridays and Sundays and forgot the long middle. Rather than sit in the gap with them, we push them across it. We mistake our own impatience for their healing. We call it encouragement. It is abandonment with a Bible verse attached.

To sit with someone on their Saturday is to do the one thing the disciples managed and we mostly cannot, to stay in the room with the dead and the silence and the absence of any timeline, and to ask for nothing, and to fix nothing, and to simply not leave. That is harder than a casserole. It is harder than a verse. It costs you the comfort of being useful. You will sit there with empty hands and feel them empty, and the staying will be the whole gift. It is what love requires, and most of us run from it.

## What you carry out of this

I am not going to promise you that your Sunday is coming this week. I do not know your calendar and I will not pretend to. Some Saturdays last a season. I have walked beside people whose Saturday lasted years, and a few whose Saturday, as far as I could see, did not break this side of their own grave. I will not lie about that to make this end gently, because the lie would cost you your trust the moment the next Tuesday arrived unchanged.

What I can tell you is that Saturday is not godforsaken, even when it feels like the very definition of forsaken. The day with no miracle in it is still a day the Lord was in. He lay in the dark of it. He kept the silence of it. He waited the length of it, with no more evidence of Sunday than you have now, and he had less, because he was the dead one.

So you are not waiting alone, and you are not waiting outside the faith. You are waiting inside the one day we forgot to write about. The stone is still sealed. The body is still cold. The morning has not come.

It is Saturday. He is in the tomb with you.
posts.excerpt: We have a theology of the cross and a theology of the resurrection. We have almost nothing for the day in between, which is the day most of the grieving are actually living in.

posts.title: When Grief Doesn't Lift
posts.body:
They told you it would lift. It did not lift.

The literature of grief is full of stages, and the stages imply a destination. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance, laid out like a hallway you walk down, with a door at the end marked *recovery*, on the other side of which the weight is gone and you are yourself again. People wait for that door. They count the months. At the one-year mark they expect to have arrived, because someone implied that the first year was the hard one and the second year was the better one, and when the second year turns out to weigh exactly what the first one did, they conclude that something has gone wrong with them. They grieved incorrectly. They failed the assignment. The grief that doesn't lift becomes, on top of everything else, a verdict against the griever.

I want to tell you that when grief doesn't lift, it is not your failure. I have watched it stay in faithful people for decades. It is not a malfunction of grief. It is what grief is.

## The lie of the closed wound

Somewhere we got the idea that the goal of mourning is to return to the person we were before. To close the wound so completely that the scar disappears and the loss stops registering, and we are, in some sense, restored to factory condition.

We speak of *getting over it*, *moving on*, *finding closure*, language borrowed from the marketplace and from the therapeutic, neither of which has any business legislating how long a mother may miss her son. Listen to where the words come from. We close a deal. We move on to the next thing. We process and finish. The whole vocabulary is the vocabulary of transactions completed and tasks discharged, and we have laid it over the one experience in human life it fits least.

Closure is a real estate term. It means the deal is done and the parties walk away. It has no place at a grave. The people you love are not deals to be closed. The relationship did not end when the breathing did; it changed its form, but you are still in it, still oriented toward someone who is no longer where you can reach them, and the ache of that orientation is not a problem to be solved. It is love with nowhere to go. It is love that has outlived its object and refuses to die on schedule.

So of course it stays. **It stays because the love stays, and you would not want the love to stop, which means you cannot honestly want the grief to stop either, because they turn out to be the same substance.** To ask for the grief to end completely is to ask to stop loving the one you lost. No one who has truly loved will pay that price for relief. You would not trade the ache away if the price of the trade were the love that aches. Nobody would. And so it stays, and the staying is not the wound failing to heal. The staying is the love refusing to die.

## Wolterstorff and the wound that becomes you

Nicholas Wolterstorff, after his son Eric died on a mountain in 1983, wrote one of the few honest things ever published about this. *Lament for a Son* came out in 1987, and it refuses the closure on every page.

*I shall look at the world through tears,* he wrote. *Perhaps I shall see things that dry-eyed I could not see.* He did not expect the tears to stop. He expected to see differently because of them, permanently, for the rest of his life. He was not describing a phase. He was describing a new and permanent way of having eyes.

And then the line I return to most. He wrote that grief does not get smaller; we get bigger around it. The loss stays the same size, it was always the full size of the person who died, and that does not shrink. A child is not a smaller loss in year ten than in year one. But a life can grow up around the wound, the way a tree grows around an iron stake driven into its trunk, the bark slowly enfolding the metal without ever expelling it. The stake is still there. It is inside the wood now, grown over, carried. The tree is larger, and it is also, permanently, a tree with iron in it. That is healing, but it is not the healing we were sold. Nothing was removed. Something was incorporated. The tree did not get its old shape back. It built a new shape around what it could not get rid of.

This is a truer picture than the hallway with the door. There is no door. There is only the slow widening of a life around a thing it will carry to its own grave.

## Why the resurrection does not erase the grief

I am a Christian, and I believe in the resurrection of the dead, and I need to say carefully what that does and does not do, because the church has badly misused it on the grieving, and I have watched the misuse leave a second wound beside the first.

The resurrection is not a reason to stop grieving now. Notice that Jesus, who is the resurrection and the life, wept at the tomb of Lazarus before he raised him. He had the resurrection in his own hands, minutes away, the power to undo the whole catastrophe already coiled in his chest, and he grieved anyway. He did not treat the coming joy as a cancellation of the present sorrow. He let both be fully real at once, in the same body, at the same grave. The Christian is not asked to skip the weeping because Sunday is coming. The Christian is asked to weep as one who weeps toward a morning, which is a different thing entirely than not weeping at all.

Paul wrote it precisely, and we misquote it constantly. We do not grieve *as those who have no hope.* He did not write that we do not grieve. He wrote that our grief has a horizon the hopeless do not have. The grief is the same grief. The tears are the same tears, the same salt, the same exhaustion. What changes is the direction we are facing while we shed them. The resurrection does not lift the weight in this life, it promises that the weight is not the final word, which is exactly not the same as promising you will stop feeling it on a Tuesday in the tenth year. You may feel it on that Tuesday. Many faithful people do. The hope is not that you will stop. The hope is what waits on the far side of all the Tuesdays, after the last of them.

This is why the cheap version of resurrection hope wounds. When we wave the empty tomb at a fresh grief as though it should end the crying, we are not preaching the resurrection. We are preaching against the tears of Christ. He cried at the grave of a man he was about to raise. If the coming resurrection did not stop his weeping, no one should be telling you it must stop yours.

## The widow at the second Christmas

I have learned to distrust the first Christmas after a death. Everyone is watching it. The family closes ranks, the church remembers, the casseroles are still arriving, and the grieving person is carried through the day on a current of attention.

It is the second Christmas I have learned to fear. By then the world has decided the grief should be over. The attention has moved on to a newer sorrow, a fresher crisis, someone else's hard year. And the person is left to discover that the second one is, very often, worse than the first, because now they are grieving alone, without the current to carry them, and they are grieving a second loss on top of the first: the discovery that the grief did not keep its promise to leave.

I have sat with people in that second year and watched them apologize for still being sad. Apologize. As though they had broken a contract they never signed. Someone, somewhere, had taught them that a year was the allotment, and they had gone over, and now they were ashamed of a love that would not shrink to the size the calendar permitted. I have spent more of my ministry talking people out of that shame than almost anything else I do. The grief is not the problem. The lie that it should be gone, that lie is the problem, and it does more quiet damage in the second year than the loss did in the first.

So I have learned to do the opposite of what the calendar wants. I have learned to come back in the second year, and the third, when no one else is coming. To say the name of the dead out loud, on purpose, because the grieving are starving to hear it and everyone around them has decided that saying it would only stir things up. The name was already stirring. It never stopped. The only question is whether they have to carry it alone or whether someone will say it with them.

There is a quiet ministry in that, and the church has nearly lost it. To remember out loud. To mark the anniversary the rest of the world has forgotten. To send a note in March, when the casseroles stopped in January, that says only: I was thinking of him today. The grieving do not need to be reminded of their loss, they have not forgotten it for an hour, they need to be told that someone else has not forgotten it either, that the one they lost still has a place in the memory of more people than the one carrying the grief. That is a thing love can do for the long haul, and it costs almost nothing, and almost no one does it past the first month.

## The faith always made room for the long grief

We act as though lifelong grief were an embarrassment to faith, a thing to be hidden in the back pew. The Scriptures never treated it that way.

Walter Brueggemann spent his life recovering the lament tradition the modern church had quietly abandoned, and his central observation lands directly here: a faith that only knows how to praise has no language for the person whose grief did not end on schedule. Israel kept the laments in the songbook precisely because grief outlasts the funeral. Jacob mourned Joseph for years and refused to be comforted, *I shall go down to my son to the grave mourning*, and the text does not rebuke him for it. David wept over Absalom until his soldiers were ashamed of him, and the wail he made, *my son, my son*, has never stopped being read aloud at gravesides three thousand years later. The Bible is full of people whose grief did not lift, recorded without apology, because the people who assembled it knew what the calendar-keepers forgot.

The longest griefs in Scripture belong to the most faithful people in it. That ought to settle something. If lifelong grief were a failure of trust, the patriarchs and the king after God's own heart would be the great failures. They are not. They are the witnesses. Their tears are in the book on purpose, the way Psalm 88 is in the book on purpose, to tell the person grieving in year ten that they have not wandered outside the faith. They have wandered deeper into it, into the part the brochures left out.

## What you carry, and what carries you

So here is what I will not say. I will not say time heals all wounds, because it does not, and you already know it does not, and you would stop trusting me the moment I said it. I will not give you a stage you are about to graduate from. I will not promise that next year is lighter. I do not know your next year, and I will not lie about it to make this end gently.

What I will say is that the staying of the weight is not a sign that your faith is weak or your grief is broken. It is the shape that love takes once death has had its turn. The people who told you it would lift were trying to be kind, but they were describing a country none of us has ever actually visited, and you are not failing to reach it. You are doing the harder and more faithful thing, which is to keep carrying what cannot be set down, and to keep walking anyway, toward a morning you have been promised and have not yet seen.

The weight stays. I will not pretend otherwise.

But you do not carry it alone, and you do not carry it nowhere. There is a hand under the load that has held heavier ones, and a grave already emptied that tells you which way the dark finally breaks. Not yet. Not on your schedule. But that way, and not the other.

The weight stays. So does he.
posts.excerpt: You were promised the grief would lift. It did not lift. It is time someone told you that the staying is not your failure, it is the shape love takes once death has had its turn.

posts.title: Is It Okay to Be Angry at God?
posts.body:
You are angry at God, and you have been told to stop.

Maybe not in those words. The church rarely says it that bluntly. It says it sideways, *be careful with that; you don't want to put God in the dock; who are you, O man, to answer back to God.* It says it with a verse fired like a warning shot. And the grieving person, already carrying the loss, now carries a second thing: the suspicion that the rage rising in their chest is itself a sin, a failure of faith, evidence that they were never as devoted as they thought. So they swallow it. They go quiet. They say the right things at the funeral, and then they stop talking to God altogether, because the only thing they have to say to him is the one thing they have been told they are not allowed to say.

So the question sits there, unasked out loud, behind the polite face at the potluck: is it okay to be angry at God? I want to tell you what the prayer book of the Bible actually does with that anger. It is not what you were taught.

## A third of the songbook is complaint

Open the Psalms. This is the hymnal Israel sang, the prayers Jesus prayed, the words the church has carried for three thousand years. And roughly a third of them are laments, not gentle, not composed, but raw complaints flung directly at God by people who believed he had wronged them or abandoned them or fallen asleep at the post.

*How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?* That is Psalm 13, and notice the accusation buried in it. The psalmist is not asking whether God has forgotten him. He is asserting it, and demanding to know how much longer it will go on. The question is not theological. It is the question of someone pounding on a locked door, and it is preserved, word for word, as Scripture. *Rouse yourself. Why do you sleep, O Lord.* That is Psalm 44, the prayer of people who have been faithful and been crushed anyway, and they say so to his face, *all this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you.* They are not confessing sin. They are filing a grievance.

This is in the Bible. God did not leave it out. He could have given us a songbook of pure praise, sanitized, untroubled, the kind of worship music that never asks an awkward question, that we could pipe into a sanctuary without anyone in the room having to feel anything they would rather not. Instead he gave us a songbook with the complaints left in, and he called it Scripture, and his Son sang from it as he died.

## Brueggemann and the prayers we stopped praying

Walter Brueggemann spent his life on these psalms, and he noticed something about the modern church that should disturb us. We have edited them out.

Quietly, without a vote, the contemporary church has stopped praying the laments. Our worship runs almost entirely in what Brueggemann called the psalms of orientation and the psalms of new orientation, the everything-is-good and the everything-is-restored. The psalms of disorientation, the ones for the season when life has come apart and God seems to have done it, we have dropped from the rotation. Look at what we sing. Count how many of the songs would survive being sung honestly by a woman who buried her husband on Thursday. Most of them would die in her throat.

Brueggemann's point was sharp, and it should sting. By cutting the laments, we did not make our faith more reverent. We made it dishonest. We created a worship in which the only permitted speech to God is gratitude, so the person whose life is in ruins has no sanctioned language and must either fake the gratitude or fall silent. We taught people that the way to be close to God is to lie to him about how they feel. And a relationship in which one party is not allowed to say the hard thing is not a close relationship. It is a managed one. It is the relationship you have with someone you are afraid of.

The lament psalms refuse the management. *You have made us like sheep for the slaughter. Rise up; come to our help.* That is covenant speech. It is the speech of someone who is angry precisely because they still believe God is supposed to be on their side, and the anger is the proof that the relationship is still load-bearing. **You do not rage at a God you have given up on. You rage at the one you are still holding to his promise.**

## The accusation that is still prayer

Here is the line we keep missing. The lament is always addressed to God.

The psalmist does not write God off. The psalmist does not turn to the congregation and complain about God, the way we complain about a difficult boss in the parking lot after the meeting. The psalmist turns to God's own face and complains to him directly. *Why have you forsaken me? Why do you hide? How long?* Every accusation is a second-person accusation. You. You did this. You are absent. You are too slow. The anger is not a turning away from God. It is the most intense possible turning toward him.

This is the difference the church flattened into a single forbidden thing. There is a way to be angry at God that is unbelief, the anger that walks out, slams the door, and never addresses him again, that takes the loss as final proof he was never there. And there is a way to be angry at God that is faith holding on with bloodied hands, the anger that stays in the room and keeps yelling at the one it refuses to stop believing in. The Psalms are full of the second kind. The Psalms canonize it. They make it liturgy. They hand it to the whole people of God as the right way to pray when the world has broken and God appears to have allowed it.

Jesus prayed it from the cross. *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me.* He did not pray *I accept this in serene submission.* He prayed Psalm 22, the lament, the why, the accusation, the question with no answer coming back from the dark sky over Golgotha. The sinless one, in his last conscious words, reached for the complaint. If the lament were a failure of faith, the most faithful human who ever lived would not have died with one on his lips. He would have died quoting something tidier. He chose the lament. He made the why his last word.

## The imprecations we are most afraid of

There is a darker corner of the Psalter, and the church has quarantined it almost entirely. The imprecatory psalms, the ones where the praying person asks God to do violence to those who have harmed them. *Break the teeth in their mouths.* *Let death take them by surprise.* The hundred and thirty-seventh psalm, written by exiles weeping by the rivers of Babylon, ends with a line so terrible we never print it on a coffee mug, a blessing pronounced on whoever would dash the infants of Babylon against the rocks. We read past it. We pretend it is not there. We skip the verse in the reading and hope no one notices.

I am not going to defend the sentiment as a moral instruction. It is not one, and I will not pretend it is. But notice what the praying person is doing with the rage, and notice what they are not doing. They are not picking up a stone. They are not on the road to Babylon with a weapon. They are handing the rage to God.
