There is a consolation buried in the Incarnation that does not reach you until you need it, and as a pastor I have watched it reach people in the worst rooms there are.

Most religions, and most of the vague spirituality that has replaced religion, offer a God who looks down on suffering from a clean distance, sympathetic, perhaps, but untouched, the way a wealthy man might pity the poor from a window. The Christian claim is categorically different. The letter to the Hebrews says that because Jesus shared our flesh and blood and was tested in every way we are, "he is able to help those who are being tested" (Hebrews 2:18). The God of the creeds is not a stranger to your worst day. He has had worse. He knows hunger from the inside, because he went hungry. He knows exhaustion, because he slept in the back of a boat too tired to wake in a storm. He knows betrayal by a friend, the death of someone he loved, the specific terror of facing a death he could see coming and dreaded. On the night before he died he sweated and begged and asked, if there were any other way, to be spared, and there was no other way, and he went anyway.

This is the difference between a God who explains suffering and a God who enters it. Christianity has never given a tidy answer to why there is pain; the book of Job spends forty chapters refusing to give one. What it gives instead is stranger and, when you are in the dark, more durable than an answer: a God who climbed down into the pain himself, who did not stay safe, who has the scars. When I sit with someone whose life has come apart, and I have sat with many, I have nothing useful to say about why. What I have is this: the one you are angry at, the one who seems absent, is not absent in the way you think, and he is not untouched. He came down into exactly this. He has a body that remembers the nails.

That is the practical payload of an ancient doctrine. The Incarnation means your suffering is not observed from a window. It is shared from the inside by the one who made you, and that changes what it is possible to believe about him when everything else has failed.

## What it means for what you are

This is where it stops being ancient and becomes yours.

C. S. Lewis, who came to faith out of the same unbelief I came from, kept circling one phrase for what happened at the Incarnation: he called it the great miracle, the central event after which everything else is comment. And he said something about it that reframes the whole arc of human longing. We had always suspected, in our myths and our hungers, that the divine and the human were meant to meet. Every culture told stories that ached toward it. In Jesus, Lewis said, the thing all the myths had been reaching for actually happened, myth became fact, in a particular place, on a particular date, in a body you could have touched. The longing was real because the answer was real.

N. T. Wright presses the same point toward what it does to the material world. The Incarnation means God is not embarrassed by matter. He made it, and he was willing to wear it. Your body is not a cage your soul is trying to escape; it is part of what God came to save, which is why the Christian hope has never been a disembodied heaven of floating souls but a resurrection, bodies remade, the whole creation set right. The same logic runs through Paul's great hymn about Christ: "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created... And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:15–20). The one holding the atoms together is the one who became an atom-built body. Matter was never the problem. Matter was always good. He proved it by becoming some.

And then there is the hymn Paul quotes in Philippians, which may be the oldest Christian poem we have, and which tells you what direction God moves: Christ, "though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men... he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:5–11). Note the direction. Down. The whole movement of God in the Incarnation is downward, from glory to a feeding trough, from the throne to the cross. That is the most counterintuitive thing about the Christian God and the thing I, as an atheist, was least prepared for. The gods I had dismissed were all climbing, demanding, looking down. This one came down. He did not wait at the top for us to ascend. He descended to where we actually were, which is the bottom.

## The doctrine that dignifies ordinary life

There is one more consequence of the Incarnation that a newcomer rarely hears, and it quietly reshapes how a person values their own days.

Before he was a public teacher, before any of the miracles, Jesus spent roughly thirty years doing nothing the world would record. He grew up in an unimportant town, learned a trade, worked with his hands, ate ordinary meals, kept ordinary company. The Gospels give us almost nothing of it, and the silence is itself the point. God did not skip the unremarkable part of being human. He did not arrive as a grown teacher and start working. He was a child who had to be taught, an adolescent, a young man at a workbench, a son in a household. The eternal Word spent the overwhelming majority of his human life doing the kind of unrecorded, unglamorous things that fill almost all of every human life.

This is why Christianity has never been able to draw a clean line between the sacred and the ordinary, between the holy work of the temple and the unremarkable work of the home or the field or the shop. If God himself spent thirty years in obscurity before three years of ministry, then the obscure years are not a waste, not a holding pattern before real life begins. They were real life, and he sanctified them by living them. The changing of diapers, the long day of unnoticed labor, the meal cooked again, the child taught to walk, God did not consider these beneath him. He did them, or grew up needing them done for him. The Incarnation means there is no such thing as a merely secular Tuesday. The maker of the universe spent thousands of them at a bench in Nazareth, and called it good.

For a person measuring their life and finding it small, this is heavier than it first sounds. The God who could have arrived in glory chose, first, to be unremarkable for three decades. Whatever your ordinary life is made of, he has been there, in the ordinary, and it did not embarrass him.

## The weight in the manger

So go back to the card on the mantel, the baby in the straw, and refuse for one minute to find it cozy.

That is God, having limits for the first time. That is the maker of light learning to focus his eyes. That is the source of all words unable yet to speak one. He did this not as a stunt and not as a story, but as a rescue mission that required him to become the thing that dies, in order to die the death we were dying, and to carry our broken flesh up through the grave and out the far side into a life that cannot end. The smallness was the strategy. The weakness was the point.

What I could not see as an unbeliever, and what I would give anything to hand to someone still standing where I stood, is that the offensive part is the saving part. A god who stayed safely divine could never have reached me. The whole hope of the thing hangs on the scandal: that he became what I am, down to the dying, so that I could become what he is, all the way up to the life that has no end. He became a baby. That is not the sweet part of the story. That is the whole astonishing weight of it.
posts.excerpt: The Christmas story has been sentimentalized into harmlessness. Strip the tinsel off and you find the most outrageous claim any religion has ever made, and the one that changes what it means to be human.

posts.title: Easter Was Never Meant to Be One Sunday
posts.body:
Picture a typical Easter. The lilies appear at the front of the church, the building is fuller than it has been since Christmas, there is a sunrise service for the devoted and a late service for everyone else, and by early afternoon the good clothes are off and the ham is on the table and the children are hunting plastic eggs in the yard. By Monday it is over. The lilies will be dead by Wednesday. The decorations come down. The world, and the church with it, moves on to whatever is next.

This is how nearly everyone experiences Easter, as a single, bright, slightly exhausting Sunday, the spring counterpart to Christmas morning. And it is, when you stand back and look at it, one of the strangest things the modern church has done to itself.

**Because Easter was never meant to be a day. It is a season, fifty days, called Eastertide, the longest celebration in the Christian year, and the church built it that long for a reason: what happened on that first Sunday is too enormous for the human heart to take in over a single morning.** We have shrunk the central event of our entire faith into an afternoon. We spend more time celebrating the end of a war or the start of a new year than the church historically spent celebrating the one event it stakes everything on. Something has gone wrong with our sense of scale.

## A celebration longer than the fast

Notice the imbalance in how most of us keep the year, because it reveals what we actually believe. Lent, the season of fasting and repentance that leads up to Easter, runs forty days, and serious Christians keep it with real discipline, giving things up, going without, walking into the wilderness. Then Easter arrives, the thing all that fasting was preparing for, and we celebrate it for one morning and quit.

The historic church did the opposite. It fasted for forty days and then feasted for fifty. Eastertide runs from Easter Sunday all the way to Pentecost, seven full weeks, and during those weeks the ancient church refused to fast at all, refused even to kneel in prayer, because kneeling was a posture of penitence and this was not a season for penitence. This was a season for standing up, for celebration so sustained it changed your body's posture for nearly two months. The feast was longer than the fast. The joy outlasted the sorrow. The proportion preached its own sermon: that the resurrection is bigger than everything it answered, that the celebration of life must run longer than the discipline of facing death.

We have reversed the proportion. We are rigorous about the fasting and careless about the feast. And I suspect that reversal is not an accident of scheduling. It is a confession. We find it easier to believe in our own sinfulness, which we experience daily, than in the resurrection, which we have never seen. The forty days of Lent feel true to us. The fifty days of Easter feel like a stretch. So we keep the one and abandon the other, and in doing so we quietly tell the truth about which we actually find more believable.

## Why one Sunday cannot hold it

To see why the resurrection needs fifty days, you have to grasp how large the New Testament thinks the event is. We have domesticated it into a happy ending, Jesus was dead, now he is alive, the story works out. But the first Christians did not experience it as a happy ending to a sad story. They experienced it as the beginning of a new creation breaking into the middle of the old one.

Paul, writing to the Corinthians in what is the earliest detailed account of the resurrection we possess, treats it not as a comforting belief but as the load-bearing wall of reality itself. "If Christ has not been raised," he writes, "your faith is futile and you are still in your sins" (1 Corinthians 15:17). Everything hangs on it. And then he widens the lens until it takes in the whole cosmos: the risen Christ is the firstfruits, the first sheaf of an entire harvest of resurrection that will eventually include all who belong to him and the renewal of creation itself. Death, the last enemy, will be destroyed. This is not a man surviving his own funeral. This is the hinge of history turning.

N.T. Wright, the New Testament scholar whose book *Surprised by Hope*, published in 2008, has done more than any modern work to recover what the resurrection actually means, argues that the church lost the plot when it reduced Easter to a story about going to heaven when you die. That, Wright insists, is not the New Testament's hope at all. The resurrection of Jesus is the launch of God's project to renew the entire world, to raise bodies, restore creation, and bring heaven and earth together at last. Easter is not God's reassurance that we will escape this world. It is God's announcement that he is reclaiming it. A new creation has begun, in a garden, on a Sunday, in the body of a crucified man who walked out of his tomb and ate breakfast with his friends. You cannot fit that on a single morning. You can barely fit it in fifty days.

## What the fifty days are for

So what does the church do with the seven weeks after Easter Sunday? It does what the first witnesses did. It lives inside the astonishment, slowly, as the implications land one after another.

Read the resurrection accounts in John 20 and 21 and notice how gradual the believing is, even for the people who saw it with their own eyes. Mary mistakes him for the gardener. The disciples lock the doors in fear even after they have heard the reports. Thomas refuses to believe until he can put his hand in the wounds. And then, in the final chapter, the risen Jesus does the most ordinary thing imaginable, he builds a fire on a beach and cooks fish for breakfast and asks Peter, three times, whether he loves him. The resurrection does not arrive as a thunderclap that settles everything at once. It arrives in walks and meals and conversations, over weeks, as people who had watched their hope die learn, slowly, to trust that it is alive again. Eastertide is the church rehearsing that same slow believing. It takes time to absorb that death has been defeated. The season gives you the time.

And it builds toward something. The fifty days are not an aimless victory lap. They lead to Pentecost, the day the Spirit was poured out and the church was born. In Acts 2, Peter stands up in Jerusalem, the same Peter who had denied even knowing Jesus, and preaches the resurrection to a crowd, and three thousand people are added in a day. The resurrection does not stay private. It moves outward, from an empty tomb to a locked room to a public square to the ends of the earth. Eastertide traces that expansion. It begins with a few stunned witnesses in a garden and ends with the Spirit launching the church into the world. The season has a direction: from the resurrection of one man to the resurrection of everything.

This is why Eastertide cannot be a single Sunday. A single Sunday can hold the fact of the resurrection. It cannot hold the consequences, and the New Testament is almost entirely about the consequences.

It is worth pausing on how completely the resurrection reorganized the lives of the people closest to it, because that reorganization is the historical fingerprint of the thing. These were not men predisposed to belief. They had watched their leader executed in the most degrading way the Roman world could devise, a death that to every observer meant the movement was finished and the claims were false. They scattered. They hid. By every expectation of history, that should have been the end, one more failed messiah in a century full of them, his followers melting back into the obscurity they came from. Instead, within weeks, the same frightened men were standing in public proclaiming that the executed man was alive and was Lord, and they did not stop when it cost them everything, and most of them died for refusing to stop. Something happened in the gap. Whatever it was, it was strong enough to turn cowards into martyrs and to launch a movement that the most powerful empire on earth could not extinguish. The fifty days of Eastertide are the church's way of staying in that gap long enough to feel its force, rather than rushing past it to the next thing on the calendar.

## Living as resurrection people

Here is where the season stops being history and starts making claims on the ordinary Tuesday. Paul tells the Colossians: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above... Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:1–4). Notice the tense. *You have been raised.* Not will be, have been. Paul speaks of the believer's resurrection as something that has, in some real sense, already begun. The same power that raised Jesus is already at work, and the Christian is meant to live now as a person on the far side of death, no longer ruled by the fear that organizes most human life.

That is what Eastertide is supposed to form: people who live as though the resurrection were true on a normal weekday, not just on a decorated Sunday. And this is harder than it sounds, because the world we wake up to every morning does not look like a world in which death has been defeated. It looks like a world where death is still winning, where people we love still get sick, still grieve, still die. The fifty days are the church's deliberate practice of insisting, against all the available evidence, that the deepest truth about reality is the empty tomb and not the full graveyard. Schmemann, again, saw the whole Christian life as fundamentally Paschal, shaped by Pascha, the resurrection, so that every Sunday is a little Easter and the believer learns to carry the joy of the empty tomb into the most unremarkable hours.

I have kept Easter as a single Sunday for most of my life, and I can tell you exactly what it produced. A spike of feeling on one morning, real but brief, and then a return to a Monday that looked indistinguishable from the Monday before, as if nothing cosmic had occurred, as if the most disruptive event in the history of the world had no bearing on my actual week. The fifty-day season is the church's correction to exactly that. It refuses to let the resurrection be a feeling you have once a year. It insists that it is a fact you live inside, all the way to Pentecost and beyond.

The difference this makes is hardest to feel and most important at a graveside. Every person who lives long enough stands eventually beside a coffin that holds someone they cannot imagine living without, and in that moment all the comfortable religion in the world is worth nothing, and the only question that matters is whether the resurrection is true. Wright is relentless on this point: the Christian hope is not that the soul of the departed has floated off to a better place while the body is discarded, but that the body itself, the actual person, raised and remade, will rise, because Christ's body rose, the firstfruits of all the rest. That is a far wilder and far more consoling hope than the vague spiritualism that passes for comfort at most funerals. It says the grave is not the end of the person but a waiting room for the person, that death is real and terrible and also, now, defeated, that the one we buried will be raised as surely as the One who walked out of the tomb in the garden. Eastertide is the season that trains us to hold that hope before we need it, so that when the graveside comes, and it always comes, we are not reaching for it for the first time, fumbling for a comfort we never practiced, but standing on a fact we have lived inside for fifty days a year, every year, for as long as we have kept the season.

## The day that refused to end

There is a reason the early church called Sunday the eighth day. The week has seven days; the resurrection happened on the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath, which they began to call the eighth, a day outside the old count entirely, the first day of a new creation that the old calendar had no room for. Every Sunday since has been, in their understanding, a small Easter, a weekly return to the morning the tomb came up empty. This is the deepest reason Christians gather on Sunday rather than the Sabbath day their tradition had kept for centuries: they had been given a new day, an eighth day, because they were living in a new creation that began on a particular Sunday morning and has not ended. Every week the church returns to that morning. Every week is, in miniature, the fifty days compressed into one, a refusal to let the most important fact in the universe slip out of view between Easters.

And once you see Sunday as a weekly Easter, the whole rhythm of the Christian week changes shape. The day off stops being merely a rest from labor and becomes a celebration of resurrection, a small fifty days inside the seven, a recurring insistence against the gray evidence of every week that death has been beaten and the new creation has begun. The early Christians did not invent a new calendar because they were fond of tradition. They invented it because something had happened that the old way of counting time could not contain, and they needed a day that pointed past the closed circle of the week toward the open future the resurrection had cracked open. We inherited that eighth day. Most of us spend it like any other, never asking why the church set it apart, never feeling the strangeness of a people who reorganized the very week around an empty tomb.

That is the scale we have lost. We treat Easter as a single point on the calendar, a bright dot we touch once a year and leave behind. The church that knew what had happened treated it as a season too large for a day, a celebration too important to end on schedule, a fact that had cracked the old calendar open and started a new kind of time running underneath it.

The lilies die by Wednesday. The tomb is still empty. Easter was never one Sunday because the thing it celebrates was never finished, it was begun, that morning, and it is still unfolding, and it will not be complete until the firstfruits become the full harvest and death itself is the last thing to die.

Fifty days is not too long. Fifty days is barely a start.
posts.excerpt: We treat Easter as a single morning, lilies, a sunrise service, ham by noon, done. The church has always known it as fifty days, because what happened that morning was too large for the world to absorb in one sitting. Here is what we shrank.

posts.title: What the Boring Middle of the Year Teaches You
posts.body:
Ask someone what they know about the church year and you will hear about two things. Christmas, with its candles and its carols and its manger. And Easter, with its lilies and its empty tomb. The high seasons. The ones the whole culture half-remembers, the ones with the good music and the full pews. These are the parts of the Christian calendar everyone can name.

What almost no one can name is the part in between, the long, green, unspectacular stretch that fills most of the year, that has no famous music and no special decorations and no cultural footprint at all. The church calls it Ordinary Time, and it runs for something like half the year, the longest season by far. It is the part of the calendar nobody puts on a card. And I have come to believe it is the part that actually does the work.

**Ordinary Time is the church's deliberate decision to give its longest, least dramatic season to the ordinary, to insist that the unremarkable Tuesday, and not the mountaintop Sunday, is where most of a faithful life is actually lived and where most of it is actually formed.** The boring middle is not the church year's filler. It is its main event, disguised as nothing.

## The season with the honest name

First, a correction, because the name misleads almost everyone. Ordinary Time does not mean *boring time* or *ordinary-as-in-nothing-special.* The word comes from *ordinal*, as in the ordinal numbers, first, second, third. Ordinary Time is simply the counted time, the numbered weeks that run between the great festivals: the weeks after Epiphany before Lent begins, and then the long stretch after Pentecost that runs all the way to Advent. It is called ordinary because the weeks are counted in order, one after another, the way ordinary days actually pass.

But the accidental meaning turns out to be the true one. Ordinary Time really is the season of ordinary life, and the church was wise to make it the longest. Because if you are honest about your own life, you will admit that the mountaintop moments are rare. The dramatic conversions, the answered prayers you can point to, the Sundays the worship genuinely lifts you off the ground, these are real, but they are occasional. Most of life is not that. Most of life is the long middle: the same commute, the same dishes, the same prayers that feel like they hit the ceiling, the same faithfulness asked of you on a Wednesday that no one will ever notice. The church calendar tells the truth about this. It gives the most weeks to the kind of time you actually have the most of.

This is itself a quietly radical thing to do in a culture addicted to the spectacular. We are trained to measure our lives by peaks, the highlights, the achievements, the moments worth posting. We treat the ordinary stretches as dead time to be endured until the next significant thing. The church year refuses that. It dignifies the middle. It says the counted, uneventful weeks are not less holy than the festivals; they are simply where most of the following of Jesus gets done.

## Where Jesus spent most of his life

Here is the fact that should reorganize how we think about the unspectacular, and almost no one notices it. The Son of God, given roughly thirty-three years on earth, spent thirty of them doing nothing the Gospels found worth recording.

Think about that. We have four accounts of Jesus' life, and they are almost entirely about the final three years, the ministry, the miracles, the cross, the resurrection. The first thirty years are dispatched in a handful of verses. We get the birth, a single episode at age twelve in the temple, and then a sentence that should stop us cold: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man" (Luke 2:52). That is the entire record of three decades. Thirty years of growing up, learning a trade, working with his hands, living in an unremarkable town that produced a proverb about how nothing good comes out of it. Thirty years of Ordinary Time before there was ever a public ministry.

God, given a human life, chose to spend the overwhelming majority of it in obscurity, doing ordinary work no one would have called significant. The carpenter's shop in Nazareth was not a waiting room before the real life began. It was real life, thirty years of it, and it was where the wisdom and the stature and the favor were formed that the three famous years would draw on. The hidden decades were not wasted. They were the foundation. If the incarnate God gave thirty years to the ordinary and three to the spectacular, perhaps we have our proportions exactly backwards.

## The lie of the dramatic life

We are formed, most of us, by a story that says the meaningful life is the dramatic one, that significance lives in the big moments, the visible impact, the things that can be pointed to and measured and admired. This story is everywhere, and it is a quiet poison, because it teaches us to despise the very texture of the life we have actually been given, which is mostly small and mostly unwitnessed.

Eugene Peterson saw this clearly. His book *A Long Obedience in the Same Direction*, published in 1980, takes its title from a line about discipleship and aims it straight at the American hunger for the instant and the spectacular. We have, Peterson wrote, a religion of the dramatic conversion and the mountaintop experience, and almost no patience for the long, plodding, unremarkable faithfulness that is actually what discipleship consists of. The Christian life, he insisted, is not a series of peak experiences strung together. It is a long obedience in the same direction, the same small fidelities repeated across years until they become a life. There are no shortcuts to the things that matter. There is only the long way, walked faithfully, mostly in the dark, mostly unseen.

This is the spirituality of Ordinary Time, and it cuts against everything the surrounding culture trains into us. Paul, of all the apostles the most dramatic in his own conversion, told the Thessalonians the least dramatic thing imaginable: "Aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands" (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Aspire to live quietly. That is not advice we know what to do with. We aspire to live loudly, visibly, impactfully. Paul holds up the quiet, hand-working, attention-avoiding life as something to aim at, as itself a form of faithfulness. The ordinary, minded well, is not beneath the spiritual life. It is the spiritual life.

The technology of our moment has made this lesson harder to hear than it has ever been, because the screen in everyone's pocket is a machine for despising the day of small things. It serves a relentless feed of other people's peaks, the highlights, the achievements, the dramatic moments, edited and filtered and stripped of all the ordinary hours that surrounded them, and it sets that curated spectacle against the unremarkable reality of your own Tuesday. The comparison is rigged and constant, and its effect is to make the ordinary life, which is the only life any of us actually has, feel like a failure to launch. We scroll through everyone else's festival days and wonder why our own life feels so much like Ordinary Time, never grasping that everyone's life is mostly Ordinary Time, that the peaks we are comparing ourselves against are the rare exceptions other people also spend most of their hours waiting for. Ordinary Time is the church's quiet refusal of that whole rigged comparison. It says the unedited middle is not the part of life to be ashamed of and hidden. It is the part where you actually live, and where God actually works, and the sooner you stop despising it the sooner you can start being formed by it.

I have spent years measuring my own ministry by the dramatic, the big Sunday, the numbers, the visible result, and treating the ordinary weeks, the hospital visits no one saw, the long unspectacular discipling of one stubborn person, as the part that did not count. I had the proportions backwards. The ordinary weeks were the ministry. The dramatic moments, when they came, were built entirely out of the faithfulness no one had noticed.

## God in the dishes

Tish Harrison Warren, in her widely loved book *Liturgy of the Ordinary*, published in 2016, structures the whole thing around a single ordinary day, waking, brushing teeth, losing her keys, eating leftovers, fighting with her husband, going to bed, and finds in each unremarkable moment a place where God is forming her. Her argument is that we keep waiting for the spiritual life to happen in the extraordinary, and it keeps happening in the dishes and the commute and the small frustrations we treat as interruptions to the real thing. The ordinary is not the interruption. The ordinary is the real thing. The dishes are where the formation happens, precisely because that is where most of life happens.

Scripture says the same in its own way. Paul tells the Colossians, "Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Colossians 3:17). Whatever you do. Not just the religious acts, not just the dramatic obediences, the whatever, the ordinary, the work of your hands and the words of your mouth on a normal day. The entire ordinary life is gathered up and offered. There is no part of it too small to be holy.

This cuts against a division most of us carry without examining it, the assumption that life is split into the spiritual parts and the secular parts, the moments that count toward God and the long stretches that are just life. We treat prayer and church and the visibly religious as the real spiritual content, and we treat the commute, the email, the laundry, the meeting as neutral filler in between. But the New Testament knows no such division. The whole of a life is offered, or none of it is, and the ordinary hours are not the gaps between the holy moments. They are the holy moments, if they are done as unto God. A parent feeding a child at three in the morning, a worker doing an unseen task with care, a friend listening to the same complaint for the hundredth time, these are not lesser than the dramatic spiritual experiences we keep waiting for. They are very often more, because they cost more and ask for a faithfulness no one is applauding. Ordinary Time is the church's annual insistence on exactly this: that the secular-sacred divide is a fiction, and that God is just as present in the green months of nothing-much as in the festival weeks of everything.

And then there is the line from Zechariah that I have come to love more than almost any other in this connection. The people are rebuilding the temple after exile, and the new foundation looks pathetic compared to the glory of the one that was lost, and the older people who remember the first temple are weeping at how small the new beginning is. And God speaks through the prophet: "For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice" (Zechariah 4:10). The day of small things. God's whole work in that moment looked small, unimpressive, hardly worth the effort, and God names the despising of small things as the actual error. The kingdom, it turns out, comes mostly in small things, in days that do not look like much, in faithfulness that no one would film.

## The season that finally tells the truth

So what does Ordinary Time teach the newcomer who has never thought about the church year at all? It teaches the one thing the rest of the culture will never tell you, because the culture has nothing to sell you in the ordinary.

It teaches that your real life, the one you are actually living, the unremarkable one, the one mostly made of repetition and small duties and unwitnessed fidelity, is not the waiting room for some more significant life that keeps failing to arrive. It is the life. It is where God is forming you, week by counted week, into the shape of Christ, and he is doing it not in spite of the ordinariness but precisely through it, the way he formed his own Son through thirty hidden years in a carpenter's shop.

There is one more thing Ordinary Time quietly insists on, and it is the hardest for a results-driven person to accept. It teaches that faithfulness is not the same as fruitfulness, and that you are responsible only for the first. We want to see the harvest. We measure ourselves by outcomes, the marriage that turned out, the child who kept the faith, the work that finally got noticed, and when the outcomes do not come, we conclude that the faithfulness was wasted. But the long green season says no. You sow in the ordinary weeks without seeing what grows. You teach the child, love the spouse, labor at the task, keep the prayer, and you may never see the result, because the result is God's province and not yours. The farmer in Jesus' parable scatters seed and then sleeps and rises, night and day, and the seed grows he knows not how. That is the posture Ordinary Time forms, the willingness to be faithful in the dark without demanding to see the crop, trusting that the One who counts the small things is also the One who, in his own time and not ours, brings the harvest in.

The festivals are real, and we need them. But you cannot live on festivals. You live in Ordinary Time, in the long green stretch where nothing seems to happen, and the church was telling the truth when it made that stretch the longest. Most of your faithfulness will be invisible. Most of your obedience will go unnoticed. Most of the following of Jesus is the same small turning, repeated, in the same direction, for years.

That is not the consolation prize. That is the thing itself. And the day you stop despising it is the day the boring middle of your life turns out to have been, all along, the place where God was actually at work.
posts.excerpt: The church year has two famous seasons and one long stretch nobody talks about, the green months between Pentecost and Advent called Ordinary Time. It is the least exciting part of the calendar, and it may be the part that actually forms you.

posts.title: What Is Advent, and Why Wait for Something That Already Happened?
posts.body:
There is a particular kind of restlessness that arrives in December, and almost nobody names it correctly. We call it stress, or busyness, or the holidays, and we treat it as a logistics problem to be solved with better planning and more sleep. But underneath the errands there is something older and stranger moving, a low ache that the lights and the music are designed to cover and never quite do. A sense that we are waiting for something, and that whatever it is has not arrived, and that the wrapped boxes are not it.

The church has a name for that ache, and a season built to hold it. The season is called Advent, and it does the one thing the surrounding culture cannot bear to do in December.

It waits.

**Advent is the four weeks before Christmas in which the church deliberately refuses to celebrate yet, sitting instead in darkness and longing, rehearsing what it was to wait for a Savior who had not come, in order to learn how to wait for the one who has not come back.** That is the strange double motion of the season, and it is the thing newcomers find most confusing. The word *Advent* means *coming.* But we already know Christ came. So why spend a month waiting for an arrival the calendar has already filed under history?

The answer is the most useful thing the church year has to teach a restless age.

## The season the culture deleted

Notice first what has happened to December. The culture has collapsed Advent and Christmas into a single, frantic thirty-day sprint of celebration that begins the day after Thanksgiving and ends, abruptly, around two o'clock on Christmas afternoon, when the paper is in the trash and a strange flatness settles over the house. We have all felt that flatness. We rarely ask what it means.

It means we did the season backwards. We spent a month celebrating an arrival and then, at the precise moment the church year is just beginning to feast, we quit. The secular December is front-loaded with joy and ends in exhaustion. The Christian December is the reverse: it begins in the dark and builds, slowly, toward a light it will not let you have early. Advent is not the Christmas warm-up. It is a season with its own integrity, and the first gift it gives is permission to feel, in a culture that demands relentless cheer, the thing many people are actually feeling under the lights, which is some mixture of grief and hope and a longing they cannot place.

Fleming Rutledge, the Episcopal preacher whose collection of Advent sermons, published simply as *Advent* in 2018, has become the season's modern handbook, insists that Advent is the most countercultural season in the church year precisely because it refuses to rush to the manger. It begins, she writes, in the dark. It takes the darkness seriously. It does not pretend the world is fine and only needs a little holiday sparkle to be reminded of it. Advent looks at the actual condition of things, the wars, the cruelty, the long silence of God that so many people feel and so few will admit in church, and it says: yes. This is what we are waiting to be rescued from. And it does not flinch.

That honesty is the first thing that makes Advent feel less like religion and more like the truth.

## Two comings, not one

Here is the piece that resolves the puzzle of waiting for what already happened. Advent has never been about only one arrival. It holds two, and it holds them at the same time, and the whole season vibrates with the tension between them.

The first coming is the one everybody knows. A child born in an occupied backwater of the Roman Empire, to a teenage mother, in conditions so ordinary they were nearly squalid. The prophet Isaiah had seen it coming centuries out: "The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shined" (Isaiah 9:2). Luke records the long human waiting that surrounded the birth, Mary's astonished song, Zechariah's recovered voice, old Simeon and Anna in the temple who had been waiting their whole lives to see the consolation of Israel and would not die until they had (Luke 1–2). The first coming is the answer to all that waiting. It is the arrival that Advent's first half remembers.

But the church discovered early that it was now living in a second waiting, stranger than the first. Christ had come. Christ had died and risen. And then Christ had gone, with a promise to return and finish what he started, to set right everything that is still, visibly, catastrophically wrong. The last words of the entire Bible are a prayer of waiting: "Come, Lord Jesus" (Revelation 22:20). So the Christian lives suspended between two advents. One has happened. One has not. And Advent is the season that names this exact position, the now-and-not-yet, the kingdom that has broken in but has not broken through, the deposit received and the inheritance still outstanding.

This is why waiting for something that already happened is not absurd. **In Advent the church rehearses the first coming in order to train itself for the second**, using the long-ago birth, which we know turned out, to learn how to keep faith through the long-still-coming return, which we do not yet see. We wait for Bethlehem so that we will know how to wait for the day God makes all things new. The first arrival is the church's evidence that the second one is not a fantasy. He came once. He keeps his appointments.

## Why waiting is not wasted time

We are, as a people, almost incapable of waiting. We have engineered our entire economy to abolish it, same-day delivery, streaming, the swipe that summons a car, the feed that refreshes the instant attention flags. Waiting now registers to us as a malfunction, a problem to be solved, a sign that the system is broken. And so we have lost an entire spiritual capacity, because the deepest things God does in a person, he does almost entirely in the waiting.

Paul knew this. In one of the most piercing passages in the New Testament he writes that the whole creation is groaning, straining like a woman in labor, and that we ourselves groan inwardly while we wait for our adoption to be completed, for our bodies to be redeemed. And then the line that Advent is built on: "But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience" (Romans 8:22–25). Hope, Paul says, is not the same as having. Hope is precisely the posture of the one who does not yet see and waits anyway. The groan and the hope are not opposites. They live in the same breath.

This is the discipline Advent restores, and it cuts against everything the surrounding age has trained into us. The world tells you that the gap between desire and fulfillment is a problem to be eliminated as fast as money allows. Advent tells you the gap is holy ground, that the waiting itself is where longing is purified, where you find out what you actually want underneath all the things you thought you wanted, where the soul learns to ache for God rather than for the next delivery. Bobby Gross, in his book *Living the Christian Year*, describes Advent as a season that teaches Christians to inhabit their longing rather than anesthetize it. Most of us spend enormous energy anesthetizing ours. Advent asks us to stop, and to feel the ache, and to let it point somewhere.

There is a deeper reason waiting matters, and it has to do with what hope actually is. We tend to use the word *hope* the way we use the word *wish*, a vague optimism that things will turn out, a pleasant expectation with no particular ground. That is not the biblical word. Hope, in Scripture, is a settled confidence in a promise from someone trustworthy, held onto precisely in the stretch of time before the promise comes true. Which means hope can only exist in the waiting. A hope that has already received what it hoped for is no longer hope; it is possession. The waiting is not the obstacle to hope. The waiting is the only place hope can live. Abolish the waiting and you do not get more hope. You get less, because you have removed the very condition that makes hope possible. This is why a culture that cannot wait is also, not coincidentally, a culture that has nearly lost the capacity for hope, and traded it for a thin, anxious optimism that collapses the moment things stop trending up.

Advent trains the older, sturdier thing. It puts you back in the position of the people of Israel, who waited centuries for a Messiah on the strength of a promise, who died without seeing him, who held the hope across generations because the One who made the promise was faithful. That kind of hope is a muscle, and like any muscle it atrophies without use. Most of us have let it waste away. We have not had to wait for anything in so long that we have forgotten how, and when the real waiting comes, for healing, for reconciliation, for a prodigal to come home, we find we have no strength for it. Advent is the annual rebuilding of that strength, four weeks of practiced waiting so that when the unchosen waiting arrives, we are not starting from nothing.

I have spent Decembers numbing the ache with activity, more events, more obligations, more noise, a calendar so full there was no quiet space in which any longing could speak. I called it the Christmas season. It was avoidance wearing tinsel. Advent is the season that takes the activity away and leaves you alone with the question the noise was covering: what are you really waiting for. For most of us, the honest answer is not a thing on a list. It is closer to a Person.

## Living in the dark, on purpose

So what does it actually look like to keep Advent if you have never done it?

It is quieter than you would expect, and slower. It means letting the four weeks before Christmas be different from Christmas itself, not jumping straight to the feast, but holding off, the way you hold off on a meal you are genuinely hungry for so that the eating, when it comes, means something. It often means a single candle, then two, then three, then four, a little more light each week of a darkening month, so that the room you sit in is teaching your body what the season is about before your mind has framed it. It means reading the parts of the prophets that ache, the parts about people walking in darkness and the parts that promise a light, and letting both halves stay true at once.

And it means resisting the enormous cultural pressure to skip it. This is harder than it sounds. Everything around you in December is already celebrating, has been since before December started, and to keep Advent is to stand slightly out of step with all of it, to be the household still waiting while the rest of the world has moved on to the party. That out-of-step quality is not a flaw in the practice. It is the point. Advent makes you a little strange in December, and the strangeness is itself a kind of witness, a quiet refusal to pretend the arrival has happened when, in the deepest sense, the world is still waiting for it to be completed.

I should be honest that the keeping of it is awkward at first, especially if you came up with no church calendar at all, as I did. The first year you try to hold off on Christmas while everyone around you has already started feels less like devotion and more like deprivation, as if you are the only one who did not get the memo that the celebration began weeks ago. The candles feel like a quaint gesture. The waiting feels like pretending. This is normal, and it passes, because what you are actually doing in that first awkward Advent is unlearning a December that the culture installed in you before you had any say. The strangeness fades as the season does its slow work, and one year, usually without warning, you notice that the early waiting has made the eventual feast taste like something, that Christmas, when it finally comes, lands with a weight it never had when you started celebrating it in November. The discipline of not-yet is what gives the at-last its force. You cannot feel the arrival of a light you were never sitting in the dark for.

There is also something the season does for grief, and this is the part newcomers least expect. December is, for an enormous number of people, the hardest month of the year, the season when the empty chair at the table is emptiest, when the forced cheer of the culture makes the private sorrow feel unspeakable, when everyone seems to be celebrating and you are quietly falling apart. The secular December has no room for these people. Its relentless brightness makes their darkness a kind of failure. Advent does the opposite. It begins in the dark, names the world's brokenness without flinching, and tells the grieving that their ache is not a malfunction but the very thing the season was built to hold. For the person carrying a loss into December, Advent is often the first time the church year stops feeling like decoration and starts feeling like the truth, a season honest enough to admit that we are not all fine, and faithful enough to insist that the light is coming anyway.

There is a reason the church put this season first, at the head of its whole year. It wanted to begin not with achievement but with longing. Not with the light but with the dark and the promise. It wanted the Christian year to open the way the gospel actually opens, with a people in the dark, waiting for a God who has promised to come, and who, against every probability, did.

He came once into a night no one expected. The whole of Advent is the church learning to trust that he will come again into a darkness we can barely name. Until he does, we light the candles one at a time, and we say the oldest prayer there is, and we wait.

Come, Lord Jesus.
posts.excerpt: Advent is not the Christmas warm-up. It is four weeks the church spends in the dark, on purpose, waiting for a birth that happened two thousand years ago. Once you understand why, you may find it is the most honest season there is.

posts.title: Why Would Anyone Give Something Up for Lent?
posts.body:
A coworker mentions she is giving up wine for Lent. Someone else is off social media until Easter. A friend has sworn off chocolate, again, the way he does every year, and will break by the second week, the way he does every year. From the outside it looks like a religious version of a New Year's resolution, a seasonal diet with a theological label, a quaint exercise in willpower that the modern world has mostly outgrown. Even many Christians treat it that way, picking a vice to suspend for six weeks and then forgetting why.

But the people who keep Lent seriously are not on a diet, and they are not testing their willpower. They are doing something far older and more deliberately uncomfortable, and once you understand what it is, the whole practice stops looking quaint and starts looking almost dangerous.

**Lent is forty days in which Christians deliberately remove the comforts that numb them, not to prove they can, but to expose what those comforts have been covering, and to walk, with Jesus, into the wilderness where a person finds out who he actually is when the easy things are gone.** Giving something up is not the point. It is the method. The point is what the absence reveals.

## What the fasting is actually for

Start with the misunderstanding, because nearly everyone holds it. We assume fasting is about deprivation, that the spiritual value lies in the suffering, as if God is pleased by our small miseries and keeps a ledger of foregone desserts. That is not the logic of Christian fasting, and it never was. Fasting is not about the thing you give up. It is about what becomes visible when you give it up.

Consider what actually happens when you remove a daily comfort. Take away the glass of wine at the end of the day and you discover, sometimes for the first time, exactly how much you had been depending on it to take the edge off, how the day's tension had nowhere to go but that glass. Take away the phone you reach for in every idle moment and you discover, in the sudden silences, just how restless you are, how unable to sit with your own thoughts, how relentlessly you have been managing your own discomfort with a screen. The fast does not create these things. It uncovers them. It pulls back the anesthetic and lets you feel what you have been medicating.

This is why Lent matters for people who think they have no particular problem. Most of us are not aware of our compulsions, our small idolatries, the dozen comforts we use to keep ourselves from ever sitting still long enough to face what is underneath. We are too well-supplied to notice. Lent is the deliberate removal of the supply. And what surfaces in the absence, the irritability, the craving, the strange grief when the comfort is gone, that is the real spiritual data. That is the season showing you, gently and without judgment, where your heart has actually been living.

Alexander Schmemann, in his slim and demanding classic *Great Lent*, published in 1969, argued that Lent is not a sad season but a season of return, a long act of remembering who we are and what we were made for, by stripping away the things that have made us forget. The fasting, he wrote, is meant to bring us back to a hunger deeper than food: the hunger for God that our endless small satisfactions have been quietly suppressing. We eat and drink and scroll and buy not because we are so hungry, Schmemann suggests, but because we are starving for something else and have mistaken the symptoms. Lent removes the substitutes so the real hunger can speak.

## Forty days, and why exactly that many

The number is not arbitrary, and the pattern goes deep into Scripture.

Before Jesus began his public ministry, the Spirit drove him into the wilderness for forty days, where he ate nothing and was tempted by the devil (Matthew 4:1–11). Read that account closely and notice what the wilderness does. It strips Jesus down to nothing, no food, no comfort, no crowd, no role to play, and in that stripped-down state the temptations arrive with full force. Turn the stones to bread. Throw yourself down and let the angels catch you. Bow to me and take the kingdoms without the cross. Every temptation is an offer of comfort, of shortcut, of glory without suffering. And Jesus, hungry and alone, refuses all three, answering each with the word of God rather than the relief his body was screaming for.

That is the template Lent follows. The forty days are not a random length of penance. They are a deliberate echo of those forty days in the wilderness, and behind them, of Israel's forty years in the desert, and Moses' forty days on the mountain, and Elijah's forty days of travel to the mountain of God. The wilderness, in Scripture, is the place where God's people are stripped of everything they were leaning on and learn, painfully, to lean on God instead. Lent is the church choosing to enter that wilderness on purpose, once a year, in the company of Jesus, who went there first.

This is the part that moves me most about the season. We do not go into the wilderness alone, and we do not go to earn anything. We go to walk where Jesus walked, to feel a fraction of what he felt, to let the hunger of forty days connect us to the One who was hungry so that we could be fed. The fasting is not a transaction. It is a kind of companionship.

And the timing of the church's forty days is itself instructive. Lent does not float somewhere convenient. It is anchored to the calendar so that it lands in the weeks leading to the cross, which means the wilderness it puts you in is not a detour away from Holy Week but the road directly into it. You fast through the gray end of winter, and the fasting is meant to mirror the season, the bare trees, the long nights not yet broken by spring, the sense of a world waiting for something it cannot yet see. The early church, in placing Lent here, was reading the natural year and the gospel year against each other, letting the dying-back of the world outside the window preach the same sermon as the dying that Holy Week remembers. None of this is sentimental. It is the church using everything available to it, the season, the body, the empty stomach, the bare branch, to make sure the truth gets all the way in, past the part of us that can affirm the cross intellectually while feeling nothing.

## Repentance without the shame

Now the word that scares people off, and the place where I have to be careful, because the church has often gotten this exactly wrong. Lent is a season of repentance. And many people, when they hear that word, hear shame, the grim, groveling, self-loathing religiosity that has driven so many away from the church and back into the very comforts Lent is trying to expose.

Biblical repentance is not that. The prophet Joel, calling a comfortable and complacent nation back to God, frames it like this: "Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). And then immediately, in the same breath, the reason: "for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love." The turning is serious. The God you are turning toward is not standing over you with a ledger. He is gracious and merciful and abounding in steadfast love, and the whole reason repentance is possible at all is that he is the kind of God who runs toward returning children rather than away from them.

Psalm 51, the great penitential prayer, written after a catastrophic moral failure, holds both truths in tension without ever collapsing into despair. It names the sin plainly, no minimizing, no excuse, and in the same prayer asks God to create a clean heart and restore the joy of salvation. The grief over sin and the confidence in mercy live together. That is the emotional register of Lent. Not shame. Honesty, in the presence of a God you trust enough to be honest with.

James puts it as bluntly as anyone: "Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts. Be wretched and mourn and weep" (James 4:8–10). That sounds harsh until you read the promise wrapped inside it, *draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.* The mourning is not the destination. It is the door. You grieve what is broken precisely because you believe it can be healed, and you believe the One who heals it is already moving toward you.

I have avoided this honesty for long stretches of my own life, and I avoided it the way most of us do, not by denying my failures but by staying too comfortable and too busy to ever sit with them. Comfort is a wonderful place to hide. You can run from God for years without ever doing anything dramatic, simply by keeping yourself perpetually soothed. Lent is the season that takes away the soothing and lets you finally stop running, not into condemnation, but into the arms of a mercy you had been too distracted to receive.

This is the thing the church understood about repentance that the modern world has almost entirely lost: that it is a gift, not a punishment. We hear the word and brace, as if repentance were the bill we have to pay before grace will be extended. It is the reverse. Repentance is only possible because grace has already been extended, you can only turn back toward a God you already trust is waiting, and you can only name your failures honestly to a love you are already sure of. The penitent in Psalm 51 does not grovel in the hope of earning his way back. He pours out the truth precisely because he knows the character of the One he is pouring it out to. The honesty is the fruit of the confidence, not the price of it. And so Lent's repentance, kept rightly, does not make a person smaller. It makes a person freer, because there is nothing so exhausting as the management of a self you will not look at honestly, and nothing so unburdening as finally setting it down in front of a God who already knew and already loved and already paid.

## What it forms in you

So why would anyone do this? Why choose discomfort in a world engineered to eliminate it? Why give something up when the entire surrounding economy exists to make sure you never have to?

Because the alternative is to be formed entirely by comfort, and comfort makes weak people. This is not a moralism; it is an observation about how souls actually grow. Richard Foster, in *Celebration of Discipline*, the book that reintroduced a generation of Protestants to the practices they had abandoned, argued that fasting reveals the things that control us. We cover up what is inside us with food and other good things, he wrote, but in fasting these things surface. If pride controls us, it will surface. If anger, fear, bitterness, they surface. The fast does not make us holy. It shows us the truth, and only the truth can be healed.

What Lent forms, over the years, is a person who is no longer at the mercy of his own appetites, who has learned, through repeated practice, that he can be hungry and not collapse, can be uncomfortable and still choose God, can sit in silence without reaching for the screen, can want something badly and not need it. That freedom is rare and precious and almost impossible to acquire any other way. You cannot think your way into it. You have to fast your way into it, a little at a time, year after year.

Consider what the absence of that freedom looks like, because most of us are living inside it without noticing. A person who has never learned to be uncomfortable is a person who can be steered by anyone willing to offer him comfort or threaten him with its loss. He cannot tell the truth if the truth is costly, cannot keep a hard promise if keeping it hurts, cannot stand against a crowd if standing alone is painful, because every one of those things requires the capacity to choose something good over something easy, and that capacity is precisely what comfort, uninterrupted, never develops. We have raised entire generations, and I include myself and my own ministry in this, on the unexamined assumption that the goal of life is to reduce discomfort as far as possible, and we are now surprised to find ourselves fragile, easily manipulated, unable to bear much of anything. Lent is the ancient correction to exactly this fragility. It is strength training for the soul, and like all strength training, it works only through resistance, only by asking of you something slightly more than is comfortable, repeated until the muscle grows.

And the culture, for all its talk of wellness, has no equivalent. It will sell you a juice cleanse and a digital detox and a hundred forms of self-improvement, but every one of them is aimed back at the self, at making you healthier, more productive, more optimized, more you. Lent is aimed somewhere else entirely. Its fasting is not in service of a better you. It is in service of a deeper hunger for God, and that difference is the whole difference. A self-improvement fast leaves you more curved in on yourself than before, prouder of your discipline, more invested in your own betterment. A Lenten fast, kept rightly, turns you outward and upward, empties you of yourself just enough that God can fill the space. The disciplines look identical from the outside. They are pointed at opposite gods.

And the season has an end. This is the mercy built into its structure. Lent does not last forever. It walks toward something, toward the cross, and then through the cross to the empty tomb. The wilderness is real, but it is not the destination. After forty days of hunger comes a feast that the hunger was preparing you to taste. You give something up for a season precisely because there is a Sunday coming when everything will be given back, and more.

That is why anyone would do it. Not to suffer. To get free. And to arrive at Easter as someone who has walked the long road there, hungry enough, at last, to know what the bread is for.
posts.excerpt: Giving up coffee or chocolate for six weeks looks like a quaint religious diet. It is something far stranger and more serious: forty days of deliberately removing what numbs you, to find out what is actually underneath. Here is what Lent is really for.

posts.title: Why Does the Church Have Its Own Calendar?
posts.body:
Pull out your phone and look at the calendar. Not the appointments, the shape of the year underneath them. You will find it already full before you add a single thing. There is a season for spending and a season for resolutions. A season for love that you buy in February and a season for fear that arrives every fall in the form of pumpkins and discount candy. There is a long climb toward a single day in late December that begins, in most stores, before the leaves have turned. You did not choose any of this. It was handed to you, and it tells a story so familiar you have stopped hearing it: that time is a series of occasions to want things, and to get them, and to want the next thing.

Everyone keeps a calendar. The only question is whose.

That is the claim this whole essay is built to earn, so I will say it plainly now. **The Christian year is not religious decoration laid over an otherwise neutral calendar. It is a rival calendar, a deliberate, centuries-old attempt to tell the truth about time, so that the shape of your year slowly retells the story of Jesus instead of the story of the market.** Most people who have never set foot in a liturgical church assume the seasons of the church year are quaint, the leftover furniture of an older world. They are something stranger and more interesting than that. They are a form of resistance you can live inside.

## Time is never empty

We talk about time as if it were a blank container, twenty-four hours a day, three hundred sixty-five of them a year, neutral until we fill them. That is not how time actually reaches us. Time always arrives pre-loaded, already shaped by somebody's story about what it is for.

The philosopher James K.A. Smith spent a book, *You Are What You Love*, published in 2016, making an argument that sounds obvious once you hear it and changes everything once you believe it. We are not primarily thinking things, he says. We are loving things, desiring things, and our desires are not formed by the ideas we hold but by the practices we repeat. What we do over and over, in rhythms we barely notice, quietly tells us what to want. He calls these rhythms liturgies, and he insists that the mall has them, the stadium has them, the screen has them. The shopping center is a temple with its own calendar of feasts, and you have been catechized in it since before you could read.

Hear what that means. The retail year is not neutral. It is a discipleship program. It has seasons of longing and seasons of release, days set apart and days of obligation, and it is forming the people inside it into a particular kind of person, one who experiences the passage of time as the recurring ache of not-yet-having and the brief relief of finally-buying. You can refuse to believe this. You cannot refuse to be shaped by it. The only thing you get to decide is whether some other story gets a vote.

This is why the question of the church calendar is not a question for religious specialists. It is a question for anyone who suspects their own year is being authored by forces they never agreed to.

## The pattern was there from the first page

The instinct to shape time around the truth about God is not a medieval invention. It is on the first page of the Bible, and it is built into the structure of the cosmos as Scripture describes it.

Genesis opens not with a list of objects but with a rhythm. Evening and morning, evening and morning, a cadence of days falling toward a day unlike the others, when the Maker of everything stops. The creation account is, among other things, a calendar. It establishes that time itself has joints and seams, that the week has a shape, that there is a difference between the six and the seventh, that rest is woven into the order of things and not bolted on afterward. Before there is a single command about worship, there is a pattern in the days. God does not make a timeless world. He makes a world that keeps time.

By the time we reach Leviticus 23, the rhythm has become a full liturgical year. God gives Israel a calendar, Passover, Firstfruits, the Feast of Weeks, the Day of Atonement, the Feast of Booths, and the logic of every one of them is the same. Remember. Each feast freezes a moment of God's action so that a generation that did not stand at the Red Sea can taste what it was to be delivered. The feasts exist because human memory is short and human attention drifts toward whatever is loudest, and a people without a calendar of remembrance will, within a generation or two, forget what God has done and start telling some other story about who they are. Israel did not invent these feasts out of nostalgia. They were given them as a defense against forgetting.

And then, into a world already keeping time, comes the strangest sentence in the New Testament about the calendar. Paul writes that "when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son" (Galatians 4:4). The fullness of time. As if all those centuries of evenings and mornings, all those Passovers, all that waiting, had been moving toward a single hour, and that hour had a date. The eternal God did not stay above time. He entered it. He was born under a particular emperor, in a particular town, on a day that actually happened. Christianity is the most aggressively time-bound religion there is, because its central claim is not a timeless principle. It is an event. And events have to be remembered, or they are lost.

The church calendar is what the church built to keep from losing the event.

## What the year actually does

Walk through it once and the architecture becomes clear. The Christian year does not begin in January with the rest of the culture. It begins in late November or early December, in the dark, with Advent, a season of waiting for a Light that has not yet come, even though we know it already has. Then Christmas, twelve days of it, not a single morning of paper and exhaustion but a stretch of celebration that begins where the culture's celebration ends. Then Epiphany, the slow widening of the news to the whole world. Then the long discipline of Lent, forty days in the wilderness with Jesus, walking toward a cross. Then the dark hinge of Holy Week and the impossible morning of Easter, and Easter is not a day but fifty of them, a season of resurrection longer than the season of fasting that prepared for it. Then Pentecost, the Spirit poured out. And then the longest stretch of all, Ordinary Time, the green months of ordinary Sundays where the church learns to follow Jesus through the unspectacular middle of a life.

Now stand back and see what you are looking at. **The Christian year walks you through the entire gospel every twelve months, not as information to be recalled but as time to be inhabited.** You do not read about waiting in Advent. You wait. You do not study repentance in Lent. You repent, with your body, by giving something up. You do not affirm the resurrection on Easter. You feast for seven weeks because something happened that the universe cannot contain in a single Sunday. The year preaches without words. It catechizes through the calendar.

Alexander Schmemann, the Orthodox theologian whose small book *For the Life of the World* reshaped how a generation thought about worship, argued that the liturgical year is not the church's way of commemorating past events at a safe distance. It is the church's way of entering them, of letting the time of Christ become the time we actually live in, so that the gospel stops being a story we believe and becomes a story we are inside. Robert Webber, the evangelical scholar who spent his life calling low-church Protestants back toward the ancient rhythms, made the same case in plainer terms: the Christian year, he wrote, is a way of ordering all of life around the central truth that Jesus is Lord of time itself. Webber was not writing for monks. He was writing for Baptists and Bible-church people who had quietly assumed the calendar was someone else's tradition. He thought they had thrown away something they needed.

I think he was right, and I say that as someone who grew up with no church calendar at all.

## "But isn't this just empty ritual?"

This is the objection I owe an honest answer, because it is the one I once made myself, and it is the one most newcomers feel before they will admit it. Doesn't a calendar of seasons just turn faith into routine? Aren't we supposed to be free of all that, to worship in spirit and in truth, not by the clock?

Here is what I missed for years. The objection assumes that the alternative to ritual is freedom. It is not. The alternative to one set of rhythms is always another set of rhythms. The person who rejects the church calendar does not float free above all calendars, sustained by pure spontaneous devotion. He simply gets discipled by whatever calendar is left running in the background, which, in our world, is the calendar of consumption and the calendar of the news. There is no neutral ground. There is no year that forms you into nothing. The choice was never between ritual and freedom. The choice is between a year shaped by the gospel and a year shaped by something that does not love you.

And I have felt the pull of the something else. I have caught my own attention organized around the next purchase, the next holiday weekend, the next quarter, while the death and resurrection of the Son of God sat somewhere on a shelf marked *believed but not remembered.* I did not stop being formed by time when I stopped keeping a calendar. I just stopped having a say in who was doing the forming. That is not freedom. That is surrender with the lights off.

## The slow work of a different year

What the church calendar offers is not intensity. It is duration. It works the way a riverbed works on water, not in a moment but over years, the same seasons returning, wearing a channel in you so deep that eventually your sense of time itself runs through it.

This is its quiet genius and its hardest sell. We want formation that is fast and felt. The calendar is slow and mostly unfelt. You keep one Advent and nothing seems to happen. You keep twenty Advents and you discover you have become a person who knows, in your body, how to wait for God in the dark, because you have done it, December after December, until waiting is no longer a concept but a competence. The fruit of the church year is not a feeling. It is a self, formed over decades into the shape of the story it kept telling.

There is a further thing the calendar does that the culture's year cannot, and it took me a long time to notice it. The retail year runs in a flat line. It has no story, only a loop, the same cycle of wanting and buying, over and over, going nowhere, arriving at no destination, because the only purpose of the loop is to keep you inside it. The Christian year is not a loop. It is a story told in a circle, which is a different thing entirely. Every December you return to Advent, but you are not the same person who kept it last year, and the story has not changed, Christ still comes, still dies, still rises, so what happens over a lifetime is that the unchanging story keeps meeting the changing you, at a different point in your grief or your faith or your exhaustion every time, and says the same true thing into a new wound. The repetition is not monotony. It is the patience of a story willing to be told to you again until you finally hear it.

This is something Schmemann understood that the consumer calendar can never replicate. The world's year takes from you, your money, your attention, your restlessness renewed on schedule. The church's year gives, the same gospel, returned to you annually, deepening each time it comes around. One calendar exists to keep you hungry. The other exists to feed you. And you cannot serve both, because they are organizing your time toward opposite ends, and over the span of a life the difference between them is the difference between a person who has been formed by longing for things and a person who has been formed by the death and resurrection of God.

The early Christians understood something we have nearly lost. They believed that time was contested ground, that the Roman calendar with its imperial festivals and its emperor-worship was a rival liturgy, and that to keep the Christian year was to declare, quietly and stubbornly, that the world belonged to Christ and not to Caesar. Their calendar was a form of allegiance. It said: this is whose time we keep. When a believer in a city full of festivals to the gods refused to mark the imperial holy days and instead kept the days of Christ, that refusal was costly and visible, a small public treason against the order of things. Time, to them, was never private. To keep a different calendar was to belong to a different kingdom, in public, where it could be seen and could be punished.

We are not so different from them as we like to think. We have our own Caesars now, and they too keep a calendar, and they too would like to author your year. The question the church calendar puts to you is the same one it put to a believer in the second century, sitting in a city full of festivals to gods he did not serve.

Whose time are you keeping. You are keeping someone's. You always were.
posts.excerpt: You already live by a calendar, it tells you when to spend, when to hurry, when to want more. The church year tells a different story about time. Here is what it is for, and what it does to you over years.

posts.title: The Meal That Was Supposed to Make Us One
posts.body:
A newcomer to Christianity figures out the central claim quickly enough: there is one God, one Lord, one faith, one people gathered from every nation into a single body. It is repeated everywhere, sung in the hymns, printed on the websites. *One.* The church loves the word.

Then the same newcomer visits a few churches and runs into something that does not fit. At one, they are told gently that the bread and cup are only for members in good standing of that communion, that they may watch but not receive. At another, the table is open to anyone who loves Jesus. Down the road a third church believes something about that bread the first two consider an error serious enough to keep them apart. The newcomer does the obvious math. The one meal that this religion says makes its people *one* is, in practice, the single most visible place where they are divided. You can worship near each other. You frequently cannot eat together.

This should trouble Christians far more than it does. We have grown so used to it that we explain it away as a technicality, a matter of church order, the sort of thing that need not bother the spiritually mature.
