Surveys of working scientists consistently turn up a sizable minority who hold religious belief of some kind, not a fringe, not a remnant, a standing share of the people doing the actual research. The war model has to treat them all as confused, compartmentalized, or quietly embarrassed. It is a strange theory that has to explain away that many of the very people it claims to speak for.

## A finding that did not fit my expectations

There is one development in twentieth-century physics that I genuinely did not expect when I started reading as a skeptic, because it ran against the direction I assumed the science was heading. I had assumed that the more we learned, the more the universe would look like an accident, vast, indifferent, our presence in it a fluke of no significance. Some of what physics turned up pointed the other way, and honesty requires me to report it even though it does not prove what believers sometimes claim it does.

The constants that govern the universe, the strength of gravity, the force binding atomic nuclei, the rate of cosmic expansion, turn out to sit within extraordinarily narrow ranges, and had several of them been even slightly different, no stable stars, no chemistry, no life of any conceivable kind could have formed. Physicists call this fine-tuning, and it is not a religious claim; it is a feature of the equations that secular cosmologists describe and debate. What it means is the open question. Some read it as evidence of design. Others propose a vast or infinite ensemble of universes, so that ours is simply one of the rare ones where the numbers happened to permit observers. I am not going to pretend the design reading is forced; the multiverse is a serious proposal made by serious people. But notice that the multiverse is itself a leap beyond what any instrument can observe, posited largely to absorb the strangeness of the tuning. The universe stopped looking obviously accidental somewhere in the last century, and the people working hardest to keep it accidental have had to reach for an unobservable infinity of other universes to do it. That is not the picture the war story prepared me for. The cosmos did not get more indifferent as we looked closer. It got stranger, and the strangeness has a shape that does not rule God out.

## Where science genuinely stops

Here is the move I have to make honestly, because it is where the real intellectual action is, and where the easy Christian answers go wrong by claiming too much.

Science is extraordinarily good at one kind of question and silent on another. It can tell you how the universe behaves, the mechanisms, the processes, the laws. It cannot, by its own method, tell you why there is a universe at all rather than nothing, or whether your life means anything, or whether the moral weight you feel when you watch cruelty is tracking something real or just firing neurons. These are not questions science has failed to answer yet, awaiting a better instrument. They are questions of a different kind, outside the reach of the method by design. The instrument that measures wavelengths cannot weigh a duty. That is not a defect in the instrument. It is the boundary of what the instrument is for.

The mistake of my old atheism was to take the silence of science on those questions as the answer no. Because the laboratory could not find God, I concluded there was nothing there, without noticing that the laboratory cannot find justice or beauty or obligation either, and I had not stopped believing in those. I had quietly exempted the values I liked from the standard I was using to dismiss the God I did not want. That is not skepticism. It is selective skepticism, which is another word for prejudice.

## What holds it together

Colossians makes a claim that the war story has no category for. It says that in Christ all things hold together (Colossians 1:17), that the coherence of the world, the very lawfulness that makes science possible, is not an accident the universe happens to have but a feature it is held in. Genesis 1, read not as a science textbook it never claimed to be but as the theological poem it is, makes the same foundational claim in different language: that the world is made, ordered, called good, separated out from chaos by a word. Whatever you make of the timeline, the deep claim is that reality is intelligible because it is authored.

You do not need that claim to do science. Plenty of brilliant scientists work without it. But it is striking that the assumption science cannot prove and cannot do without, that the universe is orderly and the order is knowable, is exactly the assumption the doctrine of creation hands you for free, and exactly the assumption a purposeless cosmos has no obvious reason to grant. Why a blind, unguided process should produce minds capable of reading the deep mathematics of reality, and why that reality should be written in mathematics legible to such minds at all, is not a question science answers. It is a question science assumes its way past every morning before the first experiment. The believer at least has a reason the world is comprehensible. The strict materialist has a remarkable coincidence he has agreed not to find remarkable.

## The choice you were told to make

So here is where I land, and I want to be careful not to overclaim, because overclaiming is how this conversation usually dies. I am not telling you the science proves God. It does not, and the Christians who say it does have not understood either the science or the God. I am telling you something narrower and, I think, harder to dodge.

The choice you were told you had to make between faith and science is a false one, sold by two nineteenth-century writers with an agenda and absorbed by people who never read them. The choice that actually remains is the older one, and the laboratory cannot make it for you: whether the order you study points to anything beyond itself, whether the meaning you cannot help feeling is real or a trick of the wiring, whether the world is authored or accidental. Science hands you a magnificent description of the house. It is constitutionally unable to tell you whether anyone lives there.

That question was never going to be settled by a microscope. It was never that kind of question. And the longer I pretended the microscope had settled it, the more I was hiding a decision I had already made from the evidence I claimed to be following.
posts.excerpt: Everyone knows faith and science are at war. The trouble is that the war is largely a story invented in the nineteenth century, and the man who led the human genome project is a believer. Here is where the conflict actually came from, and where it doesn't exist.

posts.title: If God Is Good, Why Is There So Much Suffering?
posts.body:
I will not start this one by being clever, because the subject does not allow it. The strongest argument against the existence of God is not the one made in philosophy seminars. It is the one made by a hospital ward full of children who did nothing to deserve what is happening to them. If there is a good and all-powerful God, that ward should not exist. It does exist. For a great many thoughtful people, that single fact has closed the question, and I do not think they are stupid or shallow for letting it. The problem of suffering is the best reason not to believe, and any apologetics that treats it as a debating point to be scored has already failed the people it claims to be helping.

So I am going to take it at full strength before I say anything in reply, and I am not going to pretend my reply dissolves it.

**My claim is deliberately modest, because anything less than modest here is a lie: the problem of suffering does not disprove God, but it does not need to be solved to be survived, and the alternative, a universe in which the suffering means nothing at all, is harder to live in than skeptics let on.** I am not going to tie a bow on this. There is no bow.

## Let the strongest version stand

The cheap Christian move is to soften the objection so it is easier to answer. I refuse to do that, because the strongest version is the one I actually believe, and the only honest way through it is straight in.

Dostoevsky put it more devastatingly than any modern atheist, and he put it in the mouth of a man named Ivan, in *The Brothers Karamazov* (1880). Ivan does not deny God exists. He does something worse for the believer, he says that even if God exists, even if there is some grand harmony at the end of all things in which every tear is wiped away and every wrong made right, he wants no part of it, because no future harmony can be worth the torture of one innocent child. He piles up real cases, atrocities done to children, and then he refuses the ticket. *It is not God I do not accept,* Ivan says in effect, *it is the world he made; I most respectfully return him the ticket.* That is the argument at full power. It is not a logic puzzle. It is a moral refusal, and it is more honest than most defenses of God I have heard.

The philosophical version is tidier and almost as hard. If God is all-powerful, he could prevent suffering. If God is all-good, he would want to. Suffering exists in staggering quantities. So either he cannot, and is not all-powerful, or will not, and is not all-good, and either way the God of traditional theism seems ruled out. For most of my life I thought that argument was airtight, and I thought anyone who believed had simply not let themselves feel its force.

I no longer think it is airtight. I do still think it should be felt with full force, and the believer who has not felt it is not believing in the real God. He is believing in a smaller one who never had to answer for the ward.

## Why the logical version weakened

The philosophers have actually moved on this, and it is worth a skeptic knowing where the conversation stands, because the version of the argument most people carry is a generation out of date.

For a long time the claim was that the existence of any evil at all was logically inconsistent with the existence of an all-powerful, all-good God, that you could not coherently hold both, the way you cannot hold a married bachelor. Alvin Plantinga is generally credited with ending that strong version. His free-will defense does not claim to explain why God permits any particular evil. It makes a narrower, more durable point: it is at least possible that a world containing free creatures, capable of genuine love and genuine evil, is more valuable than a world of puppets who cannot do wrong because they cannot do anything, and that even an all-powerful God cannot create free creatures and also guarantee they never misuse the freedom, because forced love is a contradiction. If that scenario is even possible, and almost no one now argues it is not, then the bare logical contradiction collapses. The coexistence of God and evil is not a contradiction in terms.

That settles less than it sounds like. It addresses the evil we do to each other. It does not touch the earthquake, the cancer in a child, the suffering no free human chose. And it does not make the suffering hurt less. Plantinga himself never claimed it did. It moves the argument from disproof to something murkier and more human: not *God cannot exist given this,* but *how could a good God allow this*, which is not a proof at all. It is a cry, and it deserves to be treated as one.

## The honest limit of every answer

Here is where I have to disappoint anyone hoping for the knockout, because the knockout does not exist and pretending it does is the cruelty I most want to avoid.

There are partial answers, and they carry some weight. The free-will defense covers moral evil. The argument that real virtues, courage, compassion, sacrifice, require a world with real stakes covers some of the rest. The observation that a creature cannot see the whole from inside the story covers the rest in principle. C.S. Lewis worked these through in *The Problem of Pain* (1940) with rigor and some real insight, and then, years later, after his wife died of cancer, he wrote *A Grief Observed* and discovered that none of his own arguments touched the wound. Both books are true. That is the thing about this subject. The intellectual answers can be sound and the wound can stay open, and a faith worth having has to hold both without letting either cancel the other.

Tim Keller, in *Walking with God through Pain and Suffering* (2013), made the observation that finally reframed it for me, and it is not a solution but a redistribution of the difficulty. Every worldview faces the problem of suffering. The secular one does not escape it, it relocates it. If there is no God, the suffering of the child is not a problem to be explained; it is simply a fact with no meaning, no redemption, no final accounting, a burst of pain in an indifferent universe that will forget it ever happened. The atheist does not get to keep the moral outrage that powered Ivan's argument and also keep the universe that makes outrage incoherent. If there is no God, on what ground is the child's suffering an *outrage* rather than merely an event, the way a landslide is an event? Ivan's refusal borrows a moral law to indict the universe, and a universe with no God supplies no such law to borrow.

That is not a proof of God. It is an observation that the problem of evil cuts both ways, and the side that thinks it has escaped the problem has only stopped naming it.

Press the point one turn further, because it is the turn that did the most to unsettle my own atheism. The problem of evil is not just an emotional difficulty for the unbeliever; it is a logical one, and it runs in the opposite direction from where I had aimed it. To call the suffering of a child *evil*, not unfortunate, not statistically regrettable, but evil, a violation of the way things ought to be, is to appeal to a standard of how things ought to be. But where does a purely material universe get an "ought"? Atoms do not have oughts. A process of blind selection produces creatures that survive; it does not produce a cosmic standard of justice that the universe is failing to meet. The atheist who is genuinely outraged at suffering is standing on a moral floor his own worldview cannot pour. He is using the reality of evil to argue against God, while the very category of evil, real, objective, binding wrong, is far easier to account for if there is a God whose character defines the ought than if there is not. I had thought the problem of evil was my strongest weapon against belief. It turned out to be borrowing its ammunition from the thing it was firing at.

## What Scripture does not do

The thing that disarmed me, when I finally read it rather than assuming its contents, was what the Bible does not do with suffering. I had expected it to explain. It refuses.

When Job, who has lost his children, his health, everything, finally gets the audience with God he has demanded, God does not answer the question. God does not explain the wager in the prologue, does not justify the loss, does not produce the theodicy Job's friends kept manufacturing. Instead, out of the whirlwind, God asks Job questions for four chapters (Job 38–42): where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth, can you bind the stars, do you give the horse his strength. It reads at first like evasion. It is not. It is the refusal of a glib answer from the only source entitled to give one. God will not reduce Job's agony to a lesson. He offers, instead, himself, his presence, his reality, the sheer scale of a wisdom Job cannot audit. And Job, strangely, is satisfied, not because he got the explanation but because he got God.

Habakkuk does the same thing from the other side. The prophet opens by shouting the problem straight at God, how long shall I cry for help and you will not hear, why do you make me look at injustice (Habakkuk 1), and the book never resolves the complaint into a clean answer. It resolves into trust held in the dark. The Bible authorizes the protest. It puts the strongest version of the objection into the mouths of its own heroes and does not rebuke them for it.

And then there is the line of Jesus that should stop the believer cold. When people brought him the news of a massacre and a fatal accident, clearly fishing for the explanation, *what did those people do to deserve it*, he flatly denied the premise that suffering maps to guilt (Luke 13:1–5). Those who died were not worse sinners. The clean accounting we crave, where suffering is the receipt for sin, he tore up. He left the why unanswered and turned it back on the askers as a question about themselves.

## The strange location of the Christian answer

If Christianity had an explanation for suffering, it would be one more theodicy among many, and I would not have found it more persuasive than the others. It has something stranger, and the strangeness is the point.

The center of the faith is not a God who explains suffering from a safe distance. It is a God who entered it. The claim is that the One who could have answered Ivan from the throne instead came down into the ward, was betrayed, tortured, and executed, and cried from the cross the exact question every sufferer cries, *why have you forsaken me.* Romans says the whole creation groans as in childbirth, and we groan with it, waiting (Romans 8:18–25), not denying the groan, naming it, locating it inside a labor that is going somewhere. The Christian answer to suffering is not a syllogism. It is a wounded God and a promised end, offered to people in the middle who cannot yet see either clearly.

I do not say this resolves the problem. It does not. The child in the ward is still in the ward. But it changes what kind of universe the ward is in. Not a universe where suffering is meaningless noise, and not a universe where a distant deity watches unmoved, but one where the suffering is real, and named, and entered, and not the last word.

## Where I leave you, because I cannot do better

I am not going to end this with a resolution, because to resolve it would be to betray everyone who is actually suffering while they read it. The problem of evil is not solved in this essay or any other. It is the hardest thing, and the people who tell you they have it figured out have usually not been near the worst of it.

Here is the most I can honestly say. The suffering does not disprove God; the logical version of that argument did not hold, and the moral version turns out to need a moral law that a Godless universe cannot supply. But the suffering does not get explained away either, and the faith that pretends otherwise is not worth having. What is left is a choice between two unprovable things: that the agony of the world means nothing and will be forgotten, or that it is real and seen and will somehow be answered by a God who did not stay out of it. Neither can be proven from inside the story. But one of them I have watched people die holding, with a peace the other never gave anyone.

The question was never going to get a clean answer. The God of Job never gave one. What he gave was himself, in the whirlwind and finally on a cross, and the people who have met him in their worst hour do not come back saying they understand. They come back saying they are not alone in it. That is less than you wanted. It may be more than you expected.
posts.excerpt: The strongest argument against God is not made by philosophers. It is made by a suffering child, and Dostoevsky put it better than any atheist since. Here is the problem of evil taken at full strength, no glib answers, no comfort that isn't earned.

posts.title: Was Jesus Really Just a Good Teacher?
posts.body:
The most respectable thing you can say about Jesus in polite company is that he was a great moral teacher. It costs nothing and offends no one. You get to keep the Sermon on the Mount, the love of enemies, the care for the poor, all the parts modern people still admire, without the embarrassing supernatural machinery. Wise man, ethical genius, perhaps the finest teacher who ever lived, on a shelf next to Socrates and the Buddha. It is the verdict of the thoughtful, secular, generous-minded person, and for years it was mine.

C.S. Lewis thought it was the one verdict the evidence would not let you keep, and he said so in a paragraph that has annoyed clever people ever since.

**Here is what I will argue, and I will sharpen the objections to it before I rest any weight on it: the comfortable verdict, great teacher, nothing more, is the one position the historical Jesus makes almost impossible to hold, because the teaching you admire and the claims you want to discard come from the same mouth, in the same breath, and cannot be cleanly separated.**

## The argument that will not leave you alone

Lewis made it in *Mere Christianity* (1952), and even people who reject it concede it has teeth. A man who was merely human and said the kinds of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher. He would either be a liar, or a lunatic, or something far worse. The teacher who tells you to love your neighbor is one thing. The teacher who also tells you that he can forgive your sins, that he existed before Abraham, that he and the Father are one, that man is not handing you ethics. He is making a claim about himself that, if false, is either deliberate fraud or delusion of a clinical kind. You can call him Lord, Lewis said, or you can call him a madman or worse, but the one thing you cannot call him, on the evidence, is simply a wise teacher, because no merely wise teacher talks that way. *That is the one thing we must not say.*

It is a sharp argument. It is also, in the popular form, too quick, and a skeptic is right to push on it. So let me push on it myself, harder than most defenders do.

## The objections, taken seriously

The trilemma, liar, lunatic, or Lord, has at least two real holes, and pretending otherwise is how Christians lose people who can think.

The first hole is the one most often named: legend. The trilemma assumes Jesus actually said these things. But what if he did not? What if the high claims were put in his mouth by a later church that had already decided he was divine, while the historical Jesus was a humble rabbi who would have been horrified to hear himself called God? This is not a fringe position. It was, for a long stretch of the twentieth century, the mainstream scholarly default, the assumption that the divine Jesus was a slow theological accretion, layered onto a simpler human figure over generations. If that is right, the trilemma collapses, because there is a fourth option Lewis left out: legend. Not liar, lunatic, or Lord, but a good teacher whose followers mythologized him after the fact.

The second hole is subtler. Even granting Jesus said remarkable things about himself, the categories may be too clean. Sincere religious figures across history have made elevated claims without being either frauds or psychiatric cases in any simple sense. Human self-understanding is stranger and more layered than three tidy boxes allow. The trilemma can feel like a forced choice that rigs the outcome by limiting the options.

There is a third objection, the gentlest and in some ways the most modern, and it deserves naming because it is the one most thoughtful people actually hold today. It is the pluralist move: that Jesus, like other great teachers, was pointing past himself to a universal truth, and that his followers misunderstood a humble mystic's self-effacement as self-exaltation. On this reading he is closer to a sage who said "the kingdom of God is within you" than to a man claiming to be God. It is an attractive picture. It keeps Jesus admirable and keeps him safely one option among many. The difficulty is that it requires setting aside not stray verses but the entire shape of how he spoke and acted and died, and replacing it with a figure no first-century source actually describes, a serene mystic invented largely in the modern West, retrofitted onto a Galilean who got himself crucified for blasphemy. The pluralist Jesus is the most recent of the legends, and the least anchored in the record.

These objections are fair, and the first is the one that matters most, because if the legend theory holds, the rest is moot. So that is where the historical work has to be done, and it is here that the conversation has shifted in a way most skeptics have not caught up with.

## The legend theory ran out of time

The whole legend account depends on time, on a long enough gap between the human Jesus and the divine Jesus for the myth to grow. Take the time away and the theory has nowhere to stand. And the time has been taken away.

Larry Hurtado spent his career on exactly this question, and his major work, *Lord Jesus Christ* (2003), assembles the evidence that the worship of Jesus as divine did not develop slowly over centuries. It erupted astonishingly early, within the first years after his death, among Jewish monotheists, the very people whose entire religious identity was built on the refusal to worship anyone but the one God. These were not pagans for whom another god was no scandal. These were people who would die before bowing to an idol, and they began, almost immediately, to pray to Jesus, sing to him, baptize in his name, treat him with the devotion reserved for God alone. Hurtado's point is that this is historically extraordinary and demands explanation. Devotion this high, this fast, among these people, does not behave like a legend slowly accreting. It behaves like a response to something that had already detonated their categories.

The early creed Paul quotes in his letters, material older than the gospels, traceable to within a few years of the crucifixion, already treats Jesus in the highest terms. The divine Jesus is not the end of a long evolutionary chain. He is there at the documentable beginning. N.T. Wright has argued the same across his historical work: the evidence does not show a human teacher gradually promoted to godhood by a forgetful church, but a movement that, from its earliest recoverable moment, was already doing the unthinkable thing of worshiping a crucified man within the framework of Jewish monotheism. The legend needed centuries. The record gives it years, and barely that.

N.T. Wright has added a dimension to this that closes a different exit. The popular debate often gets stuck on whether Jesus walked around announcing "I am God" in so many words, and a skeptic can fairly point out that the most explicit statements cluster in John's gospel, which is generally dated later. But Wright's historical work shows the claim does not depend on the explicit formula. It is built into what Jesus did, in the earliest and most securely historical layers, and it is built in the way a first-century Jew would have read it, not the way a modern reader scanning for a creedal statement would. Jesus acted as though he carried an authority the Scriptures reserved for God alone. He spoke as if the temple, the center of Israel's entire encounter with God, was being relocated around himself. He behaved as though Israel's God was returning to his people, in person, in him. To his contemporaries this was not a vague spirituality. It was a set of actions with a single unmistakable meaning, and they tried to kill him for it well before any gospel was written. The high claim is not a late verbal addition. It is the earliest layer's account of why he was executed.

## What he actually said

Strip the question to the texts, and the claims are not buried in later editorializing. They are woven through the earliest layers, often in the most Jewish material, exactly where invention would be hardest.

To a paralyzed man he said, simply, *your sins are forgiven*, and the scribes watching understood the offense instantly, asking who can forgive sins but God alone (Mark 2:5–7). They were right to be scandalized. He was not pronouncing a general truth about God's mercy. He was personally absolving, taking to himself a prerogative that belonged, in their entire theology, to God and no one else. He did not correct their reading. He doubled down by healing the man to prove the point.

To his opponents he said, *before Abraham was, I am* (John 8:58), and they picked up stones, because the construction was not merely a claim to predate Abraham by centuries. It echoed the divine name God spoke to Moses from the bush. They reached for rocks because they heard, correctly, a man applying the name of God to himself. Elsewhere, plainly, *I and the Father are one,* and again the stones come out, and when he asks which good work they are stoning him for, they answer that it is not for any work but for blasphemy, because *you, being a man, make yourself God* (John 10:30–33). The hostile witnesses in the text understood the claim better than the modern admirer does. They did not hear a great teacher. They heard a man claiming the unclaimable, and they responded the way first-century monotheists would.

And when he asked his own disciples directly who they thought he was, and Peter answered that he was the Messiah, the Son of the living God, Jesus did not deflect or correct the title (Matthew 16:13–16). He received it. He blessed the man for seeing it. A merely humble rabbi, horrified to be called divine, had every opportunity in these scenes to say *no, you misunderstand, I am only a teacher.* The texts never record him saying it. The texts record him accepting worship, forgiving sins, and applying the name of God to himself, and dying, in the end, on the specific charge of blasphemy.

## Why the comfortable verdict fails

Now the trilemma can be put back together, stronger for having survived its objections, and aimed where it actually bites.

The legend escape is closed, or at least badly weakened, by Hurtado and the early creeds and the speed of the devotion: the high claims are not late additions but early bedrock. And once that escape is closed, the comfortable position is in real trouble, because the comfortable position depends on cleanly separating the ethics you admire from the claims you reject, keeping the Sermon on the Mount and discarding *before Abraham was, I am*, when both come from the same person, in the same sources, in the same voice. You cannot run a scalpel between them. The man who told you to love your enemies is the man who told you he could forgive their sins against God. If he was wrong about the second, you have no obvious grounds to trust him on the first, because a man that wrong about himself is not a reliable guide to anything, however lovely his aphorisms.

That is the force of Lewis's argument once it has been pressure-tested. It does not prove Jesus was God. A skeptic can still conclude he was deluded, or that the sincere claims of a remarkable figure resist the neat categories. Those remain open. The one position that does not remain open, on the actual evidence, is the flattering middle, the wise teacher who never disturbs you. That man is the invention. The historical Jesus is the one who disturbs.

Consider what the trilemma's remaining options actually cost, because the comfortable view survives partly by never pricing them. Take the lunatic reading: a man under a delusion of divinity grand enough to forgive sins and accept worship. Clinical grandiosity of that order does not generally coexist with the teaching attributed to Jesus, the precision, the moral depth, the penetrating realism about human nature, the steadiness under interrogation. The Sermon on the Mount is not the work of a disordered mind, and the parables are not the productions of a man who has lost contact with reality. The same evidence that makes us want to call him a great teacher is the evidence that makes the lunatic verdict hard to sustain. Now take the liar reading: a deliberate fraud who manufactured the claims for gain. But he gained nothing a fraud seeks. He acquired enemies, poverty, and an execution he saw coming and walked toward. Frauds do not generally die for the con when recanting would save them. Each remaining option carries a weight the admirer rarely weighs, and the weight is what makes the comfortable verdict feel light by comparison, it is light because it has quietly declined to pay anything at all.

## The verdict you cannot avoid

I held the comfortable view sincerely, and I want to name what was really going on in it, because I think it is common. I admired Jesus. I quoted him. And I had arranged the admiration so that it never cost me anything, I had filed him under great teachers, which is the file you keep things in when you want to honor them without obeying them. The great-teacher verdict is not the conclusion of careful thought. It is the most comfortable place to set down a person you find too compelling to dismiss and too demanding to follow.

The historical Jesus will not stay in that file. He made claims that a great teacher does not make, that the legend theory cannot explain away, that his earliest Jewish followers responded to with the worship they owed to God alone. You are left with the choice his contemporaries faced, and it was never the polite three-way of the seminar. It was the one he put to his friends on the road, and then waited for the answer.

*Who do you say that I am.* He is still standing there, and the one reply he has made unavailable is the one most people reach for first.
posts.excerpt: The polite modern verdict on Jesus is that he was a great moral teacher, nothing more. C.S. Lewis said that was the one thing he never left open to us. The trilemma gets attacked, fairly, so here it is pressure-tested against the best objections.

posts.title: Why Would Anyone Trust the Bible?
posts.body:
The most common objection I hear to the Bible is not really an objection to the Bible. It is an objection to a story about the Bible, a story most people absorbed without ever checking, the way you absorb the rules of a game you have never read. The Bible was copied by hand for centuries, the story goes, so it must be like the telephone game, garbled past recovery. It was assembled by a council of bishops with political motives who voted on which books would make Jesus divine and burned the rest. It contradicts itself constantly. By the time the story is finished, you would be a fool to take it seriously, and most people I talk to have never gotten past the story to the thing itself.

I lived inside that story for years. It was load-bearing for my unbelief. When it collapsed, it did not make me a Christian, but it took away an excuse I had been leaning on hard.

**Here is what I will argue, and I will try to give the objections their full weight before I answer them: the case against trusting the Bible is built almost entirely on claims that the relevant scholarship, much of it produced by non-Christians and skeptics, does not support.** That does not settle whether the Bible is true. It clears away the underbrush so the real question can be asked.

## The telephone game is the wrong picture

Start with the most popular objection, because it is the most quickly answered and the most stubbornly repeated.

The telephone game works because each player hears the message once, from one source, and passes it to exactly one other person, with no way to check. That is the opposite of how the New Testament was transmitted. The texts were copied many times, in many places, by many hands, and the copies spread outward in a branching tree, not a single fragile line. F.F. Bruce, the Manchester scholar whose *The New Testament Documents: Are They Reliable?* (1943) is still a sober starting point, made the basic point that the sheer volume of manuscripts is itself the safeguard. We have thousands of Greek manuscripts and many thousands more in other ancient languages, vastly more than for any other document of the ancient world. Caesar's *Gallic Wars* survives in a handful of late copies, and no one writes books questioning whether Caesar really wrote it.

Abundance is not a weakness. It is how scholars catch errors. When you have one copy, a mistake is invisible. When you have thousands branching from different regions, a copyist's slip in Egypt shows up against a clean reading in Syria, and the original is recoverable by comparison. The vast majority of the variations among manuscripts are spelling differences and obvious slips of the pen. The places where a genuinely meaningful, disputed variant affects anything are few, well known, and printed right in the footnotes of any decent modern Bible. The text is not hidden from you. The uncertainty is disclosed on the page.

This is not the same as proving the contents true. A perfectly transmitted false claim is still false. But the specific charge, that the words were garbled in transit until we cannot know what was originally written, does not survive contact with the manuscript evidence. We know what they wrote with a confidence that embarrasses the comparison to every other ancient text.

## The council did not invent the canon

The second story is more dramatic and more wrong: that a council of bishops sat down centuries later and voted Jesus into godhood, choosing four gospels and suppressing dozens of others to consolidate power. It is a good plot. It is not history.

The canon was not decided by decree. It emerged by recognition, slowly, from below. The four gospels were functioning as authoritative across scattered, often persecuted churches long before any council ratified them, the church recognized the books it had already been reading and dying for, rather than conferring authority on them by vote. The criteria were not political: a book had to trace to the apostolic circle, be in wide use across the churches, and cohere with the faith already received. The famous alternative gospels usually invoked here were written considerably later, mostly in the second century and after, often carrying a theology the apostolic churches had already rejected on its face. They were not suppressed by a conspiracy. They lost because they arrived late and said things the eyewitness communities knew to be foreign.

Luke states the method out loud at the start of his gospel. He says many have undertaken to compile accounts, that he has carefully investigated everything from the beginning, drawing on those who were eyewitnesses from the first, so that his reader may know the certainty of what he was taught (Luke 1:1–4). That is not the preface of a man inventing a religion. It is the preface of a man doing research and showing his work.

It is worth pausing on why the conspiracy version is so attractive despite being so weak, because the attraction tells you something. The story of a power-hungry council voting Jesus into godhood gives the skeptic a villain, a motive, and a clean exit, if the whole thing was a power grab, you can dismiss it without engaging it. That is a great deal more comfortable than the actual history, which is messy and bottom-up and full of ordinary people in scattered towns recognizing books they were already reading aloud and dying over. The conspiracy is the easier story to disbelieve, which is exactly why it gets believed. I preferred it for the same reason most people do. It let me close the file without reading it. The trouble is that the real history of the canon refuses to supply the villain the story needs, and a dismissal aimed at a villain who was never there is a punch thrown at a shadow.

## The eyewitness question is where it gets interesting

For a long time the scholarly fashion held that the gospels were anonymous folk traditions, shaped and reshaped by communities over generations until whatever historical core they had was buried under invention. That model dominated, and it is the assumption sitting underneath most educated dismissals today.

Richard Bauckham took it apart in *Jesus and the Eyewitnesses* (2006), and the argument is worth a skeptic's attention precisely because it cuts against the academic grain. Bauckham marshals the evidence that the gospels are not anonymous community products but testimony tied to named individuals who were there. He points to the strange specificity of named minor characters who serve no literary purpose, why name the man who carried the cross, and his sons, unless those sons were known figures in the church who could be asked? He shows that the patterns of names in the gospels match the actual statistical frequency of Jewish names in first-century Palestine, a fingerprint almost impossible to fake from a distance or a later generation. He argues that the period between the events and the writing was not the silent gap legend requires but a span in which the eyewitnesses were living, teaching, and available to correct the record.

You can disagree with Bauckham, scholars do. But you cannot any longer treat the eyewitness question as settled in favor of the legend model, because a major work of mainstream scholarship reopened it and put the weight back on the side of testimony. That is the honest state of the field, and it is not the state of the field most skeptics think they are standing on.

## The texts touch the ground

There is a quieter line of evidence that rarely makes the popular debates, and it mattered to me precisely because it was checkable against things outside the Bible. The documents are not free-floating tales set in a vague never-land. They are studded with the names of real rulers, real places, real political arrangements that we can verify from sources that had no stake in the Christian claim.

Luke in particular reads like a man who expected his readers to be able to look things up. He anchors his account in datable reigns and named officials, governors, tetrarchs, high priests, many of whom turn up in Roman records, in the Jewish historian Josephus, and in inscriptions pulled out of the ground centuries later. An inscription confirming Pontius Pilate as the Roman prefect of Judea was recovered in the twentieth century, long after anyone could have planted it to help the gospels. The titles Luke gives to local officials in various cities, which earlier critics flagged as errors, turned out to be precisely correct for the specific places and periods he was describing, a kind of accuracy a late forger writing from a distance would have been unlikely to get right. None of this proves the resurrection, and I will keep saying that, because the line between corroboration and proof is exactly the line careless apologists erase. But it does undercut the picture of the gospels as floating myth. A myth does not bother to get the provincial bureaucracy right. A myth has no governor to name.

## What about the contradictions

This is the objection I respect most, because it is the one with real texture, and the glib Christian answers to it are genuinely bad.

The gospels do not agree on every detail. How many angels at the tomb, the order of events on Easter morning, the exact wording of sayings reported differently, these differences are real, and pretending they are not is a kind of lying that does the Bible no favors. But here is what serious historians notice, and what should give a skeptic pause: ancient testimony that agrees on every detail is the suspicious kind. It signals collusion, a single source dressed up as many. Independent witnesses to the same event always differ at the edges and converge at the center, and that is exactly the pattern the gospels show. They differ on the number of angels. They do not differ on the crucifixion, the burial, the empty tomb, the appearances. The variation at the periphery is evidence of independence, not evidence of fraud.

N.T. Wright has made this point across his historical work: the differences in the resurrection narratives are precisely what you would expect from separate witnesses describing a real, confusing, overwhelming event, and precisely not what you would expect from a committee inventing a story to agree on. The flat, harmonized account would be the forgery. The textured, partly-divergent account is what testimony looks like.

There is a further detail in those narratives that a committee bent on persuasion would have edited out. In a culture where a woman's testimony carried little legal weight, all four gospels make women the first witnesses to the empty tomb. If you were fabricating a story to win converts in the first century, you would not anchor your central claim in the testimony of the witnesses your own society discounted. You would put the men there first. The gospels do the opposite, and the most economical explanation for an embarrassing detail that works against the storyteller's interest is that it happened that way and the writers were not free to change it. Historians call this the criterion of embarrassment, and the gospels are full of it, the disciples are dull, cowardly, and slow; their leader is baptized by a man preaching repentance; he dies the death reserved for the lowest criminals. These are not the flattering details a movement invents about its origins. They are the details a movement reports because it is stuck with them.

## The claim the Bible makes about itself

There is a move I have to make carefully here, because it can sound circular, and a skeptic is right to flag circular reasoning. I am not arguing the Bible is true because the Bible says so. I am noting what kind of claim its authors thought they were making, because it bears on how to read them.

Peter, writing about what he had seen, insists he was not passing on clever myths, that he had been an eyewitness of Jesus' majesty (2 Peter 1:16). John ends his gospel saying plainly that Jesus did many other things he did not record, and that the ones he did record were written so the reader might believe (John 20:30–31). The selection is admitted. The purpose is admitted. And Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, correcting, training (2 Timothy 3:16), a claim of inspiration, not of magical transmission, made by men who also told you they did research and selected their material.

These are not the moves of people who think they are writing fiction. Whether they were right is the question that remains. But the texts present themselves as testimony and selection and investigation, and they should be examined as that, not as the garbled rumor of the telephone-game story, which the documents themselves refuse.

## Where this leaves the question

Clearing the underbrush does not get you to faith, and I will not pretend it does. You can grant every point I have made, that the transmission is reliable, that the canon emerged by recognition, that the eyewitness case is live, that the contradictions are the signature of independence, and still conclude the witnesses were sincerely mistaken about what they saw. That is a coherent position. It is a far more honest one than the position I held, which was to reject the whole thing on the strength of stories about it I had never checked.

That is the part I have to own. My unbelief had felt like the brave, clear-eyed option, the refusal to be fooled. It turned out to be the credulous option, I had simply transferred my faith from the Bible to the secular folklore about the Bible, and never noticed I had believed something on worse evidence than the thing I was rejecting.

So the question I would leave you with is not whether the Bible is convenient or comfortable or flattering. It is older and simpler than that. Have you actually read it, with the attention you would give a hostile witness you suspected of telling the truth? Or have you, like me, been quoting the trailer and calling it the film?

The book is not asking to be trusted blindly. It is asking to be opened. Most of the people most confident it cannot be trusted have done everything with it except that.
posts.excerpt: Translated through telephone games, edited by councils with agendas, full of contradictions, that's the story most people inherit about the Bible. Almost none of it survives contact with the actual scholarship. Here is what the evidence really shows, objections included.

posts.title: Does God Change His Mind?
posts.body:
Open the Bible at random and you can come away with two flatly opposite pictures of God. In one, He is the fixed point, the one thing that does not move while everything else does, "I the LORD do not change" (Malachi 3:6). In the other, He seems as movable as a parent worn down by a long argument: He sees Nineveh repent and "relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them" (Jonah 3:10); He hears Moses plead and "the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people" (Exodus 32:14). So which is it? Does God change His mind or not? Skeptics treat this as a contradiction caught red-handed. Believers often just look away from it. Both responses miss something worth having.

I missed it for years. As someone who came to faith out of unbelief, I had been trained to hunt for exactly this kind of seam in a text, the place where the story trips over itself, and the God who "repents" looked like an obvious trip. It took me a long time to see that I was reading the seam the wrong way around.

Here is the claim, and I want to make it gently because it is easy to make it coldly. **God does not change His mind the way you and I do, not because He is rigid, but because He is complete. He has no new information, no second thoughts, no improved plan He wishes He had thought of sooner. And precisely because He does not change, the verses where He "relents" mean something far more reassuring than they appear to.** The unchanging God is not the frozen God. He is the only God you could ever actually lean your whole weight on.

## Why an unchanging God sounds cold, and isn't

Let me name the resistance first, because I felt it and you may too.

"God does not change" sounds, on first hearing, like bad news. We want a God who responds, who is moved by our prayers, who can be reached, who is not a marble statue staring past us. An "unchanging" God sounds like an indifferent one, sealed off in His perfection, untouchable. If nothing I do can move Him, why pray? Why love a being who is the same whether I show up or not? The doctrine the theologians call *immutability*, God's unchangeableness, has a public-relations problem, and the problem is that we hear it as *unresponsiveness.*

But run the opposite all the way out and see if you actually want it. A God who changes is a God who can change *for the worse.* A God who has new thoughts is a God who can be surprised, which means He did not see this coming, which means tomorrow may bring something He has not accounted for. A God who can be talked into things can be talked out of them; the love He has for you today is, in principle, revisable. Every quality you love about God, His mercy, His faithfulness, His goodness, is only as reliable as His changelessness. If He can change, then His promise to you is a mood, and moods pass. I wanted a God who would not move. Not because I wanted Him distant, but because I had spent enough time around people whose love was weather, and I could not bet my life on weather again.

So the question is not whether you want a changeable God. The question is what kind of unchangeableness we are talking about, and the tradition is far more careful here than its critics assume.

## Aquinas, Boethius, and the God who is not in time the way we are

Two old thinkers worked this out with a precision worth recovering, and you do not need Latin to follow them.

Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, reasoned about it this way. To change is to gain something you lacked or lose something you had, to move from potential to actual. A seed changes into a tree; it had the capacity for treeness and now realizes it. But God lacks nothing. He is not on His way to becoming more fully Himself; He is already, completely, all that He is, "pure act," Aquinas called it, with no unrealized potential waiting to be filled in. A being like that cannot change, not because He is stuck, but because there is no improvement available to Him and no diminishment possible. He does not grow wiser, because He was never less than perfectly wise. He does not cool toward you, because His love was never a temperature. Immutability, for Aquinas, is not God's limitation. It is the overflow of His fullness.

Boethius, seven centuries earlier, writing in prison while awaiting his own execution, added the piece that makes the puzzle verses snap into place. We experience our lives as a moving line, one moment, then the next, the past gone and the future not yet here. We are inside time, carried along it. But God, Boethius argued in *The Consolation of Philosophy* (around 524), is not on the timeline. God's relation to time is not "before" and "after" but a single, complete present, what Boethius called the possession of life "all at once and complete," *tota simul.* God does not wait to find out what Nineveh will do and then react. He holds the whole of Nineveh's history, the warning, the repentance, the sparing, in one undivided sight. The change is real, but the change is in Nineveh, not in God. The city moves. The sun does not move because the shadows do.

This is what the New Testament means when it says of God that "with [Him] there is no variation or shadow due to change" (James 1:17). The image is astronomical: stars and planets shift, cast shadows, rise and set. God does not. He is the fixed light by which everything else is seen to move.

## So what is happening when God "relents"?

Now we can return to the troublesome verses, and they stop being an embarrassment and start being a comfort.

When Jonah preaches doom and God "relents," nothing changed in God. What changed was Nineveh. God's character, His settled disposition to judge unrepentant evil and to spare the repentant, is exactly the same before and after. A city walking toward judgment turns around, and the same unchanging God who opposes the unrepentant now, by the very same fixed principle, spares the repentant. From inside time it looks like God changed His mind. From God's vantage it is the steadiest thing imaginable: His response to repentance is utterly reliable, which is the whole reason Jonah was sent to warn them in the first place. The warning was never a prediction of what would certainly happen. It was an invitation that assumed God's unchanging mercy toward anyone who turns.

The theologians have a useful phrase: God is *immutable in His character and His purposes, not static in His relationships.* He genuinely relates to us as the story unfolds, He warns, He responds, He answers prayer, but His relating flows from a center that never wobbles. Think of it less like a man changing his mind and more like the way the unchanging law of gravity produces wildly different outcomes depending on whether you jump or stay on the ground. The law did not change when you jumped. Your relation to it did. Scripture describes God in the language of relationship, "relented," "was moved," "remembered", because that is the only honest way to describe what it is like to deal with Him from inside time. The language is true. It is just true the way a sunrise is true: real, vivid, exactly what it looks like from here, and not a statement about the sun moving.

This is why prayer is not pointless before an unchanging God. God does not change in response to prayer, but He has, unchangingly and from before the world began, ordained that He will act through the prayers of His people. Your prayer is not new information that updates His plan. Your prayer is part of the plan, woven in from the start. You are not changing God's mind. You are taking the place He always meant you to have in what He was always going to do.

There is a serious objection here, and it deserves a serious hearing rather than a brush-off. Some thoughtful Christians have argued in the last few decades that all of this is too tidy, that the God who "relents" really does adjust, really does respond to a future He left genuinely open, and that the older view turns Him into a statue who only pretends to interact with us. They are reaching for something true: that God's relationship with us is real, not theater. But notice the cost of the trade. If God is genuinely surprised by Nineveh, if He did not know until the cloth and ashes whether the city would turn, then He is, in the most literal sense, learning. And a God who is still learning is a God who does not yet know how your story ends, which means the comfort He offers is only as good as His current guess. The older view is not colder than this. It is warmer. It says God's interaction with you is real *and* that He already knows, holds, and has accounted for everything you are walking toward, including the parts you cannot see. He is not improvising His love as new facts arrive. He committed to you with His eyes fully open, having already seen the whole of you, the worst of you, the end of you, and loved you anyway.

## The mountain you can actually stand on

Let me put the whole thing where it lands, which is not in the seminar room but in the worst night of your life.

The reason this doctrine matters has nothing to do with winning arguments and everything to do with what you reach for when the ground goes. Malachi gives the verse a context we usually drop: "For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed" (Malachi 3:6). Read the "therefore." The reason a faithless people has not been wiped out is that God's commitment to them does not rise and fall with their performance. His covenant love is not responsive to their merit; it is anchored in His own unchanging character. They are spared not because they are lovable but because He is constant. That is the only kind of love that can hold a person who knows what they actually are.

I have sat with enough people in collapse to know that what fails them is rarely their theology of God's existence. What fails them is their suspicion that His care is conditional and revisable, that He loved them last year, when they were doing better, and may have cooled since. The doctrine of immutability is the sledgehammer that breaks that suspicion. The God who does not change cannot love you more on your good days or less on your worst, because His love was never a reaction to you in the first place. It is older than you. It does not update. It will be exactly what it is today on the day you die and the day after.

The skeptic asks the question as a "gotcha." It turns out to be the most stabilizing thing a frightened person can be told.

## The hardest case, and the deepest comfort

There is one event that seems to break everything I have said, and a newcomer deserves to have it raised rather than hidden, because it is the place where immutability becomes almost unbearably good.

If God does not change, what do we do with the central claim of Christianity, that God became a man? That the eternal Son took on flesh, grew up, got tired, wept at a grave, and died? That looks like the largest change imaginable: from infinite to infant, from beyond time to bleeding inside it. The church wrestled with this for centuries and arrived at something careful and strange. In the incarnation, God did not stop being God or trade His unchanging nature for a changeable one. The eternal Son took *to* Himself a full human nature, added it, entered it, lived a real and limited human life within it, without subtracting anything from who He eternally is. The fixed point did not move. The fixed point came near. And here is what that means for you. The unchanging God did not stay safely above our changing, suffering world, observing it from a distance the way Boethius's watchman observes the road. He came down onto the road. He took the changing, the tiring, the grieving, the dying into Himself, while remaining the One who does not change, which is the only way the steadiness could reach us where we actually are. An immutable God who stayed remote would be solid but useless to a drowning man. An immutable God who came all the way down, without ceasing to be the rock, is solid ground walking out onto the water to where you are going under. That is not a God who changed His mind about us. That is the unchanging mind, made flesh.

## What remains

So I will leave the contradiction standing where it belongs, resolved, but not flattened.

God does not change His mind, and God relents. Both are true, and holding them together is not a clever trick but a clearer sight: the steadiness is in Him, the movement is in us, and the verses where He "turns" are simply what it looks like, from the inside of time, when an unmoving mercy meets a moving world. The doctrine does not make God colder. It makes Him the one warm thing that will still be warm when everything else has gone out.

Paul, after eleven dense chapters wrestling with the inscrutable ways of God, finally gives up trying to map Him and just worships: "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" (Romans 11:29). Irrevocable. Not subject to revision. Not a mood He might be talked out of. The same yesterday, and today, and on the day you most need Him to be.

Everything in your life is going to move. The question has only ever been whether anything underneath it does not. The oldest answer is also the steadiest, and it is the only thing I have found that holds.
posts.excerpt: The Bible says God does not change. The Bible also says God 'relented' and 'changed his mind.' Both are right, and the resolution is not a dodge, it opens onto the strangest and most stabilizing thing anyone has ever said about God.

posts.title: Is God Angry?
posts.body:
Ask a hundred people who have left church what made God seem unbelievable, and a surprising number will say the same thing. Not the science. Not the suffering, exactly. The temper. Somewhere along the way they were handed a God who was easily set off, a being who watched you closely, kept a tally, and waited for the moment your number came up. The thunderbolt was always loaded. You spent your childhood trying not to draw it. And one ordinary adult morning you woke up and decided you would rather have no God at all than that one.

I understand the instinct, because for years I lived on the other side of it as an atheist, and the God I was rejecting was exactly this God, the cosmic short fuse, the divine sulk. I had a picture of God. It was a bad picture. And it would take me a long time to learn that the thing I had rejected was not God but a cartoon someone had drawn over Him.

So let me say the hard thing plainly and then spend the rest of this essay earning it. **The Bible insists that God is angry, and that this is good news, not bad. A God who could look at the worst of what human beings do to each other and feel nothing would not be more loving than the God of Scripture. He would be a monster.** The problem was never that God gets angry. The problem is what we assumed His anger was.

## What we mean by "angry", and why it misleads

Start with the word, because the word is where the trouble begins.

When we say a person is angry, we usually mean something has gone wrong inside them. They have lost control. Some insult landed, some need went unmet, and now the temperature is up and the judgment is down. Human anger is mostly weather, it blows in, it blows out, and the wise learn to wait it out. So when we hear that God is angry, we import all of that. We picture moodiness in the sky. We picture a being we have to manage, soothe, stay on the good side of. We picture, in short, a very large and very dangerous version of ourselves.

The theologians have a word for what we are doing there. We are anthropomorphizing, reading our own emotional machinery up into God. And Scripture itself warns us off it. "God is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind" (Numbers 23:19). His anger is not the divine version of your bad afternoon. It is something else entirely, and to see it you have to stop watching the sky for lightning and start watching what the anger is *about*.

Here is the turn that changed everything for me. **God's wrath is not the opposite of His love. It is a function of it.** Anger, rightly understood, is what love does when it meets the thing destroying its beloved. You are not angry at strangers. You are angry on behalf of what you love, at what threatens it. The mother whose child is harmed does not respond to the harm with serene neutrality, and we do not admire mothers who do. Her fury is the exact measure of her love. Take away the capacity for that fury and you have not made her more loving. You have made her care less.

## The God who is slow to anger, and angry

The Old Testament knows this distinction better than we do. The book most people assume is wall-to-wall divine rage actually contains the most careful self-description God gives of His own character, and it is worth slowing down over.

In Exodus, after Israel has betrayed Him at the worst possible moment, God passes in front of Moses and announces who He is: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exodus 34:6–7). Read that twice. The self-portrait leads with mercy. It is *slow* to anger, the Hebrew is literally "long of nose," long-breathed, the opposite of a short fuse. And then, in the same breath, without contradiction, it refuses to pretend the guilty are innocent. Both clauses are God. The mercy and the refusal to whitewash evil are not in tension. They are the same holiness seen from two sides.

The Jewish philosopher Abraham Heschel saw this more clearly than most Christians have. In *The Prophets* (1962) he argued against the long Greek-influenced habit of treating divine emotion as a defect, as if a perfect God must be a cold one. The prophets, Heschel said, did not encounter an unmoved abstraction. They encountered a God of pathos, a God who is *affected* by what happens to the vulnerable, who is not indifferent to cruelty and injustice. The wrath of God, in Heschel's reading, is not a blemish on His character to be explained away. It is the proof that He is not neutral about evil. "The God of the philosophers," he wrote, is unmoved; the God of the prophets is moved to the depths. A God who could watch the trafficking of children, the grinding of the poor, the murder of the innocent, and remain unbothered, that God would be worse than no God. His anger is His refusal to be that.

## What the New Testament does with wrath

Now to the move most modern readers want to make, and where it goes wrong.

The standard hope is that the New Testament quietly retires all this. Jesus shows up, God mellows, the thunder is over. It is a comforting story. It is also not what the texts say. Paul opens the most important letter in Christian history not with comfort but with this: "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Romans 1:18). And the gospel writer most associated with love, John, the one who tells us God *is* love, ends his third chapter with a sentence that should stop us cold: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36). The wrath *remains*. It is not introduced by the New Testament. It is the standing condition the cross addresses.

The British scholar D. A. Carson spent a career insisting that Christians not soften this, and his point is theological, not temperamental. If you remove the wrath of God, Carson argued, you do not get a more loving gospel. You get an unintelligible one. The cross stops making sense. Why would God go to the trouble of the crucifixion if there were nothing to deal with, no real opposition to evil, no debt, no judgment, nothing that needed to be borne? Strip out the wrath and Good Friday becomes a pointless tragedy, a good man dying for no reason. Keep the wrath, and the cross becomes the most extraordinary thing ever claimed: the God who is rightly opposed to evil absorbing that opposition into Himself, in His own Son, rather than letting it fall on us. The wrath does not contradict the love at Calvary. The wrath is what makes the love cost something.

This is the thing the cartoon God can never do. The cartoon God throws lightning. The God of the cross steps in front of it.

## How we lost the category

It is worth asking how we arrived at a culture that finds divine anger embarrassing, because the discomfort is not timeless. It has a history.

For most of human history, people assumed that whatever was ultimate cared intensely about right and wrong, that the moral order was not a human invention but a feature of reality with weight behind it, and that to violate it was to run up against something that would push back. That assumption began to thin out over the last two centuries as the Western mind quietly relocated the source of morality from God to the self. The sociologist Robert Bellah described the endpoint in *Habits of the Heart* (1985): a culture in which each person becomes the sole author of their own values, answerable to no standard outside their own preferences. Once morality is just my preference, the idea of a God who is *angry* about anything becomes incoherent, anger implies a real violation of a real standard, and we no longer believe there is one. So we kept the parts of God we liked, the affirming and accepting parts, and quietly retired the part that judges, not because we examined the doctrine and found it false, but because it no longer fit the picture of the universe we had already decided to live in. We did not lose the doctrine of wrath in an argument. We lost it by drift. And I drifted with everyone else; the God I rejected as a young man was already this pre-trimmed God, the one with the inconvenient parts filed off, which is to say I rejected a God who had already been edited down by the very culture I thought I was rebelling against.

## Wrath as settled opposition, not a mood

Let me give you the working definition I wish someone had given me at twenty.

The wrath of God is not an emotion that comes and goes. It is His settled, permanent, holy opposition to everything that ruins what He has made. It does not flare up because He had a bad day; it is constant, because His character is constant. The prophet Nahum, writing against the empire of Assyria, a regime that flayed its captives and stacked their skulls as monuments, describes a God who "will by no means clear the guilty" (Nahum 1:3), whose anger burns against the empire precisely because the empire built its glory on other people's blood. To the Assyrians that is terrifying. To the Assyrians' victims it is the only good news there is. The wrath of God against Nineveh is the promise that the strong will not get away with grinding the weak forever. Take that promise away and you have not made the universe kinder. You have abandoned every victim who ever cried out and got silence.

Miroslav Volf, who lived through the wars in the former Yugoslavia, made this point with a credibility most of us have not earned. In *Exclusion and Embrace* (1996) he wrote that he used to find the idea of a wrathful God distasteful, a holdover from a less enlightened age, until he stood in a land where villages had been burned and neighbors had butchered neighbors. There, he wrote, the belief that God will not finally judge such things came to seem not noble but obscene. A God who merely shrugs at genocide is not a God of love. He is an accomplice. Volf went further: it is precisely the conviction that God will judge that frees the victim to lay down the sword, because vengeance has a rightful Owner, and it is not me. The doctrine of divine wrath, he argued, is what makes human nonviolence possible. We can forgo our own vengeance only because we trust there is a Judge who will not let evil have the last word.

So the question is not really "Is God angry?" The question is whether you want a God who can be.

## The anger you actually fear

But I have to come back to where most of us actually live, because the doctrine is one thing and the 3 a.m. dread is another.

The fear is not abstract. The fear is that the wrath is *at me*, personally, with my name on it, for the specific things I have done and cannot undo. The cartoon God does its worst damage right here, because it turns every failure into evidence that the thunderbolt is finally coming. I know this fear from the inside. There were years when the word "God" meant, to me, the one who had it in for me, a suspicion I never quite outgrew even after I stopped believing He existed. You can be an atheist and still be afraid of God. I was.

Here is what the cross does to that fear, and it is the whole point. If the wrath of God is real, then the cross is not God working up the nerve to forgive you while still secretly seething. It is God Himself, in the person of the Son, walking into the place where the judgment falls and taking it, so that the settled opposition to the evil in you is fully, finally, and lovingly resolved, not ignored. Your sin was not minimized. It was carried. That is a completely different God than the one who keeps the tally. The tally was paid. And a debt that has been paid cannot be charged twice.

This does not make God's anger smaller. It makes it more serious than the cartoon ever imagined, serious enough to cost a death, and then it places that whole weight on Himself instead of on you. The God you were afraid of would have made you pay. The God of the Bible paid.

## What remains

So I will leave you where the doctrine left me, which is not at ease but somewhere better than ease.

A God who never got angry would be a God who did not love you enough to be bothered by what is killing you. He would watch the abuse, the betrayal, the slow theft of everything good, and feel about it roughly what you feel about a stranger's weather. That God is not the God of Scripture, and He is not, when you really look at Him, a God worth wanting. The God who is there burns, at the cruelty, at the lie, at the empire built on blood, and yes, at the evil that has its hooks in you and me. His anger is the heat of a love that refuses to call the cancer healthy.

The only question is where that heat finally lands. Scripture says it can land on you, or it can land on the One who stepped in front of it on a Friday afternoon and said, in effect, *put it here.* That is not a God to manage. That is not a fuse to avoid tripping.

That is a love with fire in it, and it has already decided what to do with the fire.
posts.excerpt: Most people picture God's anger as a temper, a short fuse, a thrown thunderbolt. That cartoon has done real damage. The truth is harder and far better: a God who never got angry could not possibly be good.

posts.title: If God Is in Control, Why Doesn't It Feel Like It?
posts.body:
Somebody says it at the funeral. *God is in control.* Somebody says it after the diagnosis, after the layoff, after the marriage finally comes apart in the kitchen at eleven at night. It is meant as comfort and it often lands as an insult, because the person hearing it is looking at a piece of reality that does not look controlled by anyone, least of all by a good God. The sentence and the situation will not sit in the same room. And so a lot of people file the doctrine of God's sovereignty under things Christians say that they do not really mean, a verbal tic for hard moments, a way of filling a silence that should have been left alone.

I have heard that sentence land wrong. I have probably said it when I should have said nothing. And I came to faith late, out of unbelief, partly through wrestling with exactly this, because the version of "God is in control" I had been handed as a younger man was so glib, so untouched by how the world actually goes, that rejecting it felt like the only intellectually honest thing to do.

So let me try to say what the doctrine actually claims, because I think we have been defending a caricature of it. **To say God is sovereign, that He is in control, is not to say that everything that happens is good, or that He authored the evil, or that your pain is part of some cheerful plan you would applaud if you could see the spreadsheet. It is to say something both smaller and far larger: that there is no event, including the worst one in your life, that has escaped Him, fallen outside His reach, or defeated His purpose.** That is a harder claim and a stranger comfort than the bumper sticker. It does not ask you to call the wreckage good. It asks you to believe the wreckage is not the end of the sentence.

## Two pictures, both wrong

Begin by clearing away the two cartoons, because most people are choosing between them and both are unworthy of belief.

The first cartoon is the micromanaging puppeteer, a God who personally pulls every string, so that the drunk driver, the tumor, and the collapsing bridge are all His direct, intended handiwork, scripted in advance for reasons He is not sharing. People who hold this picture end up either blaming God for everything or contorting themselves to praise Him for things no decent person would praise. It makes God the author of evil, and Scripture will not allow that: "God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one" (James 1:13).

The second cartoon is the absent landlord, a God who got the universe going, set the rules, and stepped back, so that what happens now happens on its own, indifferent, mechanical, unwatched. This is the God of the deists, and frankly the God a lot of practicing Christians actually believe in without admitting it: present in theory, absent in fact, a being who would not notice if you stopped praying. This picture spares God the blame but at the cost of His care. He is in control the way a retired founder is in control of the company, on the letterhead, not in the building.

It is worth seeing what each cartoon does to a real person in a real crisis, because the choice is not academic. The puppeteer God leaves the grieving mother believing that God personally selected her child's death off a menu of options and willed it for reasons she is forbidden to question, a belief that produces either a crushed silence or a slow, corrosive resentment she is too frightened to name. The absent-landlord God leaves her believing her child died into a void, unwatched, unheld, a random outcome in a machine that would have ground on identically whether she prayed or not. One God she cannot trust because He seems cruel. The other she cannot reach because He is not there. Most people who say they have lost faith in God's sovereignty have actually only lost faith in one of these two cartoons, and they were right to. The tragedy is that no one ever offered them the third thing.

The classical doctrine of providence threads between these, and the threading is the whole point. It claims that God governs all things, actively, continuously, down to the sparrow and the hair, and yet does so without being the author of the evil within them, and without cancelling the real freedom and real causes of the creatures He governs. How both can be true is genuinely hard, and the tradition has never pretended it is easy. But it has insisted that the alternatives, a God who does evil, or a God who does nothing, are both worse, and both false.
