That is the world as it left the Maker's hands. Webbed together. In delight.

Hold that picture, because everything that follows is the tearing of that web.

## The fracture

The third chapter of Genesis is the most consequential short story ever told, and it is told with terrible economy.

There is a command, one tree, one limit, the single mark that the humans are creatures and not the Creator. There is a question, hissed by the serpent, and notice that it is not first a temptation to do something but a temptation to doubt something: *Did God really say?* The whole catastrophe begins as a suspicion about the goodness of God, the suggestion that the Maker is holding out, that the limit is not love but envy, that the way to become fully human is to stop trusting and start seizing. And then the act. They take. They eat. They reach past the one boundary that defined them as creatures and grasp at being gods.

What happens next is not a thunderbolt. It is worse. It is a series of fractures, quiet and total. They hide, the relationship with God, severed, replaced by fear. They blame, the man accuses the woman, the woman accuses the serpent, the relationship between them already poisoned in its first crisis. The ground itself turns against the man, yielding thorns, making his work a struggle (Genesis 3:17–19). And finally they are sent out of the garden, east of Eden, and an angel with a flaming sword stands where the way back used to be. The web of shalom does not so much snap as unravel, every strand at once. God. Neighbor. Self. World. All of it pulling loose in a single afternoon.

This is the biblical diagnosis, and it is crucial to see what kind of diagnosis it is. The problem is not located in any one place where we could surgically remove it. It is not in the economy, though it corrupts the economy. It is not in the systems, though it deforms every system. It is not in the other tribe, though it animates the other tribe and ours. It is in the relationship, the broken trust between creatures and their Creator, and from that center it radiates into everything else. Plantinga's whole book is a recovery of the old word for this radiating fracture, a word we have nearly stopped being able to say without flinching: sin. Not a list of misdeeds. Sin as the *condition*, shalom violated, the web torn, the world bent away from the One who holds it together.

## Why this diagnosis explains what the others cannot

Here is where the biblical account earns its keep, because it explains the one thing the popular diagnoses keep tripping over.

If the problem were only ignorance, then knowledge would cure it, and the most educated century in human history produced the most efficient atrocities in human history. If the problem were only bad systems, then good systems would cure it, and we keep building good systems and watching them rot from the inside, because the rot was never only in the system. If the problem were only *them*, then removing them would cure it, and every revolution that has ever guillotined the oppressor has discovered the appetite for oppression intact in the new regime, sometimes by the following Tuesday. The reason these solutions keep failing is that they all locate the wrong somewhere outside the self. The Bible locates it, finally, inside, and then has the nerve to say it is inside everyone, no exceptions, the diagnosis that no one is exempt from and that is therefore the only one that ever describes the actual room.

This is the doctrine modern people most resist and most quietly confirm. We cannot stop grading the world. We are moral animals to the marrow, we rage at injustice, we are wounded by betrayal, we expect the world to be other than it is, and we expect it with a fierceness that makes no sense if the world is merely matter in motion with no should about it. Where did we get the ruler we keep measuring reality against and finding it short? The Bible's answer is that we remember the garden. We were made for shalom, and the ache we feel at every broken thing is the memory of a home we lost. The longing is not naïve. The longing is evidence.

Plantinga makes a further observation that has stayed with me for years, because it names something I see in myself. Sin, he argues, is a parasite. It has no power of its own to create; it can only corrupt good things. Pride is a corruption of proper self-respect. Lust is a corruption of desire, which is good. Greed is a corruption of the legitimate care a person owes his own household. Cruelty often masquerades as a corruption of justice. This is why sin is so hard to see and so hard to root out, it never arrives as something obviously alien. It arrives as a good thing slightly bent, a right desire aimed one degree off, a love that has curved in on itself. The man who wrecks his family for an affair did not set out to worship destruction; he set out chasing a real good, intimacy, by a ruinous road. The fracture works by spoiling, never by inventing. That is exactly why we keep mistaking it for something else, and exactly why no reform that only rearranges our goods will reach it. You cannot legislate the bend out of a heart.

And here is the part that should stop us. The same capacity that lets us recognize evil so sharply in others goes strangely quiet when it turns inward. We are prosecuting attorneys about the world's wrongness and defense attorneys about our own. I have watched it in myself, the speed with which I can diagnose a colleague's pride and the slowness with which I notice the identical thing in me. That asymmetry is not an accident of personality. It is the signature of the very condition the Bible is describing. A fracture that ran neatly outside us would be visible. The reason it is so hard to see is that it runs through the one instrument we are using to look.

## The whole creation, not just us

There is one more turn in the biblical diagnosis, and modern Christians often miss it because we have privatized sin into a personal matter of individual guilt. Scripture refuses that shrinking. The fracture, it insists, did not stay inside the human heart. It went out into the world.

Paul says it plainly, and it is one of the strangest sentences in the New Testament. The whole creation, he writes, "was subjected to frustration" and is "groaning as in the pains of childbirth," waiting to be liberated from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:20–22). The damage is cosmic. It is in the thorned ground and the failing body, in the predator and the famine and the slow running-down of everything. N. T. Wright, writing on this passage, points out that we have badly misread our problem if we think the trouble is merely that human souls have sinned and need rescuing *out* of a doomed world. The world itself is wounded and the world itself is groaning, and what it groans for is not evacuation but healing. The wrongness Paul describes is not a stain on an otherwise fine machine. It is a creation-wide grief, and creation knows it, the way a body running a fever knows something is wrong even when it cannot name it.

This is why the Christian account of wrongness is not, in the end, a counsel of despair, though it is more honest about ruin than any rival. To say the world is fractured the way a marriage is fractured is also to say that the world is the kind of thing that *can* be reconciled. You do not reconcile a machine. You repair it or you scrap it. But a broken relationship can be restored, by a costly act of love from the side that was wronged. And that, though it is the next chapters of the story, not this one, is precisely the shape of everything the Bible says God does next.

## Why naming it right is mercy

I want to say plainly why this diagnosis matters, especially for the reader who has only ever heard "sin" used as a club.

A wrong diagnosis is not neutral. It kills. The doctor who tells you your tumor is indigestion is not being kind; he is being lethal with a smile. And the cultural diagnoses we prefer, you are fine, the problem is out there, you only need more information or a better system or the defeat of your enemies, are comforting in exactly the way the cheerful doctor is comforting, and just as deadly. They send us to fight the wrong war, year after year, generation after generation, and they leave the actual fracture untouched at the center of us.

The Bible's diagnosis is harder to hear and is the beginning of mercy. It tells you the truth you already half-know in your most honest moments: that the line between the world as it is and the world as it should be does not run neatly between you and your enemies. It runs through your own chest. I know that line. I have crossed it in private in ways the people who admire me have never seen. The relief is not in pretending the line is not there. The relief is in finally being told the truth by Someone who knows exactly where it runs and has already moved, at unspeakable cost, to mend the thing it cut.

Something is wrong with the world. You knew that before you opened this. What the Bible adds is harder and, in the end, kinder than every other answer: the something that is wrong is not only out there, and the One who made the garden has not walked away from it groaning.

He went down into the wreckage himself. But that is the next part of the story.
posts.excerpt: Everyone knows something is wrong with the world. We disagree violently about what. The Bible opens with a diagnosis older and stranger than any of ours, that the world is not broken the way a machine breaks, but the way a marriage breaks.

posts.title: Why God Started With One Family
posts.body:
There is a question that quietly bothers honest readers of the Bible, and it surfaces somewhere around the twelfth chapter of Genesis. The first eleven chapters are about everything, the cosmos, the human race, the whole groaning world. And then, abruptly, the camera stops sweeping and zooms all the way in. It lands on one man. An old, childless herdsman in the Bronze Age Near East, somewhere around the region of Ur, with a barren wife and no particular distinction the text bothers to mention. And from that chapter to nearly the end of the book, the story is about him and his descendants, one family, then one tribe, then one small, frequently humiliated nation pressed between empires.

The question is obvious and worth asking out loud. If God meant to rescue the whole world, why spend most of the book on one family? Why the narrowing? It looks, on its face, like favoritism, like a God who loves everyone in theory and one ethnic group in practice. A great many people have walked away from the Bible at exactly this point, offended by what they took to be tribalism with a divine warrant.

They misread it, and the misreading is understandable, and clearing it up opens the entire middle of the Bible. **God did not choose one family instead of the world. He chose one family for the sake of the world.** The narrowing is not the abandonment of the rescue. The narrowing is the strategy of the rescue. Election in the Bible is never a privilege held against others; it is a vocation carried on behalf of others. Miss that, and the whole Old Testament looks like a long ethnic detour. See it, and the Old Testament becomes what it actually is, the slow, costly setup for a blessing that was always aimed at everyone.

## The promise has the whole world in it from the first sentence

Go to the moment of the choosing, and read it without skipping the last line, because the last line is the one we always skip.

God says to Abram: leave your country and your people and your father's household, go to a land I will show you, and "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing." And then the sentence that explains everything: "all peoples on earth will be blessed through you" (Genesis 12:1–3). Read that final clause slowly. The choosing of Abram is, in the very breath that announces it, aimed past Abram. He is blessed *to be* a blessing. He is chosen as a conduit, not a terminus. The promise has the whole earth inside it from the start, *all peoples, all families of the ground*, the same ground that Genesis 3 said was cursed. The rescue of everything has not been narrowed away. It has been planted, like a seed, in one old man.

This is the structural genius of the move, and it is worth pausing on. God responds to a universal catastrophe, the fracturing of the whole world in Eden, the scattering of the nations at Babel, not with a universal announcement but with a particular person. He does not address humanity in the abstract. He grabs one man by the collar and makes a promise, and he stakes the future of everything on it. The British scholar Christopher Wright, in his 2006 book *The Mission of God*, calls this the hinge of the entire Old Testament. Genesis 1 through 11, Wright argues, lays out the problem, the world in ruins, the nations divided. Genesis 12 launches the solution, and the solution is not the election of Israel away from the nations but the election of Israel *for* the nations. Wright puts it in a single line that reorders everything: it is not that God has a mission for his people in the world; it is that God has a people for his mission in the world. The people exist for the mission. The mission was always the world.

## Chosen, and told why

Lest anyone think this is a clever Christian reading imposed backward, the Old Testament says it out loud, repeatedly, to Israel's face.

At Mount Sinai, just freed from Egypt, the new nation is told its purpose in terms no one could mistake. "You will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:5–6). Sit with the word *priests.* A priest is not a person God loves more than other people. A priest is a person who stands between God and others, who represents God to the people and the people to God. To call Israel a kingdom of priests is to define the whole nation by its function toward the outsiders. Israel is chosen the way a priest is chosen: set apart, yes, but set apart *for* somebody. The holiness is not a trophy. It is a job. They are meant to be the people through whom the watching nations finally see what the living God is like, what justice looks like, what mercy looks like, what it looks like for a society to be ordered around the One who made it.

And in case Israel should ever mistake the choosing for a compliment, Moses removes the last possible ground for pride. Why did God set his love on you, he asks the nation in Deuteronomy. Not because you were impressive. "The Lord did not set his affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. But it was because the Lord loved you" (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). There it is, stated flatly. You were the smallest. You were nothing. The choosing was never a reward for your size or your virtue; it was sheer, unearned love that landed on you and then sent you out. This is the opposite of tribal arrogance. It is the deliberate dismantling of it. You have nothing to be proud of and everything to be responsible for. That is what it means, in the Bible, to be chosen.

## The exodus is the pattern of the whole rescue

The defining event of this whole middle act, the one the Old Testament returns to again and again, the one Israel was commanded to retell to its children every single year, is the exodus, and it teaches the same lesson at the level of action rather than statement.

Israel is in Egypt, enslaved, crushed, anonymous. And God says a sentence that contains the heart of the biblical God: "I have indeed seen the misery of my people. I have heard them crying out. I have come down to rescue them." He hears the groaning, the same groaning the whole creation does in Romans, and he comes down, into the mess, to get his people out. He does not send advice. He does not improve their circumstances from a distance. He comes down. And he brings them out, through the sea, into a covenant, toward a land. The exodus becomes the master pattern of everything God does: a God who sees suffering, descends into it, pays its price, and leads his people out into freedom and into a calling. Every later rescue in Scripture is told in exodus language. The whole Bible learns to hope by remembering Egypt.

And notice what the rescued people are immediately told. You were slaves; therefore you shall not oppress the slave or the foreigner among you, for you know the heart of a foreigner. The rescue is meant to reshape the rescued. Having received mercy, they are to become a society organized around mercy, a living demonstration, in the middle of a brutal ancient world, of how human beings flourish when they live under the God who came down. They were chosen for the sake of someone else. The someone else was the watching world, and the watching world included the very strangers they were now commanded to love.

This is why the law that follows the exodus, all those statutes we find so foreign, is not arbitrary religious housekeeping. Christopher Wright, who spent much of his scholarly life on the ethics of the Old Testament, argues that Israel's law was a kind of public exhibit. Gather the years of jubilee, the gleaning laws that left the edges of every field for the poor, the prohibitions on charging interest to a brother in need, the sabbath that gave rest even to slaves and animals, and you are looking at the blueprint for a society deliberately unlike its neighbors. Other ancient peoples had gods who served the powerful. Israel was given a God who heard the cry of the weak and wrote their protection into the founding documents of the nation. The watching nations were supposed to look at this strange little society and ask what kind of God could produce it. The law was missionary before it was anything else. It was the shape that the blessing of Abraham was meant to take in the streets, so that the families of the earth could see it and want it.

## Why the long, frustrating middle had to happen

The middle act does not read like the romance I have just described. Israel mostly fails. They forget Egypt. They want a king like the other nations. They chase the gods of their neighbors instead of showing their neighbors the living God. The prophets spend centuries indicting a people who were supposed to be a light and had become indistinguishable from the dark around them. By the end of the Old Testament, the chosen nation is conquered, exiled, scattered, a remnant clinging to a promise that looks, by every visible measure, to have failed.

Why would God run his rescue of the world through a vehicle so obviously unequal to it? This is not a flaw in the story. It is the point the story is patiently making. The long middle act demonstrates, across a thousand years and at enormous cost, that the chosen people cannot themselves be the blessing the world needs. They were given the law, and they could not keep it. They were given the land, and they lost it. They were given the priesthood, the temple, the prophets, every advantage, and still the fracture in the human heart ran straight through the chosen as much as through everyone else. The middle act is not God's failure. It is God proving, beyond all argument, that the rescue of the world will finally have to come not merely *through* the chosen people but *as* one of them, a true Israelite who succeeds where the nation failed, who is the blessing rather than merely carrying it.

The whole long, frustrating, beautiful middle is a setup. Every unkept promise is a debt being moved onto a single account that One descendant will eventually have to pay. When the New Testament opens by calling Jesus the son of Abraham, it is not decoration. It is the claim that the promise made to one old man in Genesis 12, *all peoples on earth will be blessed through you*, is about to come true through his greatest grandson, and that the blessing aimed at the world from the first sentence is finally going to arrive.

## What the choosing means for you

There is a personal weight in this for anyone who has ever wondered where they stand with the God of the Bible, and it is the opposite of what the favoritism reading would suggest.

The pattern of Scripture is that God chooses not the impressive but the small, not to hoard them but to send them, not because they earned it but because he loved them, and never, ever for their sake alone. If that is how God works, and the whole Old Testament insists it is, then being chosen by this God is never a status to sit on. It is always a commission to carry. The church inherits Abraham's call exactly, named in the New Testament in the same priestly language: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, called out of darkness to declare the praises of the One who called them, for the sake of the nations, as always, never for the sake of the club.

This is also the quiet rebuke the story aims at people like me. Every group that has ever believed itself chosen by God has faced the same temptation, and most have failed it the same way, to read the choosing as a verdict on their superiority rather than a draft into someone else's rescue. Israel did it; they began to treat the covenant as a wall against the nations instead of a door for them, and the prophets thundered against exactly that distortion. The church has done it for two thousand years, mistaking its calling for a comfort and its election for a status, building walls where God commanded doors. I have done it in miniature, more times than I would like to count, caught the warmth of belonging to God's people and forgotten that belonging is a sending. The hardest part of grace is not receiving it. It is remembering that it was never given to be kept.

So if you have ever suspected the Christian story of being a tribal arrangement, a divine in-group with a velvet rope, read Genesis 12 to its last line and Deuteronomy 7 to the bottom. The God of the Bible does not choose people the way an empire recruits favorites. He chooses them the way you would choose a messenger you trusted to carry something to people you loved who could not be reached any other way. He started with one family. He started with one family because he was after every family. He has been keeping that one ancient promise the entire time.

And the day he kept it in full, he kept it on a cross. But that is where the whole story turns.
posts.excerpt: If God meant to rescue the whole world, why start with one obscure herdsman in the Bronze Age and his barren wife? The answer opens the entire middle of the Bible, and it is the opposite of what favoritism looks like.

posts.title: The Restless Man Who Couldn't Outrun God
posts.body:
Around the year 397, a middle-aged African bishop sat down and did something no one in the ancient world had really done before. He wrote the story of his own soul. Not his accomplishments, he had plenty. Not his battles or his travels. He wrote the story of his interior life, the wantings and the failures and the long detour he had taken before he finally stopped running. He addressed the whole thing to God, as a prayer, which means we are reading over his shoulder while a man talks to his Maker about everything he is most ashamed of. The book is called the *Confessions*, and sixteen hundred years later it is still in print, still being read by people who have never set foot in a church, because they open it and find, to their alarm, that it is about them.

His name was Aurelius Augustinus, Augustine. He was born in 354 in a town in what is now Algeria, in Roman North Africa. He was not born into power or wealth, but he was born brilliant, and everyone around him knew it early. His mother, Monica, was a Christian who prayed for his soul for decades. His father was not. Augustine grew up smart, ambitious, hungry, for sex, for status, for the applause that comes to a man who can speak well, and he spent the first half of his life chasing every one of those hungers down to the bottom and finding nothing there. The most famous sentence he ever wrote sits on the first page of the *Confessions* and explains the whole rest of it: "You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you."

That is the thesis of his life. He had a restless heart, and he tried to quiet it with everything a person reaches for, and none of it worked, and the not-working is the story.

## The most honest book anyone had written

You have to grasp how strange the *Confessions* was. Ancient autobiography, where it existed, was a monument. A great man told you about his great deeds so you would admire him. Augustine did the opposite. He told God, and us, about the time he stole pears as a boy, not because he was hungry but for the pure thrill of doing wrong, and then he spent pages agonizing over what that small theft revealed about the rottenness in the human will. He wrote about his sexual life with a candor that still makes readers shift in their seats. He had a long-term partner, a woman he never names, with whom he lived for years and had a son he loved, and he wrote about the wrenching pain of leaving her for the sake of an ambitious marriage that never happened. He prayed one of the most famous and honest lines in religious literature: "Grant me chastity and self-control, but please, not yet." He wanted to be good. He did not want it badly enough to stop, and he knew it, and he said so.

This is why the great historian Peter Brown, whose 1967 biography *Augustine of Hippo* is still the book scholars hand you first, called him essentially the inventor of the inner self as we know it. Before Augustine, people did not generally write as though the most interesting and most contested territory in the universe was the inside of one's own divided heart. After Augustine, the West could not stop. Every memoir you have ever read that turns its gaze inward and tells the truth about the gap between who we want to be and what we actually do, every one of them is, whether the author knows it or not, walking in tracks Augustine cut sixteen centuries ago.

And this is also why a newcomer to the faith should read him before almost anyone else. Augustine does not start with answers. He starts with the wanting. He starts exactly where most of us actually live, restless, divided, reaching for the next thing in the hope that it will finally be enough. He is not a man who had it figured out lecturing you from above. He is a man who was a mess, writing up from inside the mess, telling you how he got out.

## The years of running

For most of his twenties and into his thirties, Augustine ran. Not from God, as he understood it at the time, he would have told you he was searching for truth, and he was. He tried a fashionable religious movement of the day, a sect called the Manichees, who offered a tidy explanation of evil that flattered his sense of being one of the enlightened few. He left it disillusioned. He flirted with the skeptics, who said you couldn't really know anything for certain. He chased a career as a teacher of rhetoric, the ancient equivalent of a high-end communications consultant, and it carried him from Africa to Rome to Milan, the imperial capital, where he landed a prestigious post and the kind of platform an ambitious provincial dreamed of.

And he was miserable. He tells the story of riding through Milan in his fine clothes on his way to deliver a grand speech praising the emperor, a speech full of lies he knew were lies, and passing a drunk beggar in the street, laughing, happy. And Augustine realized the beggar had, by sheer dumb luck, gotten to the joy that Augustine was killing himself to reach and never reaching. He had everything the world told him to want. It was ash in his mouth.

What broke the spell, slowly, was two things. First, he encountered Christian preaching he could not dismiss, in Milan he heard the great bishop Ambrose, and discovered that the faith of his mother, which he had written off as simple, was in fact intellectually serious in ways that embarrassed him. Second, he could not get free of the wanting. He could see the good. He could not will himself into it. He describes the agony of a divided will with a precision no one had matched: the part of him that wanted God and the part of him that wanted everything else, locked in a war he kept losing.

If you want the older biblical echo of this, it is the apostle Paul on the road to Damascus in Acts 9, a man dead set on his own course, certain he is right, knocked flat and remade against everything he had planned for his life. Augustine knew that story well. He just did not yet know it was about to become his.

## The garden

It came to a head in a garden in Milan, in the late summer of 386. Augustine tells it as the hinge of his whole life, and it is worth slowing down for, because it is one of the most vivid conversion scenes ever written.

He was in torment. A friend had just told him the story of two Roman officials who had given up their careers to follow Christ, and the story landed on Augustine like an accusation: *the unlearned rise up and take heaven by storm, and here we are with all our learning, wallowing.* He fled into the garden of the house where he was staying, weeping, tearing at his hair, throwing himself down under a fig tree. His will was at war with itself and he could not break the deadlock. He cried out the question that anyone who has ever wanted to change and couldn't has cried out: *How long? How long this "tomorrow and tomorrow"? Why not now? Why not an end to my uncleanness this very hour?*

And then he heard, from a neighboring house, the voice of a child, he could not tell if it was a boy or a girl, singing a little phrase over and over as part of some game: *Tolle, lege. Tolle, lege.* Take up and read. Take up and read.

He took it as a command from God. He ran back to where he had left a copy of Paul's letters, snatched it up, and read the first passage his eyes fell on. It was Romans 13:13–14: "Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not think about how to gratify the desires of the flesh." He says he did not need to read further. "Instantly, as I reached the end of the sentence, it was as though the light of certainty flooded my heart, and all the shadows of doubt were swept away." The war was over. The wanting that had ruled him for thirty-one years let go.

He went and told his mother, Monica, who had prayed for this day longer than he had been alive. The *Confessions* records her joy. She died not long after, content, and he buried her, and you can feel in the pages how much that ordinary grief, a son burying his praying mother, sat at the center of his understanding of grace.

## What he saw that we keep forgetting

Here is why Augustine still matters, and not just as a good story. Out of those running years he drew a conclusion about the human heart that the modern world has spent a great deal of effort trying to forget, and that keeps proving true anyway.

The conclusion is this: our problem is not mainly that we lack information. It is that we love the wrong things, or we love the right things in the wrong order. Augustine called it *disordered love*. We are not empty vessels who need to be told what is good. We can usually see what is good. We want the lesser thing more. The drunk beggar in Milan was happier than the celebrated rhetorician because Augustine's loves were pointed at things that could not hold the weight he was putting on them, applause, status, the next pleasure. Psalm 139, which Augustine prayed constantly, says God has searched us and known us, knows our sitting down and our rising up, has hemmed us in behind and before. "Where can I go from your Spirit? Where can I flee from your presence?" the psalm asks (Psalm 139:7). Augustine read that not as surveillance but as rescue. The God who knows the inside of you, all of it, the part you would never confess to your closest friend, that God is the only one who can finally reorder what you love, because he is the only one who already sees what you actually love.

This is the architecture of his whole thought, and it is why Tim Keller, who learned more from Augustine than from almost anyone, kept returning to it in our own day: you are not what you think. You are what you love. And you cannot simply decide to love differently by force of will, Augustine tried that for years in the garden of his own effort and failed every time. Love is reordered by a greater love breaking in. That is what happened under the fig tree. He did not finally muster the willpower to choose God. God, as he tells it, finally became more desirable than the things that had owned him, and the chains he could not break fell off because he no longer wanted them on.

## The bishop, and the long shadow

Augustine did not vanish into private piety after the garden. He went home to Africa, was more or less drafted into the priesthood by a congregation that recognized what it had, and spent the last thirty-four years of his life as the bishop of Hippo, a working pastor in a provincial town. This is the part that endears him to me, and that ought to encourage anyone who imagines the great figures of church history lived on some higher plane. The man who wrote the most influential spiritual autobiography in history spent most of his days doing what pastors have always done: settling petty disputes among his people, preaching week after week to an ordinary congregation, burying the dead, answering letters from the anxious and the argumentative, and trying to keep a small church together in a crumbling empire. He wrote his greatest works in the cracks of an exhausting ministry, not in a scholar's leisure.

And the shadow he cast is almost impossible to overstate. For more than a thousand years, Western Christianity essentially thought with Augustine's mind. The reformers, Martin Luther was an Augustinian monk before he was anything else, read him as the great witness to grace, to the truth that we are rescued by God's mercy rather than by our own moral achievement, which was the thing Augustine had learned the hard way in the garden when his own willpower failed him over and over. His insistence that human beings are not basically fine, that there is something genuinely disordered in us that we cannot fix by trying harder, ran against the optimism of his age and ours alike, and it keeps being confirmed by anyone honest enough to watch their own behavior for a week. He died in 430, an old man, as an army of invaders besieged his city and the Roman world he had known collapsed around him. He had spent his life pointing past every collapsing thing to the one rest that does not fall.

## The restlessness was the mercy

I want to end where he began, because it is the most pastoral thing he ever said and the easiest to miss.

We tend to treat our restlessness as a defect. The dissatisfaction that follows us through one accomplishment after another, the way the thing we were sure would finally settle us turns out, once we have it, to settle nothing, we treat that as a sign that something is wrong with us, or that we just haven't found the right thing yet. Augustine spent half his life on that assumption and it nearly destroyed him. Then he turned it around. The restlessness was not the disease. The restlessness was the symptom that pointed to the cure. *You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.* The ache was not random. It was a homing signal. It was the part of him that had been made for God refusing to be satisfied by anything less than God, no matter how hard he tried to drug it quiet.

If you have felt that, the strange poverty in the middle of having what you wanted, the hunger that the next thing never fills, Augustine would tell you not to despair of it and not to try to kill it. He would tell you it is the truest thing about you. He chased it down every wrong road for thirty-one years and it would not let him go, and in the end he was grateful, because the only reason he was still restless was that the One who made him had refused to let him settle for less than himself.

He could not outrun God. He tells the whole story as the discovery, late and astonished, that he had never been the one doing the chasing.
posts.excerpt: Sixteen hundred years ago a brilliant, ambitious, sexually compulsive young man wrote down the story of how God chased him through every pleasure he tried to hide in. We have been reading ourselves in his pages ever since.

posts.title: Christianity Was Never a Western Religion
posts.body:
Most of us, if we are honest, carry a mental picture of Christianity that goes something like this. It is a Western religion. It started, more or less, in Europe, or it became itself in Europe, and then European and American missionaries carried it out across the world to Africa and Asia and Latin America, where it took root among people who had nothing like it before. The faith flows outward, in this picture, from the West to everyone else. Christianity is the home team's religion, exported.

That picture is not just incomplete. It has the map upside down. Jesus of Nazareth was a brown-skinned Middle Eastern man who never set foot in Europe and would not have recognized a European. The very first person recorded as converting after the day of Pentecost was an African official going home to the African continent. The church was flourishing in Egypt, Syria, North Africa, Ethiopia, and as far east as India and China for centuries before most of Europe had heard the name of Christ, and some of those churches are still there, having outlasted empires. The story of Christianity as a Western faith that went out to the world is a story Europe told about itself during a few centuries when it happened to be powerful. It is not the actual shape of the thing. To understand the people who came before us, we have to recover the truth that the family is far older, far larger, and far more global than the picture lets us see, and always was.

## It began in the wrong place for the story we tell

Start with the obvious thing we manage to forget: the geography of the New Testament is not European. It is the eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, North Africa. Jesus lived and died in Roman-occupied Judea, in the Middle East. The faith first spread through cities like Jerusalem, Damascus, and Antioch, Antioch being in what is now Turkey, near the Syrian border, and a place that matters enormously to our story.

Acts 11:19–26 records that after persecution scattered the first believers, some of them came to Antioch and began preaching to non-Jews, to Greeks, to Gentiles, and a great number believed. The church there became the launching point for the spread of the faith across the empire, and the text records, almost as an aside, one of the most important sentences in the whole history of the church: "The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch." The name we all carry was first given not in Rome or anywhere in Europe but in a multicultural Middle Eastern city, to a community of Jews and Greeks and others who had become, in the eyes of their neighbors, something new enough to need a new word. The faith was multiethnic from almost the first breath. It did not start as one nation's religion and later open up. It started open.

## The African at the side of the road

Now to the convert. Long before any missionary set out for Europe, before Paul had written most of his letters, the book of Acts records a conversion that should reorder the whole picture in our heads. It is in Acts 8:26–39.

An Ethiopian, a court official of the Kandake, the queen of the Ethiopians, a man in charge of her entire treasury, is traveling home on a desert road, riding in his chariot, reading aloud from the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He has been to Jerusalem to worship, which tells us he was already drawn to the God of Israel. Philip, one of the early Christians, is sent by the Spirit to run alongside the chariot, and he hears the man reading the passage about a lamb led to the slaughter, and Philip asks him, "Do you understand what you are reading?" The official says the human thing: "How can I, unless someone explains it to me?" And he invites this stranger up into his chariot, and Philip, starting from that very passage of Isaiah, tells him the good news about Jesus. They come to some water. The official says, "Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?" And he is baptized, right there on the road, and goes on his way home to Africa rejoicing.

Sit with what that scene actually is. The first individual conversion narrated in detail after Pentecost is an African, a Black African official from the kingdom that sat south of Egypt, and he takes the faith home with him, to a continent, before the gospel had reached most of the places we now think of as its heartland. Ancient tradition connects this conversion to the deep early roots of Christianity in the Horn of Africa, and to this day Ethiopia has one of the oldest continuous Christian communities on earth, one that predates the conversion of most of Europe by centuries. The faith was in Africa, carried by Africans, from the very beginning of the story. It was never waiting for the West to bring it.

And this fits a pattern, not an exception. North Africa produced some of the greatest minds of the early church, Augustine of Hippo, whom we met as the restless man, was a North African. Egypt gave us the desert monks and the great theological school of Alexandria. The church in Syria, in Persia, and along the trade routes carried the faith east; there were Christian communities in India that trace their founding to the apostle Thomas, and by the 600s Christianity had reached China. While much of Europe was still pagan, the church was already a sprawling, multilingual, multicontinental thing.

## The churches we never learned about

Part of why this comes as a surprise is that the version of church history most of us absorbed, if we absorbed any at all, runs along a single track: Jerusalem to Rome to Europe to America, as though the faith traveled one road westward and the rest was a footnote. But there were other roads, older than the one to Rome, and the churches at the end of them are some of the most remarkable communities the faith ever produced. We were simply never taught they existed.

There was, for centuries, a thriving Christian world to the east of the Roman Empire entirely, in the lands of Persia and beyond, the Church of the East, often called Nestorian, which sent its missionaries not west but east, along the Silk Road. A stone monument unearthed in China, dating to 781, records in Chinese and Syriac that Christian monks had arrived in the Tang capital more than a century earlier and that the emperor had received them. There were bishops in Central Asia. There were Christian communities in India, the Thomas Christians of the southwest coast, who hold to this day that the apostle Thomas himself brought the faith to them, and who were worshiping in their own ancient liturgy long before any European arrived to "discover" them. There were the churches of Egypt, the Copts, who can trace their tradition to the evangelist Mark and who endure as a living community after two thousand years. There were the Armenians, whose kingdom became, around the year 301, the first state in the world to adopt Christianity as its official faith, years before the Roman emperor Constantine had legalized it.

Hold those facts next to the picture we started with. Armenia was officially Christian before Rome tolerated it. Christian monks were preaching in China while most of northern Europe still worshiped the old gods. The faith was being read in Syriac and Coptic and the languages of India and the Persian court while the conversion of the English and the Germans and the Scandinavians lay centuries in the future. The map in our heads has Christianity radiating outward from a Western center to a waiting world. The actual map has it spreading in every direction at once from a Middle Eastern origin, and reaching much of Asia and Africa long before it had finished reaching Europe at all. Many of those eastern and African churches later suffered terribly, shrank under pressure, and dropped out of the story the West chose to tell. They did not drop out of existence. A good number of them are still there, still praying, having outlasted every empire that ever tried to end them.

## Why we forgot

So how did we end up with the map upside down? How did a Middle Eastern faith with deep African and Asian roots come to feel, to so many of us, like a Western possession?

Mostly by an accident of power and timing. For a few centuries, roughly from the rise of European colonial empires through the twentieth century, the West was the dominant force on earth, and during that stretch a great deal of Christian missionary activity did flow outward from Europe and America. That era was real, and it left the impression, especially in the West itself, that Christianity was a Western thing being shared with the world. But that era was a chapter, not the book. It came late, it is already ending, and it sat on top of a far older and more global story that it temporarily obscured.

The scholar Andrew Walls spent his career making this argument and is one of the people most responsible for the recovery of it: that there has never been a single cultural home for Christianity, that the faith has been "translated" into culture after culture from the start, and that its center of gravity has always been on the move. It began in the Middle East, shifted toward the Mediterranean and then Europe, and is now shifting decisively south and east again, back, in a sense, toward where it started.

## The center has already moved

This is where it stops being merely history and becomes the present, and where the historian Philip Jenkins delivered the news the Western church is still absorbing. In his 2002 book *The Next Christendom*, Jenkins documented what the numbers had already made undeniable: the typical Christian in the world today is not a white Westerner. The typical Christian is far more likely to be a Nigerian woman, a Brazilian, a Filipino, a Chinese house-church member, a believer in Kenya or Korea. Christianity is growing fastest, by far, in the global South, in sub-Saharan Africa, in parts of Asia, in Latin America, even as it declines in the Europe that once thought it owned the franchise. The future of the faith, Jenkins argued two decades ago and the data has only confirmed, is southern and global, not Western. In many ways it already is.

There is a piece of this that should especially move anyone who comes to the faith as an outsider, and it comes from the scholar Lamin Sanneh, a Gambian convert from Islam, in his book *Translating the Message*. Sanneh noticed something distinctive about Christianity that the colonial picture obscures. Unlike some religions that bind their sacred text to a single holy language, Christianity has translated itself, from the very beginning, into every tongue it touched. There is no one holy language of Christianity. The early church did not even preserve Jesus' own words in his native Aramaic; it wrote them down in Greek, the common language of ordinary people, so the most people possible could understand. And this translatability, Sanneh argued, is not a weakness but the heart of the thing. A faith that insists on being spoken in your own mother tongue is a faith that takes your culture seriously enough to enter it rather than erase it. Christianity does not have a home culture it asks you to adopt. It comes home to wherever you are. That is why it could be African and Asian and Middle Eastern and European all at once, with no contradiction, from the start.

## The picture at the end of the book

There is an image at the very end of the Bible that I think is the truest portrait of what the church actually is, and it has been there the whole time, waiting for us to notice. In Revelation 7:9, John sees a vision of the final gathering of God's people, and here is what he sees: "a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and before the Lamb."

Every nation. Every tribe. Every language. That is not a hope that someday Christianity might become diverse if the missionaries do their job. It is a description of what it has been aiming at, and quietly always been, from the first African on the desert road and the first mixed crowd in Antioch who needed a new name. It is worth saying plainly what this means for how we hold the faith now. If the church was global before it was European, and is global again now that the European chapter is closing, then no culture gets to own it and no culture is merely a guest in it. The African believer is not receiving a Western inheritance. The Western believer is not the keeper of a family heirloom that others are lucky to share. We are all latecomers to something older than any of us, all equally at home and equally dependent on a story that began on the wrong continent for our pride. The crowd before the throne is not a Western crowd with guests. It is the whole human family in every color and tongue, and no one language is the holy one, and no one nation is the home team.

So if you come to this faith feeling like an outsider to something that belongs to other people, to a culture or a country or a kind of person you are not, let the actual history correct you. You are not joining someone else's religion. You are coming home to the most global, most translated, most multinational movement in the history of the world, one that was African and Asian and Middle Eastern before it was ever anything else, and that has been waiting, since a man read Isaiah aloud in a chariot on a desert road, to be spoken in your own language too. The map was never the one we drew. The family was always larger than the room we were shown.
posts.excerpt: Jesus was a Middle Eastern man. The first convert recorded after Pentecost was an African. The church was thriving in Asia and Africa for centuries before most of Europe heard of it. The story we tell about a Western faith going out to the world has the map upside down.

posts.title: The Fight to Put the Bible in Your Hands
posts.body:
Reach over and pick up a Bible. Any Bible, the one on the shelf, the app on your phone, the hotel-drawer copy. Notice how ordinary it feels. You can read it. You did not have to ask anyone's permission. You can underline it, argue with it, leave it in the bathroom, lose it and buy another for the price of lunch. It is the most printed book in human history and one of the cheapest objects you own. The thing in your hands is so easy to get that it is easy to forget it was ever hard.

It was hard. For most of Christian history, ordinary people could not read the Bible for themselves, and a great many powerful people intended to keep it that way. The book you can pick up without a thought was, for centuries, locked behind a wall of Latin and law and fear, and the men who set out to break that wall down were hunted for it. One of them, a brilliant, stubborn Englishman named William Tyndale, was strangled and his body burned in 1536 for the crime of putting the New Testament into plain English. He died for the sentences you can now read on a screen while waiting for coffee. This is the story of how the book got to you, and it is one of the most consequential stories in the history of the West.

## The wall, and why it stood

To feel the story you have to understand the wall. By the late Middle Ages, the Bible existed in Western Europe almost entirely in Latin, a translation called the Vulgate, made by the scholar Jerome around the year 400. In Jerome's time, Latin was the common tongue; the whole point had been to put the Bible into the language people spoke. But a thousand years later, Latin was a dead language that only the educated clergy could read. The Bible was, in effect, locked in a box only the professionals had the key to. The ordinary farmer or weaver or mother heard the Scriptures recited in a language they did not understand, and received their content secondhand, filtered entirely through what the church chose to tell them it said.

Now, plenty of churchmen defended this honestly. The Bible is a difficult book; left to untrained readers, they argued, it would be twisted into a thousand private heresies. There is a real concern buried in that, and it would be unfair to pretend the whole motive was control. But control was certainly part of it. A people who cannot read the source for themselves cannot check the institution against it. If you alone hold the text, you alone decide what it means, and your authority is unchallengeable because no one else can open the book. The wall was not only about protecting truth. It was also about protecting power, and the two had become difficult to tell apart.

Into that situation, across two centuries, came a series of men who decided that the people had a right to read the words of God in the language of their own kitchens.

## Wycliffe: the morning star

The first great Englishman to push hard against the wall was John Wycliffe, a sharp and controversial Oxford scholar in the 1300s. Wycliffe had a radical conviction for his time: that the Bible, not the institution, was the final authority, and that ordinary Christians ought to be able to read it. Under his influence, around the 1380s, the first complete English Bibles were produced, translated by hand from the Latin, copied by hand, since the printing press did not yet exist in Europe.

Think about what that meant. Every single copy had to be written out by hand, word by word, by someone who risked punishment for owning it. They were precious, rare, and dangerous to possess. Wycliffe's followers, mockingly called Lollards, carried them in secret and read them aloud in homes. The authorities responded with fury. Owning an English Bible could get you tried for heresy. The hostility to Wycliffe was so deep that decades after he died of natural causes, the church had his body dug up, burned, and the ashes thrown into a river, a posthumous execution of a man they could no longer reach. He has been called the morning star of the Reformation, the first light before the dawn. He saw what was coming a hundred and fifty years early.

It is hard, from here, to feel how shocking his conviction was. We take it for granted that a Christian reads the Bible. For most of the people in Wycliffe's England, the Bible was not something you read; it was something that was done to you, in a language you did not know, by men who alone could open it. The idea that a weaver in her own kitchen might hold the words of God in her own tongue and weigh for herself what they meant, that was not a small reform. It was a reordering of who had access to God, and everyone understood that reordering authority over the book meant reordering authority over the people who lived by it. That is why a scholarly question about translation could get a man's bones dug up and burned. It was never only about translation.

## Tyndale: the man who would not stop

The dawn came with William Tyndale, and his is the story that should be told in every church that owns an English Bible, because we mostly do not know it.

Tyndale was born around 1494, a Gloucestershire man, fiercely gifted in languages, he eventually worked in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and several living European tongues. He came of age just as two things converged that Wycliffe never had: the printing press, which could now produce thousands of identical copies cheaply, and the recovery of the original Greek and Hebrew, which meant a translator no longer had to work from the Latin but could go back to the source. Tyndale wanted to translate the Bible directly from Greek and Hebrew into an English so plain that, in his famous boast to a learned clergyman who scorned the idea, "the boy that driveth the plough" would know more of Scripture than the scholar did.

The English authorities refused him permission and made it clear they would stop him. So Tyndale did something extraordinary: he left England, never to return, and spent the rest of his life on the run on the European continent, translating and printing the Bible in exile and smuggling the copies back into England hidden in bales of cloth and sacks of grain. His English New Testament appeared in 1526. The bishops bought up copies to burn them, sometimes unwittingly funding the printing of the next batch. He worked under constant threat, moving from city to city, betrayed more than once.

He was betrayed for the last time in 1535, near Brussels, by a man who had pretended to be his friend. He was imprisoned for over a year in a damp castle cell, where he wrote a letter, it survives, asking his captors for a warmer cap, a coat, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar, and dictionary, so he could keep working in prison. In October 1536 he was condemned, strangled at the stake, and his body burned. The tradition records his final words as a prayer: "Lord, open the King of England's eyes."

Here is the staggering part. Within three years of his death, the King of England did exactly that. Henry VIII authorized an official English Bible to be placed in every parish church in the land, and that authorized Bible, and nearly every major English Bible after it, including the celebrated King James Version of 1611, drew enormously on Tyndale's own translation. The very words the church burned him for printing became the words England read in church on Sundays. Phrases we think of as simply "biblical English", "let there be light," "the powers that be," "the salt of the earth," "fight the good fight", are Tyndale's. He lost his life and won the language. His prayer was answered within his own decade.

## Why anyone thought this was worth dying for

A newcomer is entitled to ask the obvious question. It is a book. Why would a sane, brilliant man throw away his life, on the run for a decade, to put it into English? Why not let the scholars keep their Latin and find some less fatal cause?

Because Wycliffe and Tyndale and the reformers who came after them believed something specific about this particular book, and it is the conviction that drove the whole upheaval we call the Reformation. They believed that the Scriptures are, as 2 Timothy 3:16 puts it, "God-breathed", that through these words the living God actually speaks, not merely about ancient matters but to the reader, now. If that is true, then keeping the book locked in a dead language is not a neutral administrative arrangement. It is keeping people from the voice of God. It is standing between a person and the One trying to speak to them. They had taken God at his word in Isaiah 55:11, that the word which goes out from his mouth "will not return to me empty, but will accomplish what I desire", and they reasoned that a word with that kind of power had no business being locked away from the people it was sent to. Tyndale was not risking his life for literature. He was risking it for access, for the conviction that a plowboy had as much right to hear God speak as a bishop did, and that no institution had the right to stand in the middle.

The historian Alister McGrath, who has written the standard popular histories of this whole drama in *In the Beginning* (2001, on the making of the King James Bible) and *Christianity's Dangerous Idea* (2007, on the Reformation), names the dangerous idea precisely. The dangerous idea was that ordinary Christians could read and interpret the Bible for themselves. It was dangerous because it was destabilizing, it did, in fact, fracture Western Christianity into the many traditions we have today, for better and for worse, and McGrath does not pretend the costs were small. But it was also, he argues, one of the most powerful and liberating ideas in the history of the West, because it put the source back into the hands of the people, and a people who can read the source can never again be told, unchallenged, what it says.

It is worth pausing to be fair to the other side of this, because a newcomer should not be handed a simple story of heroes and villains. The men who wanted to keep the Bible in Latin were not all cynics guarding their power. Some of them had watched untrained readers take a verse out of context and build a destructive movement on it, and they were genuinely afraid of what would happen if everyone became their own interpreter. They were not entirely wrong to be afraid. The centuries after Tyndale did produce a great deal of confident misreading, a great deal of division, a great many people sure that their private reading of a difficult passage settled a question the wisest minds had argued for a thousand years. McGrath is candid about this. The dangerous idea was dangerous in both directions. It liberated, and it fractured, and it did both at once, and the same conviction that freed the plowboy also armed every crank with a proof text.

But the reformers made a wager about which danger was worse, and it is the wager worth understanding. They decided that a people kept from the source, dependent entirely on what they were told it said, was in greater peril than a people given the source and trusted, at real cost, to wrestle with it. They bet that a difficult freedom was better than a comfortable dependence. They bet that the God who breathed out these words was capable of reaching ordinary people through them without an official standing in the middle to license the meaning. It was a bet on the competence of ordinary believers and on the clarity of God's own voice, and they staked their lives on it. You can argue about whether they were entirely right. You cannot argue that they were cowards, and you cannot argue that the bet did not change the world.

There is an old picture of what this is supposed to feel like, and it is in Nehemiah 8. The people of Israel have returned from exile, and the scribe Ezra stands on a wooden platform and reads the Book of the Law aloud to the whole assembled people, from morning until midday, "and all the people listened attentively." Others translated and explained it so the people could understand the meaning. And the people wept when they heard it, because they grasped the words for the first time. That scene, ordinary people, hearing the words of God in a language they understand and weeping at what they finally grasp, is exactly what Wycliffe and Tyndale wanted to give their own people. The wall had kept it from them for a thousand years. These men tore it down with their lives.

## What you are holding

So pick the book up again, and feel it differently this time.

The reason it is in a language you can read is that men were burned for translating it. The reason it is cheap enough to own three copies is that a printing press once smuggled it past soldiers in sacks of flour. The reason you do not need a priest to tell you what it says is that a plowboy's right to read it for himself was bought at the cost of William Tyndale's life, strangled at a stake in 1536 with a prayer on his lips that his enemies' eyes would be opened. John 1:1 calls Christ himself the Word, the Word who was with God and was God and became flesh and lived among us. The reformers risked everything on the belief that this Word still wanted to be heard, by everyone, in their own tongue, without a wall in the way.

We treat the book as common because it is everywhere. They knew it was the most uncommon thing in the world, and they spent their lives to get it into ordinary hands. The least we can do, having been handed it at no cost, is to open it, and remember, when we do, the price someone paid for the simple, astonishing fact that we can understand the words.
posts.excerpt: The Bible on your shelf, in a language you can read, cost people their lives. One man was strangled and burned for translating it. This is the story of how the book got to you, and why anyone thought it was worth dying to deliver.

posts.title: The First Christians Died for This
posts.body:
There is a letter, written around the year 155, from one church to another, describing the death of an old man. The old man's name was Polycarp, and he was the bishop of a city called Smyrna, on the coast of what is now Turkey. He was eighty-six. The Roman governor had him brought into the arena, where a crowd was waiting, and offered him the simplest way out anyone has ever been offered. All Polycarp had to do was say the words *Caesar is Lord*, drop a small pinch of incense onto a fire, and curse the name of Christ. Three small actions. A few seconds of his life. And then he could go home to his church and his old age and his bed.

The letter records what he said. "Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" They burned him alive. The letter says the believers gathered his bones afterward, which they considered "more precious than gold," and buried them, and met there on the anniversary of his death to remember him with joy.

I want you to sit inside the strangeness of that for a moment, because it is the doorway into everything that follows. A pinch of incense. That is all it would have taken. Not a renunciation of his whole moral life, not a betrayal of his friends, not anything that would have made the morning paper. A gesture so small that a modern person can barely understand why he didn't just do it and cross his fingers. He had eighty-six years of reasons to live. He chose the fire instead. To understand the people who came before us, the people on whose graves the entire Christian story stands, you have to understand why that pinch of incense was the one thing he could not do.

## The world that made the question impossible to dodge

Start with the Roman world, because we have flattened it in our imaginations into something it never was. We picture Rome as a secular state with a hobby of feeding Christians to lions. It was nothing of the kind. Rome was drenched in religion. The gods were everywhere, at the door of every house, over every meal, in the founding myths of the city, in the calendar, in the army, in the marketplace. Religion was not a private opinion you held on the weekend. It was the glue of public life, the thing that held the whole vast empire together. To be a good Roman was to honor the gods who had made Rome great, and at the center of it all, by the first century, stood the emperor himself, increasingly treated as divine.

This is the part that matters. When a Roman official asked a Christian to burn incense to the emperor, he did not, in his own mind, think he was demanding much. He was asking for a loyalty oath. It was closer to standing for a national anthem than to a profession of theology. The gesture said: *I am a good citizen, I wish the empire well, I am one of us.* Refusing it was not refusing a creed. It looked, to Rome, like sedition. It looked like a person announcing they did not belong to the human community at all.

And the Christians knew exactly how it looked. That is what makes their refusal so striking. They were not confused. They understood they could keep their heads down, honor Caesar in this one symbolic way, and go right on worshiping Jesus in private. Plenty of people in the ancient world held many gods at once; adding one more cost nothing. The Christians would not add one more. They had read the first commandment and taken it with a literalness that baffled their neighbors. There was one Lord, and his name was not Caesar.

The sociologist Rodney Stark, in his 1996 study *The Rise of Christianity*, asks the hard-nosed question that a historian has to ask: how did a tiny, persecuted, illegal movement of perhaps a few thousand people grow, in less than three centuries, into the dominant faith of the Roman Empire? His answer is not what you would expect from a man writing as a social scientist. Part of it, he argues, is precisely this willingness to die. A faith that asks nothing of you is worth nothing to you. A faith that people will pay for with their lives is a faith that announces, with total clarity, that it believes its own claims. The martyrs were not a public-relations disaster the church had to survive. They were, in a strange and terrible way, the church's most persuasive argument.

## Who they actually were

We say "the martyrs" and the word goes abstract, like "the casualties" or "the fallen." So let me give you two of them by name, because they were not a category. They were people.

Polycarp you have already met. He mattered enormously to the early church for a reason beyond his courage: he was a living wire back to the beginning. The tradition, well attested in the early sources, is that Polycarp had been a disciple of the apostle John, that as a young man he had sat at the feet of someone who had walked with Jesus. When he died in 155, he was one of the last living links to the eyewitness generation. The early church held onto men like him the way a family holds onto the last grandparent who remembers the old country. When he refused the incense, it was not theology refusing a gesture. It was memory refusing to lie.

The second is harder to read about, and you should read about her anyway. Her name was Perpetua, and she died in Carthage, in North Africa, around the year 203. She was about twenty-two. She was a young mother, well-born, educated, and still nursing her infant son. We know her not from a stranger's letter but, remarkably, from what scholars believe to be her own prison diary, one of the earliest surviving pieces of writing by a Christian woman, set down in her own voice in the days before her death. In it she describes her father coming to the prison again and again, begging her to recant. He is not a villain. He is a frightened old man who loves his daughter and cannot understand why she will throw her life away over a word. At one point he takes the baby. At one point he tears at his own beard and throws himself on the ground. She writes that she grieved for him, and that she would not deny the name. She was killed in the arena for the entertainment of a crowd, alongside her pregnant slave, Felicity, who had given birth in prison days before.

Read Perpetua's diary and the abstraction shatters. This is not a stained-glass saint. This is a young woman with a baby at her breast and a weeping father at the bars, making the one decision none of us can imagine making, and writing it down so we would know it was real. We tend to picture the early Christians as old men with beards. A great many of them were young, and a great many of them were women, and a number of them were enslaved people like Felicity who owned nothing in this world and gave up the one thing they had left.

## Why the incense, of all things

Here is where a newcomer's honest question deserves an honest answer. Why was a pinch of incense the line? Why not just do it?

Because the Christians had grasped something about worship that we have largely lost, and it is worth recovering even if you are not sure you believe any of it. They understood that worship is not a feeling. It is an act of allegiance, and allegiance cannot be divided. To offer incense to Caesar was to say, with your body, *Caesar holds the place that belongs to God.* It did not matter that you didn't mean it. The act meant it for you. They had inherited this conviction from the Jewish people, who had spent centuries dying rather than bow to the gods of whatever empire happened to be occupying them at the time, and who had handed the early church a story like the one in Acts 7, the death of Stephen, the first Christian killed for his faith, stoned while he looked up and said he saw the heavens opened. Stephen set the pattern. He did not curse his killers. He prayed for them, and then he died.

The Christians read that story and others like it and drew a conclusion that the book of Revelation states with brutal economy. Speaking of the believers who overcame the great accuser, it says: "They triumphed over him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony; they did not love their lives so much as to shrink from death" (Revelation 12:11). *They did not love their lives so much as to shrink from death.* That is not a description of fanatics. It is a description of people who had relocated the center of gravity of their existence. Their lives were no longer the thing they were protecting. Something else had become the thing, and their lives had become negotiable in its service.

Jesus had told them this would be the shape of it. "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, be afraid of the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28). To a modern ear that sounds harsh. To Polycarp it sounded like freedom. If the worst the empire could do was kill his body, then the empire had already lost its grip on him. There was nothing left to threaten. A man who does not fear death cannot be ruled by anyone who trades in death, and that, more than any army, is what Rome could not finally defeat. The apostle Paul had said the same thing from a prison cell of his own: "For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain" (Philippians 1:21). Polycarp simply lived out the arithmetic.

## What they were not

It is important to say what the martyrs were not, because the word "martyr" has been dragged through a great deal of mud in the centuries since, and the early Christians would not recognize most of what now travels under their name.

They were not people who went looking for death. The early church was, in fact, suspicious of believers who courted martyrdom, who turned themselves in or provoked the authorities. That was considered a kind of spiritual pride, a grasping after a crown you were supposed to receive, not seize. Polycarp himself had withdrawn to a farmhouse outside the city when the persecution began; he did not march into the arena. He went when he was found. The model was not a death wish. It was a refusal to lie when the lie was finally demanded.

And they were not haters. This is the detail that the Roman world found most disorienting, and the one Stark argues did the most to grow the church. The Christians prayed for the emperors who killed them. During the plagues that swept the empire, when the pagans, terrified of contagion, fled the cities and abandoned their own dying relatives in the streets, the Christians stayed. They nursed the sick, including the sick who were not their own, and many of them caught the diseases and died doing it. A faith that would die rather than worship Caesar would also die nursing a stranger's fever. It was all one thing. The historian Robert Louis Wilken, in *The Spirit of Early Christian Thought* (2003), spent his career insisting that we will never understand these people if we treat their faith as a set of opinions they happened to hold strongly. It was a whole way of seeing, of seeing God, the world, the body, the neighbor, and death itself, and the dying made no sense apart from the loving, and the loving made no sense apart from the God they refused to deny.

## What this asks of us

I have to be careful here, because the easy move is to turn the martyrs into a rebuke. To point at Polycarp in the fire and say to a comfortable modern church: *look how soft you have become.* And there is a truth in that, but it is not my truth to wield, because I have never been asked to do anything that cost me what it cost them. I have never been offered the incense. None of us reading this likely have. To stand at a safe distance of eighteen centuries and use their courage as a stick is its own kind of cowardice, and I will not do it.

What I will say is gentler and, I think, harder. The martyrs are not mainly a measuring stick. They are a family. When you become a Christian, you are not joining a movement that started with your favorite preacher or your grandmother's church. You are being grafted into something that runs back through Perpetua's prison cell and Polycarp's farmhouse and Stephen's bloodied face, all the way to an empty tomb. These people are not historical curiosities. They are the relatives you never met whose decisions made your faith possible. The reason there was a church for you to walk into at all is that an eighty-six-year-old man in Smyrna decided that eighty-six years of mercy were worth more than one more morning of his life.

So I do not ask you to die. I ask you to recognize whose house you have walked into. There are bones under the floor, "more precious than gold," and the people who gathered them did so with joy, not grief, because they were sure, surer than we tend to be about anything, that the King they served had already walked out of his own grave and would not leave them in theirs. They built the room you are standing in. They are still in it. And the question they leave on the table is not whether you could die like them. It is whether you believe, as plainly as they did, that there is anyone worth it.
posts.excerpt: Before there were cathedrals or denominations or a single complete Bible, there were people who would rather burn than offer a pinch of incense to the emperor. This is who they were, and why they did it.

posts.title: Why People Fled to the Desert to Find God
posts.body:
Picture a young man in Egypt, around the year 270. He is maybe twenty. His parents have just died and left him a comfortable inheritance, good land, a household, a sister to look after, a settled future. One Sunday he walks into church and hears the Gospel reading, the moment in Matthew 19 where Jesus tells a rich young man, "If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me." The rich young man in the story walks away sad, because he had great wealth. This young man in Egypt does not walk away. He hears those words as though they were spoken directly to him, that morning, in that building. He goes out, sells the land, gives away the money, arranges for his sister, and walks into the desert to live alone with God for the rest of his life.

His name was Antony. He lived to be over a hundred. And the strange thing he did, walking away from a comfortable life into the wilderness, caught fire. Within a generation, thousands were doing it. By the fourth and fifth centuries the deserts of Egypt, Syria, and Palestine were dotted with hermits and small communities of men and women who had left everything to seek God in the silence. To a modern person this looks like madness, or at best like an extreme nobody should imitate. But to understand the people who came before us, you have to understand why the desert pulled at them, because the thing that drove them out there is a hunger we still have, even if we have forgotten what to do with it.

## What happened to make the desert necessary

For the first three centuries, being a Christian was dangerous. As we saw in the age of the martyrs, you could be killed for it. The faith was illegal, costly, and absolutely serious, you did not drift into it, because drifting in could get you killed. Then, in the early 300s, everything changed.
