It is a deduction from a specific reported event: that Jesus of Nazareth, executed and buried, was bodily alive on the third day. Peter, writing to scattered and suffering Christians, says it with precision, that God has given us new birth into a *living* hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Peter 1:3–9). Living, as opposed to dead. A hope with a pulse, because it is tethered to something that, if it happened, changes the status of death itself for everyone. Peter writes to people in real trials, and he does not tell them to cheer up. He tells them their hope is anchored in an event, and that the event guarantees an inheritance that cannot perish or fade, kept for them.

This is the structure N. T. Wright has spent a career laying out: that the resurrection is not a comforting symbol the early Christians adopted but the load-bearing historical claim on which everything else rests, and that without it the whole edifice is, as Paul himself admitted, a fraud worth pitying. Wright's point, made again and again, is that Christianity stuck its neck out in a way no myth ever does. It did not say "be at peace, the soul is immortal." It said a corpse stood up, here, in our history, under a named governor, and that this is the first instance of what is coming for the world. That is either false, in which case the hope collapses, or it is true, in which case the hope is the most reasonable conclusion a person could draw. What it cannot be is "wishful thinking," because wishes do not get crucified, buried, and reported alive by frightened witnesses who then died rather than recant.

## The hope that produces patience, not passivity

There is a charge against hope worth answering before going further: that it makes people passive, that a hope fixed on the next world breeds indifference to this one. Let the world burn, the accusation goes, because the believer has his eyes on a better address. The history of the church gives that charge some real ammunition; there have been Christians who used the hope of heaven as an excuse to ignore hunger and injustice at their feet. But that is the hope misused, not the hope itself, and the New Testament cuts directly against it. Paul, having grounded everything in the resurrection in his long argument to Corinth, does not conclude "therefore relax." He concludes "therefore stand firm, let nothing move you, give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor is not in vain." The resurrection is offered as the reason your present work *matters*, not the reason it does not, because if the world is going to be raised rather than scrapped, then what you build in it now is not wasted.

Moltmann, who knew real despair, drew exactly this conclusion. A hope grounded in the resurrection, he argued, does not pacify; it agitates. It makes the believer restless with the way things are, unwilling to accept the present as final, precisely because he has seen a future that contradicts it. The person who genuinely believes death has been defeated is not the person who shrugs at a deathly world. He is the person who can no longer make peace with it. Hope that breeds passivity was never the resurrection's hope. It was always a counterfeit wearing its clothes.

## The hope was built for the worst day, not the best

Notice where the New Testament deploys this hope. Not at celebrations. At funerals. Paul, writing to Thessalonica, addresses people grieving believers who have died, and his explicit aim is that they not grieve like the rest, who have no hope. And then he does not tell them grief is wrong. He tells them *why* their grief is different: because if Jesus died and rose again, then God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him, and the dead in Christ will rise, and the living and the dead together will be with the Lord forever (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Look closely at what he does and does not say. He does not say "do not grieve." He says do not grieve *as those who have no hope*. The tears are allowed. The loss is real. What is added is not a denial of the loss but a horizon beyond it, and the horizon is fixed to the resurrection, the same anchor, thrown past death and caught on the far side.

That is the test of whether a hope is wishful or real: bring it to the worst day and see if it stands. Optimism cannot come to a graveside; it has nothing to say there, and it knows it, which is why it changes the subject. Christian hope was *built* for the graveside. It is most itself there. It does not minimize the death. It out-narrates it, insisting that the story does not end in the box, because it did not end in the box for the one the whole hope hangs on.

## What the first Christians did with it

Test a hope by what it makes people do. The early Christians did not treat the resurrection as a private comfort to be kept indoors. They treated it as a fact so large that it reorganized how they lived and, repeatedly, how they died. They went to lions and to crosses and to the executioner's sword across three centuries, and the Roman authorities who killed them noted, with bafflement, that these people did not behave like the frightened or the deluded. They nursed plague victims that everyone else had abandoned, because they did not believe death was the worst thing that could happen. They freed slaves and buried the poor and refused, under torture, to recant a claim about an empty tomb. You do not do that for a wish. You do not walk into an arena for positive thinking. Whatever else can be said about them, they staked their lives on the conviction that the resurrection was not a metaphor but an event, and that the event meant the world was not ending in death after all.

That is the behavioral signature of hope rather than wishful thinking. Wishful thinking is comfortable and costs nothing; it lets you feel better and changes none of your decisions. The resurrection hope cost the early church everything it had, and they spent it gladly, because they were not betting on a mood. They were betting on a morning, and a body, and a tomb that would not stay shut.

## Why this is harder to dismiss than it looks

Here is what changed for me, coming at this from the outside. I expected Christian hope to be the soft part of the faith, the part that asks nothing and merely soothes. I found it to be the most exposed part, the part that takes the biggest risk. A myth designed to comfort would never have anchored itself to a checkable event in recent history. It would have stayed safely in the realm of feeling and symbol, where it could never be disproved. Christianity did the opposite. It bet the entire farm on a public claim about a particular weekend, and it told its own followers that if the claim were false they were fools to be pitied. That is not the behavior of wishful thinking. Wishful thinking protects itself. This staked itself.

I am not going to tell you the evidence forces the conclusion; honest faith is not a math proof, and anyone who tells you it is has oversold it. There is a real step to take, and it is a step, not a calculation. But I will tell you that the choice is not between brave realism and cowardly hope. It is between two accounts of the same facts: a world where death has the last word and our longing for more is a cruel joke, or a world where one death was reversed and that reversal is the first light of a dawn coming for everything. Both are stances. Both reach beyond what can be proven. Only one of them has an empty tomb to point at.

So when someone tells you that hope is just refusing to face facts, you can agree about the cheap kind and then ask them about the other kind. The cheap kind is a mood, and it fails exactly when you need it. The other kind is an anchor, and it is fixed to a morning two thousand years ago that either happened or did not. If it did not, then the honest thing is to let the hope go and grieve like those who have none. But if it did, if the stone really moved, if the grave really emptied, if the witnesses really saw what they said they saw and went to their deaths insisting on it, then hope is not the soft option at all. It is the conclusion. And the anchor holds, not because the sea is calm, but because of where the line is tied.
posts.excerpt: Hope has a bad reputation among honest people, it sounds like the polite word for refusing to face facts, a coat of paint over the void. But Christian hope is not optimism, and it is not the power of positive thinking. It rests on a claim about something that did or did not happen on a Sunday morning.

posts.title: Will There Really Be a Judgment Day?
posts.body:
The phrase has been ruined by the people who shouted it. *Judgment Day.* Say it and most of us hear a sandwich board on a street corner, a red-faced preacher promising fire, a threat aimed at keeping the nervous in line. It sounds like the worst of religion, fear dressed up as faith, a God whose main feeling toward you is displeasure, waiting at the end of life to catch you out. No wonder the modern mind files it under "things we have outgrown." We do not want a cosmic prosecutor. We would rather, thank you, be left alone.

I understand the recoil. I shared it. But I want to make a claim that will sound strange at first and, I think, will not sound strange by the end. **The longing for a final judgment is not a primitive fear we have outgrown. It is one of the deepest moral instincts we have, and the people who feel it most fiercely are not the comfortable but the crushed, the ones for whom a universe with no final reckoning is not a relief but a horror.** Judgment Day, rightly understood, is not first of all a threat held over the well-fed. It is a promise made to the wronged. It is the announcement that the story is not over, that the powerful do not get the last word, that the blood spilled in secret will one day be answered. Take judgment away and you have not made the world kinder. You have abandoned every victim to the verdict of the strong.

## Whether you want it depends on where you stand

Begin with a fact the comfortable forget: how you feel about a courtroom depends entirely on whether you are the defendant or the plaintiff. If you have spent your life safe, well-fed, and unwronged, "judgment" sounds like a risk, an audit you would rather skip. But stand somewhere else. Stand in the position of the people history actually ground under its wheels, and the word changes completely.

The theologian Miroslav Volf knows this from the inside. He is a Croatian, and he wrote his great book *Exclusion and Embrace* while the Balkans were tearing themselves apart in the 1990s, while villages were being cleansed and mass graves dug a few hours' drive from where he sat. He set out, as a Christian, to write about forgiveness and the embrace of the enemy, and he found that he could not, honestly, ask the victims to forgive and release their tormentors unless there was a God who would *not* let the atrocities pass unjudged. A non-judging God, he wrote, in a world this violent, would be unworthy of worship. It is precisely the certainty of God's judgment that makes it possible for a human being to lay down the sword, because you can stop demanding vengeance with your own hands only if you believe the wrong will not, in the end, simply be ignored. Volf's point is sharp and it is permanent: the doctrine of divine judgment is what stands between a victim and the abyss of either despair or endless retaliation.

## The question is not abstract for them

For most of the people who have ever lived, this is not a seminar question. Think of the slave who died in chains having never once seen the man who owned her face a single consequence. Think of the child worked to death in a mine whose owner died rich and respected and was buried under a marble stone. Think of the millions whose suffering left no record, whose names no one wrote down, whose murderers prospered and aged and passed away in their beds. If there is no judgment, then that is simply how it ends for them. The strong wrote the history, kept the wealth, and dissolved into the same nothing as their victims, and the only difference between them was that one set enjoyed the ride. A world with no final reckoning is not a tolerant, easygoing world. It is a world in which the powerful have permanently won and the weak have permanently lost, and the universe shrugs.

The Christian claim is that the universe does not shrug. Paul, standing in Athens among the philosophers, told them that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world with justice, by a man he has appointed, and has given assurance of this by raising that man from the dead (Acts 17:31). Notice the logic: the resurrection is the *proof* that judgment is coming, the down payment, the public guarantee that this world is heading toward a reckoning and not toward a fade-out. To the Athenians, the resurrection was the strange part and the judgment was unremarkable. To us it is reversed. But the connection is the heart of it: because one man was raised, the books will be opened.

## The instinct we cannot talk ourselves out of

Watch what happens to people who claim not to believe in any final justice. They cannot live it. The same person who says, over coffee, that morality is just evolved preference and there is no cosmic court will, an hour later, be undone by a news story about a child harmed and a perpetrator who walked free. The outrage is not optional for them. It rises unbidden, and it carries an absolute quality, *that should not be, that must be answered*, that their stated philosophy has no room for. You can call the outrage a leftover instinct, a trick of the genes. But notice that no one actually treats it that way. We treat injustice as a real feature of the world that makes a real claim on us, demanding a response that mere preference could never demand. The hunger for a final reckoning is not a quirk a few religious people have. It is universal, and it is one of the most stubborn facts about human beings.

The Christian claim is simply that this hunger is not a cruel joke. It corresponds to something. The reason "that should be answered" feels like a true statement and not a passing mood is that it *is* a true statement, there is an answer coming, a court that will sit, a verdict that will be rendered. The doctrine of judgment is the universe taking your moral outrage as seriously as you cannot help taking it yourself. To deny judgment is not to escape the burden of justice. It is to declare that your deepest convictions about right and wrong are noises with no referent, and almost no one can actually believe that for longer than a sentence.

## Judgment cuts toward the truth, in every direction

Now the part that keeps it from becoming a weapon for the self-righteous. The same Scripture that promises judgment for the oppressor refuses to let the rest of us stand smugly in the gallery. Paul, writing to Rome, warns specifically the person who judges others while doing the same things, and says that God will repay each one according to what they have done, glory and peace for everyone who does good, but wrath for the self-seeking, and, he adds twice, for the Jew first and also for the Gentile, there is no favoritism with God (Romans 2:5–11). Judgment is not a tribe sorting itself above another tribe. It is the truth told about every life without exception, including mine. And Jesus says the standard reaches further than any of us would set it: that we will give account on that day even for every careless word we have spoken (Matthew 12:36). Not only the public crimes. The casual cruelties. The throwaway contempt. The whole record.

That should sober the comfortable Christian as much as it consoles the victim, and it is meant to. The vision in Revelation of the great white throne, the dead, great and small, standing before God, the books opened, each judged according to what they had done (Revelation 20:11–15), is not a scene in which a few obvious monsters are dealt with while the rest of us watch. It is a scene in which *everyone* stands, and the great and the small stand on the same floor, and the only thing that finally matters is what is written. The day that vindicates the wronged is the same day that strips every one of us bare. You cannot want the one without facing the other. That is the honesty the doctrine forces, and it is why it is good news and frightening news in the same breath.

## What forgiveness needs in order to be possible

Volf's deepest insight is one the comfortable rarely grasp, because they have never had to forgive anything that cost them. We tend to imagine that belief in judgment makes people vengeful and that letting go of it makes people gracious. The reality runs the other way. It is precisely because there is a God who will set things right that a victim can release the demand to set things right himself. If there is no final justice, then forgiveness means letting the wrong simply vanish unanswered, which no one who has truly suffered can do, and should not be asked to do. But if the wrong will be dealt with, fully, truthfully, by one who sees what no human court could see, then the survivor can lay down the sword without laying down the truth that a wrong was done. Forgiveness becomes possible only when vengeance is taken out of human hands and placed in God's. Remove judgment and you do not get more mercy. You get either despair or an endless cycle of people taking justice into their own hands because no one else will.

This is why Paul, immediately after telling the Romans not to take revenge, grounds the command in judgment: leave room for God's wrath, he says, for it is written that vengeance belongs to God, who will repay. That is not an afterthought. It is the load-bearing beam. You can stop demanding payment yourself only because Someone trustworthy has guaranteed the account will be settled. The doctrine that looks like the engine of human cruelty turns out to be the only thing that makes laying down cruelty possible.

## Why this is not the threat you think

So return to the sandwich board, and see how badly it misrepresented the thing. The street preacher made judgment a threat aimed *outward*, at the sinners over there, the ones not like us. But biblical judgment is aimed at the truth of every life, and its first beneficiaries are the people the world refused to see. The doctrine does not exist to frighten the anxious into church attendance. It exists to declare that reality is *moral all the way down*, that there is no act so hidden it escapes the record, no victim so forgotten that their suffering goes unweighed, no power so great that it stands above the bench. The atheist materialist I used to be had no resources for this at all. On that view, the words "that was unjust" are just noises we make; there is no court in which the claim could ever be heard, no verdict that could ever be rendered, no difference, in the end, between the tyrant and his victims except the order in which they decomposed. I called that the brave, grown-up view. I have come to think it is the one that cannot account for the very outrage that makes us human.

There is a hard mercy buried in the doctrine, too. The same throne that judges is, in the Christian claim, occupied by the one who was himself judged unjustly, condemned in a rigged trial, executed by an empire, the supreme victim of human injustice, and who took the verdict that the rest of us deserve into his own body so that the judgment might, for those who will have it, fall on him instead. The judge has the wounds. He is not a stranger to the dock. That does not soften the seriousness of the reckoning. It locates it. The God who will judge the world is the God who first let the world judge him.

## The careless word and the long memory

There is a detail in Jesus' teaching that I find almost unbearable, and it is the one that finally persuaded me the doctrine was not a crude scare tactic but something far more searching. He says we will give account for every careless word. Not only the great public sins, the careless ones. The remark made to wound and then forgotten by the speaker, though never by the one it landed on. The contempt tossed off in passing. The lie told for convenience. A crude religion of judgment would care about the headline crimes and ignore the rest. The God Jesus describes has a longer memory than that, and a finer one. He notices the small cruelties the world files under nothing, the ones no human court would ever hear, the ones we ourselves have already excused.

This should level the ground completely. It means there is no clean separation between the monsters who face judgment and the decent people who watch. The same scrutiny that exposes the tyrant exposes the man who has merely been quietly unkind for forty years and called it being honest. N. T. Wright observes that the biblical hope of judgment is not the cosmic equivalent of a tabloid exposing the famous; it is the truth told about every life, including the unremarkable ones, including the religious ones, including mine. That is what makes it good news and terrible news at once. The wronged are vindicated, and no one in the room gets to feel superior about it, because the books opened are everyone's.

## What it asks of you

Here is where it lands, and I will not soften it into advice. If there is a Judgment Day, then your life is not a private affair that ends in silence. It is a public matter, headed for a court, and the verdict will be true. That is terrible if you are counting on getting away with things. It is the best news imaginable if you are one of the countless people who have been wronged and watched the wrong go unanswered, or if you are the kind of person who lies awake aching for the world to be set right and despairing that it never is.

I cannot tell you the day or the hour; no one can, and the ones who claim to are not to be trusted. I can tell you that the Christian faith refuses the two consoling lies our age keeps offering, that there is no such thing as final justice, and that you personally have nothing to answer for. It insists instead on something harder and, I have come to believe, truer: that justice is real and coming, that you and I are inside its reach, and that the only safe place to stand on that day is not behind your own record, which will not hold, but behind the one who already stood in the dock for you. The wronged will be vindicated. The truth will be told. And the question is not whether the day comes, but whose name you are counting on when it does.
posts.excerpt: Judgment Day sounds like a threat invented to keep people in line, a cosmic courtroom with God as the angry judge. But ask the people history actually crushed whether they want a final reckoning, and you will hear a very different answer. For them, judgment is not the bad news. It is the only hope left.

posts.title: Can You Be a Christian on Your Own?
posts.body:
Try to find the solo Christian in the New Testament. Go looking. Search the letters and the gospels for the believer who follows Jesus privately, accountable to no one, gathered with no one, a faith of one. You will not find him. Not because the writers forbade him, they barely thought to forbid what they could not imagine. The category does not exist. There is no Greek word in the entire New Testament for a Christian who belongs to no church, for the same reason there is no word in an anatomy textbook for a hand that has decided it would rather not be attached to an arm.

I want to make this argument gently, because the people most likely to be reading it have usually been burned by people who made it harshly. You have been told you *must* go to church in a tone that made church sound like a debt collector. Set that tone down. I am not here to collect. I am here to describe something you may not have been shown, that the loneliness you have felt in your private faith is not a personal failing, and not a sign you're doing it wrong. It is the predictable ache of a thing that was built for two or more, running on one.

**Here is the claim, and I'll spend the rest of the essay being fair to the version of you that resists it: the New Testament knows no solitary Christian, not as a rule it enforces, but as a reality it cannot picture, because in the mind of the first believers, to belong to Christ was to be grafted into a body, and a severed member is not a smaller Christian. It is a member in trouble.**

## The metaphor that was not a metaphor

Begin with the image Paul reached for when he wanted to describe what a church is, because he reached for it more than any other, and we have softened it into a poster.

*Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ* (1 Corinthians 12:12). We read that and nod. Nice picture. Teamwork. But Paul is not handing us a motivational image about cooperation. He is making a claim about what kind of thing a Christian *is.* He goes on: the eye cannot say to the hand, *I don't need you.* The head cannot say to the feet, *I have no need of you* (1 Corinthians 12:21). And then the line we skip: *If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it* (1 Corinthians 12:26).

Sit with what Paul is actually saying. He is not saying the church *functions like* a body when it cooperates well. He is saying you, the individual believer, are a body *part.* A hand. An eye. A foot. And the defining fact about a body part is that it has no independent life. A hand on a table is not a more autonomous hand. It is a dying hand. Its wholeness is not located in itself. Its wholeness is located in its attachment.

This is why the question *can I be a Christian alone* would have confused Paul the way *can I be a hand without an arm* confuses a surgeon. The hand can be detached. It just cannot stay a hand for long.

## What the first Christians actually did when they believed

The clearest answer to "can you do this alone" is to watch what the people did the very day the church was born, because they tell you what they thought belief *was* by what they immediately did with it.

Three thousand people believe in a single afternoon in Acts 2. What happens next is not three thousand individuals going home to pray privately. *They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer* (Acts 2:42). And then the description thickens: they sold property and shared it, they ate in each other's homes, they met daily, they had, and the word is startling, *all things in common* (Acts 2:44–47). Belief, for these people, did not produce a private spirituality that occasionally socialized. It produced a shared life so immediate and so total that the believing and the belonging were the same motion.

We have nearly reversed this. We treat the believing as the real thing and the belonging as the optional follow-up, first you get saved, privately, and then, if you have the energy and find a church you like, you join one. To the people in Acts 2 this would have read backward. There was no gap between trusting Jesus and joining his people, because joining his people was *how you trusted Jesus.* The fellowship was not the reward for faith. It was the shape faith took the moment it became real.

The experiment has been run, in other words. We know what conviction-plus-community does, because we watched three thousand people do it in a single chapter. We are the ones running the new experiment, conviction alone, and we are running it without a control group, on ourselves, with our own souls as the variable.

## The family you didn't choose

Here is where a New Testament scholar named Joseph Hellerman has done more to help me than almost anyone, because he recovered a word we have sentimentalized into nothing.

In *When the Church Was a Family* (2009), Hellerman shows that the earliest Christians used family language for the church not as warm decoration but as their primary social reality. They called each other brother and sister, and in the ancient Mediterranean world, the sibling bond was the strongest bond there was, stronger, in many ways, than marriage, because you could divorce a spouse but your brother was your brother for life. When the New Testament calls fellow believers your brothers and sisters, it is not offering you a friendly vibe. It is reassigning your family. It is telling you that the people in that room have a claim on you, and you on them, of the kind you do not get to walk away from when it stops being convenient.

This is the part our individualism cannot stand, and the part the wounded most need to hear honestly. A family is not a thing you consume. It is a thing you are *stuck with*, gloriously and impossibly. You cannot fire your sister for being annoying. You cannot decline your brother because his politics embarrass you. And the modern church, this is our sin, not yours, let people treat it like a service precisely by stripping out the family claim, so that when the service disappointed, leaving cost nothing. We made church a thing you attend instead of a people you belong to, and then we were shocked that people left it like a restaurant with a bad review.

You may have left a service. I understand leaving a service. But Hellerman would gently ask you whether you have ever actually been offered a family, and whether the loneliness in your faith right now is the specific loneliness of someone who has a Father and a Lord but no brothers and sisters in the room.

## Bonhoeffer, who learned this with the secret police outside

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote the most piercing book on Christian community while training pastors in an underground seminary the Nazi state was trying to shut down. *Life Together* (1939) is not the soft book the title suggests. It is the testimony of a man who knew exactly how fragile and how necessary the body is, because his was being hunted.

Bonhoeffer says a thing that I have never been able to shake: that the Christian needs other Christians because of Jesus Christ, that I cannot reliably speak the word of God to myself. My own heart is biased toward me. It excuses what should be confessed and condemns what should be forgiven. When I tell myself the gospel alone, I am both the preacher and the only one checking whether the preaching is true, and I will, over time, preach myself a gospel shaped suspiciously like my own preferences. But when a brother or sister says it to me, *your sins are forgiven, Christ is risen, you are not alone*, it comes from outside me, with the authority of a word I did not author and cannot revise to suit myself.

This is the deepest reason the solo Christian struggles, and it has nothing to do with rules. It is that a faith with no outside voice slowly becomes a conversation you are having with yourself. The most dangerous heresy is never the dramatic one. It is the slow drift you cannot detect because there is no one beside you who would notice the drift and say, gently, *that isn't him. That's you.*

Bonhoeffer also said the opposite, which is why I trust him: that the one who cannot be alone should beware of community, and the one who cannot stand community should beware of being alone. He was not romantic about it. Community wounded him; he names the wounding. He simply refused to conclude from the wound that the body was optional.

## The objection I take most seriously

There is one response to all of this that I respect more than any other, and I will not pretend it away. It goes like this: *the church in Acts 2 sounds nothing like the church that hurt me. You are describing a family that sold its property to feed each other. I attended a building that took my money and ignored my name. Don't tell me to rejoin a body when what I experienced was a business.*

That objection is not faithless. It is accurate. And the honest answer is that the gap between the church Paul describes and the church many of you experienced is enormous, and the gap is not your fault. Much of what calls itself church in this country has drifted so far from the body in Acts 2 that the word barely connects the two. You were promised a family and sold a service, and when the service disappointed, you were blamed for leaving, which is exactly backward, because a family you cannot leave and a service you can, and they handed you the second while using the language of the first.

So I am not arguing that the buildings you left were the body. Some of them were a long way from it. What I am arguing is narrower and harder to dodge: the body is real, the New Testament insists on it, and the failures of the counterfeit do not abolish the original any more than counterfeit money proves there is no treasury. The fact that you were handed a fake does not mean there is nothing real to be handed. It means you were robbed, and being robbed is a reason for grief and caution, but it is not, by itself, evidence that the thing stolen never existed.

The solo Christian, in other words, is often not someone who rejected the body. They are someone who was shown a forgery, recognized it as a forgery, and concluded, understandably, that the whole category was fake. I am asking you to consider that you recognized the forgery *because* you know, somewhere, what the real thing is supposed to look like. The disappointment is itself a kind of evidence. You cannot be disappointed by a counterfeit unless you carry, somewhere, the image of the genuine article it failed to be.

## The building, the body, and the house

Paul has one more image, and it answers the part of you that wants to believe your private faith is structurally fine.

He tells the Ephesians they are *no longer foreigners and strangers, but fellow citizens with God's people and also members of his household*, and then he changes the metaphor mid-sentence into a building, *joined together* and *rising to become a holy temple*, *built together to become a dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit* (Ephesians 2:19–22). Read the verbs again. *Joined together. Built together.* A brick by itself is not a small temple. It is a brick. Its whole purpose waits on the other bricks, and the mortar, and the joining. A brick in a field is not expressing its brick-nature more purely by being unencumbered. It is just a brick the builder hasn't placed yet, or a brick that fell out of the wall.

I think some of you fell out of the wall. You were not thrown, you fell, in the chaos, when the wall was shaking, and no one caught you, and you have lived in the field so long that the field feels like home. I am not going to tell you the wall that dropped you was a good wall. Some of them weren't. But I will tell you what a brick is for, because no one may have told you: you were shaped to bear weight and to have weight set on you, to hold and be held, to be part of something that houses the presence of God. You cannot do that on the ground. Not because it's against the rules. Because it's against your nature as the kind of thing you are.

So, can you be a Christian on your own? I will give you the honest answer, which is neither the harsh one nor the comfortable one. You can believe alone. People do. The thief on the cross believed alone and Jesus received him without a membership card. God is not so small that he loses track of the isolated. But *believing alone* and *being a Christian alone* are not the same sentence, because being a Christian is not finally a belief you hold. It is a body you have been made part of, a family you have been adopted into, a brick set into a wall that holds the weight of God.

You can hold the faith by yourself. I just don't think it can hold you. And the day it can't, the day the wind comes and there's no one beside you saying *that's him, not you*, is the day you find out what the body was always quietly doing, by being the thing that wasn't there.
posts.excerpt: The New Testament has no category for the solitary Christian. Not because the writers were authoritarian, but because they could not conceive of a hand that had decided it no longer needed the body. A gentle argument for why faith was built for company.

posts.title: What If You're Done With Church but Not With Jesus?
posts.body:
There is a sentence people say to me in coffee shops and parking lots, lowered, almost confessional, as if they are admitting to something shameful. *I still believe. I just can't do the building anymore.* They say it the way you'd admit to a debt. They expect me to argue. They have braced for the argument, because the last time they raised it someone handed them a verse about forsaking the assembly and changed the subject.

I am not going to argue with you. Not yet. First I want to tell you that you are not rare, you are not the first, and you are not, by saying that sentence, doing anything that puts you outside the reach of the God you still love.

In 2023 two pastors, Jim Davis and Michael Graham, published a book on this exact phenomenon, drawing on what they call the largest study of dechurching ever conducted. They called it *The Great Dechurching*. Their finding was not that America stopped believing. Their finding was stranger and harder. Around forty million American adults have stopped attending church in the last quarter-century, more people leaving in a single generation than were added in the First Great Awakening, the Second Great Awakening, and the Billy Graham crusades combined. And here is the part nobody expected: a large share of them did not deconvert. They did not become atheists. They still pray. They still believe Jesus rose. They simply stopped going, and most of them did not leave in a blaze of argument. They drifted. They moved cities. They had a baby. They got burned. Sunday came and they did not, and then it kept not happening, and one day they realized the not-going had hardened into a life.

**You are not a problem the church needs to solve. You are a person the church mostly failed to notice leaving. And the question in front of you is not whether your faith is real, it plainly is, but whether a faith this real was ever meant to be carried alone.**

That is the whole essay. Everything after this is me earning it.

## The most common spiritual position in America

Start with how ordinary you are, because the loneliness of your position is half its weight.

For most of Christian history, "I believe but I don't belong" was nearly unthinkable. Not because people were holier, but because faith was social before it was anything else. You were born into a people, baptized into a community, and your belief and your belonging arrived in the same package. The idea that you could hold the one while setting down the other would have struck a believer in the year 400, or 1400, as roughly like saying you loved your family but had decided to live as an only child.

What changed is not your sincerity. What changed is the air. Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* (2007), described the slow shift from a world where faith was assumed to a world where faith is one option among many, chosen and held by the individual, defended by the individual, and, this is the crucial turn, increasingly *located* in the individual. We did not just make belief optional. We privatized it. We moved it indoors, into the self, where it became a matter between you and God with the door closed. And once faith lives entirely indoors, the church starts to look like an accessory. A nice add-on for people who like that sort of thing. Optional, the way a gym membership is optional for someone who has decided to run outside.

So when you say *I still believe, I just can't do the building*, you are not being rebellious. You are being a perfectly formed product of the last three hundred years. The whole culture taught you that the realest part of faith is the part inside your chest, and the building is just where some people go to express it. If that is true, then leaving the building costs you nothing essential.

The trouble is that it isn't quite true. And some part of you already suspects it, or you would not lower your voice when you say the sentence.

## Why you left is not the same as why you stayed away

Be honest about two different things, because we tend to collapse them.

There is the reason you left. And there is the reason you have stayed gone. They are rarely the same, and confusing them keeps a lot of people stuck.

The reason you left might be a real wound. A pastor who lied. A community that closed ranks around an abuser and against a victim. A church that loved its politics more than its people, or its building fund more than its widows. If that is your story, I will not rush you past it, and a later essay in this set is written entirely for you. Some of you left for reasons that were not betrayal at all, a move, an illness, a season of exhaustion, a Sunday you missed that turned into a year. And some of you, if you are willing to be searched, left because the convenience of staying gone is simply enormous. Sunday morning is the last unclaimed acreage in an overcommitted life. The bed is warm. The coffee is yours. Nobody asks anything of you. That is not a sin worth shaming. It is just worth naming, because it is a different thing than a wound, and it asks for a different answer.

The reason you stay away is almost always inertia plus relief. And inertia plus relief, repeated for enough Sundays, will hollow out a faith without ever once attacking it directly. It does not argue you out of believing. It just slowly removes everything that fed the belief, until one day you notice the fire is mostly memory.

## What Jesus did when the crowds left him

Here is a scene that should comfort you and unsettle you in the same breath.

In John 6, Jesus says something so hard that the text reports the result plainly: many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66). This was a mass dechurching, two thousand years early. The crowd thinned. The institution of the moment, such as it was, collapsed around him. And Jesus turns to the Twelve, the ones still standing in the emptied field, and asks a question with no defensiveness in it at all: *Do you want to go away as well?* (John 6:67)

Peter's answer is not triumphant. It is almost desperate, and that is why I trust it. *Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life* (John 6:68). Notice what Peter does not say. He does not say *the community is so warm.* He does not say *I love the singing.* He says, in effect, *I have nowhere else to take this. There is no other door.* Peter stays not because the institution was working but because the Person was irreplaceable.

That is your sentence too, isn't it. *I still believe. I can't do the building.* You have kept Peter's clause, *to whom shall we go*, and set down the field he was standing in when he said it. The reason your faith feels lonelier than it used to is that Peter never said that line alone. He said it standing next to eleven other people who had also just decided not to leave. The staying was personal. It was not solitary.

## The thing the building was carrying that you can't see yet

You experienced church as a place you went to receive something, a sermon, a song, a feeling, a service to consume. And when the service got bad, or the feeling went cold, or the people hurt you, it was entirely rational to stop consuming a product that had gone sour. I would have stopped too.

But the church was never primarily a service you attended. It was a body you belonged to, and bodies do something for their members that the members cannot do for themselves. Hebrews names it without sentimentality: *Let us consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds, not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another* (Hebrews 10:24–25). Read it slowly and notice the verbs. *Spur. Encourage.* These are not things you do to yourself. You cannot spur yourself on any more than you can tickle yourself. The writer is not scolding people for skipping a meeting. He is describing a kind of strengthening that only happens between people, the way a coal stays hot in the pile and goes cold pulled out alone.

The faith you are carrying by yourself right now is a coal you pulled out of the fire. It is still glowing. I am not denying the glow. I am telling you what happens to coals over time, away from the others, and I am telling you because I would rather say it now than meet you in five years when the glow has gone gray and you can't remember why it went.

## The slow cost no one warns you about

No one described this to me, and I wish they had.

The first year out is almost always fine. Better than fine. The relief is real and the freedom is sweet. You sleep in. You take the morning slow. Your faith, unhooked from a disappointing institution, feels purer, more yours, less cluttered by other people's noise. You read Scripture when you want to. You pray on a walk. You tell yourself, honestly, that you are closer to God now than you were in the pew, and a lot of the time you are right, because the pew had become a performance and the walk is sincere.

The second year is quieter. You notice you read less than you meant to. The walk-prayers get shorter and then occasional. Nothing dramatic happens. There is no crisis of faith, no argument that knocks you over. There is just the slow withdrawal of the thousand small pressures that used to keep faith in the foreground, the Sunday rhythm, the friend who would ask how you were really doing, the song that put words to a thing you could not say, the sermon that interrupted the story you were telling yourself about your own life. None of those were the gospel. But all of them were scaffolding, and faith, it turns out, is a thing that needs scaffolding, not because it is weak but because it is alive, and living things grow toward the things that feed them.

By the third or fourth year, for a lot of people, what is left is a warm memory of having believed, narrated in the past tense without their ever deciding to change tenses. They have not rejected anything. They could still tell you, sincerely, that they believe Jesus rose. It has simply stopped costing them anything, stopped shaping a Tuesday, stopped being the thing the rest of life bends around. The fire did not go out in a storm. It went out the way fires go out when no one tends them and no one else is keeping coals beside yours.

I am not saying this is your story. I am saying I have watched it be too many people's story for me to stay quiet about the pattern, and that the pattern is not a moral failure. It is physics. A coal alone goes cold. That is not a verdict on the coal.

## What you actually want

The dechurched but believing, and that is most of you reading this, are not running from God at all. A lot of you are running toward the God you found, and away from the people who handled him carelessly. That is grief, not contradiction.

And there is one verse for you that I have watched do more work than any argument. David, who spent years hunted and exhausted with nowhere safe to lay his head, writes down the one thing he still wants when everything else has been stripped away: *One thing I ask from the Lord, this only do I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the Lord* (Psalm 27:4). The man who wrote that had every reason to be done with the institutional religion of his day. It was run, much of the time, by people trying to kill him. And the one thing he asks for is not relief from the people. It is the house. Not the building as real estate. The house as the place where the beauty of God is gazed upon in company.

That ache in you, the one that makes you lower your voice and say *I still believe*, is Psalm 27 still running in your bones, not the residue of an old habit. You want to dwell in the house. You have just never been shown a house worth dwelling in, or you were shown one and it burned, and you have confused the fire with the architecture.

I am not asking you to walk back into the room that hurt you. I am asking you to consider that the thing you actually long for was never the room. It was the gazing, and the man who wrote that line knew you cannot do it alone.

You are done with church. I understand. I have been done with it too, and I am a pastor.

But you are not done with Jesus. And he has never once, in two thousand years, handed himself out one isolated soul at a time. He comes with a body attached. That is not the fine print. That is the gift. The question is not whether your lonely faith is real. It is real. The question is how long a real thing can stay alive in a field that everyone else has left, and whether the ache you keep lowering your voice to admit is, in fact, the oldest prayer in the book, asking to come home.
posts.excerpt: Millions of Americans have walked out of church without walking away from Jesus. That is not a contradiction to be corrected. It is a wound to be named, and a question that will not stay quiet.

posts.title: How Do You Find a Church Worth Joining?
posts.body:
Maybe you have read the rest of these essays and something in you has loosened. You are not ready to promise anything. But you are willing to consider that the lonely faith you have been carrying was built for company, and that the building that hurt you was not the bride but the men who betrayed her, and that the thing church is actually for is something you may never have been offered. And now you are standing at the hardest practical question of all, the one that follows you out the door: *fine, but how do I find one that won't do it to me again?*

I am not going to pretend that question has a clean answer. There is no inspection that guarantees you won't get hurt, because a church is people, and people will eventually fail you, the way your own family eventually fails you. But there is a difference between a church that will disappoint you the way every family disappoints, and a church that will wound you the way the last one did. The first is the cost of belonging anywhere. The second you can learn to spot and avoid.

**Finding a church worth joining is not about finding a perfect one, there isn't one, and the hunt for it is its own kind of disease. It is about learning to tell the difference between the failures you can forgive and the failures you must flee, and refusing to let the consumer instinct pick the church for you when belonging, not performance, is what you actually need.**

## You are not shopping for a product

Start by killing the instinct the last twenty years trained into you, because it will steer you wrong every time.

You will be tempted to evaluate churches the way you evaluate everything else, by the experience. Is the music good? Is the preacher compelling? Is the building nice, the coffee decent, the kids' wing impressive? These are the questions a consumer asks, and they are nearly useless, because the church most engineered to win them is often the one least able to give you the body, the family, and the witness you actually came for. A spectacular Sunday production can coexist with a congregation where no one knows your name and no one will come when you are sick. The qualities that make a church *impressive* and the qualities that make it *worth joining* are not the same list, and they sometimes run in opposite directions.

Eugene Peterson spent a lifetime warning pastors against the very thing you are tempted to shop for. He called it the church run on the logic of religious consumerism, where the pastor becomes a shopkeeper arranging an attractive display, and the congregation becomes customers whose appetites must be satisfied, and the gospel becomes one more product competing for attention. Peterson's whole pastoral vision was a protest against this, a stubborn insistence that the church is a place of slow formation, not fast satisfaction, closer to a farm than a store, where things grow at the speed things grow and nobody can rush the harvest. When you look for a church, the consumer in you will want the store. What you need is the farm. The farm looks less impressive on a first visit and changes your life over twenty years. The store dazzles on a Sunday and forms nothing.

So the first discipline is this: refuse to let your eyes do the choosing. The best church for you may have worse music and a plainer building than three others you could pick, and be the one that actually makes you into someone who can love.

## What to actually look for

If not the experience, then what? Acts gives you the original checklist, and it is short. The first church *devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer* (Acts 2:42). Four things. Real teaching, real fellowship, the table, and prayer. Notice what is not on the list, production, size, polish, relevance. Watch for the four.

*Is the Bible actually taught, or merely referenced?* In a church worth joining, Scripture is the authority that even the leaders submit to, not a springboard for the leader's own opinions. You can tell the difference quickly. In one, the preacher is under the text. In the other, the text is under the preacher, used to decorate whatever he already wanted to say. Hebrews points you here: *Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith* (Hebrews 13:7). Note the two-part test, what they *say* (the word of God, not their own brand) and how they *live* (an outcome worth imitating). Both, or neither.

*Do the people actually know each other, or just attend together?* Look for evidence of a household, not an audience. Are there people there who would notice if you disappeared? Do they eat together, carry each other, show up in crises? This is harder to see on a first visit, which is why a first visit is never enough. You have to stay long enough to watch whether the fellowship in Acts 2 is real or advertised.

*Is the leadership accountable, or unaccountable?* This is where you must be most careful, especially if you were wounded before. Paul tells Timothy what to look for in those who lead, and the qualifications are almost entirely about character, not talent: a leader must be *above reproach, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money*, and, tellingly, one who *manages his own household well* and *must have a good reputation with outsiders* (1 Timothy 3:2–7). Read that list and notice what is missing. Charisma. Vision-casting. Stage presence. The biblical qualifications for leadership are a character résumé, not a talent résumé. A church that selects its leaders for gifting over character is building the exact conditions that hurt you before. A church that takes 1 Timothy 3 seriously, where leaders are plural, accountable to each other, and chosen for who they are when no one is watching, has built a guardrail against the thing that wounded you.

## What to forgive

Now the harder discipline, and the one that will determine whether you can ever belong anywhere again. You have to learn what to forgive.

Because here is the trap waiting for the church-hurt: having been wounded by a bad church, you can become a person no church can ever satisfy, scanning every congregation for the flaw that confirms your fear, leaving the moment you find it, and you will always find it, because there is no flawless church, and the search for one is just your wound wearing the costume of discernment. The same instinct that protects you from another abusive church, untrained, will keep you out of every healthy one too.

So forgive the small things, and forgive them generously. Forgive the awkward greeter. Forgive the sermon that didn't land. Forgive the worship style that isn't yours. Forgive the building that needs work and the bulletin with the typo and the small group that felt clumsy the first night. Forgive the people for being, like you, in process, *Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring praise to God* (Romans 15:7). Paul wrote that to a church full of people who annoyed each other across ethnic and cultural lines, and his instruction was not *find people who don't annoy you.* It was *accept each other the way Christ accepted you*, which is to say, before you had your act together. A church worth joining is full of people you will have to forgive, repeatedly, for being human. That is not a defect in the church. That is the assignment.

The distinction is not how much a church fails you. Every church will fail you. The distinction is whether it fails you the way a family fails, out of weakness, in ways that can be named and repaired, or the way a predator fails, out of corruption, in ways that are hidden, denied, and defended.

## What never to overlook

And so, finally, the things you must never forgive into invisibility, the warning signs that mean *leave*, no matter how good the teaching or warm the people.

Watch how the church handles power, because this is where the last one likely failed. Is the leader accountable to anyone who can actually say no to him? Or is the structure arranged so that all the no-saying authority belongs to people he chose and can remove? Watch how it handles money. Is it transparent, or is the budget a mystery only the inner circle is allowed to see? Watch how it handles the vulnerable, the one who raises a hard question, the one who reports being hurt, the woman who says something happened. Is the impulse to protect that person, or to protect the image of the church *from* that person? The day you watch a church close ranks around its reputation and against a victim is the day you have your answer, and no quality of preaching should keep you in the room after that.

Rosaria Butterfield, in *The Gospel Comes with a House Key* (2018), describes what the healthy version actually looks like, and it is almost shockingly ordinary. She writes about a Christianity practiced through what she calls radically ordinary hospitality, the open door, the shared table, the daily, unglamorous willingness to let your home and your life be interruptible by the needs of others, including strangers and the people the world has written off. The remarkable thing about her account is how unremarkable it is. No stage. No production. No charismatic leader. Just people whose faith had become a table long enough for the neighbor, the doubter, the addict, the lonely, to sit down and be known. That is the witness Jesus pointed to. That is the church worth joining, not the one that dazzles you on Sunday, but the one whose ordinary members keep setting another place at the table.

When you visit a church, in other words, do not only watch the stage. Watch the table. Watch who gets fed, who gets carried, who gets believed when they are hurting, and who gets protected when their truth threatens the institution. The stage will tell you how talented they are. The table will tell you who they are.

## How to actually start, when starting feels impossible

The practical reality, for many of you, is not that you don't know what to look for. It is that the front door of any church now triggers a fear response, and no checklist gets you across a threshold your body has learned to dread. So a word about how to actually begin, slowly, in a way that respects what you have been through.

Go expecting to visit, not to join. Give yourself explicit permission to leave at the end and never return, with no guilt and no explanation owed to anyone. The pressure people feel to commit on a first visit is one of the things that keeps the wounded out entirely; remove it. You are not deciding anything. You are gathering information about whether this particular body resembles Acts 2 or resembles the place that hurt you. That is reconnaissance, not commitment, and you are allowed to do it as many times, at as many churches, as you need.

Go more than once before you decide anything, because the things that matter, whether the people actually know each other, whether the leaders are accountable, whether the table is open, are invisible on a first Sunday and only show themselves over weeks. The polish shows up immediately; the substance shows up slowly. A church that looks unremarkable the first week and turns out to be a genuine family by the second month is worth a hundred that dazzle on a single visit.

Find the one or two people, not the whole congregation. You do not need to bond with three hundred strangers. You need to find one person who is honest, one household whose table is open, one couple or friend who will tell you the truth and notice when you are gone. The body becomes real to you not through the service but through specific people, and you only need to find a few to begin. Rosaria Butterfield's whole vision is built on this, that the church becomes real one open door, one shared meal, one ordinary act of hospitality at a time, not through a program but through a person who set another place at the table.

And go, if you can, with your guard *partly* down, not all the way, you have earned your caution, but not so far up that no church could ever reach you. The discernment your wound gave you is a gift. Let it screen for the corrupt ones. Do not let it screen for every flawed one, or you will screen out the whole human race, which is the only material the church has ever had to work with.

## The cost, and the only way through

I cannot promise you that the next church won't hurt you. I would be lying, and you have been lied to by enough pastors. People who belong to each other eventually wound each other; that is the price of belonging anywhere, and a church is not exempt. What I can tell you is that the wound a healthy family inflicts is survivable, namable, and reparable, and the loneliness of belonging to no one is not, it just kills you slower and calls itself safety.

So you will have to risk it again. Not recklessly. Not by walking back into the room that hurt you, or by silencing the discernment your wound earned you the hard way. But by going, slowly, with your eyes open, watching the table more than the stage, forgiving the small things, fleeing the corrupt ones, and giving a healthy body enough time to prove itself, which is the only way a body ever can.

The church that is worth joining will not be the one that promises it will never disappoint you. It will be the one honest enough to admit it might, structured carefully enough to make sure it can't do it the way the last one did, and ordinary enough to keep setting a place at the table for someone like you, who is still here, still believing, and finally, cautiously, ready to be known again.
posts.excerpt: If you are ready to try again but afraid of getting hurt again, you need more than a vibe check. A pastor on what to actually look for, what you can forgive, and the one or two things you must never overlook.

posts.title: What Is Church Actually For?
posts.body:
Ask most Americans, churched or not, what church is *for*, and you will get a version of the same answer. It is where you go to worship. It is where you hear teaching. It is where you get fed, encouraged, recharged for the week. Even people who love their church usually describe it this way, as a place you go to receive a thing. And if that is what church is, then leaving it is the most reasonable decision in the world the moment the thing it provides drops in quality, becomes available elsewhere, or gets ruined by the people running it. You don't keep going to a restaurant after the chef leaves and the food turns. Why would you keep attending a service that has stopped serving you?

The logic is airtight. It is also built on a definition of church that the New Testament never once uses.

**Church was never a religious service you attend. It is a body you are joined to, a family you are adopted into, and a public witness you are made part of, and not one of those three is a thing you can consume, replace, or do alone. We have spent fifty years selling church as a service, and then acting surprised that people treat it like one and leave it like one.**

I want to recover what it is actually for, because I think a lot of you left a thing that was never the real thing, and you deserve to know what the real thing was before you decide you're done with it.

## How we turned a body into a venue

Begin with how the confusion happened, because it was not your fault and it was not an accident.

For most of American history, the church was the center of a community's life because it had to be, it was the place people gathered, the source of their relief work, their schools, their funerals, their belonging. Then, slowly, the culture got richer in options. Entertainment got better. Community moved online. And the American church, watching its crowds thin, made a fateful decision, mostly unconsciously: it would compete. It would become a better product. Better music, better lighting, better preaching, better children's programming, a better experience. We professionalized the stage and we measured success in attendance, and in doing so we trained two generations of Christians to evaluate church exactly the way they evaluate every other experience they buy, by how it makes them feel, and whether the competition has a better one.

Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon saw this coming and named it in *Resident Aliens* (1989). The church, they argued, had made a quiet and disastrous deal: it agreed to become a helpful institution that supports the lives people were already living, rather than a colony of heaven that produces a different kind of life altogether. It became a service provider to the surrounding culture instead of an alternative to it. And a service provider can always be out-served. The moment church exists to meet your felt needs, it is competing with everything else that meets your felt needs, most of which require less of you on a Sunday morning.

So when you found church boring, or redundant, or worse than the podcast you could hear in bed, you were responding rationally to a thing the church had told you it was. The tragedy is that it was lying, mostly to itself, about what it actually is.

## A body, where the parts cannot quit

Paul's most common word for the church is *body*, and Ephesians shows you what the body is for in a way that demolishes the service model entirely.

Christ gave the church its leaders, Paul says, apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, *to equip his people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up until we all reach unity in the faith... attaining to the whole measure of the fullness of Christ* (Ephesians 4:11–13). Read who does the work in that sentence. The leaders do not do the ministry. The leaders *equip the people* to do the ministry. The whole point is to get every member functioning, so that the body grows itself. *From him the whole body, joined and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love, as each part does its work* (Ephesians 4:16).

This is the exact opposite of a service. At a service, a few professionals perform and the audience receives. In a body, there is no audience. There are only members, each one carrying something the others need and cannot get anywhere else. Your absence from a body is not like an empty seat at a concert, which the performers barely notice. It is like a missing ligament. Something does not hold that used to hold. Someone goes uncarried who would have been carried by the part of the body that was you.

When you stopped attending, you experienced it as *I stopped receiving a service.* But from the body's side, what happened was *a ligament went missing, and the rest of us are working harder to hold what you used to hold.* You felt your own loss of supply. You could not feel the body's loss of you. That asymmetry is exactly what the service model hides, and it is why leaving feels so cheap from the inside and costs so much from the outside.

## A family, where you are stuck with each other

The second thing church is for, and the one most foreign to a consumer, is that it is a family, which means you cannot consume it, you can only belong to it.

Acts 2 describes the first church and the description is relentlessly familial. *They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer... All the believers were together and had everything in common. They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. Every day they continued to meet together... They broke bread in their homes and ate together with glad and sincere hearts* (Acts 2:42–46). This is not a description of a weekly service. It is a description of a household. People eating in each other's homes. People selling property to cover each other's needs. People so entangled in each other's daily lives that the line between the meeting and the rest of the week dissolved.

You cannot consume a family. You can only be in one. A family does not exist to make you feel good on Sunday; it exists to be the people who show up when the diagnosis comes, who bury your parent with you, who feed you when you cannot get out of bed, who tell you the truth you do not want to hear because they have earned the right to. The reason this kind of church is rare is not that the model failed. It is that we replaced it with the venue, where nobody knows your name and nobody is coming when the diagnosis lands, because you were an attender, not a member of a household.

And here is the part that should make the wounded among you ache rather than scoff: the reason consumer church disappoints so reliably is that it is offering you a family's claim on your heart while delivering a venue's level of commitment. You showed up looking for the household in Acts 2 and got a concert with a sermon. Of course it left you empty. It was the wrong genre. You were starving for a family and they sold you a service, and then they blamed you for not being filled.

## A witness, which only a community can give

The third thing church is for points outward, and Jesus tied it not to our programs but to something only a community can produce.

*A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another* (John 13:34–35). Notice what Jesus did *not* say. He did not say the world will know you are mine by your individual morality, or your private prayer life, or the depth of your personal convictions. He said the world will know by the love *between* you. The witness is plural. It is the thing visible in the spaces between Christians, how they treat each other, carry each other, forgive each other. A solitary Christian, however sincere, cannot produce this witness, for the same reason one note cannot produce harmony. The testimony Jesus pointed to lives in the relationship, not the individual.

Lesslie Newbigin spent forty years as a missionary in India and then came home to a Britain that had quietly stopped believing, and he gave the rest of his life to a single argument: that the way the gospel becomes credible to a watching world is not primarily through argument but through a community that visibly lives a different life. The church, Newbigin said, is the hermeneutic of the gospel, the lens through which the world reads whether the message is true. People do not first believe the gospel and then join the community. They watch the community, find it strange and compelling, and through it come to wonder if the gospel might be real. Take away the community and you have taken away the world's primary evidence.

Peter says the same thing in a single dense sentence: *You are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light* (1 Peter 2:9). Every noun is plural and corporate. A *people.* A *priesthood.* A *nation.* You cannot be a nation by yourself. You cannot be a people of one. The witness Peter describes is something a gathered, visible, peculiar community produces by existing, and no individual, however devoted, can be a nation alone.

## Why the three cannot be unbundled

You might be tempted, having heard all this, to take the parts you like and leave the building behind. Keep the body language as a metaphor for online Christian friendship. Keep the family feeling through a small group that meets in a living room and never bothers with the rest. Keep the witness by being a good and visibly kind person at work. Assemble your own church out of components, à la carte, without the institution that disappointed you.

I understand the appeal, and I want to be honest about why it does not quite work, not because the components are bad, but because the three things church is for are not three separate features you can order individually. They are three faces of one reality, and they hold each other up.

The body needs the family, because a body where the members do not actually know each other is just a crowd performing unity. The family needs the witness, because a family turned inward, existing only for its own warmth, curdles into a clique and stops being good news to anyone outside it. And the witness needs the body, because the love-between-Christians that Jesus said would convince the world cannot be produced by individuals who have assembled a private spiritual life, it can only be produced by people genuinely bound to each other, including the ones they did not choose and would not have picked. The à la carte version keeps failing for the same reason a hand kept in a jar of nutrients is not a functioning hand. You can preserve the parts. You cannot make them live apart from the whole.

This is also why the local, committed, physically gathered, frustratingly specific congregation matters and cannot be replaced by a stream or a network of like-minded friends. You can learn from a teacher online; you cannot be carried by one. You can feel inspired by a podcast; it will not sit with you in the hospital. The body, the family, and the witness all require the same thing the consumer model was built to eliminate, actual, durable, inconvenient commitment to a specific group of people who can see you, need you, fail you, and hold you. Unbundle that, and you have kept the brochure and lost the thing the brochure described.

## What you actually walked away from

So let me say, gently, what I think happened to a lot of you.

You did not walk away from the body, the family, and the witness. You probably never got offered them. You got offered a service, and the service was mediocre or wounding or simply replaceable, and you made the rational call. The error was not yours. The error was a church that forgot what it was for, dressed itself up as a venue, and trained you to evaluate it as one, and then could not understand why you left when the venue down the street, or the one on your screen, or the one called Sunday morning in bed, offered a better experience for less.

But the thing church is actually for cannot be gotten any other way. You cannot be a ligament in your living room. You cannot be a family of one. You cannot, by yourself, be the love-between-Christians that Jesus said would make the world wonder. These are not features the church offers. They are the church. And the ache you feel, the suspicion that your private faith is missing something it cannot name, is the precise shape of a body part that has forgotten it is part of a body, and a family member who has been eating alone so long they have started to call it freedom.

You are not done with church. You may have never met it. The question is not whether to go back to the service that failed you. The question is whether you have the courage to go looking for the thing the service was always a counterfeit of, and to be, for someone else, the ligament that holds when their diagnosis comes.
posts.excerpt: If church is a service you attend, then a bad service is reason enough to stop. But the New Testament never describes a service. It describes a body, a family, and a witness, and that changes everything about whether you can replace it.

posts.title: When the Church Is the Thing That Hurt You
posts.body:
If you are reading this, there is a real chance you have a specific face in your mind. A pastor. An elder. A small group leader. A whole congregation that closed around something it should have exposed. The wound has a name and a date and a smell, the particular smell of the room where it happened, and you have spent years being told, directly or by implication, that the wound is your problem. That you are bitter. That you need to forgive and move on. That you left because you couldn't handle accountability, or because you wanted to sin, or because you were never really one of us.

I want to say something I am afraid the church has not said to you nearly enough, and I want to say it before I say anything else, because everything else depends on it being true.

What happened to you was real. Your anger is not your faithlessness. And the God you are afraid you have offended by leaving is, on the matter of what was done to you, angrier than you are.

**The church can be the thing that hurts you. Scripture does not flinch from this, it says it more violently than you would dare to. And the path back from church hurt does not run through pretending it didn't happen. It runs through a God who hates what was done to you, and through the hard, slow work of learning the difference between the bride and the men who betrayed her in her name.**

## The shepherds who ate the sheep

You may have been handed a Bible full of green pastures and gentle shepherds. You were not handed Ezekiel 34, and someone should have handed it to you years ago.

Listen to how God talks about religious leaders who use the people instead of feeding them. In Ezekiel 34:2–4 he pronounces woe on the shepherds of Israel who only feed themselves while the flock goes hungry, who eat the curds and wear the wool and slaughter the best animals, but do not strengthen the weak or heal the sick or bind up the injured, and who rule the people harshly and brutally. This is God speaking. This is not a disgruntled ex-member writing an angry post. This is the voice of God describing leaders who fattened themselves on the people they were supposed to protect, and the verb that follows is not gentle. *I am against the shepherds and will hold them accountable for my flock* (Ezekiel 34:10).

Read that and let it land. The thing you have felt, the fury that someone in God's name used God's people for their own appetite, is not your bitterness corrupting your faith. It is the echo of God's own fury running through you. You did not invent that anger. You inherited it from the heart of God, who looked at the same kind of leader and said *I am against them.* When you left a church that protected a predator, or covered a fraud, or crushed the weak to preserve its image, you were not abandoning God. In some real sense you were taking God's side against people who had stopped being on it.

## Jesus and the millstone
