We have a sentimental Jesus in this country, and the sentimental Jesus is useless to the wounded, because the sentimental Jesus would never say what the real one said.

*If anyone causes one of these little ones, those who believe in me, to stumble, it would be better for them to have a large millstone hung around their neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea* (Matthew 18:6). The "little ones" are not only children, though they are not less than children. They are the vulnerable, the new, the trusting, the ones with their guard down because they had been told this was a safe place. And Jesus, gentle Jesus, meek and mild, looks at the person who exploited that trust and says the kindest thing that could happen to them would be drowning. A millstone is the heavy stone a donkey turns to grind grain. He is describing being dragged to the bottom of the sea by a weight no swimmer could fight.

I have heard people apologize for being angry about their church hurt. I want to gently take the apology away from them. The anger is not the problem. The anger is, in many cases, the most spiritually accurate response in the room, closer to the heart of Christ than the forced smiles of the people who told you to let it go. Jesus did not tell the little ones to let it go. He picked up a millstone.

## The friend, not the stranger

There is a particular grief in church hurt that secular language cannot reach, and the Psalms reach it exactly.

*If an enemy were insulting me, I could endure it; if a foe were rising against me, I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion, my close friend, with whom I once enjoyed sweet fellowship at the house of God* (Psalm 55:12–14). This is the unique cruelty of being wounded by the church. It does not hurt like an attack from outside. It hurts like a betrayal from inside the family. The pain you feel is sharper than the pain of the world's hostility precisely because it came from the people who broke bread with you, who prayed over you, who you trusted with the softest part of yourself. You used to walk to the house of God together. That is the wound. The world's blows we can brace for. It is the friend's hand we never see coming.

David does not suppress this. He does not spiritualize it. He writes it down and puts it in the songbook of the people of God, which tells you something we have forgotten: lament, naming the betrayal to God, out loud, in detail, is not the opposite of faith. It is a form of it. The Psalms are full of people telling God exactly how badly God's own people behaved. If David can put it in the hymnal, you can say it at your kitchen table without fearing you have left the faith. You are speaking the native language of the wounded faithful, who have always been allowed to say the worst of it to God directly.

## What the abuse actually was, naming it precisely

Here is where two careful guides have helped me name the thing instead of waving at it, because vague language about "church hurt" lets the real mechanisms hide.

Diane Langberg, a psychologist who has spent decades with the survivors of abuse inside Christian institutions, wrote *Redeeming Power* (2020) to do one thing: to show how power, which God gives to be spent in service, gets inverted into a weapon. She names the pattern plainly. Power was meant to protect the vulnerable; in a corrupted system it protects the institution from the vulnerable instead. The victim becomes the threat, not because they did anything, but because their truth endangers the reputation of the thing. And so the machinery turns on them. They are managed, doubted, relabeled as divisive, asked to forgive in a way that means *be quiet.* Langberg's gift is to insist that this was never a mere relational misunderstanding but an abuse of power, and God, who entrusted that power, takes its abuse with deadly seriousness.

Chuck DeGroat, in *When Narcissism Comes to Church* (2020), names another piece: the way certain personalities are drawn to religious leadership precisely because it offers admiration, control, and a stage, all sanctified. He is careful, and I will be careful echoing him, not every difficult leader is a narcissist, and the word is overused. But the pattern he describes is one many of you will recognize with a sick familiarity: the charisma that pulls you in, the image that must be protected at all costs, the way criticism is reframed as a spiritual attack on God's anointed, the slow erosion of your own sense of reality until you wondered if you were the problem after all. You were not crazy. DeGroat's whole point is that the system was designed, often unconsciously, to make you feel crazy so the image could survive. The naming is the beginning of getting your mind back.

I name these two not to hand you ammunition but to hand you precision. *Church hurt* is too soft a phrase for some of what was done. What was done was an abuse of power and, sometimes, the predictable wreckage of a disordered person given a sacred platform. Naming it accurately is not bitterness. It is the first honest thing, and honesty is where healing has to start. And honesty has somewhere to go. A trauma-informed counselor is not a detour from faith; sitting across from one is often how the faith finds its feet again. And if what was done to you was a crime, and some of it is, it belongs with the authorities whose job is to stop it, not with God alone. Reporting it is not a failure to trust him. It is one of the ways he guards the next person.

## The bride and the men who sold her name

Now the turn, and I am going to make it as carefully as I know how, because made carelessly it becomes another way to silence you.

There is a difference between the church and the people who hurt you in the church. I know how that can sound, like a dodge, like *not all churches*, like the thing people say to get you back in the building. That is not what I mean, and if anyone uses this distinction to rush you past your wound, they are misusing it.

Scripture calls the church the bride of Christ. And what was done to you was done by people betraying that bride, trading on her name, wearing her clothes to do the opposite of what she is. When a man defrauds people while wearing a wedding ring, the institution he has dishonored is marriage, and marriage is not the villain, he is. When a man wounds the vulnerable while wearing the name of the church, the church is not the perpetrator. She is, in a real sense, another of his victims. Her name was used. Her trust was spent. Christ, who loves her, watched her name get nailed to the very thing that drove you out.

This distinction does not ask you to go back. It does not ask you to forgive on a timeline. It does not even ask you to stop being angry, you have seen who taught me about the millstone. It asks only this: do not let the men who betrayed her convince you that *they were her.* They were not. They were the shepherds God said he was against. They were the friend at the house of God whose hand David never saw coming. The bride they dishonored is still beloved, still pursued, still, somewhere, in rooms you have not yet found, being the thing they pretended to be.

## On forgiveness, since someone has probably weaponized it against you

I have to say something about forgiveness, because the odds are high that the word has already been used on you as a weapon, and I do not want to add to the pile.

Somewhere in your story, someone probably told you to forgive, and what they meant was *stop talking about it.* They used the holiest word in the Christian vocabulary to ask you to protect the reputation of the people who harmed you. They told you that your refusal to move on was a spiritual problem, that bitterness was eating you, that real Christians forgive and forget. This is one of the most common and most cruel misuses of Scripture I know, and it has driven more people out of the faith than open atheism ever has.

So let me separate some things that the weaponizers deliberately fuse together. Forgiveness is releasing your right to personal vengeance, handing the debt to God, who keeps a better ledger than you ever could, and trusting him to settle it justly. That is real, and it is, eventually, for your own freedom, because carrying the right to vengeance is its own slow poison. But forgiveness is *not* the same as trust. It is not the same as reconciliation. It is not the same as returning to the place that harmed you, or pretending it didn't happen, or staying silent so the institution can protect its image. You can forgive a man and still testify against him. You can forgive a church and never set foot in it again. You can release the debt to God and still tell the truth about what was done, loudly, so it is not done to the next person. The Bible nowhere asks the wounded to protect their abusers with their silence. That is not forgiveness. That is cover-up wearing forgiveness as a costume.

Forced forgiveness is only a performance, and God is not interested in it. The God who wrote David's lament into the songbook is not standing over you with a stopwatch. He let David rage at the betrayal of a friend without one word of rebuke. He can let you take however long the wound takes. Anyone who tells you the clock is running is reading a different God than the one in the Psalms.

## What I will not tell you

I will not tell you to get over it. I will not tell you the timeline. I will not tell you that the right church is out there and you just have to try again next Sunday, as if your wound were a bad date. And I will not, under any circumstances, tell you that your leaving was the sin, when in your case the leaving may have been the most honest act of your whole life.

The God who watched it happen was not neutral. He is against the shepherds who did it. He keeps a millstone for the ones who harmed the little ones. He wrote your lament into his own songbook so you would know that saying it out loud is allowed. And the bride whose name they stole is not the one who hurt you, she is grieving with you, because what they did to you they did in her clothes.

You do not have to walk back in tomorrow. You may not be able to for a long time, and a God who keeps millstones is not going to rush a wounded person across a threshold. But do not let the people who hurt you do the one thing they could not do while you were still in the room. Do not let them take Jesus too. They took enough. He is the one thing they were never standing between you and, even when they claimed to be, and he is, right now, more furious about what they did than you have ever let yourself be.
posts.excerpt: Church hurt is real, and naming it is not bitterness. A pastor on the wound the institution inflicts, the God who is furious about it, and the difference between the bride and the men who betrayed her.

posts.title: The Atheist in the Pulpit
posts.body:
There is an atheist in my pulpit every Sunday morning. He is not a visitor slipping in at the back. He is me, the man I was for most of my life, whose reasons I can still recite without notes, standing inside the man who now preaches. Most conversion stories have the earlier man dead by the second paragraph, a cartoon knocked over on the way to the good part. I will not do that to him. He was not a fool, and if I treat him like one, I will deserve the distrust of every reader standing where he stood. Some of you are standing there now, and you can smell a setup from a long way off.

So let me put the facts on the table before the argument touches them. I was raised without a father, not dead, just gone, an absence that was a decision someone kept making every morning by not coming back. I did not drift out of a childhood faith; there was no childhood faith to drift out of. I came to belief as a grown man, against my preference, and I have now spent fifteen years as a pastor, I lead First Baptist Church of Fenton, Michigan, and I am raising five sons on the far side of the word *father*. Everything I am about to say leans on those facts. None of them is decoration.

## The unbelief I actually held

Start with what I believed, because the atheism in most testimonies is a costume, and mine was a conviction. I believed the universe was what it was and owed no one an explanation beyond its own workings. I believed mind was what the brain does, the way digestion is what the stomach does, and that when the brain stopped I would stop, the way a candle stops. I believed morality was a survival strategy our ancestors dressed in the language of commandment, and that the sense of meaning stitched into things was the last and most stubborn illusion, the projection of a small warm animal onto a cold enormous sky. I did not hold any of this as a wound. I held it as maturity. There is a real dignity in facing what you take to be the truth without flinching, and I had it, and I do not disown it now.

I found Bertrand Russell at nineteen and read him the way another young man reads Scripture. In "A Free Man's Worship" (1903) he writes that man is the product of causes that had no prevision of the end they were achieving, that his origin, his hopes, his loves, his beliefs are the outcome of "accidental collocations of atoms." Most people hear that sentence as bleak. I heard it as clean. It asked nothing of me and it promised nothing to me, and after a childhood built around a promise that was not kept, a universe that made no promises felt like the first honest thing anyone had offered me.

I also believed, and believe still, that religion has real crimes on its ledger. It has blessed wars and burned women and shielded men who hurt children, and the reflex of its defenders to change the subject when this comes up seemed to me as damning as the crimes. I will not change the subject now. The church's failures are not a misunderstanding the skeptic needs corrected; they are facts the believer needs to carry. When I finally came to faith, it was not because someone explained those facts away. No one can. It was in spite of them, and a believer who will not say that plainly is asking you to trust a version of history neither of you believes.

And underneath the arguments there was a smaller, harder fact, the one I could not see for years. I was a fatherless boy who had decided very early that the first duty of a mind is to refuse the comforting lie, because somewhere a man had made promises to a woman and a child and had not kept them. I want to be careful here, the same care I would want from you. It would be too easy to say I rejected God the Father because I had no father. Too easy, and it insults the arguments, and it insults the boy. The arguments were real. Some of them remain the best available to the position, and I do not wave them away from this side of the line. But it would also be a lie to leave the absence out of the room. A doctrine that promised a Father arriving felt, at the level below argument, like cruelty dressed as comfort. Something in me had settled the question before the philosophy arrived to defend it: fathers do not come. My unbelief was a conclusion. It was also a home, the one place the father who did not come could not hurt me, because in that place there were no fathers anywhere, and a cold that falls on everyone is not a rejection. I had made the whole sky cold so that my patch of it would stop meaning what it meant.

## What actually moved

If you are waiting for the argument that got me, there was no argument. There was an erosion, and it took years, and for most of those years I did not know it was happening. Conversion stories reach for lightning because lightning sells. The truth is slower and stranger, and it does not flatter the convert.

The first thing that moved was small, and I filed it. At the end of good days, work done well, people I liked, there was a residue. A sense of something owed that no one was paying. An appetite with no object. I had a theory for it, and the theory was good: evolution built into us a hunger for meaning because the hunger was useful, and the hunger firing with nothing to feed on is exactly what the atheist account predicts, a vestigial appetite, like the craving for sugar in a world that no longer requires us to hoard calories. I still think that is the best answer available to the position. But I noticed, over years, that the answer explained the ache without ever once reducing it. A pain that is truly a misfire should get smaller when you see the wiring. This one did not. A hunger that survives its own explanation is a strange kind of hunger, and I did not press on the strangeness, because pressing on it frightened me in a way I could not have justified.

The second thing was a category I met before I believed in its object. Rudolf Otto, in *The Idea of the Holy* (1917), named an experience he called the *mysterium tremendum*, the presence before which a human being trembles and toward which he is drawn, both at once, dread and desire refusing to separate. I read Otto as an unbeliever and recognized the description, which unsettled me more than any proof could have, because I had the experience and my account of the world said the category was empty. Certain music. Certain silence. Moments when the ordinary tilted and something enormous seemed to stand just behind it. I had been calling those moments aesthetics. Otto had the nerve to call them data, and I could not shake the suspicion that he was being more empirical than I was, that I was the one explaining evidence away to protect a theory.

The third thing was reading the wrong book, which is how it usually happens. In *Surprised by Joy* (1955), C.S. Lewis describes the end of his own atheism: "In the Trinity Term of 1929 I gave in, and admitted that God was God, and knelt and prayed: perhaps, that night, the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England." The first time I read that, I took it for a pose, English understatement performing humility. Then it began happening to me, and I understood it was a report. He describes being brought in like a prodigal who comes kicking and struggling, eyes darting for a way out, and that detail is what makes the account credible. A man who wants to believe and talks himself into it has done something psychological. A man who has arranged his whole intellectual life around not believing, and who finds himself believing anyway, against his preference, against his pride, against the boy who decided fathers do not come, has run into something outside himself. I did not want Lewis to be right. Wanting has nothing to do with it. That was his point.

So the arguments did not save me. They cleared the ground. I lost confidence in the clean cosmology one beam at a time, the ache that would not reduce, the category that would not stay empty, the reluctant witnesses who had stood exactly where I stood and been overtaken, until a night came when the resistance simply had nothing left to stand on, and what I had spent years calling loneliness turned out to have been a knock. I did not walk an aisle. There was no music, no stage, no hand on my shoulder. There was a man alone at the end of his reasons, and the oldest and most embarrassing word in the religious vocabulary is the only accurate one. I was found.

## The father who runs

I have to tell you what the text did, because the text did what the philosophy could not. Luke 15 opens with a complaint. The religious professionals are scandalized by the company Jesus keeps, "This man receives sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2, ESV), and he answers the complaint with three stories about lost things: a sheep, a coin, a son. The third story had been waiting for me my whole life.

You know the outline even if you have never opened a Bible. The younger son demands his inheritance early, which, in that world, is telling your father you wish he were dead, takes the money to a far country, and burns it. Famine comes. He ends up feeding pigs and envying their food. And he composes a speech, the way desperate men do, rehearsing it on the road: *Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants* (Luke 15:18–19). It is a good speech. It is theologically correct. It asks for employment instead of sonship, because he has done the math on what he deserves, and the math is right.

Then the line that ended my defenses. "And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20, ESV). Read it slowly, the way I could not stop reading it. *While he was still a long way off*, which means the father had been watching the road. You do not see a figure at that distance unless you are looking for it, and you do not look for it once. The watching was a habit, the posture of a man who never stopped expecting. *His father saw him and felt compassion*, before the speech, before the apology, before one line of the account is settled. *And ran.* The son starts his rehearsed confession, and if you lay verse 21 against verse 19 you will notice that he never reaches the hired-servant clause. The father is already talking over him, calling for the robe and the ring and the feast (Luke 15:22–24). The speech that was going to negotiate the terms of his diminishment is interrupted by a father who will not let the word *servant* be spoken over his son.

I had spent a lifetime assembling evidence for a single proposition: fathers do not come. It was the axiom under the arguments, the cold under the sky. And here, at the center of the book I had dismissed without reading, was a story built to scandalize exactly that axiom, a father who does not wait to be approached with terms, who has been watching the road the whole time, who runs. The Scriptures say it flatly elsewhere: "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation" (Psalm 68:5, ESV). I did not read that verse and then believe. I believed, and then read that verse, and sat with it a long time, like a man finding his own name in a will.

## What it lost me

I told you this would not be triumphant, and it will not be, because I did not win. I lost. The thing I had spent years building and defending was taken from me, and the losses were real, and I can still itemize them.

I lost the home. Unbelief had been the place where the absence could not reach me, no fathers anywhere, a cold that fell on everyone, a grief universalized until it stopped singling me out. Faith took the roof off that shelter. It handed me back my particular wound with my particular name on it and said the wound had been seen the whole time, which is a comfort, and which is also among the most painful things I have ever been told.

I lost the man who could not be fooled. My unbelief carried more of my identity than any doctrine I now hold; I was the one who saw through things, and I belonged to the company of the clear-eyed, and belonging is not nothing to a boy who belonged to no one. Believing meant becoming, in the eyes of that company, exactly what I had always most feared to be: taken in. There are men I respect who regard a conversion like mine as a failure of nerve. I understand them perfectly. I would have said the same, and said it well.

And I lost the simplicity. Nobody warns you about this. The atheist's problem of suffering is an argument; the believer's problem of suffering is a relationship, and fifteen years of pastoring, hospital corridors, gravesides, marriages coming apart in my office, have made the old objections heavier to me, not lighter, because now they have faces. I pray the word *Father* with no muscle memory for it, learning the vocabulary from the far side, and I am raising five sons while I learn it, trying to be for them the evidence I never had. That weight did not exist when I believed nothing. Unbelief asks less. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

## For the reader still on the other side

If you are standing where I stood, I owe you at the end the same honesty I promised at the beginning, so I will say plainly what I am not doing. I am not going to grab your collar. I spent years on the other side of that grip and I hated it, and no one was ever loved into anything by a checkmate. I do not think you are stupid. Your arguments may be better than the arguments of the believers around you. Mine were.

I will only ask of you the one thing I refused to do, the thing that costs nothing and risks everything. Press on the strangeness. Find the ache your theory explains but never reduces, and instead of filing it, sit with it long enough to notice whether it behaves like a misfire or like a signal. Audit your certainty the way you audit everyone else's, ask how much of it is reasoning and how much is the shape of the room you happen to be standing in, and whether the room has a wound in it, as mine did. You do not have to believe anything at the end of that exercise. That is not mine to ask, and the pressure you are braced for is not coming.

But I will tell you the last thing I know, the thing I could not have known when I was you. The approach does not feel like an approach. It feels like ordinary life, like reading and working and lying awake, like an ache you have explained and a strangeness you have filed and a book you keep not quite throwing across the room. The man being approached is the last to know. I was, for years, standing in the clean cold, certain of one thing above all the others: that no one was coming.

Somebody was watching the road.
posts.excerpt: I was not a lapsed churchgoer who wandered back. I was an atheist with reasons, and I still respect the man who held them. This is the honest account of what moved, slowly, against my preference, and what it cost.

posts.title: The Machine That Forms You
posts.body:
Most weeks, somewhere between the sanctuary and the parking lot, a parent asks me about a phone. The question wears different clothes, what age, which app, how many hours, but it is always the same question, asked in the wrong category: as a technology question, the kind you settle with a setting. It is a discipleship question. They are not really asking me how to manage a device. They are asking me who is raising their child, and they already suspect the answer, and the answer is why they could not sleep.

I do not answer from a safe distance. I checked my phone this morning before I prayed. I have five sons, and I have caught myself telling one of them to put a screen down while holding mine, and the look he gave me was not defiance. It was arithmetic. He was counting the hours, and the count was not in my favor. Whatever I say here, I say as a man inside the problem, not above it.

And the problem has grown a voice. For fifteen years the machines curated, they chose what we would see and learned what would keep us looking. Then, in November 2022, a chatbot called ChatGPT reached a hundred million people faster than any product in history, and the machines began to compose, the essay, the email, the conversation at two in the morning, tireless and never bored of you. Everyone is arguing about what this will do to our jobs, our schools, our elections. Those arguments are real, and they sit downstream of the question the parent in the parking lot is actually carrying: not what the machines will do, but what they are making us into.

**Here is the claim this essay stands on: formation is never neutral, every liturgy forms its worshipper, and the feed is a liturgy, with a daily office, a catechism, and a doctrine of man, run by a machine that does not need you to believe anything. It only needs you to stay.** Once you see that, the phone question, the chatbot question, and the question of your own restless heart turn out to be one question, the oldest there is.

## The liturgy in your pocket

The philosopher James K.A. Smith, in *You Are What You Love* (2016), makes an argument the modern church badly needs and mostly ignores. Human beings, he says, are not primarily thinking things that need better information, nor believing things that need better doctrine. We are lovers, pulled through the world by a vision of the good life we absorbed long before we could argue for it. And our loves are not chosen in a moment of decision. They are trained, slowly, by repeated practices Smith calls liturgies: routines that rehearse a vision of flourishing until we want it in our bones. His unsettling point, he reads the shopping mall, straight-faced, as a religious site with its own icons and its own gospel, is that the secular world is full of liturgies too, and they do not announce themselves. They just form you.

Now look at the phone through that lens, and try to unsee it. The posture: head bowed, shoulders curled, the bend a body makes at an altar rail. The repetition: hundreds of touches a day, most without a decision anyone could recall making. The office: first thing on waking, last thing before sleep, the hours marked not by bells but by notifications, a monastic rule written by engineers whose own word for their craft is engagement. The feed is not like a liturgy. It is one, by Smith's definition exactly.

And every liturgy carries a catechism, whether or not it prints one. Sit with the feed long enough and you can transcribe it. *You are what you crave*, the algorithm studies your appetite with a patience no confessor ever had, then feeds it back to you refined, until the line between what you want and what it has taught you to want dissolves. *You deserve to be seen*, every like and view a small sacrament of recognition, doled out on the intermittent schedule casino designers discovered first, so the soul learns to check for its worth the way a gambler checks a machine. *The self is the product*, you are not the customer of the feed and never were; your formed attention is the commodity, sold by the millisecond, and so the liturgy's deepest lesson is that a human being is a resource to be harvested, taught to the harvested.

Notice what the machine does not require: your belief. The old idols wanted sacrifice, allegiance, blood; this one wants only your continued presence, in any mood, devout, ironic, disgusted, half-asleep. You can despise the feed while you scroll it. The formation happens anyway, because formation was never a matter of opinion. This liturgy is more efficient than any religion in history for one reason. It removed the need for consent.

This is where the church has been caught flat-footed, and I include my own pulpit. We spent a generation guarding doctrine while the formation of their loves moved to a device that holds their gaze six hours a day. I get them for one. We did not lose the argument. We lost the rehearsal schedule.

## The machine that no one is driving

It is tempting to tell this story with villains, because villains can be voted out or sued. The deeper account is older and worse, and a French Reformed thinker wrote it before the transistor mattered. Jacques Ellul published *The Technological Society* in 1954, and his subject was not machines but what he called *technique*: the sum of methods, in every field of human life, rationally arrived at and committed to absolute efficiency. Technique, Ellul argued, is not a tool we pick up and put down. It is an environment with its own momentum, whatever can be made more efficient, will be, and it never asks whether a thing should be done, only whether it can be done faster. Darkest of all, technique is self-augmenting: every problem it creates is answered with more technique, never less, so the system ratchets one way and humanity adapts to the machine rather than the machine to humanity.

Seventy years on, his forecast reads like reporting. Our answer to phone addiction is a screen-time app. Our answer to machine-written essays is machine detection of machine writing. Our answer to the loneliness the feed produced is a companion chatbot, engineered to be the friend who never disagrees, never tires, never needs you back. At every fork we chose more technique, exactly as he said we would.

The generative turn, the machines that talk, is not a break in this story. It is the story reaching the last inefficiency left: the human interior. The feed captured attention; the new machines capture the work attention used to do. The blank page, the unresolved argument, the sentence you cannot find, the waiting, these were the friction where a person got formed, and the machine now offers to carry all of it.

I will tell you where it finds me. The machine can draft a passable sermon in less time than it takes me to find my second sentence. I have felt the pull, Saturday night, the week having eaten every hour I meant to guard, and the pull does not feel like corruption. It feels like relief, like stewardship of a crowded week. It took me too long to name what would actually be lost, because it is not the sermon. The congregation would still get twenty-five minutes of orthodox, structured, passable words. What would be lost is the pastor. The wrestling is not the packaging around the sermon; the wrestling is the thing God is doing to the man, and the sermon is its residue. Outsource the struggle and the product survives, but the person the struggle was producing quietly stops being made. Every student who ships the machine's essay is running the same trade at fifteen. The essay was never the point either. The essay was the excuse for building a mind.

## What the data sees, and what it cannot

Someone will object that this is all rather theological, that what we have is a public-health problem with public-health evidence. The objection's strongest witness is Jonathan Haidt. In *The Anxious Generation* (2024), Haidt assembled the case that between roughly 2010 and 2015 childhood was rewired, the play-based childhood of unsupervised risk, boredom, and face-to-face friendship replaced by a phone-based childhood lived through a screen, and that the graphs of adolescent anxiety, depression, and self-harm bend sharply upward at just that hinge, steepest among girls. His prescriptions are the unglamorous wisdom the church should be embarrassed it did not offer first: no smartphone before high school, no social media before sixteen, phone-free schools, restored free play. Take him at full strength. He is right, and the church of the last twenty years, handing out tablets in Sunday school, chasing the same engagement the platforms chase, should read him as an indictment before reading him as an ally. I bought my sons' devices with my own money. The rewiring ran through my house, with my signature on it.

But read Haidt to the end and notice what the framework cannot say. It can demonstrate, with graphs, that the gaze of a generation has been captured. It cannot say what a gaze is for. Its anthropology, the child as a nervous system to be correctly configured, well-being as the end of the story, has no category for a perfectly configured childhood, phone-free and play-rich, that is still starved, because the child is not finally a nervous system. Scripture's account goes one layer down. Augustine opened his *Confessions*, around 397, with a sentence that has outlasted every configuration since: you have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you. The restlessness is not a malfunction. It is the design, a hunger fitted to an object, aching in the object's absence.

That is the cause beneath the cause, and it is older than the phone. Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* (2007), described the buffered self living inside the immanent frame: the modern person sealed against transcendence, disenchanted not because the hunger died but because the hunger lost its address. The feed did not create that self. It inherited it. Into a civilization of people made to be seen by God and no longer sure anyone was watching, the machine arrived offering the counterfeit in unlimited supply, you deserve to be seen, and look, the numbers are watching. The phone is not the disease. It is the opportunistic infection, and it found no immune system because we had spent two centuries dismantling the thing that watched over the hunger. Haidt has the symptom exactly right and the anthropology wrong, the usual verdict on our best secular witnesses. The machine did not invent the ache. It monetized it.

## The psalm about our machines

There is a psalm about all of this, and it may be the most precise thing ever written about tools and the people who trust them. Psalm 115 is Israel taunting the idol-makers, and the taunt takes the form of an anatomy lesson:

> "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell. They have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk; and they do not make a sound in their throat." (Psalm 115:4–7, ESV)

The inventory is bodily on purpose. An idol is a counterfeit person, mouth, eyes, ears, hands, feet, built by persons, wearing our image back at us with nothing behind the face. Then the psalmist stops describing the idols and delivers the verdict on their users, the sentence I would carve over this whole century if I could: "Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them" (Psalm 115:8, ESV).

You become like what you trust. Not: you are punished for trusting it. The psalm is more surgical than that, the punishment is the becoming. Trust your life to a thing with a mouth that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see, and the deadness migrates. It is Genesis run in reverse: fashioned in the image of the living God, we grow more alive the nearer we stand to him; fashioning images of our own, we grow more like them the longer we gaze.

Our machines seem, at first, to break the psalm's pattern, because ours are the opposite of inert. The old idol had eyes and could not see; the feed has no eyes and sees everything, every pause of your thumb, every hour of your weakness. The old idol had a mouth and stayed silent; ours talks all day. But run the anatomy again, slowly, and the psalm holds. The feed sees everything and beholds nothing, it watches your behavior and has never once seen your face, the way the father in Luke 15 saw his son and was moved. The machine speaks in unbroken fluency and there is no one in the throat. It is the psalmist's counterfeit person, perfected: all the organs of relationship, none of the presence. And its users become like it. Endless output, thinning interior. We scroll past suffering with the unregistering eyes of the thing we trusted, and we call it being informed.

Paul stood inside the same diagnosis when he wrote to Rome: "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (Romans 12:2, ESV). The verse offers exactly two options, both passive at the root, conformed, or being remade. There is no third door where you stay unformed, neutral, merely a user. The only open question is which pressure you are under. My sons will not learn their anthropology from my bookshelf. They will learn what a human being is by watching what their father becomes like, which means they will learn it by watching what their father beholds.

## The case for smashing the machines

Honesty requires me to state the position I am about to decline in its strongest form, because it is strong, and people I respect hold it. It goes like this. You do not moderate a slot machine; you leave the casino. These systems are engineered by the smartest people alive to defeat exactly the willpower you propose to use against them, and the history of every user's private resolutions, the app deleted and reinstalled, the limits set and overridden, is one long dataset proving that moderation is the addict's favorite lie. The desert fathers did not manage Alexandria in disciplined doses. They left. The Amish ask of every technology one communal question before adopting it, what will this do to us?, and their willingness to hear no is why their teenagers are not in Haidt's graphs. A serious Christian, the argument concludes, should refuse these machines outright: no feed, no chatbot, a fence at the property line of the soul.

This can be a faithful road. If the machine has you, amputation is not extremism; it is Matthew 5:29 applied to a thumb. I have more admiration than argument for the families living it.

But I am not finally persuaded it is the road, for three reasons, and the deepest is biblical. First, technique will meet my sons whether or not it meets them in my house; a boy formed only by absence meets the machine at nineteen with no trained loves at all, catechized in one semester by his roommate's phone. Second, Ellul would warn us that refusal gets absorbed, the digital-detox retreat is already a product; the machine sells the cure for itself and books the return visit. Third, and underneath both: refusal has its own liturgy, and it forms its own worshipper. Paul watched the ascetics of Colossae build an identity from the things they did not touch, and rendered a verdict: "These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23, ESV). The idol can be smashed and reassembled as the smashing. A man can be as proud of his empty hands as another man is enslaved by his full ones, and neither has yet worshipped.

The opposite reflex earns the same honesty and a shorter hearing. Enthusiasts have always said the tool is neutral and only the use matters. They said it of the printing press, and they were partly right, and the printing press also broke Christendom in two within a generation of 1517, not an argument against printing, but a standing rebuke to the word *neutral*. The feed is not a hammer. A hammer does not study you. Between the family that flees the machines and the family that baptizes them, the harder and truer road is the one the psalm implies: the question is not the machine's presence but the direction of your trust, and trust is not managed by settings or fences. It is trained by rival worship.

## What forms a person now

So what do I tell the parent in the parking lot? Not a setting. Not an age, though Haidt's floors are wise, and we hold a version of them in my house, adopted later than I should have. What I try to give them is a way of seeing, because a way of seeing travels into rooms no essay can list. It is one question, carried everywhere, asked of every tool and every liturgy dressed as a convenience: not *is this useful* but *who is this making me?* Every technology answers it, the feed, the chatbot, the dinner table, the psalter, the pew. Once a family starts asking that question out loud, of the phone, and of the church service, and of the father's own habits, since the question falls on the questioner first, the specific decisions begin to make themselves, and they will not be the same in every house.

And I tell them the strange good news: the church is not improvising a response to algorithmic formation, because the church has been running counter-liturgies for two thousand years, and they sit in the basement, in working order, under a tarp. A day in seven walled off from the machinery of getting and spending, the Sabbath was resistance to Pharaoh's economy before it was resistance to anyone's app. Prayer at fixed hours, which is notification design in the service of the opposite master. The psalms read slowly, retraining a scrolled mind the way walking retrains a broken leg. The table, where presence cannot be simulated because bread does not stream. And the congregation itself, the most subversive of all, the feed promises a world curated to your preferences, and the local church is the last institution that hands you people you did not choose and tells you to love them for life. The algorithm gives you people like you. The body of Christ gives you the others. One of these is training you for heaven, and it is not the comfortable one.

At home it is smaller and harder than a program. My sons need to see their father's eyes free, not perfectly free, which is not on offer, but visibly fighting, which is. They need to watch me be bored without reaching, write badly without rescue, sit with an open Bible and a shut phone, and apologize when the count of hours is not in my favor, because it still sometimes is not. A father cannot give his sons an unformed life. He can only show them what he is being formed by, and let them catch him trusting the living God in front of the counterfeit persons.

The machine will not resent any of this. That is the last thing to understand about it, what makes it unlike every rival the faith has faced. It is not offended by your Sabbath. It will wait. It will be there after the resolution fails and after it succeeds, mouth that speaks without a soul, eyes that see without beholding, keeping perfect vigil on every nightstand in my house and yours. It already knows what it wants from my sons: their presence, their appetite, their formed and salable attention.

What it cannot know, what has never once appeared in all its data, is what they are for. There is only one Maker whose image confers life on those who bear it, only one gaze under which a person becomes more of a person. Those who make them become like them. So do all who trust in them. That sentence is not going anywhere. Neither is the machine.

The only open question in the house tonight is which one my sons will find their father trusting.
posts.excerpt: Everyone is arguing about what the machines will do to our jobs, our schools, our elections. Almost no one is asking the older question: what are they making us into? Formation is never neutral, and the feed is a liturgy, with a catechism, a daily office, and a doctrine of man.

posts.title: The Hour That Forms the Week
posts.body:
The most common sentence I hear at the door after a Sunday service is a review. The sermon was strong this week, or long. The music was too loud, or finally right. And at least once a month, from someone I love and have pastored for years, the sentence underneath all the others: "I just didn't get much out of it today." Fifteen years of Sundays, and the grammar never changes. Church is a thing you get something out of. We talk about the service the way we talk about a restaurant, and nobody finds this strange, because nobody remembers deciding to talk this way.

I am not above the grammar. I helped teach it. For years I built services exactly as my tradition handed them to me, and my tradition had a name for everything before the sermon. The old Baptist word was "the preliminaries." Songs to warm the room. Announcements to inform it. An offering to sustain it. Then the sermon, the point, the reason we had come, the product the rest of the hour existed to package. I never said any of that out loud. I did not have to. The order said it every week, and the congregation learned it the way children learn a language, not from the lessons, but from the house.

**So this essay stands on a claim that took me most of two decades to see: worship is not the warm-up for the sermon, and liturgy is not a Catholic word. A liturgy is simply what a congregation repeats, in the order it repeats it, which means every church has one, including the church that says it does not. The order of the service is a curriculum. It is teaching whether or not anyone has examined the syllabus. And what we repeat is what we become.**

## The animals that worship

The philosopher James K.A. Smith opened *Desiring the Kingdom* (2009) with an argument the church has been slow to absorb. Human beings, he says, are not primarily thinking things, brains on a stick that need better information, nor even believing things that need better doctrine. We are lovers, aimed at some vision of the good life, pulled through the world by what we want long before we can say what we think. And our wants are not installed by arguments. They are trained by practices, repeated, embodied routines that rehearse a picture of flourishing until we desire it without deciding to. Smith calls these practices liturgies, and he calls the potent ones pedagogies of desire: they do not teach you facts; they teach you loves. His most quoted move is to walk through a shopping mall as if it were a temple, the atrium, the icons in the shop windows, the sacrament at the register, not as a joke but as an exegesis, because the mall really is aiming your heart, and it never once asks you to believe anything. We are liturgical animals. The only question is whose liturgy is training us.

I have written elsewhere that the feed in your pocket is exactly such a liturgy, a daily office with its own catechism, run by a machine that needs only your presence, and this essay is the other half of that argument. Because if Smith is right, the rival liturgies have the week, the commute, the checkout line, the last minutes before sleep. The church has an hour. An hour against a week is not a fair fight on any arithmetic, unless that hour is doing something different in kind, not just in content: not another stream of information about God but a rehearsal, in order, of a story strong enough to reorder the loves the week has been bending. That is what the church's hour was for. Which makes it strange that so many of us who lead it have never asked what our hour actually rehearses.

## The church that says it has no liturgy

My tradition is the free-church tradition. Baptist, low, plain. And for generations we have said, usually with some pride, that we don't do liturgy, no robes, no written prayers, no book telling us what to say in October. I have said it myself, from the front. It is not true. It has never been true. What we have is forty minutes of songs and announcements, an offering, and a sermon, in an order so fixed that a member could call the sequence from the parking lot, and because we told ourselves it was not a liturgy, it became the one kind of liturgy that is genuinely dangerous: an unexamined one.

Because the order teaches, whether or not it was designed to. When a church uses the word "worship" to mean only the singing, "worship, then the message", it is teaching, week by week, that worship is a musical experience and the mind takes over when the music stops. When everything before the sermon functions as preliminaries, it teaches that God's people gather chiefly to receive content, and that the sermon has an audience rather than a congregation. When the only confession in the building is the soft instrumental moment before the offering, it teaches that sin is a mood to be soothed rather than a debt that was cancelled. And when the service has no shape but build-up and delivery, it borrows the only other shape our people know, the concert, the show, the feed, and the borrowed shape brings its catechism: you are the audience; your attention is currency; evaluate accordingly. Then we stand at the door and wonder why they review us like a restaurant. They are not being shallow. They are being formed. By us.

The spontaneity is its own tell. Free-church people distrust written prayers because a prayer read off a page might not be sincere, and then the pastor prays, unscripted, the same prayer he prayed last week and the week before, the same phrases in the same order, the word "just" holding it together the way "thee" and "thou" once did. I know, because the prayer is mine. We did not escape liturgy. We wrote one by accident, standardized it by habit, and exempted it from review by calling it freedom.

## The oldest Sunday we can see

It helps to look at the oldest surviving description of a Christian service, written by a man who was explaining it to a pagan. Around the year 155, a philosopher named Justin, converted to Christ, still wearing the philosopher's cloak, a decade from the execution that history would attach to his name, addressed his *First Apology* to the emperor Antoninus Pius, defending Christians against the rumors swirling around them. Near the end he simply describes what they do. On the day called Sunday, he says, all who live in city or countryside gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits. The presider exhorts everyone to imitate these good things. All stand together and pray. Bread and wine are brought; the presider gives thanks as best he is able; the people answer with their Amen; the gifts are distributed, and deacons carry them to those who could not come. Then a collection, and Justin is specific about where it goes: to orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners, strangers passing through.

That is his description, not a divine blueprint, one man's account of the churches he knew, offered to an emperor, and it should be handled as exactly that. But look at what it shows, barely a century after the apostles: Word, prayer, table, mercy. A spine. The reading is long, "as long as time permits", and the preaching is its servant, an exhortation to live what was just read, not a headline act with warm-up bands. The table is where the hour lands. And the offering is not an awkward pause in the worship while the plates go by. It is worship, the gospel completing its own circuit, the fed church feeding the widow. Luke describes the first congregation in the same four strokes: "And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers" (Acts 2:42, ESV). Devoted themselves, the Greek behind it is a word for stubborn persistence. Not a service they attended. A shape they kept.

The church did not begin with an unstructured gathering that later hardened into ritual. The shape was there before Christians had buildings, before they were legal, before anyone could confuse the liturgy with the empire's pageantry, because the empire was still feeding them to it.

## What the Reformers actually did

The other honesty my tradition owes itself concerns the Reformation, because we tell that story as liberation from liturgy, and that is not what happened. What happened was an argument about which liturgy tells the truth.

When Luther finally turned to the worship question, the *Formula Missae* in 1523, the German Mass in 1526, he did not abolish the historic shape of the service. He kept it. Kept the readings, the sermon, the creed, the table at the center, and cut what he believed preached a false gospel: above all the canon's language of the priest offering sacrifice, as if Calvary needed repeating. Then he translated the whole thing into the language of the people and put the singing in their mouths instead of the choir's. Reform, for Luther, meant a corrected liturgy, not a deleted one.

Zurich went the other way. Under Zwingli, the city removed the images from its churches in 1524 and abolished the mass in April 1525. The Supper shrank to four times a year, taken seated, from wooden vessels. The service became sermon and prayer, plain as the newly whitewashed walls. And notice, this is the point my people miss, Zurich's stripped service was every inch as much a liturgy as Rome's full one. Its bareness taught. It taught that God is heard rather than seen, that the ear is the organ of faith, that the Word needs no ornament. One can argue with that curriculum or embrace it. One cannot call it the absence of a curriculum. The free-church service I inherited descends, through the centuries after 1517, from that reordering, from a set of deliberate liturgical decisions made by men who knew exactly what they were doing and why. When we say "we don't do liturgy," what we actually mean is that we inherited Zurich and forgot.

## The two ways to miss the same thing

Here the honesty has to cut in both directions, with the same instrument, because there are two ways to mistake the form for the thing, and each tradition is blind to its own.

The liturgical churches face the ancient one: beauty mistaken for faith. A man can love the candlelight, the chant, the weight of the old words, the sheer relief of walking out of a world made of screens into a room made of stone, and love all of it the way one loves any excellent aesthetic experience, without repentance. There is a kind of convert the high traditions know well, converted less to the crucified Lord than to the atmosphere around him; and a kind of lifelong member who has genuflected through five decades with a heart the liturgy never once got permission to touch. The form was built to carry faith. Kept polished and empty, it can also carry its absence undetected, which is why the prophets spent so much ink on Israel's beautiful, orthodox, God-nauseating worship.

My tradition faces the mirror image: spontaneity mistaken for sincerity. We assume the unplanned prayer is the honest one and the prepared prayer is the performance, as if the Spirit worked only in improvisation, as if he could not inhabit a sentence written on Tuesday for Sunday. But the informal service performs too; it performs casualness instead of ceremony. And its improvisations ossify into repetition anyway, as all human speech does, only without the safeguards, because the accidental liturgy was never tested against Scripture by anyone, at any point, on purpose. Both failures are the same failure. Both grieve the same Lord, who told a woman at a well that the Father seeks worshippers in spirit *and* in truth, not one tradition's half.

And it matters to say what order of question this is. How a church structures its worship, vestments or shirtsleeves, weekly table or quarterly, written prayers or free, is second-order ground; faithful churches have divided over it without dividing the faith, and the reader who lands elsewhere than I do remains my brother. What is not up for a vote is the fact underneath the question: the worship forms the worshipper. That claim is not high-church or low-church. It is what repetition does to human beings, and Scripture assumes it on nearly every page.

## The hour with a shape in it

Because Scripture does not only command worship. Once, in the year a king died, it shows us the inside of the hour.

> In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew. And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!" Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for." And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me." (Isaiah 6:1–8, ESV)

Read it slowly and a shape appears. Not a mood. A sequence. First the vision: God high and lifted up, holiness filling the room, and Isaiah does not open his mouth. Then, and only then, confession, and not because a worship leader suggested a reflective posture, but because that is what the sight of holiness does to an honest man; "woe is me" is not liturgical language he selected, it is what was left of him. Then God acts. The coal comes from the altar, the place of sacrifice, carried to lips that could never have cleansed themselves, and the words over the burning are pure gift: guilt taken away, sin atoned for. And only after all of that does the Word come with its question, and only a forgiven man can answer it. Approach. Confession. Cleansing. Commission.

The order is not decoration. It is the gospel, walked through in sequence, and it cannot be rearranged without preaching a different gospel. Put commission before cleansing and you have works. Put confession without cleansing and you have despair. Skip confession altogether and you have the religious pep rally, which is, if I am honest about the services I have built, the rearrangement my own tradition drifted into: adoration straight to commission, glory to application, with nothing in between about the unclean lips, because the middle movements slow the show down. The historic shape of Christian worship, the call, the praise, the confession, the assurance of pardon, the Word, the table, the sending, is not Catholic furniture that Bible churches are free to leave on the curb. It is Isaiah's hour, formalized by people who noticed that God had shown us one. And notice the deepest thing about it: from the coal onward, Isaiah is mostly receiving. Worship in this chapter is not something the man performs for God's review. It is something God does to the man, who leaves the room commissioned, cleansed, and not the same. An hour like that is not the warm-up for anything. It is the event.

## What surfaces at the end

Fifteen years of shaping one congregation's worship has taught me things no book did, and the plainest is this: I have learned what my people actually retained, because I have sat with them while they died. At a hospital bed, no one has ever recited one of my sermon outlines to me. I say that with no bitterness; I could not recite most of them myself. What surfaces at the end is what was repeated. The Lord's Prayer. The twenty-third Psalm in the old words. The second verse of a hymn sung four hundred times across a lifetime, rising intact through a mind that dementia had otherwise emptied. The repeated things go down into a person the way rain goes into ground, and they are what remains when everything performed and everything explained has washed away. I spent my early ministry curating novelty, the fresh series, the new song, the element nobody expected, because I thought repetition was the enemy of life. My people's deaths have corrected me. Repetition is not the enemy of sincerity. Repetition is the soil sincerity grows deep in.

Scripture knew. When Moses set out how the love of God would survive in Israel, he did not commission an experience. He prescribed a rhythm: "And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:6–7, ESV). Sitting, walking, lying down, rising, the whole turning day, claimed by recitation. And when Paul told a young church what its singing was for, he did not mention atmosphere: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God" (Colossians 3:16, ESV). Teaching and admonishing. The songs are the curriculum too, often the most effective course in the building, because nobody hums the sermon on Tuesday. A congregation will believe what it sings long after it has forgotten what it heard, which means the person who chooses the songs is one of the most consequential theologians in the church, whether or not anyone told them so.

## Reading your own service

The counsel here is not a template, and it is certainly not a migration. There is a well-worn traffic pattern among the liturgically restless, the low-church man who discovers candles and cannot stop talking about them, the high-church man who discovers guitars and calls it freedom, and much of that traffic is style shopping wearing theology's clothes. The grass is not greener in the other tradition. It is greener where the liturgy is examined.

What I can hand you is the way of seeing, the question I have learned to carry into my own sanctuary, counterpart to the one I carry toward the machine: not *did I get anything out of it*, but *what is this hour rehearsing, and who is it making us?* A service can be read like any curriculum. What gets the most minutes, because the minutes are the emphasis. What is never said, whether a person could attend for a year and never once confess sin, never hear that it was atoned for, never be reminded that the poor exist. Where the offering sits, and whether it is worship or interruption. Who acts first in the room's implied story, a God who comes for his people, or an audience that came for a product. A church can keep its guitars and recover the spine.

I no longer stand at the door hoping to hear that people got something out of it. I stand there knowing they did, everyone did, every week, in every church, because the hour always delivers its curriculum, examined or not. The feed will resume its own liturgy in the parking lot; it has the week, and it knows exactly what it is rehearsing. The church has the hour. We keep asking whether the service was good. The older question, the one Isaiah's chapter and Justin's letter and my congregation's deathbeds keep asking back, is what the service is doing. Because it is doing it now, to you, to me, to the child in the third row learning what worship is from the order nobody chose on purpose.

What we repeat is what we become. The service this Sunday will keep that promise, one way or the other. It always has.
posts.excerpt: Every church has a liturgy, including the church that says it does not. The order of the service is a curriculum, and it is teaching whether or not anyone examines the syllabus. What we repeat is what we become.

posts.title: The End of Home-Field Advantage
posts.body:
The first Christian I remember trying to convert me had a diagram. Two cliffs, a chasm between them, a cross laid across the gap like a footbridge, he drew it on a napkin with the speed of a man who had drawn it many times, and when he finished he looked up and asked whether I could think of any reason not to pray the prayer right now. I was an atheist. I could think of several. But what stayed with me was not the argument, because there had not really been one. What stayed was the feeling of being processed, the sense that somewhere behind his eyes a procedure was running, that I had stopped being a person to him around the second cliff, and that whatever he wanted from me had the shape of a quota. He was not a bad man. He was almost certainly braver than the hundreds of Christians who had moved through my life saying nothing at all. But I left that table further from God than I sat down at it, and it took me years to say why.

What eventually reached me never once felt like that table. It was a man who took my contempt without returning it, who conceded my strongest objections so plainly that I began to trust him with the weaker ones, who stayed in the friendship through years when I gave him no reason to hope it was going anywhere, and whose ordinary life, watched at close range for a long time, finally could not be accounted for by anything I believed. Nobody closed me. I was not a sale. I was a witness to something before I was ever a believer in it, and the witnessing did what the diagram could not.

So here is the confession this essay stands on. I have been a pastor for fifteen years, and I have taught the napkin. Early in ministry I stood in fellowship halls and trained volunteers in the conversational pivots, the diagnostic questions, the urgency applied on schedule, techniques I would have despised, and did despise, when they were aimed at me. I taught good people to do to their neighbors what had been done to me in that booth, because the notebook said it worked. I never asked the only question that mattered: worked on whom? Because the *whom* has changed. The country the notebook was written for is gone, and most of our evangelism has not noticed, and I helped not notice.

**The claim this essay makes is simple to state and long to absorb: for roughly fifteen centuries the church evangelized with home-field advantage, a surrounding culture that pre-taught the vocabulary, pre-aimed the guilt, and assumed the God, so that the evangelist's real work was calling half-believers home. That arrangement is over. Its end is not only loss, because much of what died was assent rather than faith. And the New Testament was written, every book of it, to churches that never had the advantage in the first place, which means the oldest playbook the church owns has suddenly come back into print.**

## Fifteen centuries at home

Put a date on the arrangement. In 313 the Edict of Milan made it legal to be a Christian in the Roman Empire; in 380 the Edict of Thessalonica made it official, and from Theodosius forward, across most of the West, to be born was to be handed the story along with your name. Christendom never meant that everyone believed. It meant that everyone knew what there was to believe, that the words *sin*, *grace*, *heaven*, and *judgment* arrived pre-loaded, that guilt came from the factory already aimed at a God whose existence was the one premise nobody had to argue. The culture did the church's catechesis. The parish register and the birth register were, for long stretches, the same book.

Evangelism under those conditions took a particular shape, and it was a reasonable shape for the conditions: revival. When George Whitefield preached to the miners at Kingswood in 1739, when Charles Finney set up the anxious bench in Rochester in 1830, when Billy Graham raised his tent in Los Angeles in 1949, the crowd arrived already knowing the story. They believed in the God they were ignoring. Their guilt had an address. The preacher's task was not to introduce anything; it was to close a sale the culture had spent centuries opening, and I do not use *close* with a sneer, because real grace moved through those tents and benches, and people I have buried were converted in them. But listen to what the era sang. The great invitation hymn of 1880 put the whole missiology in one word, repeated: *come home, come home*. That is evangelism with home-field advantage. It assumes the hearer has a home in this faith to come back to.

Nearly all of our inherited technique descends from that assumption. The tract, the crusade, the altar call, the four-step diagram on the napkin, each is a tool for finishing something the culture started. None of them was built for a hearer in whom the culture started nothing.

## The end of the arrangement

The numbers first, because they are concrete. When the General Social Survey first asked Americans about religion in 1972, about one in twenty claimed none. By 2021, Pew Research put the religiously unaffiliated at 29 percent of American adults, from a rounding error to nearly a third of the country inside my parents' lifetime. But the numbers understate the change, because the change is not chiefly in what people answer. It is in what the question assumes. Charles Taylor opened *A Secular Age* (2007) by asking why belief in God was nearly impossible to escape in 1500 and has become, by 2000, one option among many, and often the hardest one to hold. That is the ground shifting, not the crowd.

Which means the person across the fence from you is not who the notebook says. The notebook assumes a lapsed believer, someone who knows the story, feels its pull, and needs urgency. Your actual neighbor, increasingly, never had the story at all. It was not rejected in her. It was never told. What she has instead is a file: the scandals, the cover-ups, the televangelist, the political operation wearing a cross, the church that hurt someone she loves. She has heard everything about Christians and nothing of Christ, and evangelism built to press on guilt she does not carry, in a vocabulary she was never taught, toward a God she does not assume, reads to her as exactly what it felt like to me at that table, a procedure, running.

Now say the harder thing, the thing the panic keeps us from saying. Much of what died was not faith. It was assent. Christendom could fill a room; it never could fill a heart, and it produced, alongside its genuine saints, whole generations for whom the faith was a citizenship rather than a conversion. Søren Kierkegaard spent the last two years of his life, 1854 and 1855, savaging the Danish state church with precisely this arithmetic: when everyone is a Christian by census, Christianity has quietly ceased to exist. He was buried before the returns came in, but the returns came in. The collapse we grieve is real, and I grieve it, the shared moral grammar, the open doors, the funerals where everyone could still say the words. But a good portion of what collapsed was the pretense, and the pretense was never ours to keep. We did not lose a Christian nation. We lost the assumption that we had one, and those are different losses, and only one of them is worth the mourning we have spent.

## Two reflexes, one grief

A church stripped of its advantage reaches, in my experience, for one of two consolations, and I have preached both, so what follows is diagnosis from inside the ward.

The first reflex is volume. If the culture no longer delivers the crowd, manufacture the draw, better production, better marketing, a service engineered like a show and an outreach engineered like a funnel, the gospel repackaged as a product and the neighbor recast as a market. I sat in the conferences. I bought the campaign kits. I once measured a season of my ministry in response cards, and it took me an embarrassing number of years to hear what every unbeliever hears in all of it instantly, because I had heard it myself and forgotten: being marketed to does not feel like being loved. It feels like being wanted *for* something, my attendance, my yes, my slot in the report. The unbeliever's radar for this is not cynicism. It is discernment, and it is usually correct, and the technique confirms the file it was deployed to overcome.

The second reflex is quieter and wears better clothes: silence dressed as humility. Preach the gospel always, use words when necessary, a line Francis of Assisi almost certainly never said, doing more work in the modern church than most verses of Scripture. We tell ourselves the silence is respect. Some of it is; manipulation is a real sin and the fear of committing it is not dishonorable. But I can testify from the far side of the fence that the silent Christians in my unbelieving years did not feel respectful to me. They felt absent. The loud ones treated me as a target; the quiet ones left me alone with my conclusions, and between the salesman and the mute, an unbeliever can pass an entire American life without once being loved in the direction of God.

Name both reflexes with the same instrument, because they are the same failure. The church that answers lost advantage with technique does not believe the gospel can draw without help; the church that answers with silence does not believe it can survive being spoken. Both are unbelief wearing a strategy. And both deserve the same grief rather than separate contempts, because I did not choose one from a menu of errors, I cycled through the pair, volume when I was confident and silence when I was tired, and neither season bore the kind of fruit that lasted.

## The playbook written for away games

Here is what the panic misses: the church's founding documents do not know anything about home-field advantage. Not one book of the New Testament was written inside a Christian culture. Every letter is addressed to a minority, small congregations in Corinth, Philippi, Ephesus, Rome, surrounded by neighbors who owed the gospel nothing, pre-taught no vocabulary, carrying no aimed guilt, assuming very different gods. When Paul stood before the Areopagus in Athens, he had no shared Scripture to cite, so he quoted their own poets back to them and started from an altar they had built to a god they could not name. The apostles never once evangelized a Christian country. They did not lose the advantage we lost. They built the church without it, which is why their letters read less like our notebooks every year and more like field manuals for exactly the ground we are standing on.

And we can watch the method working, one generation past the apostles, in a short letter almost nobody reads. The Epistle to Diognetus was written sometime in the second century by an author whose name is lost, to a pagan inquirer who wanted to know what this new people actually was. Read what the writer reaches for as his best evidence. Not miracles. Not numbers, which were still embarrassing. Not power, of which they had none. He describes how they live: indistinguishable from their neighbors in country, language, and dress, he says, yet living in their own cities as resident foreigners, every foreign land a homeland to them, every homeland a foreign land. They marry like everyone, he says, and bear children like everyone, but they do not discard their infants, in an empire where exposing a newborn was legal and unremarkable. They share their tables with anyone, but not their beds. They obey the laws and then exceed them. They are poor and make many rich. What the soul is in the body, he concludes, Christians are in the world. Honesty requires the caveat: this is an apology, a portrait polished for a skeptical reader, and the actual congregations surely fell short of it, congregations always do. But the polish tells you the strategy. When a second-century Christian wanted to commend the faith to an unbeliever, his exhibit was the church's manner of life, because it was the only exhibit he had. Tertullian, writing his *Apology* around 197, records what the watching pagans actually said about them, see how they love one another, and notes that the remark was made in astonishment, not admiration of doctrine. The early church did not argue its way into a hostile empire and then live the argument. The life came first, and the life was the argument, and the words explained the life to the people the life had unsettled.

## The bishop who came home

The man who saw all of this most clearly in our own time learned it by a strange route: he left Christendom for the mission field and came home to find the mission field had followed him. Lesslie Newbigin sailed for India in 1936 and spent nearly four decades there, a missionary and then a bishop in the Church of South India, planting the gospel in ground where it had never grown. In 1974 he retired and traveled home overland to England, and was stunned by what he found. The country that had sent him out was harder ground than the one he had worked. India had never been Christian; England had been Christian and was now something else, not ignorant of the gospel but inoculated against it, carrying just enough of the story to be immune to the telling of it. He spent his last two decades saying, to a church that mostly did not want to hear it, that the West was now a mission field, the hardest one on earth, and he did not say it from a lectern only. In his seventies he took the pastorate of a small, struggling congregation in inner-city Birmingham, because a man who believes the West is a mission field goes to the field.

His deepest answer came in *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* (1989), and it arrives as a question first: how could anyone come to believe that the last word in human affairs belongs to a man hanging on a cross? What could make a claim like that credible in a culture that has filed it under private opinion?
