His answer: "the only hermeneutic of the gospel is a congregation of men and women who believe it and live by it." A hermeneutic is what makes a text legible, the frame that lets you read it as what it is. For fifteen centuries, the culture was the gospel's hermeneutic; the world around the text taught you how to read it before you ever opened it. That interpreter has retired. What remains, the only interpreter left, Newbigin insisted, is a community living as though the story were true, close enough to be watched. This is Diognetus again, sixty generations later. And notice what Newbigin was not saying, because both of our reflexes will try to claim him. He was not saying the church should perform better; the congregation he means is not an attraction but an argument, and arguments made of lives cannot be staged. And he was not counseling silence, the man preached, debated, and wrote to the end of his life. He was saying the words have lost their translator, and the church's shared life is the only translation the unbeliever can still read. The congregation does not replace the message. It makes the message legible.

## The letter to exiles

If the New Testament has an after-Christendom book, it is 1 Peter. The address alone tells you the situation: "To those who are elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1, ESV), scattered households of believers across Asia Minor, socially marginal, politically powerless, already being slandered as enemies of the human race. Peter writes to people with no advantage of any kind, and his strategy for them is stated early: "Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation" (1 Peter 2:12, ESV). Then, in the third chapter, he compresses the whole missiology of the powerless church into two verses that the modern church quotes at half strength:

> but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. (1 Peter 3:15–16, ESV)

Unfold it slowly, in order, because the order is the instruction. It begins in the heart, not the mouth: *honor Christ the Lord as holy*. Witness is downstream of worship, and the first audience of the sentence is the believer's own interior, before Peter says a word about the neighbor, he addresses the throne room of the person speaking, because an evangelist whose heart is not settled will reach for pressure to make up the deficit, and pressure is what pressure produces.

Then the verse makes an assumption so quiet we read past it: *to anyone who asks you*. Someone asks. Peter takes it for granted that the exile's life, hope held under slander, good rendered for evil, a household that does not run on the empire's fuel, will be strange enough to generate the question. The witness he describes is not an opening move. It is an answer. And this is the hinge on which everything I have written here turns, because I can tell you from the unbelieving side exactly what the difference feels like. An answer to a question I never asked arrived as an intrusion, however true it was; it taught me only that this person needed something from me. But the friend who finally told me why his life held together was answering a question I had asked, it had taken me years to ask it, and the same sentences that would have bounced off me in a parking lot landed like news, because by then I wanted to know. You cannot rush the question. You can only live the kind of life that raises it, and be unashamed when it comes.

Then the content: *a reason for the hope that is in you*. Not a worldview, not a rebuttal, not the napkin, hope, and hope located somewhere: *in you*. The thing to be explained is not an argument the Christian carries but a life the Christian is visibly living, which is why no technique can substitute for it; there is no method for explaining a hope you do not have.

And then the clause we trained ourselves to forget: *yet do it with gentleness and respect*. Peter puts the manner inside the command, not beside it. The word behind *respect* is the old word for fear, reverence, and whether Peter means reverence before God or before the conscience of the questioner, the effect is the same: no contempt survives it, no procedure survives it, nothing that treats the person as terrain survives it. This is not packaging. A gospel of unearned grace delivered as a conquest contradicts itself in the delivery; the manner is part of the message, and the hearer, I promise you, having been the hearer, reads the manner first. Verse 16 finishes the thought: the good conscience, the good behavior, the slander answered not by a counterattack but by a life the accusation cannot be made to fit. The exiles' whole apologetic, like Diognetus's, like Newbigin's, stands or falls on how they live between the questions.

## What remains to be asked

I owe a word to the reader who does not believe any of this, because I know you are here, I read essays like this one for years, the way a man reads letters not addressed to him, checking whether the writer would tell the truth about people like me. So: you were right to resent the diagram. The feeling of being processed was not oversensitivity; something really was treating you as terrain, and it was not the gospel, and the parts of the church that learned evangelism from the sales floor owe you the apology I am attempting here. Nothing in this essay is a subtler technique aimed at you. It is, if anything, the dismantling of the techniques, an argument to my own people that you are not a market, not a quota, not a project with a closing date, and that any Christian who befriends you with a conversion deadline in mind has already misrepresented the faith he came to commend. What I hope you find among us is what I finally found: people whose kindness is not a strategy, who can hear your strongest objection without flinching or needing to win, and whose lives raise a question you are free never to ask. If you never ask it, the kindness was still real. That is the whole test of whether it was ever kindness at all.

And to the church: nothing here is a case for silence. The news must still be told, it is news; a watched life can raise the question, but no casserole ever explained an empty tomb, and the generation that mistakes its quietness for witness will comfort itself into extinction. What has changed is not whether we speak but where the speaking sits. It sits after love, inside trust, in answer to questions our common life has raised, which is to say it sits where it sat for the church's first three centuries, before the empire made it easy, back when the whole enterprise ran on nothing but the Spirit of God and the strangeness of the saints. The exiles Peter wrote to had no tents, no campaigns, no cultural memory to press on, and they buried the empire that slandered them. They did not have the advantage. They had a hope that required explanation.

That is the sentence I cannot get out from under, and I will not resolve it for you, because it does not resolve. Peter's instruction has a prerequisite no technique can fake: it only works on a church that is asked. The old arrangement asked on our behalf for fifteen centuries, and the old arrangement is dead, and no amount of volume will resurrect it, and no depth of silence will excuse us from the question it used to answer. I think of the man with the napkin more charitably now than I did then. He believed the chasm was real and could not bear to watch me walk toward it politely. What he lacked was not courage but a country that still did his catechesis for him, and that country is gone for good, which leaves the matter where it was in the year 155, where it was in Pontus and Bithynia, where it is on my street and yours tonight. The advantage is over. The question is whether anything about us is still strange enough, hopeful enough, gentle enough, unaccountable enough, to be asked about. My neighbors are not asking me the reason for my hope this week. Before I teach one more class on what to say, I have to sit with why.
posts.excerpt: For fifteen centuries the church evangelized a culture that already half believed, the vocabulary pre-taught, the guilt pre-aimed, the God assumed. That arrangement is over, and its end is not only loss, because much of what died was assent, not faith. The New Testament was written entirely to churches playing away from home. The oldest playbook is current again.

posts.title: What a Christian Owes the City
posts.body:
The sermon had gone the way those sermons go. I had said, as carefully as fifteen years of practice allows, that the cross is not a party asset, that a church which cannot tell the difference between the kingdom of God and a November outcome has already lost something no election can return. People nodded. Some of them meant it. And then in the foyer a man I have known for years, a deacon's steadiness in him, a man who reads, shook my hand and asked the question that has been working on me ever since. All right, he said. I hear you. The flag comes off the altar. Then what? Do I still vote? Do I still care who wins? What do you actually want from me on a Tuesday in November?

I gave him something warm and inconclusive, and he was gracious about it, and I drove home knowing what had happened. I had handed him a whole theology of what not to worship and half a page on what to do. A diagnosis with no prescription leaves the patient two doors, and both are wrong. The first goes back into the tribe, the sermon fades, the feed resumes, and by the next election the idolatry has been forgiven for the excellent reason that it never left. The second looks like repentance and is really resignation: politics is dirty, both sides are compromised, I am done, withdrawal from the city, renamed purity. I have watched members of my own congregation walk through each door, sometimes the same member through both, one election apart.

**So this is the essay the diagnosis has been pointing toward, and its claim is easy to say and hard to hold. After the idolatry is named, the question is not whether a Christian loves the city. It is how. And the answer Scripture gives is a both/and that neither tribe can carry: genuine, costly care for the city's welfare, and a flat refusal to seek salvation from it. Engagement without worship. Love without trust. The tribes split that sentence and take half apiece, one keeps the engagement and loses the refusal, the other keeps the refusal and loses the love, and each half, alone, becomes a lie.**

## A letter to people who lost

Begin where God begins the constructive work, because the address matters as much as the instruction. In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar's army took Jerusalem, and the first great deportation carried the young king, the elders, the craftsmen, and the smiths, the whole functioning class of the city, east to Babylon. The temple still stood; it had a decade left. And among the deportees a market in hope sprang up at once, stocked by prophets. One of them, Hananiah, put a date on it: within two years the temple vessels would come home and the yoke of Babylon would snap (Jeremiah 28 records the scene, and records that Hananiah was dead within the year). Notice what the false prophecy in Babylon was not. It was not paganism. It was optimism about power, the announcement that the political situation would shortly be corrected. The exiles' strongest religious temptation was a rescue on a political timetable. Some things do not change.

Into that market Jeremiah sent a letter, and it said the unforgivable thing, seventy years, and then it said this:

> "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease. But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare." (Jeremiah 29:4–7, ESV)

Read the address line first. This is written to people who did not hold power and were not going to, no vote in Babylon, no seat at court, no path to the throne, no return ticket inside their own lifetimes. Whatever this command is, it cannot be a strategy for taking the city, because the people it was given to could not take a city block. And read the strange claim buried in the greeting, *whom I have sent*. Not whom Nebuchadnezzar dragged. God puts his own name on the catastrophe, which means the exile is an assignment before it is a punishment, and the address they did not choose is the address where obedience now lives.

Then the instruction, and its shape is almost insultingly ordinary. Houses. Gardens. Weddings. Grandchildren. No underground, no counter-court, no siege engines of the military or the cultural kind, just the patient machinery of settled life, planted in enemy soil. And then the sentence that breaks the categories: seek the welfare of the city. The word is *shalom*, not the city's mere order but its flourishing, the knitting-together of its common life. Pray to the LORD *on its behalf*. This is Babylon. These streets run with the wealth stripped out of Jerusalem. Seek its shalom, says the God of Israel, for in its shalom you will find your own, your welfare and its welfare have been tied together, on purpose, by me.

Hold the two edges of that text and you can feel it cutting both ways. It cannot be conscripted for conquest, because it was issued to the powerless: seeking a city's welfare is not seeking its throne, and the letter pointedly offers no throne. And it cannot be conscripted for withdrawal, because *build, plant, marry, invest, pray* is a command to entangle yourself with a pagan city's flourishing until its good becomes your good. The exiles were forbidden both the fantasy of rescue-by-regime-change and the purity of the sealed enclave. What remained was harder than either. Love the city. Expect nothing from it that only God can give.

## Two cities in one ruin

Eight centuries of Roman confidence ended on August 24, 410, when Alaric's Goths sacked the city the whole Mediterranean world had assumed was permanent. The refugees who washed up in North Africa carried an accusation with them: Rome fell because it abandoned the old gods for Christ. So in 413 the bishop of Hippo began the book that took him thirteen years to finish, *The City of God*, among a dozen other things, the church's deepest sustained answer to what Christians are doing in a political order at all.

Augustine's answer runs on a distinction. There are two cities, he argued, and they are not church and state, not Rome and Jerusalem, not any pair you can find on a map, because their citizens live on the same streets and their memberships are invisible until the end. What distinguishes them is what they love. Two loves built two cities, his famous formulation, near the close of Book XIV, the earthly city by love of self swollen to contempt for God, the heavenly city by love of God carried to contempt for self. Everything else hangs off that hinge, including his account of virtue as rightly ordered love, *ordo amoris*, loving each thing as much as it deserves and nothing more. Sin, on this reckoning, is rarely loving a bad thing. It is loving a good thing out of order.

Now set that beside the political air we breathe, because the diagnosis translates without remainder. There are two ways a Christian's loves and politics can relate, and only one of them is faith. Politics can order your loves: the coalition tells you whom to love and whom to fear, which sufferings count and which are propaganda, which sins are emergencies and which are quirks, until the party has done the precise work Augustine assigned to God, arranging the heart's priorities, and has thereby become, in the only sense that matters, your god. Or love can order your politics: the city becomes one of the goods you care for, a real good, worth real labor, but a created good, loved in its place, beneath the God who will outlast it. Augustine grieved Rome; the book is not a shrug. But he had watched the thing every political theology must reckon with: the city that called itself eternal, wasn't. He wrote from inside the rubble that the earthly city's peace is genuinely valuable and genuinely temporary, that the heavenly city makes grateful use of it while refusing to call it home. He was not lowering the reader's care for the city. He was moving its foundation off the city's permanence, an illusion, and onto the command of the God who assigns his people to cities the way he assigned exiles to Babylon.

## The servant and the beast

Whoever wants a one-verse political theology has to suppress a canonical fact: the New Testament looks at the same empire twice and reports two different things, and both reports are Scripture. Writing to the Christians of Rome around the year 57, Paul is unambiguous: "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (Romans 13:1, ESV). The ruler, he adds, "is God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:4, ESV). The emperor Paul calls God's servant was Nero. A generation later, most scholars place it in the mid-90s, under Domitian, John, exiled on Patmos, sees the same empire as a beast rising from the sea, wearing blasphemous names, demanding the world's worship: "Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation" (Revelation 13:7, ESV).

Romans 13 and Revelation 13. The same Rome. The canon is not confused; it is teaching. Government is God's servant for your good, really, even when its ministers never heard of him, *and* government can swell into a beast demanding what belongs to God alone, and the same government can travel from the one to the other within a Christian's lifetime. A political theology that can only read Romans 13 will baptize whatever holds the sword. One that can only read Revelation 13 will find the beast under every statute and never honor anything. The apostles held both, and Peter compressed the both/and into four clauses: "Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor" (1 Peter 2:17, ESV). Honor for the emperor; fear reserved for God. The same sentence bows and refuses to kneel.

And here is where the tribes give themselves away, because each of them owns both chapters and switches between them on schedule. Romans 13 when our man holds the sword; Revelation 13 the moment the other man takes it. Submission preached as godliness in one administration becomes resistance preached as godliness in the next, and the exegesis tracks the election returns to the decimal. Both sides run the same play; only the years change. I am not describing it from a safe distance, I know which verse rises in me unbidden depending on who won. A man whose canon rotates with the White House has not submitted his politics to Scripture. He has submitted Scripture to his politics and kept the leather cover.

## What faithful presence actually asks

The best-known modern name for the constructive posture is James Davison Hunter's, and it is worth stating what he actually argued, because "faithful presence" has been worn as a brand by people recommending nearly the opposite. In *To Change the World* (2010), Hunter, a sociologist at the University of Virginia, not a culture-war chaplain for either side, dismantled the theory of change both Christian tribes run on: that culture is transformed by changing individual hearts, or by winning political power. Cultures do not mainly change that way, he argued; they change slowly, through networks of institutions and elites near the center, which is why a century of Christian mobilization produced so little of what it promised. Worse, he showed what the mobilization did produce. When the church made politics its master frame, and he indicts the Christian right, the Christian left, and the neo-Anabaptist purists together, which is why partisans of all three dislike the book, it absorbed the politics of *ressentiment*, a settled grievance that became the church's public face regardless of its stated creed. His prescription scandalized activists: the church might need to be silent for a season about politics, not because the public square does not matter but because the church's speech there had become toxic to its own witness.

What he offered instead is the phrase everyone quotes and fewer have read: faithful presence. Not withdrawal, Hunter rejects the sealed enclave. Not conquest, the book exists to bury that theory. Faithful presence means Christians fully committed to the people, places, and vocations where they already are, the school, the shop, the block, the county, working for the flourishing of everyone within reach, believer and unbeliever alike, without needing to run the world or win the era. It is Jeremiah's letter translated into sociology: build, plant, seek the shalom of the city, and let go of the timetable.

Lesslie Newbigin, home in England after nearly four decades as a missionary bishop in India, reached the same place by a different road. In *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* (1989) he asked how the gospel could be found credible in a culture that no longer grants its premises, and his answer was not an argument but an address: the only hermeneutic of the gospel, he wrote, is a congregation of men and women who believe it and live by it. Which means the church's first political act is not a statement, an endorsement, or a march. It is being the church, a visible community where the gospel is legible in how enemies are treated. A congregation that cannot hold two yard signs at one table is not merely failing at fellowship. It is failing at evangelism, because the community was the argument, and the argument just collapsed.

## One table, two yard signs

Which brings me to the room I actually serve, because everything above this line I learned the hard way, standing in it. My congregation is small-town Michigan, politically mixed the way small towns are: not a debating society, just neighbors, the retired shop teacher and the nurse, the farmer and the schoolteacher, people who cancel each other's votes every cycle and know it. Every election year the country's argument arrives at our door dressed as a member. And every communion Sunday I watch something the country would not believe: people whose yard signs face each other across the street kneeling at the same rail, served from the same loaf, by each other. I can count on one hand the rooms left in my town where that happens. The church is one of the last places in America where the two tribes still touch the same bread, and I have stopped treating that as a scheduling accident. It is a political fact, maybe the most political thing we do.

Now the confession, because this essay does not get to indict from the gallery. Over fifteen years I have preached bravely against the idolatry my room already distrusted and carefully about the one it brought in the door. I knew which applause was cheap and I banked it anyway. I called the caution pastoral wisdom, and some of it was, and some of it was cowardice wearing wisdom's jacket, and on the honest days I can tell which was which. A guardrail that only fires in one political direction is not orthodoxy; it is a tribe in robes, and for stretches of my ministry I wore them. My pews deserved a shepherd who grieved both captivities at the same volume. Getting there cost me approval I had grown used to. It was owed.

## The scale you actually live at

So what should the man in the foyer do? Here the essay has to refuse two temptations at once: the voter guide, which would betray everything above, and the shrug, which would betray him. What Scripture and the tradition hand us is not a platform. It is a posture, and it takes flesh at the scale where you actually live, which is, for nearly everyone reading this, not the national scale. The national argument is the one you can do least about and the one built to occupy you most; the county you live in is the reverse. Faithful presence begins by trading the politics you can only watch for the politics you can actually touch.

That means the school board meeting, attended, or the seat itself, held the way a deacon holds an office rather than the way a soldier holds a hill: read the budget, learn the names, pray for the superintendent whether or not you voted for the levy, and when the vote goes six to one against you, lose like a Christian, without contempt and without leaving. It means the food pantry, quietly the most political square footage in town in the old sense of the word, the *polis*, the shared life, because the line outside it does not sort by party. It means the neighbor whose sign opposes yours: his name learned, his driveway shoveled, his kids known, so that whatever the feed says his kind of people are like, you are disqualified from believing it, having eaten at his table. None of this will trend. That is much of its value. The future does not belong to stronger tribes; it belongs to deeper disciples, and the school board, the pantry line, and the fence line are where the depth is formed, one unspectacular Tuesday at a time.

And the vote. Cast it. Abstention is also a political act whose costs land on neighbors, and the exiles were not told to keep their hands clean of Babylon's common life. But cast it the way you would use any tool that cannot love you back, soberly, prayerfully, with a loose grip, and walk out of the booth exactly as free as you walked in, belonging to no one you just voted for. The lever is a stewardship. It is not a sacrament, and it was never a confession of faith.

What I will not tell you is where the lever should land, and the refusal is not cowardice this time; it is doctrine. Christians have always distinguished what the faith settles from what it leaves to judgment, and almost every policy mechanism, the tax rate, the zoning variance, the immigration number, the healthcare design, the school funding formula, lives in the second category, where serious believers reading the same Bible reach different prudential conclusions and remain brothers. What the faith settles is smaller and far more demanding: the person on the other side bears the image of God and is therefore permanently off-limits to your contempt. James would not let his churches split the tongue's allegiance: "With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9, ESV). Fight your opponent's proposal with everything lawful and honest. You may not despise the man. Contempt is the one truly bipartisan sin of this era, the habit both tribes teach as virtue and reward as loyalty, and the one thing on the whole political menu a Christian is flatly forbidden to order.

## The welfare of a city that is not home

The exiles who received Jeremiah's letter mostly died in Babylon. They built the houses, planted the gardens, raised the grandchildren, prayed for the city that had burned their city, and were buried in its soil, seventy years short of the return their obedience made possible for someone else. That is the address the constructive answer was mailed to, and it has not changed. Seek the welfare of a city that is not your home, will not thank you, and cannot save you. Expect the work to outlast your lifetime and the credit to skip your generation.

It would be easier to be told to conquer the city. It would be easier to be told to abandon it. We were told to love it, and love is the costlier instruction, it always is. I owe the man in the foyer a better answer than the one he got, and this is its beginning, not its end; he will have to work out the school board and the shovel and the lever in the county where he actually lives. But the two truths he carries into November are not in tension after all. The city cannot save you. You are commanded to seek its welfare anyway. The space between those sentences is not a contradiction to resolve. It is the address, and we were sent to it.
posts.excerpt: The critique of political idolatry is finished only when it builds something. Jeremiah told exiles to seek the welfare of the city that burned their home, a both/and neither tribe can hold: genuine care for the city, and no salvation from it.

posts.title: Excavation, Not Demolition
posts.body:
The word arrives across a table, usually with the coffee going cold, and it arrives braced. Someone I have pastored for a decade, or someone who drove forty minutes because they could not risk saying it at their own church, looks down and says it the way people report a diagnosis. *I think I'm deconstructing.* Then they wait, because they have learned to wait. They know the two speeches. There is the alarm speech, where the pastor hears the word as a positive test result and reaches for the apologetics shelf, and there is the celebration speech, available these days one podcast over, where the same word is treated as a graduation. Panic or applause. Both speeches make the same mistake. Neither one asks what the person is actually doing with the crowbar in their hands.

I have never been able to give the first speech, because I am disqualified. I came to faith from atheism, which means I met Christianity the way an inspector meets a building he has been assured is condemned. Every argument the deconstructing Christian discovers at two in the morning, the contradictions, the crusades and the cover-ups, the suspicion that the whole thing is a coping mechanism with a steeple on it, I did not have to discover. It was my native language. I stood outside the house for years agreeing with the demolition order, and when I finally went in, I went in swinging. I hit everything in that house as hard as any insider mid-crisis ever could, because I had no sentiment to protect and no grandmother watching. So the word does not frighten me.

But I cannot give the celebration speech either, and this is the harder confession. I have been a pastor for fifteen years, and in some of those years I preached a faith that could not survive the questions my own people would eventually ask it. I taped things together, the gospel and the country, the gospel and the party, the gospel and the quiet promise that God's chief interest was the smooth operation of a middle-class life, and I called the bundle Christianity, and I handed it to families who trusted me, and when the bundle failed in their hands, some of them concluded that God had failed. Some of the deconstruction happening in my county is the disassembly of sermons with my name on them. I do not write about this from a safe distance. There is no safe distance.

**So this essay stands on the one claim I owe every person at that table: deconstruction has a direction problem, not a tool problem. Demolition and excavation use the same instruments, the pry bar, the shovel, the refusal to respect a wall just because it is standing. From the street the two look identical. The difference is what you are digging for. One digs to get out. The other digs to get down, because under the additions, under everything the last few centuries nailed onto the house, there is something older, and the digging can be the way down to it rather than the way out of it. Demolition, or excavation. Nearly everything anyone will tell you about deconstruction sits downstream of that distinction, and almost nobody names it.**

## The grief is the honest part

Start where the tearing starts, because it rarely starts with an argument. It starts with a wound, and the wounds are not imaginary. In May 2022, Guidepost Solutions released its independent investigation into the Southern Baptist Convention's Executive Committee and found that leaders of the largest Protestant denomination in America had kept a private list of ministers accused of sexual abuse, hundreds of entries, maintained for years, while telling survivors who called for help that nothing could be done. The year before that, a posthumous investigation commissioned by his own ministry confirmed that Ravi Zacharias, the most celebrated apologist of his generation, a man whose books sat on my shelf, had used the cover of that ministry to prey on women. Beneath the covered cases run the unreported local ones: the church that protected the deacon and exiled the girl, the youth group where a kid's honest question was treated as a discipline problem.

And the pulpits that should have named all of it were often busy with other business. Over the last half century, large sections of the American church bound themselves to partisan politics so tightly that millions can no longer find the seam between the faith and the platform. I have written about that fusion elsewhere. Here it is enough to say that when a young woman concludes the church is a voting bloc with a music budget, she did not reach that conclusion irrationally. We handed her the evidence.

Then there are the answers, which for many people were the deepest wound, because they came from the people who were supposed to know. You asked why your father left, and got a slogan about God's plan. You asked how a good God watches a children's oncology ward, and were handed a verse like a coupon. I asked the first of those questions myself, as a boy growing up without a father, and I remember the coupons. A faith that answers its hardest questions with merchandise is training its most serious people to leave, and then blaming them for the training.

I know the counter-speech, and it deserves its strongest form: some deconstruction is appetite looking for an alibi, a decision already made, out shopping for respectable reasons. That is true of some. I have met them. But it is not true of most of the people at my table, and a diagnosis that flatters the diagnostician should always be checked twice. Because the person taking the faith apart is very often the one who took it most seriously. You do not tear at a thing you never expected to hold. The kid who actually read the whole Bible and noticed what is in it. The woman who actually believed the church was the body of Christ and therefore could not shrug when it behaved like any other corporation protecting its brand. The pew beside them can relax precisely because it never leaned its full weight on any of it. The deconstructor leaned, and something cracked, and the cracking sound was faith being taken seriously. Deconstruction is not usually rebellion. It is usually grief with a crowbar.

## The same tools

The word itself carries thirty seconds of useful history. Jacques Derrida coined *deconstruction* in the 1960s as a term of art for a way of reading texts; by the time it reached the hashtag it meant something simpler and sadder, the taking apart of an inherited evangelical faith, piece by piece, usually in public, usually in grief. I am not interested in policing the vocabulary. I am interested in the direction of the digging.

Because the alarm speech omits a fact it cannot afford to admit: most of what American deconstruction removes deserved to be removed. In 2005 the sociologist Christian Smith and his colleague Melinda Lundquist Denton published *Soul Searching*, the largest study of American teenage religion yet conducted, and gave the country's actual folk faith a name, moralistic therapeutic deism. Its creed, as they summarized it, runs roughly so: a God exists who watches over things; he wants people to be good and nice; the point of life is to be happy and feel good about yourself; God does not need to be involved unless you have a problem; good people go to heaven when they die. Read that list slowly and notice what is missing, sin, cross, resurrection, judgment, grace, cost, which is to say, notice that Christianity is missing. That is the deity a great deal of deconstruction is deconstructing. Beside him stand his colleagues: the tribal god who blesses one party's platform, the prosperity god who pays out for faith like a slot machine, the national god whose cross doubles as a flagpole. When a person takes that pantheon apart, they are not attacking the faith. They are agreeing with its first commandment. The church has a word for the demolition of false gods, and the word is not apostasy. Most of the rubble deserved to be rubble.

But now the question that decides everything, the one nobody at the demolition site wants to stop and answer: what are you digging *for*? A wrecking crew and an archaeological dig look identical from the road, the same dust, the same debris pile, the same disrespect for the existing structure. The difference is entirely in what the diggers believe is down there. The demolisher digs to clear the lot. The excavator digs because he has reason to think the ugly additions were additions, that under the vinyl siding and the drop ceilings and the seasonal flags there is a structure older than everything he hates about the house. Same shovel. Opposite prayer.

And I have watched what happens when the digging has no downward direction, so I will name it, gently, because I have loved some of these people. The crater becomes an address. There are men and women ten years into the demolition whose entire creed is now the list of things they no longer believe, who have made a settled identity out of the taking-apart, and taking apart is genuinely easier than building: the same feeling of progress at a fraction of the cost, and always an audience for the sound of breaking glass. Rubble is honest. Nobody can live in it. And the voices selling permanent demolition as freedom have usually found a way to bill by the swing.

## What the shovel hits

Dig down through the American additions and you do not reach empty dirt. The shovel rings. There is stone under this house, and the stone has dates carved into it.

In the year 325, the emperor Constantine convened bishops at Nicaea, among them, tradition remembers, men still carrying the marks of Diocletian's persecution, a missing eye, a maimed leg, to settle the teaching of an Alexandrian presbyter named Arius. Give Arius his due, because he was no cartoon. He was guarding the majesty of God the only way he could see, reasoning that the Father alone is without beginning, and that the Son, however exalted, must therefore be the first and greatest of creatures, nearest to God, but on our side of the line. It is a clean, plausible, reverent-sounding position; forms of it get reinvented every century. The council heard it and answered with a word chosen precisely because it could not be bent back into cleanliness: *homoousios*, the Son is of one being with the Father. Not the greatest creature. God from God, light from light. The church looked at the most reasonable reduction on offer and refused it, at a moment when some of the men refusing had already bled for less.

In 451 the Council of Chalcedon did the same service at the other pole of the mystery, confessing Christ as one person in two natures, fully God, fully man, and fencing the confession with four negations, usually translated *without confusion, without change, without division, without separation*. Notice what kind of sentences these are. They are not the product of comfortable men smoothing over a quarrel. They are the product of a church under pressure refusing every available simplification, from every direction, at cost, because each simplification would have made the faith easier and false.

That is the bedrock, and it has been under demolition for seventeen centuries. It is still there. Arius swung at it. The philosophers of the eighteenth century swung at it. The scholars who voted on the sayings of Jesus with colored beads swung at it. Empires that outlawed it and empires that domesticated it swung at it from opposite sides. Durability is not proof. But an honest demolisher, hearing the shovel ring like that, should at least grow curious about what kind of stone survives every crew that ever pronounced it finished.

And notice how small the floor is. Nicaea says nothing about your politics. Nothing about worship styles, the age of the earth, the timeline of the end, the schooling of children, or most of the fence lines the church that hurt you treated as matters of salvation. The creed that defines the faith is shorter than that church's membership covenant. Which means a large share of what is currently falling off your house was never load-bearing. Much of it was never in the blueprints at all.

## A monk with a pry bar

The church has been through this before, and the record is worth reading before you decide how your own dig ends. On October 31, 1517, an Augustinian friar and university professor named Martin Luther posted ninety-five theses for academic debate in Wittenberg, in Latin, addressed to scholars, opening with the claim (I paraphrase his first thesis) that when Christ said "repent" he meant the whole of a believer's life, not a transaction at a booth. Luther was not founding a movement. He was filing a repair request. He aimed at something specific, the indulgence trade, the machinery that had turned grace into revenue, and he expected the house to accept the repair. It excommunicated him instead, in 1521, and what we call the Reformation is in large part the story of a repair the institution refused.

What Luther declined to demolish tells you what kind of digger he was. He kept the creeds, all of them. Kept the Trinity of Nicaea and the two natures of Chalcedon, kept baptism and the Supper, kept the shape of the worship service with the false parts cut out, and put the Scriptures back at the center in the people's own language. The movement's slogan was a digging word: *ad fontes*, back to the sources, down through the medieval additions to Scripture and the fathers underneath. Luther swung as hard at the church of his day as anyone has ever swung, and he swung downward, toward a floor he was certain was there. It was an excavation that the institution experienced as a demolition, and the difference between those two descriptions is the entire argument of this essay.

I will not romanticize it. The digging cracked Europe. Wars followed it, and the fragments are still fragmenting five centuries later; an honest telling holds the wreckage in the same hands as the recovery. Excavation is not safe. Nothing about any of this is safe. The claim was never that digging costs nothing. The claim is that direction decides what the cost buys.

There is an older scene that catches the strange grief of rebuilding. When the exiles came home from Babylon and laid the foundation of the second temple, Ezra records that the young men shouted for joy while the old men who had seen the first house wept aloud, and the sound of weeping could not be told apart from the sound of joy (Ezra 3:12–13). Every rebuilt faith sounds like that. What rises on the old foundation will not look like what you lost, and there will be weeping mixed into the shouting, and the mixture is not failure. It is what recovery has always sounded like.

## Six verbs, one calling

There is one place in Scripture where God himself hands a man the wrecking bar, and it repays slow reading. In the thirteenth year of King Josiah, around 627 BC, the word of the LORD comes to a young man in the priest-town of Anathoth, and the commission runs like this:

> "See, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant." (Jeremiah 1:10, ESV)

Count the verbs. Six. Four of them are demolition, pluck up, break down, destroy, overthrow, and two of them are construction, build, plant, and all six are one calling, issued in one breath, to one man. God did not commission an optimist. He commissioned a demolisher, and he put the demolition first, because what Judah called faith had grown additions that had to come down before anything true could stand: the fusion of God and nation, the certainty that the temple guaranteed their safety, a religion that had become the state's chaplain. Jeremiah spent his life swinging at it. God sends him to the temple gate to say to the worshippers, "Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD'" (Jeremiah 7:4, ESV). Their holiest slogan. Their deepest security. A lie, and he was sent to break it in the doorway of the building it advertised. No one who has read the prophets imagines that, walking into an American sanctuary this Sunday, they would leave the additions standing.

But the commission does not stop at overthrow, and here the whole matter turns. The last two verbs govern the first four. *To build and to plant*, and notice what kind of verbs they are: the slow ones. Anyone can overthrow in an afternoon. Demolition is loud, fast, and photogenic. Building takes years, and planting takes seasons, and the planter has to stay, through the winters, after the audience that gathered for the breaking glass has drifted off. Four verbs of wrecking, two of building, and the two are the point of the four, because a prophet authorized only to tear down would be half a prophet, and God does not commission halves. The demolition is in the calling. It is not the calling.

## What was under my house

I told you I went into the house swinging, so I owe you the end of it, though I will keep it short, because I promised no speech. When my demolition was finished, and it was thorough, years of it, what I found at the bottom was not the Christianity I had refused. That religion, the suburban chaplaincy, the mascot god of the comfortable, the vending machine with a fish on the side: my demolition was right about it, and I have never rebuilt one plank of it. What was under the house was older and stranger and harder. A first-century rabbi who could not be recruited by anyone's empire, including the ones that fly his cross. A God who demands death before he gives resurrection. A grace that costs nothing and then claims everything. A tomb that the best counterarguments I owned could not keep sealed. I did not find a faith that answered every question I had carried in. I found one that could hold the questions' weight, which is different, and better, and nobody had told me it existed.

And I found that the only prayer a rebuilder gets had already been written, by a man out of arguments, standing in front of Jesus with a dying son: he "cried out and said, 'I believe; help my unbelief!'" (Mark 9:24, ESV). Both halves in one breath, and the miracle came anyway. That is not the prayer of a finished man. It is the prayer of a standing one. It has held my weight ever since.

So, to the person at that table: no speech, and no deadline. Nobody standing in a half-taken-apart house needs a schedule shouted through the window, and the pressure you feel to land somewhere, anywhere, so that everyone around you can exhale, is not coming from God. Paul's instruction to a young church holds both edges of your situation in one sentence: "but test everything; hold fast what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21, ESV). Test everything, the verse authorizes your crowbar. Hold fast what is good, the verse assumes the testing finds something, and that you will need your hands free to grip it.

You are allowed to keep the question inside the faith. Whatever they taught you, doubt is not the exit, and certainty was never the entrance fee, the father in Mark 9 got his answer mid-sentence, unbelief still on his lips. And you are allowed to dig past the point where the podcasts stop, past the crater where demolition sets up its gift shop, down through the additions, through the politics and the merchandise and the coupons they handed you instead of answers, down to where the shovel rings.

I do not know how long your dig takes. Mine took years, and I started with more wreckage than most. I only ask you to notice, some night when the house is quiet and the pile of what you no longer believe has grown taller than what you still do, that there are two ways to hold a shovel, and that they look identical from the street, and that they are not the same. One is how you leave. The other is how you get to the bottom.

Take it apart, then. Take it all the way apart, toward something. The bedrock is not going anywhere. It never has.
posts.excerpt: Demolition and excavation use the same tools, the pry bar, the shovel, the refusal to respect a wall just because it is standing. The difference is what you are digging for. Most of what deconstruction removes deserved to go. Under the additions there is something older.

posts.title: Not Every Darkness Is a Doctrine Problem
posts.body:
Fifteen years of pastoring keeps sending me the same two people.

The first sits down in my office and apologizes before she says anything else. A doctor diagnosed her with depression years ago, her doctor, her word, not mine, and the medication helps, and that is what she has come to confess. A church she loved before this one taught her an arithmetic she cannot stop running: joy is a fruit of the Spirit, she cannot feel joy, therefore the branch must be bad. Someone in a Bible study told her the pills were a way of not trusting God. Someone else asked, gently and wrongly, what sin she might be harboring. So she has managed her illness the way other people manage an affair, in secret, off the family ledger, confessed to no one, and what she wants from me is permission. She wants to know whether she can take the medication and the Lord's Supper in the same week.

The second has no shame at all; he has vocabulary instead. He can name his anhedonia, his attachment style, the family system that produced him. He has a therapist he likes, and I am glad he does, that gladness is real, and it will matter later. But he is not sleeping either, and when we finally get underneath the language he tells me what the language was built over: a thing he did two years ago that he has never once called wrong out loud. Every frame he owns keeps translating the ache into symptoms, stress, rumination, an inner critic to be quieted. It has not worked, because some guilt is not a malfunction. Some guilt is working exactly as designed, like the pain that gets your hand off the stove, and there is no one left in his life with a category for that.

The church has failed them both, and failed them with the same confidence. To the first we said: this darkness is spiritual, so pray harder. To the second the culture said, and the church, tired of being embarrassed by its own record here, increasingly says along with it: every darkness is chemical or circumstantial, so there is nothing in you a professional cannot reach. Two opposite errors. One result. A person gets erased either way, reduced to a soul that happens to be haunting a body, or to a body that has somehow talked itself into believing it has a soul.

**So this essay stands on a claim I have spent fifteen years earning the right to make: depression is real, and the dark night of the soul is real, and they are not the same thing, and they can occupy the same person in the same season. A broken serotonin system is no more a verdict on your faith than a broken leg. And a soul under conviction, or in grief, or in the silence John of the Cross mapped, is not a disorder to be managed out of the way. The line between them is genuinely hard to find, which is exactly why no pastor should hunt for it alone, and no Christian should be ashamed of needing both a doctor and a church.**

## The sermon I preached wrong

I know the first error from the inside, because I committed it from a pulpit.

Early in my ministry a man in my congregation stopped being able to feel his own life. He said it almost that plainly, the color had gone out of things, prayer included, work included, his kids included, and I gave him what I had. Philippians 4. A reading plan. The assurance that the joy would return when the disciplines did. He was more faithful to my prescription than I have ever been to anyone's. He prayed more, read more, served more, and sank further, and now he carried the extra stone I had handed him: the certainty that his continued darkness was evidence against his faith, since he had done everything the pastor said and the lights had not come on. What finally helped him was a physician. What I had been treating as a doctrine problem had a body in it the whole time, sleep gone, appetite gone, concentration gone, everything grey at once, and I had walked past every one of those signals because my theology had no shelf to put them on. He forgave me before I asked. I have been slower, because I did not merely fail to help him. I baptized his suffering as his fault.

The error is not stupid, and it did not come from nowhere. Say the strongest version of it, because its defenders deserve that much: the pray-harder church is holding a truth the clinic cannot say out loud, that the soul is real, that some darkness does lift when sin is confessed and forgiven, that a human being is more than chemistry, and that handing every sorrow straight to the pharmacy is its own kind of despair. The people who say pray harder have usually watched prayer work. Their mistake is not believing too much in the soul. It is declining, in practice, to believe in the body, quietly refusing the doctrine of creation they would defend to the death on paper.

And the suspicion behind it was not invented from nothing. When the modern clinic introduced itself to the church, it introduced itself as a rival: Freud, in *The Future of an Illusion* (1927), classed religion as a wish-projection humanity would outgrow, a kind of inherited neurosis. The church took him at his word and returned fire for two generations, and our people bled in the crossfire, told, from pulpits like mine, that the enemy's medicine could not be God's provision. Add the newer teaching that equates belonging to God with feeling well, prosperity in its emotional key, and the arithmetic my first visitor runs was complete: if you are his, you should be happy; you are not happy; draw the conclusion. That arithmetic is not the theology of the psalms, half of which are written from the bottom of a well. It is a theology with no cross in it, and it breaks the people who believe it.

## The frame that swallowed the soul

The second error is younger and it is winning.

Philip Rieff saw it coming in *The Triumph of the Therapeutic* (1966): the culture's center of gravity shifting from religious man to psychological man, from the person who asks *am I forgiven* to the person who asks *am I well*, with well-being installed as the final measure and the clinic inheriting the authority the church used to hold. A person in crisis once went somewhere to be saved. Now he goes somewhere to feel better, and the difference between those two errands has quietly become invisible.

Be honest about why the therapeutic won: in large part, the church deserved to lose. The clinic sat with sufferers we had shamed. It did not ask the weeping woman what sin she was harboring. It kept people alive whom sermons like my early ones were actively harming, and its medicine works, measurably, repeatably, mercifully. None of that is the enemy of the faith. When I say I am glad the man has a therapist, it is not diplomacy.

But a frame with no category for God cannot see everything, and what it cannot see, it renames. Conviction becomes toxic guilt, and since the frame can only treat the feeling of guilt, never the fact of it, the man in my office got two years of increasingly sophisticated language for an ache that wanted one old word. Grief becomes a disorder: in 2022 the DSM's revisers added prolonged grief to the manual, so that mourning which outstays roughly a year can now be coded and billed. The clinicians who added it were not villains; they were reaching for mourners whose grief had genuinely trapped them. But notice what kind of culture needs the category, one with no practices left for carrying sorrow, so the only place to put a widow who still weeps at fourteen months is a diagnostic bin. And the dark night, the deliberate, purifying silence of God that the tradition spent centuries learning to recognize, reads, in this frame, as low-grade depression to be medicated at the first sign of dryness. The verdict on the therapeutic is the one this platform keeps reaching about every secular account worth taking seriously: it got the symptom right and the anthropology wrong. The first error erases the body. This one erases the soul, and it does it politely, with excellent intentions, one renamed reality at a time.

## The body that groans

I did not come to faith believing in souls. I was an atheist first, and the atheist I was would have sided cheerfully with the second error: the mind is the brain, the brain is matter, and everything called spiritual is chemistry that has not been explained yet. Becoming a Christian did not require me to renounce that respect for the body. It required me to stop believing the body was the whole story.

Because Scripture's picture of a human being is stranger than either error. God forms dust and breathes into it, "and the man became a living creature" (Genesis 2:7, ESV), not a soul issued a container, not meat that learned to dream, but one creature, dust and breath in a unity so tight the seam never shows. And that unity is fallen all the way through. Paul is explicit that the wreckage runs wider than the will: "For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:22–23, ESV). The brain is creation. Three pounds of it, electric and bruisable, and it groans with everything else, which is why a failing thyroid can flatten a saint, why the weeks after childbirth can turn a faithful woman's mind against her, why a man can inherit darkness down the family line the way he inherits his father's hands. Calling that inheritance a faith problem is not rigor. It is cruelty with a verse attached. And notice where Paul's sentence lands: not on escape from the body but on "the redemption of our bodies." Christianity is, in this sense, the least spiritualized of faiths. It does not promise to rescue you out of your nervous system. It promises to raise it.

## What John of the Cross actually wrote

The soul's side of the line has a map, and we owe it to a prisoner.

In December 1577 John of the Cross was seized by his own Carmelite brothers, the reform he served had enemies inside the order, and locked in a cell in Toledo scarcely larger than his body. He escaped the next summer, and out of that darkness came a poem, and out of the poem, in the years that followed (c. 1578–1585), the commentary the world knows as *The Dark Night of the Soul*. We have worn his phrase down to a synonym for any bad season, and the wear has cost us his precision. John was not describing sadness. He was describing a specific work of God: the deliberate withdrawal of felt sweetness from a believer who had, without noticing, begun to love the sweetness more than the God it pointed to, consolation removed the way a surgeon removes what the patient cannot heal around, so the soul learns to love God in the dark, for himself, with nothing in it for her. Not abandonment. Weaning.

But the detail we skip is that John wrote a differential. In the first book of the commentary he sets down signs for telling his dark night apart from its counterfeits, and he names *melancholy*, his century's word for what a clinician would now assess as depression, as a condition that can mimic the night or tangle with it. The marks he gives are worth restating in plain words. In the true night, the dryness empties prayer of all its old pleasure, yet the ache stays aimed at God: the soul is anxious *about him*, afraid of having failed him, longing without a landing place. The person still cares, painfully, in one particular direction. Mere melancholy, John says, carries no such Godward solicitude, the dryness is just dryness, weather without a compass. The founding text of the dark night refuses, on its own pages, to treat every darkness as the dark night. We kept his phrase and lost his caution.

Held alongside what medicine has learned since, John's marks still work, roughly, and I hand them to you as a pastor and not as a screening tool. The dark night tends to be strangely local: prayer goes dead while dinner still tastes like something, the work still holds some color, and the grief is *about God*, his silence is the wound. Depression tends to flatten the whole field at once, God, food, work, sleep, the faces of your own children going grey together, the body sinking with the mind. If everything has gone grey, your body is telling you something, and the faithful response is a doctor's appointment this week, not a longer quiet time. If the world still has color and only God has gone silent while you ache toward him, the tradition has a name and a map for where you are, and I have written about that country elsewhere. And often, this is the maddening part, and the true one, it is both, in the same chest, in the same month. The two travel together, each darkening the other. Which is why the sorting was never meant to be homework you finish alone.

## The preacher who kept fainting

If the pray-harder equation were true, church history would falsify it on one man alone.

On the evening of 19 October 1856, Charles Spurgeon, twenty-two years old, already the most famous preacher in England, stood before thousands at the Surrey Gardens Music Hall when someone shouted fire. There was no fire. There was a stampede, and seven people died in it, and Spurgeon was carried from the pulpit a different man than the one who had mounted it. By the testimony of those closest to him, and by his own, the darkness that opened that night revisited him for the rest of his life.

He did not hide it. He built a lecture for his pastoral students, it sits in *Lectures to My Students* under the title "The Minister's Fainting Fits", and told them, in substance, that seasons of causeless despondency had fallen on him so heavily he would not wish the acquaintance on any of them; that the mind can sink to depths the body never reaches; that such fits visit most who carry the weight of souls, and that the men who comfort best are the ones who have been in the dark themselves. He refused to call the darkness sin, in himself or anyone. He prescribed what his century had, rest, time away, the company of friends, and he kept preaching, heavy, for decades, to the largest congregation in the world. His theology did not cure him. His theology carried him, and the difference between those two verbs is nearly the whole argument of this essay. No one audits Spurgeon's orthodoxy. If the medicine of his century had been better, he would have been right to take it, and we would have lost nothing of him but some of the agony.

## Bread before the whisper

Scripture got to all of this first, and it got there with a story the church keeps preaching around the edges of.

First Kings 18 is the triumph: fire from heaven on Carmel, the prophets of Baal routed, the long drought broken, Elijah vindicated in front of the whole nation. Then one queen sends one threat, and the man who called down fire runs for his life, south past Beersheba, out into the wilderness, alone.

> But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers." And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat." And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again. And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God. (1 Kings 19:4–8, ESV)

The text says it as plainly as it can be said: he asked that he might die. Scripture does not flinch from the sentence, does not dress it up, and does not linger over it, and I will follow the text on all three. If that sentence has taken up residence in you, notice that God does not argue with Elijah about it. What he does instead is stranger and better than an argument.

Count what is missing from God's response. No rebuke. No sermon. Not one word, yet, about the theology of despair, and there was plenty to correct; Elijah's claim to be the last faithful man in Israel was factually wrong. Instead: sleep. A touch. Bread, warm, and water. More sleep. Bread again. The first thing the LORD of hosts does for a prophet who wants to die is feed him and let him rest, twice, and the only sentence spoken under that tree may be the most pastoral in the Old Testament, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." Not: your faith is too small. The road is too long, the strength is gone, and God addresses the body first because the man is a creature and his Maker has never once been embarrassed by that.

Only later, at Horeb, comes the question, "What are you doing here, Elijah?", and Elijah's answer, given twice, word for word, is the isolation talking: I alone am left, and they want my life. Then the wind that tore the mountains, "but the LORD was not in the wind"; the earthquake and the fire, and the LORD was not in them either; "and after the fire the sound of a low whisper" (1 Kings 19:11–12, ESV). And even then God never explains the darkness. He re-gives the man his work, kings to anoint, a successor to call. He gives him a companion; Elisha will not leave his side. And he corrects despair's arithmetic with a number: seven thousand in Israel who have never bowed to Baal. The despair claimed *only I am left*. God did not debate the claim. He outnumbered it.

The order of the text is the theology. Body, presence, word, work, company, in that sequence, none skipped. One of our errors starts at the word and shames the body; the other stops at the bread and starves the soul. God ran the whole sequence, in order, for a man at the bottom, and any care that calls itself biblical has to keep his order.

And if the broom tree is where you are tonight, if the darkness has begun to tell you that you should not be here, that the people you love would be lighter without you, then hear one thing said with no art at all: that thought is a symptom, not a verdict, and it lies with tremendous fluency, and it is lying now. In the United States you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any hour, and a human being will answer. Do that, and then tell one person who loves you, out loud, today. God's first answer to a prophet who asked to die was to keep him alive and feed him. Let the people near you be the angel with the bread.

## Both a doctor and a church

Some of what this essay claims is doctrine, and most of it is not, and the difference matters. That bodies are real, created, fallen, and destined for resurrection, that is first-order ground, creed-level, not up for a vote. That souls are real, that guilt can be true, that God sometimes withdraws sweetness on purpose, doctrine as well, old as the psalms. But where the line falls in any particular life, whether this Tuesday's darkness is a body failing, a soul in surgery, or both at once, is not doctrine at all. It is wisdom, and Scripture is blunt about how wisdom arrives: "in an abundance of counselors there is safety" (Proverbs 11:14, ESV). Plural on purpose. A pastor alone is not an abundance. Neither is a prescription pad.

So let me say the plain thing in my own voice rather than in fine print: I am a pastor, not a clinician, and nothing in this essay is medical advice. It is one shepherd's account of the territory, written so that you will be quicker, not slower, to put real help around you. What fifteen years has actually built in me is a shorter road to the phone, the names of counselors and a psychiatrist I trust, handed out the way we hand out casseroles, as ordinary church. And two questions I did not know to ask the man I failed: Has everything gone grey, or is the ache aimed at God? And, before any of that, when did you last sleep through a night? The people I have pastored through both darknesses tell me the same two things from opposite directions. The medication did not medicate God away; it cleared enough fog for them to find him in the dark, still there, un-offended by the pill. And the therapy did not absolve them; a session cannot forgive sins, and the honest therapists never claimed it could, but it taught them to sleep, and forgiveness is easier to believe at seven in the morning than at three.

I told the woman in my office what I will tell you: take the medication and take the Supper, in the same week, with the same clean conscience, because both come from the hand of the same Lord, one through the common grace he gives to medicine, one through the covenant grace he gives to his church, and he is not divided against himself. I told the man the old word for what he did, and then the older word, forgiveness, and what it cost, and we needed no scare quotes for either. And I keep the memory of my wrong sermon where I can see it, because the man I preached it to deserves to be more than my regret. He is my instruction.

The line between the body's darkness and the soul's is hard to find. That is not a flaw in the map; it is a fact about creatures, we are dust and breath in one piece, and the seam does not show. So the darkness, when it comes, will rarely announce its department. Go to the doctor. Stay in the church. Say the psalm you cannot feel and take the pill you wish you did not need, and let no one, not the deacon with the verse, not the culture with the diagnosis, talk you out of half of what you are. Elijah ate the bread before he heard the whisper. Both came from the same God, tending the same man, who was one creature the whole way down. So are you.
posts.excerpt: The church has told the clinically ill to pray harder and told the spiritually dry to get their chemistry checked, with the same confidence, and both answers erase a person. On depression, the dark night of the soul, and the line no one should have to find alone.

posts.title: A Whole Life
posts.body:
Some years ago I went back through my old sermon notes looking for something I no longer remember, and I found something I had never once noticed while writing them. The illustrations. Year after year of them, my wife, my sons, the dinner table, the minivan, the argument at bedtime about brushing teeth. If you reconstructed my congregation from my sermons alone, you would conclude that every adult in the room went home to a full house. On any given Sunday, a third of them went home to an empty one. I had been preaching to my own kitchen for fifteen years and calling it application. And no one ever complained, which is the detail that should have alarmed me most, because it means the single members of my church had learned, long before I stood up, that church is a place where other people's lives are the examples.

They are not a niche. In 1960, roughly seven in ten American adults were married; by 2010, Pew Research Center found the share had fallen to barely half, and it has not recovered. Add together the never married, the divorced, and the widowed, and the unmarried are the fastest-growing presence in the American pew, and the American church, especially my wing of it, has spent those same decades building as if the household were the unit of membership. The nursery wing, the youth wing, the marriage retreat, the family camp, the sermon series every February. We called ourselves a family of families and never heard what the phrase said to the person who walked in alone.

**So this essay stands on a claim I have no natural right to make and every scriptural obligation to: the New Testament does not treat singleness as a waiting room, a consolation prize, or a problem God has been asked to fix. It calls the unmarried life good, Paul's own word, a calling with its own content, kept to the end by the Lord of the church and by the apostle who planted half of it. A church that cannot say this plainly has not overvalued marriage. It has misread its own book. And I write this as a man with a wedding ring and five sons, which is exactly why it needs writing, and exactly why you should watch my hands while I write it. The people who built the family-shaped church were people shaped like me.**

## The chapter married preachers skip

Paul takes up the question directly, in a letter to a church that had asked him about marriage. His answer has been read aloud at almost no weddings, for reasons that will become obvious.

> I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another. To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. (1 Corinthians 7:7–8, ESV)

Sit with the first sentence before the qualifications arrive. *I wish that all were as I myself am.* Paul is unmarried, and he wishes everyone were. Not tolerates it. Not makes pastoral peace with it. Wishes it, for the whole church. If a preacher stood up on a Sunday and said those words as his own, his elders would meet with him by Thursday. Paul says them as Scripture. And the word he chooses for the unmarried state is the word the family-centered church has never quite managed to say without a comma after it: *good*. Not good-for-now. Not good-until. Good, the same verdict God pronounced over creation.

Later in the chapter he explains why, and this is the passage that gets skipped hardest, because it does not merely permit singleness. It ranks it.

> I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife, and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord. (1 Corinthians 7:32–35, ESV)

Read it without flinching. The unmarried person is anxious about the things of the Lord; the married person's interests are *divided*, and Paul does not mean that as a rebuke of the married, because the division is right and owed. A husband who was not anxious to please his wife would be sinning against her. That is precisely the point. Marriage is a good that divides you, lawfully and necessarily, and singleness is a good that leaves the whole self available for undivided devotion. On the one axis Paul actually measures, freedom for the things of the Lord, the advantage runs toward the single. Fifteen centuries of family-pew Christianity has read this chapter upside down: marriage as the norm requiring no defense, singleness as the exception requiring an explanation. The chapter itself argues the reverse. If either estate has to justify itself before this text, it is not the unmarried one.

Paul is careful, and honesty requires tracking his care. He commands no one; "each has his own gift from God", marriage one gift, singleness another, neither the default issue of being human. He is blunt that celibacy without self-control is a fire hazard: "For it is better to marry than to burn with passion" (1 Corinthians 7:9, ESV). And he says he intends "not to lay any restraint upon you." The chapter is not anti-marriage; the man who wrote Ephesians 5 cannot be. But the direction of its argument is unmistakable, and we have spent a very long time preaching it as if it ran the other way.

## The strongest case against me

The family-centered reading of Scripture is not stupid, and it deserves its best form before any verdict. It runs like this. The first command God gives humanity is "Be fruitful and multiply" (Genesis 1:28, ESV), and the first problem God names in creation is solitude: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him" (Genesis 2:18, ESV). Marriage is a creation ordinance, older than Israel, older than the fall. The household is the Bible's ordinary school of faith, Deuteronomy 6 assigns the teaching of the children to the home, not the temple. The Psalms call children a heritage from the Lord and picture blessing as a table ringed with olive shoots. And when Paul commends singleness, he flags his own context: "in view of the present distress" (1 Corinthians 7:26, ESV), counsel for a persecuted minority in a hostile empire, the argument goes, not a permanent ranking of estates. Scripture even warns, in 1 Timothy 4, against those who forbid marriage as a mark of false teaching. A defender of the family-shaped church would sign every sentence of that paragraph, and every sentence of it is true.

Two things it cannot do. It cannot make "not good that the man should be alone" mean "not good that the man should be unmarried", because the Bible answers Adam's solitude twice, once with Eve and once with the church, and the second answer is the one the New Testament spends its pages building. And it cannot quarantine 1 Corinthians 7 inside a first-century emergency, because the grounds Paul actually gives in verses 32 through 35 are not crisis-grounds. They are devotion-grounds, anxieties, interests, the undivided heart, and they hold in a suburb as firmly as under Nero. When Paul says "the appointed time has grown very short" (1 Corinthians 7:29, ESV), he is not misjudging the calendar. He is naming the church's permanent address: between the resurrection and the return, every generation lives in the shortened time, and the unmarried life is one of the two faithful ways to keep house there.

And beneath both answers stands a fact the family-centered reading has never had a comfortable place for. Jesus of Nazareth, the one human being in whom our nature exists without defect, the man Chalcedon confesses as fully God and fully man, never married. If the unmarried life were a lesser or incomplete humanity, the incarnation would be its refutation. He was not waiting for his real life to begin. He was not half a person hoping to be completed at an altar. He is the standard of the completed human, and he lived and died single. The church can say marriage is good with its whole chest. What it cannot say, while looking at its own Lord, is that marriage is the norm from which singleness deviates.

## The single Savior and the dry tree
