Jesus said so himself, in a passage nearly as unpreached as Paul's. When his teaching on divorce landed so hard that the disciples blurted out that maybe it is better not to marry at all, he did not correct them. He said something stranger:

> For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it. (Matthew 19:12, ESV)

Eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom, people who set marriage aside not because they failed to find it but because the kingdom claimed the space it would have filled. Jesus names a category of person the modern church barely has vocabulary for: not single-because-unlucky but single-because-called. And he had already redefined the family in a scene that scandalized his own. Told that his mother and brothers were outside asking for him, "looking about at those who sat around him, he said, 'Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother'" (Mark 3:34–35, ESV). The exclamation is his, not mine. Blood built the old family; the will of God builds the new one, and it is the only family Jesus ever calls his own in that scene. Later, pressed with a riddle about a much-married widow, he says plainly that marriage belongs to this age and not to the resurrection, the children of the age to come "neither marry nor are given in marriage" (Luke 20:34–36, paraphrased with the reference so you can weigh it yourself). Every marriage in your congregation is temporary. Every single believer in your congregation is living, now, in the estate the whole church will share forever. They are not behind the times. They are ahead of them.

None of this fell out of the sky. Seven centuries before, Isaiah had already heard God make a promise to the person the covenant community treated as its most obvious dead end, the eunuch, cut off from the one thing the ancient world counted as a future:

> Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, "The LORD will surely separate me from his people"; and let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree." For thus says the LORD: "To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off." (Isaiah 56:3–5, ESV)

A name *better* than sons and daughters. Not a consolation matching what the childless man lost, an exceeding of it, spoken to the man whose family tree ends with him. I have heard a thousand sermons on family legacy. I have preached my share. I cannot remember hearing this text preached once, and I know I never preached it, though I might have noticed that when Luke narrates the gospel's first great leap outward in Acts 8, the convert in the chariot is a eunuch, reading the scroll of Isaiah, a few columns from the promise written to him. The Bible kept honoring the people my sermon file forgot.

## Fifteen centuries, two ditches

The early church took all this literally enough to build institutions on it. Paul's instruction that widows over sixty be "enrolled" (1 Timothy 5:9) hardened into a recognized order, the unmarried not as a pastoral problem but as a roster, with duties and honor. By the year 251, a letter from Cornelius, bishop of Rome, preserved in Eusebius's *Ecclesiastical History*, could report more than fifteen hundred widows and distressed persons supported by that one church's rolls. And the celibates were not the church's leftovers; in a Roman world where the family line was the empire's pension plan and childbearing a civic duty, the Christian who renounced marriage for the kingdom was a public scandal, a living claim that a person's future did not depend on producing heirs, because God had promised the dry tree a name.

Then the church drove into the first ditch. Honor for celibacy curdled into a caste system: the celibate as spiritual athlete, the married as the crowd in the cheap seats. When a monk named Jovinian argued, around 390, that marriage and virginity stood equal in merit before God, synods at Rome and Milan condemned him in 393, and Jerome's treatise against him disparaged marriage so ferociously that Jerome's own friends tried to pull the book out of circulation. The medieval settlement that followed made celibacy mandatory for the clergy and marriage a concession to weakness, and it took the Reformation to break it. When Luther married Katharina von Bora in 1525, an ex-monk marrying an ex-nun, to the delight of every pamphleteer in Europe, he was not lowering the church's standards. He was restoring Paul's actual sentence: each has his own gift.

But Protestants did not stop at the correction. Over four centuries we drove, slowly and with the best intentions, into the opposite ditch. Marriage went from despised to permitted to celebrated to assumed, until the family was no longer one calling among two but the shape of the church itself. The postwar suburban congregation finished the job: programming by household, discipleship routed through the nursery and the youth group, "family church" as a selling point, and the unmarried adult filed in a ministry named like a junk drawer. Singles ministry, as if the widows Paul enrolled and the eunuchs Jesus blessed were a demographic to be matched off. Two ditches, fifteen centuries apart, and the same error at the bottom of both: one estate crowned the norm and the other made to explain itself. The medieval church demanded a reason you would marry. We demand a reason you have not. Paul refused both demands in a single verse, and neither age could hear him.

I did not inherit this from a distance. I built it. My church calendar, my programming instincts, my sermon file full of minivans, a man with five sons constructing, in perfect sincerity, a church where his own life was the template. The father of five is exactly the wrong man to write this essay comfortably, which is why he has to write it uncomfortably or not at all.

## The culture's version of the same mistake

It would flatter the church to say the surrounding culture got this right, but the culture has simply dug the same hole from the other side. The secular script for singleness is not a waiting room; it is a showroom, the optimized self, the curated feed, the options kept permanently open, the app that renders other persons as inventory to be swiped through. It sounds like freedom and functions like weightlessness: a single life with no calling in it, answerable to nothing, pointed at nothing but its own refinement. And notice what this script shares with the church's script, because underneath they agree. Both assume the single life is about the self. The church says: the self on hold, waiting to be chosen. The culture says: the self as the project, endlessly under renovation. Paul says neither. His single person is not waiting and not self-curating; she is *anxious about the things of the Lord*, seized, occupied, spent on something. The Christian answer to the church that pities singles and the culture that flatters them is the same answer, delivered with the same instrument: the unmarried life is not an absence. It is a vocation with content.

## A calling with content

Name the content, because a calling with no substance is just a compliment. Devotion is the first, the undivided heart Paul describes, the whole self available to God without the lawful, honorable division a family requires. Availability is the second, and church history is largely a record of it: the missionaries, the scholars, the pastors of impossible parishes, the ones who could go because no one at home would be abandoned by their going, who could stay late in the crisis, give away the savings, take the assignment. My own divided interests are not a failure; they are my vows working. But I know what my vows cost the church in my availability, and the single believer's freedom is not what is left over from a marriage that failed to happen. It is a resource the kingdom has spent lavishly in every generation.

And the third is friendship, not as consolation, but as covenant. Around the 1160s, Aelred, the Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx, wrote *Spiritual Friendship*, a book by a celibate man that takes friendship more seriously than nearly anything written since. Aelred had renounced marriage and family entirely and did not experience this as exile from intimacy, because for him friendship was intimacy of the highest order, two souls knit in the love of God, with Christ himself making a third between them. He dared to say one might almost rephrase Scripture: God is friendship. Our age hears that as sentimentality. It is actually an indictment, of a church that has made marriage the only covenant it knows how to honor, so that every other love in the building floats, unpromised and unprotected. The single life Scripture commends was never meant to be a solitary life. It was meant to be lived inside a family that does not run on blood, the one Jesus pointed to when he looked around the room at those seated near him.

That family carries a claim the modern church has almost forgotten it makes. Stanley Hauerwas argued, in *A Community of Character* (1981), that Christian singleness is the church's boldest wager: a congregation that honors the unmarried is declaring that its future comes by witness and conversion, not by birthrate, that God, not biology, secures the church's tomorrow. Every honored single believer in a pew is that doctrine, standing up. And Sam Allberry, a pastor for whom singleness is not a season but the whole road, and who has written about it from inside a lifelong celibacy, puts the complementary claim in *7 Myths About Singleness* (2019): if marriage bears witness to the shape of the gospel, Christ's covenant love for his church, then singleness bears witness to its sufficiency, that Christ is actually enough for a whole human life. Both estates preach. A church with only married members has lost a sermon it cannot get from anyone else.

Hear what is not being said. Marriage is not lowered an inch by any of this; the house rule of this essay is that no calling gets softened to sharpen another. Scripture opens with a wedding in a garden and closes with one at the end of the age, and marriage is a mystery that refers to Christ and the church, I believe that, I preach it, I live inside it with gratitude. But the wedding at the end is the only one that lasts, and both estates are testimonies to it: marriage a portrait of that covenant, singleness a proof it can fill a life. Two gifts, Paul said. One of one kind and one of another. Neither is the default human.

## The people in the room

I have been writing about singleness as a doctrine, and no one lives inside a doctrine. In the rooms I pastor, the unmarried life has many faces, and a faithful church learns to meet each without diagnosing any. There are the contentedly single, who mostly need the church to stop treating their contentment as denial, to stop auditing their peace for the sadness it assumes must be underneath. There are the painfully lonely, and their ache is real and owed no minimizing: the empty side of the bed, the long Sunday afternoon, the absence of one person whose whole job is to know you. Genesis is still true, it is not good for a human being to be alone, but the New Testament's answer to that verse is bigger than matchmaking, and if a single believer is alone inside a congregation, the church is failing its own doctrine of the household of God; the single person is not failing theirs. There are the divorced, carrying a grief with a verdict stapled to it, who have learned that some churches treat a broken marriage as a contagious condition. There are the widowed, Paul's first addressees, the original enrolled order, too often thanked for their casseroles and forgotten by the calendar. And there are believers whose same-sex attraction has led them, at real and continuing cost, into a celibacy most married Christians have never priced for a single day, often inside churches that praise the sacrifice in the abstract while building no household in which a person could actually live it. Isaiah 56 was written to the one whose obedience costs the future everyone else takes for granted. A name better than sons and daughters. The church that will not make that promise audible has no business quoting the rest of the chapter.

And one sentence in this whole subject needs to be retired from married mouths, or earned before it is spoken. *Singleness is a gift.* Paul said it, and Paul could, he lived it to the end. When a man with a wedding ring says it from a stage and drives home to a loud table, the single person in the third row hears exactly what he means: a gift he is glad someone else received. I have said the sentence that way. I am the man in that sentence. The words are true, and in my mouth they were cheap, because a church earns the right to call singleness a gift only by becoming the kind of family in which it functions as one, where the unmarried are hosts and not perpetual guests, godparents and elders and not a demographic, woven into households and wills and Tuesday dinners, honored the way the church of Cornelius's Rome honored its fifteen hundred.

I will go home tonight to the full house. Five boys, a loud table, the life my sermons kept mistaking for everyone's. Somewhere in my congregation a woman my age will let herself into a quiet apartment, and the question this essay finally asks is not whether her life is whole. Scripture settled that; her Lord lived her estate, and his apostle called it good, and Isaiah promised her a name that outlasts my genealogy. The question is whether her church believes its own book, because he was thirty-three, unmarried, and no one's father, and if he walked into most of our lobbies we would welcome him warmly, hand him a card, and wonder quietly when he was going to settle down. The church that has no honored place for the unmarried has not overvalued marriage. It has undervalued Christ.

Two gifts, one of one kind and one of another. He kept the one we pity.
posts.excerpt: Jesus was single. Paul was single and called it good. The church that treats the unmarried life as a waiting room has not overvalued marriage, it has misread its own book. A father of five on the chapter married preachers skip.

posts.title: The Work Nobody Watches
posts.body:
My husband works in public. He stands in a pulpit on Sunday mornings and a few hundred people watch him do his work, and when he does it well they tell him so at the door. I hear those sermons from the pew, with our five sons in a row beside me, five boys in shoes that were found, after searching, under five different pieces of furniture. His work has an aisle where people shake his hand. Mine has no door to stand at. Nobody has ever congratulated a woman because her sons know how to sit through a service, and nobody knows what it cost to get them there.

I am not complaining. I am describing. There is a kind of work that holds a household and a generation together, and its defining feature is that it does not show. It has to be done again tomorrow, which is why it never looks finished. It is spread across ten thousand small acts, which is why it never looks large. Ask a mother at the end of the day what she did and watch her reach for an answer, not because she did nothing but because she did a thousand things, and not one of them will still be done by Thursday. The meal was eaten. The floor is dirty again. The argument I settled at breakfast has been reopened for renegotiation by supper. If you measure work by what remains visible when the day ends, motherhood measures near zero, forever.

The question is who is doing the measuring, and by what.

## The two verdicts

Two verdicts get handed down on this work, from opposite benches, and they disagree about everything except the sentence.

The first comes from the culture, and it says the work is a waste of a mind. It rarely says it that plainly anymore. It says it in the shape of a question at a dinner party, *and what do you do?*, and in the particular quality of the silence after the answer. It says it in the word *just*, as in *just a mom*, a word mothers now say about themselves, preemptively, the way you flinch before a blow you have taken before. It says it in every framework where a résumé gap is a wound to be explained and the formation of five human beings is the gap.

I want to be fair to that verdict, because it did not come from nowhere. For a long stretch of history the home was not a calling offered to women; it was a sentence imposed on them. It was the only room a woman was permitted to occupy, the door was locked from the outside, and the lock was often quoted in the King James. I cannot pretend not to know this. I was raised in a late, sour version of exactly that world, where a woman's smallness was preached to her as her sanctification. So when the door finally gave way and a generation walked out cursing the room itself, I understood the cursing. But somewhere inside it a false equation got made: because women were confined to this work, the work must be small. That conclusion punishes the work for the sins of the men who made it a cage. Feeding people you love was never the insult. The lock was the insult.

The second verdict comes from the church, and it arrives wearing a carnation. In 1908 a woman named Anna Jarvis organized the first Mother's Day observance, in Grafton, West Virginia, to honor the kind of unrecorded labor her own mother's life had been made of, and then spent her remaining decades fighting, bitterly and in vain, against what the day became once the florists and the card companies found it. The church should have listened to her harder than it did. One Sunday a year we set our mothers on a pedestal, and the other fifty-one weeks the church runs on their unbilled labor, the nursery, the meal train, the funeral casseroles, the vacation Bible school that does not staff itself, honored in the abstract and invoiced in the particular, loaded like a mule and addressed as an angel. Sentimentality is what honor turns into when it has decided not to pay anything. The culture's verdict at least has the dignity of open contempt. The church's comes with a corsage.

Both verdicts miss the same fact, and the fact is not sentimental at all.

## The first theologian

Begin with something so large it is hard to see. Every Christian who has ever lived learned the faith from somebody. Doctrine does not fall on a person out of the sky; it is handed over, that is all the word *tradition* means, the handing, and for most people in most centuries, the first hand was a mother's. Before a child can hold the word *God*, he has already learned, in someone's arms, whether the universe answers when he cries. That is not preparation for theology. That is theology, the first draft of the doctrine of God, written into a person, revised for the rest of a life. The question is never whether a mother teaches theology. The question is only which theology she is teaching, in the hours nobody grades.

Moses knew where the faith of a generation actually lives. When he handed Israel the words that were meant to outlast him, he did not lodge them in the sanctuary:

> And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. (Deuteronomy 6:6–7, ESV)

Read the schedule. Sitting in the house. Walking on the road. Lying down. Getting up. That is not the timetable of a classroom or a temple. It is the timetable of a household, supper and errands and bedtime and morning, and whoever keeps those hours keeps the catechism of the next generation. In most houses, in most of history, I know who has kept them. So does the book of Proverbs, which opens by binding two voices into the child's ear, not one: "Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching" (Proverbs 1:8, ESV). The Bible assumes instruction from a mother's mouth. The world I was raised in read that Bible constantly and never once drew the conclusion.

And once, near the end of his life, Paul wrote the conclusion down as a family tree. His last surviving letter is to Timothy, the young pastor he loved best, his true child in the faith, and when he reaches back for the origin of Timothy's faith, he does not name a preacher:

> I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well. (2 Timothy 1:5, ESV)

Two women's names, preserved in Scripture, for one reason: they were the line the faith ran down. Luke supplies the household detail without comment, Timothy was "the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek" (Acts 16:1, ESV). As far as the record shows, the faith did not come to Timothy through his father at all. It came grandmother to mother to son, and Paul does not treat this as irregular or second-best. He treats it as the credential. Later in the same letter he tells Timothy to continue in what he has learned, "knowing from whom you learned it," and reminds him that "from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings" (2 Timothy 3:14–15, ESV). From childhood. Somebody put Scripture into that boy years before any congregation did, and Paul has already told us her name, and her mother's. I want to be careful here, because verses like this get inflated into arguments they never made, and I refuse to do to the text what was done to it around me. This passage settles no debate about offices. It records something better than a debate: the actual pedigree of the man Paul trusted with the churches he was leaving behind. The pedigree is two women deep.

The New Testament keeps doing this, reaching for mothers when it wants to describe the holiest work. When Paul defends his apostleship to the Thessalonians, the image he chooses is not a soldier or a builder: "we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children" (1 Thessalonians 2:7, ESV). And when Luke tells the story of the incarnation, he pauses to show us where the memory of it was kept for the long years before anyone wrote a Gospel: "But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luke 2:19, ESV). The church's first archive was a mother's memory. The manger had one contemplative in attendance, and she was the one who had just given birth.

A woman saw all of this clearly a generation before mine. In 1971 Edith Schaeffer, who with her husband Francis had opened their home in the Swiss Alps in 1955 to any questioning student who knocked, the community that became L'Abri, published a book called *Hidden Art*, known in later printings as *The Hidden Art of Homemaking*. Her argument was simple, and it has been condescended to ever since: we are made in the image of a Creator, and so the ordinary rooms of life, a meal, a garden, a table set with intention, music in a house, are fields for real art. Hidden art, she called it: art whose audience is a household rather than a gallery. She was not dressing up drudgery. She was naming the creative act inside work the world had filed under leftovers. What the Christian subculture later did with the genre she started, hardening a vision into a law, turning the open home into a stage and the homemade into a tournament, was not her doing, and it proves her point in reverse. The moment the work became a display, it stopped being the thing she was describing. The art she meant was hidden. That was not its weakness. That was its species.

## A woman raising men

There is one more room in this argument, and it is the one I live in. I am not raising children in general. I am raising men, five of them, coming toward manhood in a culture that cannot agree on what a man is for. And it has settled on me slowly, the way the largest facts do, that the most consequential theology of womanhood my sons will ever hold is not going to come from a book, a sermon, or an argument they lose online. It is going to come from the woman at close range. A boy learns what a woman is years before anyone tells him. He learns it across a kitchen: whether a woman's voice carries authority or only volume; whether her tiredness registers as information or as weather; whether her mind is something you argue with honestly or something you manage; whether her work is thanked or simply absorbed. My sons will meet a hundred theories about women. They met a woman first. Whatever this house teaches them, that is the doctrine they will default to under pressure, at nineteen, at forty, in kitchens of their own.

So the work in front of me is precise. I am teaching five men what to expect of a woman: a whole person, whose mind was doing something before they interrupted it and will go on doing something after. And I am teaching them what a woman may rightly expect of a man: strength that spends itself on someone else's behalf, honesty that does not require an audience, hands that clear a table without being asked because they have watched it done ten thousand times and finally understood that it was being done by someone. Their father carries the other half of this, sons learn how to treat a woman most deeply by watching how their father treats her, and he has written elsewhere about what fatherhood requires. This essay is the other side of that house. But there is a portion only I can do, because I am the woman they know first, and the first womanhood a man believes in, for good and for ill, for the rest of his life, is his mother's.

## The books I kept

Now the part I would rather leave out.

I have kept books in this house that I never showed anyone. A ledger: every unthanked task entered neatly, every load of laundry no one acknowledged, every invisible sacrifice recorded with the date, and the whole account read aloud in my own head at midnight, with interest compounding. There is a version of motherhood that looks like service from the outside and is debt collection underneath, and I have practiced it. Scorekeeping is what serving becomes when the servant has quietly stopped believing anyone else will do the accounting. And it ruins the thing it records, because a gift with a ledger behind it is an invoice. Paul says of love that "it is not irritable or resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5, ESV), and there have been seasons of my life when I could not have read that verse aloud without my voice going strange.

I have mistaken exhaustion for holiness, and this one has older roots. I was raised in a world that measured a woman by how little she asked for, where depletion was proof of devotion, and a tired woman was a good one by definition, no further questions taken. I walked out of that world. And then, with my own two hands, I rebuilt its arithmetic inside my own house and called it motherhood. Nobody assigned me the martyrdom; I volunteered, partly because it was the only holiness I had ever been shown, and partly, this is the truest version, because exhaustion is a form of scorekeeping too. It feels like evidence. It is the self manufacturing a righteousness out of depletion. And it forms sons wrongly: boys who watch a woman erase herself learn, wordlessly, that erasure is what women are for. The old world preached a woman's smallness as her glory. I have preached the same sermon in my own kitchen, in the liturgy of my own collapsing, to a congregation of five.

And I have taught a rule before a reason. Fear is efficient. It produces compliance faster than formation produces love, and on the hard days efficiency wins. I know the mother tongue of fear, I was raised speaking it, and there are still days it is out of my mouth before the better language arrives. But a rule without a reason forms a child who obeys a voice; any voice; whichever voice is nearest and loudest. I am not trying to raise men who obey the nearest loud voice. I am trying to raise men who love a Person, which is slower, and which requires me to be unafraid, which is the actual cost. The rules were never the hard part. The reasons are the hard part, because to hand a child a reason you must have faced it yourself.

## The God who sees

So the work is invisible. The culture calls it a waste, the church calls it precious and pays it nothing, and the worker herself will corrupt it the day she starts keeping books. Where does that leave a woman on an ordinary Tuesday, folding what she folded on the last one?

It leaves her where an Egyptian slave named Hagar once stood, which is deeper into the Bible than my girlhood ever took me. Hagar was used by the household of Abraham and then blamed for the arrangement, and she fled pregnant into the wilderness, which is what a woman does when she has run out of rooms. No one watched her go; that was rather the point of her. And the LORD found her by a spring in the desert, and spoke to her, and made her a promise, and this discarded woman did something no patriarch and no prophet had yet done in the whole of Scripture. She gave God a name.

> So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me." (Genesis 16:13, ESV)

The first person in the Bible to name God is a runaway slave woman, pregnant and alone, and the name she chooses is the one every unwatched worker since has needed: the God of seeing. Not the God of applause. Not the God of the annual carnation. The God whose attention is native to the hidden, Jesus's own claim, and notice what he fastens it to: "And your Father who sees in secret will reward you" (Matthew 6:4, ESV). The entire category the résumé cannot record and the church forgets by Monday is precisely the category Jesus says the Father keeps.

And when Jesus wanted to say what the kingdom of God itself is like, not what it decorates, but how it works, he did not choose a battle or a throne. He chose a woman's hands, in flour, working alone. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened" (Matthew 13:33, ESV). *Hid.* The word is right there in the sentence. The kingdom operates the way a mother operates: buried inside the ordinary mass, invisible while it is happening, doubted by everyone in a hurry, and then the whole loaf rises. Three measures of flour is a feast's worth of bread; the woman in the parable is baking for a crowd she cannot yet see. So am I. The men my sons will become, the women those men will honor or fail, the grandchildren who will learn the first name of God in somebody's arms, that is the loaf. None of it is visible from my kitchen tonight. All of it is in the flour now.

I will set a table this evening that will need setting again tomorrow, and no one will inspect either one. This is the work. It will not be watched. It was never going to be watched; watching was never the promise. Seen is the promise, seen by the only audit that outlasts the house, the God who found Hagar by the water, who keeps the books I have finally stopped keeping, who put his kingdom into the flour where nobody could find it and let it rise.

Leaven works in the dark. So does he.
posts.excerpt: The culture calls mothering a waste of a mind. The church hands it a carnation one Sunday a year and loads it like a mule the other fifty-one. Both are wrong about the same fact: the first theologian in every generation is a mother, and her work was never unseen. Only unwatched.

posts.title: The Womanhood They Preached Was Small
posts.body:
You will not get details from me. Not because I cannot supply them, and not because anyone is owed my silence, but because details become spectacle, and spectacle is a way of not listening. The pattern is the point. And the pattern is common enough that some of the women reading this will not need the details filled in. You have your own set.

I was raised inside a fundamentalism that preached its rules as though the rules were the gospel. Fear was the engine of everything it called formation. And womanhood, in that world, was a discipline of shrinkage. Modesty was taught not as dignity but as fear of the body, a girl's body presented to her as a hazard to be managed, other people's sins pre-assigned to her hemline. Submission was taught not as anything the New Testament describes but as erasure: the will treated as a defect awaiting surrender. Silence was a virtue, the crowning one. A woman's godliness was measured by how little room she took up, how little she asked, wanted, said, weighed upon the world. And every inch of it came stapled to Bible verses, because Scripture, in that world, was not the bread of the household. It was the leash.

These days I hear preaching from a different kind of pulpit, my husband's, sitting in a pew with our five sons beside me, which is its own quiet astonishment for a woman with my beginnings, because the pulpit was where the leash used to be held. It took me years to hear a sermon without bracing. This essay is about what happened between that world and this pew, and about the strange road I took to get here: not away from the book they weaponized, but further into it.

## The small god of the small womanhood

The first thing to say about that world is not what it did to women. It is what it did to God, because the two are a single error. The god of my girlhood was small. He needed managing. He watched for infractions the way an anxious man watches a till, and his favor was a thin surface you could fall through at any hour. Whatever the doctrinal statement said, the gospel as actually preached was *behave*. A small god makes everyone underneath him small, and the people most underneath him smallest of all. Women were most underneath him.

I want to be exact here, because exactness is owed in both directions. The problem with the world I grew up in was not that it took the Bible too seriously. That was its claim about itself, and the claim was false. It took fear seriously and called the fear Scripture. I know churches that hold convictions about men and women that some of my readers do not share, I worship in one, and hold them with warmth and open books, where the women are large-souled and nobody's silence is enforced. Faithful churches genuinely disagree about women and ordained office; that is an old argument among people who love the same Bible, second-order by any honest reckoning, and nothing in this essay depends on where you land in it. What I am naming lives beneath that argument. Whatever a church concludes about office, a womanhood of fear, managed smallness, and Scripture-as-leash is not among the options the text leaves open. That is not one side of a debate. That is the abuse of the book, carried out in the book's own name, and I watched it done.

## Two ways out

Nearly every woman I have known from a world like mine left it by one of two roads.

The first is the obvious one: burn the book. When a book has been the handle of the whip, throwing the book away looks less like rebellion than like sanity, the first sane act, maybe, in a life that had been arranged to prevent it. I will not stand at a safe distance and scold the women who took that road. They are not weak, and about what was done to them they are not even wrong; they are witnesses, and a church that wonders aloud why they left should first sit down and hear what was preached to them as the word of the Lord. If tearing down means taking apart a thing that was built wrong, their demolition was overdue. My only quarrel with that road is where it ends. It ends in the rubble. You can spend a whole life proving the old house deserved condemning, it did, and still have nowhere to live.

One thing before I go further, because I know who may be reading this. Some of you are not out. If you are inside a home or a church where obedience is kept in place by fear, or by anything worse than fear, then the first faithful thing is not to win the theological argument. It is to be safe. Safety comes before theology; it is not a detour from faithfulness but the ground of it, and getting safe from an abusive place usually takes help from outside its walls, a person you trust, a professional, someone the people who control you do not control. Ask for that help. God is not on the side of what is being done to you. The rest of this essay will keep.

The second road is harder to see from inside, and it is the one I took, not out of courage, I want that on the record, but out of something closer to stubbornness. They had always told me the Bible was on their side. Every rule came with a verse; every verse arrived pre-read. And it occurred to me, later than I like to admit, that I had never actually checked. I had heard the book quoted my whole life and had never once read it as though it might be a witness for the other side. So I read it, not devotionally at first; forensically, the way you read a contract someone has been enforcing against you. And this is what I found, and what the rest of this essay is about: the book did not say what they said it said. Page after page, the book was worse news for them than it ever was for me.

## The first page

They should never have let me read Genesis. On the first page of the book they used to shrink me, before a single command about marriage, before any curse, before the fall itself, there is this:

> So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. (Genesis 1:27, ESV)

Male and female, in the same verse, in the same breath, at the same instant. The image of God is not conferred on the man and then extended to the woman as a courtesy. It is spoken over both, first, before anything else is true of them, and the commission that follows lands on both as well: "And God blessed them. And God said to them, 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion'" (Genesis 1:28, ESV). *Them.* The world I was raised in taught, without ever quite writing it down, that the image of God reached a woman secondhand, routed through a father, then a husband, the way electricity reaches a lamp. The first page of the Bible refuses it. Whatever else Scripture goes on to say about men and women, and it says things Christians argue over in good faith, it says this first, and it never takes it back.

## A word they read small

In my girlhood, Proverbs 31 was a measuring stick. The "excellent wife" was read at women, her rising while it is yet night, her distaff and her merchant ships, as a to-do list nobody could finish, which was, I came to think, the point of reading it that way. A woman kept permanently behind an impossible standard is a woman easy to govern.

Then I looked at the word. "An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels" (Proverbs 31:10, ESV). The word translated *excellent* is the Hebrew *chayil*, and it is not a domestic word. It is the Old Testament's word for might, the word for armies, for wealth, for warriors. When the angel of the LORD appears to Gideon, the greeting is "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor" (Judges 6:12, ESV), the same word. The poem in Proverbs 31 is an acrostic, a victory hymn built on the alphabet, and it crowns not a chore chart but a campaign: "Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come" (Proverbs 31:25, ESV). She laughs at the future. That is not the posture of a woman being kept small. And in observant Jewish homes to this day, the poem is sung at the Sabbath table, sung *to* the woman, in her hearing, as praise. It was composed to be sung to a woman, not read at her.

Ruth settles what the word cannot mean. Boaz calls Ruth "a worthy woman", *eshet chayil*, the exact phrase of Proverbs 31:10, "for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman" (Ruth 3:11, ESV). At that moment Ruth is a destitute foreign widow gleaning other people's fields. No husband, no household, no output the old checklist could score. Whatever valor is, it is not domestic production. They translated a war-word into a chore list, and the mistranslation was not linguistic. It was convenient.

## The names nobody read to me

Then there were the women in the text itself, there the whole time, in the plain reading of the plain Bible that world claimed to live by, and somehow never once read to me.

Deborah. "Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time" (Judges 4:4, ESV). Judging Israel, and the next verse says the people of Israel "came up to her for judgment." The men of a nation climbing a hill to hear a woman render verdicts, in the era my girlhood held up as the Bible's own world. The text records it without apology and without a flicker of embarrassment. In the victory song that follows, she is given the title in her own voice: "I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel" (Judges 5:7, ESV). The Scripture I was handed had somehow misplaced her.

Huldah. When the Book of the Law was rediscovered in the temple in the reign of Josiah, and the young king tore his robes and demanded to know what the LORD's word meant for his people, he sent the highest delegation his kingdom could assemble, Hilkiah the high priest among them, to inquire of the LORD. They went to "Huldah the prophetess" (2 Kings 22:14, ESV). This while Jeremiah and Zephaniah were both alive and prophesying in those same years. The high priest of Israel carried the newly found Scripture to a woman to hear the LORD's verdict on it, and she gave it, "Thus says the LORD", to the king's own officials. I grew up under men who would not let a woman read announcements. Nobody ever mentioned Huldah.

The women of Luke 8. Jesus's traveling ministry ran on money, and Luke tells you plainly whose it was: "and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means" (Luke 8:2–3, ESV). The itinerant preaching of the Son of God was funded by women, named, particular women, one of them ranking gentry from Herod's own court. And one of the three names is Susanna. I have carried that name my whole life, and no one in the world that raised me ever once showed me hers.

Junia. Near the end of Romans, Paul greets two coworkers: "Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were with Christ before me" (Romans 16:7, ESV). A woman who went to prison with Paul and was in Christ before him. Honesty requires the footnote, so here it is: the Greek phrase can be read "well known to the apostles," as my translation has it, or "outstanding among the apostles," as others do, and scholars argue the grammar in good faith. But John Chrysostom, a fourth-century preacher no one has ever accused of flattering women, read the verse, took Junia for a woman, and marveled that she should be counted worthy of the title of apostle. What happened afterward is its own small parable: for centuries, editors and translators quietly gave her a man's name, Junias, a name otherwise unattested in the ancient world. A woman stood in the text, and generations of readers corrected her. I know how she must have felt.

## The witness they would not have called

And then there is Jesus, who is the argument underneath all the other arguments.

Watch him with the sisters at Bethany. Martha is doing what my girlhood would have blessed, the kitchen, the serving, the being useful, and Mary "sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching" (Luke 10:39, ESV), which is not a posture of sentiment; sitting at a rabbi's feet is the posture of a disciple, the seat Paul says he took at the feet of Gamaliel. When Martha objects, Jesus defends the woman in the student's chair: "Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:42, ESV). Will not be taken away. He said that knowing exactly how many hands, over how many centuries, would try.

But the morning that ends the argument is the one at the tomb. Some context first, because the text deserves it: in the first-century world, a woman's testimony carried almost no legal weight, the historian Josephus records the assumption of the age plainly, that evidence from women was not to be admitted. Every early Christian knew this. Which is why no one inventing a resurrection story in that world would have written the story we have.

> But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. (John 20:11, ESV)

She had come to tend a body. She stayed because grief does not follow instructions. And the risen Christ, with all of history to choose from, Peter was available; John had already been to the tomb and gone home, appeared first to her, and she mistook him for the gardener until he said one word:

> Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher). (John 20:16, ESV)

Her name. The small god of my girlhood knew girls only by their infractions. The risen Lord of the actual Scriptures knows this woman by name, in the dark of the greatest morning there has ever been, and then he does the thing that should have ended womanhood-as-silence forever. He gives her the news, and he gives her the sending: "go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God'" (John 20:17, ESV). And she goes: "Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, 'I have seen the Lord'" (John 20:18, ESV).

The first human being entrusted with the message on which everything since has rested was a woman whose testimony a court of her own day would not have taken. The church's older memory gave her a title for it, the apostle to the apostles. If the story were fabricated, she would never have been in it; her presence in that garden is there for the reason unflattering details are always there, which is that it happened. The first sermon of the new creation was five words long, and a woman preached it to preachers, because the risen Christ told her to. Whatever your church concludes about offices and order, and mine has its convictions, no honest reading of that morning can ever again call a woman's silence her glory. He did not ask Mary to be small. He asked her to be a witness, which is the opposite thing.

## The other smallness

Now the harder honesty, the one the house rules of this platform require and my own history makes me slow to say: the culture that would rescue me from all this carries a leash of its own.

The world I fled taught me to need permission for everything. The world I fled into teaches women to need nothing and no one, the self as fortress, every attachment a liability, every need a failure of the project, rescue defined as requiring no rescue ever again. It sounds like the antidote. It is the same instrument held at the other end. Fundamentalism shrank a woman to a role; this shrinks her to a résumé of self-sufficiency, and both hand her an identity smaller than the image of God. One forbade her voice; the other forbids her need. Neither can imagine what Genesis says at the start and the garden tomb says at the end, a woman whose dignity is conferred, not performed; who can be strong precisely because she does not have to be invulnerable.

I say this from inside it. When I first got out, I built the fortress. A woman leaving a world that punished her needs learns to stop having any, and calls the amputation strength, I confused being hard to hurt with being healed, and they are not the same thing, and the people who lived with me in those years paid the difference. The old fear had not left. It had straightened its posture. Erasing yourself for God's supposed sake and armoring yourself against everyone made in his image are two failures of the same confession: that you were made an image-bearer, which means made for communion, seen, needed, needing, from the first page.

## What was under the house

So no, I did not keep the faith I was handed. It could not be kept; it was not load-bearing. But I did not burn it down either, in the end, and the difference between those two sentences is the whole road. I dug. Under the small womanhood, under the rules preached as gospel, there was an older house, the one the counterfeiters had been imitating badly all along. In it I found the God who wrote women into every hinge of the story: naming himself to a slave woman in the desert, raising up a mother in Israel to judge a nation, sending his high priest to a prophetess, funding his Son's ministry out of women's purses, seating Mary in the disciple's chair, choosing the witness no court would call. When Matthew opens the New Testament with a genealogy, he breaks the conventions of the form to name the women in the Messiah's line, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, "the wife of Uriah," and Mary (Matthew 1:3–16), and not one of them is the kind of name polite religion puts on the wall. Nothing about this book was ever small except some of the hands it got read through.

I think of the women still inside, the ones this essay has been quietly addressed to since the first paragraph. I cannot hand you the years it took me. I can hand you the one thing I wish someone had said over the fence: the book they are holding is not on their side. I checked. Read it yourself, all of it, in the light, and see whose witness it turns out to be.

And I think of my five sons, who are learning what a woman is by living with one, and who will someday sit in pews and read texts and vote in churches I will never see. The womanhood preached over my girlhood was small, and it did not survive contact with the Scriptures it claimed. The woman in the text is not small. On the first morning of the new creation, the risen Christ had one sentence to deliver and all the world to choose a herald from, and he said a woman's name, and told her to go and say it.

He did not tell her to be small. There is no verse where he tells her to be small. He told her: go and say. He has not changed the instruction.
posts.excerpt: The world I was raised in preached a womanhood of shrinkage, modesty as fear of the body, submission as erasure, silence as virtue, Scripture as a leash. Most women who leave that world burn the book. I read it instead, and found it did not say what they said it said.

posts.title: Does God Actually Exist?
posts.body:
Nobody talks themselves out of God the way the debates pretend. There is no evening when you weigh the cosmological argument against the problem of evil, tally the columns, and conclude that the universe is unattended. That is not how unbelief actually happens, and I say that as someone who lived inside it for most of my life. Unbelief happens the way weather happens. You grow up breathing an air in which God is simply not a live presence, in which the burden of proof sits permanently on the believer and never on the doubter, and one day you notice you stopped expecting anyone to be there. The philosopher Charles Taylor gave this the best name it has. He called it the immanent frame, the sense, so deep we no longer feel it as a choice, that the world is a closed system of natural causes with no window cut in the ceiling. Taylor's point, in his history of how the West got secular, is that five hundred years ago belief was the water everyone swam in and unbelief was nearly unthinkable, and now the position has exactly reversed, and the reversal happened underneath argument, not through it. I did not reason my way out. I was raised in the frame. It felt like clear sight. It was a set of walls I had mistaken for the horizon.

So I am not going to try to reason you into anything. You cannot be argued into the kingdom, and anyone selling a proof that closes the case like a math problem is selling something that has never once worked on a living person. What I can do is tell you the thing I did not expect, which is that the frame started to cost more than I could afford. The atheism I held was not a neutral absence of belief. It was a full account of everything, and that account kept running up debts it quietly refused to pay.

Let me name the strongest version of the case I was defending, because a version you can knock over is not worth leaving. The most serious atheism is not the sneering internet kind. It is the one that says: the world looks exactly as we would expect it to look if no one were in charge. The innocent suffer at random. The universe is vast beyond meaning and indifferent beyond appeal. If there were a God who wanted to be known, he has done a strange job of it, hiding behind a silence that looks identical to absence. The philosopher J. L. Schellenberg built a rigorous argument out of that last point alone, that a perfectly loving God would not permit the honest seeker to find only silence, and the silence is real, and so perhaps the God is not. I felt that argument in my body long before I could name it. Do not let anyone tell you it is weak. The hiddenness of God is the best card the other side holds, and pretending otherwise is how believers lose the honest people in the room.

Grant it. Grant the silence and the suffering and the sheer indifferent scale of things. Now watch what my old account had to spend to keep the ledger closed.

It started with the simplest question anyone can ask, the one Leibniz put three centuries ago and no one has retired since: why is there something rather than nothing. Not why is there this particular something, but why is there anything at all, why is there a universe here to be indifferent instead of the clean silence of nothing whatever. The honest atheist answer is that there is no answer, that the universe is just there, a brute fact with no account of itself. And maybe that is where it ends. But notice that this is not a discovery. It is a refusal to keep asking, dressed as maturity. I had called my refusal courage. It was closer to a man who stops opening the mail.

Then there was the fine-tuning, which I first heard and dismissed and could not make stay dismissed. The physical constants that govern the universe, the strength of gravity, the balance of the forces that let matter clump into stars instead of flying apart or collapsing, sit in a range so narrow that a small nudge in almost any of them yields a cosmos with no stars, no chemistry, no observers, nothing. The naturalist has a reply, and it is a real one: perhaps there are countless other universes with other settings, and we necessarily find ourselves in one of the rare ones that works, because we could not find ourselves anywhere else. A multiverse. But sit with what that costs. To avoid the conclusion that the one universe we can observe looks set up, we posit an infinity of universes we cannot observe, in principle, ever. That is not the humble empirical move. That is an enormous act of faith wearing a lab coat, and I had been making it without noticing that it was faith.

The bill I could least afford came due over something smaller and closer than cosmology. It came due over the fact that I could not actually live as though cruelty were merely something I disliked. When I read of a child tortured for someone's pleasure, everything in me said not I disapprove of this but this is wrong, wrong in a way that would still be wrong if every person on earth applauded it, wrong the way a false equation is false regardless of the vote. C. S. Lewis pressed exactly here, and I resented it before I conceded it. If there is no God, then that overwhelming sense of a real moral law standing over me and over the torturer alike is a chemical event in a primate brain, useful for keeping the tribe together, and nothing more. It does not report a truth. It only feels like it does. I could say that sentence. I could not live it. I went on treating some things as really evil and some things as really owed, and every time I did, I was writing a check on an account my worldview swore was empty.

That is the pattern I did not see until I was most of the way out. The atheism I held could be stated, but it could not be inhabited. It told me the universe was meaningless and then could not stop me from grieving as though a death were an outrage rather than a rearrangement of molecules. It told me my reason was the accidental byproduct of blind selection and then asked me to trust that same reason to deliver the truth about everything, including the truth of atheism, which is a bit like trusting a random number generator because it told you it was reliable. It told me the person across the table was a bag of chemicals and then expected me to treat her as though she had a dignity that no chemistry confers. At every one of those points the account said one thing and I lived the other, and I had called the gap between them realism. It was not realism. It was a man refusing to notice that he already believed the world was the kind of place that only makes sense if someone made it.

None of this is a proof, and I will not insult you by calling it one. The arguments do not march anyone across the line at gunpoint, and they are not meant to. Blaise Pascal saw this better than the debaters do. He said God has given enough light for those who desire to see, and enough darkness for those who do not, that the evidence is calibrated not to overwhelm a mind but to meet a heart that is actually looking. That used to sound to me like an excuse for a God who would not show up. It sounds different now. It sounds like the difference between a proof, which compels a mind and changes nothing else, and a person, who can only be known by those willing to be changed by the knowing.

Scripture does not argue for God's existence. It is worth noticing that. It never once treats the matter as an open question to be settled by evidence, and for years I read that as evasion. Now I read it as a diagnosis. Paul, writing to Rome, says that what can be known of God has been plain, that "his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse" (Romans 1:20). The claim there is not that the argument is airtight. The claim is that the problem was never mainly the evidence. The problem is that we are practiced, all of us, believer and atheist alike, at not seeing what we would rather not owe. I know that practice from the inside. I was very good at it.

So I am not going to hand you a syllogism and tell you the debt is settled. I am going to tell you what I found on the other side of the frame I mistook for the sky. The question is not really whether you can prove God, because you cannot prove, in that hard sense, most of the things you would die for. The question is which account can carry the weight of what you already know and cannot stop knowing: that some things are truly wrong, that your mind can reach real truth, that the person beside you is more than meat, that the universe's being here at all is stranger than your silence about it admits. Atheism can say those things are illusions. It cannot get you to live as though they were. I tried, longer than most. In the end the unbelief was not too rational to keep. It was too expensive, and I had been paying, all along, in a currency it told me did not exist.
posts.excerpt: I did not stop being an atheist because someone won an argument. I stopped because the account I was defending kept sending me a bill it could not pay.

posts.title: Is Jesus Really the Only Way?
posts.body:
The question almost never arrives as a question. It arrives as a face.

Someone is sitting across from you, and they have just buried a grandmother who prayed five times a day toward Mecca for sixty years, or lit lamps to a god whose name you cannot pronounce, and prayed with a devotion that shames your own. And the person across from you says the thing that is really being asked whenever anyone asks whether Jesus is the only way. They say: are you telling me she is in hell. They are not asking for a doctrine. They are asking whether the God you believe in is the kind of God who would do that, and whether you have the nerve to say it to their face.

I want to be honest about where I am standing when I write this. I did not come to this question as a believer defending home turf. I came to it as the objection itself. For most of my life I was an atheist, and of all the things the church claimed, this was the one I found not merely improbable but obscene. The idea that the accident of where a person was born, the family that raised them, the book that happened to be on the nightstand, would decide their eternity, struck me as the clearest evidence that the whole system was invented by men who wanted to believe they alone had the map. I did not think the exclusive claim was hard to believe. I thought it was easy to see through.

So when I say the objection is serious, I am not being generous. I am remembering.

Here is the objection in its strongest form, and I will not soften it, because a version you can knock over is not worth answering. The philosopher John Hick spent a career pressing it, and he pressed it well. Hick called for what he named a Copernican revolution in the way Christians think about other religions. For centuries, he said, we placed our own faith at the center and made every other tradition orbit around it, counted as true only insofar as it reflected ours. But what if the center is not Christianity at all. What if the center is God, or what Hick carefully called the Real, and Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, and the rest are all planets in orbit around that one sun, each catching the light at a different angle, each a genuine human response to the same infinite reality no one of us can see whole. On this account the sincerity of that grandmother is not a problem to be explained away. It is evidence. A God worth the name would not hide himself so that only the people handed the right pamphlet could find him.

And underneath the philosophy sits an intuition even harder to shake, because it does not require a philosophy degree to feel. If you had been born in Riyadh instead of a small town in Michigan, you would almost certainly be a Muslim, and you would hold it with exactly the confidence you now hold this. Your deepest convictions track your zip code. That should unsettle anyone. It unsettled me for years.

Grant all of it. Grant that the church has often held this doctrine like a weapon, has used the word only to bless conquest and baptize contempt, has said to the grieving what should never be said to the grieving. Grant that a great deal of what passes for defending the exclusivity of Christ has been the ugliest thing in the room. If you do not feel the force of that, you are not ready to say the next sentence.

Now watch what the argument does when you turn it over.

Hick loved to tell the old parable of the blind men and the elephant. One grasps the trunk and says the elephant is a snake, one the leg and says a tree, one the ear and says a fan. Each has part of the truth, none has the whole, and how foolish for any of them to insist his piece is the animal. It is a devastating little story. It has been used against Christian confidence for a century. But notice the one thing the parable cannot survive being asked. Who is telling it. The man narrating the story is not one of the blind men. He is standing above the whole scene with his eyes open, describing the entire elephant that all the others are too limited to see. To tell the parable at all, he has to claim the exact thing he is denying to everyone else: a view of the whole. Lesslie Newbigin, who spent forty years as a missionary in India and thought harder about this than almost anyone, put his finger on it. The person who says all religions are partial glimpses of a reality none can grasp is not standing nowhere. He is standing somewhere, and it is a very particular somewhere, and from it he is making the largest and most exclusive claim in the room. He is claiming to know the real shape of God well enough to correct every prophet and every scripture that ever said otherwise.

This is the thing I did not see when I was on the other side. I thought pluralism was the humble position and exclusivity the arrogant one. It is the reverse. Pluralism does not refuse the total claim. It makes a total claim and calls the refusal humility. Everyone at the table is making a truth claim about the whole. The Buddhist who says the self is an illusion and the Christian who says the self is loved by name are not describing the same elephant from two angles. They are saying incompatible things about what is finally real, and the pluralist who says they are both partial is not standing outside that disagreement. He has joined it, on a third side, and pretended he floated above it.

So the question was never whether we can avoid an exclusive claim. No one avoids one. The question is which exclusive claim is true. And that is a different kind of question, a harder and more honest one, and it deserves better than the charge of arrogance, because the charge applies to the one making it just as much.

Then there is the history, which almost everyone gets backwards. When people hear the church say there is no other name, they hear Christendom talking. They hear cathedrals and crusades, the strong telling the weak that the weak must convert or be damned. But go back to where the sentence was first spoken. Peter says it in the fourth chapter of Acts, and the scene is not a throne room. Peter is a fisherman standing trial. He and John have been arrested, hauled before the very council that arranged the execution of Jesus a few weeks earlier, and asked by what power they had healed a lame man. It is into that, powerless before the people who could kill him as easily as they killed his teacher, that Peter says it: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). That is not the language of empire. That is a condemned minority refusing to add the emperor's name, or the council's, to the name of the crucified man they will not stop preaching. The exclusivity did not begin as a boast of the powerful. It began as the defiance of the powerless, and it cost most of them their lives.

The scandal of the claim was never that it grabbed too much power. The scandal was where it located salvation. Not in a philosophy the clever could master, not in a law the disciplined could keep, not in a birthplace or a bloodline, but in an executed provincial nobody from an occupied backwater. That is the offense. Christianity does not say the way is narrow because God is stingy with the map. It says the way is a person, and a person is the one thing you cannot earn your way to or reason your way to or be born into. You can only receive him. Which means the door the doctrine seems to close on merit and pedigree and geography is the same door it throws open to the grandmother who never had the right book, because if salvation is a gift and not a grade, then the one thing that cannot disqualify her is that she was born in the wrong place.

I need to be careful here, because two questions get fused and they are not the same. One is whether Jesus is the only Savior, whether the cross is the sole ground on which any human being is ever reconciled to God. The historic church answers yes, and it is bound to, because the whole faith stands on it. The other question is whether every person must consciously hear and name him in this life to be reached by what he did. That question is genuinely harder, the church has held more than one faithful answer to it, and it is not the one I am settling today. Hold it open. What the exclusivity of Christ settles is the mechanism, that all grace runs through one cross. It does not by itself hand you the roster of who is saved, and anyone who tells you it does has said more than the text does.

Which brings the whole thing back to the face across the table, and to the verse people quote at that face without ever reading where it sits. "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). We hear it as a bouncer at a door. Read the sentence before it. Thomas, frightened, says, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" The line about the only way is not spoken to an outsider to keep him out. It is spoken to a terrified friend who asked how to find God, and it is the tenderest possible answer: you do not have to know the way, because I am the way, and I am not leaving you to find it alone. The exclusivity and the comfort are the same sentence. They were never meant to be pried apart.

I do not know the eternal standing of your grandmother, and I will not pretend to, and anyone who says it easily has not understood either the doctrine or the grief. What I know is that the claim I once thought was Christianity's cruelty is closer to its whole hope. A God you reach by being born right, or thinking right, or behaving right, is a God who belongs to the lucky and the strong. The God who comes down to one cross, and offers himself as the way rather than posting the way on a wall, is the only kind of God who could ever be good news for the person who got everything wrong.

That is not a smaller God than the pluralist's. It is a more dangerous one. He will not stay a symbol you assemble from all traditions at your convenience. He has a name, and he was killed under it, and he asks to be received rather than admired. You can refuse him. People did, to his face, and he let them walk. But do not refuse him for being arrogant. Refuse him, if you must, for being too particular, too specific, too unwilling to be one glimpse among many. And then sit with the possibility that the particularity you resent is the only shape love could take if it meant to reach the ones who could never have found it themselves.
posts.excerpt: For most of my life I was an atheist, and of all the things the church claimed, that Jesus is the only way struck me as not merely improbable but obscene. Then I noticed the one question the parable of the blind men and the elephant cannot survive being asked.

posts.title: What About Those Who Never Heard?
posts.body:
The question that undoes people is not usually the one about whether God exists. It is the one a teenager asks on the drive home from a mission conference, and it goes like this: what about the man who lived and died on some mountainside a thousand years before a missionary ever crossed the water, who never heard the name of Jesus, not once, not from anyone. Is he in hell for missing a message that was never sent to him. Ask it out loud in most churches and watch the room get careful. It is the soft place in the exclusive claim, the one that makes even settled believers change the subject, because it seems to make salvation a lottery run by geography, and a God who runs that lottery is a God a decent person cannot worship without lying.

I want to take this one slowly, because it is the kind of question people leave the faith over, and they usually leave holding an answer they were handed too fast, in either direction. I have been handed both. I have been told, briskly, that yes, of course the man is condemned, that is what the seriousness of missions depends on, and any softness here is the first step out the door. And I have been told, just as briskly, that a loving God would never, that everyone is fine in the end, sleep well. Both answers share a family resemblance I have learned to distrust. They both resolve the ache too quickly, and they both claim to know something the Scriptures guard more carefully than either camp admits.

Let me give the hard position its full due first, because it is not the cartoon its critics make of it. The case that saving faith requires actually hearing and trusting Christ is not cruelty for its own sake. It is built on a text. Paul writes to Rome, "How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?" (Romans 10:14). That is a chain, and it runs from hearing to believing to being saved, and it is the engine of every missionary who ever left home. Take it away and you have, the hard position warns, cut the nerve of the Great Commission. If the unreached are already safe in their unreachedness, then the most loving thing the church could do is stop telling them, leave them undisturbed, let sleeping nations lie. The restrictivist is guarding something real: that the message is not decoration, that it matters eternally whether it arrives. Do not wave that away. A gospel it makes no difference to hear is not the gospel the apostles died to carry.

But hold that against another set of texts, ones the confident restrictivist tends to hurry past. In the very same letter, two chapters earlier, Paul says something that does not fit the tidy chain. He writes that "when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts" (Romans 2:14-15). Paul is willing to say that people who never received the revelation still have something of God's requirement inscribed in them, and that God's judgment will reckon with what they actually had, not with what they never received. And then there is Peter, standing in the house of a Roman soldier who had never been a Jew and had certainly never been a Christian, saying, "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him" (Acts 10:34-35). Whatever that means, and it is debated, it does not mean that God is trapped by a man's zip code.

So the church has held more than one faithful answer here, and honesty requires naming them rather than pretending yours is the only one a serious Christian could reach. There is the restrictivist answer: explicit faith in this life, and God is just in ways we must trust past our sight. There is the inclusivist answer, held by many who love the Scriptures no less: that the only ground of anyone's salvation is still the cross of Christ and nothing else, but that God may apply that finished work to a person who never heard the name, the way, everyone agrees, he applied it to Abraham and Moses and every saint who died before Bethlehem, none of whom ever heard the name either, all of whom were saved by a Christ they knew only as promise and shadow. C. S. Lewis reached for this in a story, when he let a lifelong worshiper of a false god be received in the end by the true one, on the grounds that the man's honest seeking had, without his knowing it, always been aimed at the only God there is. You may find that too generous. Others find it the only reading that lets God be both just and the Savior of the OT saints in the same breath. The point is not that the question is easy. The point is that it is genuinely open, that Scripture speaks to it in more than one register, and that this is not first-order ground where the creeds have bound us. It is a place where brothers disagree and remain brothers.

What I want to say is that we have been arguing about the wrong thing, or at least arguing about it in the wrong order. We keep trying to settle the mechanism, to get God to hand over the roster so we can stop feeling the ache. He has not handed it over. What he has handed over is something better and harder to hold, which is his own character, put on the record in the one place the question was first raised. Long before any missionary conference, Abraham stood in front of God, who was about to judge a wicked city, and Abraham did not flatter him. He argued. He said the thing every honest doubter since has wanted to say: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). And the staggering thing is that God does not rebuke the question. He honors it. He lets Abraham press him, again and again, down to a handful of righteous, and he yields ground every time. The Bible does not treat the worry about God's fairness as impertinence to be silenced. It puts that worry in the mouth of the father of the faithful and lets it stand.

That is the pivot the whole matter turns on, and I missed it for years because I wanted the list instead. We are not given the list. We are given the Judge. And the Judge is not a distant sovereign applying a policy from behind glass. The Judge is the one who did not stay behind the glass, who crossed every distance himself, who was born into an occupied backwater precisely so that no one could say God ruled on human life from a safe remove. When you ask whether the man on the mountainside will be dealt with justly, you are asking about the character of the specific God who went to a cross rather than spare himself. You already know more about his fairness than the question assumes. You know what he was willing to spend.

None of this loosens the church's feet from the road. This is the part the soft answer never sees. If I do not know that the unreached are automatically safe, and I do not, then their reaching is not optional, and my comfort is not the point. The uncertainty cuts toward the mission, not away from it. It was never our job to calculate who God can and cannot reach without us. It was our job to go, because the message is not decoration, and because the God who wrote his law on every human heart clearly wants that law answered by a face and a name and a cross, not left as a rumor in the conscience. The inclusivist who uses his hope as a reason to stay home has betrayed the very grace he claims to trust.

So I will not tell you where the man on the mountainside stands, because I do not know, and the people who told you they knew, in either direction, were telling you something the text withholds. What I will tell you is the one thing the text does not withhold. The Judge of all the earth will do what is just. He proved what he was willing to pay for that justice on a hill outside Jerusalem, in public, where anyone could watch. You are allowed to press him, the way Abraham did. What you are not allowed to do, having watched him die, is go on suspecting he is the kind of God who would damn a man on a technicality. That accusation died with him and got up without him. Whatever he does with the ones who never heard, he will not do it from a distance, and he will not do it unjustly, and if that is not enough to quiet the ache entirely, it was never meant to. It is meant to send you back to the road.
posts.excerpt: A missionary asked me the question that has emptied more pews than atheism ever did. Not is God real, but is God fair to the ones who died having never once been told his name.

posts.title: Can You Be Good Without God?
posts.body:
The best man in my old neighborhood did not believe in God, and neither did I.
