The denial of the cross is not a small historical footnote in Islam. It follows from everything Islam believes about how God treats the ones he sends.

And it lands on the single fact Christianity cannot give away. Because for the Christian the cross is not the tragic interruption of the story. It is the center of it. Remove it and there is nothing left standing. "For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Paul knew exactly what he was staking. "And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). The two faiths do not merely interpret the cross differently. One says it did not happen, and the other says nothing else finally matters if it did not. That is not a difference of emphasis. It is a fork in the road with no path between the branches.

## How a person is made right with God

Then the question all the others were leading toward. How is the distance between a holy God and a failing human being ever closed. Islam's answer is coherent and demanding: a person submits. The word islam means submission. You surrender to the one God, you keep his commands, you pray and fast and give and confess his oneness and his prophet, and you throw yourself on the mercy of a God who is merciful, and your deeds are weighed. There is no atoning death in it, because none is thought to be needed; God can simply forgive, and the notion that God would require a death before he forgives can look, from inside Islam, like a limit placed on a mercy that ought to be limitless.

Christianity says the distance is too wide for submission to close, and that God knew it, and so God closed it himself, from his own side, at his own cost. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Here the two faiths are not describing one salvation in two vocabularies. One says a person climbs, helped by mercy, toward a God who commands the climb. The other says a person cannot climb, and God came down. It is grace as reward and grace as rescue, and they do not meet in the middle.

I will not pretend those four disputes are misunderstandings that a patient afternoon could clear away. They are not. They are the load-bearing walls of two different houses, and the people living inside them are not fools on either side. But naming the disputes honestly is the opposite of the contempt that usually stands in for this conversation. The pluralist who says the faiths are all the same has not honored Islam. He has erased it. A Muslim does not believe God is a Trinity, does not believe Jesus died on a cross, does not believe he was God in the flesh, and telling him he secretly agrees with the Christian is not respect. It is refusing to hear him. Taking a person seriously means letting him disagree with you all the way down.

When I was an atheist I kept every religion in one bin marked "things people believe to feel better," and the bin let me avoid all of them at once. Then I started reading them as if they might be making claims about what is actually real, and the bin came apart in my hands, because they were not saying the same thing in different keys. They were saying different things, and the differences could be examined, and at least some of them could in principle be true or false. Whether a crucified man walked out of a tomb outside Jerusalem is not a matter of preference. It happened or it did not.

The Christian faith stakes everything on the claim that it did. Not that Jesus was a great teacher, which Islam grants. Not that he was a prophet, which Islam honors. But that the one God, without ceasing to be one, entered his own creation as a man, was handed over to be killed, and was not defeated by it; and that this is not God brought low but God showing at last what his greatness was always for. I hold that as confession, not as a point scored against a neighbor I respect. I could be wrong, and if I am, I have built my life on a rumor. But I cannot make it smaller than it is to keep the peace at the table, and neither can the devout Muslim across from me make his smaller, and the honesty we owe each other is not the pretense that the gap between us is narrow.

It is to look at it plainly, name what stands on each side of it, and refuse to lie about its width.
posts.excerpt: People say the two faiths are basically the same, or that they share nothing at all. Both are ways of not having the conversation. When I was an atheist, lumping every religion together was not tolerance; it was how I kept all of them at arm's length.

posts.title: Can a Life Mean Anything Without God?
posts.body:
The question does not usually announce itself. It waits for a good day.

You have done the work well, the people you love are asleep in the next rooms, the bills are covered this month, and you are standing in a dark kitchen with a glass of water when the thought arrives without being invited. None of this finally matters. Not that it feels bad in the moment. It feels like nothing, which is worse, a sudden weightlessness where you expected the floor. The children you would die for will die too, and their children, and one day the last human being will close his eyes on a cooling planet under a sun that is itself running down, and no one will be left to remember that you loved anyone or built anything or stood in this kitchen afraid. Then the moment passes and you go to bed. But you have seen it now, and you cannot un-see it.

I know the thought from the inside, and I need to say where I am standing before I say anything else. I did not first meet that 2 a.m. weightlessness as a pastor with an answer ready. I met it as an atheist who thought he had already made his peace with it. For most of my life I believed the universe owed me no meaning and I did not resent it for the silence. So when the church tells you that people without God are secretly miserable, that they lie awake in despair and only pretend to be happy, I want you to know that a man who lived on the other side is telling you the church is wrong. That story is a lie we tell to comfort ourselves, and it is an insult besides.

## The strongest form of the other answer

Let me put the secular account in the form its best defenders actually gave it, because a version you can knock over is not worth the paper.

Albert Camus opened *The Myth of Sisyphus* in 1942 with a sentence that has never stopped being true: "There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide." He was not being morbid. He was being honest in a way most people never are. If the universe is silent, if there is no given purpose written into things, then the first question is not what to have for dinner or how to get promoted. It is whether a life with no external meaning is worth continuing at all. Camus refused the two easy exits. He would not lie to himself and pretend the cosmos cared, and he would not step off the ledge either. He chose a third thing he called revolt: to live fully and defiantly inside the absurd, to squeeze the day for everything it holds precisely because nothing guarantees it, to keep pushing the rock without the consolation of a summit. His book ends where every honest reader remembers it ending. "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."

Jean-Paul Sartre pressed the same ground from a different angle. For a manufactured object, he argued, essence comes first: the knife is designed for cutting before it exists. For a human being it runs the other way. Existence precedes essence. You arrive with no blueprint, no assigned purpose, no maker's intent, and that terrifying vacancy is also the only real freedom there has ever been. You are, in his phrase, condemned to be free. No god hands you a meaning, which means no god can take it from you or shrink you to fit it. You author it yourself, and you are wholly responsible for what you write.

And here is what I will not let the believer skip. This is not a recipe for despair, and the people who live by it are not frauds. I have known atheists who loved their spouses with a fidelity that shamed the elders of my church, who gave to strangers with no heaven watching the ledger, who faced a terminal diagnosis with a steadiness I would want at my own bedside. They built meaning the way Sartre said you could, out of love and craft and loyalty and the refusal to look away, and it was real meaning, not a stage set. Any Christian who has watched that up close and still says it is secretly empty is not defending the faith. He is protecting his own comfort by slandering better men. Concede this fully, or do not bother turning the page.

## The seam

Now turn it over, gently, and look at the seam.

There is a difference between a meaning you invent and a meaning you discover, and the whole question lives in that difference. What you invent, you can also un-invent. What you author, you can revise, and on the worst night you can delete. A purpose I assign to my own life is answerable to me, which sounds like power until the hour comes when I am the very thing that has broken, and then the author and the sinking ship are the same person, and there is no one on the shore. Meaning you make cannot save you, because it is downstream of you. It has exactly as much authority over you as you are willing to grant it, and the granting can be withdrawn.

And under even that, the second problem, the one Camus was too honest to hide. The heat death does not care what you authored. If matter and time are all there is, then every cathedral and every symphony and every child taught to be kind is a pattern that the running-down of the universe will eventually smooth flat, and the smoothing is not a tragedy the cosmos will mourn, because there will be no one to mourn and nothing that was ever owed. A meaning that is finally erased and never even registered as a loss is in a strange position. It is real to you now and null to the universe always, and you are asked to hold both of those at once and call it enough.

I am not scoring a debating point. I lived here. I want to show you two men who lived here harder than I did.

## Tolstoy in the study

Leo Tolstoy had, by any accounting the world keeps, won. By the time he wrote *A Confession* in 1882 he had produced *War and Peace* and *Anna Karenina*, he had land and wealth and international fame, a wife and children, health, and the full use of a mind that ranks among the strongest his century produced. He had built meaning by every method Sartre would later prescribe, and more of it than almost anyone alive. And in the middle of that life he was ambushed by a question he could not answer and could not silence: was there any meaning in his life that the death waiting for all of it would not destroy. He could not find one. He described hiding a rope so that he would not hang himself from the beam of his own room, and giving up hunting with his gun for fear of what he might do with it alone in the woods. This is not the confession of a failure drowning his regrets. It is the confession of the most successful man in Russia discovering that success was never the thing that answered the question, and that he had no idea what was.

That is the seam I mean. The invented meaning worked beautifully right up until the moment he looked past its edge, and then it held nothing, because it had never been anchored to anything outside the man holding it.

## The values they could not fund

Here is the tell I find most telling, and I offer it as diagnosis, not as a gotcha. The great atheist thinkers kept reaching past their own systems for something their systems could not pay for.

Camus could not stay inside pure absurdity, and he knew it. In *The Rebel*, in 1951, he argued that the man who rebels against oppression is not merely expressing a preference. In saying no to the tyrant he appeals, whether he admits it or not, to a value he believes holds for every human being and not only for himself. But a value that binds everyone, that would still condemn the torturer even if the torturer felt fulfilled, is exactly the kind of objective moral fact a silent and indifferent universe does not stock. Camus wanted justice to be more than his taste in the matter. His cosmos could not make it so.

Sartre did the same with his body as well as his pen. In 1966 he sat as executive president of the tribunal Bertrand Russell convened to judge war crimes in Vietnam, and he judged them, as crimes, as things that were wrong and not merely disliked. A philosophy in which each of us authors his own values from nothing has no floor under the word *crime*. Yet Sartre stood on that floor as though it were solid, because at the level below argument he knew some things are wrong for everyone whether or not anyone authored the rule. He borrowed the plank. He could not have milled it in his own shop.

I do not say this to sneer at two serious men. I say it because I did the identical thing for years and called it maturity. I insisted the universe was meaningless and then lived, minute to minute, as though my son's life had a worth no atom of me had voted on. The account I defended in argument was not the account I trusted with my child.

## The nihilist inside the canon

Here is what took me longest to believe about the Bible, once I finally opened it instead of dismissing it. It is not afraid of any of this. It got there first.

There is a book in it that stares straight into the void Camus described and does not blink. "Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The Hebrew word behind *vanity* means vapor, breath, the mist your mouth makes on a cold morning that is gone before you finish looking at it. The Preacher has money, pleasure, projects, wisdom, work, and he weighs each one and files the same verdict. "Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). That is Sisyphus and his rock, written two thousand years before the Frenchman named it. The scandal is not that the skeptic has a hard question the Bible cannot handle. The scandal is that the Bible put the hardest form of the question in its own canon and canonized it, and no council ever voted it out.

But the Preacher leaves one seam of his own, and it is the whole difference. God, he says, "has put eternity into man's heart" (Ecclesiastes 3:11). The reason the mist grieves us, the reason a temporary meaning cannot finally satisfy a creature who keeps demanding a permanent one, is that we were built to want something the running-down world was never able to supply. The ache is not a malfunction to be medicated. It is a piece of evidence about what kind of creature is doing the aching.

## What I would tell the man I was

So I will not tell you that you cannot make meaning without God. You obviously can, and you may be making finer meaning than half the people in my pews. That was never the real question, and pretending it was is how Christians lose the argument they should win.

The real question is quieter and it does not go away when you succeed. It is whether the meaning you are making can carry your weight on the night it has to. Whether it is a thing you hold up, which fails exactly when your arms do, or a thing that holds you, which is only good news if it came from somewhere other than you. Invented meaning has one fatal property: on the day you can no longer believe in it, it is gone, because it was only ever your believing. Discovered meaning has the opposite property, and it is the only property that finally helps. It is still there when you stop feeling it. It was true while you slept.

The Christian claim is not that we escaped the vapor by refusing to look at it. Paul looked straight at it and wrote that if the dead are not raised, then "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (1 Corinthians 15:32), which is to say that if the grave is the end he would concede the whole nihilist case and pass the wine. The claim is that a man walked out of a tomb on the far side of the vapor, and that this makes love and labor and a kindness no one will remember into something the heat death cannot reach, not because we authored them but because they are held by someone the cooling universe does not get to erase.

I made my own meaning for years, and it was good, and it worked, right up until it did not, on a night when I was the thing that had broken and there was no one on the shore because I had spent my whole life proving the shore was empty. I am not going to tell you what to conclude from that. I will only tell you not to trust the peace you have made with the silence more than you trust the silence itself. Test it. Wait for the good day, the dark kitchen, the glass of water, the weightlessness. Ask whether what you have built is holding you up, or whether you are holding it.

Then notice which one of you gets tired first.
posts.excerpt: The atheist is not the miserable nihilist the church invented to feel better. He builds real, loving, meaningful lives. The question is not whether he can make meaning. It is whether meaning you make can hold you when you stop believing in it.

posts.title: The Suffering God Never Ordered
posts.body:
There is an objection I have never fully answered, and I am not going to spend the next two thousand words pretending I finally have.

I can make my peace with the evil we do to each other. Give me an afternoon and I will walk you through the free-will defense, the case that a world of creatures who can genuinely love has to be a world of creatures who can genuinely wound, that forced love is a contradiction and God cannot both hand us freedom and confiscate every misuse of it. I believe that argument. I have made it elsewhere. It answers the concentration camp and the abusive father and the drunk driver, the whole ledger of what human beings choose. It answers cruelty.

It does not answer the fawn.

The philosopher William Rowe put the harder problem into a single image in 1979, in a paper called "The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism," and it has not lost a step since. Picture a forest, somewhere no person has ever walked. Lightning strikes a dead tree and the fire spreads. A fawn is caught in it, badly burned, and lies in the undergrowth for several days in agony before death finally reaches it. No human being started the fire. No human being sees the fawn. No human being is ennobled by its death or learns a thing from it, or is even aware that it happened. The suffering arrives, runs its full course, and ends, and as far as anyone can tell it accomplishes exactly nothing.

That is not the problem of moral evil. No freedom is being protected in this story, because no one in it is free; there is only a fire and an animal and a length of pain with no witness and no fruit. And the fawn is not a special case. It is a single frame from something enormous. Predation is not a recent human arrangement. It is hundreds of millions of years old, written into the fossil record long before anything that could sin had evolved to sin. For most of the history of life on this planet, animals have torn other animals apart in order to live, and parasites have grown inside living hosts by consuming them slowly. Darwin, in an 1860 letter to the botanist Asa Gray, confessed he could not persuade himself that a good and omnipotent God would have deliberately designed the ichneumon wasps to feed within the living bodies of caterpillars. He was not being flippant. He was looking at the actual mechanism of the world and finding it hard to reconcile with the God he had been handed. So do I.

Bring it up out of the forest and into a hospital. A child gets leukemia. No one did it to her. There is no villain, no choice, no freedom being defended; there is a cell that copied itself wrong. A fault line that has been storing pressure since before there was a written word slips one afternoon, and a wave crosses the Indian Ocean, and a quarter of a million people are gone by nightfall. The plates were not angry. The virus has no malice. This is the suffering that no free will explains, and it is, I think, the strongest form of the case against the God I preach. Its technical name is the evidential problem of evil, and its honest version is not the claim that suffering proves there is no God. It is the quieter, heavier claim that the sheer quantity of apparently pointless suffering, the fawn multiplied by every unwitnessed agony in the long dark of natural history, makes a good and all-powerful God look, on the face of the evidence, unlikely. I felt the weight of that for years. I still feel its edge on the bad nights.

So let me say first what I will not do with it, because the church has done all of these to people in grief and I have winced from the back pew. I will not tell a mother in an oncology ward that God needed another angel, because that is not Christianity and it is not true. I will not tell her the earthquake was a punishment, because Jesus was asked that exact question about a tower that fell and killed eighteen people, and he refused the premise flatly (Luke 13:4-5). And I will not reach for the reflex that blames the whole groaning order on the sin of one couple in a garden, as though a man eating fruit rewired plate tectonics and installed the second law of thermodynamics. The Bible does not require me to say that, and the geology will not let me. Predation and decay are older than humanity by a margin no reading of Genesis can shrink. If I am going to be honest with the skeptic, I have to be honest here first, where it costs me something.

What I have instead is smaller than an answer and larger than a shrug. A few things I have come to think are true, none of which closes the case, offered to a reader I am assuming is intelligent and may be in pain.

The first is about the kind of world this is. A world in which embodied creatures can act at all is a world that runs on stable law, and stable law does not bend to spare the creature. The reason your body can heal is the reason it can break; the chemistry that knits bone is the chemistry that lets it shatter under enough force, and you cannot keep the one property and delete the other, because they are the same property described from two sides. The tectonic churn that buries carbon and renews the soil and keeps this planet habitable across deep time is the same churn that slips one afternoon and drowns a coast. Water that can bear a boat can fill a child's lungs; it is not a different substance on the two occasions. You begin to see the shape of the difficulty. A world regular enough to act in, regular enough to build a boat and set a bone and love a creature whose behavior you can predict and trust, seems to be a world whose regularities will sometimes fall on that creature and crush it. I am not claiming this proves the arrangement good. I am claiming it may be the necessary price of any world in which anyone can do anything at all, and that a world without the price might be a world without embodied life in it. That is not comfort. It is a reason to think the situation might not be the plain negligence it looks like.

The second is that the Bible itself does not call the present arrangement the intended one. This surprised me when I read it instead of assuming its contents. I had expected Scripture to defend the world as it stands, to pronounce the whole system very good and dare me to argue. It does something stranger. Paul writes: "For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now" (Romans 8:20-22). Read what that does not say. It does not say the groaning is good. It does not say the futility is the last word. It calls the present order subjected, bound, in labor, straining toward a release it does not yet have. The name Scripture gives the fawn's agony is not justice and it is not design fulfilled. It is groaning. The Bible looks at the same world Rowe looked at and refuses to call it finished. Whatever this is, it files it under childbirth, not under the way things are meant to stay.

The third thing is Job, and I have to be careful, because Job is the book everyone reaches for and almost everyone uses to deliver the very lecture the book was written to demolish. Job loses everything, his children included, to raiders and a collapsing house, human evil and natural disaster braided together. His friends arrive with theodicies, tidy accounts of what he must have done to earn it, and God's verdict at the end is that the friends were wrong and Job, who protested, had spoken rightly. But when God finally answers Job out of the whirlwind, he does not explain. He asks questions for four chapters, and the strangest thing about those chapters is their content. God offers no moral defense of the universe. He gives Job a tour of the wild. He points to the lioness on the hunt and the young ravens crying for food, to the wild donkey who scorns the noise of the city, to the ostrich who deals cruelly with her own young, to the hawk and the wild ox and two untamed monsters no man can bring under a yoke (Job 38-41). It is a parade of exactly the parts of creation that do not revolve around human comfort or even human sight, a world with predation and wildness built into its frame, and God claims all of it as his, on purpose, without apology and without explanation. Job wanted the transcript of the trial. What he got was the living God and the wild otherness of what that God had made, and Job says he is satisfied, not because the ledger finally balanced but because he had been arguing about someone he had never met and now had met him. I do not fully understand that ending. I have watched it happen to people at gravesides, which is why I no longer wave it off.

And the last thing is the one that finally held me, not because it answers the argument but because it moves who is standing where. The God of Christianity does not issue the fawn a statement from outside the fire. The claim at the center of the faith is that he came into the world that groans and took its worst onto his own body. Not a symbolic body. A nervous system. He starved in a wilderness, wept at a friend's grave, and died of the ordinary brutal physics of asphyxiation and blood loss under a Roman crossbeam, crying the sufferer's own line, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). Whatever this is, it is not a comfortable deity narrating our pain from a safe altitude. It is a God who declined the altitude. That does not tell me why the fawn burned. It tells me the maker of the fawn is not exempt from the fire, and for reasons I can defend better with my life than with a syllogism, that turned out to be the thing I could stand on when the argument could not be won.

I promised at the start that I would not pretend I had solved this, so at the end I will keep the promise where it costs the most. None of that resolves the fawn. Line the four considerations up and the animal is still in the undergrowth, still burned, still alone, and I have not produced the reason its days of pain were worth it, because I do not have that reason, and the man who tells you he does is selling you something he has never held. The evidential problem is not dissolved. It is, at most, held. What Christianity offers the skeptic here is not a proof that the suffering makes sense. It is two claims the suffering on its own terms cannot reach: that this is not the arrangement God intends to keep, and that he did not stay outside it.

I still feel the edge of this one, and I want you to know that, because the church usually hands you the man who has stopped feeling it, and you are right not to trust him. I have five sons, and I have buried other people's children, and there are nights the argument comes back at full force and I do not have the answer, only the person. The fawn's fire is real. It is also, if the gospel is true, not the last word and not the intended word, and there is a difference wide enough to build a life on between a universe where that pain is finally nothing and a universe where it is finally seen.
posts.excerpt: Free will explains the evil we do to each other. It explains nothing about the fawn burning alone in a forest fire, the child's leukemia, the long ages of animal agony before anyone could sin. This is the objection I have never fully answered, and I will not pretend here that I finally have.

posts.title: What the New Atheists Got Right
posts.body:
I owned the books. Not borrowed, not skimmed at a table in a store: bought, underlined, argued from at dinner tables where I already knew I would win. When Richard Dawkins published *The God Delusion* in 2006, I read it the way a soldier reads dispatches from a front where his side is advancing. Christopher Hitchens came the next year with *God Is Not Great: How Religion Poisons Everything*, and I read that one twice. Sam Harris had fired the opening shot in 2004 with *The End of Faith*, written in the smoke still rising off September 11th. Daniel Dennett rounded out the four in 2006 with *Breaking the Spell*. Someone nicknamed them the Four Horsemen, and I would have followed all four off a cliff.

I have to say that before I say anything else, because the easiest thing a pastor can do with these men is build a version of them out of straw and knock it down in front of an audience that was never going to read them anyway. I refuse. I stood where they stood. I made their arguments better than most believers I now know could answer them. And here is the sentence it took me years to be able to write without flinching: they were right about a great deal, and a believer who cannot say so has understood neither the men nor the faith he imagines he is defending.

## The four, at full strength

Take them at their most serious, because a version you can knock over is not worth the paper.

Harris wrote first and wrote angriest, and his anger had a specific occasion. Nineteen men had flown planes into buildings because they believed something about the next life, and Harris argued that the moderate believer who calls their faith a perversion has no principled ground to stand on, because he too holds beliefs he cannot test and will not surrender to evidence. Religious moderation, he said, is not a solution. It is the cover that keeps the whole enterprise beyond criticism. Faith is belief without sufficient reason, and in a century of engineered viruses and portable warheads, belief without reason is not a private comfort. It is a public danger.

Dawkins pressed a cleaner claim. The existence of God, he insisted, is not a separate kind of question fenced off from investigation. It is a hypothesis about what is really out there, and a hypothesis can be weighed. Weigh it, he argued, and it fails: the universe looks exactly as we would expect if there were no one behind it, and the God most people actually worship is a bronze-age tribal figure whose recorded conduct, laid out plainly, would disgrace a human being. He catalogued that conduct at length, the jealousy and the slaughter and the sanctioned cruelty, and dared the believer to read his own scriptures with the flinch removed.

Dennett was the quietest and, in a way, the most subversive. He did not mainly argue that religion is false. He argued that we have made it rude to ask. His book proposed to break a spell: the unspoken agreement that faith is the one human phenomenon we do not study the way we study everything else. Treat religion as a natural thing, he said, a product of human minds and human history with causes we can trace, and watch how quickly its claim to have descended from heaven begins to look like something that grew up from the ground.

And Hitchens. Hitchens did not build a system. He indicted. Religion, he wrote, is man-made, and its title tells you where he landed: it poisons everything. It corrupts our view of our own origins, sets us at the center of a cosmos that plainly does not revolve around us, promises eternity to buy obedience now, and reserves its special energies for the policing of sex and the shaming of the body. He had watched clerics of every flag bless armies and cover for the men who harmed children, and he had the memory and the malice to name every instance. I laughed out loud reading him. I also, in the honest hours, could not answer him.

## What they got right

So let me stop performing balance and simply concede the ground, because it is real ground and it is soaked.

Religion has blood on it. Not metaphorically, not in the soft sense a sermon uses before the reassuring turn. The church blessed the conquest of peoples and called it mission. It burned dissenters and lit the fires with Scripture. In my own lifetime it moved men who abused children from one parish to the next and spent more energy protecting the institution than the children, and when the accounting came it reached for lawyers before it reached for repentance. Hitchens did not invent any of that. He read it off the record, and the record is public, and the reflex of the church's defenders to change the subject the moment it comes up is very nearly as damning as the thing itself.

They were right about the anti-intellectualism too, and this one I feel personally, because I was on the receiving end of it before I ever left. I asked hard questions as a young man and I was handed slogans. I raised the problem of suffering and got a bumper sticker. I noticed the contradictions honest readers have always noticed, and I was told that noticing was the sin, that a good heart does not ask. Faith was offered to me not as a conviction that could survive scrutiny but as a fortress built to avoid it, and Harris is exactly right that a faith which forbids the question has already conceded it cannot answer it. The apologetics I was given were thin, and I could feel their thinness the way you feel a floor that will not hold your weight, and the men who gave them to me mistook my leaving for rebellion when it was closer to disappointment.

And they were right about the poison in the specific place it does its quietest work: the shutting down of the mind in the name of God. This is the hit I most want to dodge and will not. Every time the church has answered a real question with a demand for silence, every time it has treated doubt as disloyalty and curiosity as pride, it has taught its own children that the faith cannot bear examination. It taught me that. I did not walk away from Jesus of Nazareth. I walked away from a version of him that came with the instruction to stop thinking, and I was right to walk away from that, and it took me a long time to learn that the instruction had never come from him.

Grant all of it. If you cannot grant it, you are not ready for the next paragraph, and neither was I.

## Where the argument overreaches

Now turn the argument over and look at its underside, slowly, the way I finally learned to.

Watch first what each man does with the evidence when it runs the other way. The worst of religion is presented as its essence, the thing it truly is once the pleasantries are stripped off. The worst of secularism is presented as an aberration, a betrayal of principles that remain clean. But the twentieth century will not sit still for that division. The regimes that killed on the largest scale the world has ever recorded were not priest-ridden. They were built by men who had read their Feuerbach and their Marx, who abolished God by decree and put the state in the empty chair. Stalin's cellars, Mao's famine, the killing fields of Cambodia: these were not the church's crimes. They were carried out by movements that shared the horsemen's diagnosis and drew the practical conclusion. When Hitchens was pressed on this, he answered that those regimes were religious in structure, cults of personality with their own liturgies. It is a clever answer. It is also the whole argument collapsing, because if every organized cruelty counts as religion, then religion is just a name for the human capacity to organize cruelty, and the word has stopped meaning what his book needed it to mean.

That is the deeper flaw under all four, and it has a name older than any of them: the genetic fallacy, the mistake of thinking you have shown a belief false by exposing where it came from. Dennett is right that religion has natural causes, that it grew in human minds and human tribes and can be studied like anything else. But so did mathematics. So did his own confidence in reason. Show me the evolutionary account of why a hominid came to trust its own reasoning, and you have explained the origin of trust without touching the question of whether the reasoning is any good. A belief is true or false on the merits, not on its pedigree. Trace the faith all the way back to the anxious ape at the fire, and you have still not said one word about whether, at the end of that long chain, there is anyone there.

And Dawkins made the cleanest category mistake of the four, the one I repeated for years without noticing. He treated God as a hypothesis inside the universe, a large invisible object whose existence should leave fingerprints his instruments could detect. But the God the historic creeds confess was never advanced as an item within the world, one more thing alongside the galaxies to be found or ruled out. He is offered as the reason there is a world at all, the ground the whole experiment stands on. You do not test the foundation by searching the house for it. To demand that God show up as data within the system is to have decided in advance that nothing could count as him, and then to announce, with the air of discovery, that nothing does.

There is a fair objection here, and I will not hide from it. The believer who says God is beyond all testing can sound like a man moving the goalposts to a field where he can never lose. That is a real danger and the church has abused it. But there is a difference between a claim that explains nothing and a claim that is simply the wrong shape for a microscope, and the honest atheist knows the difference, because he applies it to his own foundations without blinking every day.

## What I finally saw

I have saved the hardest concession for the end, and it is a concession I make against my old self.

Jesus said harder things about religion than Hitchens ever managed. "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness" (Matthew 23:27, ESV). That is not a skeptic writing from outside. That is the center of the faith turning on the religious professionals with a fury the horsemen would have envied, and it means the critique the four thought they were leveling at Christianity from without had been sitting inside it, in red letters, the whole time. The book they were attacking already contained the indictment. It also contained the standard by which the church stands condemned: "Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world" (James 1:27, ESV). By that measure most of what the four attacked deserved attacking, and the New Testament said so first.

What I could not see while I held their books, because I was too busy winning, was this. They were right about the church I was leaving. They were wrong about the God I had never actually met. Every crime they catalogued was real, and not one of them was Jesus of Nazareth. They had assembled a brilliant, furious, documented case against religion as a human machine for control, and I cheered because I thought that machine was the whole of it, and I had never once been shown the man at the center who was executed by exactly that machine for exactly the reasons the horsemen despised it. I left over the poison. Nobody told me the poison was the thing he came to name, and that they had crucified him for naming it.

So I do not stand over these men now. I owe them too much. Harris taught me that a faith which forbids the question is already dead. Dawkins taught me to read my own scriptures with the flinch removed, and when I finally did, they were harder and stranger and more honest than the sanitized version I had been sold. Hitchens taught me that the church must carry its crimes as facts and not misunderstandings, and I have carried them into hospital rooms and gravesides ever since. They cleared a great deal of rotten ground, and the God I found was standing on the far side of it, where I would never have looked as long as I mistook the rot for the thing itself.

The test they never let me apply to my own certainty is the one their own hero recommended. "Thus you will recognize them by their fruits" (Matthew 7:20, ESV). Apply it to the church and it draws blood, and it should. Apply it to the confident secular century that promised to do better once God was gone, and it draws blood too. Neither of us gets to walk away clean. That is not a victory for my side. It is the end of the idea that either of us had a side that was clean, and it is exactly where an honest man, believer or not, should have to stand before he says one more word about who poisons everything.
posts.excerpt: I owned the books. I underlined them, I argued from them, and I would have followed all four horsemen off a cliff. This is the honest account of where they were right, where they overreached, and the one thing they got wrong that I could not see until I had stopped being one of them.

posts.title: What the Bible Says About Angels, Demons, and the Unseen
posts.body:
Of everything in the Bible, this was the easiest to mock. Not the miracles, which at least kept their dignity, and not the moral demands, which I could respect while refusing. Angels and demons were something else. They were the part a grown man was supposed to have outgrown, the pageant furniture of a species that had not yet discovered what actually moves the world. I could dismiss the resurrection with an argument. I dismissed the unseen order with a smile, which is worse, because a smile does not have to think. And I want to say at the start that I have come to believe the man smiling had understood this less than anything else he was sure of. But he had a case. I am not going to pretend he did not.

## The case for disenchantment

Here is the reasonable person's objection, and it is reasonable. You tell him there are angels and demons, an invisible traffic of spirits behind the visible world, and he hears the cosmology of people who did not know what he knows. People who thought illness was a curse instead of a pathogen. People who read a storm as a mood in the heavens instead of a pressure system, who heard a seizure and saw possession, who buried a stillborn child and looked for the witch who had done it. For most of human history the space we now fill with germ theory and meteorology and neurology was filled with beings, and the beings did the work no one could yet explain. Then we learned better. We found the bacterium under the plague and the misfiring neuron under the fit, and one by one the demons were evicted from the rooms they had been squatting in, until there were no rooms left. That is not a small point. That is most of what a modern person means by the word progress.

And the objection has a harder edge than the history, because the history is only half of it. The philosopher Charles Taylor, tracing how the West became secular, described the change not as a set of arguments we won but as a shift in the very texture of experience. He called the modern self the buffered self. The older self, the one Taylor calls porous, felt itself open to a world thick with forces, vulnerable to spirits and blessings and curses that could cross into it from outside. The buffered self is sealed. It draws a line at the edge of the skin and the meaning stays inside it, and everything past the line is just nature, matter running its causes with no one home. We live now, Taylor says, inside an immanent frame, a world felt as a closed system of natural cause and effect with no window cut in the ceiling. The point is that most of us did not decide this. We inhabit it the way we inhabit a language. When the buffered man hears "demon," he is not rejecting a claim. He is failing to feel that the category could contain anything at all.

I was that man, and I did not experience my disenchantment as a position. I experienced it as adulthood.

## What the church earned

Before I say a word for the other side, I have to concede what my side was right to hold against the church, because a believer who skips this has forfeited the honest reader in the first paragraph.

The church earned the smile. It has spent centuries handing the skeptic his best material. There is a whole industry of deliverance that plays possession like theater, a man in a good suit shouting at demons under stage lights while an audience films it, and the spectacle is not reverence. It is entertainment wearing the costume of warfare. There is the long, ugly habit of naming a demon for what was in fact an untreated illness, of praying over a depression that needed a physician and a prescription, of telling a woman her intrusive thoughts were a spirit when they were a diagnosable and treatable condition, and of leaving her ashamed on top of sick. And there is a fear-market that sells this, books and conferences and ministries priced to a Christian's anxiety, teaching him to read a flat tire and a bad mood as enemy fire, keeping him scared enough to keep buying. I will not defend any of it. It has done real harm, it has driven thoughtful people out the door, and when the skeptic points at it he is not being cynical. He is being accurate. If that is what the doctrine of the unseen produces, the doctrine deserves the contempt.

So the church has to answer for the circus before it says anything about the thing the circus is a counterfeit of. I am answering for it now. And having answered, I have to tell you that the counterfeit is not the original, and that the smile I wore was aimed at the counterfeit, and that I had never once looked hard at what the text actually claims.

## What the text actually claims

Start with what the Bible does not say, because most of what a modern person is rejecting is not in it.

It does not teach dualism. This is the correction that reorganized everything for me. The picture I was mocking, God and the devil as matched opponents locked in a cosmic contest whose outcome hangs in doubt, two roughly equal powers of light and dark, is not the Christian claim. It is closer to the plot of a film. Scripture will not give the devil that dignity. God has no equal and no opposite. "I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 45:5). The devil in the Bible is a creature, a made thing, existing at every moment on borrowed being, no more a rival to his Maker than a shadow is a rival to the sun. Evil is real, but it is derivative, a good gone wrong, a defection. It has no kingdom of its own and no future. The moment you grasp that the unseen order is not a balanced war but a defeated rebellion inside a creation with one Lord, you have already left superstition behind, because superstition runs on fear of a power that might win, and this power cannot.

Then the angels, who are not what the greeting cards made them. They are not the souls of the dead. They are not soft ornamental infants. The word means messenger, and in the text they are servants, dispatched, given errands, sent to speak and to guard and to carry out the will of the one who made them. "Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?" (Hebrews 1:14). When one appears, the first thing it usually has to say is do not be afraid, which tells you these are not the tame decorations of a nursery. But the point the text keeps making is that their weight is borrowed too. They serve. They are creatures with jobs. The interest is never in the messenger; it is in who sent him.

And then the sober center of it, the part that survived my scorn and eventually undid it. The New Testament does not spend much time on lurid possession stories, which is itself worth noticing, given the reputation. It speaks instead of what it calls principalities and powers, and it locates the real conflict somewhere I had not expected. Writing to the church at Ephesus, Paul says: "For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 6:12). Read that slowly, because it is doing something precise. It is telling you the battle is not mainly the theatrical kind. It is telling you the enemy is not the person across the table, not flesh and blood, which means the doctrine of the unseen, rightly held, is the one thing that could have pulled me back from the easiest sin of the political animal, which is to believe my opponent is the darkness. The powers named there are the things that organize human evil into something larger than any single wicked man, the ideology that swallows a nation, the machinery of a lie that outlives the liars who built it, the momentum by which ordinary people do monstrous things together and each feels innocent. A materialist can watch that happen and call it sociology. Scripture says there is a personal malice behind it, and, having read the twentieth century, I am no longer certain sociology is the deeper account.

## The note is victory, not fear

Now the turn the fear-market cannot afford to let you hear, because a customer who hears it stops paying.

If the New Testament wanted you afraid, this is where it would press. It does the opposite. The whole tone of the thing, once you actually read it instead of quoting it in the dark, is not terror but a strange settled confidence, and the reason is a single event the writers keep returning to. Of the cross, Paul says: "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). Disarmed. Not fought to a draw, not held at bay pending some later rematch, but stripped and paraded, the way a conquering general marched a beaten enemy through the streets so the whole city could see the war was already over. Whatever the powers are, the claim is that they have been publicly and decisively broken, and that the breaking is finished, and that it happened in the one place I would never have looked for a victory, on an instrument of execution, in what looked to every eye present like total defeat.

That is why the Christian posture toward the unseen is not the posture the circus sells. The word the text keeps using is not fear. It is sobriety. "Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour" (1 Peter 5:8). Watchful, yes, awake, not naive, taking the reality seriously. But sober, which is the opposite of the fevered eye that finds a demon in every setback. A lion is real and a lion is dangerous and you do not walk toward it, and also you are not to spend your life screaming at the grass. The Christian is told to stand, to be clothed in truth and righteousness and the readiness of the good news, and to leave the outcome where it already rests, with the one who has no equal. There is exactly enough seriousness here to keep you honest and exactly enough victory to keep you from panic, and the tradition that gets loud and afraid has lost the second half of its own book.

## What I had misunderstood

So let me stand inside the indictment where I belong, because I did not merely disbelieve this. I disbelieved a version of it that I had never checked against the source, and I called the not-checking rigor.

I had mistaken the counterfeit for the claim. I had taken the worst practitioners as the fair sample, which is a move I would never have permitted anyone to make against a scientific theory, and I made it against this one because it cost me nothing and flattered me to make it. I had assumed the doctrine was pre-scientific, a gap-filler waiting to be evicted by better knowledge, when its real subject was never the seizure or the storm at all, but the thing modern people are least equipped to see and most desperately need to, that evil is larger than the individuals who carry it and personal in a way our machinery cannot register. The buffered self is very good at not being afraid of demons. It is not at all good at explaining how a whole civilized nation can be marched into atrocity by something none of its people would have chosen alone. I had a category that named that and I had thrown it out with the greeting-card angels, and I was proud of the housecleaning.

What I could not have known, standing in the immanent frame and mistaking its walls for the sky, is that the sober version was there the whole time, underneath the circus and older than my scorn. A creation with one Lord and no rival. Messengers who serve. Powers that are real, and personal, and already beaten. And a reader I would have pitied, the ancient Christian who believed in all of it, holding it not with a frightened eye but with a peace I did not have and could not, from inside my closed and tidy world, so much as feel the shape of.

I smiled at people who could see something I had trained myself out of seeing. The joke, it turned out, was on the buffered man who thought the room was empty because he had sealed the windows himself.
posts.excerpt: As a materialist this was the easiest thing in the Bible to mock, and later the thing I had understood least. Angels, demons, an unseen order. Here is the sober version, with the fear taken out and the claim left in.

posts.title: Is My Anxiety a Spiritual Failure?
posts.body:
The verse arrives at three in the morning, and it does not come as comfort. You are awake again, heart going faster than the room warrants, running the list of everything that could break, and somewhere underneath the list a second fear is waiting, quieter and worse than the first. If you really trusted God, you would not be lying here like this. The racing is not only racing anymore. It has become evidence. A verdict on your faith, delivered nightly, in your own voice.

I want to meet you there before I say anything else, because that second fear does more damage than the first, and almost no one names it out loud. The anxiety is hard. The shame stacked on top of it, the suspicion that a stronger Christian would have prayed this away by now, is the part that keeps you from telling anyone, and the hiding is what lets it grow. So let me be plain at the start, and then spend the rest of this earning it: your anxiety is not a report card on your soul. It is not the measure of how much you believe. Before we get to why, I have to be honest about the two answers you have probably already been handed, because both of them contain enough truth to keep you trapped.

## The two answers that did not help

The first answer is the one that comes with a Bible verse and a faint smell of shame. Be anxious for nothing, it says. Scripture commands you not to worry, so if you are worried, the problem is spiritual. Pray harder. Trust more. Confess the sin of unbelief. And I have to grant this answer its due before I take it apart, because it is holding on to something real. God does call his people out of fear. The command "fear not" runs through the whole of Scripture, not as scolding but as invitation, and a faith that never quiets any anxiety has missed something God actually offers. The people who hand you this answer are usually pointing, however clumsily, at a genuine peace they have tasted and want for you.

But here is where it turns cruel. It takes a feeling and reads it as a moral failure, and in doing so it adds the exact weight it claims to remove. Tell an anxious person that their anxiety is sin and you have not given them less to carry. You have given them more. Now they are anxious, and ashamed of being anxious, and anxious about the shame. I have watched this in my own congregation, and I have to confess I once preached closer to it than I like to remember, mistaking a bruise for a rebellion and pressing on it in the name of God. That is not pastoral care. It is a heavier chain with a verse stamped on the lock.

The second answer comes from the opposite direction and wears a lab coat. It says the spiritual talk is beside the point. Anxiety is chemistry. It is cortisol and a nervous system that will not stand down, wiring and hormones and sleep you did not get, and the soul has nothing to do with any of it. I want to grant this one its due as well, and generously, because a great deal of it is simply true. Your body is not a rumor. Anxiety is not only in your head in the dismissive sense; it is in your chest and your gut and your bloodstream, and a real physiology is running underneath the fear. The people who say this are often rescuing you from the first answer, and they are right that your racing heart is not a character flaw.

Where this one fails is not in what it sees but in what it flattens. If you are only chemistry, then the dread that keeps you up is a malfunction with no meaning, a machine misfiring, and nothing you are afraid of actually matters because there is no you underneath the neurons to matter to. That is not comfort. That is a smaller room with the lights turned off. The body is telling the truth. But you are more than the body, and a person is not a set of symptoms to be managed down to quiet.

So one answer says it is all soul and the other says it is all chemistry, and both leave you alone. The truth is that you are not a soul trapped in a machine, and you are not a machine with a rumor of a soul. You are a whole person, body and spirit at once, made that way and loved that way, and any answer that has to cut you in half to work is not the answer.

## What Paul actually wrote

Now to the verse that has been used against you, because it does not say what the shame taught you it says. Paul writes, "do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:6-7, ESV).

Read where he was when he wrote it. Paul is in prison, writing to a church he loves and cannot get to, and this is not a man on a stage telling you to cheer up. Read the shape of the sentence and notice what it is not. It is not "stop feeling anxious or else." It is not a command to grab the feeling by the throat and strangle it into silence by force of will. It is a door, held open. Do not carry this alone, he says. In everything, bring it. Every request, named out loud, handed over. The verse is not asking you to manufacture calm and then present the finished calm to God as proof of your faith. It is asking you to bring him the mess while it is still a mess.

The word Paul uses for anxious is the same word Jesus uses in the Sermon on the Mount when he says "do not be anxious about your life" (Matthew 6:25, ESV). It is the word for a divided mind, a heart pulled in two directions at once, torn between the God who holds tomorrow and the tomorrow you cannot control. Jesus is not condemning the torn feeling. He is calling the torn person home, back to a Father who feeds birds and clothes fields and has not forgotten you. The peace on offer is not a technique you perform. It is a Person you go to. That is the whole difference, and it is the difference between a command you will always fail and an invitation you can always accept.

## The body is not a spiritual afterthought

If you still suspect that a truly faithful person would not need anything as ordinary as sleep or food or help, I want to take you to a prophet flat on his back in the desert. Elijah has just won the loudest victory of his career, and days later he is running for his life, done, sitting under a bush and asking to die. "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers" (1 Kings 19:4, ESV). This is one of the great men of Scripture, and he has hit the bottom of himself.

Watch what God does, because it is not what the shame answer would predict. God does not open with a lecture on Elijah's weak faith. He does not hand him a verse and tell him to claim it. "And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, 'Arise and eat.' And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again" (1 Kings 19:5-6, ESV). Sleep. A meal. Then more sleep, and a second meal. God treats the exhausted body first, gently, twice, and only later, rested and fed, does Elijah get the word from heaven he needs. The God who made you knows you are dust, and he does not despise the dust. He feeds it. If God met the crushed prophet with rest and bread before theology, you can stop believing that needing rest and bread and help is a sign he has given up on you.

## Lament is not the failure of faith. It is faith.

There is a whole language in Scripture for exactly where you are, and the church has largely forgotten how to speak it. Roughly a third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of people in genuine anguish who do not tidy themselves up before they come. "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?" (Psalm 42:5, ESV). That is in the songbook of the people of God, on purpose. God did not edit the turmoil out. He inspired someone to write it down and gave it to the church to pray.

And then there is the garden. On the last night, Jesus himself, fully God and fully a man with a nervous system, says to his friends, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38, ESV). Luke, who was a physician and noticed such things, records that "being in an agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44, ESV). Whatever anxiety is, it is not something the sinless Son of God stayed safely above. He went into the deepest distress a body can hold, and he did not sin in it, and he prayed through it rather than around it. Your dread does not disqualify you from his company. He has been where you are, in a garden, in the dark, asking the Father if there is any other way. Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith with its eyes open, refusing to pretend, still talking to God.

## Getting help is a gift, not a defeat

So let me say the practical thing without a bait and switch, because someone needs to hear it plainly tonight. If your anxiety is heavy enough to steal your sleep, your appetite, your work, or your ability to be present to the people you love, please tell someone this week. Tell your doctor. Talk to a counselor. Tell one trusted person who can sit with you and not flinch. If there is medicine that helps your body carry what it cannot carry alone, that is not a failure of faith any more than glasses are a failure of eyesight. I am a pastor and not a physician, and none of this is medical advice; it is a door I am pointing you toward and asking you to walk through, because the God who fed Elijah works through ordinary bread and ordinary people and ordinary means of care.

And if you have gone to the place Elijah went, where you no longer want to be here at all, hear this with everything I have: that is not a verdict on your soul either, and it is not something to hide. It is a reason to tell someone today, out loud, and to let them help you get real support now. You are not a burden for needing it. You are a person God made and has not stopped watching over, and reaching for help is one of the most faithful things you will ever do.

You did not fail a test tonight. There was no test. There is a Father who feeds the exhausted, a Savior who sweat in a garden, a songbook full of people who prayed their turmoil and were not turned away, and a room full of ordinary help he is not too proud to use. Your anxiety is not the measure of your faith. Bring it to him as it is, and tell someone in the morning. He was never keeping score. He was watching the road.
posts.excerpt: The verse arrives at three in the morning and does not come as comfort. Underneath the racing heart is a second fear, quieter and worse: that the anxiety itself is the verdict on your faith. It is not. Let me tell you why.

posts.title: Can Christians Fight? Just War and the Case for Peace
posts.body:
The question does not usually arrive in a seminar. It arrives at a door.

Someone is on the other side of it, and they mean to come through, and behind you in the house are the people you would die for. You have seconds. And in those seconds a man who spent his life reading the Sermon on the Mount has to decide whether the words he has underlined a hundred times mean what they seem to mean, or whether there is an exception written in ink he cannot see. I have five sons. I know exactly which way my body wants to move. What I do not know, and what I want to be honest that I do not know, is whether the wanting is obedience or the oldest sin dressed as love.

So I am not going to tell you where I land. Not because I am hedging. Because the church has held this both ways for two thousand years, has canonized saints on both sides, and has never once resolved it into a rule you can carry into that hallway. The most honest thing I can do is hand you both cases at full strength and refuse to spare you the weight of choosing.

Start with the case for peace, and refuse the cartoon of it first. Pacifism is not the belief that violence is unpleasant. Everyone believes that. It is the belief that Jesus meant it.

Read the words without the escape hatch already installed. "But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also" (Matthew 5:39). And a few sentences later: "But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44). The pacifist reads these and asks a question the rest of us work very hard not to ask. What did he mean by enemy. Not the annoying neighbor. The Greek word carries the enemy who wants you dead, the occupying soldier, the one with the sword. Jesus is not describing an unpleasant coworker. He is describing Rome. And into a crowd that had every earthly reason to take up arms against an empire, an armed rebellion any of them would have called just, he said love them, and he did not add a footnote for the hard cases.

Then he did the thing that is harder to argue with than any verse. In the garden, when the soldiers came for him, one of his own men drew a sword and used it, and struck, and drew blood in the one situation every one of us would call justified. This was not aggression. This was the defense of an innocent man, the most innocent who ever lived, against an unjust arrest by a mob in the dark. If self-defense is ever righteous, it was righteous there. And Jesus stopped him. "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). He healed the wound his defender had inflicted. Then he let them take him. The pacifist stands on that ground and asks the rest of us a question we cannot easily answer: if the sword was wrong there, in the clearest case of just defense in human history, where exactly does it become right.

And this is not a modern softness invented by people who never bled. For its first centuries the church leaned hard against the sword. Tertullian, writing around the year 200, argued that when Christ disarmed Peter he disarmed every soldier, that the Christian could not serve in an army whose trade was killing. Origen, answering the pagan Celsus a generation later, said plainly that Christians do not take up arms against anyone, that they fight instead by prayer. The historical record is not perfectly clean, and honest scholars argue over how many Christians were in the legions. But the moral center of gravity in the first three centuries pulled away from the sword, and it pulled that way while the church was being fed to lions, which is to say it was not the pacifism of the comfortable. It was the conviction of people who were themselves the ones being killed and still would not kill back.

The modern voice that pressed this hardest was John Howard Yoder, whose 1972 book The Politics of Jesus argued that the church misread its whole vocation the day it decided its job was to run the empire responsibly rather than to be a different kind of people inside it. Jesus, Yoder said, was not a spiritual teacher indifferent to politics. He was intensely political, and his politics was the cross, a refusal to secure the good by the world's means. Stanley Hauerwas carried the same fire into a thousand lecture halls: the first task of the church is not to make the world's history come out right, because that was never something God asked us to control. The first task of the church is to be the church, a community that can afford to lose, because it has already been told how the story ends. The pacifist is not naive about evil. He simply refuses to believe that the answer to a cross is a sword, when the whole faith turns on a man who took the first and would not take the second.

That is the case for peace, and it should cost you something to read it. Now turn, and give the other side the same refusal to caricature. Because the just war tradition is not the church baptizing what it wanted to do anyway. It began as an attempt to say no.

Augustine did not develop it to unleash violence. He developed it to leash it, in a world where the empire that had finally stopped feeding Christians to lions was now the only thing standing between ordinary people and the men who would burn their villages to the ground. And Augustine asked a question the pacifist has to answer and often does not: what do you owe the person being murdered in front of you. Love your enemy, yes. But your neighbor is also being killed by that enemy, and love has a second object in the room. To stand by with clean hands while the defenseless are slaughtered is not obviously innocence. It may be a way of loving your own purity more than your neighbor's life. The just war tradition was born from taking that question seriously.

Thomas Aquinas gave it the shape the church has argued over ever since, in the Summa Theologiae, laying down the tests: a just cause, a legitimate authority rather than a private grudge, and a right intention aimed at peace rather than plunder. Later hands added the rest, the criteria a war must pass before it can be called just: it must be a last resort, its violence proportional to the wrong it answers, waged with reasonable hope and never with the deliberate targeting of the innocent. Read that list honestly and notice what it is. It is not permission. It is a wall of conditions so high that almost no war humans have actually fought could climb it. The just war tradition, done right, disqualifies far more than it blesses. It is the church's way of saying that if force is ever used, it is used the way a surgeon uses a knife, under strict limit, to save a body, and never for the joy of the cut.

And there is a text the tradition will not let the pacifist read past. Paul, writing to Christians under the very empire that would eventually kill him, says of the governing authority that "he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:4). Paul is not describing a spiritual sword. He is describing the coercive power of the state, and he is calling that power, restrained and just, a servant of God. The just war Christian stands there and asks the pacifist: if all sword-bearing is sin, why does Paul call the sword-bearer God's servant. There is a place, the tradition says, for a soldier who steps between a killer and a child, and calling that soldier a murderer is a moral confusion that the Sermon on the Mount, rightly read, never asked for.

Now let me put the two questions in the same room, because that is where they actually live, and refuse to let either off the hook.

To the pacifist, the just war Christian says: your hands are clean, but are they clean because you are righteous or because someone else did the bleeding you were unwilling to do. When the killers come and you will not lift a hand, it is not only your life you are laying down. It may be your daughter's. You have called that faithfulness. Are you sure it is not just the luxury of never having been the only thing standing between evil and the people it wants.

To the just war Christian, the pacifist says: every empire that ever marched believed its cause was just. Every soldier was told he was the one protecting the child. You have given the sword a doctrine, and the doctrine has never once, in all of history, stopped a nation from finding its war on the approved list. You say you use force like a surgeon. The graveyards say you use it like everyone else and quote Aquinas afterward. Where is the war your tradition actually stopped.

Neither of them has a clean answer. That is the point I will not spare you.

And both have paid. Do not imagine this is a debate between people who have risked nothing. The martyr paid, the Christian who would not raise a hand and was killed for it, and the church counts that blood holy. The soldier paid too, the believer who went to the border and stood between his town and the men who meant to erase it and did not come home, and the church has buried him with honor and meant it. Two graves. Both of them Christian. Both of them, the church has dared to say, faithful. If your position requires you to spit on one of those graves, your position is too small for the people who are actually in them.

I told you I would not tell you where I stand, and I will keep that, because this is one of the questions the church has held open with its eyes open, not out of cowardice but out of the honesty to admit that the Sermon on the Mount and the letter to the Romans are both Scripture and both true and do not, on this side of the kingdom, resolve into a single command you can hand a soldier or a martyr and settle the matter. You are trusted here. You can read this and pick up the rifle and remain my brother. You can read this and lay it down and remain my brother. What you cannot do, what none of us can do, is pretend the other one made the easy choice.

So I leave you where the garden leaves us. A sword, drawn in the one case we would all call just. A voice telling the man to put it away. And a cross that the man on it could have called ten thousand angels down to prevent, and did not. I do not fully understand what that scene demands of me in the hallway with my sons behind me. I only know that whichever way I move, I will not get to move as though it were obvious. He did not leave it obvious. He left it costly, on purpose, and told us to follow him into a garden where the right thing to do with a sword is the hardest question a Christian ever has to hold.
posts.excerpt: Two Christians read the same Sermon on the Mount. One picks up a rifle to stop a slaughter. One lays the rifle down and lets them kill him first. The church has produced both, called both faithful, and never resolved it. Neither will I.

posts.title: Does the Evidence for Near-Death Experiences Prove Anything?
posts.body:
A bestselling book about a boy who came back from heaven sold by the millions, and then the boy grew up and said he had made the whole thing up. I remember the satisfaction that news gave me, back when I held that the brain was a machine and death was the machine going dark. I kept a whole shelf of contempt for these accounts. The tunnel, the light at the end of it, the dead relatives waiting there, the warm voice saying it was not yet time. I filed all of it under wishful thinking, the last chemical panic of an organ shutting down, and I was not entirely wrong. I am no longer sure I was entirely right. That uncertainty is the only honest place to start.

Set the thing on the table before either side reaches for it. A near-death experience is what some people report after being pulled back from the edge: the cardiac arrest, the operating table, the crash that nearly finished them. Raymond Moody gave the phenomenon its name in 1975, in a book called *Life After Life*, and since then the reports have been gathered by the thousands. They are strange, and they are consistent, and both of those facts have to be accounted for by anyone who wants to be taken seriously here.

## The case a believer can honestly make

Start with the case for taking these accounts seriously, because it is stronger than my old contempt allowed. The reports rhyme across people who have nothing in common. A retired machinist in Ohio and a woman in a village that never heard his language describe the same architecture. The passage. The enveloping light. The sense of a love so total it reorders everything the person thought they wanted. Many describe a review of their own life, every unkind thing felt again from the other side, from inside the person they wounded. And a striking number come back angry to be back, grieving the return to their bodies the way you would grieve a country you were deported from. A hallucination, you would think, would be as various as the people having it. This one keeps its shape.

Then there are the accounts that are harder to wave off. The ones where a patient with no heartbeat and a flat reading later describes something they should not have been able to describe: the instrument the surgeon called for, a conversation out in the corridor, an object on a ledge no one in the room had reason to mention. I hold these loosely, because such stories are hard to verify after the fact and easy to round up in the retelling, and I will not build anything on them. But I no longer pretend they are not there. The honest skeptic ought to be at least unsettled that they exist at all.

What moved me most, when I finally looked instead of sneering, was not any single story. It was that some of the people studying this are not credulous at all. A handful of cardiologists and neurologists have spent careers on the phenomenon, working in ordinary hospitals and publishing in ordinary medical literature, precisely because it would not sit still under the easy explanations they started with. You can decide they are chasing a mirage. You cannot decide they never looked. I had assumed the only people interested were the ones already sure of the answer, and that assumption was the tell of a man who had not done any looking himself.

## The case a skeptic can honestly make
