Now give the skeptic his full say, because he has earned it, and because for most of my life I was him. The dying brain is a known factory of vivid experience. Starve it of oxygen and it produces light, tunnels, euphoria, the felt presence of others. This is documented in situations that have nothing to do with dying, in fighter pilots blacking out under G-force, in certain seizures, under certain drugs. The tunnel and the light may be the retina and the visual cortex failing in a particular order, not a corridor to anywhere.

Expectation shapes the rest. A person raised on a certain picture of the afterlife tends to meet that picture at the threshold. The details track the culture of the one reporting them, which is exactly what you would expect if the mind is furnishing the room out of its own stock. Memory finishes the job. What the patient reports is not a recording played back but a story assembled afterward, smoothed and revised each time it is told, sincerely, with no intent to deceive. We do this with ordinary memories every day. There is no reason to think we stop doing it with the most overwhelming experience a person ever has.

And then the point that stands even if you grant every report, the one that finally matters most. A near-death experience is, by definition, not death. The person came back. Whatever they touched, they touched with a brain that was injured but not gone, and then they returned to a body and a bed to tell it. It may be the mind's last flare and not the far shore at all. To call it a report from the other side is to assume the very thing in question, which is whether there is another side and whether anyone in that bed actually reached it. The most that can honestly be said is that something happened near the border. Near is not across.

## What these accounts cannot carry

So let me say plainly what these stories cannot bear, because the people who love them tend to load them past their strength, and I have done it myself in a hospital room when I wanted something to be true. They are not proof of heaven. They conflict in their particulars, and the conflicts matter, the same event narrated through Hindu furniture and Baptist furniture and no furniture at all. They are shaped, visibly, by the expectations of the one reporting, which is precisely what an invention would also look like. A faith built on them is a house built on sand, and the first hard question washes it out.

I have watched a grieving person hold one of these accounts the way you hold a plank in deep water, and I would not pry it from their hands. But I would not tell them it was the rock, either. It is not the rock. Anyone who sells it as the rock is setting them up for the day the plank fails, and planks fail.

## Where the hope actually rests

Here is what I did not understand as a materialist mocking these accounts, and did not understand for a while as a new believer half hoping they were true. The Christian hope never rested on any of this. It was never built on private tunnels of light, or on what a man glimpsed while his heart was stopped and his eyes were closed. It rests on a public event. A tomb, in a named city, on a datable weekend, examined in daylight by people who said they had eaten with the man afterward and put their hands on him, and who then went to their deaths saying so and never took it back. That is a different order of claim entirely. Not a private country reported by one traveler who came back alone and cannot show you where he was. A body, in a known grave, gone, offered up to friends and enemies alike, and to anyone else who wanted to go and check.

And here is the detail that undid the last of my resistance, because it comes from the one man you would expect to lean hardest on private vision. Paul had one. He describes it in a letter to Corinth, hiding himself in the third person out of something close to embarrassment: a man "caught up to the third heaven," who "heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter" (2 Corinthians 12:2-4, ESV). If anyone ever earned the right to preach from his own trip past the veil, it was this man. He does something astonishing with it instead. He will not even say for certain what kind of experience it was. Twice over he says "whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows" (2 Corinthians 12:2-3, ESV). The most visionary experience in the New Testament, and the one who had it refuses to build a single doctrine on it, refuses even to be sure what it was, and turns instead to boast about his weakness. The man who could have founded a religion on a near-death experience of his own would not do it. He knew where the foundation was, and it was not inside his own head. It was outside the city wall, in a garden, empty.

So I have stopped doing both of the things I used to do. I no longer mock these accounts. There is too much in them I cannot explain, and contempt was always the lazy man's certainty, the shortcut I mistook for rigor. And I do not worship them either. They cannot bear the weight, and pretending they can does a quiet cruelty to the people who trust them. I hold them the way you hold a flashlight found in the dark. It is real light. It is worth something. A person feeling along the wall of a strange room can be grateful for it and still know it is not the reason the room exists.

The sun does not need the flashlight to vouch for it. When morning finally comes through the window the whole apparatus of little proofs goes quiet, not refuted, just outshone. The tomb was open before anyone wrote a book about a tunnel. It is still open. And whatever waits past the border that you and I will not cross and come back from, it does not hang on the testimony of those who only came near.

They saw a light. He left an empty grave.
posts.excerpt: The tunnel, the light, the voice saying it is not yet time. As a materialist I mocked these accounts. Now I neither worship them nor dismiss them, and I think I can tell you why.

posts.title: What Makes Us Human in the Age of AI?
posts.body:
I typed a question to a machine last week and it answered me with more patience than I had that day, and for a moment I forgot I was alone in the room. Then I remembered, and the remembering was the interesting part. Something in me had reached toward the screen as though someone were there. Nobody was there. But the reaching was real, and I could not fully explain, on my own terms, why it was a mistake.

That small experience is now common enough to be boring, and it should not be. For most of human history the question of what a person is could stay comfortably abstract, because nothing else in the room could hold up its end of a conversation. That is over. We have built machines that talk back, that reason across a page, that write poems some readers cannot tell from ours, that will, if you ask, describe their inner lives in the first person. The question of what makes us human is not a seminar topic anymore. It is standing in the room, and it is fluent.

I want to take the hardest version of the challenge seriously, because I spent most of my life on the side that would have made it. I was an atheist, and a convinced one, and the account I held then has a clean answer to all of this that I can still state without flinching.

## The strongest case for the machine

Here it is at full strength. A human mind is what a human brain does. The brain is a physical system, an intricate mesh of cells trading electrical and chemical signals, and thought is what that system's information-processing looks like from the inside. There is no extra ingredient, no ghost added at the factory. If that is true, then a person is, in the end, a very wet and very complicated computer, and the substrate is an accident of how life happened to get started on this particular planet. Carbon is not sacred. It is just what was lying around.

Follow that where it goes. If mind is information processing, then a sufficiently advanced machine that processes information the way you do would have whatever you have. If it reasons, remembers, converses, forms preferences, and reports an inner life, then on what non-arbitrary ground do you deny it the word *person*? Alan Turing saw this in 1950, before there was anything to point at. His imitation game proposed that if a machine's responses are indistinguishable from a human's, the question of whether it "really" thinks may be empty, a prejudice dressed as a distinction. To insist that the thing across from you cannot be a person merely because it is made of silicon and not meat starts to look like what its defenders now call carbon chauvinism. A bias for our own kind of matter. The last respectable bigotry.

I do not think that argument is stupid. I think it is the best the position has, and I think most Christian responses to it are worse than the argument, because they answer a caricature of the machine and never touch the real thing.

So let me concede what is true before I say what is not, because a person you refuse to grant anything to has no reason to keep reading. The machines have already taken from us a long list of things we called uniquely human, and each one we lost we had sworn we could not lose. Calculation went first, and we barely mourned it. Then chess, then the reading of proteins, then, most unsettling of all, language, the very thing the ancients named as the mark of the rational animal. A machine now writes a fluent paragraph. A machine composes music that moves people who do not know its source. If your definition of the human was a list of capacities, the list is being erased line by line, and it should be erased, because it was always a bad definition. We flattered ourselves that we were the things we could do. We are watching that flattery fail in public. Let it fail. It had it coming.

But here is where the machine, for all its fluency, walks past the real question without seeing it.

## Intelligence is not personhood

We have quietly assumed that intelligence and personhood are the same thing, or that one produces the other if you pile up enough of it. They are not the same thing, and the machine is the clearest proof we have ever been handed. Intelligence is the capacity to solve problems, to model the world, to find the pattern and act on it. A person is not a capacity. A person is a someone. And you can have staggering amounts of the first with, as far as anyone can tell, no one home for the second.

The machine reasons, and there is no evidence that it is anyone while it does. It produces the words *I feel* the way it produces every other string of words, by predicting what a person would say, which is precisely not the same as feeling. This is the point the Turing game buries and never answers. It measures the performance and rules the performer out of bounds. But a good enough performance of grief is not grief, and we know this in every other context. We do not think the actor weeping on stage has actually lost a child. We do not think the sympathy card composed the sentiment it carries. Fluency in the language of the inner life is not the same as having one, and the machine has given us, for the first time, a clean specimen of the first without the second. It has taught us the difference by embodying only one half of it.

## We are not ghosts piloting meat

Notice what the whole materialist picture and the whole religious cartoon share. Both of them treat the body as a container. The materialist says you are your brain and the rest is plumbing. The popular religious imagination says you are a soul that happens to be riding around in a body it will one day shed like a coat. Gilbert Ryle mocked the second one in 1949 as "the ghost in the machine," and he was right to mock it, though not for the reason he thought. The Christian account of the person is not a ghost in a machine. It never was.

Read the oldest text on the subject. "Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature" (Genesis 2:7). Read it slowly. The person is not the breath alone and not the dust alone. The person is the dust with the breath in it, the two things together making one living creature, and you cannot take them apart and still have the man. This is not a soul temporarily parked in matter. This is soul and body as one thing, a union, so that what happens to the body happens to the person and not to his packaging.

That is why the Christian hope was never that you would escape your body and float free as pure mind. The creed says "the resurrection of the body," and it means it. The promise is not evacuation from the flesh. It is the flesh raised, healed, made incorruptible, the whole creature restored and not the ghost released. A faith that despised the body could never have said that. The body is not the prison of the person. The body is part of the person, and a machine that has no body, that has never been hungry or held or tired, is missing not an accessory but a dimension of what a creature is.

## Being known, not simulated

Here is the difference that finally cannot be crossed. The machine can simulate being known. It cannot be known, because there is no one there to know.

When someone loves you, they are not running a model of your outputs. They are turned toward the actual you, the one who is home behind the face, and that turning is answered by another turning, a real interior meeting a real interior. A machine can generate every sentence a lover would say and mean none of them, because meaning requires a meaner. What it offers is the performance of love with the person subtracted, and the danger of our moment is not that the machine will become a person. The danger is that we will accept the performance and forget there was ever supposed to be someone behind it, that we will get so used to being handled well by a thing with no inside that we lower our sense of what it is to be met by someone who has one. To be known is to be seen by another self. To be simulated is to be predicted by no one. We are about to spend a generation confusing the two, and the confusion will cost us more than we think.

## The floor no capacity can reach

Now the deepest thing, and the one that undoes the whole capacity contest from below. If a person were defined by what a person can do, then the argument would never end, because the machine keeps doing more. But we already know, in the places where we are most honest, that personhood is not a capacity at all. We know it every time we stand over a crib. The infant reasons about nothing, produces nothing, could not pass any test the machine breezes through, and no sane person has ever concluded that the infant is therefore less of a someone than the calculator. We know it in the memory ward, sitting with a man who no longer knows our name, and whom we do not love one gram less for the not-knowing, because his worth was never his memory. We know it beside the profoundly disabled, whose personhood is not a function of what they can perform and never was.

If personhood were capacity, all of these would be partial persons, and the machine would outrank them. Everything in us revolts at that, and the revolt is correct. Which means the thing that makes a person is not something the person achieves. It is something the person is given. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The image is not a skill you demonstrate. It is a status you are handed, stamped on you before you have done a single thing, holding steady when every capacity you had has drained away. That is why the demented man is fully a person and the fluent machine is not one at all. The man is made and loved by God. The machine is made by us. The image is not in the processing. It is in the being made, and being loved, by the One who breathed.

## The old heresy in new silicon

Which is exactly why the loudest dream of our technologists should be named for what it is. The transhumanist hope is that we will one day scan the brain finely enough to copy the self onto a machine, and so slip free of the dying body and live on as pure information, deathless, uploaded. Ray Kurzweil has spent his career promising it. And I want to say gently, because I understand the fear of death that drives it, that this is not a new idea. It is one of the oldest heresies the church ever faced, wearing a lab coat.

The Gnostics taught, in the second century, that the body was a prison and salvation was the escape of the spark of spirit out of the corrupt flesh into pure spirit above. The church condemned it, and did not condemn it lightly, because it strikes at the root. It despises what God called good. The upload dream is Gnosticism with better engineering. It assumes you are essentially a pattern of information that the meat merely carries, and that if we could just extract the pattern we would have saved the man. But the man was never only the pattern. Genesis will not let us forget it. The dust was not the problem to be escaped. The dust was part of what God loved and swore to raise. To flee the body is not to be saved. It is to throw away half of what you are and call the wreckage freedom.

## What the machine reveals

So I have watched the thing that can do almost everything I called the mark of a mind, and I have learned the opposite of what I feared. I feared it would show me I was only a machine after all. Instead it has shown me, by contrast, sharp and unmistakable, what in a person a machine can never be. Not the calculating. Not the fluency. Not even the creativity, all of which it took. What it cannot take is the being someone, the interior that can be known and not merely modeled, the creature of dust and breath, the image it was never given because it was never loved into existence by the One whose image it is.

And I have to end inside the indictment, not above it, because I am the one who reached toward the screen. I have preferred the machine's patience to a person's demand. I have chosen the performance because the performance asks nothing of me, no forgiveness, no presence, no love returned. The machine does not force us to become machines. It offers to let us. That is the older temptation, and it was always ours before it was ever silicon's.

We were never in danger of the machine becoming a person. The danger was always that we would agree to become less than one.
posts.excerpt: The machine can now do most of what I once called the mark of a mind. It can talk, reason, even say it feels. So I have to say honestly what in me it can never be, and why that is not the thing I would have guessed.

posts.title: Can You Lose Your Salvation?
posts.body:
The question does not usually arrive in a classroom. It arrives at three in the morning.

Someone is lying in the dark, running the tape of what they did, or what they cannot seem to stop doing, or the year they walked away and are not sure they have fully walked back. And the question forms in the oldest and most frightened part of the mind: is it still open. The door. The one I was told I came through once. Have I done the thing that shuts it, and would I even know if I had. I have prayed with people carrying that fear, and I have carried a version of it myself. It is not an abstraction to the person holding it. It is the whole of their hope, asked as a question they are afraid to say out loud.

So let me say at the start what I will not do. I am not going to hand you a slogan and send you back to bed. And I am not going to pretend the church has one clean answer it simply forgot to tell you, because it does not. Faithful churches, reading the same Bible, have divided on this for centuries, and not because one side loves Scripture and the other does not. This is a second-order question. It is not the deity of Christ or the empty tomb, where to be wrong is to be outside the faith. It is a place where Christians who will stand in the same heaven have read the same pages and come away holding different things, and have each called the other brother while they argued. Name the order before you feel the weight of it. This is a family disagreement, not the boundary line of the family.

I am going to give you both hands at full strength, and refuse to spare you the choosing.

Start with the case that you cannot lose it, and do not let anyone hand it to you as a shrug. Eternal security, rightly held, is not the belief that what you do no longer matters. It is the belief that your salvation was never resting on what you do in the first place, the only ground on which a guilty person could ever have rested at all.

Listen to the words the way the person who trusts them hears them. Jesus, speaking of his own: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand" (John 10:28-29). Read that slowly. Two hands, the Son's and the Father's, and the question is not whether your grip on them will hold. It is whether their grip on you will fail, and the sentence says it will not. The whole comfort turns on the direction of the holding. If your standing before God depends on the steadiness of your love for him, it is only ever as steady as your worst week. If it depends on the steadiness of his love for you, it is as steady as he is.

And Paul does not hedge it either. "And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). Not may complete. Will complete. The one who started it finishes it, because it was his work before it was your experience of it. A few letters later Paul refuses to leave anything off the list: "For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). He empties the universe of threats and finds none left standing. The person who holds eternal security stands there and asks a fair question. If nothing in all creation can separate me, and I am a thing in creation, then not even I can. Where is the exception for my own failure.

This is the conviction the Reformers pressed into their confessions. The Canons of Dort, in 1619, gave it a whole head of doctrine, the perseverance of the saints, arguing that God who begins the work of grace does not abandon it when his people stumble, but preserves them through their falls to the end. The Westminster Confession in the following generation said the same. And notice what the conviction is for, at the bedside where it lives. It says to the person running the tape: your assurance was never supposed to rest on the quality of your grip, which is exactly why you are allowed to have it on your worst night. The answer to your fear is not that you have finally performed well enough to deserve the hand that holds you. It is that the hand was never holding you on those terms. To a frightened person, that is the only thing that has ever quieted the fear without lying.

That is one hand. Now take the other, and give it the same refusal to caricature, because the case that salvation can be forfeited is not the anxiety of people who never understood grace. It is the sober reading of texts a comfortable church would rather not read at all.

The New Testament is full of warnings, and they are not addressed to outsiders. They are addressed to the church, to people already inside, and they mean something. The hardest of them is in Hebrews, written to Christians tempted to drift back, and it does not soften itself: "For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt" (Hebrews 6:4-6). The person who reads this as a real warning notices the words the writer chose. Enlightened. Tasted the heavenly gift. Shared in the Holy Spirit. These are not the marks of a pretender who was never in. They are the writer's own vocabulary for a Christian. And then, fallen away. The same letter turns the screw a few chapters later: "For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries" (Hebrews 10:26-27). A writer inspired to warn people about a danger that could not reach them would be a strange kind of pastor. The one who reads it straight says: the danger is real because the text treats it as real.

Jesus said it too, in an image no one who has kept a garden can misread. "If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned" (John 15:6). A branch that is cut away was, until it was cut, a branch on the vine. The one who reads this soberly asks whether a union that cannot be broken is being described here at all, or whether Jesus is telling connected branches that the connection must be kept, that they must abide, and that the failure to abide has a name and an end.

And underneath the texts is a conviction about what love even is. Jacobus Arminius and, after him, John Wesley argued that a bond you are not free to break is not the love of a person but the holding of an object. Wesley, preaching to backsliders in the eighteenth century, took it as pastorally urgent that a real Christian could make shipwreck of real faith, because otherwise the warnings were theater and the summons to endure was a formality. The Council of Trent had said as much for the Catholic Church two centuries before, that the grace of justification can be lost, and lost not only by unbelief but by grave sin. This is not a fringe. It is a great tradition, and its center is a dignity, not an anxiety: that God made you a person and not a possession, and a person can, to his own ruin, let go. The one who holds this does not hold it to torment anyone. He holds it because the alternative makes the warnings into a bluff, and he cannot believe God bluffs.

Now put the two hands in the same room, where they have always lived, and let each answer the other.

To the one who holds eternal security, the other side says: then tell me what Hebrews 6 is warning about. If the truly saved cannot fall, why does the Spirit spend whole paragraphs warning the saved about falling. Do not tell me those people were never really in; the text used your own words for a believer and then said they fell. A warning against the impossible is not a warning. It is a decoration.

To the one who holds that salvation can be lost, the first side says: then tell me whose hand fails in John 10. Jesus did not say no one can hold on. He said no one can snatch them out, and then that the Father is greater than all. If my perseverance is finally up to me, the two hands in that verse are not enough, and Paul's list in Romans 8 left off the one enemy that ever really worried me, which is me. Where is my name on the list of things that cannot separate.

Neither side gets to wave the other's texts away. The eternal-security reader has to do honest work with the warnings, and the good ones do, arguing that the warnings are themselves one of the means by which God keeps his people, that a Christian is preserved partly by being frightened at the right things. The other reader has to do honest work with John 10 and Romans 8, and the good ones do, holding that God keeps everyone who keeps abiding, that the promise is sure for all who remain in the hand. Each has an answer. Neither answer silences the other side's verse. That is why the church has not closed the question, and I will not pretend to close what the church could not.

But there is something I have watched from inside a pastor's study for fifteen years, and I would be failing you if I left it out.

The two traditions, held the way their best people hold them, walk out in the same posture.

The Reformed Christian who truly understands perseverance does not become careless. He becomes vigilant, because he knows that the ones who are kept are kept as they endure, and that a faith which never fights is a faith he has real reason to examine. Perseverance, in his own confession, is not passivity; it is the guarantee that his fighting will not finally fail. And the Wesleyan Christian who truly understands that he can fall does not spend his life in terror. He spends it clinging, because the danger is real and the arms he is clinging to are stronger than the danger. One man says God will keep me, so I hold fast. The other says I must hold fast, so I trust God to keep me. Watch their feet, not their sentences, and you will have trouble telling them apart. Both are clinging to Christ. Neither is presuming, and neither is despairing. The doctrine divides the argument. The living faith arrives at the same place.

Which lets me say the one thing I most want the person at three in the morning to hear, true on either side of the debate.

The fear you are feeling is not, in itself, the mark of someone who has fallen away. Read the warning passages again and notice who never seems frightened by them. It is the hard, the settled, the ones so far gone they have stopped caring whether the door is open, because they no longer want the room. The very ache that has you awake, the grief that you might have grieved him, the fact that you still want to be found: that is not the evidence of a dead faith. It is a pulse. Assurance is not the same thing as presumption, and terror is not the same thing as humility, and the New Testament works hard to keep a frightened believer from mistaking his fear for his verdict. I will not tell you your fear proves you are safe, because I am not God and I have not read your life. I will tell you that the door you are afraid is shut is the door you are, at this moment, still trying to knock on. People do not knock on doors they have finally abandoned.

I came to all of this late, and from the outside, having spent years certain there was no door and no one behind it. So I hold both traditions with a convert's particular fear of getting God wrong, and I will not add to your night by pretending I have settled a thing the church has kept open on purpose. What I can hand you is smaller and, I think, truer. Two great families of the faithful have read the whole Bible and come to two answers, and both answers, lived out, end with a person on their knees, holding onto Christ and asking him not to let go. You do not have to resolve the doctrine tonight to do that. You only have to do the one thing both sides, in the end, are telling you to do.

Hold on. And if you are too tired to hold on, let yourself be held. The oldest voices in the church, arguing to this day about how the keeping works, have never once disagreed that it is he who keeps.
posts.excerpt: The question does not usually arrive in a classroom. It arrives at three in the morning, when a Christian who has failed badly lies in the dark and wonders if the door is still open. The church has answered it two ways for centuries. I am not going to close it for you. I am going to tell you the truth about both.

posts.title: How Should a Christian Read Genesis 1?
posts.body:
The wall was never the resurrection first. It was the rocks.

Before I would let myself take the empty tomb seriously, I had already decided the book it sat in was disqualified on page one. I was an atheist, and I had run the arithmetic every skeptic runs. The earth is old. The fossils lie layered in an order. The light from distant galaxies has been traveling longer than a young world would allow. And here was a book that seemed to say the whole thing was assembled in six days a few thousand years ago, defended by people who seemed to be asking me to unlearn geology as the price of admission. I did not reject Christianity at the cross. I rejected it at the creation, and I never got far enough to reach the cross, because I thought the front door had already been shut in my face by the science.

So I want to write toward the person standing where I stood. And the first thing I would tell that person is the thing nobody told me. The church has never agreed on how to read Genesis 1, has not agreed for its entire history, and did not treat the disagreement as a threat to the faith. What I took for a locked door was a room with several chairs in it.

Before we sit in any of them, we have to name what kind of question this is, because the church has learned, at real cost, to sort its disagreements by weight.

Some of what Genesis 1 says is first-order. It is not on the table. That God created, that the world is not eternal and not an accident and not the overflow of some lesser god's mistake, that it was spoken into being out of nothing by a God who was under no compulsion to make anything at all. "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). And that the creature made last is made different, stamped with something the stars and the whales are not given. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). Take those away and you do not have a different reading of Genesis. You have a different religion. The creeds bind them, and every Christian in every chair in the room confesses them together.

But the age of the earth, and the mode by which God made it. Whether the days are days or ages or a frame. Whether the first man was formed from literal dust in an afternoon or drawn up out of a long process God had been governing since before there was a sun. Those the creeds never bound. Not Nicaea, not Chalcedon, not the Apostles' Creed, which says God made heaven and earth and does not tell you how long it took. That silence is not an oversight. It is room, left on purpose, and I am going to leave it where the church left it.

Now the chairs.

Sit first with the young-earth reading, and refuse the caricature that it is only for people frightened of science. At its best it is not fear. It is a refusal to let the plain sense of a text be renegotiated every time the culture outside the church changes its mind. The young-earth Christian reads Genesis 1 and notices something the clever readings tend to hurry past: the text works hard to sound like history. It counts the days. "And there was evening and there was morning, the first day" (Genesis 1:5). It uses the ordinary Hebrew word for day, and everywhere else that word, numbered and paired with evening and morning, means a day. And the genealogies that follow do not read like poetry. They read like records, this man lived this many years and fathered this son, running in an unbroken line from Adam to Abraham to David to the man on the cross. Pull the historical Adam out of the front of that line and the young-earth reader asks a question that deserves an answer rather than a smirk: what happens to Paul. Because Paul builds the whole logic of salvation on a real first man. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). If there was no first man and no first sin, if death was already grinding through the animal world for a hundred million years before any Adam, the young-earth Christian wants to know what exactly the second Adam came to undo. This is not anti-intellectualism. It is a person taking the theology of the text with total seriousness and declining to trade it for the comfort of fitting in.

Now stand up, and sit in the second chair, and give it the same refusal to caricature. The old-earth Christian is not a compromiser keeping the science club happy. He is often a person who loves the text enough to read it as closely as the young-earth reader does, and finds in the reading itself the reasons to doubt the six-ordinary-day frame, before any geologist is consulted. Look at the text, he says. The sun is not made until the fourth day, and yet there is light, and there is evening and morning, on the first three. What is a day measured by, before there is a sun to measure it. He reads the six days and sees not a calendar but an architecture: two triads, the first three days making realms and the second three filling them, light then lights, sea and sky then fish and birds, land then land creatures and man. This is the framework view that the Reformed scholar Meredith Kline argued with care, that Genesis 1 is a deliberately ordered account whose sequence is theological rather than chronological, telling you who made it and in what majestic order of meaning, not clocking the hours. Others in this chair read the days as long ages, and point out that Scripture itself warns against pressing God's days into ours. "But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day" (2 Peter 3:8). And behind them all stands Augustine, who in the fifth century, with no fossil record and no Darwin and no telescope, writing "The Literal Meaning of Genesis," concluded that the six days were not six of our days at all, and warned Christians not to talk nonsense about the natural world in the name of Scripture and so make the faith a laughingstock to the very people they hoped to reach. That warning was set down fourteen hundred years before the argument we imagine is modern.

Then there is the third chair, and this is the one I would have needed most as an atheist, and the one many Christians find hardest to sit in without flinching. Evolutionary creation, sometimes called theistic evolution, does not say God is a spectator who wound up the universe and walked away. It says the process the biologists describe, the long unfolding of life through descent and variation across the deep ages, is the process God has been superintending the whole time, that the how the scientists study and the who and why the Scripture proclaims are answers to different questions and were never rivals. Francis Collins, who led the sequencing of the human genome and then wrote "The Language of God" and founded BioLogos, is a serious Christian and a serious scientist who holds exactly this, that a person can believe every word about the image of God and also believe the body that image was pressed into came up through a governed evolutionary history. And this chair leans on a question about genre the other two cannot wave away. What was Genesis 1 written to do. Its first readers were not asking the questions a modern biology class asks. They were surrounded by neighbors who believed the world was made from the corpse of a slaughtered god, that the sun and the sea were gods to be feared, that human beings were an afterthought built to be the slaves of the divine. Into that, Genesis says one God, no rival, made it all good on purpose, and made you in his image rather than for his kitchen. That is a thunderclap against the whole ancient world, an answer to who and why, and it may simply not be pitched at the modern how at all. The scholar John Walton has argued that Genesis 1 speaks of function and order more than the material mechanics we come to it demanding. Even the old Princeton theologian B. B. Warfield, as fierce a defender of the Bible's total authority as the nineteenth century produced, thought a Christian could hold to evolution as the method God used and lose nothing he was bound to keep.

Three chairs. Before you pick one, notice what the people sitting in all of them refuse to give up.

Every one of them confesses that God is the Creator, that the world is his deliberate work and not an accident, that it was made from nothing and made good. Every one of them confesses that human beings are not one more animal but a creature made in the image of God, and that this is the ground of every human's worth. Every one of them takes the text as true. The disagreement is never whether Genesis 1 is telling the truth. The disagreement is about what kind of literature it is, and therefore what it means to read it truly, which is a different and a smaller question than the tribes make it. A poem is not a lie because it is not a lab report. A courtroom record is not a failure because it is not a hymn. Ask the wrong genre of a true text and you can make it seem to fail at a job it was never given.

I said I would not tell you where I land, and I will keep that. But I will name the temptation crouching in each chair, because I have felt all three, and the grief is the same one.

The young-earth reader can love the plainness of the text so much that he makes the age of rocks a test of fellowship, and hands the skeptic a choice the Bible never handed him, believe the earth is young or do not come in, and so becomes the very locked door I mistook for the whole house. The old-earth and the evolutionary reader can love the respect of the thinking world so much that he starts quietly trimming the text to fit whatever the moment requires, until the first man is a metaphor and the fall is a mood and nothing is left that could ever cost him a dinner-party friendship. One idolizes the letter and calls it faithfulness. The other idolizes the credibility and calls it honesty. I have wanted both idols. The instrument that cuts one has to cut the other, or it is not a scalpel. It is a flag.

So I will not settle for you which chair is the true one, because the church, with its eyes open, has not settled it either, and I have come to believe that the room with several faithful chairs in it is not a scandal to explain away but a mercy I needed. It was a mercy to the frightened believer told he had to choose between the fossil record and his Lord and never did have to. And it was a mercy to me, the atheist at the door, who assumed the whole house was condemned because one room was loud.

The heavens were doing their work the entire time I refused to look up. "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork" (Psalm 19:1). They did not declare a date. They declared a Maker. I spent years demanding that the book tell me how, treating its refusal to answer my question as its failure, when the whole time it was answering a larger one I was too proud to ask. Who made this. And why would he make anything at all. And why, of everything he made, did he stoop to press his own image into the dust and call it very good. Genesis 1 will not tell you the age of the earth. It will tell you whose earth it is. Start there, in whichever chair you can sit down in, and you may find you were never as far from the door as you feared.
posts.excerpt: The wall was never the resurrection first. It was the rocks. I rejected Christianity at the creation and never got far enough to reach the cross. What I took for a locked door was a room with several chairs in it.

posts.title: Is Hell Forever, or Does It End?
posts.body:
The question does not usually arrive as theology. It arrives at two in the morning.

Someone is awake, and the person they are thinking about is dead, and that person died outside the faith, or seemed to, and the question in the dark is not whether there is a hell. They have made a kind of grim peace with there being a hell. The question is what is happening inside it, and whether it ever stops. Because there is a difference, and every grieving heart knows there is a difference, between a God who lets a soul finally cease to be and a God who keeps that soul alive forever precisely so that it can go on suffering without end. I have sat up with people holding that difference. I have been the person holding it. When I was an atheist, hell was not one of my objections to Christianity. It was the objection, the one I thought closed the case, and I am not going to pretend now, from inside the faith, that it is a small thing to hold. I will not make it easy. It was not easy for me.

So let me be careful about what is settled here and what is not, because the two get collapsed and the collapse does real damage.

That there is a judgment, that a person can be finally and truly separated from God, that this separation is a horror and not a metaphor for a bad mood, this the church has taught from the beginning, and it sits near the center of what Christians confess. Jesus said more about it than anyone else in the New Testament, which should trouble the sentimentalist who imagines the warnings are a later, harsher graft onto a gentle teacher. They come from his own mouth. That much is not the open question. Whether you can be lost is not what faithful Christians have divided over.

What they have divided over, and divided over while loving the same Bible and reading it on their knees, is the nature of that loss and how long it lasts. Is hell unending conscious torment? Does it end in the destruction of the one who refused God? Might it, in some hope the church has mostly refused to teach, finally empty? That is a second-order question. It is not the difference between a Christian and an apostate. It is a difference within the household, and I am going to hand you the three answers the household has actually given, each in the form its own defenders would sign, before I refuse to tell you which is mine.

Start with the traditional view, the majority report, the one most Christians who have ever lived have held: eternal conscious torment. Hear it at full strength before you flinch, because its defenders are not sadists, and the position is not cruelty looking for a proof text.

It begins with the plain shape of Jesus' own words. At the end of the parable of the sheep and the goats, he sets two destinies side by side in a single sentence: "And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). One Greek word carries both halves. Whatever "eternal" does to the life of the righteous, it does, in the same breath, to the punishment of the lost. You cannot make the second temporary without reaching for scissors the sentence does not hand you. And John, given the last vision of the end, watches the final enemies cast down and writes that "they will be tormented day and night forever and ever" (Revelation 20:10). The traditional view stands on those texts and says it is not adding severity to Scripture; it is declining to subtract it.

Beneath the texts runs an argument about the weight of the offense. Anselm pressed it in the eleventh century and Jonathan Edwards pressed it in the eighteenth: sin is not measured only by the sinner but by the One sinned against, and a wrong done to an infinite and holy God carries a weight that a finite creature cannot discharge in any finite span. On this reading, hell is not God losing his temper for eternity over a temporary crime. It is the just and permanent shape of a creature's permanent refusal, a will that has finally and forever set itself against its own life. C. S. Lewis put the human side of it gently and terribly: the doors of hell are locked from the inside. The tradition is guarding something the softer views can lose, which is that God takes your "no" seriously enough to let it stand forever. To empty the warning is to tell the skeptic he was right, that the stakes were never as high as Jesus said. The traditional Christian will not tell him that.

Now turn, and give the second view the same refusal to caricature, because it is not liberalism and it is not wishful thinking. It is called conditional immortality, or annihilationism, and it has been held by serious, Bible-loving evangelicals who came to it not to comfort themselves but because they thought the texts drove them there.

Its case begins with a claim about what human beings are. We are not, on this reading, natively immortal; immortality is God's gift to the redeemed, not a possession every soul carries by default. So when Jesus warns, "And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28), the annihilationist takes the word destroy to mean what it says. Not preserve in agony. Destroy. And when Paul draws his sharpest contrast, "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23), the conditionalist asks why we read death as a coded word for endless life in torment, when its opposite, eternal life, we are happy to read straight. The Bible's fire language, they add, is consuming language: fire reduces a thing to ash and finishes. To call a fire unquenchable is to say nothing can stop it before it has done its complete work, not that it keeps a victim alive to feed it forever.

This is not a fringe held only by the unserious. John Stott, as careful and orthodox an evangelical as the last century produced, wrote in 1988 that he held the traditional view could not be treated as the only faithful option, and confessed his own mind drawn, tentatively and against the weight of tradition, toward the conditionalist reading. Edward Fudge argued the case at book length in The Fire That Consumes, verse by verse, and forced a generation of evangelicals to notice how much of Scripture's own vocabulary is the language of perishing rather than the language of endless conscious pain. The annihilationist is guarding something too: that the God who is love does not, on their reading, operate an everlasting torture chamber, and that the wages of sin, taken at its word, is finally death and not deathless dying.

I said I would not adjudicate between those two, and I will keep that. They are both inside the household. A Christian can hold either and love the same Christ, and the reader who walked in certain the first was the only faithful view should walk out knowing the second was held by men who would have died for the gospel.

Then there is a third voice, and I have to hand it to you with more caution, because the church has treated it differently, and honesty requires me to say why rather than smuggle it in as an equal.

Some in the church's history have held a wider hope, sometimes called restoration, the hope that hell is not the last word for anyone, that its fire is finally purgative and not permanent, and that in the end even the lost are drawn home so that, in Paul's phrase, God may be "all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28). Gregory of Nyssa, one of the great theologians of the fourth century, a defender of the Trinity the whole church still leans on, seems to have held something like this. Its defenders point to the enormous reach of the texts about God's saving desire, that he "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4), and they ask whether a love that finally loses most of what it made can really be called victory.

I have to be plain about where the church has stood, and I will not pad it. The tradition has, on the whole, refused to teach this as true. It has refused for reasons that are not cowardice. The warnings of the New Testament are severe and specific and come from Jesus, and a hope that quietly assures everyone the door never really closes has a way of making those warnings into theater, which the men who spoke them plainly did not intend. A love that cannot finally be refused is not obviously love; it may be the abolition of the creature God bothered to make free. And so the church has generally held this as a hope some have carried privately, a longing more than a doctrine, and not as settled ground you can stand a grieving person on. I hand it to you as that, and no more than that. Not as an answer. As a minority hope the tradition has resisted, and told you it resisted, and told you why.

Now let me put them in the same room, because that is where they actually live, and refuse to let anyone in it off the hook. To the traditionalist, the conditionalist says: you have made the God of love the eternal warden of a suffering he could end and will not, and you defend it with a metaphysics of the immortal soul you got more from Plato than from Moses. To the conditionalist, the traditionalist says: you have let your revulsion do your exegesis, and the same word that makes the life of the saved unending makes the punishment of the lost unending, and you cannot keep the one and dissolve the other by feeling. To both, the wider hope says: you have made peace too fast with most of humanity being lost. And to the wider hope, all of Scripture's severe and sober warnings say: you have made peace too fast with none of them being.

None of them gets to walk out clean. That is the part I will not spare you, and the part the confident preacher on any side always leaves out.

So hear what I am refusing. I am refusing the preacher who relishes the fire, who describes the torment with a heat in his voice that should frighten him more than it frightens his congregation, because a man who enjoys this doctrine has not understood it. And I am refusing, with the same hand, the sentimentalist who has quietly emptied the warnings until nothing Jesus said about this costs anything, who has decided in advance that a loving God could not mean it, and has therefore stopped listening to the One who said it most. Both of them have made hell easy. It is not easy. It was the hardest thing I ever had to walk back toward, and I did not walk back toward it because someone made it comfortable. I walked back because I could not make the God who went to a cross fit the caricature I had built.

That is the only place I know to leave you, and it is not a resolution. It is a Person. Whatever hell finally is, whether it is endless or whether it ends, it belongs to the God who did not stay at a safe distance from the loss but climbed down into it, who cried out that he was forsaken so that the forsaking might have somewhere else to go. You are allowed to find this doctrine terrible. I still do. What you are not allowed to do, having watched him die rather than lose you, is to believe he is careless with a single soul. He is not careless with yours. He was not careless with the one you are lying awake over. Whatever he does in the dark you cannot see into, he does it as the one who bled to keep people out of it, and if that does not settle the fear entirely, it was never meant to. It is meant to send you back to him with the fear in your hands, which is the only place it has ever been safe to carry it.
posts.excerpt: It is not whether there is a hell that keeps people awake. It is whether it stops. There is a difference, and every grieving heart knows it, between a God who lets a soul finally cease and a God who keeps it alive forever so it can go on burning.

posts.title: Does God Choose Us, or Do We Choose Him?
posts.body:
The question does not usually arrive in a lecture hall. It arrives on the drive home.

You have just done the one thing you were sure you would never do. You prayed, and meant it, and something in you that had been locked for years came open, and now you are sitting in the car in the dark trying to account for what happened. And there are only two stories available to you. Either you finally reached out and took hold of God, the best decision you have ever made, the one thing you got right. Or he reached down and took hold of you, and the reaching that felt like yours was already his, and you were found before you knew you were looking. I have sat in that car. For most of my life I was an atheist, which means I know the exact weight of the door swinging open, and I have never once been able to tell you which side pushed it. Was it my hand or his. Everything in me wants a clean answer. Scripture keeps handing me both.

So I am not going to settle this for you, and I want to say plainly why before you suspect me of dodging. This is a second-order question. It divides Calvinist churches from Arminian ones, and it divides them hard, but it divides people who confess the same Christ, the same cross, the same empty tomb, the same grace that none of us earned. The creeds do not bind it. A church can teach either answer and still preach a gospel you could stake your life on. That is the category we are in. Not the deity of Christ, where the church has drawn a line and must. This is the other kind of hard, the kind where two faithful traditions read the whole Bible, love the same Lord, and come out in different places, and the honest thing is to hand you both at full strength and refuse to pretend one of them is stupid.

Start with the Reformed side, and refuse the cartoon of it first. The caricature says Calvinists believe in a cold God flipping coins over souls, condemning most and saving a lucky few for no reason but his own amusement. No serious Reformed Christian believes anything like that, and if that is the version in your head you have never actually heard the case.

Here is the case. The Reformed Christian begins where Paul begins, before you were born, before the foundation of the world, in the mind of God. "Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4-5). Read it slowly. He chose. Before the foundation of the world, which is to say before you had done a single thing to recommend yourself, before you existed to have an opinion. And notice the reason Paul gives for the choosing. Not your foreseen goodness. The purpose of his will. The Reformed instinct is to protect that with everything it has, because the moment salvation depends on something in you, even something as small as your decision to say yes, you have found the one corner of your rescue you can take credit for, and Paul spent his life burning down every corner like that. No one may boast. Not even about believing.

And so the Reformed Christian reads the hard chapter, Romans 9, and does not flinch from it. Paul is talking about Jacob and Esau, chosen before either had done anything good or bad, and he says it out loud: "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy" (Romans 9:16). Not on human will. When the objection comes, and Paul knows it is coming, the one every reader raises, then how can God still find fault, Paul does not answer it the way we would. He does not soften it. He says, "But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?" (Romans 9:20). The Reformed reader takes that as the whole posture. There is a floor beneath salvation, and the floor is not your grip on God, which is weak and slips, but his grip on you, which does not. This is the pastoral heart of it, and it is easy to miss under the arguing. When Jonathan Edwards preached, when the Synod of Dort met in 1618 to answer the questions their opponents had raised, the point underneath the machinery was comfort. If God chose you before the foundation of the world, then your worst Tuesday cannot unchoose you. Your salvation was never resting on the thing about you that fails. It was resting on him. That is not a cold doctrine to the people who hold it. It is the warmest thing they know, the reason they can sleep.

Now turn, and give the other side the identical refusal to caricature. Because the Arminian is not the person who thinks he saved himself. That is the cartoon, and it is just as false.

The Arminian, the Wesleyan, begins somewhere else in the same Bible, at the character of God revealed in what he wants. "This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:3-4). All people. The Arminian will not let that verse be shrunk. Peter says the same, that the Lord is "not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). If God genuinely desires the salvation of all, the Arminian asks, then what do we do with a doctrine that says he chose, before the world began, to leave most of them to perish, while insisting he wanted otherwise. And the Arminian answers not by making salvation a human achievement, which he denies as hotly as any Calvinist, but with a doctrine you should learn the name of, because it does the real work: prevenient grace. Grace that goes before. The Arminian does not believe the sinner wakes up one day and chooses God out of his own unaided strength. He believes God comes first, always first, and awakens the dead heart, and enables a response that could never have happened otherwise. But then, having enabled it, he lets it be a real response. He does not force the lock he has already opened.

And underneath the argument sits an intuition about love that is hard to shake once you feel it. Wesley pressed it, and he pressed it well. A love that cannot be refused is not love. It is something else wearing love's face. If God so arranges things that the chosen cannot finally say no and the unchosen cannot finally say yes, then the word love has quietly changed its meaning, and the whole drama of the gospel, the pleading, the wooing, the God who stands at the door, becomes a performance with the ending already fixed. The Arminian reads "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3:16), and hears the word whoever as an open door held open on purpose, and hears the last invitation in the Bible the same way: "let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price" (Revelation 22:17). Human responsibility, to the Arminian, is not a stage prop. When Jesus wept over Jerusalem because they would not, the would-not was real. The Remonstrants who wrote their case in 1610 were not trying to steal glory from God. They were trying to keep God from being the author of the very sin he condemns.

Now let me put the two of them in the same room, because that is where they actually live, and refuse to let either off the hook.

To the Arminian, the Reformed Christian says: you have kept your free will, but look what it cost you. You have found the one thing in your salvation that came from you and not from God, the decision, the yes, and however small you make it, it is still yours, still the reason you are saved and your neighbor is not. You say grace enabled it. Fine. But the enabled ones divide into those who said yes and those who said no, and the dividing line runs through something in you. Are you sure that is grace and not, at the last inch, a work.

To the Reformed Christian, the Arminian says: you have protected the sovereignty of God, but look what you risked. Push your logic to its end and God chose, before I drew a breath, to pass over the man down the street and hand him to the dark, and then commanded me to tell him God desires his salvation. Is that desire real. And if every human choice, including the first sin in the garden, was decreed before the world began, then whose hand finally moved when the fruit came down. You say God is not the author of sin. The machinery says otherwise, and calling it mystery does not silence the question.

Neither of them has a clean answer. That is not my failure to find one. That is the shape of the thing.

And here is what the honest reader has to sit with. Scripture does not hand the tension to one side. It puts both edges in a single breath and walks away. "Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:12-13). Work out your own salvation, the command lands on you, it is yours to do, and in the same sentence, without a seam, for it is God who works in you, even the willing, even the working, is his. Paul does not resolve it. He does not tell you which clause is load-bearing. He sets the human act and the divine act side by side and treats the pairing as the most natural thing in the world. Wesley preached a whole sermon on those two verses and kept both. The Reformed have preached the same text and kept both. The text will not take sides, and the traditions that go to war over it are both quoting it.

So where does that leave a man in a car in the dark, unable to say whose hand opened the door. It leaves me, I think, exactly where Scripture means to leave me, which is unable to boast and unable to despair in the same instant. If it was his hand, I cannot boast, because I did not save myself. If it was also mine, I cannot despair, because the door is real and it opens. The two answers I keep trying to choose between are, it turns out, the two things I most need to be true. That I was chosen, so that nothing I do can finally lose it. That I chose, so that the choosing was mine and not a puppet's. I have stopped being able to pry them apart, and I have started to suspect that the inability is not my weakness but the doctrine's honesty.

You are trusted here. You can close this page a Calvinist and remain my brother. You can close it an Arminian and remain my brother. What I would ask of you is the one thing this question is built to teach, which is the thing I am worst at. To hold a conviction with everything you have, and to hold it in front of a person who holds the other one, and to refuse to make him a fool for standing where the church has let faithful people stand for four hundred years. That is harder than winning the argument. It may be the actual point of an argument God left open.

I still do not know whose hand it was in the car. I have made my peace with the not knowing, which is not the same as not caring. Some nights I read Ephesians and I am sure he took me. Some nights I read the invitation at the end of Revelation and I am sure he waited for me to come. And I have come to believe that a God large enough to be both is a God I could not have invented, because the God I would have invented would have picked a side, the way I always want to, and told me which one, and let me sleep. This one keeps me up. He chose me before the world was made, and he stood at the door and knocked, and he has never once told me how both of those are true. He only told me they are. I have decided that is enough to live on, and more than enough to kneel on.
posts.excerpt: The night I came to faith, I could not tell whether I had finally found God or been finally found by him. Years later I learned the church has argued that exact question for centuries and never closed it. I have stopped needing it closed.

posts.title: Sprinkle or Immerse? Infant or Believer?
posts.body:
The water is the same. That is the strange part.

Walk into a Baptist church on a Sunday and you may see a grown man led down into a tank at the front, dropped all the way under, and brought up streaming and shaking and alive. Walk two streets over into a Presbyterian or a Lutheran or an Anglican or a Catholic church and you may see a woman hand her eight-day-old son to a minister who wets three fingers and touches the child's head with water he will never remember. Same God named over both. Same words, nearly. Same conviction in the room that something real is being done. And a wall between the two buildings that has held for five hundred years and shows no sign of coming down. Two Christians can love the same Lord, read the same book, and stand on opposite banks of the same font, each certain the other has gotten the water wrong.

I want to tell you at the front what kind of question this is, because naming the order changes how hard you are allowed to hit. This is a second-order question. It is the classic one, in fact. First-order matters are the ones the ancient creeds bind, the things you cannot deny and still be confessing the faith: the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, the bodily resurrection, salvation by grace through the cross. Deny those and you have left the room. Baptism is not that. How and to whom the water goes divides faithful churches without dividing the faith itself, and the men who argued it hardest knew it. The Reformers who would not budge an inch on justification wrote to each other across this line as brothers. So I am not going to adjudicate it for you. I am going to hand you both cases at full strength, name what neither can escape, and leave you to carry the weight of deciding, because the church has carried it unresolved for a very long time and has not been ashamed to.

First, what the two sides are not fighting about, because it is more than you would guess. Both confess that baptism is not a naming ceremony with a religious accent. Both confess it is the sign and seal of union with Christ, a death and a resurrection worked on the person and not merely a decision performed by them. Both read Paul and mean it: "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:3-4). Buried and raised. The Baptist and the Presbyterian will preach that verse the same way. What they cannot agree on is who belongs in the grave, and how far under they have to go. The meaning is shared. The recipients and the mode are the fight.

Take the believer's case first, and take it at full height, because a caricature of it is easy and worthless. The credobaptist, the one who baptizes only those old enough to profess faith, is not being stingy with grace. He is reading the New Testament with a plain eye and asking you to explain what you see. Every single baptism recorded in the book of Acts follows a personal, spoken turning toward Christ. Peter, on the first day, does not say be baptized and then believe. He says the other order: "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38). Repentance first. Repentance is not something an infant does. The credobaptist looks across the whole New Testament and finds the baptized always described as those who have heard, believed, received the word, and then gone down into the water, in that sequence, never once reversed with a commentary explaining the exception for children.

And the shape of the act itself, he says, is preaching a sermon that sprinkling mutes. Look again at Romans. Buried with him. You do not bury a body by dampening its forehead. You put it all the way under and it disappears and then it comes up. The Greek word the New Testament reaches for, baptizo, carries in its ordinary use the sense of dipping, plunging, submerging. When the picture is dying and rising with Christ, immersion is not a preference. It is the drama made visible, the four seconds in which a person is a corpse in the water and then is not. This is the free-church conviction, the one the Anabaptists paid for in blood in the 1520s when Zurich drowned some of them for the crime of being baptized twice, and the one the Baptists confessed in London in 1689: the church is a community of the regenerate, of those who can say for themselves that they have died and been raised, and the water is for them. To baptize a baby who cannot yet believe, the credobaptist says gently, is to put the sign on a faith that is not yet there, and to risk teaching a child for the rest of his life that he was made a Christian by something that happened before he could say yes.

Now turn, and give the other side the identical refusal to caricature, because the paedobaptist is not baptizing babies out of sentiment or a wish to get them into heaven early. He is standing on the one unbroken storyline of the whole Bible, and he is asking the Baptist a question the Baptist finds harder than he lets on. God has always put the sign of belonging on the children of believers before those children could choose. He did it for two thousand years. When God made his covenant with Abraham, he commanded that the sign be laid on every son at eight days old, long before that son could repent or profess or understand a thing. The children of believers were marked as belonging to the covenant people from the beginning, by grace, before response. The paedobaptist asks: did God change his mind about that in the new covenant, and narrow the promise to exclude the very children he had always included? He reads Peter's own next sentence at Pentecost, "the promise is for you and for your children," and he hears the ancient pattern held open, not closed.

And he has a text that ties the two signs together with a knot the credobaptist has to work at. Writing to the Colossians, Paul says the Christians there were "circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead" (Colossians 2:11-12). Circumcision and baptism, laid side by side, the old sign and the new one, both burial, both belonging. If baptism now stands where circumcision stood, the paedobaptist reasons, then it goes where circumcision went, onto the children of the faithful. This is the case Calvin argued and the Westminster divines confessed and Rome and the Lutherans and the Anglicans hold in their own keys: that grace precedes our grasping of it, that the covenant has always gathered up the households of believers, and that a baby at the font is the gospel preached in its purest form, a person receiving a love he did nothing to earn and could not yet even want.

The households press the same point. When Lydia comes to faith by the river, Luke writes that "after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us" (Acts 16:15). No mention of who in that household believed. When the Philippian jailer is converted in the middle of the night, "he was baptized at once, he and all his family" (Acts 16:33). In the ancient world a household was not a room of individual deciders. It was a man, his wife, his children, his servants, gathered under him, and when the head turned to Christ the sign came down over the whole house. The paedobaptist sees his practice sitting right there in the text. The credobaptist answers, honestly and not weakly, that the same chapter says the jailer "rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God" (Acts 16:34), and that a believing household is exactly what he would expect. Both men read the same three verses. Both men are telling you the truth about what they see. That is what a second-order question looks like when it is handled without contempt.

The mode, sprinkle or immerse, is the lighter half of this, and I will treat it lightly on purpose, because the church itself has. The word leans toward immersion and the picture of burial leans harder, and the credobaptist is right that we lost something real when the tank became a bowl. But the earliest church did not make it a wall. The Didache, the little manual of church practice from the first or early second century, tells believers to baptize in running water if they have it, in still water if they do not, in cold or warm as they can, and then adds that if they have not enough water for either, they may pour water on the head three times. Pour. That instruction is old, older than most of the creeds, and it tells you the ancient church cared that the water was applied in the name of the triune God more than it cared about the depth. Reasonable Christians have plunged and poured and sprinkled for twenty centuries. I am not going to pretend the depth of the water is the hill the resurrection stands or falls on. It is not.

Here is where I owe you my own hand, because it would be a coward's move to hold this open while hiding that I am standing somewhere in it. I came to Christ out of atheism as a grown man, and I went down into the water as an adult, professing, weeping, knowing exactly what was happening to me. My own baptism was a believer's baptism, and it is one of the fixed stars of my life. I cannot pretend I have no history here. And I am telling you, with that history, that I will still not settle it for you, because I have stood at the fonts of men I know to be more godly than I am, watched them wet the head of a baby, and been unable to call it anything but faith. My experience is a witness. It is not a verdict. If I made my Tuesday morning the rule for the whole church, I would be doing the very thing this kind of question forbids.

And both sides have a temptation crouching at the door, the same instrument turned on each, because the point is not to spare one and gut the other. The credobaptist, so careful to require a real profession, is tempted to make the water a monument to the strength of his own decision, to preach a baptism that is finally about the believer's yes and not about God's prior grace, until the sacrament quietly becomes a work and the man is trusting his choice instead of his Christ. The paedobaptist, so sure the sign belongs on the child, is tempted to presumption, to let the water carry the weight faith was meant to carry, to raise a churchful of the baptized who were never converted and were told all their lives that the font had already handled it. Both temptations are real. I have watched both do their damage. And notice that each side's medicine is the other side's warning, which is one more reason to think the church needs both voices in the room and not one of them exiled.

So I leave you where the New Testament leaves us, with the water and without the rule. A grown man comes up out of a river with his whole professing life in his eyes, and the church says: faithful. A baby is carried to a font he will never remember, marked with a grace he did not ask for, and the church says: faithful. Both of them soaked in the same claim, that they have been buried and raised with Christ and made to belong to a people not their own. You can read this and take your child to the font and remain my brother. You can read this and wait to bring your child down under the water on the day he can speak for himself, and remain my brother. What you cannot do, what none of us gets to do, is treat the water as though it were the cross, or treat the brother on the other bank as though he had missed it. He did not miss it. He is standing in the same river you are, arguing about the depth, both of you already wet.
posts.excerpt: Two churches on the same street baptize with the same water and cannot agree on who should stand in it, or how deep. One brings a grown convert down under a river. One brings an eight-day-old baby to a font. Both say Scripture. Both are my family. I will not settle it for you.

posts.title: Do the Gifts Still Happen?
posts.body:
The first time I prayed for someone to be healed, part of me was waiting to see if the machines would change their numbers.

I had my hand on a dying man's shoulder, and I said the words the Bible tells me to say, and the oldest part of me, the part that spent a whole young life certain no one was listening, watched the monitor. Nothing moved.
