I have also sat across from a woman who told me, without theater, that she had been prayed over and a thing her doctors could not account for had simply lifted, and I could not prove she was lying and did not think she was. I came to faith out of atheism. That means the miraculous is not a doctrine I inherited and quietly stopped examining. It is the exact seam where my old life and my new one still rub against each other, and the rubbing has never fully stopped.

So when a Christian asks me whether the gifts of the Spirit still happen, the tongues and the prophecy and the healing that run all through the book of Acts, I know they are not asking me a trivia question. They are asking whether the God who acted then acts now, or whether he has gone quiet on purpose. And I have to tell them the same thing I am about to tell you. The church has not agreed. It has divided into serious, Bible-loving traditions that read the same New Testament and walk out into different rooms, and it has never once resolved the division into a rule you could carry into a hospital hallway and lean on.

Let me name what kind of question this is before I say anything else, because the category decides how hard you are allowed to hold it. This is a third-order question. It divides Pentecostal churches from charismatic ones from cessationist ones, in earnest, but it divides people who confess the same Christ, the same cross, the same grace none of us earned. No creed binds it. A church can teach that the gifts stopped, or teach that they continue, and still preach a gospel you could build your life on. That is the ground we are standing on. Not the deity of Christ, where the church has drawn a line and had to. This is the other kind of hard, where two faithful families love the same Lord, read the whole Book, and land in different places. The honest thing is to hand you both at full strength and refuse to pretend either one is foolish.

Start with the cessationist, and refuse the cartoon first. The caricature says the cessationist is a dried-up rationalist who has explained the Holy Spirit into a footnote and would be embarrassed if God actually did something. No serious cessationist believes anything close to that. If that is the version in your head, you have never heard the case.

Here is the case. The cessationist begins with a question about what the miraculous gifts were for. In the New Testament, signs and wonders travel with revelation. They accredit the messenger. When the writer of Hebrews describes how the gospel reached the second generation, he says it "was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will" (Hebrews 2:3-4). Notice the logic. The signs bore witness. Paul says the church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation, by its nature, is laid once. The cessationist reasons from there. If the miraculous and revelatory gifts existed to accredit new revelation, then when the revelation was complete, when the last apostle died and the canon of Scripture closed, the accrediting work was done, and the gifts that served it were done too. B. B. Warfield laid this out at length in Counterfeit Miracles in 1918, arguing that the age of miracles belonged to the age of the apostles and the founding of the church, and that later claims of miracle-working would not survive honest scrutiny.

And underneath the argument is a pastoral fear worth honoring, not sneering at. The cessationist has watched what happens when people hunger for a fresh word more than they trust the finished one. He has seen the manipulation, the healer who blames the sick man's faith when the healing does not come, the prophecy that flatters the crowd, the Bible left closed on the lap while someone waits for a whisper. He has concluded that the sufficiency of Scripture is a wall worth defending, because the alternative is a church tossed around by whoever claims the hottest line to heaven. When Warfield wrote, and when careful Reformed voices after him, like Richard Gaffin in Perspectives on Pentecost, pressed the same case, the point underneath was not a small God. It was a settled God, who has spoken finally in his Son, and who does not need a stream of new signs to prop up a word that is already complete. That is not unbelief. To the people who hold it, it is reverence.

Now turn, and give the other side the identical refusal to caricature. Because the continuationist is not a gullible enthusiast chasing goosebumps. That is the cartoon, and it is just as false.

The continuationist begins with a simple observation about the text. Nowhere does the New Testament put an expiration date on the gifts. The chapters that deal with the gifts most directly, 1 Corinthians 12 through 14, do not read like a description of a temporary phase. They read like instructions for an ongoing life. Paul does not say the Corinthians once had these gifts. He tells them how to use them without wrecking the church, and then he says, plainly, "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). That is a command in the present tense, aimed at a church and, the continuationist argues, at every church after it. A few lines later Paul writes, "earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues" (1 Corinthians 14:39). It is difficult to obey a command to earnestly desire something you have been told God withdrew.

And there is the famous passage the cessationist leans on, which the continuationist reads the other way. Paul writes that "as for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:8), and then gives the timing: "but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:10). The whole question is what the perfect is. The cessationist has sometimes read it as the completed canon. But look at what Paul says next, in the same breath: "For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" (1 Corinthians 13:12). Face to face. Known as fully as God knows me. That is not the arrival of a book, the continuationist says. That is the return of Christ. And if the gifts pass away when we see him face to face, then they were meant to run until that day, not until the last page of Revelation was copied out.

Serious Reformed scholars have made a careful case for it. D. A. Carson, in Showing the Spirit, worked through 1 Corinthians 12 through 14 and concluded that the burden of proof sits on the one who says the gifts have ceased, because the text nowhere says so. Wayne Grudem has argued at length for the continuation of prophecy, understood not as new Scripture but as a lesser, fallible gift that must always be tested against the Book that cannot fail. And then there is the plain fact of the last hundred years. Much of the explosive growth of the church across the global south came through Christians who prayed expecting God to act and testified that he did. The movement that traces back to the Azusa Street revival of 1906 is now counted in the hundreds of millions. The continuationist offers that not as proof but as a fact the cessationist has to explain, because it is hard to say the Spirit stopped giving gifts while looking at where the church is actually growing.

There is a middle, and it deserves to be named honestly rather than used as a hiding place. Many thoughtful Christians land in a posture often called open but cautious. They cannot find the verse that shuts the gifts off, so they will not say God does not still give them. But they have seen too much abuse to go looking for signs, and they read the New Testament's own commands to weigh and to test as the reason for their caution. They hold the door open and stand back from it, unwilling to deny what Scripture never denied and unwilling to chase what it never told them to chase. It is not a dodge. It may be the most exact reading of a Bible that both refuses to end the gifts and refuses to let them run wild.

Now let me put them in the same room, because that is where they actually live, and refuse to let either off the hook. And I have to start with myself, because I have leaned both ways in the same week.

To the continuationist, the cessationist says: you say you are earnestly desiring the gifts, but look at what your movement has produced when it stops testing. You have people manufacturing a spiritual experience and calling it the Spirit, prophets who are never wrong because no one is allowed to check them, a hunger for the next sign that has quietly grown louder than your hunger for the God who already spoke. You call it faith. Are you sure it is not appetite. This is the continuationist's besetting temptation, and it has a name he does not like to say: credulity, the spiritual theater that mistakes intensity for the presence of God, and every honest continuationist has watched it happen and winced.

To the cessationist, the continuationist says: you say you are guarding the sufficiency of Scripture, but look at what your reasoning does to your Tuesday. You have built a theology in which the God of the Bible acted powerfully for one generation and then, functionally, went silent, and you pray without expecting an answer you would recognize, and you call your low expectations maturity. You have a doctrine of the Spirit and a life that could run without him. That is the cessationist's besetting temptation, and it also has a name: a functional deism that has boxed God into the first century, that believes in principle he could act and in practice would be startled if he did. And I know that temptation from the inside, because the old atheist in me finds it the most comfortable room in the house. It asks nothing of me. It lets the machine stay silent and calls the silence theology.

Neither side has a clean answer to the other. That is not my failure to find one.

And here is what the honest reader has to sit with. The New Testament that will not put an expiration date on the gifts is the same New Testament that will not let you swallow every claim uncritically. To one church Paul writes both halves in a single breath: "Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21). Do not quench. Do not despise. And also, test everything. The text hands the eager one a warning and the cautious one a rebuke, in the same sentence, and walks away without telling you which clause is load-bearing. The traditions that go to war over the gifts are both quoting a Book that refused to take their side.

I told you the miraculous is the seam where my two lives still rub, and I am not going to pretend I have sewn it shut. I will not tell you the gifts have ceased, because I have met the woman I could not prove wrong. I will not tell you to go chase them either, because I have watched what the chasing does to people who stopped testing, and I have felt in my own chest how easily a man can want a sign more than he wants God. You are trusted here. You can close this page a cessationist and remain my brother. You can close it a continuationist and remain my brother. What neither of us gets to do is treat the other one as a fool for standing where the church has let faithful people stand.

So I leave you where the hospital room leaves me. My hand is still on the shoulder. I do not know, going in, whether God will act the way Acts describes or hold his peace, and I have stopped pretending I know. I only know I am not allowed to close the door in either direction, because the God who could has not told me to, and the God who does has not asked my permission. He is quieter than the continuationist sometimes promises and louder than the cessationist sometimes allows, and he has never once let me settle which. I have decided to keep praying with my hands open and my eyes open, which is the only honest posture left to a man who used to be sure the room was empty and is now only sure that it is not.
posts.excerpt: I have stood in a hospital room with my hand on a dying man and waited to see if the machines would change. They did not. I came to faith out of atheism, so the question of whether God still acts is not a doctrine I inherited. It is the seam where my old life and my new one still rub.

posts.title: When a Marriage Ends: Divorce, Remarriage, and Grace
posts.body:
The paper comes in an envelope, or it comes as a sentence at the kitchen table, or it comes as the slow understanding that the person across the bed left the marriage years before either of you said the word out loud. However it arrives, it does not feel like a doctrine. It feels like a death.

You may be reading this with the ring still on and a house gone quiet. You may be reading it a decade later, with a second spouse in the next room and a shame that walks into church a step ahead of you. You may be the one who was left, or the one who did the leaving, or the one who can no longer tell which of those is true. I am not going to hand you a verdict. The church has carried this question for two thousand years without once setting it down, and the most honest thing I can do is carry it into the room beside you and refuse to pretend it is light.

Start with what is not in dispute, because nearly everything true here begins there. Marriage is good. Not good the way a policy is good, something the culture assembled and can therefore amend. It is older than the culture. Jesus, asked about divorce, does not begin with Moses. He reaches past Moses to the garden, to the way it was from the beginning, and he says of husband and wife, "So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matthew 19:6). The New Testament will later make that one flesh a picture of Christ and his church, which is why the vow is not a convenience and the breaking of it is never small. That much the whole church confesses, and it sits near the center of Christian ethics, not out at the edge where we are free to trade things away. Hold onto it. Everything I am about to describe is an argument among people who all hold onto it.

Now the actual dividing line, and let me name its weight before I walk into it. Whether there are grounds on which a believer may rightly divorce, and whether a divorced believer may rightly remarry, is a question on which faithful churches have genuinely differed. This is not the deity of Christ. It is not the resurrection. It is a second-order question, the kind that has divided sincere Christians from one another without dividing any of them from Christ, and I am going to treat it as exactly that. Serious enough to labor over. Open enough that a brother on the other side is still a brother.

Take the strict view first, and take it at full strength, because the world has spent fifty years making it easy to sneer at, and it does not deserve the sneer. The strict reading says that what God joins, no one on earth has standing to pull apart, and that includes the two people standing inside it. Jesus did not loosen Moses. He tightened him. Moses permitted the certificate of divorce, and Jesus calls that permission a concession to hard hearts, not the will of the God who made them one. On this reading the bond is not a feeling that can die or a contract that can be breached. It is an objective thing God did, and a human court dissolving it on paper does not dissolve it in heaven. This is not a fringe severity. In various forms it has been the conviction of much of the church across the centuries, and it remains the formal teaching of the Roman Catholic Church, which holds a consummated Christian marriage indissoluble until death and will not call a second union, contracted while the first spouse lives, a marriage at all. The strict Christian looks at a culture that files for divorce more easily than it breaks a lease, at vows treated as sentiment that expires the moment it costs something, and says the thing no one wants to hear. Someone has to hold the line the world has erased. Someone has to testify with their own life that the promise meant what it said, and if the church will not, no one will. They are not being cruel when they say it. They are guarding the one human institution that still tells a child what a covenant is, and they are willing to pay for it in their own comfort to keep it true.

Now turn, and give the other side the same refusal to caricature, because it is not the party of loose vows. It is the party that took the exceptions Scripture actually wrote down and would not erase them to make the rule cleaner. Because Jesus himself, in the same breath where he raises the standard, names an exception. "And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery" (Matthew 19:9). Read the exception clause honestly and it will not disappear. He could have said whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery, and stopped. He did not. He carved out a case, and a plain reading finds in it one truth the strict view has to work hard to hold down: a spouse's betrayal of the one flesh is a wound that can end the marriage in fact before any court ends it on paper. Then Paul, facing a situation Jesus had not addressed, adds a second. When an unbelieving spouse walks out on a believer, "if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15). Not enslaved. Paul will not chain a deserted believer to a marriage the other person has already abandoned.

And there is the word from Malachi that both sides have to hold with care. Malachi 2:16 in the ESV reads, "For the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence, says the LORD of hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be faithless." Older translations render the opening as God saying "I hate divorce," and the anger survives in either rendering. It falls on the treachery, on the violence done under the roof, on the covenant a man breaks against the wife he swore to cover. Read that way, the verse is not a wall built against the abandoned. It is a verse standing on the side of the betrayed. And many faithful Christians reason from exactly there: that a spouse who batters, or who deserts, has already torn the covenant with their own hands, and that the church works its own kind of violence when it orders a battered woman back under that roof and calls her staying obedience. If you have ever watched that happen, you know it does not look like holiness. It looks like a man protecting a doctrine with someone else's body.

So here is the honest tension, and I am not going to relieve it for you. The same Jesus who says let not man separate says except for sexual immorality. Both sentences are his. The strict Christian is guarding something real, the permanence the world has cheapened until it means nothing. The Christian who permits divorce in some cases is guarding something just as real, the abandoned and the abused whom a flattened rule would crush under the weight of the very covenant the other person already broke. Refuse both of the easy men. Refuse the rigorist who binds a burden onto the wounded and steps back to watch them carry it. Refuse the sentimentalist who empties the vow of everything that made it cost, until "till death" quietly comes to mean "till it gets hard." Both of them have found a way to stop feeling the weight. The rigorist stopped feeling the person. The sentimentalist stopped feeling the promise. The gospel will not let you set either one down.

I have been the rigorist. I will tell you that plainly, because I am inside this indictment and not standing over it. I have reached for the rule in a counseling room because the rule was clean and the person in front of me was not, because a principle asks nothing of me and a bleeding human asks everything I have. I was raised without a father, in the wreckage a broken home leaves in a boy who never got a vote, and I have five sons of my own now, and none of that has handed me the verdict. It has only made me unable to hold this question at a safe distance. When I have gotten it wrong, I have gotten it wrong in the direction of protecting my theology from somebody's pain. That is a sin the strict and the loose can both commit. I have committed it.

Which is why I have to tell you the one thing this page cannot do. It cannot know you. A website does not know whether you were the betrayer or the betrayed, whether the marriage died of one catastrophic blow or ten thousand small withdrawals nobody could see, whether staying is faithfulness or is slowly ending you. A real decision about a real marriage does not belong to an essay. It belongs in a room, with a pastor who knows your name and will still know it a year from now, and often with a wise counselor beside him. If you are in danger, it belongs first with people who can actually keep you safe, and reaching for them is not a failure of faith. It is faith with its eyes open. Do not carry this alone because you are ashamed. Shame is the one counselor in the room who is always lying.

And hear this, whichever line you have already crossed. The blood of Christ was not spilled for the people whose marriages held. Grace is not the wage paid out on a record you kept clean. It is the thing that walks toward you precisely because you could not keep it. If your marriage has ended, you are not standing outside the reach of God, filed under some category his mercy has learned to skip. The woman Jesus met at the well had five husbands behind her and a sixth man who was not her husband, and he did not open by counting them. He asked her for a drink. Then he told her who he was, and she left her water jar and went back to the town that knew her whole story, and many of them believed because of what she said. He began where the grace was, not where the failure was.

So I leave you where the question actually lives, which is not in a rulebook but in a covenant that was always meant to image a faithfulness stronger than ours. Marriage is good, and its breaking is a grief God himself calls violence, and there are cases where faithful Christians have stood over the same wreckage and disagreed, in the fear of God, about what love requires next. I will not settle it for you from here. Settling it from here would be its own kind of violence, the cheap kind, done to a person I cannot see. But I will tell you the one thing I am sure of. Whatever your marriage became, you have not out-sinned the cross. It was built taller than your worst day on purpose. Go find the people who can help you carry this, and do not believe the voice that tells you the door is shut. It is not the door that is closed. It is only the night, and the night has never once been the end of the story.
posts.excerpt: You may be reading this with the ring still on and a house gone quiet, or a decade later with a second spouse in the next room and a shame that walks into church a step ahead of you. The church has carried this question for two thousand years without setting it down. I will not hand you a verdict. I will refuse to pretend it is light.

posts.title: Should We Keep People Alive at Any Cost?
posts.body:
The question does not arrive in an ethics seminar. It arrives in a room with a bed in it.

Someone you love is in that bed, and a machine is doing the breathing now, or the pain has stopped answering the medicine, and a doctor with kind eyes is asking you what you want to do. Or it is not someone you love. It is you. The scan came back, and you have started doing the math on how many of the months ahead are the ones where you are still yourself. I need to say something before I say anything else, because a man in a room like that deserves it said plainly. I am a pastor. I am not a physician and I am not a lawyer, and nothing in this essay is medical or legal advice. The decisions in that room are not mine to make and not mine to grade. They belong to you, to the people who love you, to the doctors who actually know your body, and to a pastor who knows your name. What I can do is refuse to hand you a slogan on the way in.

Because the slogans are waiting on both sides of that door, and both of them are lying to you about how hard this is.

So start with the case I am supposed to be against, and refuse the cartoon of it first. The people who argue for a chosen death are not, mostly, people who hold life cheap. Many of them arrived at the argument the hard way, at a bedside, watching. They watched someone take a very long time to die and suffer nearly every hour of it. They watched a person they loved become a body that pain moved through, a mouth that could no longer form the names of the people in the room. And they came away with a conviction that deserves to be stated at full strength, not swatted down. It is this. When there is nothing left but the suffering, when the medicine has run out of mercy and the only thing modern hospitals are good at is making the dying last longer, it is not compassion to prolong it. It is cruelty wearing a lab coat. We would not do it to a dog. We call it kindness when we spare an animal this, and then we force it on our own mothers and tell them to offer it up.

Under the compassion sits a second argument, and it is harder. It is the argument from your own hands. If anything in this world is yours, surely your own death is yours. You did not choose to be born; the least the universe owes you is a say in how you leave. A man who has run his own life, made his own bed, paid his own way, should not have to spend his final chapter as a problem to be managed, kept alive past the point he recognizes himself because a law or a religion he never signed decided his suffering was necessary for reasons that are not his. The word we reach for is dignity, and behind it is a real fear, one I will not pretend is unreasonable. It is the fear of a medicalized dying. Of ending not in a bed at home with the people who know you, but in a fluorescent room among strangers who are efficient and gentle and cannot stop, wired to machines that beep your heart back from every exit it tries to take, your death postponed one intervention at a time until it happens anyway, later, worse, and further from anyone you love. The Greek word euthanasia means, at its root, a good death. The people asking for it are not asking for death. They have that already. They are asking that it be good.

I want you to feel the weight of that before I say anything else, because if you cannot feel it you are not ready to disagree with it. I have felt it. I have stood at enough bedsides to know that the suffering behind this argument is not theoretical, and that the people making it are often the ones who loved most and watched longest. Anyone who answers them with a bumper sticker about the sanctity of life has not been in the room.

Now let me stand somewhere else, and try to earn the standing.

The Christian account does not begin with a rule about dying. It begins with a claim about owning, and the claim is that you do not. Your life is not a possession you hold; it is a gift you were handed. Paul says it to a church that thought its bodies were its own business: "You are not your own, for you were bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The psalmist says it looking backward at his own beginning: "Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them" (Psalm 139:16). And Job, who had more reason than any of us to curse the arrangement, says it having lost everything: "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21). This is not the tidy answer it can sound like from a pulpit. It is the whole quarrel, stated. If my life is mine, then the autonomy argument is close to unanswerable, and the only real question is whether I am choosing well. If my life was given, then even my death is not a thing I own outright, and I hold it the way I hold everything else that was given, with open hands and not a clenched fist. The two arguments are not really about pain. They are about whose life it is. That is the whole disagreement, and it is worth naming honestly instead of pretending the compassion case is the only thing on the table.

But here is where the church has to be more careful than it usually is, and where a lot of frightened people have been handed a cruelty in God's name. Saying life is a gift is not the same as saying we must cling to every hour of it at any cost. It is not. Scripture itself will not let me say it. "For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:1-2). There is a time to die. Christianity has never taught that death is the ultimate defeat to be resisted with every machine we own; that is closer to the creed of a culture that has stopped believing in resurrection and so has nothing left but the fight. The faith that says a man rose from a grave is not the faith most desperate to keep everyone out of one.

Which is why the tradition drew a line a long time ago that the current debate keeps blurring, and the line matters more than almost anything else I can tell you. It is the difference between allowing a death and causing one. For centuries Christian moral thought distinguished between what it called ordinary and extraordinary means, between the care you owe a dying person and the interventions that only prolong a dying already underway. Declining a fourth round of chemotherapy that will buy weeks of misery and no cure. Turning off a ventilator that is breathing for a body that will never breathe on its own again. Choosing comfort over one more surgery. The tradition has generally permitted all of these, and called none of them killing, because in each of them the disease is what takes the life. You are not reaching for death. You are declining to wage a war against a death that has already won, and letting a person go home. That is not the same act as putting the death in the syringe. One removes an obstacle and lets nature finish; the other makes the ending happen by your own hand. A skeptic will tell you the line is a fiction, that a dead patient is a dead patient and the rest is Catholic hairsplitting to salve the conscience. I understand why it looks that way from outside. But every parent knows the difference between failing to save a child and harming one, and every court knows the difference between letting a man die and killing him, and the difference does not evaporate because the case is sad. What this means for you, in the room, is freedom you may not know you have. You are not required to torture someone you love into a few more days. Letting go is not the sin the machines want you to think it is.

So if the tradition already lets us stop, what is left to argue about? Only the last step. Only the hand on the syringe. And here the Christian objection is not mainly about the sufferer, who has my whole sympathy. It is about everyone standing behind him. Because the moment a society makes killing a medical option, it changes what it means to be old, to be disabled, to be expensive, to be a burden. The offer, once available, becomes a question, and the question does not stay unasked. A frail woman who would never have thought of it starts to wonder whether she is costing her children too much, whether the decent thing, the loving thing, would be to stop being in the way. Nobody has to coerce her. The mere existence of the door does the work; her sense that she ought to consider walking through it is the coercion. Wherever assisted dying has been made law, the criteria that began narrow, for the terminal and the imminently dying, have tended over years to widen, toward the chronically ill, the disabled, the mentally anguished, the merely tired of life. I am not going to hand you invented numbers, and I am not going to pretend every expansion is a scandal. I am going to say the plain thing the disability rights community has been saying, from the left, for a long time, and being ignored: a right to die, in a society that treats some lives as less worth living, has a way of becoming a duty to die for the people that society was already tired of carrying. The most vulnerable person in that hospital is not the one with the strong family and the good insurance who wants control. It is the one with neither, who is about to learn what his society thinks he is worth.

There is a better thing than the argument, and the church half-forgot it and had to be reminded by a woman most of us have never heard of. In 1967, a British physician named Cicely Saunders, a Christian, opened St Christopher's Hospice in London and more or less founded the modern hospice movement out of one conviction: that a dying person is a living person, that the pain of dying is not only in the body but in the mind and the spirit and the fear, what she called total pain, and that all of it could be met. Not cured. Met. She proved something the whole assisted-dying debate is starving for. That the choice is not really between agony and the needle. That a death can be attended, its pain actually managed, its terror actually company-kept, the person actually accompanied to the door instead of hurried through it. Most of the horror driving the case for a chosen death is the horror of dying abandoned, dying as a medical problem in a room full of strangers. The answer to being abandoned is not to be killed. It is to not be abandoned. Hospice at its best is the church remembering an older word for this than dignity. The word is unabandoned. There is such a thing as dying well, surrounded and unafraid, and we let it become exotic.

Now I have to be careful about a different kind of person, because I have watched this get bungled too. There is a distance the width of a life between the debates I have been describing and the private darkness of someone who wants to die because the pain of being alive has become unbearable. If that is where you are as you read this, I am not handing you a verdict. That is not a bioethics question and I will not treat it as one. It is a wound, and it wants company and care, not an argument, and it wants them now. Please tell someone today. A doctor, a pastor, a crisis line, a person in your house. In the United States you can reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. The despair is lying to you about how permanent it is and about how little you would be missed. Do not believe it alone in a room. The church's word to you is not a position paper. It is: stay, and let us stay with you.

I have been writing as if I were only the pastor at the bedside. I am also going to be in the bed. I have five sons, and one of the quiet arithmetic problems of loving them is knowing that one day I will most likely be their burden, that the strong father who carried them will become the old man they have to lift. And I have felt, already, in preview, the exact fear the autonomy argument is built on: the fear of being too much, of costing them their years, of the loving thing being to get out of the way. I understand the man who wants to spare his children that. I am that man on the bad afternoons. Which is exactly why I do not trust the fear to write my ending. It is not asking to die. It is asking not to be a burden, and a faith worth having tells me that being carried is not beneath my dignity, because I was never the source of my dignity in the first place. "For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's" (Romans 14:8). I do not get to be useful all the way to the end. I get to be his. That will have to be enough, because it is what is true.

Let me leave you with the man who I think understood this best, because he wanted to die and did not. Paul, in a prison cell, tired, with the executioner somewhere down the hall, wrote: "I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account" (Philippians 1:23-24). Read what that is. It is a man who genuinely wanted to go, who was not clinging, who had made his peace with death and honestly preferred it. And who stayed. Not because dying was forbidden to want, but because his life was not his own to spend, and there were still people it was for. He held his own death with open hands and then handed even that back.

I cannot tell you what to do in the room. I told you that at the start and I meant it, and anyone who would tell you is a stranger to how heavy that room is. What I can tell you is that you do not have to fight death like an enemy at every cost, and you do not have to reach for it like a friend to escape the cost, and there is a whole territory between those two panics that the church knew once and is trying to remember. It is the territory of dying well. Attended, not abandoned. Unafraid, because carried. Given back the way it was given. If you are in that room tonight, I am not going to hand you a rule. I am going to tell you that you are not the first to stand there, that the people who love you are the ones to stand there with you, and that whatever you decide, you were never as alone in it as the room makes you feel. Do not decide it by yourself. That is the only thing I am sure of. Not by yourself.
posts.excerpt: The question does not arrive in an ethics seminar. It arrives in a room with a bed in it, and a doctor with kind eyes asking what you want to do. I am not going to hand you a slogan on the way in. Both sides of that door are lying to you about how hard this is.

posts.title: Is the Historic Christian View of Sex Homophobic?
posts.body:
The question does not usually arrive as a question. It arrives as a person who has already decided you are not safe.

I have watched it happen more than once, and it tends to go the same way. A man sits in the church for the better part of three years. Second row, most Sundays, singing like he means it, and he does not say he is gay until he is most of the way out the door, and by then he is telling you why he is leaving, not asking whether he can stay. He did the math a long time before anyone noticed him. He watched how the room talked about people like him when it thought no one like him was in it, the jokes that were not quite jokes, the certainty that cost the certain nothing. He learned what we would do with the truth before he ever risked it on us. Three years of his voice and none of his life, and then he was gone, and we found out what we had been pastoring only after we had failed to.

I have to say that before I say anything else, because if I do not, the rest of this is just a man arranging arguments over a wound he refuses to look at. The church has been cruel here. Not in the abstract. In rooms I have stood in, from pulpits I have shared, in a tone I have used myself before I knew who was listening. We singled out one sin, made it the sin, the one you could be known by and defined by and kept at the door for, while the gossip and the greed and the divorces in the third pew got a nod and a casserole. If you are gay and you grew up in the church, you already know all of this in your body, and you do not need me to perform sorrow about it. You need me to not lie. So I will not. The cruelty was real, it was ours, and a great deal of what has been said in defense of the historic teaching has been the ugliest thing in the room while claiming to be the holiest.

If you cannot feel the weight of that, you are not ready for the next sentence.

Because here is the harder thing. Naming the cruelty does not by itself settle what the church should teach, and pretending it does is its own kind of dodge. There is a live disagreement here, and it runs down the middle of serious, Scripture-loving Christians, and whole traditions have come down on opposite sides of it without either side being stupid or evil. Some hold it as a boundary of the faith. Others hold it as a difference between brothers who will be in the kingdom together. I am not going to tell you today which of those is right, and I want to be honest that the not-telling is not cowardice. It is the shape of the thing. So let me do the one useful thing I can. Let me hand you both cases at their strongest, in the form their best defenders would actually sign, and refuse to let you off the weight of it.

Start with the affirming case, and refuse the cartoon of it first. It is not a shrug. It is not people who stopped believing the Bible and dressed it up.

The most serious version begins with the texts themselves, read closely rather than shouted. There are only a handful, and the affirming scholar asks what each one is actually looking at. When Paul writes in Romans that "their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another" (Romans 1:26-27), the argument is that the frame is idolatry and excess, desire boiling over its own banks, the exchange of the Creator for the created, and not two people building a faithful covenant. The world Paul knew, the argument goes, had no category for a marriage between two men. What it had was the older man and the boy, the master and the slave, the temple and its excess. When Paul reaches for a word in 1 Corinthians, one of the words the ESV renders "men who practice homosexuality," the affirming scholar points out it is a term so rare we are partly guessing at its edges, and asks whether Paul is condemning an orientation the ancient world did not name or the exploitation it saw everywhere. Matthew Vines and James Brownson have pressed this at length and in good faith, and they are not hacks. They love the book they are arguing about.

Then the affirming case does the thing that is hardest to wave off. It points at the fruit. "Thus you will recognize them by their fruits" (Matthew 7:20), the Lord said, and the affirming Christian says: look, then. Look at the gay believer who prays, who serves, who has been faithful to one person for thirty years, whose life grows patience and kindness and self-control, the very fruit of the Spirit Paul names in Galatians. If the tree is bad, where is the bad fruit. And it makes the trajectory argument, the one that should not be dismissed with a joke: the Spirit has led the church to go back and read its own Bible again before. We quoted chapter and verse for slavery, whole libraries of it, and we were wrong, and it was the Spirit working through the excluded that dragged us to see it. What if we are standing in that same place again, defending with a handful of verses a cruelty our grandchildren will not believe we could not see. That argument has moral seriousness. Refuse to feel it and you have not understood it.

Now turn, and give the other side the identical refusal to caricature. Because the historic teaching is not bigotry with a proof-text stapled on, and treating it that way is its own failure of honesty.

The traditional case starts further back than any of the disputed verses, which is exactly why its defenders think the affirming reading is fighting on the wrong ground. It starts in Genesis, with a pattern laid down before any prohibition: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). Male and female, made for each other, the difference itself part of the design. And the traditional Christian notes who reaches back for that verse. Jesus does. Asked about marriage, he goes to the beginning: "he who created them from the beginning made them male and female" (Matthew 19:4), and grounds the whole of marriage in that pattern. The historic reading does not hang on Paul being angry in Romans. It hangs on a shape the Lord himself treats as the given.

And it goes one step further, into why the shape might matter that much. When Paul quotes the one-flesh verse in Ephesians, he says something staggering about it: "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32). Marriage, on this reading, is not merely a good arrangement for raising the young and easing loneliness. It is a living icon, the union of two who are genuinely other, the way Christ and the church are other, made one without being made the same. Take away the difference of male and female, the traditional Christian argues, and you have not adjusted a rule. You have blurred the picture the thing was made to paint. That is why they cannot treat it as a small matter, and it is not homophobia that makes them say so. It is a theology of the body they think they did not invent.

Then comes the part that gets left out, and it is the part that matters most for whether the teaching is cruel. The historic call is not a special burden built for gay people. It is the call to chastity, and it falls on a crowd. It falls on the single man who wanted to be married and never was. On the widow who buried the only person she ever touched. On the divorced woman who did nothing wrong and is alone anyway. The church has always taught, however badly it has lived it, that a faithful life outside of marriage is not a lesser life, that Jesus himself lived it whole and unmarried, that Paul commended it. Wesley Hill, who is gay and celibate and writes about it without a shred of self-pity, keeps insisting the tradition is not asking him for something it does not ask of millions of straight believers too. If chastity outside marriage is a death sentence for the gay Christian, it is the same sentence for a great many others, and either it is livable for all of them or the church has been lying to the single and the widowed for two thousand years.

The people inside this argument have even given themselves names for it, Side A and Side B, the affirming and the celibate-traditional, and the reason they needed names is that they are both trying to follow Jesus and both refuse to leave. That should tell you something about how far this is from a simple case of the faithful against the faithless.

So put the two questions in the same room and refuse to spare either.

To the affirming Christian, the traditional one says: you have read the fruit honestly, but you have made experience the judge of Scripture, and once you do that, tell me what it cannot revise. Every generation finds its own desires natural and the text embarrassing. If the plain sense of Genesis and the words of Jesus about male and female can be dissolved by how sincerely we want them dissolved, what survives the next thing we sincerely want. You called it the Spirit. How do you know it is not just the age you happen to live in, wearing the Spirit's coat.

To the traditional Christian, the affirming one says: you say it is not a special burden, but look at what you actually did with it. You did not treat gluttony as a boundary of the faith. You did not fence the table against the gossips. You found the one prohibition that costs straight people nothing and made it the wall, and then you told the gay teenager it was about your high theology of the body when it was about your comfort. Your doctrine may be right. Your fruit has been rot. Do not hand me Ephesians with the same mouth that drove that boy out of my church.

Neither of them has a clean answer to the other. That is not a failure of my writing. It is the actual shape of a question the church has not closed.

And I have to name where I am standing, because I am not above this scene, I am in it. I am the pastor who did not notice for three years. When I line up the arguments I can feel my own hands wanting the version that would cost me the least, and I do not fully trust the wanting, on either side. The temptation on the traditional side is to love being right more than I love the person the rightness lands on. The temptation on the affirming side is to love being kind more than I love telling the truth, to buy peace in the room with a softness that is really just my fear of being hated. Both of those are in me. Neither of them is the Holy Spirit. I know that much.

Here is what I will not do. I will not stand over your particular life and hand down a ruling on who you should marry or how you should carry a desire you did not choose, as though I could read your years off a page. The historic teaching of the church is what it is, and I have set it in front of you at full strength, and I have set the serious case against it there too, and I have told you plainly that faithful Christians who love this book are not agreed. What order of question this is, whether it is a boundary or a difference, is itself part of what they are not agreed on, and I am not going to pretend from a keyboard that I have settled for you what the church has not settled for itself.

What I can tell you is that you are not an issue. You never were. You are not a position I am arguing against or a talking point I am defending. If you are gay and you have read this far, past everything the church has already done to make sure you would not, then you have shown more willingness to sit in the hard room than most of the people who talk loudest about you have ever shown you. You are welcome to keep reading here. You are welcome to argue with every line. The door is not the thing my church made you think it was.

I keep going back to that second row. To three years of a voice and none of a life, and to the fact that I got the doctrine into all my sermons and missed the boy entirely. Whatever the right answer is to the question this essay refuses to close, I am sure of one thing about the day I stand before God to give an account of that pew. He is not going to ask me first whether I was Side A or Side B. He is going to ask me why the boy did not think he could tell me the truth. And I do not yet have an answer that will hold.
posts.excerpt: A gay teenager sat in my church for three years and never told me, because he had learned exactly what we would do with it. Before I say one word about the texts, I have to say that. The church earned his silence, and it is the first thing that has to be true on the page.

posts.title: What Should Christians Think About Abortion?
posts.body:
The word that starts most of these arguments is not a word. It is a wall.

Two people stand on either side of it, each holding a sign the other cannot read, and the volume goes up in exact proportion to how little either of them intends to look at the person across from them. I have stood on both sides of that wall in my life, and I want to tell you the truth about what I was doing there. I was not thinking. I was belonging. The certainty felt like conviction, but most of it was the warm feeling of being on a team that had already agreed the other team was either a murderer or a bully. That feeling is available on both sides. It costs nothing. It has never once helped a woman make it through a Tuesday.

So before I say anything else, I want to name who is actually in the room when this subject comes up, because she is almost never the person the argument is about. She is a woman who has already made this decision, or is making it now, or watched someone she loves make it and has never said a word about the weight she still carries. She is reading this. If everything I write is aimed past her at a political opponent, I have done the exact thing I am about to accuse both sides of doing. So I am writing to her too, the whole way, and I am telling her at the top: there is no sentence coming that is designed to make her smaller.

Now let me do the hard work, which is to give each side the version its serious people would actually sign, before I weigh a single thing.

## The strongest case for abortion rights

Start here, and refuse the cartoon of it, because the cartoon is where Christians usually begin and it is a lie. The serious case for abortion rights is not a shrug about human life. It is not people who think a pregnancy is nothing. Its best defenders are often the ones most awake to how much a woman's body, her health, her whole future, is on the line in a way that no man's body ever is.

The argument runs like this. A pregnancy does not happen to a woman the way weather happens to a field. It happens inside her, at real cost to her blood and bone and years, and no one else can carry it for her or bear the risk in her place. To say the state may command her to carry a pregnancy she did not choose, or cannot survive, or cannot endure, is to say her body is finally not her own, and that is a thing we say to no one else about any other organ or any other risk. Then come the cases that are not abstractions. The girl who was raped and is now told the pregnancy is a gift. The woman whose own life is failing as the pregnancy advances, whose doctors are weighing whether she goes home to her other children. The couple who wanted this child desperately and learned the pregnancy will never become a living baby, and are now asked to carry a certain death to term for a principle. The serious defender says: whatever you think in general, look at her, and tell me the law knows her situation better than she does.

And the last move, the one that ought to land hardest on a Christian, is this. If you actually want fewer abortions, the evidence points less at the courtroom than at the conditions. A woman with paid leave, with a doctor she can afford, with a partner who stays, with a church that will not vanish when the belly shows, chooses differently than a woman staring down all of it alone. So the serious defender says the loudest voices against abortion are often the quietest about the things that reduce it, and that a movement more interested in banning than in helping has told on itself. Grant that. Do not flinch from it. Some of it is aimed at me.

## The strongest case that the unborn is not nothing

Now turn, and give this side the same refusal to caricature, because it too has a cartoon, and the cartoon is a man who stops caring the moment the baby is born.

The case begins not in the Bible but in the biology, because it does not require you to share my faith to feel it. From conception forward there is no later line at which something switches on. There is no morning the thing in the womb becomes a different kind of thing. It is, from the start, a distinct and continuous human life, the same organism that will one day argue about abortion, only younger and more dependent than it will ever be again. Every line we draw after that first moment, a heartbeat, a trimester, a breath, is a line we chose, and the person on the far side of it was already there. The defender asks a question that does not go away by being called a slogan: if it is not a human life, what is it, and if it is, what exactly permits ending it.

Then the church's witness, which is older and stranger than most people fighting about it today realize. This is not a position American Christians invented in 1973. In the first century, in a document called the Didache, the earliest Christians wrote down their ethic for a pagan world that exposed unwanted infants on hillsides as a matter of course, and they forbade abortion by name. They did it as a persecuted minority with no political power, no court to appeal to, nothing to gain. They did it because they believed the God who made every person had made these ones too, the unseen and the unwanted. That conviction runs straight back into the Scripture they read. "For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13). The claim is not that a fetus is precious because it is useful or wanted or viable. The claim is that God is already at work in there, on a person he already knows, before the mother knows and before the world assigns a value.

And the last move, the one that ought to land hardest on the other side. The measure of any society is what it does with the members who cannot argue for themselves, who have no vote and no voice and no way to make the powerful look at them. Proverbs puts the duty plainly. "Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter" (Proverbs 24:11). The defender says the unborn are exactly the kind of voiceless the whole of Scripture keeps commanding us to see, and that a culture which has learned to look away from them has practiced a skill it will use again on someone else. Grant that too.

## Naming the order, because it is the whole thing

Here is the part both teams skip, and skipping it is how the shouting stays possible.

These two claims are not the same size, and pretending they are is the tribal shortcut. The conviction that a human being bears the image of God, and that the life in the womb is not nothing, is deep and old and near the center of Christian ethics. It is not a policy preference the church picked up recently. It goes back to the hillsides where the first believers gathered up the infants Rome had thrown away. On that, the church's voice across two thousand years is not divided, and I will not pretend it is to make peace in a paragraph. That is high ground, and the church has stood on it a long time.

But the hardest cases, and the question of what a law should therefore be, and how a state should weigh a mother's life and a doctor's judgment and a rape and a dying pregnancy, are exactly where sincere people, including sincere Christians who share the conviction above, disagree sharply and in good faith. A woman can hold that the unborn is a human life and still weep at a bill that offers her nothing but a threat. A man can believe every life is God's image and still not know what the statute should say when two lives are failing at once. To treat the deep conviction and the contested policy as one indivisible package, so that touching the second means betraying the first, is the move that has made this subject unspeakable in most churches. It is not honesty. It is a way of not thinking, dressed as courage.

So I am not going to hand you my ballot. Not because I have no convictions, and not to hide, but because the thing this platform owes you is the shape of the question stated truly, and the church's ancient witness named as the church's, and then the trust to carry it into a voting booth I do not get to enter with you.

## The two cheap versions, refused together, with the same grief

Now let me criticize both sides with one instrument, because the moment I only ever swing it in one direction, I have stopped doing theology and started doing party work.

There is a pro-life that loses interest at birth. It will fight for the child in the womb and then vanish when that child is a hungry six-year-old, or a terrified nineteen-year-old holding a test in a gas station bathroom. It has sometimes meant pro-birth and no more, a passion for the unborn that cools the instant a life would actually cost the movement something. I have sat in rooms where that was true and said nothing, because the room was mine. That is not a full doctrine of life. It is the easy half.

And there is a pro-choice that will not look at the ultrasound. That keeps the language abstract precisely because the picture is not, that says clump of cells to avoid the harder word, that treats any grief the woman feels as false consciousness to be corrected rather than a truth she is telling about what happened. It has sometimes meant a refusal to look at what is ended, because looking would cost the argument its comfort. That is not honesty either. It is the other easy half.

Same instrument. Same grief. If my guardrail only ever fires at the people I already disagree with, it was never a guardrail. It was a flag.

## The woman in the room

I said I would keep her in view the whole way, so let me end with her and not with the argument.

If you have had an abortion, hear this before anything else. You are not a talking point, not to God and not on this page. Whatever you carry from that day, whether it is grief you have never been allowed to say out loud, or relief tangled up with shame you did not expect, or a numbness you have learned to live behind, none of it puts you outside the reach of the only voice that finally matters. The gospel is not that you were never in the wrong. It is that Christ came for people who were, all of us, me first, and that there is no sin his cross was too small to cover. Grace is not the reward for having a clean history. It is the thing that walks into the history you actually have and refuses to leave. If the church ever taught you that this one was the exception, the church was wrong, and I am sorry for the part of it that was mine.

And if you are standing in that decision right now, in the dark, feeling like there is no one to tell and nowhere soft to land, please do not carry it alone. There are people who will sit with you and not perform at you, a pastor, a doctor you trust, a pregnancy center or a counselor who will tell you the truth without shaming you for needing it. You are worth more than the worst hour of your life, and the feeling that you are not is a liar, however loud it gets tonight.

I do not get to hand you a formula that makes this weightless, and I would not trust myself if I tried, because the flourish a man uses to make this weightless is almost always a flourish over someone's grave. What I can tell you is that the God who knits a person in the womb is the same God who knits the broken back together, and that he has never once been more interested in winning an argument than in finding the person the argument forgot. That is where I have to leave it. Not resolved. Held. The way you hold something you were never meant to set down cheaply.
posts.excerpt: The argument is loud because it is easy. Two slogans, thrown past each other, by people who have already decided the other side is either a killer or a bully. I have been both kinds of certain. Neither one was looking at the room.

posts.title: What Does the Church Owe Transgender People?
posts.body:
Before it is a debate, it is a person.

It is a fourteen-year-old who cannot explain to you why the body they woke up in feels like a coat that belongs to someone else, only that the feeling does not lift when they are told to pray it away, and does not lift when they are told it is a phase, and has been there so long they cannot remember being without it. It is a mother in a car in a parking lot, not going in yet, because she does not know how to hold her child and hold her church in the same two hands, and she is terrified that whichever one she puts down, she loses. That is where this actually lives. Not in the panel discussion. In the car.

So I want to say the first thing plainly, and I want it to cost the people on my own side of the aisle something to read. The distress is real. It is not invented, it is not a trend a kid tried on for attention, and for most people who carry it, it was not chosen any more than you chose the color of your eyes. Gender dysphoria, the deep and persistent ache of being at war with your own body, is a real form of suffering, and it is documented, and the church does not get to wave that away because it finds the subject uncomfortable. I am not a physician, and nothing here is medical advice. But I have sat with enough people in enough dark rooms to know the difference between a person who is faking and a person who is drowning, and the first thing the church owes anyone drowning is to stop debating the water and get in it.

We have not done that. Much of the time we have done the opposite. We have taken one of the smallest and most frightened populations of human beings and turned them into a plank in a platform, a thing to be against, a line in a fundraising letter. I have to name that as sin before I say anything else, because it is mine to name. I have stood in rooms where a trans person was discussed the way you would discuss a policy, and I did not always stop it, and the silence was a kind of consent. If a suffering person cannot walk into a church without becoming somebody's political point, we have already failed them before the theology ever gets a word in.

## The case I am asked to caricature, at full strength

Let me give the accommodating view the strongest form its most serious holders would actually sign, because if I beat a straw man here I have lied to you.

It goes like this. A person in the grip of dysphoria is not confused about a doctrine. They are in pain, sometimes the kind of pain that does not let them see a future. The compassionate reading of Scripture, this view says, begins where Jesus began, with the person in front of him and not with the rule about them. He touched the untouchable. He let himself be interrupted by the bleeding woman the law said made him unclean. He was found, over and over, on the wrong side of the respectable, and the people he was hardest on were never the suffering. They were the ones who used holiness as a wall.

And so, this view continues, when we meet someone whose distress lifts, whose sleep returns, whose desire to be alive comes back when they are allowed to live as the gender they experience themselves to be, we are not looking at rebellion. We are looking at relief. To withhold that relief in the name of a principle, when the alternative may be a person who does not survive their own body, is to love an abstraction more than a neighbor. The people who hold this are not, at their most serious, trying to abolish the idea of male and female. They are trying to keep a child alive, and they are asking the church a question it has been very slow to answer honestly: what is your certainty worth, if it is paid for with their life?

That question deserves to land. I am not going to pretend it away.

## The conviction I am asked to abandon, at full strength

Now turn, and give the historic Christian conviction the same refusal to caricature, because it is not what its critics say it is either. It is not disgust with a fancy vocabulary. At its best it is not about controlling anyone. It is about a claim regarding what a human being actually is.

The claim is this. The body is not a costume the real self wears and may exchange. It is not luggage the soul is carrying. It is you, part of the actual you, given and not chosen, and that givenness is a mercy and not a prison. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27, ESV). The historic reading hears in that verse something good and load-bearing: that being made male and female is not an accident evolution left on us to be corrected, but a created reality, spoken by God over the world before anything went wrong, and called good along with the rest of it. On this account the ache to be free of your body is real, and it is also part of the deep wrongness that runs through the whole world after the fall, the same wrongness that puts cancer in good cells and grief in good love. The answer to a body at war with itself, this view says, is not finally to remake the body to match the mind, because the mind is no more infallible than the body. The answer, the one we are all still waiting on, is resurrection, the day the whole self is made whole.

And there is a second thing in this view that the culture war never lets you hear, so let me say it slowly. A person's worth has nothing to do with how well they perform masculinity or femininity. Nothing. The boy who is gentle and hates the things boys are supposed to like is not less a man, and the church that told him so was preaching a culture, not a Christ. Half the freight a dysphoric kid is carrying was loaded onto them by a world, sometimes a church, that decided there was one narrow way to be a boy or a girl and made them a stranger for failing it. The historic conviction, held rightly, does not add to that weight. It lifts it. "I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well" (Psalm 139:14, ESV). The body you have is not a mistake you must escape to be loved. That is meant to be good news, and we have too often preached it as a threat.

## Naming the order, and refusing the shortcut

So I have to be honest about what kind of question this is, because we sort questions badly and it kills people.

There is a first-order center here that the creeds do bind: that the human being is God's good creation, made in his image, body and soul together, and destined not for deletion but for resurrection. That is not up for a vote. But the pastoral and medical particulars, what compassion actually requires in a given life, at a given age, in a given body, with a given history, are hard and genuinely contested, and they are contested among people who share every word of that first-order faith. Serious, Christ-loving believers who agree entirely that the body is a good gift still disagree, sometimes sharply, about what faithfulness looks like across the desk from a suffering fifteen-year-old. Anyone who tells you that part is simple is selling you the comfort of a tribe, and it does not matter which tribe.

And this is where I refuse both shortcuts with the same hand, because I have watched both of them do damage.

The church's shortcut is cruelty dressed as conviction. It is the mockery, the sneer, the man in the pulpit who gets a laugh at the expense of a category of people he has never once sat with. It is turning a doctrine of the body's goodness into a weapon against particular bodies. Whatever the historic view is, that is a betrayal of it, because you cannot preach that a person is fearfully and wonderfully made and then treat them as a punchline in the same breath. I have to own that my own side produced that sneer, and often excused it, and called the excusing courage.

The culture's shortcut is the pretense that none of it is hard. It is the confidence that every question here is already settled, that there is no cost anywhere, no grief, no wisdom required, that the only possible reason for hesitation is hatred. That is not true, and it is not kind, because it hands a frightened family a certainty that the actual research and the actual medicine and the actual long human record do not yet support, and it does it with the same untroubled ease the church uses on the other side. Both shortcuts spare the speaker the weight. Both make the suffering person carry it instead.

## What I will not do, and what I will

I am not going to stand on a website and rule on your child's medicine. I do not know your child. I do not know their body or their history or the particular edge they are standing on, and a man who does not know those things and issues a verdict anyway is not being brave. He is being reckless with a life that is not his. Those decisions belong to the person living them, to the family who loves them, to doctors who can actually examine them, and to a pastor who has earned the right to be in the room by staying in it. Not to me, and not to a stranger with a strong opinion and no skin in your family's grief.

What I will do is tell you what I am fairly sure the church owes, underneath the part we cannot yet resolve.

We owe presence before position. A trans person, or a parent in that parking lot, should be able to walk into a congregation and be known by their name and their face before they are known by this, and be loved in a way that does not depend on the argument coming out where we would prefer. We owe honesty about our own failures, the boy we shamed for being soft, the family we let walk out alone. We owe the refusal to lie in either direction, neither pretending the questions are cost-free nor pretending a hurting person is a threat. And we owe a path to real help kept always in view: a wise pastor who will stay, a counselor trained for this weight, real medical care from people who know you, and, if you are reading this and you have reached the place where you are not sure you want to be here at all, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which you can call or text right now, tonight, because staying is not weakness and reaching for help is one of the most faithful things a person can do. That last one is not a footnote. For someone reading this, it is the only sentence that matters, and I would rather you skip everything else and keep that number.

## Where I leave you

I am not going to resolve this for you, and I want to be honest that it is not because I am hiding my hand. It is because the thing itself is not yet resolved on this side of the kingdom, and the people who claim otherwise, on the right and on the left, are the ones I trust least in the room with an actual child.

But I can tell you the company you are in. You are in the company of a Savior who was himself, in the words of the prophet, "despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3, ESV), who knows exactly what it is to be looked at and turned away from, who was not fooled by the world's confidence about who was worth touching. When his disciples looked at a suffering man and asked whose fault it was, he said, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him" (John 9:3, ESV). He would not let the suffering be a verdict. He would not let it be a debate. He went to the man.

So if you are the teenager who cannot stand to be in your own skin, hear at least this: you are not a category, you are not a mistake, and you are not alone in the dark as much as it feels like it. And if you are the mother in the parking lot, still not going in: go in. Not because the church has all of this figured out. It does not, and I have told you so. Go in because you should not have to carry your child by yourself, and the whole point of the thing, when it is being what it is supposed to be, is that you do not have to. Bring the child God gave you, exactly as afraid as you both are. That is not the failure of faith. On the worst nights, it is the whole of it.
posts.excerpt: Before it is a debate, it is a person. A teenager who cannot stand to be in the body they woke up in, and a mother in the parking lot who does not know how to keep her child alive and keep her faith at the same time. The church has owed both of them something for a long time, and mostly sent an argument instead.

posts.title: Can a Woman Preach?
posts.body:
The question does not usually arrive in a debate. It arrives after the service, in the emptying room.

A woman has just done a thing. She stood up in front of your people and opened the text, and the room went quiet the way it only goes when someone is actually being fed, and old men who have heard a thousand sermons leaned in, and something true got said better than most of the men you have watched try. And then the room clears, and she finds you by the door, and she asks the question she has carried up the aisle. Was I allowed to do that. Not was it good. She knows it was good. The people told her so on the way out. She wants to know whether the thing that just happened, the thing God appeared to use, was obedience or trespass. I have stood in that emptying room. I did not have a clean answer for her then, and I am not going to pretend I have grown one since.

So I am not going to tell you where I land, and I want to say why before you suspect a dodge. This is a second-order question. It divides complementarian churches from egalitarian ones, and it divides them hard, but it divides people who confess the same Christ, the same cross, the same empty tomb, the same grace none of us earned. The creeds do not bind it. Chalcedon says nothing about who may stand behind the pulpit. A church can teach either answer and still preach a gospel you could stake your life on. That is the category we are in. Not the deity of Christ, where the church has drawn a line and had to. This is the other kind of hard, where two faithful traditions read the whole Bible, love the same Lord, and come out in different rooms, and the honest thing is to hand you both at full strength and refuse to pretend one of them is stupid.

Start with the complementarian case, and refuse the cartoon of it first. The caricature says these are men protecting their turf, who think women are less intelligent, less spiritual, a rung down the ladder of being. No serious complementarian believes anything like that, and if that is the version in your head you have never actually heard the case.

Here is the case. It does not begin with the fall. It begins before it, in a garden with no sin in it yet. When Paul tells Timothy how the assembly is to be ordered, he does not reach for the curse and he does not reach for the culture of Ephesus. He reaches all the way back to the sixth day. "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet" (1 Timothy 2:12). And then the ground he stands it on: "For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (1 Timothy 2:13). Read what he did there. He could have said the women in Ephesus were causing a specific problem, and he did not. He anchored the instruction in the order of creation itself, before there was any sin to correct, which means the pattern is not a wound the gospel came to heal. It is a design the gospel came to restore. The complementarian takes that seriously because Paul took it seriously, and grounding a command in Eden rather than in a local mess is Paul telling you the reach of the thing.

And the pattern holds when Paul lists the men who will lead. The overseer, the elder, is described in terms that assume a man: "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2). Not as an insult to women but as a shape, a particular calling given a particular form, the way a father is a particular thing a mother is not, and no one insults a mother by saying she is not the father. The complementarian vision, at its best, is not a ladder at all. It is equal worth in distinct roles, and its holders insist on that word equal with everything they have. They will point you to the life inside God himself, where the Son submits to the Father and is in no way less than the Father, fully God, eternally beloved, and yet ordered under him, so that submission and equality are revealed to be not enemies but the deepest grain of reality. The men who wrote the Danvers Statement in 1987, who gathered under the banner of what they called biblical manhood and womanhood, were not trying to shrink women. They believed they were receiving an order they did not invent and had no authority to revise, and that the loving thing, the true thing, was to keep it and not to congratulate themselves for improving on God.

Now turn, and give the other side the identical refusal to caricature. Because the egalitarian is not the person who reads the Bible with an eraser, cutting out what the age finds embarrassing. That is the cartoon, and it is just as false.

The egalitarian begins somewhere else in the same Bible, at a wall that came down.
