"There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). And then they do the thing that is harder to answer than any single verse. They walk you through the actual women in the actual pages. Paul commends "our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae" (Romans 16:1), and the word under servant is diakonos, deacon, the same office he uses of himself. When a gifted preacher named Apollos got the gospel not quite right, it was a married couple who corrected him, and the wife is named first: "Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26). Philip "had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied" (Acts 21:9), and to prophesy in the assembly is to speak God's word to God's gathered people, which is most of what preaching is. And Paul sends greetings to a woman named Junia: "they are well known to the apostles" (Romans 16:7). For the first thousand years of the church the fathers read that name as a woman, and John Chrysostom, no soft liberal, marveled that a woman had been counted worthy of the name apostle. It was only later that translators, sure the text could not mean what it said, changed her into a man named Junias, a name otherwise unknown in the ancient world.

Then the egalitarian turns the complementarian's own strongest text back toward him. If women are simply to be silent, why does Paul, in a letter he wrote himself, regulate how "every wife who prays or prophesies" (1 Corinthians 11:5) should do it in the gathered church, assuming as settled that she does. And what was actually happening in Ephesus when Paul wrote to Timothy, a city ruled by the temple of Artemis, a cult led by women, drowning in exactly the false teaching Paul spends the whole letter fighting. Read the sentence before the prohibition and you find something a first-century man was not supposed to say: "Let a woman learn" (1 Timothy 2:11). The egalitarian, the scholar like Gordon Fee or Craig Keener, does not delete the restriction. They read it as Paul silencing untaught women spreading a specific error in a specific church, the way you would tell any untaught person to sit down and learn before they teach, and they hold that local correction next to Galatians and Phoebe and Junia and refuse to let one verse in Ephesus overrule the pattern of the whole.

Now let me put the two of them in the same room, because that is where they actually live, and refuse to let either off the hook.

To the egalitarian, the complementarian says: you keep telling me the ban was local, tied to Ephesus and Artemis and a specific mess. But read what Paul actually reached for. He did not say the women there were causing trouble. He reached past Ephesus, past the whole first century, back to the order of creation, to Adam formed first in a garden with no false teaching in it. You have given me a brilliant reading of the context. Paul gave you Eden. Whose context is that. If the reason is creation and not culture, then your local explanation has to answer why the apostle grounded a passing correction in the permanent shape of the world.

To the complementarian, the egalitarian says: if the silence is universal and permanent, then explain your own apostle to me. In the same breath he tells women to keep quiet, he greets a woman deacon, salutes a woman known to the apostles, corrects his theology by way of a woman named first, and regulates the women who prophesy out loud in the assembly. You have told me which verse is the rule and which is the exception. Are you sure you have them the right way round. Are you sure the thing you are defending as the order of creation is not, at least in part, the order of the world you happened to be handed.

Neither of them has a clean answer. That is not my failure to find one. That is the shape of the thing.

And here is where each is tempted to overreach, and I have seen both up close, so I will not point from outside. A complementarianism held wrong does not stay a doctrine of equal worth. It curdles. It becomes a room where a man never has to listen to a woman and calls the not-listening faithfulness, where a woman who can plainly teach is felt as a threat to be managed, where distinct roles quietly shrinks to a smaller and smaller room until the equal has bled out of it and only the ranking is left. I have sat in those rooms. I have nodded in them. And an egalitarianism held wrong does the opposite thing and it is no better. It starts treating the hard text as an embarrassment to be handled, a relic of a darker age Paul would surely renounce if he could see us now, until Scripture stops being the thing that judges the culture and becomes a mirror that only ever reflects what the culture already decided, and the word of God is quietly demoted to the amen of the age. One tribe makes a footstool of women. The other makes a footstool of the text. Both call it obedience. I have been near enough to each to know I could have been at home in either.

I told you I would not tell you where I stand on this, and I will keep that, because it is one of the questions the church has held open with its eyes open, where a woman who submitted to a conviction and served faithfully in the room she was given and a woman who believed God had called her to preach and answered him are both, the church has dared to say, faithful daughters. If your position requires you to make a fool of the woman on the other side, or a fool of Paul, your position is smaller than the Bible it claims.

So I owe that woman by the door an answer, and the truest one I have is not the one she wanted. The church that has read this book longer than either of us has been alive has not agreed. It has produced her, and produced the men who would tell her to sit down, and called them all brothers and sisters, and gone on breaking the same bread. What I can tell her is that the thing that happened in that room, the quiet, the leaning in, the true word landing, was not nothing, and any doctrine that makes it nothing should frighten the one who holds it. And what I cannot tell her, what I will not manufacture to end the ache, is a verse that closes the case. Paul reached back to Eden. Paul greeted Junia. Both are on the page. Both are Scripture. And on this side of the kingdom they have not, for two thousand years, resolved into a single rule you can hand a woman in an emptying room and settle what God was doing when he used her.
posts.excerpt: A woman taught the room better than most men you have heard try, and then asked whether she had been allowed to. Two faithful traditions read the same Bible and answer that question in opposite directions. I am going to hand you both and refuse to spare you the choosing.

posts.title: Morality Without God, and With Him
posts.body:
We didn't come to faith because we ran out of arguments. We came because the argument we were most proud of turned out to be the weakest one we owned.

Let me start by conceding the thing my own side keeps getting wrong, because it embarrasses me every time I hear it. The claim that an atheist cannot be good is false. It is not subtle-false. It is obviously, publicly, humiliatingly false, and the unbeliever reading this knows it in his bones, because he has watched a churchgoer lie and watched a secular humanist keep his word, and he has done the arithmetic. I have too. I spent years outside the faith, and I was not a monster. I gave blood. I told the truth when it cost me. I would have run into traffic for a stranger's kid without stopping to consult a worldview. When I hear a believer suggest that people like the man I was are one philosophy seminar away from the gulag, I want to leave the room. It is a slander. Drop it.

And it is not only false. It is strategically suicidal, because every skeptic can see the counterexample in his own kitchen. He has an atheist mother who is kinder than most deacons. He has read about the quiet unbelievers who hid the hunted while baptized Christians looked away. The moment a Christian argues that goodness requires belief, he has handed the honest doubter a reason to stop listening, and the doubter is right to take it. So I will say it as plainly as I can, from inside the church that keeps forgetting: you do not need God to be good, and anyone who tells you otherwise is not defending the faith. He is defending his own comfort. Those are not the same thing.

So that argument is dead. Good. Let it stay dead.

But killing the bad argument is not the same as ending the conversation, and I think the skeptic knows that too, because there is a different question underneath, and it is harder, and it does not go away just because the cheap version got buried. The cheap question was: can you behave well without God? Obviously yes. The real question is quieter and stranger. When you say something is *wrong*, not distasteful to you, not disfavored by your society, but wrong, what exactly are you saying? And why does it feel like a wall instead of a wish?

Here is the test case, and I want to hand it to you the way it was once handed to me, because it did not let me sleep. Somewhere tonight a man is hurting a child for his own pleasure. Now hold still and notice what you believe about that. You do not believe it is wrong *for you*. You do not believe it is wrong *in our culture*. You believe it is wrong, full stop, everywhere, in every century, and that it would remain wrong if every human being on earth were persuaded to applaud it. If the whole species voted tomorrow to call it good, you would not conclude that it had become good. You would conclude that the whole species had gone to hell. That conviction is not a preference. It has the texture of a fact. It presses on you from the outside like a law you did not write and cannot repeal.

I want to give the naturalist his strongest account of where that pressure comes from, because he has one, and it is not stupid, and Christians who wave it away have not read it. The account runs like this. We are social primates, shaped by a few million years of living or dying in groups. The creatures who felt a hot, non-negotiable revulsion at the betrayal of the vulnerable were the creatures whose bands held together, and held-together bands out-survived the bands that came apart. So evolution did not install a preference. It installed something that *feels* like a law, because a mere preference would have been too weak to hold a tribe through famine and war. On top of that biological floor we built social contracts, rules we agree to because a world where the strong may torture the weak is a world none of us would rationally sign up to live in, since any of us might end up the weak one. Add reason, add empathy, add the slow accumulation of moral progress, and you can explain the entire moral life without invoking anything supernatural at all. This is a serious position. It is held by serious people. It got a great deal right, and I will not pretend otherwise.

But I want to press it exactly where it is thinnest, and only there. Notice what that account has actually explained. It has explained why we *feel* the pressure. It has given a story about the origin of the sensation of obligation. What it has not done, what by its own logic it cannot do, is tell you whether the pressure is tracking anything real. There is a difference, and everything hangs on it. An account of why I experience the number seven as prime is not an account of whether seven is prime. If our horror at cruelty is fully explained as a survival mechanism that helped our ancestors pass on genes, then the horror is a very useful feeling, and the child's torture is disfavored by a feeling evolution gave us for reasons that had nothing to do with the child. On that story, the wrongness is not in the act. It is in us. And a thing that is only in us is a thing that could have been otherwise, and might yet be revised, and cannot finally judge a society that has revised it. This is not my clever objection. It is a worry raised by philosophers on every side of the God question, that a purely evolutionary account explains the moral emotions without underwriting the moral facts, that you can have the whole apparatus of conscience and still have no ground under it. The theme runs through Dostoevsky like a crack through a wall: pull the floor out, and everything is permitted, not because the atheist will suddenly start doing evil, but because he loses the standing to call anything evil in the last analysis.

Steelman it once more, because the naturalist has a reply and it deserves the room. He can say: I do not need a cosmic guarantee. The wrongness of torturing a child is more obvious to me than any theory you could offer me about its source, and I will trust the datum and let the metaphysics fall where it may. If my ethics floats free of a foundation, so much the worse for foundations. That is an honest answer, and it is a brave one, and I respect the man who gives it more than I respect the Christian who has never once felt the vertigo underneath his own certainties.

But notice what he has actually done. He has treated the wrongness as more certain than any naturalist explanation of it, which means he is trusting the moral fact and quietly demoting the theory that was supposed to account for it. He is behaving, in the one place it counts most, as though the wrongness were simply *there*, woven into the structure of things, binding whether he evolved to feel it or not. He is living as though morality were discovered and not invented. And that is precisely the intuition a naturalist worldview has the hardest time paying for. C.S. Lewis built the whole moral argument on this pivot in *Mere Christianity*, not that unbelievers behave badly, he never said that, but that the *ought* pressing on all of us behaves less like an appetite we happen to have and more like a command from somewhere we did not manufacture. You can reject his conclusion. I did, for a while. But you have to reckon with the shape of the thing, and the shape is stubborn.

Let me be careful about what this is and is not. This is not a proof. I have no interest in selling you a proof, because I do not have one, and a man who came to faith from atheism is allergic to being handed certainties he did not earn. This is evidence. It is the fact that when you and I stand over the worst thing in the world, we both reach for a word, *wrong*, that means more than "I don't like this" and more than "we don't do this here," and that neither of us can talk himself out of at three in the morning. Your naturalism can explain the feeling. It has a harder time explaining why you are right to trust it. That gap is not nothing. It is at least worth sitting in.

And I have to say the last part, or I have said nothing, because the theist can misuse this worse than the atheist ever could. Christians have hurt children too, and covered for the men who did, and quoted the God of the moral law while breaking it in the parish house. Having a foundation is not the same as standing on it. I know men with the whole architecture of grounded morality who are crueler than the honest unbeliever I used to be. So I am not handing you a trophy. I am handing you a question I could not answer as an atheist and can only half-answer now.

You already know some things are wrong even if everyone approves.

The only question is what that knowledge is resting on.
posts.excerpt: The argument that you can't be good without God is false, insulting, and should be dropped. The harder question is not whether you can be moral, but what moral obligation is resting on, and why it feels binding rather than merely preferred.

posts.title: The Bible Without the Marketing
posts.body:
The people who tried to hand me the Bible when I was an atheist did me a strange favor. They gave me a version so brittle it was easy to break. One error and the whole thing was supposed to collapse, a single mistranslated word, one number that did not match between two accounts, one command from a bronze-age chapter that made my stomach turn, and the entire edifice was rubble. They told me this. They told me the book was a load-bearing wall where every brick held up the roof, and then they seemed surprised that I went looking for a loose brick. I found several. I walked away thinking I had refuted Christianity.

I had refuted a marketing campaign.

Let me concede the ground first, because you have earned it and because I am not interested in selling you the same thing again. The problems are real. There are passages that appear to contradict each other, the order of events at the tomb, the count of the same census told twice, small seams that anyone reading honestly can see. There is a long and human transmission, centuries of copying by hand, scribes who nodded off and scribes who tidied up, textual variants a scholar can lay out for you in a footnote. And there are texts that do not merely puzzle. They wound. The conquest of Canaan reads like a warrant for slaughter. The household codes were quoted, chapter and verse, by men who owned other men and called it obedience. There are psalms that end with a blessing on whoever kills your enemy's children. I am not going to soften those for you. If you had told me at twenty-four that a good Christian just makes peace with those pages, I would have been right to keep walking.

So this is not a defense of the book you were handed. It is an argument that you were handed the wrong book, or rather, the right book wearing a costume it did not always wear.

Here is the fact almost no skeptic knows, and it changes the shape of the argument. The specific doctrine you are probably rejecting, total, flat, all-or-nothing inerrancy, the claim that Scripture is without error in every incidental detail of history and science, and that the whole faith stands or falls on it, is not the ancient consensus of the church. It is largely a modern construction. Its most famous formal statement, the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, was written in 1978. That is not a typo. The tightest, most defensive version of the doctrine you have been arguing against is younger than color television.

I want to be careful here, because the wrong lesson would be that Christians only recently started taking the Bible seriously. That is false. The church has held Scripture as inspired, as authoritative, as the word of God, from the beginning. What is new is the particular grammar of the modern claim, the demand that the Bible perform like a scientific textbook, that it be defended on the terms of a courtroom, that its truth be measured by whether it would satisfy an eighteenth-century empiricist. That demand did not come out of the ancient church. It came out of the fight with modernity. When the Enlightenment made "verifiable fact" the only respectable kind of truth, a certain kind of Christian agreed to fight on exactly that battlefield, and inerrancy in its hardest form is the fortification they built there. It is modernity's own weapon, turned around and aimed back.

Which means the flat, brittle Bible is not the deep tradition resisting the modern world. It is the modern world, wearing a Bible.

The older way of reading is stranger and much harder to break. For most of Christian history, the church did not treat Scripture as a single seamless rulebook dropped from the sky. It treated it as a library. Sixty-six books, many hands, many centuries, and, this is the part that matters, many kinds of writing. Law is not lament. Poetry is not chronicle. A proverb is not a promise, and a letter written to a specific church in a specific crisis is not a memo addressed to you. When the psalmist screams for God to break his enemies' teeth, that is not God instructing you to hate. That is God including, inside his own book, the sound a human being actually makes in the dark, and leaving it there, unedited, because a faith that cannot hold your rage cannot hold you. The flat reading turns that psalm into a command. The old reading knows it is a cry.

Read a library like a memo and every seam becomes a scandal. Read it as what it is and the seams become evidence of honesty, four witnesses who do not perfectly align, which is what real witnesses never do.

But a library with no center is just a shelf, and this one has a center. The whole collection is arranged around a person. The church has always read the Scriptures forward and backward from Christ, the law and the prophets bending toward him, the letters looking back at him. There is a scene near the end of Luke where the risen Jesus walks a road with two men who do not recognize him, and opens the Scriptures to show them that all of it was pointing here, to a crucified and living God. That is the interpretive key the church actually used for most of its life. Not "every verse is equally flat and equally binding." Rather: this book has a heart, and you read the hard parts in the light of the heart, not the heart in the shadow of the hard parts. The conquest texts do not get the final word. The cross does. A God who dies for his enemies is the lens you hold the sword-passages up against, and yes, some of them still cost. I am not going to pretend the light dissolves every shadow. It does not. There are pages I read and hand back to God with the honest admission that I do not yet see the bottom of them.

And it was never meant to be read alone. This is the piece my atheism could not have understood, because I thought reading was a thing a mind did in private with a text and a verdict. The church read Scripture in community, across centuries, in an argument that never closed, Augustine correcting the reading before him, someone correcting Augustine, the plain sense of a passage held in tension with the hard sense, neither one allowed to win cheaply. That is not weakness. That is a book confident enough to be argued with. The brittle version cannot afford an argument, because one lost argument is the whole building. The old version has survived every argument precisely because it was built to have them.

Now hear the self-implication, because I will not point this at "them." The church did the weaponizing. We did. The same book that says the poor are God's own concern was quoted to keep the poor in chains. Believers wielded these pages as a cudgel, against the enslaved, against the doubting, against the ones already on the floor, and I have done a smaller version of it myself, using a verse to win instead of to heal, reaching for chapter and verse the way a man reaches for a rock. When you tell me the Bible has been used to hurt people, you are not telling me anything the honest church does not confess on its knees. The problem was never that the book was too powerful. It was that we read it without its center, and a library read without its heart becomes a quarry, a place you go to dig out stones to throw.

So here is what I am actually claiming, and it is less than you were sold and more than you expected. You can take this book with total seriousness, as inspired, as authoritative, as the living word, without the flat, defensive, all-or-nothing thing that broke in your hands at nineteen. You do not have to defend a caricature to walk away from atheism. The caricature deserved to be walked away from. What is left when the marketing burns off is older, roomier, and considerably harder to refute, a library with a bleeding center, read in an argument that has lasted two thousand years, honest enough to keep its own worst pages in the record rather than sand them smooth.

I am not asking you to believe it. I am asking you to notice that the thing you rejected and the thing the church has actually confessed are not the same thing. You broke a loose brick and thought you had brought down a cathedral. The cathedral is still standing. It was never holding up the roof with that brick.

You can put it down again. I only want you holding the real one when you do.
posts.excerpt: The flat, all-or-nothing Bible you were handed is a fairly recent invention. Inspiration is older. You can take Scripture with total seriousness without the brittle thing that broke in your hands at nineteen.

posts.title: The Historical Jesus, Without the Shortcuts
posts.body:
There is a version of me that would have skimmed this essay for the trick. I spent years as an atheist, and I had learned where the sleight of hand usually hides in a Christian argument, the place where a modest claim quietly swaps itself for an enormous one and hopes you do not notice the exchange. So let me do the opposite. Let me show you my hands.

Here is what I will not do. I will not tell you that history proves the resurrection. It does not. It cannot. And a Christianity that needs it to is standing on ground that will not hold.

Start with what a careful secular historian actually grants, because it is more than the internet suggests. The claim that Jesus never existed is not a serious position among people who study the period for a living. Bart Ehrman, who is about as far from an apologist as the field produces and who does not believe Jesus rose from anything, has spent a good deal of energy arguing precisely this against the mythicists, that a Jewish teacher named Jesus lived in first-century Palestine, gathered followers, ran afoul of the authorities, and was executed by crucifixion under Roman power. That is not a devotional statement. It is a historical one, and it is close to consensus.

Add to it two more things most historians across the spectrum accept. His followers, shortly after his death, became convinced that they had encountered him alive. And they said so in the very place where saying so was most dangerous and most checkable, Jerusalem, within a few years, in the city that held his grave.

Notice what I have and have not just claimed. I have said the disciples believed. I have not said they were right. Ehrman grants the belief and denies the event, and he is not being inconsistent when he does it. A historian can establish that people were convinced. Whether the thing that convinced them was real is a different question, and it may be a question the tools of history are not built to answer.

I want to sit in that limit longer than an apologist usually does, because it is the honest place. History works by analogy and probability. It asks what most likely happened, given how the world normally runs, and the whole method assumes the world runs in the ordinary way. A miracle is by definition the world not running in the ordinary way. So the discipline is structurally tilted against ever concluding that one occurred, not because historians are closed-minded, but because their instrument does not have that setting. You cannot weigh a resurrection on a scale calibrated to weigh only what usually happens. The most a historian can honestly say is that a group of people were transformed by a conviction they would die for. Why. That word is where history hands off to something else.

This is the part the confident apologist skips. He wants the empty tomb to function as a proof, and it will not. So I will name the limit on the page and keep it there. History cannot prove the resurrection. If you walked away with only that sentence, you would have understood me correctly.

But there is a second move, and it is not a trick. Granting that history cannot prove the event, we can still ask what best explains the agreed-upon facts. That is an ordinary kind of reasoning. We do it in courtrooms and doctors' offices every day, not proof, but the best available account of a strange set of data. And the data here is genuinely strange. A crucified teacher, which in that world meant a failed and cursed one. A circle of frightened followers who had scattered. And then, fast, a movement of people insisting he was alive, willing to be flogged and killed for the insistence, in the one city where the body could have been produced to end the whole thing in an afternoon.

So let me steelman the ordinary explanations, because they deserve their strongest form, not a straw one.

The first is that the disciples hallucinated. Grief does strange things to perception, and bereaved people across cultures report vivid sensory experiences of the dead. This is well documented and not embarrassing to admit. A grieving fisherman seeing his executed teacher is not a wild hypothesis; it is a human one. The strain on it is that hallucinations are, as far as we know, private events. They do not reliably visit groups, and they do not usually persuade a hardened skeptic who was not grieving at all, which is roughly what the early sources claim happened with at least one or two figures who had no reason to want it true. The explanation covers some of the data. It stretches over the rest.

The second is legend. Stories grow in the retelling, and a movement has every incentive to gild its origins over decades. True, and any honest reader of ancient texts watches for it. But the resurrection claim does not have the profile of a slow legend. It is early, embarrassingly early, embedded in material most scholars date to within a few years of the events, before the generation that could contradict it had died off. Legends prefer distance in time and place. This one plants itself in the wrong city at the wrong moment, among the people best positioned to refute it.

The third is theft, or something like it, the body was moved, the tomb was mistaken, someone took him. This is old; it appears in the sources themselves as the counter-story, which at least tells you the tomb was empty enough to require an explanation. The weakness is not that it is impossible. It is that it accounts for an absent body without accounting for the thing that actually drove the movement, which was not an empty grave but a reported presence. An empty tomb makes people puzzled. It does not make them willing to die.

I could go further, and honest people have, in both directions. I am not pretending these explanations are worthless. Each one grips part of the evidence. My claim is smaller and, I think, harder to dismiss: none of them grips all of it cleanly, and the resurrection, the explanation the earliest witnesses gave, grips more of it than we are comfortable admitting. N.T. Wright has argued at length, and I find the argument serious, that the sheer existence of resurrection belief is itself a historical problem needing a cause, because nothing in the Jewish expectation of the time predicted a single man rising in the middle of history rather than everyone rising at the end of it. The disciples were not primed to reach for this. It was not lying ready to hand.

Which brings me to the only honest verdict. The resurrection is not the sole possible explanation of the facts. I will not say that, because it is not true. But it has stopped being an obviously stupid one. That is a real distance from where the confident unbeliever usually stands, and it is the whole distance I am asking you to travel today. Not from doubt to belief. From contempt to consideration.

I know the reflex, because it was mine. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and a resurrection is about as extraordinary as claims get. That instinct is sound, and I would not want you to abandon it. But notice what it is and is not. It is a statement about the height of the bar. It is not, by itself, a proof that nothing could ever clear it. If the bar is set so high that no evidence could in principle count, then the conclusion was reached before the evidence was consulted, and that is not skepticism anymore. It is a different faith, wearing skepticism's coat. I wore it for years and called it reason.

So here is where I leave you, and I am not going to close the gap for you, because I cannot and it would be dishonest to pretend. Everything hangs on whether one thing happened on one morning outside one city. If it did not, then the disciples were sincere and mistaken, the movement is a tragedy of misplaced grief, and you can lay this essay down without owing it anything further. That is a coherent position. I held it.

But if it did, if the tomb was empty because the ordinary machinery of death was, once, interrupted from the outside, then it is not one more religious fact to file beside the others. It is the hinge everything turns on. It would mean the universe is not closed. It would mean the man they crucified was telling the truth about who he was. It would mean death is not the last word over your life or mine, and that the ache you have learned to live with was pointing at something after all.

History cannot walk you across that line. I have been careful not to pretend otherwise. It can only bring you to the edge and show you that the edge is real, and that intelligent people have stood here without surrendering their minds.

That is all I came to do. Not to close the case. To reopen it.
posts.excerpt: What you can defend historically. What you can't. Why the discipline is structurally tilted against ever proving a resurrection, and what still changes if it happened.

posts.title: The Problem of Suffering, Honestly
posts.body:
The argument I could never answer as an atheist was not the one about miracles, or the reliability of manuscripts, or whether a man can rise from the dead. Those felt like arguments you could win with enough reading. The one I could not get past was simpler, and it did not go away when I became a Christian. A child is dying somewhere as you read this. Slowly, in pain, watched by parents who would trade their own lives in an instant and are not given the option. If there is a God who could stop it and does not, then either he is not good or he is not there. That is the argument. I want to state it at full strength, because most of what passes for a Christian answer to it is a way of not looking at it.

So look at it. Not the abstraction, "the problem of evil," a phrase clean enough to put on a syllabus. The particular. The oncology ward. The refugee column. The phone call at two in the morning. Dostoevsky put this more fiercely than any philosopher, through the character of Ivan in *The Brothers Karamazov*, who piles up the suffering of children not to score a point but to refuse the whole arrangement, who says that if the price of some final harmony is the tears of one tortured child, the price is too high, and he would return the ticket. He does not deny God. He rejects the world God runs. I have never read a stronger version of the objection, and I have never met a Christian answer that Ivan could not have anticipated and swept off the table before breakfast.

Because the answers are too clean. Let me name them honestly, the way their best defenders would.

The free will defense says God made us free, and freedom that cannot choose evil is not freedom, so the cruelty in the world is the cost of the only kind of love worth having, love that could have refused. There is something true in that. A world of puppets would not contain love, and I would not want it. But stand in a children's hospital and try the argument out loud. The leukemia did not choose. The earthquake did not choose. The tumor pressing on a four-year-old's brain stem is not exercising its freedom. Free will covers the torturer. It does not cover the cells. And even where a human will is the cause, the drunk driver, the man who hurt you when you were small, "God valued the freedom to do that more than he valued protecting you" is not a comfort. It is a second wound.

The soul-making answer says suffering forms us, that no one becomes deep or brave or kind without something to press against, that the world is a place for growing souls and growth requires resistance. Again, partly true. I have watched grief make people larger. I have been made by things I would not have chosen. But say it at the graveside of an infant and hear how obscene it sounds. What soul was made? Whose growth required that? The argument works only for the suffering that produces a visible result, and most suffering produces no result you can point to. It just grinds people down until they are gone. A theodicy that only explains the useful pain has explained almost nothing.

The greater good answer says God permits each evil because it serves a larger purpose we cannot see, that the whole will one day be revealed as good and every tear will be justified in the accounting. This is the one that finally breaks in my hands. Because it turns the child into a means. It says the suffering was instrumental, a cost paid toward an end. And the moment you say that, you have agreed with Ivan. You have said the ticket was worth buying. I do not believe God balances his books in children. I would not worship him if he did.

Here is what I have to confess. I have preached versions of all three. I have handed grieving people a tidy explanation because the explanation protected me, from the silence, from my own helplessness, from the terror of standing next to a suffering I could not fix and having nothing to say. The theodicies comfort the person who is not suffering. They are what the well say to the sick so the well can leave the room. I did that. I told a widow that God had a plan, and I watched something close in her face, and I mistook it for peace. It was not peace. It was her deciding I was not safe to grieve in front of.

And then I went back and read the Bible actually, instead of the Bible I had been taught to quote, and I found something that undid my whole apparatus.

The Bible mostly refuses to do this. The book set aside for the problem of suffering, Job, is forty chapters long, and thirty-something of them are Job's friends offering theodicies. Every answer I just listed, they say better. And at the end God shows up and tells the friends they have spoken wrongly of him, and he tells Job nothing. He does not explain. He answers out of the whirlwind with questions of his own, "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" (Job 38:4), and the strange thing, the thing that took me years to feel, is that Job is satisfied not because he got an answer but because he got a Presence. The book of Job is in the Bible to burn down the case the friends are making. It is the canon's rejection of the tidy answer, printed in full, endorsed by God.

And the prayer book of Israel is soaked in complaint. The Psalms of lament are not a minor genre, they are a large share of the whole book, and they do not resolve. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). That is in the hymnal. God authorized his people to say that to his face. Not to explain the suffering. To protest it, to him, at volume. The faith did not begin by answering the question of pain. It began by giving people permission to scream it upward and calling that prayer.

This is messier than a theodicy. It is also the only thing I have ever seen hold up at a hospital bed. Because a suffering person does not need the metaphysics of their suffering. They need to know they are not alone in it, and they need permission to be angry without being told they are failing God. Lament gives them both. It is honest about the pain in a way the explanations never are.

But lament alone would only be a permission to despair, and I will not leave you there, because the story does not.

The center of the Christian claim is not an argument about suffering. It is a crucified God. Whatever else Christianity is, it is the strange assertion that the God accused of standing at a safe distance did not stay there, that he came down into the specific human machinery of pain, the betrayal and the flogging and the slow suffocation, and that on the cross he cried the opening line of a lament psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22). Read that again. In the hour the whole edifice of Christianity rests on, God himself is praying a complaint psalm. He is not explaining suffering from above it. He is inside it, using the language Israel used, the language of a man who feels abandoned by God, while being God.

I have to be careful here, because the cross can be weaponized into exactly the tidy answer I have been tearing down. "See, God suffered too, so stop complaining." No. That is the greater-good move wearing a crown of thorns. The cross does not explain your child's cancer. It does not tell you why. It tells you something smaller and harder and more livable, that whatever this is, God has not run it from the observation deck. He has been where you are. The shortest verse in the Bible is two words at the tomb of a friend the writer says he was about to raise from the dead anyway: "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). He knew resurrection was minutes away and he still stood in the graveyard and cried. The God of the Bible does not treat your grief as a problem to be corrected by better information. He weeps in it.

I cannot tell you why there is so much suffering. I have been a pastor for fifteen years and I have buried children and I have sat with men whose wives were disappearing into a disease that eats the mind before it takes the body, and I have nothing for the question that Ivan would not knock down. I have made my peace with not having it. What I have instead is a book that refuses to hand me the answer I keep reaching for, a genre of prayer that lets me be furious and still be praying, and a God with scars.

That is not a solution. If you came here for one, I have failed you, and I would rather fail you than lie. The pain is still pain. The child is still dying. The argument still stands where it stood.

But I no longer think the people who kneel in the wreckage are fools. They are not clutching an explanation. They are holding onto a hand in the dark, and telling the truth about how dark it is.
posts.excerpt: The strongest argument against God is the child dying in the next room. The standard apologetic answers are too clean. The biblical ones are messier, and the only thing I have ever seen hold up at a hospital bed.

posts.title: The Questions That Actually Matter
posts.body:
The questions apologetics answers are not the questions I was asking.

I know this because I spent six years as an atheist, and then I spent fifteen years as a pastor watching Christians answer the atheist I never was. Someone would hand me a book, and it would be four hundred pages proving that the universe had a first cause, that the fine-tuning of the constants was improbable, that a Galilean tomb was likely empty on a Sunday morning in the spring of a year around AD 30. Good arguments, some of them. Careful. And every one of them aimed at a man standing three feet to the left of where I was actually standing.

Let me concede the strongest version of the skeptic's complaint first, because I lived inside it. Most of what gets sold as a defense of Christianity is a defense against objections the believer imagines the unbeliever has. It is a war game played against a cardboard opponent. The apologist decides in advance that my problem is intellectual, that I have simply not seen the syllogism yet, and then he wins the syllogism and looks up expecting me to convert, and cannot understand why I have quietly left the room. I did not leave because the argument failed. I left because the argument was answering a question I had stopped asking, if I ever asked it at all.

So before this track earns the right to say anything, it owes you an accounting of which questions are real. Not the ones that make for a tidy debate. The ones you actually carry.

Here is the first honest admission. I did not lie awake at night over whether the cosmological argument holds. I want to be careful here, because the argument is not stupid, and pretending it is would be its own dishonesty, some of the sharpest people I know find the question of why there is something rather than nothing to be the crack through which everything else eventually leaks. But most nights, for most people, that question does not have teeth. It is a chess problem. You can lose the game and go make a sandwich. The questions that have teeth are the ones you cannot make a sandwich after.

I lay awake over other things.

I lay awake over the fact that I was going to die, and that everyone I loved was going to die, and that on the account I then believed, the only intellectually respectable account, I was sure, this was not a tragedy but a fact, no more mournful than water finding its level. I believed we were the temporary arrangement of atoms that had briefly become able to notice itself, and would soon stop noticing, and that the noticing would leave no trace the universe could read. I believed this. And I could not make myself feel it. Every honest atheist I have ever known lives in exactly that gap, between the death he affirms with his mind and the grief he cannot stop his body from staging at a graveside. That gap is not an argument. It is a wound the worldview cannot close, and it does not care whether you have read the right books.

That is the terrain. Not the debate stage. The gap between what we say we believe about ourselves and what we cannot stop acting like is true.

Consider meaning, which is the question apologists reach for and then ruin. They tend to argue that without God your life has no meaning, as if that were a threat, and the thoughtful unbeliever rightly answers that he makes his own, his children, his work, the person asleep beside him, the particular slant of light in October. He is right. He does make meaning, and it is real meaning, and I will not insult him by pretending the meaning he has built is a delusion. But there is a harder question underneath the easy one, and it is the question that actually keeps a person up. Not "does my life have meaning?" It is: why does the meaning I make feel like something I am discovering rather than something I am inventing? Why does love feel like a country I entered, not a thing I manufactured? An invented meaning should feel like mine. This one keeps feeling like it came from somewhere.

Which is the persistence of longing, and I think it is the most undertreated fact in the whole conversation. The philosopher Charles Taylor described the condition of the modern West as living inside what he called the immanent frame, a closed room of natural cause and effect, where the transcendent is not so much refuted as simply made optional, one setting among others. And his sharpest observation was not that belief has become impossible. It is that unbelief has not become easy. The person who has fully accepted that there is nothing beyond the material world still finds himself, at a certain hour, ambushed by a longing that points at nothing the material world contains. Taylor called this being cross-pressured, haunted from both directions, unable to fully rest in the closed room and unable to walk back out of it. I have lived on both sides of that pressure. It does not resolve by reading. It just sits there, aching, pointing.

C.S. Lewis built an argument out of exactly this ache, the observation that our hungers tend to correspond to real things, that thirst suggests water and hunger suggests food, and that we carry one desire nothing in the world will feed. I am not offering that to you as a proof; Lewis's argument has real holes and a skeptic can name them in his sleep. I am offering the observation underneath the argument, which no atheism I ever held could explain away: the longing did not go when I stopped believing. It got worse. A worldview that tells me my deepest and most persistent hunger is aimed at nothing at all is asking me to believe that I am, at my core, a mistake. Maybe I am. But that is a strange thing for evolution to spend so much energy building.

Then there is the weight of right and wrong, and here I have to be most careful of all, because Christians have made a bad argument out of a real thing so many times that skeptics now flinch when the subject comes up. The bad argument says an atheist cannot be good without God. That is false, and worse than false, it is insulting, and I have known unbelievers whose integrity shamed me in my collar. So set it aside entirely. The real question is not whether you can be good. It is why, when you watch a strong man hurt a child, your reaction has the shape of a fact and not a preference. You do not feel that cruelty is distasteful the way you find a food distasteful. You feel that it is wrong the way you feel that two and two is four, as if you have bumped into something that was already there, that would still be there if every human being on earth voted to approve it. Every serious atheist I know either bites the bullet and says that moral weight is an illusion evolution installed to keep us cooperating, or he refuses to bite it and lives, quietly, as if the child's dignity were carved into the structure of things. I could never bite the bullet. I could never fully believe that my horror at cruelty was only a feeling with good press.

And underneath all of it, love, the one I saved for last because it is the one that finally cornered me. The account I held said that love is chemistry with a story attached, a set of neurochemical events that bond mammals long enough to raise the young. I believed that. It is not obviously wrong. But I stood in a room once and felt, toward another person, something that behaved in every way like a fact about the universe and not a fact about my hormones, and I had to decide whether to trust the experience or the theory that dissolved it. Every honest person eventually stands in that room. You do not get to be a human being and stay neutral on whether the thing you feel toward the people you would die for is really only the sensation of your genes protecting their investment.

Notice what I have not done. I have not answered a single one of these. I have not told you the longing proves God, or the moral weight requires him, or that love descends from somewhere. Those are moves, and if I made them now I would be doing the exact thing I accused the apologists of, winning a game you did not agree to play. This first essay has one job, and it is smaller and more honest than that. It is to say: I know which questions are real. I know the difference between the ones that make a good debate and the ones that follow you into the dark. And I am promising you, for the six essays after this one, that I will not cheat, I will not pretend the closed room has exits it does not have, and I will not pretend it is airtight when we both know, at three in the morning, that it is not.

You do not have to believe anything yet. You only have to agree that these are the questions. That death is a wound the mind affirms and the body refuses. That the meaning you make feels found. That the longing does not leave. That cruelty feels like a fact. That love asks to be more than chemistry, and you have never quite been able to tell it no.

If those are your questions, you are not standing three feet to the left anymore.

You are standing exactly where I was.
posts.excerpt: Most defenses of Christianity answer questions skeptics aren't asking. The ones that actually follow you into the dark are different, and naming them honestly is where this track has to begin.

posts.title: What Following This Actually Costs
posts.body:
We need to talk about the price before you do anything with the rest of it. Not because I want to close a sale. Because I would be lying to you if I let you walk out of these seven essays thinking the thing I have been describing is available cheap.

I came to all this at twenty-four, out of atheism, and the version of me that did not believe assumed the whole enterprise was a comfort product. Church as emotional support. God as the friend who agrees with you. I thought Christians believed because believing made them feel better, and I could not respect a thing whose only claim on a person was that it soothed them. If that is what this were, you should not want it. Neither should I.

So here is what it actually costs, said plainly, by a man who is still bad at paying it.

It costs your money. Not in the sense that there is a fee, a subscription, a tithe you calculate and resent. It costs the assumption underneath the money, the quiet certainty that what you earn is simply yours. That the number in the account is a fact about you, a measure, a defense against the future. Christianity does not ask you to give more to charity than the decent atheist already does. It asks something worse. It says the money was never yours to begin with, that you are a steward of what passed through your hands and not an owner of what landed in them, and that on the day you die the question will not be how much you accumulated but what you did with what you were lent. I have sat with that and flinched. I have five sons and a mortgage and the same animal instinct you have to build a wall of resources between my family and the dark. The faith keeps dismantling the wall. It tells me the security I am building is a smaller god than the one I claim to serve, and it is right, and I rebuild the wall anyway, and I am telling you this so you understand I am not describing a hill I have climbed. I am describing one I am still on.

It costs your marriage, and it costs your sex life, and I will not soften either one. The culture I live in, the one you live in, treats the body as private property and desire as its own justification. What you want, if it is strong enough and hurts no one who did not consent, is treated as a fact you are obligated to honor. Christianity walks into that room and says the body is not yours in that way. It says sex is a covenant language, that it means something whether or not you intend it to, that it makes a promise with the flesh that the mouth may be trying to withhold. This is not a rule about behavior. It is an account of what a person is. And it costs, it costs the freedom to treat another human being as an experience, it costs the fantasy that you can give your body without giving anything else, and inside marriage it costs the exit. Covenant means you stay when leaving would be easier and defensible and blessed by everyone you know. I have been married long enough to have wanted, on specific afternoons, the door the culture holds open. The faith closed it. Not with a threat. With a promise I had already made and a God who takes such promises more seriously than I do.

It costs your politics, and this is the one that will embarrass you, whoever you are. I watch people arrive at church having already decided which half of the country is the problem, and they expect the faith to bless the arithmetic. It will not. The cross does not belong to your party. It will not be recruited. If you are on the right, it will convict you where you have made an idol of the nation, where you have wrapped the flag around the crucifix until you cannot tell which one you are kneeling to, where you have treated the vulnerable as a threat to be managed rather than a neighbor to be loved. If you are on the left, it will convict you where you have decided the ancient moral vision of the church is simply bigotry with a longer footnote, where you have subtracted every hard word of Jesus that your tribe finds distasteful and kept only the ones that flatter you. I have felt the blade turn on my own certainties more than once, and the temptation every time is to conclude the blade is malfunctioning. It is not. A faith that only ever indicts the people you already dislike is not a faith. It is your politics wearing a robe. The real thing costs you the comfort of a clean enemy.

And it costs your image. This is the deepest one, and the last, because it sits underneath the other three. The reason we hoard money and guard the body and enlist God in our tribe is that we are each, quietly, the center of our own account of the world. The main character. The point. Christianity's most offensive claim is not about sex or money or the afterlife. It is that you are not the point. That the story is not finally about you, your growth, your happiness, your legacy, your being seen. It is about God, and you are a creature in it, loved past all reason but not central. Everything in me resists this. I built a public life. I have my name on books and on the front of a building's worth of expectation. And the faith keeps telling me the applause is not the reward, that the man who needs to be seen has already received the only wage that kind of hunger pays, and that the invisible thing done for no audience is worth more than the visible thing done for the crowd. I know this. I preach it. I still check to see who noticed. I am inside this indictment and I am not writing my way out of it.

Someone will say I am overselling the difficulty to make the thing seem important. I understand the suspicion; I would have had it. So let me put the whole argument in one sentence. A faith that asks for everything is at least not trying to sell you something cheap. The religion you are right to despise is the one that costs nothing and promises everything, the one that hands you a better life at no charge and calls it grace. There is an old and hard idea, associated most with a German pastor the Nazis killed, that grace which asks nothing of you is not grace at all, only a comfortable counterfeit. I think that idea is true, and I think the truth of it is the best evidence I can offer you that the real thing is not a scam. Con artists lower the price. They tell you it is easy. What I am describing raises the price to the top of the market and refuses to discount, and it does that because it is not selling you an enhancement to the life you already have. It is asking for that life, whole, to hand you back a different one.

This is not a better version of your existing life. It is a different one.

Jesus said the quiet part out loud, which is more than most of his followers manage. Before he asked anyone to follow, he told them to do the math. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). He was not recruiting. He was warning. And elsewhere, with no marketing softness at all: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me" (Luke 9:23). The cross was an instrument of execution. He was not using it as a metaphor for inconvenience. He meant a death, the death of the self that insists on being the point.

I am not going to ask you to decide anything today. That is the one thing I refuse to do, because the manufactured urgency, the hand raised while every head is bowed, the pressure to close before you have counted, all of it belongs to the cheap version, and the cheap version is the thing you were right to walk away from. The door does not slam. No one is standing behind it with a clipboard timing your hesitation.

I only wanted you to know the number before you priced it in your head as something small. It is not small. It is everything you have, and it does not come with a receipt you can wave at the difficulty later. I have paid pieces of it and clutched other pieces and lied to myself about the difference, and I am a pastor, which means I am telling you the cost from inside the failure to pay it, not from above it.

So I will leave it where it belongs, which is in your hands and not mine. The claim is that a man rose from the dead and that this changes what a life is for. If it is false, none of the price is worth a cent. If it is true, no price is too high, and the ones still holding on to their money and their bodies and their tribe and their name, I am one of them, are the ones who have not yet understood what we are being offered in exchange.

Count it slowly. No one worth trusting will hurry you.
posts.excerpt: The honest closer. No altar call. If Christianity is true, it is not a lifestyle enhancement, it costs your money, your marriage, your politics, your image. A faith that asks for everything is at least not selling you something cheap.

posts.title: What Secular Explanations Still Have to Explain
posts.body:
We built a world that runs without God, and it runs. That is the first thing an honest believer has to say to an honest atheist, and most of us will not say it. The lights come on. The antibiotics work. The bridge holds because a man who prayed to no one calculated the load correctly. For three hundred years the most powerful method human beings have ever devised for finding out what is true has proceeded on the working assumption that it need not consult heaven, and it has been spectacularly, humiliatingly right about almost everything it has touched. If you were an atheist because of this, you were not being lazy. You were noticing something real.

I was that atheist until I was twenty-four. And I want to grant the case at its strongest before I say anything else, because the church has a habit of arguing with a version of unbelief no serious unbeliever holds.

The strong case runs like this. Every time we did not know how something worked, we said God. Lightning, disease, the motion of the planets, the origin of species, the origin of the cosmos itself. And every time, when we finally learned the mechanism, God was not in it. Not disproven. Just unnecessary. The pattern is so consistent that betting against it looks like the only rational move left. The believer keeps retreating to the shrinking territory of the not-yet-explained and planting his flag there, and the explanation keeps arriving, and the flag keeps moving. The name for the tenant of that shrinking house is the God of the gaps, and he has been evicted so many times that a thoughtful person is right to stop renting to him. When Charles Taylor describes how the modern West came to inhabit what he calls the immanent frame, a world experienced as a closed order of natural causes, where transcendence is at most an option and no longer the air we breathe, he is not describing a mistake. He is describing an achievement. We can now give a complete account of the middle of the world without ever leaving the world. That is not nothing. That is the water we all swim in, believers included, and anyone who tells you he has stepped outside it is lying or has not noticed.

So I am not going to hand you a gap. I am going to point at four things that are not gaps at all, because they do not shrink when the science advances. They are the same size now as they were before we knew anything, and they will be the same size when we know everything a materialist account could ever deliver. I am not going to call them proof. I am going to refuse to let them be waved away.

The first is that the universe is intelligible at all. Science does not merely work; it works absurdly well, and it works by assuming in advance that reality is written in a language the human mind can read, mathematics, deep, elegant, and shockingly predictive. The steelman here is strong, so take it. Of course the universe is comprehensible to us. We are its products. Minds that could not track reality got eaten. Evolution tuned our cognition to the world because a false map gets you killed at the watering hole. Grant all of it. Then notice what it does not reach. Natural selection can explain why I can count the lions and judge the distance to the river. It has no obvious purchase on why the same organ that dodged the lion can also derive general relativity, describe the behavior of particles it will never touch, and predict, from an equation scratched on paper, a planet no one has seen. The survival value of abstract higher mathematics is zero on the savanna. We got a tool fitted for the watering hole and found it fits the deep structure of the cosmos, and no one ordered that fit. The physicist Eugene Wigner named it long ago, the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics, and naming a thing is not the same as accounting for it. The reasonable expectation was a mind that muddled through. We got a mind that reads the source code. That is strange. It should be allowed to stay strange.

The second is the one the materialist himself keeps circling back to, uneasy. Consciousness. Not intelligence, not behavior, not the information processing a machine can do. The fact that there is something it is like to be you. That the wavelength we label red is also, from the inside, the experienced redness of red, and no description of the wavelength, however total, contains that. The honest naturalist does not pretend this is solved. Thomas Nagel, an atheist, has spent a career refusing to pretend it, worrying in print that the standard reductive story leaves something out and might be leaving out something enormous. David Chalmers gave the difficulty its working name, the hard problem, and it is called hard for a reason that has not gone away. The steelman: consciousness is what a sufficiently complex brain does, we simply have not finished the science, and the confidence of the not-yet is a bad bet given the track record. Fair. But every other thing the brain does, we can at least say what a solution would look like. Here we cannot even say what would count as one. We can specify every neuron and still not know why the lights are on inside. A universe that started as dead matter and blind force has somehow, in us, opened its eyes and asked what it is. That either is the most ordinary fact in the world or the most extraordinary. It cannot be both. We have agreed to call it ordinary. I am not sure we have earned that.

The third is where I have to be most careful, because it is the one most easily cheapened. Not morality. Obligation. The materialist explains moral behavior with ease, and I concede it fully. Cooperation is fit. Empathy is selected. Kin altruism, reciprocal altruism, the whole apparatus by which a social animal comes to feel that cruelty is wrong, all of it can be told as a story about genes surviving, and told well. That is not the remainder. The remainder is that we do not experience morality as a feeling we happen to have. We experience it as a claim made on us from outside, one that stands over our feelings and judges them. When I say the man who tortures a child for pleasure is wrong, I do not mean I dislike it, or my tribe evolved to punish it, or it fails to maximize welfare. I mean he is wrong, and would be wrong if every human alive had evolved to applaud him. The steelman is the honest one: that conviction is exactly the illusion natural selection would install, because a creature that felt morality as mere preference would defect the moment defecting paid, and a creature that felt it as iron law would not. So the bindingness is a trick, useful and deep and false. That is a coherent view. Live in it. Live all the way in it, and watch what happens to the sentence the torturer is really, bindingly wrong. It does not survive. It becomes the torturer is something I was built to hate. And every one of us, the atheist included, I know, because I was him, goes on treating certain things as really wrong, wrong with a weight no story about our ancestors can hold up. We cannot get the obligation out of our mouths. We only learn to stop asking where it comes from.

The fourth is quieter and I will not press it hard. We treat truth and beauty as though they matter in themselves. The scientist who spends her life on a question that will never feed her, because the truth is worth having. The grief that a false thing is false even when the false thing was comforting. The way a theorem or a coastline or a piece of music can stop a person as if it were owed something. On the strict account these are refined appetites, byproducts, the mind's pleasure in pattern. Maybe. But we do not live as if they were appetites. We live as if we were answerable to them.

I want to say clearly what this is and is not. It is not four proofs. Each has a naturalist reply that is intelligent and might be right, and I have tried to give those replies in the form their defenders would sign. A God assembled from these four would be exactly the tenant of the shrinking house, and I already agreed he deserves eviction. This is something smaller and more stubborn. It is a refusal.

The remainder is real. The intelligibility we did not order, the light that came on in the dark, the obligation we cannot stop obeying, the truth and beauty we serve as if they could ask something of us. The mature response is not to solve them tonight. It is to stop pretending they are already solved, and to sit with the size of what a complete materialism would still have to carry.

You do not have to believe anything to admit the account is not yet closed. I only ask that when the remainder comes up, you not do the thing I used to do. I waved it away because I already knew there was nothing there. I never checked. The waving was the faith.
posts.excerpt: The case for atheism is stronger than the church admits, grant it fully. It also leaves a few things uncovered that do not shrink when the science advances. Both can be true.

books.title: When God Bless America Replaces Thy Kingdom Come
books.author: James Bell
books.description: How Patriotism Became Our Practical Savior. A direct examination of how patriotism has replaced the kingdom of God as the practical savior in American Christianity.

books.title: The Monster in the Mirror
books.author: James Bell
books.description: Why Every Generation Gets the Bible Wrong, Why Yours Is No Different, and What to Do About It. An exploration of how each generation interprets Scripture through its own cultural lens.

books.title: The Healthy & Growing Church
books.author: Pastors Connection Network
books.description: Revitalization, Real Metrics, Generation Z & Breaking Through the Plateau. Comprehensive guide on church health, decline, revitalization, replanting, and leading without losing hope.

books.title: The Patient Pastor
books.author: Pastors Connection Network
books.description: How to Lead Change Without Losing Your Church or Your Mind. Book 10 in The Hard Issues Series. Master the skill of patient leadership and strategic change management.

books.title: Change Without Casualties
books.author: Pastors Connection Network
books.description: A Playbook for Introducing Major Ministry Decisions. Book 11 in The Hard Issues Series. Strategic guide for implementing change while maintaining congregational trust.

books.title: Changing the Unchangeable
books.author: Pastors Connection Network
books.description: Leading Reform When We've Always Done It This Way. Book 12 in The Hard Issues Series. Face institutional resistance and lead real change in traditional churches.

books.title: Staying
books.author: James Bell
books.description: Marriage Through Depression, Crisis, and the Long Middle. Practical wisdom for couples carrying a marriage through life's most difficult seasons with honesty and grace.

books.title: Dangerous Calling: Why the Office of Pastor Is Not for Everyone
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A prophetic examination of pastoral calling that challenges the romanticization of ministry. Bell explores what it truly means to be called to shepherd God's people, examining both the glory and the weight of pastoral leadership. Essential reading for anyone considering pastoral ministry or supporting pastors.

books.title: The Hidden Life of a Pastor: Tending Your Soul While Tending the Flock
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A pastoral guide to spiritual formation and personal renewal in ministry. Bell addresses the inner life of pastors, their struggles, temptations, and spiritual disciplines. This book is a companion to pastoral leaders seeking to maintain their own spiritual vitality while caring for others.

books.title: The First Flock: The Church's Calling to Care for Pastors and Their Families
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A call to churches to care for their pastors and pastoral families. Bell argues that the congregation is the pastors "first flock", they must be cared for with the same intentionality as the broader church. This book challenges churches to move from taking pastors for granted to actively supporting them.

books.title: Earthen Vessels: Why Our Bodies Matter to Our Faith
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A theological exploration of embodied faith and incarnational living. Bell challenges the dualism that separates spirit from body, arguing for a whole Christianity that honors the physical. This book addresses health, sexuality, work, and the material world as central to Christian discipleship.

books.title: Preach the Word: The Primacy of Expository Preaching in the Local Church
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A defense and guide to expository preaching in contemporary ministry. Bell makes the case for text-driven preaching while addressing practical concerns about relevance and engagement. This book is essential for preachers seeking to ground their ministry in Scripture.

books.title: The Undershepherd: Pastoral Leadership, Authority, and the Care of God's People
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A comprehensive theology of pastoral leadership grounded in the metaphor of the shepherd. Bell explores the pastors role as under-shepherd, accountable to Christ the Chief Shepherd. This book addresses authority, care, discipline, and the pastors responsibility to God's flock.

books.title: The Pruning: Church Decline, Faithful Endurance, and the Promise of Renewal
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A prophetic word to declining churches about God's purposes in pruning. Bell challenges churches to see decline not as failure but as opportunity for renewal and refocus. This book offers hope and practical guidance for churches facing seasons of loss and transition.

books.title: One Body, Many Churches: A Theology of Unity for a Fractured Church
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A theological exploration of church unity across denominational lines. Bell argues for a robust doctrine of the universal church while honoring local church distinctives. This book addresses fragmentation, cooperation, and the church's witness to the world.

books.title: Necessary Words: A Pastoral Theology of Courage and Difficult Conversations
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A guide to speaking truth in love within the church. Bell addresses the pastors prophetic role in confronting sin, addressing conflict, and speaking difficult truths. This book equips leaders with biblical wisdom for necessary conversations that build rather than destroy.

books.title: Sent Into the City: The Church's Calling to Its Neighborhood and World
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A call to missional engagement and community involvement. Bell challenges churches to move beyond programs to genuine presence in their neighborhoods. This book addresses the church's prophetic voice on social justice, community transformation, and kingdom witness.

books.title: To the Ends of the Earth: Global Mission, National Partnership, and the Sent Church
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A theology of global mission and partnership in the Great Commission. Bell explores the church's role in world missions, cross-cultural partnership, and the global nature of God's kingdom. This book challenges parochialism and calls the church to think globally.

books.title: Faithful in Exile: Pastoral Leadership and the Church's Witness in a Post-Christian Age
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A prophetic guide to pastoral leadership in a secularizing culture. Bell addresses how churches and pastors can maintain faithfulness and witness in a post-Christian context. This book offers both challenge and encouragement for leaders facing cultural change.

books.title: Common Grace: What Pastors Learn When They Listen to the World
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A theology of common grace and cultural engagement. Bell argues that pastors must listen to the world to understand God's common grace at work. This book challenges Christian isolation and calls for thoughtful engagement with culture, science, art, and secular wisdom.

books.title: The Unfinished Church: Calling, Vision, and the Future God Is Building
books.author: James Bell
books.description: A vision for the church's future and God's ongoing work. Bell reflects on the church's road, current challenges, and God's promises. This book offers hope and direction for churches seeking to understand their place in God's unfolding story and their calling for the future.

settings.aboutContent: James C. Bell is a pastor, author, and ministry leader whose work spans local church leadership, global pastoral training, and public theological writing. He serves as Lead Pastor of First Baptist Church of Fenton in Fenton, Michigan, where he has shepherded the congregation since 2016. He is the husband of Susanna and the father of five sons. James is the founder of the Pastors Connection Network (PCN), a national and international ministry dedicated to connecting, mentoring, and equipping pastors and churches for sustainable, faithful ministry. James is the founder of LiveWell, a writing and ministry platform committed to biblical depth, cultural clarity, and prophetic honesty. At his core, James Bell is a pastor.
settings.pastorsNetworkContent: The Pastors Connection Network (PCN) is a national and international ministry dedicated to connecting, mentoring, and equipping pastors and churches for sustainable, faithful ministry. PCN operates from the conviction that pastoral isolation is one of the most underaddressed crises in the church today, and that every pastor, regardless of geography, denomination, or resources, deserves genuine community and meaningful development. Through PCN, we lead pastoral training initiatives reaching national church leaders serving in some of the most remote and underresourced regions in the world, with active partnerships in India, Thailand, Pakistan, South America, and across Africa. Our mission is straightforward: equip every pastor, resource every church, and carry the gospel to the last unreached corner of the earth. Join a community of pastors committed to faithful ministry, theological depth, and kingdom advancement.
